en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Essence of the Vinaya Piṭaka (First Part)
I pay homage to the Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate One; to the Dhamma, stainless and supreme;
and to the Noble Saṅgha, worthy of offerings and free from defilement.
Having crushed the enemies by the power of his sublime merit,
and having attained the consecration of sovereignty, he who desired to illuminate the Dispensation—
Parakkamabāhu, the Lion of Sīhaḷa— relied upon that [power].
Having established unity within the Saṅgha and thoroughly purified the Dispensation,
that great Elder Kassapa, the leader of the Saṅgha and the one who caused the rise of the Dispensation on the island of Tambapaṇṇi—
I pay homage to the father of the Saṅgha, who is ever devoted to practice, dwelling always in the forest,
and renowned within the Dispensation like the lunar orb in the sky,
being highly proficient in the Vinaya.
Relying upon whom I dwell, I have attained growth within the Dispensation—
Anuthera, of great merit, Sumedha, renowned for his learning,
and possessing the arising of pure qualities such as unbroken virtue.
I bow my head in reverence to the wise Gaṇavācaka, my teacher, who is learned, mindful, self-controlled, peaceful, and concentrated.
He is proficient in the Agamas and the systems of logic, and he knows the methods of the science of grammar.
In this dispensation, wherein the teaching is well-established among the resident monks,
I shall compose a commentary on the Vinaya that illuminates the hidden essential meaning— easy to understand, complete, and unconfused.
However, that elucidation of the hidden meaning composed by the ancients does not entirely accomplish the purpose for monks in every respect,
because the Sinhalese language is difficult to understand in its essential nature.
In many commentaries (*gaṇṭhipada*),
something has been written here and there by someone,
even though beginning in the Māgadhī language, yet writing some things mixed with other languages.
Even a garland made of worthless wood is often seen there;
and where a composition is confused, its meaning is difficult to discern even if it is clear.
Therefore, by means of such [a work] that is entirely incomplete, one cannot [attain the goal] here.
"How do those dwelling in various lands understand the meaning?
Having set aside differences in language and having grasped the essence in its entirety, I shall provide a clear and complete exposition."
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:
At the beginning of the commentary on the Vinaya, wishing to pay homage to the Triple Gem and for the purpose of demonstrating its possession of distinguished qualities, he said:
"He who, even in ten million aeons... For it is through the possession of distinguished qualities that one becomes worthy of veneration; and among those worthy of veneration...

And the homage performed accomplishes the intended purpose. Herein, at the commencement of the commentary, the teachers elaborate in various ways upon the purpose for making the salutation to the Three Jewels. For they explain it thus:
"The salutation to the Three Jewels at the beginning of the commentary is for the purpose of announcing the origin, the support, and the purity of the Dhamma to be commented upon."

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise regarding the expositions of the Dhamma, and for the purpose of accomplishing all benefit and happiness through right practice—
such as the correct learning and retention of that [Dhamma]. Alternatively, it is because it is auspicious,
because it constitutes a preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it has been practiced by the learned, and because others will follow one's example in the future upon seeing it.
"And this act of paying homage to the Three Jewels is for the purpose of the commentary.

We, however, shall demonstrate here only the purpose intended in this context. Therefore, it should be understood that the performance of the homage to the Three Jewels at the commencement of the commentary is for the sake of completing the commentary as promised without obstacle. For this very [purpose]...
The purpose intended here by the Teacher is as follows; for he will say:
"Thus, constantly paying homage to that Triple Gem which is worthy of worship..."
“I have obtained an abundant outflow of merit;
by its power, my obstacles have been destroyed.
And herein, by means of this homage to the Triple Gem, the commentary is brought to completion without hindrance, just as was promised.

Because through worship of the Triple Gem there arises proficiency in wisdom, and because through that proficiency in wisdom there is the destruction of the stains of lust and so forth. For this has been said:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion."
“...the mind becomes straight; at that time, his mind is indeed rectified,” and so forth.
Therefore, through the worship of the Triple Gem, proficiency in wisdom is achieved for one whose defilements have been washed away.

Alternatively, because the worship of the Triple Gem is the cause of concentration, which has wisdom as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), there is proficiency in wisdom. For its being the cause of concentration has been stated:
“Thus, Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a mind so upright gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil;
one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.”
The fact that concentration and wisdom serve as the foundation for one another has already been stated: "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
Therefore, by means of wisdom that has thus become sharp, having overcome the weariness caused by the magnitude of his undertaking, he will complete the commentary without obstruction.
Hence it is said: "for the purpose of completing it without obstruction."

Alternatively, it should be understood that the completion [of the work] without obstacles results from the increase of longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength through worship of the Triple Gem. For by bowing to the Triple Gem, longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. Indeed, this has been said:
“For one whose habit is to pay homage, who constantly honors the elders, four things increase: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.”

Therefore, it is said, "for the purpose of completing [the work] without obstacle," because through the increase of life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength, the completion of the task indeed occurs.

Alternatively, it is because reverence for the Triple Gem brings about the non-decline of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna*). For reverence toward the Three Jewels leads to non-decline. Indeed, this has been said:

"Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that lead to non-decline. Which seven? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, having virtuous friends, and being easy to admonish."
And furthermore, there is the fulfillment of one’s promise through not failing in that inspired eloquence.
Alternatively, it is because of the preeminence of merit resulting from worship toward the bases of confidence (*pasādavatthu*). For its preeminence of merit has been stated:
"For one who worships those worthy of worship—the Buddhas or their disciples..."
“To those who have transcended conceptual proliferation, who have crossed over sorrow and lamentation—
those such as these, who have attained Nibbāna and are fearless from any quarter;
for one who honors them, it is not possible for anyone to calculate even this much merit.”
Furthermore, an abundance of merit is the means for completing one's intended undertaking. As it is said:
"This is a treasure that grants all desires to gods and humans;
whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by this."
And for one who has entered upon the means, there is indeed the accomplishment of the task. For the worship of the Triple Gem is an unsurpassed field of merit;

it is an excellence of merit with immeasurable power. Thus, even amidst a worldly existence full of manifold obstacles, it is capable of destroying all defilements that constitute those obstacles, and it wards off calamities such as fear.
Therefore, it was well said: "At the commencement of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem..."
"It should be understood that [the homage] is for the purpose of completing the commentary without obstacle, exactly as promised.

Thus, wishing to perform the homage to the Triple Gem along with its specific purpose, he first offers homage to the Blessed One—since the other Gems are rooted in him—saying: "He who, for an eon... [etc. ...to that Greatly Compassionate One. Herein:

However, since the commentary he intends to compose concerns that teaching which is dominated by compassion—neither like the Sutta teachings, which are dominated by both compassion and wisdom, nor like the Abhidhamma teachings, which are dominated by wisdom—the praise of the Blessed One has begun precisely as one dominated by compassion.
For this is the custom of the Master: namely, to offer praise in accordance with the subject undertaken.

Therefore, at the commencement of the commentary on the Suttanta teaching, the praise begins with "Whose heart is cooled by compassion and whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom," emphasizing both compassion and wisdom;

whereas at the commencement of the commentary on the Abhidhamma teaching, the praise begins with "In whom, the Great Sage, wisdom dwells toward beings as does compassion," emphasizing wisdom. For the Suttanta teaching is characterized primarily by compassion and wisdom.

This is because his wisdom is capable of discerning the distinctions among various beings—such as their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), inclinations (*adhimutti*), and conduct—and because his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) functions with particular excellence toward them.

Indeed, through his teaching of the Suttantas, being frequently absorbed in the attainment of great compassion, he established profound meanings and terms within the mental continuums of those to be trained, in accordance with their respective inclinations. As for the teaching of the Abhidhamma...

Furthermore, the Abhidhamma teachings are primarily characterized by wisdom, because wisdom—which is capable of penetrating the ultimate phenomena according to their true nature—functions with particular excellence therein.

The Vinaya teaching, however, is not independent of the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) and other factors; it is motivated solely by compassion and is intended even for those who are ordinary beings and unfit to hear it.
The Blessed One established the training rule (sikkhāpada) because he would listen to what ought to be asked, would ask what ought to be asked, and would speak what ought to be spoken;

thus, his teaching was dominated by compassion. For even the Blessed One—who possessed a sense of shame (hirī) and dread of blame (ottappa) reaching the highest limit—spoke words such as "Sikharaṇī" and other reproachful words according to the offense, which were to be avoided even by worldly virtuous people, during his teaching of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
With a mind impelled by great compassion, he spoke in the midst of a great assembly;
furthermore, out of regard for the reasons for enacting various rules of training (sikkhāpada), he experienced physical hardship in Verañjā and other places.

Therefore, although the wisdom that originates the formulation of the Vinaya—like the discourses on different planes of existence, conditions, modes, and periods—is possessed of a preeminent function due to its uniqueness, it is not shared by others.

Furthermore, the duty of compassion is even greater than that; thus, the teaching of the Vinaya is dominated by compassion. Indeed, it is because the activity of compassion is predominant in the teaching that it is characterized as being dominated by compassion.
Therefore, it should be understood that the praise here is made specifically for that which is dominated by compassion, in accordance with the undertaking [of the Buddha].
And by the mention of compassion, it should be seen that all the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha are included, since they are rooted in that [compassion].

[This refers] to the remaining qualities of a Buddha. Alternatively, because Great Compassion is one of the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*), there is necessarily the inclusion of the other unique knowledges that accompany it;
thus, all the qualities of a Buddha are indeed shown by way of this method (*nayato*). For this is precisely the means for seeing the qualities of a Buddha without exception:
namely, the grasping of the method (*nayaggāha*). Otherwise, who indeed would be capable [of enumerating] the qualities of the Blessed One?
In order to show [this] word by word without remainder, he said:
"Even a Buddha, speaking the praise of a Buddha,
might do so for an eon without uttering anything else."
“An eon might pass away in the course of its vast duration, yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.
And for this very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, though intent on defining the Buddha’s qualities, said: “No...”
Having rejected [the previous suggestion] with the words, "No, venerable sir," he said, "But, venerable sir, the logical sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) is known to me.

Therefore, it should be understood that by the passage beginning with "Even in ten million eons," he praised the Blessed One in brief through his qualities of omniscience by way of compassion. This is the collective meaning here.
Now, this is the analysis of the components: the word *yo* (who) is an indefinite term. It is connected with the word *nātho* (protector).

However, by means of that compassion—by which he is called "the Greatly Compassionate"—there is the experience of suffering by the Blessed One as he performs what is exceedingly difficult for the sake of the welfare of the world for an immeasurable period of time, even by the count of tens of millions of eons (*kappakoṭi*).

He demonstrates this. Indeed, it was solely by the power of his compassion that the Blessed One, having renounced even Nibbāna which was already in his hands, performed such exceedingly difficult deeds as the giving of his eyes, his life, his son, and his wife—deeds which would have been impossible even to conceive for the sake of uplifting the multitude of beings submerged in the mire of *saṃsāra*.
As for the phrase "immeasurable time even by tens of millions of eons," it means that even by counting in tens of millions of eons, one could not say, "there were this many tens of millions of eons."

Because it is impossible to measure that time, even by way of counting millions of *kappas*, it is said to be "unmeasured" (*aparicchinnāni*), meaning four *asaṅkhyeyyas* plus a hundred thousand *kappas*.

Indeed, that time is immeasurable by way of millions of *kappas*, yet it is precisely measured by way of *asaṅkhyeyyas*. In the phrase "even by millions of *kappas*," the word "even" (*api*) [indicates this].
It shows that it cannot be measured even by way of ten million eons (*kappakoṭi*), let alone by the calculation of years.

The phrase "immeasurable time" (*appameyyaṃ kālaṃ*) uses the accusative case to express continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*), as in examples such as "he studies for a month" (*māsam adhīte*) or "he walks for a day" (*divasaṃ carati*).

"Performing what is exceedingly difficult" (*karonto atidukkarāni*) means performing the five great renunciations (*pañcamahāpariccāga*) and other deeds that are extremely hard to do. Thus, [he performed] these exceedingly difficult deeds.
If it is asked, "What does he find by doing so?"—the meaning is that he has become exhausted, fallen into physical fatigue, or reached weariness;
it is said that he experiences suffering. For suffering is called "exhaustion" (*kheda*) because it is worn out and impossible to endure.

"For the welfare of the world" means for the sake of the world of sentient beings, who have been incessantly oppressed by the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) throughout the beginningless past.

The meaning is: "Having liberated them from that suffering, I shall make them partakers of the bliss of Nibbāna"—thus, for the sake of bringing benefit to the world of sentient beings. And this connects with the phrase "performing what is exceedingly difficult.

There is also no fault in construing it as: "He has reached weariness for the sake of the world’s welfare. For in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* it is said: "Performing what is exceedingly difficult, he has reached weariness; for what purpose?"
It is said: "For what? For the welfare of the world.
As for what was stated by someone who could not conceive of such a connection—"The Blessed One does not undergo the suffering of saṃsāra for the welfare of the world;
for no one's experience of suffering brings benefit to the world"—that is merely his own opinion.
Thus, even for the Blessed One who performed such exceedingly difficult austerities, the experience of suffering was for the sake of bringing benefit to the world;

this is the meaning understood here, and not that the welfare of the world is accomplished by the mere experience of suffering. For even according to the first-mentioned interpretation, the accomplishment of the world's welfare does not come about through the mere performance of difficult tasks.
Indeed, one who performs difficult tasks does not, by that alone, establish any being in the paths, fruits, and so forth.

He establishes them; rather, having performed such an exceedingly difficult task and realized omniscience, he accomplishes the welfare of the world by establishing beings in the paths, fruits, and so forth through his teaching of the Dhamma that leads to liberation.
Although, in this context, the world is threefold—consisting of beings, formations, and the receptacle-world—it is the performance of welfare that is intended here.

The meaning here should be understood according to the world of beings (*sattaloka*) alone. For it is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their maturation, are experienced (*lokīyanti*) therein.

However, in certain instances—such as in the phrase "the world-honored one, including humans and gods" (*sanarāmaralokagaru*)—the word *loka* also carries the sense of a collection, in the sense that [a group] is experienced or designated as a whole. As for what has been stated by someone regarding this: "By this..."
"It encompasses both the world of beings (*sattaloka*) and the world of birth (*jātiloka*); therefore, having combined together the welfare of that world of beings—

consisting of benefit for this world and the next world— or the welfare known as a happy dwelling in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) for those who have transcended the next world or for whom the origin of the world has been cut off,

whether in this world of birth or in the world of space— he says simply 'for the welfare of the world' (*lokahitam*), employing the grammatical rule of *sarūpekasesa* (retaining one of identical forms) for 'the world,' 'of the worlds,' or 'in the world.'"

That [state] should not be understood as essential, because even that which is reckoned as a pleasant dwelling in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra) has the world of sentient beings as its domain;
for by the very mention of the "world of sentient beings," those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) and whose roots have been severed are also included.
In all instances where it is said "by someone," it should be understood as "by the author of the Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā. Regarding the phrase "in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada":
When either "Majjhimagaṇṭhipada" or "Cūḷagaṇṭhipada" is mentioned, it should be understood as referring to the "Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipadas.
However, when simply "Gaṇṭhipada" is mentioned, it should be understood as the "Gaṇṭhipadas" written in the Māgadha language.
"Nātha" means one who is the refuge of the world, the lord of the world, and the leader of the world; for he is preceded by the removal of all misfortune.
The Blessed One— the supreme among all beings— is the sole refuge and support for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems,
because he is devoted to providing benefit and happiness without remainder, because of his unsurpassed perfection of practice, because of his ultimate service to the generation of gods and humans,
and because he possesses infinite, incomparable, and distinguished qualities of power. Now...

Or, he is called a *nātha* because he protects (*nāthati*). The meaning is that he wishes for and aspires to the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*) by means of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that he torments (*nāthati*) the defilements residing in those to be trained; or, "he protects" (*nāthati*) means "he entreats" (*yācati*).
For the Blessed One [said]: "Bhikkhus, it is good for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time upon his own perfection," and so forth.
Even when requested by beings to practice this or that beneficial course of action, he encourages them therein out of compassion.
Or, being endowed with supreme mastery of mind, he rules over and surpasses all beings;
thus the Blessed One is the Supreme Lord (*paramissara*) and is called the "Protector" (*nātha*). And this entire meaning should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

"Of the Greatly Compassionate One" (Mahākāruṇikassa): this means of him who, because his heart was shaken by compassion, came having experienced such manifold suffering of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) through extremely difficult deeds for the sake of the welfare of the world;
that is the meaning of "of the Greatly Compassionate One. In this context, it is called *karuṇā* because it scatters (*kirati*);
the meaning is that it disperses and removes the suffering of others. Or else, it is called *karuṇā* because it is extended (*kirīyati*) or spread forth toward those who are suffering.
Compassion (*karuṇā*). Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it "wounds" (*kiṇāti*);

for when there is suffering in another, it wounds, afflicts, or destroys the compassionate one’s own happiness—the meaning being that it destroys the happiness of another. Or else, it is called *karuṇā* because, when there is suffering in another, it causes a trembling or heartache in the virtuous.
Alternatively, *kam* means happiness; it obstructs (*rundhati*) that, hence it is *karuṇā*. For its characteristic is the desire to remove the suffering of others.

"Because it obstructs and hinders the happiness of the compassionate ones by way of their disregard for their own pleasure. One who is "devoted to compassion" (*kāruṇika*) is called *kāruṇika*, just as one is called a "doorkeeper" (*dovārika*).

For just as a man—even if he is engaged elsewhere than at the door—whose livelihood is dependent on the door is called a "doorkeeper" because his conduct does not transcend the door, so too is the Blessed One.

Even when engaged elsewhere than in the dwelling of compassion (*karuṇāvihāra*) by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, because his conduct never transcends compassion, he is called "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*) due to being intent upon compassion.

From the time of his Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) until his Great Parinibbāna, the Lords of the World remain solely for the welfare and benefit of the world. One who is great and compassionate is a "Greatly Compassionate One" (*mahākāruṇika*). This is also true of the Blessed One...

Since this greatness is expressed here by means of the presence of the word "compassionate" (kāruṇika) based on other qualities as well— just as in the expression "a great grammarian" (mahāveyyākaraṇo)—
the greatness in this context should be understood as being through compassion. And by adopting this method,
through the phrase "of the Great Compassionate One" (mahākāruṇikassa), the Teacher’s great compassion is stated by way of reference to the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
Alternatively, one is "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*) because compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the act of feeling pity, is his nature (*pakati*).

The meaning is that his essential nature is the act of feeling pity—just as solidity and contact are the intrinsic natures of earth and touch—and thus it is compassion as an inherent nature. The rest is exactly as before.
Alternatively, it is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) because it is great due to its vast range, its great majesty, and its great power.
For the compassion of the Blessed One extends toward all sentient beings without exception; and as it proceeds, it proceeds in a manner not shared by others;
and it unfailingly brings about the great benefit and happiness of sentient beings, categorized as pertaining to the present life and so forth.

Thus, because he is devoted to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he is called "the Greatly Compassionate One" (*Mahākāruṇika*); all this should be understood according to the method already explained. Alternatively, *mahatī*...
One who possesses praised compassion is called *Mahākāruṇika* (the Great Compassionate One). Here, the word *maha* is a term of praise, as in expressions such as "Great Man" (*mahāpurisa*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One’s compassion is praised because it proceeds by way of the attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and because it is not shared by others.
Thus, having briefly praised the Blessed One through the aspect of compassion—by means of all the qualities of an Omniscient One—one now [praises] the True Dhamma.
To praise him, he said, "Asambudhaṃ," and so forth. Therein, "asambudhaṃ" is a designation for an action occurring in a prior time;
its meaning is "not having awakened" or "not having penetrated," which is to say, "not having penetrated according to the true nature [of things].
Here, the word *anta* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in expressions such as "he sits while reciting. The word *yaṃ* refers to the action in the prior time.
The description of the action is indefinite. "Resorted to by the Buddha" is its qualification.

Regarding that, first, the meaning of the word *buddha* should be understood according to the method of explanation as: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the world," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is because of the absolute departure from the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies, or because of the blossoming of his awakening (*buddhi*).
"Buddha" means "one who has awakened" (*buddhavā*), in the sense of waking up or blossoming.

Alternatively, because there is no knowable object (*ñeyyadhamma*) that has not been awakened to, and because there is no grasping of any particular knowable object as an object of action (*kamma*), there is an absence of a desire for a verbal expression of the object;

thus, the designation of the agent is obtained solely in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamana*). In terms of its meaning (*attha*), however, [he is called Buddha] by virtue of self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) refined by the perfections (*pāramitā*).

The Buddha is the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) which, together with its latent tendencies (vāsanā), has destroyed and utterly demolished all defilements (kilesa), and which is the substratum for an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).

As it is said: "Buddha refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), teacherless, who has personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena (dhamma) unheard of before, and who has attained omniscience therein, in the [ten] powers..."

And [the phrase] "and mastery" means that it was practiced by the Buddha, who possesses such incomparable radiance; the meaning is that it was practiced and experienced according to what was appropriate through both the practice of the field of activity (*gocarasevanā*) and the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanāsevanā*).

In this context, Nibbāna was practiced solely by way of the practice of the field of activity, whereas the Path (*magga*), moreover, was practiced by way of the practice of cultivation through its own being cultivated.
Furthermore, when one fully understands through the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) and so forth the paths and fruits produced by others,

or when one delimits those produced by oneself through the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), then they are indeed cultivated even by way of the cultivation of the object (*gocarāsevanā*). And here,
if the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) is also included under the term "Dhamma" in a figurative sense, then that too is included.
It can be understood that he is "one who has cultivated" by means of cultivating the range of the knowledge of reviewing the teachings (*desanā-sammasana-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "He reaches the ocean of the method of the Abhidhamma;

he reviews the three Piṭakas," the term "reviewing" (*sammasana*) is also applicable to the realization of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). Thus, [the phrase] "not having awakened, not awakening, not realizing" refers to this.
It should be understood that this [teaching] is also mentioned here because its purpose is present. One who does not penetrate even that goes from existence to existence;
however, one who has fully understood the Dhamma and Vinaya and is correctly practicing for the sake of that goal will, before long, make an end of suffering. For this has been said:
“Whoever shall dwell heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.

And here, although the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna are indeed accessible through the cultivation of the range of practice and so forth even by Paccekabuddhas and disciples of a Buddha, [the Blessed One alone is the source of their manifestation].
Although [these practices] have been cultivated [by others], they are nevertheless described as "resorted to by the Buddhas" (*buddhanisevita*) by way of the highest limit.
However, some state that because the word *buddha* is used in its general sense, it includes here the *anubuddhas* (those who have awakened after) and the *paccekabuddhas* (solitary buddhas) as well.

"From existence to existence" (*bhavābhava*) is a designation for karma in terms of activity in subsequent times; the meaning is "from one existence to another. Alternatively, "bhavābhava" [is explained as follows]:
The meaning is that they become small and great by way of happy and miserable destinies, and by way of inferior and superior states.

For the vowel *a* is seen in the sense of "increase," as in such expressions as “the qualities of one beyond training” (*asekkhā dhammā*). Therefore, *abhava* refers to a "great existence" (*mahābhava*).
Alternatively, *bhava* means increase, while *abhava* means decrease. Or else, *bhava* is the view of eternalism, and *abhava* is the view of annihilationism.

"Becoming and non-becoming" (*bhavābhava*) refers to the aforementioned types of existence (*bhava*) and non-existence (*abhava*). "Going to that becoming and non-becoming" (*taṃ bhavābhavaṃ gacchati*) is a description of an action occurring at a subsequent time.

"The world of living beings" (*jīvaloka*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). By using the term "living beings," he excludes the world of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāraloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), because it is impossible for them to go through states of becoming and non-becoming.
The phrase "let there be homage" (*namo atthu*) should be understood as a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhasesa*).
"Destroyer of the net of defilements beginning with ignorance" is a qualification of the Dhamma. In this context, "ignorance" (*avijjā*) means that which finds what should not be found.
In the sense of being unfit to be fulfilled, bodily misconduct and so forth are called "what should not be found" (*avindiya*), meaning they are not to be acquired.

By contrast, bodily good conduct and so forth are called "what should be found" (*vindiya*); ignorance is so named because it does not find that which should be found. Furthermore, [ignorance] is the failure to find the meaning of the aggregates as a "heap."

Or, it is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because it makes unknown the sense-field-meaning of the sense-fields, the emptiness-meaning of the elements, the sovereignty-meaning of the faculties, and the suchness-meaning of the truths;
or it is ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning—such as oppression and so forth—as stated for suffering and the rest;
[it functions] within the beginningless *saṃsāra*, amidst all the birth-places, destinies, states of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it causes beings to run about; or else, it is ignorance because it runs after things such as "woman" and "man," which do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), yet does not run after things such as the aggregates (*khandha*), which do exist.
Those things beginning with craving (*taṇhā*) of which it is the first are "ignorance and the rest" (*avijjādayo*).
They are "defilements" (*kilesa*) because beings are defiled by them. And they are a "net" (*jāla*) because they are like a net in the sense of being a bond for beings.
It is called "the destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance" because it completely shatters and utterly eradicates them through virtue (*sīla*). If it is objected:

"But surely, in this context, the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) together with the scriptures (*pariyatti*) are intended; and therein, it is only the Path (*magga*) that destroys the defilements, not the others," we reply:
Even for the Path, since it destroys the defilements by means of Nibbāna, Nibbāna itself [is also considered a destroyer of defilements].

It is called "the destroyer" (viddhaṃsī) because the function of destroying defilements (kilesa-viddhaṃsana-kicca) belonging to the Path is accomplished by the Fruit; thus, the Fruit is also called "the destroyer of defilements.

Furthermore, since the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) is a condition for the destruction of defilements, it too is worthy of being called "the destroyer of defilements," and there is no fault in this.

“Of that excellent Dhamma”: this is a statement specifying what was previously unspecified. In this context, it is called *dhamma* because it sustains one who practices according to the instruction, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery (*apāya*).
As it is said: “Whoever has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, they shall not go to the plane of misery;
having cast off the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.”

It has been said: it is called *dhamma* because it holds [the mind] so that one does not fall into the suffering of *saṃsāra*. This is because *saṃsāra* is delimited by the arising of the Path and its Fruits, such as the limit of seven more births (*sattakkhattuparama*).
Furthermore, "holding" here refers to the destruction of the defilements (*kilesa*) that produce rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*) and so forth.
And having established this, both the Noble Path and Nibbāna are, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), [called *dhamma*] because they are the causes for the accomplishment of that purpose.

It should be understood that both [the noble fruit and the Dhamma of the scriptures] are "borne" (dhāreti) in a figurative sense: the noble fruit because it is conducive to it through the subsiding of the defilements severed by it; and the Dhamma of the scriptures because it is the cause for its realization.

The "Dhamma-treasure" (dhammavara) refers to the very Dhamma described above as "excellent," "most excellent," and "unsurpassed" (anuttara) due to the absence of anything superior to itself. Of that Dhamma-treasure...
"May there be homage"—this is the connection. Up to this point, we have clarified the essential meaning (*sārattha*) herein.
As for whatever has been elaborated upon by others here, and which we have not shown, that should not be understood as the essence. This should be seen in the same way in what follows as well.
Therefore, from now on, instead of saying even this much, we shall show only the essential meaning. Where—
However, some things have been written that are utterly contradictory; we shall point those out in their proper places.

Here, by the phrase “destroyer of the web of defilements such as ignorance,” he praises the Dhamma through its well-expounded nature and other qualities. By the phrase “of the excellent Dhamma,” he indicates its perfection, because it demonstrates the absence of anything else more distinguished.
Alternatively, by the first [phrase] he shows the Dhamma’s perfection in abandonment, and by the second, its perfection in power.
Having thus praised the True Dhamma in brief by means of all its qualities, he now speaks the words beginning with “by qualities” (*guṇehi*) in order to praise the Noble Saṅgha.
The word “by qualities” (*guṇehi*) is connected with the word “endowed” (*yutto*). Now, showing those qualities by which he is endowed, he says “virtue, concentration,” and so forth.
Therein, the fourfold purification of virtue and the rest is called “virtue” (*sīla*).

It is said: "Concentration" refers to the first jhāna and so forth; for it is by way of the heading "concentration" that the first jhāna and the others are spoken of. "Wisdom" refers to path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*).

Regarding what should have been stated as "liberation and knowledge of liberation" (*vimutti-vimuttiñāṇa*), it is called "knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) by means of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining one member of a group where the members are similar).
Liberation should be understood as being included either by way of the synonym for the word "etc. (*ādi*) or by the word "and so forth" (*pabhuti*).
In this context, "liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the fruit (*phala*). "Knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

By the word "beginning with" (*pabhuti*), it should be understood that qualities such as the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*) are included. Furthermore, it should be known that herein qualities such as virtue (*sīla*)—both mundane and supramundane—are indicated according to their possibility. As for what has been stated by some here: "Although virtue and the other qualities are both mundane and supramundane..."

Although they are obtained according to possibility, nevertheless, because of the statement at the end that it is the "Noble Saṅgha," the four aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue must be supramundane—this is merely his own opinion.

For no fault whatsoever is seen in praising the Noble Saṅgha even by means of mundane qualities; for even the praise of the Omniscient Buddha himself is offered by way of both mundane and supramundane qualities.
How much more so, then, for the Noble Saṅgha!
Because it is like a field for the increase of merit for people who seek what is wholesome, he said, "the field for people who seek what is wholesome.
For a field (*khetta*) is so called because it protects (*tāyati*) the sown seed by causing it to yield great fruit.
The Noble Saṅgha is also called a "field" because it is similar to land where the crops of the previous and subsequent harvests grow.
By this, he illuminates the fact that the Noble Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world; for it has been said: "The unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
The word "that" (*taṃ*) is a definitive statement regarding what was previously mentioned without specification by the word "who" (*yo*). Regarding the phrase "the Noble Saṅgha": here...

They are "Noble Ones" (*ariya*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), because they are far removed from defilements (*kilesa*), because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, and because they proceed in the right way.

Alternatively, they are Noble Ones because they are worthy of being sought after (*araṇīya*) and approached by the world including the devas, and because for those who have approached them, their purpose is accomplished.
The "Community of Noble Ones" (*ariyasaṅgha*) is the collection or assembly of Noble Ones. Alternatively, it is both noble and that [community] in the manner already described.
And because the Saṅgha is unified by the commonality of view and virtue, it is the Noble Saṅgha, consisting of the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala). Regarding that Noble Saṅgha:

it should be understood that the statement "I bow my head" was made right here in this context to demonstrate the great benefit of the Noble Saṅgha, since after the Blessed One’s passing, the attainment of even the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma is dependent upon the jewel of the Saṅgha.
Having thus paid homage to the Triple Gem by way of briefly praising its entire range of qualities through these three verses,
he now says "Thus indeed," etc., dedicating that act of prostration toward his intended purpose. Thus, in the manner already described,
while paying homage to the Triple Gem— which is worthy of being worshipped absolutely and exclusively— ...
The connection is: "I, by worshipping with body, speech, and mind, obtained that vast outflow of merit.

In this context, the Buddha and the others are called *ratana* (jewels) in the sense of generating delight (*rati*). For when one reflects upon their qualities as they truly are, according to the formula beginning "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," a no small measure of rapture and gladness arises, which serves as the cause for attaining the Deathless. As it has been said:
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is simply straight. And when, Mahānāma, his mind is straight...”
“The noble disciple gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma;
in one who is joyful, rapture arises,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the sense of “jewel” (ratana) is the state of being honored and so on. For this has been said:
“Because it is esteemed, of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold,
and enjoyed by beings who are not ordinary, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana). Furthermore,
qualities such as being esteemed and so forth are found only in the Buddha and others, and not shared with anyone else.
“In ‘flood of merit’ (puññābhisanda), it means a heap of merit or a flow of merit,” so it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*.
However, in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, the meaning is also stated as “flood of merit” (puññābhisanda) or “the excellence of merit” (puññābhinisamsa).
But here the meaning should be understood as “flood of merit” (puññābhisanda) meaning a river of merit, a stream of merit; for that which proceeds without interruption—
Merit is called a "meritorious flood" (*puññābhisanda*) in the sense of overflowing. For this very reason, it is said in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four meritorious floods, floods of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness. What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One... [and so forth].
"‘The Buddha is the Blessed One’—this is the first flood of merit, the flood of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness.
In explaining the meaning of such a passage from the Canon, it was said: "Floods of merit, floods of the wholesome" means "rivers of merit, rivers of the wholesome.
As for what is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*—"Floods of merit" means "the fruit of merit"—that is not correct.
For one who pays homage to the Triple Gem does not obtain the fruit of merit at that very moment;
rather, at that time, one acquires a vast heap of merit, the fruit of which is to be experienced in the next world.
However, in this present life, the warding off of obstacles is merely a secondary benefit (*ānisamsa*) of that merit. Thus it is said, "By its power, obstacles were destroyed," and not...
Furthermore, if the fruit of merit had not yet arisen, it would not be possible for the state of having obstacles removed to be accomplished through its power;
nor was this [fruit] experienced in the very same moment as a result pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

Therefore, the meaning that "by the power of that great stream of merit, obstacles were removed" is indeed what is appropriate. Alternatively, because it is produced by the act of prostration, merit itself is called the "fruit of merit."
The intention behind this might be as follows: if that were so, it would be appropriate.
And showing that this stream of merit is not slight, but rather truly great, he said "vast" (*vipula*); the meaning is that it is great and not small.
"Alattha" means "I obtained"; the sense is "I reached."
"By its power" means by the power and force of that aforementioned stream of merit. "With obstacles destroyed":
an obstacle (*antarāya*) is so called because it comes (*eti*) into the midst (*antara*)—that is, within the continuum of a being—as a hindrance to various forms of prosperity;
it refers to misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth. An obstacle is "destroyed" or "dispelled" according to the method explained in the context of the act of salutation.
"Upaddavo assā" means "one whose obstacles have been destroyed. This connects with the phrase "I shall praise the Vinaya";
the sense is that, having had his obstacles destroyed, he will praise the Vinaya.

By this, he demonstrates the capacity to destroy those calamities that obstruct the flow of merit—namely, the destruction of one's own attainment of confidence and the excellence of the field consisting of the Triple Gem—through the exposition of the meaning.

Having thus shown the purpose for performing acts of personal service toward the Triple Gem, [the author] now, wishing to comment upon the meaning of the Vinaya Piṭaka, first demonstrates its status as the fundamental foundation of the Blessed One’s dispensation;
praising it as well, he says: "In which standing," and so forth. The dispensation of the Blessed One is well-established in that which stands firm.
The phrase "when that stands, it is established" should be construed here. In this context, "in which" (*yasmiṃ*) means in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Stands" (*ṭhite*) means that it exists in the sense of being practiced among persons possessed of moral shame, being neither deficient in its textual wording (*pāḷi*) nor in its meaning (*attha*).
"The Dispensation" (*sāsana*) refers to the teaching comprised of the three trainings known as higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
"Not standing" (*aṭṭhitassa*) means not standing in the two extremes, namely, devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification;
for it is said: "Friend, I have crossed the flood without a foothold and without exertion. This meaning is indeed stated in the three *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipadas*.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "'Not standing' means even for the Blessed One who has attained final Nibbāna."
"It is established" means it is established in the sense of proceeding among those very persons who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*). Regarding "of one well-proportioned":
here, in all three commentaries on the *gaṇṭhipada*, this is stated:

"The meaning is 'of one who possesses a beautiful form by way of being endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics. By this, he demonstrates his excellence of the physical body (*rūpakāya*)."

In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it is said: "He is well-proportioned in his physical body because he is endowed with the characteristics established in their proper places, and he is so also in his mental body because he is free from bodily crookedness and the like, and because he is endowed with the characteristic of being 'such' (*tādi*). But some [commentators] say:
"Or, he is well-proportioned in the sense that he is firmly and correctly established among beings by means of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*)."

For he, being well-composed, teaches the Vinaya solely out of a desire to remove the suffering of beings, a desire to bestow their welfare, and being delighted by their success, he does so without partiality.

Therefore, in this section on the commentary on the Vinaya, while praising him with appropriate verses, it was said: "Of the well-composed," and the meaning stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* is intended here in accordance with the subject matter.
"It does not exist," it is said. However, this is our own preference here:

because one does not abide in the aforementioned two extremes—namely, devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification—and because one is properly established in the Middle Way, one is "well-established. This is how the meaning should be understood.
For if this were so, the praise would be made appropriate to the undertaking, having avoided the aforementioned two extremes and [abiding] in the Middle Way.
Because it explains for the most part the training-rule (vinaya-paññatti) itself according to the way of practice (paṭipadā).
The word *taṃ* is a restrictive statement referring back to what was previously stated without specification as "in which"; its connection is with the word "training" (*vinaya*).
*Asammissaṃ* is a neuter noun in the accusative case, meaning "having made it unmixed with the tenets of other schools."
It means they will explain [the Vinaya] having made it free from confusion.

Since even for one like the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, the state of being difficult to understand is evident even regarding the mere timing appropriate for the formulation of a training rule (sikkhāpada), the statement "I shall explain the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, which is the domain of the Buddha alone, by my own power" is something that others would be unable to utter; therefore, [he says] "relying on... [nissāya].

He said, "The power of the ancient masters" (*pubbācariyānubhāva*). In terms of meaning, "the power of the ancient masters" refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) expounded by those ancient masters;
for this very reason, it is stated in all the *gaṇṭhi* (commentarial) passages that "the power of the ancient masters is the commentary.
Therefore, I shall explain [this work] relying upon the commentaries expounded by the ancient masters, and not from my own [authority] alone.
"By relying on strength" is what is meant.
Now, for one who might ask, "What is the purpose of this new commentary on the Vinaya when the ancient commentaries (porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā) already exist?", [the author] says "Kāmam ca...
and so forth, showing that the ancient commentaries are not deficient and demonstrating the specific purpose of his own commentary.
"Kāmaṃ" means "entirely" or "according to one's wish"; thus it is said "all. Its connection is with the word "saṃvaṇṇito" (expounded).
The meaning is: "It was indeed expounded; it was not unexpounded. To the question, "By whom was that Vinaya expounded?
he says: "By the bull-like former teachers. The Elder Mahākassapa and others were indeed former teachers in the sense of being immovable.
And in the sense of being supreme, they are "bulls" (āsabha); thus it is said, "by those bulls who were former teachers. But what kind of persons are these former teachers?

To this he says: "By the water of knowledge," and so forth. By the water—that is, the liquid—consisting of the knowledge of the supreme path, the three stains of lust and the rest have been washed away, cleansed, and purified through the complete production of the state of non-arising in the future.
And the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), are those by which their stains and taints have been washed away by the water of knowledge; this is the meaning.

By this, he shows that it is not only their status as teachers among these [disciples] that is intended, but rather that they are beings who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and are purified, being free from the stains of passion and so forth.
Furthermore, even in their state of having destroyed the taints, they are not merely practitioners of dry insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*), but are endowed with such powers as these.

Showing this, he said: "By means of purified true knowledge and analytical insights. Those who possess purified—that is, absolutely pure—true knowledge and the four analytical insights are "those with purified true knowledge and analytical insights.

Since there are no noble ones (ariya) who have not attained at least some portion of the analytical insights, it follows that those who have attained these have acquired a more distinguished variety of them.
The term "pure" (*visuddha*) is used in order to demonstrate this. "Knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to either the three knowledges or the eight knowledges. Among these, the three knowledges are:

the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. As for the eight knowledges, they are: insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, [the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of supernormal powers, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the future, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints].
Furthermore, the analysis of the bases of psychic power, the divine ear,
the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge following past lives;
"The divine eye and the destruction of the taints—these knowledges here are the eight forms of clear vision (vijjā).
Thus, it is precisely the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) that are encompassed by insight-knowledge and the mind-made psychic power. This is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
The four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) are: the analytical insight of the Dhamma, the analytical insight of language, and the analytical insight of eloquence.
Therein, in brief, knowledge of cause and effect is the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā); knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical insight of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā);

and knowledge regarding linguistic conventions that conforms to the cause and its corresponding effect is the analytical insight of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), [understood as] "this knowledge illuminates this meaning."
In this manner, the knowledge occurring within the three types of knowledge mentioned below is the *paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā* (analytical insight of ingenuity).

However, a detailed exposition of these is not given here because it would result in excessive prolixity. Because those who have attained the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) are skilled in the true Dhamma, it is said:
"by those skilled in the exposition of the true Dhamma. [And as it is said: "Even for those who have attained the analytical insights, regarding the teachings..."
Some also say: "He spoke thus to show the pre-eminence [of the author] among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), on account of his application.
"By those skilled in the exposition of the True Dhamma" means by those skilled (kovidehi) in the exposition of the True Dhamma—namely, the Three Piṭakas—in the complete elucidation of its meaning;
that is, by those who are proficient (chekehi), that is, by those who are adept (kusalehi).
*Sallekha* means that which scrapes away (*saṃlikhati*) or makes thin the net of defilements (*kilesajāla*) or the abundance of requisites (*parikkhārabāhulla*).

Here, however, because the subject matter concerns those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), the meaning should be understood specifically in the sense of scraping away the abundance of requisites;

for this very reason, the commentary on the *Gaṇṭhipada* states: "In the *sallekhiya*, [meaning] one who lives with limited requisites. *Sallekhiya* is the state of being *sallekha*; in that *sallekhiya*.
"By the practice of *sallekha* (effacement)" is what is meant. "With similes that are not easily found" means:
because persons suitable for comparison with those [practitioners] of the practice of *sallekha*—who are "not like anyone else"—are difficult to find, there are no easy-to-find similes for them;
thus they are "those for whom similes are not easily found. "Of the Mahāvihāra" refers to the two resident schools, namely the Cittala-pabbata and Abhayagiri.

He rejects it. "By means of the banners" (dhajūpamehi) means: just as a banner tied to a chariot serves as the cause for identifying that chariot, so too, because it serves as the cause for identifying the Mahāvihāra for those who do not know it—saying, "This is the Mahāvihāra, inhabited by such and such elders"—it is "by means of the banners of the Mahāvihāra.
"Eulogized" (saṃvaṇṇito) means praised thoroughly and without omission. This is what is eulogized.
The word-division should be made as *vinayo ti*. "By various methods" (*cittehi nayehi*) means by methods that are manifold due to their many different classifications.

"Following the excellent path of the Fully Enlightened One" (*sambuddhavaranvayehi*) means following the excellent Omniscient Buddha; what is meant is that they follow the methods according to the Blessed One’s intention.
Alternatively, the connection should be made with "following the excellent Buddha [as taught] by the preeminent former teachers" (*buddhavaram anugatehi pubbācariyāsabhehi*).

Having thus demonstrated the completeness of the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), he now says "The Commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) and so forth in order to show the specific purpose of his own sub-commentary.

This is what is meant: although this Vinaya has been fully expounded by the assembly of former teachers who were distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, nevertheless, this commentary of theirs was [composed] in the language of the inhabitants of the Island of Siṃhala.

Because it was compiled during the time when the Saṅgha was divided, it does not achieve, accomplish, or establish any purpose or utility for the community of monks residing in other islands than the Island of Ceylon; therefore, having been requested by the Elder Buddhasiri,
they will now begin this commentary, having made it conform to the method of the original text (Pāḷi).
In this context, *saṃvaṇṇanā* means that by means of it the meaning (*attha*) is fully described; thus, it is the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Furthermore, because the Elders who compiled the Dhamma first recited the Three Piṭakas and then established the path of oral transmission in accordance with the description of their meaning, it is the very path of discourse consisting of the description of the meaning of the Buddha’s word that has been ascended through the three councils (*saṅgīti*). That alone—
And it was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Great Elder Mahinda;

subsequently, it was established in the Sinhala language by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding confusion with the tenets of other schools (nikāya). Therefore, he said: "By the inhabitant of the island of Siṃhala," and so forth.
One is called *Sīhaḷa* because of seizing (*lāna*) or grasping (*gahaṇa*) a lion (*sīha*); [thus] Sīhakumāra. Because they were born in his lineage, the kṣatriyas on the island of Tambapaṇṇi...
Because they were its inhabitants, Tambapaṇṇidīpa should also be understood as having the nature of Sīhaḷa;
because it was produced in that Sīhaḷa island, it is said to be "by a Sīhaḷa sentence" or "by speech," meaning in the Sīhaḷa language.
"In accordance with the method of the Pāḷi" means having made it conform to the method of the Pāḷi, that is, having translated it into the Māgadhī language.
It exists. "Entreaty" (*ajjhesanā*) means a longing directed toward a more weighty purpose after having attended upon one who stands in the position of a teacher;
that entreaty, which is a supplication—this is the meaning. Its connection is with the word "recalling" (*samanussaranto*).
To the question "Of whom is the entreaty?", he says: "Of the elder named Buddhasiri. *Buddhasiri* is the name, that is, the appellation.
The meaning is: "properly recollecting with reverence the request of that elder named so-and-so, whose name is the glorious Buddha, and placing it in his heart.
Now, showing the manner in which he composed his own commentary, he said: "And that commentary... and so forth. Therein:
Now, commencing this commentary which is being spoken, and because the entire *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is to be taken here,
he takes the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* as the body for this commentary being spoken;

likewise, whatever exposition was stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*, and whatever exposition is found in the well-known commentaries such as the *Kurundi* and others— [The rest of the passage continues with the specific details of the expositions.]
Having been thus stated, one who does not abandon the most appropriate meaning even from that point of analysis, but rather incorporates it into the Theravāda, shall begin the commentary;
thus the connection between the words is to be understood. And here, "atthakathā" means that by which the meaning (*attha*) is told (*kathiyati*);
that very same thing is called *aṭṭhakathā* after changing the letter *tth* to *ṭṭh*, as in such expressions as "the meaning of the oppression of suffering" (*dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho*).
"Like. Regarding "Mahāpaccarī": here *paccarī* means a raft; because [the commentary] was composed while sitting upon one, it received that very name.
They say that there is a monastery called Kurundivallivihāra, and because it was composed there, it received the name *Kurundī*.
By the word "etcetera," the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā* and the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* are included. "Renowned" (*vissutāsu*)...
"Spread everywhere" means "manifested" (*pākaṭa*). Regarding the phrase "the meaning is appropriate":
here, in both the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷa-gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "'The meaning is appropriate' means that the subject to be commented upon has an appropriate meaning;
it does not mean, however, that there is no inappropriate meaning therein."
In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*, however, nothing has been stated on this point.

Someone has remarked that "the meaning is consistent with the method of the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) or with the logic of the Vinaya," and this appears reasonable, since even in works such as the *Mahāpaccarī*, there are instances where an inconsistent meaning is further clarified.
When it was said, "I shall compose the commentary by taking the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself as the basis,"...
Thinking that the Theravāda mentioned in the *aṭṭhakathās* might be considered external, he said "the Theravāda included herein" (*antogadhatheravāda*), desiring to include them within it;
thus, it is meant that they are included even within the Theravāda. The term "commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇana*) is a designation for an action performed at a later time.
However, the word "commentary" used previously refers to an action performed at an earlier time, namely "commencing" (*samārabhanto*).

It should be construed with the sense of the agent (*kammabhāva*). Although "samma" should have been used, it should be understood that the short vowel was employed for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
Having thus shown the manner of the instrument (*karaṇappakāra*), he now spoke the words beginning with "taṃ me" in order to show the method by which the listeners should proceed.
This is what is meant: "Now, this commentary on the Dhammapada-lamp of the Tathāgata, which is being spoken by me—"

Those monks who honor and revere the Dhamma—whether the Dhamma of the Dispensation (Sāsana-dhamma) or the Dhamma of the Canon (Pāḷi-dhamma)—are called *theras* because they are endowed with the stable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth;
*navas* because they have recently gone forth; and *majjhimas* because they exist between those two.
With hearts full of faith, these monks, according to the method already stated, are purposeful and possess the proper measure according to the procedure that will be explained below.
"Having placed their faith, with minds endowed with joy and gladness, let them listen and hear attentively, without being overcome by envy.
In this context, "of the lamp of the Dhamma": because it dispels the darkness of delusion within the mental continuums of sentient beings, the Dhamma itself is like a lamp;
thus, it is the "lamp of the Dhamma," namely, the Blessed One. "Of that lamp of the Dhamma."
Now, having demonstrated the purity of his source through his own self-eulogy, he spoke the words beginning with "By the Buddha" in order to show its authoritative status.
Just as the Dhamma and Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha, so too were they understood exactly as they were by those sons of the Buddha, such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and others;
for it was because the Sīhaḷa masters of the Aṭṭhakathā, who measured the wisdom of those sons of the Buddha, [transmitted them] in the past...
“They composed commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*); this is the connection here. In that context, “Dhamma” comprises the Sutta and Abhidhamma, while “Vinaya” refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
By this much, the entirety of the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) has been indicated;
for the whole of the Buddha’s word is twofold, consisting of Dhamma and Vinaya. “Spoken” means both according to the text (*pāḷi*) and according to the meaning (*attha*).
And this was spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One. For there is no sūtra-passage (tantipada) that was left unexplicated by the Blessed One;

the meaning of all of them has been told. Therefore, it should be understood that even the sequence for the commentary on the meaning of the Three Piṭakas was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself.
Indeed, the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) are simply the various discourses delivered by the Blessed One here and there.

“Known just as it was” means that it was known and understood exactly as spoken by the Buddha, without destroying even a single word or a single syllable, and without distorting the intended meaning. “Not abandoning the intention of those sons of the Buddha” means not forsaking their purpose.
“They composed commentaries” means they produced the *aṭṭhakathās*. In some places, it reads “they made the *aṭṭhakathā*.”
The reading is seen there as well, and the meaning is exactly the same; however, it should be understood that the letter *ma* has been inserted by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
By the use of the plural form "the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathā*), he includes the *Mahāpaccarī* and others.
Therefore—because they previously composed the commentaries without distorting the intention of those sons of the Buddha—
Therefore, this is the meaning. *Hi* is a mere particle, since its causal sense is already expressed by the word *tasmā* (therefore).

[The author] says, "having avoided careless scribal errors," because if everything stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) were authoritative, then even careless scribal errors therein would have to be considered authoritative;
thus he specifies "careless scribal errors. In that context, "careless scribal errors" refers to those occurring at a later time when the texts were committed to manuscripts.
This refers to an erroneous reading that occurred due to negligence during the process of writing. What is meant is this:

having excluded and removed whatever was written through negligence—due to a failure to maintain mindfulness—such as the statement "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both the true and the false" regarding the preliminary stage of taking what is not given;
all such [errors] are authoritative. For he will say there:

“In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that there is only *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for both truth and falsehood; this should be understood as a scribal error. For there is no such thing as *dukkaṭa* in the place of a *pācittiya* (offense entailing confession) regarding the preliminary stage of taking what is not given.
To whom does this apply? He says: “Of those who are respectful toward the trainings, here, the wise ones. Here means in this Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Furthermore, if one asks what the connection is for the word “because” (*yasmā*), [the answer is found] here first in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
Nothing was stated [in that regard], but in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, this is said:
"Since it is authoritative, therefore let those with confident hearts listen. Thus should its connection be understood.

Having supplied the ellipsis by thinking, "Since it is authoritative as stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), therefore what is stated here is also indeed authoritative," the Venerable Vajirabuddhi—
He speaks. In this context, "here" (idha) should be understood as meaning "in this Samantapāsādikā.

Therein, because it has been established that everything stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is authoritative by virtue of its connection with the word "since" (*yasmā*) mentioned first, the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) now being spoken is distinct from them merely by way of its verbal expression.
In order to show that, in terms of its meaning, it is indeed the *aṭṭhakathā* itself, he says: "And from that, it is merely another language," and so forth. If one asks:
why is even what is stated here an authority, given the connection with what was stated later? It is because, setting aside the mere words, this too is precisely the *aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, to show that it is an authority, he says: "And from that, it is merely another language," and so forth.
Having thus rendered [the text] confused and its nature difficult to discern, the connections were shown in the *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries;
however, the Venerable Teacher Buddhaghosa was one whose speech was unconfused. He certainly ought not to have spoken in such a confused manner.
Therefore, having made the intended meaning unconfused and easy to understand, we shall demonstrate it according to the connection as it actually stands. How so? Because in the *Aṭṭhakathās*...
"The measure has been stated; therefore, it should be studied with care"—this is how the connection here is to be understood.
If indeed the measure has been stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), one might ask: "Why then should this which is now being spoken be studied with care?
To this he says: "And having set aside even another language," and so forth. This is what is meant: because it has been stated in the commentaries...
Since this commentary is distinguished merely by its change of language and so forth, yet is not different in meaning, it will therefore be an authoritative standard;
thus, one should train in accordance with it, having shown due care and respect.
For such is the authoritative status of the ancient commentaries, and this commentary is distinguished from them merely by its change of language and so forth.
Since its meaning is non-different from that [of the ancient commentaries], both of these should be regarded as reasons for training diligently;
for it cannot be said that this commentary— despite the authoritative status of the ancient commentaries—
is different from them in meaning or something else entirely that must be trained in with diligence, nor can it be said that even though this commentary is non-different from them...
Since the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) lack authoritative status [in this context], it is appropriate to say that this sub-commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) should be studied with care;
therefore, it should be understood that both of these [the commentary and the sub-commentary] must be studied diligently for the same reason.
"From that" means from the commentary. "Having discarded the other language" means having removed the Sinhalese language, which is like a cloak.

"And having summarized the detailed path" means: having brought in even that which is stated further on in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), such as the detailed exposition of all four types of formal acts—beginning with the act of mere notification (*apalokana*)—found in various places [in the Vinaya], namely the passage:
"Monks are those who have received full ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) that is irreversible and fit for the occasion.
Just like that detailed exposition of the four formal acts, one should understand this "detailed path" to be of a similar nature.
The intention is: "I shall explain [them] by way of summary. For he will say:
"And here, only the *ñatticatuttha-kamma* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) has been mentioned;

however, it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that standing at this point, the four types of Saṅgha formal acts must be extracted and explained in detail. And these are: the *apalokana-kamma*..."

Having established them in order as "a formal act consisting of a motion," "a formal act consisting of a motion and a second [proclamation]," and "a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth [proclamation]," their textual basis has been cited in detail from the Khandhaka and from the end of the Parivāra and the Kammavibhaṅga.
We shall explain those very matters at the end of the Parivāra, in the Kammavibhaṅga itself; for when this is done, the commentary on the first Pārājika offense [will follow].
"And it will not be burdensome; the commentary on the text as it stands will be easy to understand, and those points will not be left empty.
Therefore, we shall provide a word-by-word commentary. Regarding the phrase "without omitting any of the analysis":
this means without leaving out any of the analysis set forth in the respective commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"Without leaving anything out" means without omitting even the slightest portion. It is said,
"without deviating in the slightest from the sequence of the text," because he provides a commentary on the Pāḷi as it has come down in its proper order—
being worthy of praise— and because, in the Sinhalese commentaries, he comments upon what was praised in inappropriate places by restoring it to its correct position.
The intention is: "We shall explain [the matter] in due order, without overstepping any portion of the Canon (Pāḷi).
"The meaning of the words of the Suttantas" refers to the meaning of the words found even within the Sutta-pāḷi itself.

In the Sinhalese commentaries (*Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā*), after stating "the burden of the Suttantas," there are also [explanations] of topics such as the discourse on meditation (*jhāna-kathā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-samādhi*), and so forth, which were not explicitly mentioned in the sections on Verañjā and elsewhere.
The intention is: "I shall fully elucidate the meaning of the words of the Suttantas in accordance with each respective Sutta.

"Hessati" means "it will be" or "it will be performed. And here, according to the first interpretation of the meaning, this commentary elucidates the meaning of the words of the Suttantas after having accomplished the fourfold task, beginning with the relinquishing of other languages.
The grammatical identity of the agent (*samānakattukatā*) should be understood by way of the commentary [itself] thinking, "It will be.
However, in the latter interpretation of the meaning, the identity of the agent should be understood by way of the teacher, as in:

"Having performed the aforementioned relinquishing of other languages and so forth, we shall compose this commentary which elucidates the meaning of the words of the Suttas. Thus ends the phrase "the commentary also" (*vaṇṇanāpi*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*: “Having taken the word ‘api’ here, one should connect it as: ‘Therefore, one should train diligently even [in this].
The intention there is that it combines both the specific purpose mentioned previously and its status as a standard of authority (*pamāṇabhāva*).
However, in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, the connection is stated as: “Therefore, one should train diligently even [in this]” (*tasmā sakkaccaṃ anusikkhitabbāpi*). Here—
The intended meaning is that this [commentary] not only will be an exposition (*vaṇṇanā*), but it must also be studied accordingly; thus he summarizes this point.
Here too, it is our conviction that the sense of the word *api* should be understood according to its literal position [as "also"].
This is what is meant: because the authority stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is the standard, and because this exposition is also [based] upon that.
Because it is unbroken, it will indeed become authoritative; therefore, it should be studied with diligence.
The commentary on the introductory discourse for the commencement of the book is finished.
The Discourse on the External Introduction.
Now, because he has promised, "I shall explain that Vinaya," and desiring to provide an exposition of the Vinaya as promised,

he says "Therein" (*tattha*), etc., in order to show that since the Vinaya is manifold— consisting of the Vinaya of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*), the Vinaya of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*), and so forth—
the Vinaya intended here for exposition must first be defined. Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) means...
Regarding those verses: the word *tāva* (so much/first) should be understood here in the sense of "first. By this, he indicates:

"Having first established the Vinaya, I shall subsequently provide its commentary. "To be established" (*vavatthapetabbo*) means to be determined or defined. "Therefore it is said" (*tenetaṃ vuccati*) means:
because it is to be established, for that reason, this defining statement beginning with "What is called Vinaya... is stated.

The meaning is "it is said. "Of" (assā) means "of the Vinaya. "Mātikā" means a summary. For it is called *mātikā* because, standing in the place of a mother (*mātā*) who gives birth to the words of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), it is like a mother.
Now, having established the summary (*mātikā*), he speaks the words beginning with "by whom it was spoken" in order to show the meaning that is to be explained. This is what was stated.
