There is [this]: having stated the aforementioned details—namely, by which person this Vinaya Piṭaka was spoken, at what time it was spoken, for what reason it was spoken, by whom it was preserved, by whom it was brought forth, and in whom it was established—it is adorned with the introductory formula beginning, "At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā," and then [continues with] "By him...
...[the text continues]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Vinaya Piṭaka, specifically discussing its provenance and the details of its transmission.)

I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya, demonstrating in many ways the meaning of the passage beginning with "At one time" (*samayena*). Here, although the statement "by whom, when,

and for what reason it was spoken" could have been stated separately even by one wishing to speak, it is not mentioned apart from the mere introductory formula beginning with "At that time the Buddha,

the Blessed One," because [the excellence of the teaching] is shown by the introduction as being "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*), and by the conclusion with the words "This was said" (*idamavoca*)...
And because of the statement, "beautiful in the conclusion," since both the introduction (*nidāna*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) follow the Teacher’s teaching, they are indeed included therein;

thus, because the introduction is also included within the Vinaya Piṭaka itself, he established this as a matrix (*mātikā*) by treating it as connected specifically to the Vinaya Piṭaka, [beginning with] "by whom, when, and why it was spoken. For in the matrix, it is stated: "this."
The Vinaya Piṭaka alone, in its general sense, maintains a connection throughout all [the texts].

Now, however, extracting it separately and demonstrating it, he says: "In that regard, it was stated by which... and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" (tattha) means in those sections of the Mātikā.
Then, as to why this very statement was spoken with reference to it, he says: "For this," and so forth.
The phrase "This" refers to the statement beginning with "At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One. The word *hi* should be understood in the sense of "because";
that is to say, because this is not a statement made by the Buddha, the Blessed One, from his own direct personal experience (*attapaccakkha*).

"Not a statement made from one's own direct personal experience" means it is not a statement spoken after having made it an object of one's own direct perception; it is not a statement spoken by the Blessed One [himself].
The intended meaning is that [it] exists. Some have stated: "The intended meaning of 'it is not a statement of personal realization' is that it is not spoken as a direct assertion.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is written: "'It is not a statement of personal realization' means it is not a statement uttered during one's own lifetime.
Both of these are identical in their essential meaning. Now follows the posing of the question.
Having spoken thus, while providing the answer to the question as previously stated in due order, he said, "By the Venerable One," and so forth. By this, he specifies the person;
by the words "And that," and so forth, he specifies the time. The meaning is that those words spoken by the Elder Upāli were uttered at the time of the First Great Council.
Commentary on the Account of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā).
Now, desiring to show that First Great Council and demonstrating the reason for mentioning it here—since it has been entered into the Canon (Tanti)—he said:
"This so-called First Great Council... should be understood. This is called the First Great Council.
The word *ca* in the phrase *cesā* has the sense of a collective summary (*sampiṇḍana*) of what is to be stated in such contexts;
thus it is meant that this First Great Council was held at the time of the First Great Council, and this First Great Council is to be understood in this way.

Alternatively, the word *ca* has the sense of an introduction (*upaññāsa*). An "introduction" (*upaññāsa*) is said to be the commencement of a discourse. For this is the custom of authors: namely, having stated something...
Furthermore, the employment of the word "and" (*ca*) occurs when those who begin to speak [something] intend to add further.

As for what was stated by someone else—"In the phrase 'the first Great Council (Mahāsaṅgīti) and so forth,' the word 'and' has a sense of addition (*atirekattha*), and by it, he indicates that there are others as well"—that very statement demonstrates his lack of skill in the structure of the text. For here, no sense of addition is understood through the word "and. And if here...
And it may be that the word *ca* (and) is intended for this very purpose;

if so, it need not be included at all, because the existence of the other recensions—the second and so forth—is already indicated by the word "first" (*paṭhama*) alone. For the use of the word "first" is dependent upon the second and so forth, just as the use of the word "short" (*rassa*) and so forth is dependent upon the "long" (*dīgha*) and so forth.
This is because [the suttas] were taught in various places according to the requirements of each occasion.

*Saṅgīti* means the singing or reciting together after having collected the various teachings (*dhamma*) and discipline (*vinaya*) that had been scattered because they were merely formulated (*paññatta*).

By this, the words of the compilers (*saṅgītikāra*)—which were established according to the context at the beginning, end, and intervals of each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and discourse (*sutta*)—are included.
It is called "great" (*mahatī*) because of its vast scope and its venerable nature.
*Saṅgīti* means the Great Council (*mahāsaṅgīti*); *paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti* means the first great council. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of skill in the introduction" (*nidānakosallattha*):
it is called an "introduction" (*nidāna*) because it introduces—that is, it makes known and points out—the teaching by way of its time, place, and so forth, which would otherwise remain unknown.
Skill in that is "skill in the introduction" (*nidānakosalla*); "for the sake of that" is the meaning.
Although there exist other activities of the Blessed One that serve as causes for beings to obtain the unsurpassed vision, refuge, and so forth, he stated,

"beginning with the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma," because his activity— which is the cause for the arising of the path and its fruits in those to be trained— is, in the primary sense, the Buddha’s duty (*buddhakicca*), in accordance with his promise: "The Buddha shall awaken [others]."

In this context, the very phenomena such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and so forth are called the "Wheel" (*cakra*) in the sense of proceeding; thus it is the "Dhamma-Wheel" (*dhammacakka*).

Alternatively, *cakra* means "command. Because it does not depart from the Dhamma, it is both the Dhamma and the Wheel, hence the "Dhamma-Wheel"; it is also the "Dhamma-Wheel" in the sense that it is a wheel by way of the Dhamma, that is, by way of the proper method. As it has been said:

“*Dhammacakkaṃ* means that which sets in motion the Dhamma and the wheel; it is *dhammacakkaṃ* because it sets in motion both the wheel and the Dhamma; it is *dhammacakkaṃ* because it sets in motion by means of the Dhamma; it is *dhammacakkaṃ* because it sets in motion through the practice of the Dhamma,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase *katabuddhakicce*:
it refers to the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, in whom the duties of a Buddha (*buddhakicca*) have been performed—that is, brought to completion.
By this, [the author] indicates that there remains nothing whatsoever among the tasks to be performed by a Buddha.

...he shows. For it is precisely for that reason that the Blessed One is said to have attained final nibbāna. But is it not the case that even those to be trained by disciples were in fact trained by the Blessed One himself?
For indeed, a discourse spoken by a disciple is called "the word of the Buddha," and yet those to be trained by disciples have not [yet] been fully trained.
This is not a fault, because the means for their training was entrusted to the disciples. Therefore he said:
“Evil One, I shall not attain final Nibbāna until there are monks who are mature, disciplined, confident, learned, masters of the tradition,
who have mastered the Dhamma, mastered the Vinaya, and mastered the Matikas; who,
having thoroughly refuted with reasoned argument any opposing doctrines that arise, will teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles,” and so forth.

The passage beginning with “In Kusinārā” serves to show the specific place and time of the Blessed One’s final nibbāna, as well as to demonstrate that the notion “the Blessed One has not attained final nibbāna” is false, and to show that he was born and raised in the world.
For indeed, in order to make their human nature fully manifest, Great Bodhisattvas—even in their final existence—perform such acts as taking a wife and so forth. [Thus it says: “In Kusinārā.”

"In the city named thus. This locative case is used in the sense of proximity. "In the Mallas' Sāl Grove at Upavattana" indicates the Sāl grove park belonging to the Malla kings, which served as the outskirts of that city.
There, it is called "Upavattana" because those desiring to enter the city approach and proceed (vattanti) from the park; thus, the Sāl grove is so designated.
Just as the Thūpārāma of Anurādhapura lies in the south-western direction, so too does that park lie in the south-western direction of Kusinārā.
And just as the road from the Thūpārāma leading into the city by way of the southern gate goes eastward and then turns northward,
even so the row of sāla trees from the park goes eastward and then...
Because it turned back toward the north, it is called "Upavattana. "Between the twin sāla trees" means in the middle of the twin sāla trees.
It is said that there, near the couch prepared for the Blessed One’s final passing away, one row of sāla trees was at the head end and one at the foot end;
furthermore, one young sāla tree was close to the head end and one was close to the foot end.
Therefore, it is said, "between the twin sāla trees. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"The 'twin sāla trees' are those sāla trees standing with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves intertwined with one another.

Regarding the phrase "in the element of nibbāna without residue" (*anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā*): that which is grasped (*upādīyati*) by karma and defilements is "residue" (*upādi*); [it refers to] the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandhā*) and the [kamma-]formed [matter].
And there is form. However, that [nibbāna] with residue (sopādisesa) was not relinquished at the attainment of nibbāna through the crushing of the Māra of defilements and volitional formations;

here, it is relinquished and exhausted through the crushing of the Māras of the aggregates and death. This is called the nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), because there is no residue of clinging remaining in it.
And here, by "nibbāna-element," mere extinction (nibbuti-matta) is intended.
And this is an instrumental designation used in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). "In the parinibbāna" means in the place of parinibbāna;
or, the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*), meaning "assembled for the sake of parinibbāna. "The Elder of the Saṅgha" means the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
To the question, "What is the size of that Saṅgha? he says: "of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus. Because it has a constant requirement [for a complement],...
Indeed, in such cases, a compound is certainly formed, as in the expression “Devadatta’s family.
And the phrase “of the seven hundred thousand bhikkhus” refers specifically to the seven hundred thousand bhikkhus who were elders of the Saṅgha.
For at that time, it was impossible to measure the number of bhikkhus assembled, saying, “there are this many. Thus, from the moment the pains were suppressed in the village of Veḷuva, before long—
Having heard that “the Blessed One will attain final nibbāna,” not even a single bhikkhu among those who had come from here and there departed;
therefore, the Saṅgha became beyond counting. The connection is that the Venerable Mahākassapa inspired the bhikkhus for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya.
In this context, "Mahākassapa" means the Great Kassapa because he was endowed with the great aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth;
furthermore, this Great Elder is called "Mahākassapa" in relation to the Elder Kumārakassapa.
Now, for what purpose did the Venerable Mahākassapa exert himself for the sake of the communal recitation (*saṅgāyana*) of the Dhamma and Vinaya? To this, it is said:

“Seven days after his final passing,” and so forth. Seven days brought together constitute a week (*sattāha*). One for whom seven days have passed since his final passing (*parinibbūta*) is “one who has been finally passed away for seven days”;

this refers to the Blessed One. When it is said “seven days after the Blessed One had been finally passed away,” it means that seven days had elapsed starting from the day of the Blessed One’s final passing.
By Subhadda, the elder who had gone forth late in life...
The connection is: "recalling the words that were spoken. In this context, *Subhadda* is his name;

however, because he went forth at an advanced age, he is called *Vuddhapabbajita* (the one who went forth as an elder). By the words beginning with "Enough, friend," he indicates the speech uttered by him.
For when the Blessed One had been completely extinguished for seven days, he [was present] together with the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera.
While about five hundred monks, who were not yet free from passion, were traveling on the road from Pāvā to Kusinārā,
he saw them along the way— having heard of the Blessed One’s final passing away from a certain Ājīvaka, having cast aside their bowls and robes, and having raised their arms,
lamenting in various ways— and spoke thus to them.

But why did he speak thus? Out of resentment toward the Blessed One. It is said that this man, who had previously been a barber and had gone forth in old age, was mentioned in the *Khandhaka* in the context of the story of Ātumā.

When the Blessed One departed from Kusinārā with one hundred and fifty monks and was traveling toward Ātumā, he heard, "The Blessed One is coming. Upon his arrival, [the man] thought, "I shall offer a gift of rice gruel."
To his two sons who were standing on the stage of novices, he said this:
"Sons, it seems the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā together with a great Saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty.
Go, sons, taking razors and equipment, and wander from house to house using a nāḷi-measure; [bring back] salt, oil, and rice."
“Gather some solid food as well; when the Blessed One has arrived, we shall offer him a gift of rice gruel. They did accordingly.

Then, after the Blessed One had returned from his almsround and entered the straw hut, Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, addressed the people, and having requested their labor, saying, “Give me a little work to do,” he asked, “What?”
When they said, "Venerable sir, we shall do so," he had them take all the requisites, saying, "Take this and that. Having had hearths prepared in the monastery,
and having himself put on one black *kāṣāya* robe and draped another such as that over it,
he moved about throughout the entire night, directing them, "Do this, do that," while spending a hundred thousand [pieces of money] to provide rice-gruel for eating and honey-balls.
He had it prepared. What is called *bhojjayāgu* is a gruel to be drunk after eating;
therein everything that is called "hard food" (*khādanīya*)—such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, and the juices of flowers and fruits—is included.
It is fragrant and suitable for anointing the heads of those who wish to play.
Then the Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, set out toward Ātumā for alms, surrounded by the community of monks.
People informed him, "The Blessed One is entering the village for alms;
for whom was the rice-gruel prepared by you? He, wearing those very black robes as he had put them on, with one hand—
Taking up the spoon and ladle, and placing his right knee upon the ground like Brahmā,
he paid homage and said, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice-gruel. Then,

according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka— that “Tathāgatas, though they already know, ask”— the Blessed One questioned him, and having heard [his response], [he accepted] that elder who had gone forth late in life.

Having rebuked him regarding that matter, and having laid down two training rules—the rule concerning the taking of what is improper and the rule concerning the carrying of razor implements—he said: "Monks, for many millions of eons you have spent your time merely seeking food;
yet this which is improper for you—having consumed this food obtained through unrighteous means—"
"You will be reborn in the states of misery for many thousands of existences; go away, do not take anything!
Having said this, he set out toward his alms-round, and not even a single monk took anything.
Subhadda, becoming displeased, thought, "This man wanders about saying, 'I know everything'; if he does not wish to accept it, let him send [someone]..."
"He ought to have declared it; for even 'cooked food' (pakkāhāra), though it might last at most seven days, would have sufficed for me for as long as I lived.
But he has ruined everything with this; this man wishes me harm.
Having thus harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, he was unable to say anything while the One of Ten Powers was still living. For such was his thought: "This one..."
“A Great Man has gone forth from a high-born family; if I say anything at all, he will surely rebuke me.
Thus he spoke, for having come today with the Elder Mahākassapa and hearing that “the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna,” he felt as if he had found relief and said this, joyful and delighted.
But when the Elder heard this, it was like a blow to his heart, or like a thunderbolt falling upon his head.
He thought as if [the Buddha were still there], and a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him:
"The Blessed One has been parinibbāna-ed for only seven days, yet today his golden-hued body still remains intact. Alas!

While the Blessed One’s well-accomplished dispensation was still so fresh, such a great and wicked thorn has arisen. It would be enough if this evil one, growing in power, brought about others of a similar kind."
“Having found an assistant, let us cause the teaching to decline.

Then the Elder thought: “If I were to have this old man brought out right here, dressed in rags and covered with ashes, people would say, ‘While the body of the ascetic Gotama still exists, his disciples—’”
Thinking, "They will dispute [with us] and thus expose our fault," I shall endure it for now. For the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of flowers not yet gathered;
just as flowers struck by the wind go here and there, so too, as time passes under the influence of such people, one or two training rules (sikkhāpada) will be lost from the Vinaya.
They will perish: in the Suttas, one or two sections of questions will be lost; in the Abhidhamma, one or two sections of the *bhūmi* (stages) will be lost.
Thus, in due course, when the root is lost, we shall become like *pisāca* demons. Therefore, I shall compile the Dhamma and Vinaya.
When this is done, this Dhamma and Vinaya will be as immovable as flowers gathered by strong threads.
It will come to pass. For it was for this purpose that the Blessed One came out three gavutas to meet me;
he granted me full ordination through three exhortations; he exchanged robes with me from his own body;
and while waving his hand in the air, as he spoke the "Moon-like Practice," he did so making me alone his witness, and he caused me to receive the entire jewel of the Dispensation three times.
"While a bhikkhu such as I remains, may this evil one not find growth within the Teaching, so long as unrighteousness does not flourish, righteousness is not obstructed;
so long as non-discipline does not flourish, discipline is not obstructed;
so long as those who speak unrighteously are not powerful, those who speak according to the Dhamma are not weak; so long as those who speak contrary to the Vinaya are not powerful..."
Those who speak according to the Vinaya will not be weak; for now, I shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together.
Thereafter, the monks, each taking what they can handle, will discuss what is permissible and what is impermissible. Then this evil one will come to his own downfall by himself;
he will no longer be able to lift his head, and the Dispensation will become powerful and flourishing.
Thinking, "It will be so," and reflecting, "Such a thought has indeed arisen in me," he did not inform anyone;
instead, he reassured the Saṅgha of monks and subsequently, on the day of the enshrining of the relics, inspired the monks with zeal for the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Thus it is said: "The Venerable Mahākassapa, seven days after the Parinibbāna... [etc.]"
“He inspired the bhikkhus to make an effort for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya.
In this context, *alaṃ* is a word of refusal. He addresses the weeping bhikkhus as “Āvuso” (friends). “Do not grieve” means:
do not grieve with the powerful sorrow arisen in the mind. “Do not lament” means: do not lament with speech. [The word] “lamenting” (*paridevanaṃ*)...
This is because of the statement, "lamentation. Now, showing the reason for not grieving and so forth, he said, "We are well-liberated," and so on.
In the phrase "by that Great Ascetic" (*tena mahāsamaṇena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative;

thus, the meaning is "we are thoroughly liberated from that Great Ascetic," and the intention is "and we were afflicted by him then. Alternatively, *homā* is a present tense verb used in the sense of the past; it means "we were."
The meaning is: "by way of recollecting the spiritual urgency regarding phenomena (dhamma-saṃvega)"; this is the intended sense.
Spiritual urgency regarding phenomena is the knowledge of moral dread that occurs by way of reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena. For it has been said:
"In all conditioned phenomena, it is established in the mode of moral dread."
"For those whose burden is deluded by ignorance, it is known as the spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma.

Furthermore, "this is indeed a possible occasion" (*ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjatīti*): it is called a *ṭhāna* because the fruit stands there, existing in dependence upon it; thus, it is a cause (*hetu*).
The word "indeed" (*kho*) is for emphasis, meaning that this reason certainly exists, and not that it does not exist. What is that reason?
He said: "Those wicked monks," and so forth. Here, *yaṃ* is merely a particle, or it is an indication of a cause;
the meaning is that the reason by which they would cause [the Dhamma] to disappear—that reason indeed exists. "Wicked monks" (*pāpabhikkhū*) refers to monks who are possessed of wicked, base desires.
It is called "one whose Teacher has passed away" (*atītasatthukaṃ*) because the Teacher has transcended or passed away therein, or because he belongs to such a state.
*Pāvacanaṃ*: "Excellent speech" (*padhānaṃ vacanaṃ*) is *pāvacanaṃ*; it refers to the Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Having gained a faction" means having gained a faction of those who are shameless. "Before long" means not for long at all.
"As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure" means for as long a time as the Dhamma and Vinaya remain among persons who possess a sense of shame.
"Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā" means that this was spoken by the Blessed One while he was lying on his deathbed, exhorting the bhikkhus.
"Desito paññatto" means that the Dhamma is both taught (*desita*) and laid down (*paññatta*).

For the teaching (*desanā*) of the Dhamma comprised within the Suttas and the Abhidhamma is its proclamation and awakening; it is the making known of that very same Dhamma in its various aspects within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
"Establishing" (ṭhapana) means "making known" (paññāpana); therefore, the Dhamma is said to be both "taught" (desita) and "laid down" (paññatta).
"Laid down" (paññatta) has the meaning of "established" (ṭhapita). The Vinaya is also both taught and laid down.

For, regarding that matter comprised within the body of the Vinaya which receives the designation "Vinaya" because it disciplines the body and speech, the "teaching" (desanā) consists of its authorization (atisajjana) and its proclamation (pabodhana).

The making known of that very [Dhamma] by way of its specific characteristics is its "establishment" (*paññāpana*), which is its definition according to its non-confusion; therefore, the Vinaya is also said to be both "taught" (*desita*) and "laid down" (*paññatta*).
"That, after my passing, shall be your teacher"—that Dhamma-Vinaya, after my passing, shall be your teacher. This is what is meant:
—While standing, I have [instructed] you regarding the seven classes of offenses by way of their non-transgression: "This is light; this is heavy; this is curable; this is incurable;
this is an offense against the world; this is an offense against the rule. This offense is cleared in the presence of an individual;
this, in the presence of a group; this, in the presence of the Saṅgha."
In the matter of the descent [into the world], the Great Vinaya—consisting of the two Vibhaṅgas together with the Khandhaka and Parivāra—was taught;

this entire Vinaya Piṭaka, after I have attained final Nibbāna, will perform for you the function of a Teacher by instructing through the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done, saying:
"This is to be done by you; this is not to be done. And while I am still present...
“‘These are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path’”—
having thus analyzed these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment in various ways according to the inclinations of those to be trained, the Sutta Piṭaka was taught. This...

Even the entire Sutta Piṭaka, after I have attained final Nibbāna, will fulfill for you the function of a Teacher by instructing you in right practice according to various temperaments. Furthermore, while I was still present, I taught:
"The five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments, the seven..."

“Contact, seven types of feeling, seven types of perception, seven types of volition, and seven types of consciousness—therein, so many phenomena belong to the sense sphere, so many to the fine-material sphere, so many to the immaterial sphere; so many are included [within the mundane], so many are not included;
so many are mundane, and so many are supramundane. Having thus analyzed these phenomena, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka was taught.
Even this entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, after I have attained final Nibbāna, will perform the work of a Teacher for you;

for when understood through the analysis of the aggregates and so forth, it brings about the realization of the Four Noble Truths, and thus it will accomplish the task that must be performed by the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus, all of this [teaching] spans the forty-five years from the time of his full enlightenment until his final Nibbāna.
It is spoken and uttered; it consists of the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine divisions (navaaṅga), and eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma—thus it is of such great variety.
Thus these eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma remain, while I alone am now attaining final Nibbāna, and I alone am now advising and instructing; after I have attained final Nibbāna...
"These eighty-four thousand Buddhas will exhort and instruct you for the sake of accomplishing the task of exhortation and instruction.
"The Dispensation" (*sāsana*) is the threefold Dispensation consisting of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*paṭivedha*);

but in the ultimate sense, it is the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*). "Enduring" (*addhaniya*) means "going along the path of the journey," thus it is enduring; it is capable of withstanding the journey.

The meaning is as follows: "Long-enduring" (*ciraṭṭhitika*) means that which has a long duration; it refers to the *sāsana* (the Dispensation). The connection is: "May this [Dispensation] come to be long-enduring.

This is what is intended: "In whatever manner and by whatever means this *sāsana* is capable of persisting for a long period, by that very means and in that same manner, may they recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together so that it may become long-enduring."
Now, elucidating the specific favor shown to him by the Perfectly Enlightened One, he said, “And since I was favored by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Therein, the word “yaṃ” (which) is connected with the word “anuggahito” (favored). In that context, “yaṃ” means “because” or “for which reason”;
alternatively, it is a reference to the action, whereby the act of favoring is indicated in the phrase “anuggahito.”

He touches it. However, when the Blessed One was seated at the foot of a certain tree upon the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) prepared by the Elder Mahākassapa, he spoke those words beginning with "Will you wear it?
while touching that robe with his hand, which had the color of a blooming lotus flower.
For this is stated in the *Kassapasamyutta* by the Elder Mahākassapa himself to the Elder Ānanda:
Addressing him who was speaking, he said:
"Then, friend, the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, approached the foot of a certain tree;
then, friend, having spread out my outer robe made of patches of cloth folded fourfold, I [prepared it for the Blessed One]."
I said this: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit here; it will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time.
Then, friend, the Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, friend, the Blessed One said this to me:
“Kassapa, this outer robe of yours, made of patches of coarse cloth, is indeed soft. “Venerable sir, please accept it from me.”
“The Blessed One, out of compassion, [offered] a robe made of rags from a dust-heap.
“But will you, Kassapa, wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes? “I shall wear them, Bhante; I shall wear the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag-robes.
Thus, friend, I [gave] the robe made of rags from a dust-heap to the Blessed One.
“I gave [them] away; however, I received from the Blessed One the worn-out hempen rag-robes.
Regarding that, “They are indeed soft for you” means “This [robe] of yours is indeed soft. Why did the Blessed One speak thus? Out of a desire to exchange robes with the Elder.
Why did he become desirous of exchanging them? Out of a desire to establish the Elder in his own position.
“Is it that Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not exist? “They do exist. However, this thought occurred to him: “These two will not remain for long;

Kassapa, however, has a lifespan of two hundred years. After I have attained final Nibbāna, he will dwell in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, compile the Dhamma and Vinaya, and ensure that my teaching continues for a period of five thousand years. Thus [he reflected] regarding himself...
“I shall place him in that position so that the bhikkhus will think, ‘In this way, one should listen to Kassapa. It was for this reason that he spoke thus.

However, since it is the proper custom when the praise of a robe or a bowl is spoken to say, “Take this for yourselves,” the Elder said, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept mine. But will you wear it for me?
“Kassapa,” he said, “will you be able to wear these rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) worn out by use?
This was not said with reference to physical strength, but rather with reference to the fulfillment of the practice (*paṭipatti*).
This is the intended meaning here: “I [wore] this robe after having clothed myself in it while I was a slave-girl named Puṇṇā at the raw charnel ground.”
It was discarded and surrounded by tiny creatures the size of gourds; having shaken off those creatures and established myself in the Great Noble Lineage, I took it up.

On the day I took this robe, the great earth within the ten thousandfold world-system shook while emitting a great roar, the sky resounded with a crashing sound, and the deities of the world-system gave a cry of "Sādhu! (Excellent!).

“By a monk who accepts this robe, it is fitting that he be one who wears robes made of rags from a dust-heap by birth, one who dwells in the forest by birth, one who eats only from a single sitting by birth, and one who goes for alms only from house to house by birth; will you be able to act in a manner worthy of this robe?
The Elder also possessed the strength of five elephants. Without reflecting on that, [the donor said], “I shall follow this practice...”
Thinking, "I shall fill it," and desiring with great zeal to make [the robe] suitable for the Sugata’s outer robe, he said, "Venerable Sir, I shall wear it.
"I have so practiced" means: "I have already undertaken it.
Having thus exchanged their robes, the Blessed One put on the robe worn by the Elder, and the Elder put on the Teacher’s robe. At that moment, the great earth, bounded by the waters, [shook].
It cried out and trembled.
"Sāṇa rag-robes" refers to rags made of hemp-fiber discarded after wrapping a corpse, which were gathered by shaking off the thumb-sized maggots [from them].
They are rag-robes made of hemp or bark-fiber, found anywhere such as on carriage roads, in charnel grounds, or in heaps of refuse.
It is called *paṃsukūla* because, by virtue of being situated upon dust, it has risen above [the ground] like a rag (*kūla*) among those [dust particles].
Alternatively, the meaning of the word *paṃsukūla* should be understood as: that which goes to or attains a state of worthlessness (*kucchita-bhāva*) like dust (*paṃsu*).
"Worn-out garments" (*nivāsana*) means those whose function as clothing is finished; the meaning is that they are worn out through use. Here, although there is only one...
Regarding that robe, it is stated in the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada*: "The plural number is used because it consists of many parts.
In the phrase "by means of common use with the robe," since the meaning "by means of common use with oneself" is already understood, the word "oneself" (*attanā*) was not explicitly stated;
for when the particle *ca* (and) is used in a sense that is already implied, there is freedom in its application. [He said: "Will you wear it?"
However, because it was said, “But you, Kassapa, [should use] hempen rag-robes,” it is understood that the use [of these robes] is for one’s own common enjoyment and not for another.
For the determination of the meaning is not to be made everywhere by the word alone;
rather, the meaning must generally be determined by means of the context of the subject matter (*atthapakaraṇa*) and so forth. Thus says the Elder Master Dhammapāla.

In this context, the following is stated: regarding the phrase "by means of common use of robes," one should connect it by bringing forward the word *attanā* (by oneself), thus: "by means of common use of robes with oneself. For it is said:
"Whatever is connected to something, that belongs to it even if it stands far away."
"For that which is not identical in meaning, proximity is not the cause.

Alternatively, it should be construed as: "He was favored by the Blessed One through the common use of robes," since even a single expression in the instrumental case can indicate both the agent of an action and the accompaniment.
In all instances, [the authorship is attributed] to "the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla."
It should be understood that this was stated by the commentator on the Suttanta. "Sādhāraṇa" means that which is held in common; it refers to communal use (*paribhoga*).
The connection is: "He was assisted both by communal use and by establishing things on an equal footing. Now—
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent I desire, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,

I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Kassapa too, bhikkhus, to whatever extent he desires,
secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, [enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is] accompanied by applied and sustained thought...”
He enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion and possesses rapture and pleasure.
"Monks, to whatever extent I desire, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,

I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and is born of concentration, possessing rapture and pleasure."
"I dwell [thus]. And Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...
enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
"I, monks, as long as I wish, with the fading away of rapture, dwell equanimous and mindful..."
“Clearly comprehending, I experience pleasure with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous’—entering and abiding in the third jhāna.
“Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, through the fading away of rapture, dwells in equanimity… [as before] … entering and abiding in the third jhāna.”
“Bhikkhus, as far as I wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,

I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. Kassapa too, bhikkhus, as far as he wishes, with the abandoning of pleasure...”
With the abandoning of suffering, and previously... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

"Monks, to whatever extent I desire, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' I enter and dwell in the base of infinite space."
I dwell thus. And Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, by completely surmounting perceptions of form...
[as before] ...enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
"And I, monks, as long as I wish, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, [perceive] 'it is infinite'..."

‘Consciousness’: having fully attained and dwelt in the base of infinite consciousness. Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, having completely transcended the base of infinite space... [pe] ...fully attains and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
“I too, monks, as long as I wish, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, [entering the base of nothingness]: ‘There is nothing’...”
‘There is nothing,’ and having attained the base of nothingness, I dwell therein. Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes...
[as before] ...having attained the base of nothingness, dwells therein.
“Monks, as long as I wish, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, I enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
“...and I dwell having attained it. Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes... [as before] ...dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
‘Monks, as long as I wish, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling.’”
...and I dwell having attained it. Kassapa also... [and so on] ...dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
"Monks, to whatever extent I desire, I experience various kinds of psychic power: being one, I become many;
being many, I become one; I appear and disappear; I pass through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains."
I go unhindered through a mountain as if through space; I dive in and out of the earth as if in water;
I walk on water without breaking the surface as if on earth; I travel cross-legged through the air like a winged bird;
and I touch and stroke with my hand these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic.
"I touch and stroke with my hand, and I exercise mastery with my body as far as the Brahma-world.
"And Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, experiences various kinds of psychic power... [as before] ...and exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world."

“Bhikkhus, as far as I wish, with the purified divine ear-element, which surpasses the human, I hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near. Kassapa too, bhikkhus, as far as he wishes, with the purified divine ear-element...
[as above] ...hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near.”
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent I desire, I understand the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with my own mind.
A mind possessed by lust, I understand as ‘a mind possessed by lust’; a mind free from lust, I understand as ‘a mind free from lust.
A mind possessed by hatred… [as above] …a mind free from hatred… [as above] …a mind possessed by delusion… [as above] …”
Or a mind free from delusion... [and so on] ...or a contracted mind... [and so on] ...or a scattered mind... [and so on] ...or an exalted mind...
[and so on] ...or an unexalted mind... [and so on] ...or a surpassable mind... [and so on] ...or an unsurpassable mind... [and so on] ...or a concentrated mind...
[and so on] ...or an unconcentrated mind... [and so on] ...or a liberated mind... [and so on] ...or an unliberated mind.

or he understands an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind. Kassapa too, monks, as far as he wishes, understands the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed their minds with his own mind;
he understands a mind affected by lust as ‘a mind affected by lust’...
[and so on] ...or he understands an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.’
“Monks, as far as I desire, I recollect my manifold past lives,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, and even a hundred births.”

“Even for a thousand births, even for a hundred thousand births, even for many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion, [I remember:
‘There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere, and there too I was with such a name, such a clan, and such an appearance.’”
‘Such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was the limit of my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus, monks, I recollect my manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
And Kassapa too, monks, recollects his manifold past abodes as far as he wishes—namely, one birth... [and so on].
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details.
"Monks, to whatever extent I desire, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
I see beings passing away and being reborn— lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate."
I understand beings as they fare according to their karma: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have gone to a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm."

‘...have been reborn in hell. Or else: ‘These worthy beings, having been possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, possessed of good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, holding right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—these, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye...

"With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I recognize beings according to their kamma.
Kassapa too, monks, as far as he wishes, sees beings with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, passing away..."
He understands beings as they pass away and reappear—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—according to their kamma.

"Monks, through the destruction of the taints, I have realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon and dwelt therein. And Kassapa too, monks, through the destruction of the taints..."
“Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he dwells having attained it”—

thus was this passage, which appears in the *Kassapasamyutta*, spoken by the Blessed One by way of a formulaic summary and by mentioning the beginning, in order to establish himself as equal to those superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
Showing it in brief, he said, “I, monks,” and so forth.
Therein, “as far as I wish” (yāvade ākaṅkhāmi) means “just as much as I desire.
For this very reason, it is written in both the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷa-gaṇṭhipada*: “‘Yāvade’ means ‘yāvadeva’ [just as much as]. This is also stated in the *Saṃyutta-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.
The meaning of “as far as I desire” (*yāvade ākaṅkhāmi*) is stated as “just as much as I wish.
For thus it was said in the *Līnatthappakāsinī* by the teacher Thera Dhammapāla himself: “The word ‘yāvade’ has the same meaning as ‘yāvadeva.
However, in some manuscripts, this very reading “yāvadevā” is seen. As for those [passages] following this:
By the method beginning with “quite secluded from sensual desires,” there are the four form-sphere functional jhānas;

by the method beginning with “with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form,” there are the four formless attainments; by the method beginning with “by completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling,” there is the attainment of cessation; and [the knowledge of] the manifold [powers].
The higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) have been described by way of the method beginning with "the various kinds of psychic power" (*iddhividha*).
Whatever needs to be said regarding them has been explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*, both in the word-by-word commentary and in the section on the methods of development.

Furthermore, here too, in the *Verañjakaṇḍa*, the four fine-material-sphere jhānas and the three true insights (*vijjā*) will be made manifest; therefore, whatever needs to be said concerning them [will follow].
We shall explain that very point right here.

Regarding the phrase "divided into the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges": herein, the "nine successive dwellings" are so designated because they are to be entered in successive order;
they consist of the eight attainments together with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The "six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññā*)...

"By name" means: all super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) are thus divided into mundane and supramundane, consisting of the five mundane super-knowledges together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*).
"Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to the state (*dhamma*) of those superior to humans—namely, both the meditators and the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

Alternatively, it is called "superhuman states" because they are states that transcend the human condition; the so-called "human state" (*manussadhamma*) refers to the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

For this is called "human quality" (*manussadhamma*) because it is produced by humans by their very nature, or because it brings about human existence, even without the mental attention of meditative development (*bhāvanāmanasikāra*).
Beyond that, however, the jhānas and so forth are to be understood as "superhuman qualities" (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
By "placing oneself on an equal footing": for as long a time or in as many states of attainment (*samāpatti*) as I [remain].
"I employ the direct knowledges (abhiññā), and so did Kassapa"—thus, by establishing himself as equal to the aforementioned superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
This should be understood as a mere praise based on the commonality of possessing the nine successive dwellings (navānupubbavihāra) and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā);
for Venerable Mahākassapa was not like the Blessed One, who [attained] twenty-four hundred thousand times ten million [times] daily...
He enters the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or he exercises the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) by means of the Twin Miracle and so forth.
And here, it should be understood that the phrase "by establishing himself as equal to others in superhuman qualities" is merely an illustration.

For it is said: "Exhort the bhikkhus, Kassapa; deliver a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus, Kassapa. Either I, Kassapa, shall exhort the bhikkhus, or you; either I, Kassapa, shall deliver a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus, or you."
In this way, he indeed places himself on a level with [the others]; what other state of debtlessness could there be for him, except for the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya?
This is the intended meaning. Regarding that, it is stated in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*: “*Tassa* means ‘of that Anuruddha’.
Alternatively, the meaning should be taken as “*tassa me*” (for me). For in some manuscripts, the reading is indeed “*tassa me*.”
The meaning is: "Apart from the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya, what other debt-free state or freedom from obligation will there be for me that is visible?
With the words beginning "Did not the Blessed One," he clarifies the very same point by means of a simile.
Regarding the phrase "by the granting of his own armor and sovereignty," here the mention of "armor" is used as an illustration for the robe.
Thus it is said; sovereignty is taken here by way of illustration for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"One who establishes the lineage" means one who establishes the family lineage, that is, the family tradition.

The compound should be understood as a *nityasāpekṣa* (dependent) compound, as in "one who establishes my true Dharma lineage"; what is meant is: "one who establishes and causes the true Dharma lineage to proceed. Recalling the words thus spoken—
“Anuggahesi” (he encouraged) means that, reflecting thus, he generated enthusiasm among the bhikkhus for the purpose of compiling the Dhamma and Vinaya;
the sense is that on the day of the assembly of the relics, he inspired the bhikkhus who had gathered there.
Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned meaning by means of the Pāḷi, he said “Yathāha,” etc. Therein, “ekamidāhan” means:
Here, *idam* is a mere particle. *Ekaṃ samayaṃ* is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; thus, it means "at one time. *Pāvāya* means from the city of Pāvā;
having wandered for alms there, he had set out upon the highway with the intention, "I shall go to Kusinārā"—this is what is meant.
A "highway" (*addhānamagga*) refers to a long road. It is a synonym for "long."
Here, the word *addhāna* means "journey. "Together with a great community of monks" (*mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhim*) means "great" both in terms of greatness of qualities and greatness of number.
"Community of monks" (*bhikkhusaṅghena*) refers to a group of monks; the meaning is "together with that group of recluses as one.
By the phrase "about five hundred," etc., he clarifies the greatness of number. And here, the word *matta* signifies "measure" or "limit."

“As in the passages beginning with ‘moderation in eating’ (bhojane mattaññutā). The phrase “the entire Subhadda chapter should be understood in detail” means that the entire Subhadda chapter should be brought here and shown in detail; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the expression “after that,” the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated: “After that [means] after the generation of enthusiasm among the bhikkhus.”
In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated: “‘Beyond that’ means beyond the Subhadda chapter. This alone should be understood here as the essential point; it is not mere conjecture.

For this very thing is the manner of generating enthusiasm, namely: “Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya before un-Dhamma shines forth,” and so on. Therefore, because it generates enthusiasm...
It should not be said that [the Buddha] passed away, because the manner of generating enthusiasm prior [to his passing] was not mentioned in the Canon.
This is the sequence of the Canon here: “Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
‘Friends, on one occasion I was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred bhikkhus.’”
Then, friends, having stepped off the path, I sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Now at that time, a certain Ājīvika was traveling along the road from Kusinārā to Pāvā, carrying a mandārava flower.
I saw that Ājīvika coming from afar, friends.
Having seen that Ājīvaka, I said this to him: “Friend, do you know our Teacher? “Yes, friend, I know him.
The ascetic Gotama attained final Nibbāna seven days ago; it was from there that I took this mandārava flower.
“In that case, friend, those bhikkhus who have not yet overcome passion—some of them, having raised their arms, weep, falling prostrate...”
They fell down, rolled about, and writhed, crying out: "Too soon has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna!
Too soon has the Sugata attained final Nibbāna! Too soon has the Eye of the World vanished!
But those bhikkhus who were free from lust endured it mindfully and with clear comprehension, thinking: "Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; how could it be otherwise?"
“Then, friends, I said to those bhikkhus: ‘Enough, friends; do not grieve, do not lament.
Has it not already been declared by the Blessed One that there is separation, parting, and changeability from all that is dear and beloved?
For what could be obtained here, friends, from that which is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to disintegration?’”
"It is impossible that what is subject to dissolution should not dissolve.
"At that time, friends, an elder who had gone forth as a monk named Subhadda was sitting in that assembly.
Then, friends, the elder Subhadda said this to those monks: 'Enough, friends!'"
"Do not grieve, do not lament! We have been well liberated from that Great Ascetic who said, 'This is permissible for you;
this is not permissible for you. Now, however, we shall do whatever we wish and not do what we do not wish.
Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together."
"In the past, non-Dhamma shone forth and the Dhamma was suppressed; non-discipline shone forth and discipline was suppressed.
In the past, those who spoke according to non-Dhamma were powerful and those who spoke according to the Dhamma were weak;
those who spoke according to non-discipline were powerful and those who spoke according to discipline were weak."
“In that case, venerable sir, let the Elder select the monks. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine arahants.

The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: “Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a learner (sekha), he is incapable of going on a wrong path out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; moreover, much has been heard by him in the presence of the Blessed One.”
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been mastered. Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder also choose the Venerable Ānanda,” and so forth.
Thus, regarding the phrase “from that point onwards,” the meaning should be understood as “after the Subhadda chapter.
For by the statement, “The entire Subhadda chapter should be known in detail,” this sets the limit: “Whatever we do not wish for, that we shall not do.”

Having shown the commentary on the Subhadda chapter, he now spoke the words beginning with "Come, friends," showing the remaining portion of the text that proceeds by way of generating enthusiasm. In that context,
regarding the phrase "In the past, unrighteousness (adhamma) shone forth," here "unrighteousness" refers to that which is the opposite of the dhamma consisting of the ten courses of wholesome action.

"Adhamma. "It shines even before" (*pure dippati*) means that it indeed shines [first]. Alternatively, the meaning is: "even prior to the time when unrighteousness (*adhamma*) becomes capable of obstructing righteousness (*dhamma*).
For this word *pure* refers to what is near in the future. "Shines" (*dippati*) means it will shine (*dippissati*).
Indeed, due to its connection with the word *pure*, this present tense usage occurs in the sense of the future, just as in the expression "it will rain soon" (*purā vassati*).
"A god," [he said]. However, some here explain it thus: "Just as for one traveling along a road, the path yet to be traversed is called 'ahead' (pure), so too should it be understood here.
"Non-discipline" (avinaya) means that which is the opposite of the discipline of abandonment and the discipline of restraint.
The word "iti" should also be understood here in the sense of: "The proponents of discipline are weak."

The connection is with the words, “Then, after that, they said. However, while the word *iti* is not seen in some manuscripts, it does indeed exist in the Pāḷi text and in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.
The phrase *tena hi* is a particle used in the sense of exhortation; for, while exhorting him to gather [the relics], they spoke thus to the Elder Mahākassapa.
“Let him choose the bhikkhus” means: let him select and take those bhikkhus who are suitable for the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*).

By the phrase “He encompassed all nine branches...,” it is shown that although the aforementioned persons—ranging from dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*) to those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)—possessed both scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), they were distinguished by their attainment of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) along with the qualities of the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) and so forth.

By this, he demonstrates the great utility of the Saṅgīti (the Council) due to its having reached the highest excellence. In that context, "one who bears the entire ninefold teaching of the Teacher" means:
the Teacher’s dispensation (*satthusāsana*) is called "entirely ninefold" because it consists of the nine divisions beginning with the Sutta and Geyya, or because it possesses these nine divisions.
It is called "the teaching" (*pariyatti*) because it is to be mastered by one desiring welfare, and because it constitutes the mastery of human effort pertaining to the present life and so forth.

The three Piṭakas are so called; those who bear that entire scriptural collection (pariyatti) known as the Teacher’s dispensation consisting of the ninefold division (navanga) are "bearers of the scriptural collection of the Teacher’s entire ninefold dispensation"—this is the meaning.

Because they have not destroyed the various kinds of many defilements and the view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), they produce them, or they are produced by them; thus they are "worldlings" (puthujjana). There are two kinds of worldlings.

And there are blind worldlings and noble worldlings. In this context, those who lack study, inquiry, hearing, retention, and reflection regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, are blind worldlings.
Those who possess these are noble worldlings. It is these latter who are intended here by the term "worldlings" (*puthujjana*).

Because they lack the moisture of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*), their insight (*vipassanā*) is dry, coarse, and unsullied; thus, they are called "dry-insight practitioners" (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
"Those who bear all the divisions of the *pariyatti* of the *Tipiṭaka*": the collection of the three *piṭakas* is the *tipiṭaka*;

those who bear all the various divisions of the *pariyatti*—which is designated as the *tipiṭaka* and is divided in many ways by way of the ninefold canon (*navanga*) and so forth—are "those who bear all the divisions of the *pariyatti* of the *Tipiṭaka*";
such is the meaning. That which develops and increases for those possessing it, little by little, is *anubhāva*; *anubhāva* itself is *ānubhāva*.
*Pabhāva*: "Great power" (*mahānubhāva*) refers to those who possess great majesty (*mahanto ānubhāvo yesaṃ*). Regarding the phrase "those distinguished by the three knowledges and so forth":

the three knowledges themselves are called *tevijjā*; those for whom these are the beginning—namely the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and others—are the "three-knowledge-and-so-forth" ones (*tevijjādayo*).

Those for whom these various kinds of distinctions exist are "distinguished by the three knowledges and so forth" (*tevijjādibhedā*), meaning they are *khīṇāsavas* (those whose taints are destroyed). Alternatively, it means "one who possesses the three knowledges."
"Threefold-knowledge" (*tevijja*) refers to those beginning with the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*); thus, "those beginning with the threefold-knowledge" (*tevijjādayo*).

Those for whom these are the distinctions are "those distinguished by the threefold-knowledge and so forth" (*tevijjādibhedā*), meaning those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "Of such a kind" (*tādisa*) is the meaning. "With reference to whom this was said" means that this statement, beginning with "Then the Venerable One," was spoken in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka* with reference to those bhikkhus.
"Kissa pana" means "but why? One who trains is a *sekkha* (trainee); alternatively, training (*sikkhā*) is his virtue (*sīla*), and thus he is a *sekkha*.
For, because his training is not yet completed and because he is intent upon it, he is exclusively of a training-temperament;
unlike one beyond training (*asekkha*), whose training is finished and whose effort in that regard has been laid to rest, nor like one who has abandoned training.

He is like the common folk there, lacking resolute confidence (*anadhimutta*). Alternatively, he is one who has been "born" (*jāta*) into the three trainings (*sikkhā*) of noble birth, or he exists therein;

thus he is a "learner" (*sekkha*). Alternatively, "vision" (*ikkhā*) is that by which one sees; it is the right view of the path and its fruition. One who possesses such vision is a "learner" (*sekkha*).
Because the duties of the three higher paths are not yet completed, he is "one who still has work to do" (*sakaraṇīya*). Such is he.
By this [statement], it might be argued: "Is it not true that there is nothing received in the absence of the person [face-to-face]? For it was said:
"I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks, and eighty-four thousand are the teachings that have been transmitted to me."

If it has already been stated [that there were two thousand monks], how is this [subsequent statement] consistent? Even though it was said, "two thousand monks," it was stated with the understanding that they had indeed received [the precepts] in the presence of the Blessed One;
thus, there is no contradiction. "Because of being helpful" means because of being of great assistance. Here, the word *kāra* signifies "assistance. "Assa" means "it would be."
"Excessively confident" means one who is overly trusting. "Him" refers to the Elder Ānanda; this is connected with the word "admonishes.
Because the Elder Ānanda had for the most part caused the assembly of novices to fall away [from the training], the Elder Mahākassapa said:
"This young man does not know his measure. For it was thus that, after the Teacher had attained final nibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa...
Sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled for the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, he selected five hundred bhikkhus for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya, saying:
"Friends, while spending the rains retreat at Rājagaha, let us recite the Dhamma and Vinaya;
you should sever your respective impediments before the commencement of the rains and assemble at Rājagaha."
Having spoken thus, he himself went to Rājagaha. The Elder Ānanda also, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī while instructing the great multitude;
departing from there, he traveled toward Rājagaha and wandered on alms-round in Dakkhiṇagiri.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda had about thirty resident pupils, most of whom were still youths.
Bhikkhus of one year’s standing and two years’ standing, as well as those who were not yet fully ordained, went back to the lay life. But why did they go forth, and why did they return?
It is said that their parents thought: “The Elder Ānanda is trusted by the Teacher;
having requested eight boons, he attends upon him. He is able to take the Teacher wherever he wishes to go.”

"We shall have our children ordained in his presence; he will take the Teacher with him and return, and when he has arrived, we shall be able to perform a great ceremony of honor. For this reason, their relatives ordained them.
But when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, their aspiration was cut short, and then they were disrobed all on one day.

Then, seeing the Elder Ānanda returning to Rājagaha after wandering on alms-round in Dakkhiṇāgiri, the Elder Mahākassapa said: "This young man has surely not known moderation. For this was said in the Kassapa-saṃyutta:

"But why, friend Ānanda, do you wander on alms-round with these new bhikkhus who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness? It is as if you were destroying a crop of grain."
“You are acting, friend Ānanda, as one who destroys his own family; I think you are acting as one who destroys his family. Your assembly is falling apart, friend Ānanda;
your new disciples are falling away. This young man does not know his limits.
“Venerable Kassapa, gray hairs have grown upon my head, and yet even today we [still] follow the Venerable [Kassapa].”
"We are not released from Mahākassapa’s charge that we are like children.

"For you, friend Ānanda, are wandering on tour together with these new bhikkhus who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who lack moderation in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness;
it seems you are wandering about destroying crops, it seems you are wandering about destroying families, and [the community] is falling into ruin."
"Your assembly, friend Ānanda, is falling apart; your new recruits are dispersing, yet this young man does not know his own measure.
In this context, "you wander as if intending to destroy the crops" means you roam about as if destroying the harvest.
"You wander as if intending to ruin families" means you roam about ruining families, striking them as if killing them. "It falls away" means...

"It falls apart, it breaks down. 'Friends, these nine of yours are falling apart' means, friends, that for the most part these nine of yours—the novices who are mostly one-year-olds, two-year-olds, and young boys—are falling apart.
'This boy does not know his measure' means he does not know his own limit; [the elder] is thus reproaching the Thera."
He said: "We are not released from the charge of being like children; we are not released from the charge of being like children.
But as for 'for thus you [are],' this was stated for the purpose of showing the reason why he should be addressed in such a manner. This is the intended meaning here:
because you wander together with these young bhikkhus who are devoid of restraint over the sense faculties, therefore [you are like] those with children."
“While walking, you deserve to be called a ‘boy.

In the phrase “Or perhaps this boy did not know his measure,” the word *vā* is for the purpose of completing the meter. Indeed, the word *vā* is seen in many senses, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, relinquishment, metrical completion, alternative, and so forth.
For instance, it is seen in the sense of comparison in such passages as “He is indeed wise by that [comparison].”
The meaning is "in a state of similarity. In such passages as “The wise sages experience that too,” it signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).

In such passages as “Who are these, or to whom do they belong? it signifies doubt (*saṃsaya*). In such passages as “Of all these ascetics and brahmins, this one is the most foolish and the most deluded,” it signifies emphasis (*vavassagga*).
In such passages as “Whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be, monks,” it signifies option (*vikappa*). Here [it is used in the sense of]...
However, it should be understood as serving to complete the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*). For this very reason, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated:
"When providing an analysis of the meaning of the particle *vā*, [it is used] in the sense of completing the metrical line in such passages as: 'Or rather, this boy did not know his limit.
In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as well, only this much was said: "'Or rather, this boy did not know his limit'—this boy [did not know] his own measure..."
“‘He does not indeed know,’ he said, rebuking the elder. Here too, the word *vata* is used for the sake of the elegance of expression.
As for what has been stated by someone here—“*Na vāyanti ettha vā ti vibhāsā; aññāsipi na aññāsipīti attho*” (or it means ‘they do not blow here’ or ‘it is a case of doubt’;
the meaning is ‘he both knew and did not know’)”—that should be regarded as merely his own opinion. For this meaning is not possible here; therefore...
The meaning should be understood as "he did not know his own measure. In that context, *tatra* means "this being so.
Regarding the phrase *chandāgamanaṃ viya*, the word-division should be made as *chandā āgamanaṃ viya*;
the meaning is "like an arrival by way of desire," which is to say, like performing what ought not to be done through desire. Or, it means that desire arrives [in him] by way of association.
"Going by desire" (*chandāgamana*) refers to an unwholesome mental state that, when thus arisen, leads to rebirth in the woeful states. Alternatively, "going" (*agamana*) means improper conduct;
"going by desire" (*chandāgamana*) means proceeding or acting improperly out of desire—that is, out of affection—just like performing what ought not to be done.
"One who has attained the analytical knowledges of the Asekha" (*asekkhapaṭisambhidāppatta*) refers to one who has become an Asekha...

*Paṭisambhidā* refers to the analytical knowledges of one beyond training (*asekkha-paṭisambhidā*); the meaning is "one who has attained" or "one who has acquired" those analytical knowledges of one beyond training.
*Anumatiyā* means "by permission," which is to say "by request.
As for the phrase "even though he is one in training" (*sekkho*), this is not said because those in training are capable of going on wrong paths; rather, it refers only to those beyond training.
Rather, it should be understood as "because he has been selected. For indeed, the four wrong courses are abandoned by the first path alone;

therefore, although he is still a trainee (*sekkha*), the connection here should be understood thus: "Nevertheless, let the Elder select even the Venerable Ānanda. It should not, however, be construed as:
"Although he is a trainee, nevertheless he is incapable of going on a wrong course. This is shown by the phrase beginning with "incapable" (*abhabbo*).
However, in the Dhamma-saṅgīti, those demonstrating his state of arahantship speak of the qualities that actually exist in him.
Therein, "through desire" (*chandā*) means through longing; the meaning is through affection. "To go to a wrong course" (*agatiṃ gantuṃ*) means to go where one should not go;
what is meant is to do what should not be done. These four ways of going to a wrong course [are explained] in the section on the distribution of goods and in the section on legal decisions.

And they are obtained as follows: regarding the distribution of goods (*bhaṇḍabhājanīya*), first, when goods that are undesirable arrive for those monks who are his own burden, if he exchanges them and gives what is desirable, he is said to "fall into a wrong course through favoritism" (*chandāgati*).
But when goods that are desirable arrive for those who are not his own burden, if he exchanges them and gives what is undesirable, he falls into a wrong course through ill will (*dosāgati*).
One is said to "go astray. One who, regarding goods, does not know what is the value of the articles nor their proper standing, goes astray through delusion.

Or, one who—out of fear that "if these unpleasant goods are given to me, those who are talkative or dependent on kings and such might do me harm"—turns them over and gives what is pleasant, goes astray through fear. But he who does not go astray in this way...
Being like a scale for all, acting as a standard, and remaining impartial, one gives each person exactly what they deserve;

this is called not falling into any of the four kinds of partiality (*agati*). However, in a place of legal adjudication, if one treats a heavy offense belonging to oneself as a light offense when explaining it, one falls into partiality through favoritism (*chandāgati*). [Likewise,] regarding the other’s light offense...
When one speaks after having committed a grave offense, it is called "falling into error through hatred.
When one does not know the method for emerging from an offense or the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*, it is called "falling into error through delusion.
Or, when one who is talkative or honored by kings, thinking, "He might even bring me harm if I speak of a grave offense," speaks of a grave offense as a light one; [this is also falling into error].
One is said to go to a wrong course out of fear. But he who speaks of all things exactly as they are does not go to any of the four kinds of wrong courses.
The Elder was likewise such a person, because even by the first path alone he had abandoned all four wrong courses;
therefore, when the decision regarding the Dhamma and Vinaya arrived through the recitation, he did not [alter it] otherwise through favoritism or other such motives.
"It is said that 'he speaks exactly as it is, without speaking falsely,' meaning he is incapable... [of] going to a wrong course.
*Pariyatto* means studied; the sense is "mastered.
*Uccinitena* means by what has been selected and taken up. *Etadahosi* means this reflection occurred. *Rājagahaṃ*.
Regarding the phrase "it was a great resort" (*mahāgocaraṃ*): here, it is stated in both the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada* that "Rājagaha" refers to the vicinity of Rājagaha.
A "resort" (*gocara*) is so called because cattle graze there; like a pasture, it is a place for wandering for alms.

That [place] is a "great resort" (*mahāgocara*) because it is large, or because it is a great resort; thus it refers to Rājagaha. "Stable work" (*thāvarakamma*) means work that endures for a long time.

A person of a different kind is like Subhadda. "He would reopen" means he would obstruct; the meaning is that he would prevent [the council]. He announced it by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*):

"Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize these five hundred bhikkhus to dwell in Rājagaha for the rains retreat in order to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and not by others..."
“The monks should spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha. This is the motion.

“Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: the Saṅgha appoints these five hundred monks to spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and the Vinaya; no other monks [are to spend] the rains retreat at Rājagaha.”

"It is to be authorized": whichever venerable one approves of the authorization of these five hundred bhikkhus—"that they dwell for the rains at Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and that no other bhikkhus dwell for the rains at Rājagaha"—let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.

“The Saṅgha has authorized these five hundred bhikkhus: ‘Residing for the rains at Rājagaha, they shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya; no other bhikkhus should reside for the rains at Rājagaha. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha;
therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”

In this way, he announced it by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). It was with reference to this that it was said: “This should be understood according to the method stated in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*.
Furthermore, this formal act (*kammavācā*) was performed on the twenty-first day after the Tathāgata’s final passing away (*parinibbāna*).
For this is stated in the commentary to the *Dīghanikāya*: “This formal act, however, was performed on the twenty-first day after the Tathāgata’s final passing away...”
The days were spent thus. For the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna at dawn on the full moon day of Visākha;
thereafter, for seven days, they honored his gold-colored body with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. Thus, those seven days became known as the "Days of Joyous Celebration.
Then, for seven days, the body was cremated by fire upon the funeral pyre, while for seven days it remained in the Santhāgāra Hall enclosed within a cage of spears.
Twenty-one days passed while they were performing the worship of the relics. Then, on the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, they divided the relics.

On this day of the division of the relics, having reported the improper conduct committed by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled there, the bhikkhus selected [the members] in the manner already described.
This formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has been performed. Having made this formal proclamation, the Elder addressed the monks: "Friends, you now have forty days of opportunity;
beyond that, it will not be permitted to say, 'We have such-and-such an impediment.
Therefore, within this interval, for anyone who has an impediment of illness, or an impediment of teacher or preceptor, or an impediment of mother or father—"
