"Or perhaps there is a bowl that must be fired, or a robe that must be made; let him cut off that impediment and perform what is necessary.

Having spoken thus, the Elder departed for Rājagaha surrounded by his own assembly of five hundred, while other great elders also took their respective retinues and [departed], afflicted by the arrow of grief.
Desiring to comfort the great multitude of people, they departed for various directions.

But the Elder Puṇṇa, accompanied by a retinue of seven hundred bhikkhus, remained right there in Kusinārā, thinking, "I shall comfort the great multitude of people who have come from all directions to the place of the Tathāgata’s final Nibbāna.
Venerable Ānanda acted toward the Blessed One even after his final Nibbāna exactly as he had done previously while the Blessed One was still alive.
Taking his own bowl and robe, he set out on a walking tour toward Sāvatthī together with five hundred bhikkhus;

indeed, as he went, his retinue of bhikkhus exceeded all calculation. Therefore, when twenty-one days had passed since the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, having proclaimed this formal act (*kammavācā*), [he departed].
It should be understood that the Elder had departed for Rājagaha.

If this is so, why, however, is it stated here and in the *Maṅgalasutta-aṭṭhakathā* that "when seven days of celebratory festivities and seven days of relic-worship had passed"? [This is because] when the seven days of relic-worship were counted...
Because it is invariably concomitant with that [period], the seven days for cremation on the funeral pyre in the middle are also already included;
thus, it appears as if not stated separately. If this is so, then why is it said, "Half a month has passed, one and a half months remain"?
This is not a fault. For a small deficiency or excess does not count toward the total; therefore, it is the aggregate [that matters].
Considering that even when exceeded by a small amount, it is as if it were not exceeded, it is said, "half a month has passed," even when five days are added to half a month;

this is like the statement, "of the eighty-two khandhaka-vattas, in some places there are eighty khandhaka-vattas. Likewise, considering that even when a whole is deficient by a small amount, it is as if it were not deficient, [it is said] even when [the period] is less than one and a half months...
And it is said: "Five days remain, with one and a half months left.
For this is like the statement in the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* that even when less than six months remain, "recitation should be performed for six months.
In that context, regarding each of the four pentads such as the "fivefold skin" and the two hexads, there are five days in direct order and five days in reverse order.

It is as if it were said: "Having performed the recitation separately for three sets of five days—namely, five days in forward order, likewise five days in forward order together with each of the preceding sets of five, five days in reverse order, and five days in both forward and reverse order—and having performed the recitation together for another three sets of five days, the recitation should be carried out for six months. In that regard:

For, among the three pentads beginning with the *vakkapañcaka* and the two hexads, by reciting them individually and together with those preceding them according to five pentads each, a full five months can be obtained;
however, since for the *tacapañcaka* there is only a separate period of fifteen days, only half a month is obtained. Thus, five months and an additional half-month are obtained.
This being so, just as in that case— where even when the recitation is delimited by the period of a month despite it being less than half a month—
the mention of "six months" is made for the purpose of preventing the recitation being delimited by a seventh month (by counting it as a full month),
and not for the purpose of showing that the recitation actually occurs throughout all six months; so too here.
When time is delimited by way of months, even if five days are lacking, one and a half months (diyaḍḍhamāsa) still serves as the delimiting factor;

thus, the inclusion of the term "one and a half months" (diyaḍḍhamāsa) was made in order to prevent the time being delimited from passing into another month—such as the second month—rather than remaining within the first.
This is how the meaning should be understood here. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the words of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Otherwise, a mutual contradiction arises. It should be understood that the intention of the Khuddakabhāṇakas is that the Blessed One’s body was cremated on the funeral pyre after only one day.

For if this were the case, then after the seven days of festive celebrations following the Parinibbāna had passed, the Blessed One’s body would have been cremated on the pyre on the eighth day, and thereafter, for seven days, there would have been worship of the relics.
"Akaṃsu" means that half a month has passed, and one and a half months of the summer remain.
For even in the Pāḷi of the *Parinibbāna Sutta*, the seven days for cremation on the funeral pyre are not mentioned; only two weeks are mentioned.
However, having investigated this, whatever seems appropriate should be accepted. Or rather, it should be understood in another way so that there is no contradiction.
The reason must be sought. As for what has been stated by some here—"A half-month has passed; in this context, one day is lost.
That is the first day of the month (pāṭipada), known as the day of tumult;
therefore, it is not included here"—that is not correct, because in the Pāḷi of the *Parinibbāna Sutta*, the seven days are stated starting precisely from the first day of the month.
And because in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary) three weeks are taken together with the day of the Parinibbāna;
for, since three weeks are taken together with the day of the Parinibbāna, the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha-mūla is the twenty-first day.

Regarding the phrase "on the seven days of the *sādhukīḷana*": here, *sādhukīḷana* means that by repeatedly praising the objects of spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*) and singing songs connected with impermanence (*aniccatā*) as an act of worship, it is a beautiful performance; thus it is called *sādhukīḷana*.

Alternatively, it is "good" (*sādhu*) in the sense of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others; the performance [of these songs] after repeatedly praising those objects of spiritual urgency is the *kīḷana*.
“Sādhukīḷana” means a sporting and dwelling that is not inconsistent with the welfare of future lives, because it brings forth sublime merit.
And here, because a portion of the “sādhukīḷa” was performed during the first week, those days became known as the “Sādhukīḷana Days.
However, they specifically performed the sādhukīḷana on the days of the relic worship and other such occasions. For this very reason, in the Pāḷi of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta—
“Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, having constructed a lattice of spears in the assembly hall for the Blessed One’s remains and having surrounded them with a rampart of bows,
honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped them for seven days with dance, song, music, garlands, and perfumes.”
Regarding this, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

“But why did they act in this way? During the two preceding weeks, while they were preparing places for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to stand and sit, and providing hard and soft foods and other requisites, they found no opportunity for fine amusements. Thereupon—”
It occurred to them: "We shall play this game of 'Sādhukīḷita' for these seven days;
however, it is possible that someone might come and take the relics while we are inattentive. Therefore, let us play after having established a guard.
It was for this reason that they acted in such a manner.
Therefore, it should be understood that especially on the days of the relic worship (*dhātupūjā*) and so forth, there was a thorough performance of the festival.

However, because they were performed on the occasion of the relic worship, they became well-known as "the days of the relic worship," which is why he said, "on the seven days of the relic worship. "Upakaṭṭhā" means near.
"Vassūpanāyikā" refers to that [time] where they enter or approach the rains retreat (*vassa*). "Gone by one path" refers to the wandering (*cārikā*).
Having wandered about, he went by one path in order to comfort the great multitude.
In the same way, it should be understood that the Elder Anuruddha and others also went after wandering on tour through various districts, comforting the great multitude.
"He set out on tour for Sāvatthī" means he set out on tour to where Sāvatthī was, or toward whichever direction Sāvatthī lay.
"It was time to depart from Sāvatthī; the meaning is that he set out on his wandering toward that direction. "There" means in that Sāvatthī.

"Sudam" is merely a particle. "Connected with impermanence and so forth" means occurring in the manner of "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," etc. Because the underlying tendency of craving has not been severed, [he is affected] by that which is constructed by ignorance and craving.

One is called *jana* because, through karma, one generates (*janeti*) and brings forth (*abhinibbatteti*) a personal existence (*attabhāva*)—consisting of the five aggregates—within the realms of existence, wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes of beings;

or alternatively, one is called *jana* because one generates (*janeti*), has generated (*ajani*), or will generate (*janissati*) defilements. A "great person" (*mahājana*) is one who is a great *jana*; "that great *jana*" means "the many people" (*bahujana*).

"Having consoled" (*saññāpetvā*) means having comforted (*samassāsetvā*). "Having opened the door of the fragrant chamber" (*gandhakuṭiyā dvāraṃ vivaritvā*) is said because it is a shrine of use (*paribhogacetiya*).
It should be understood that after bowing to the Gandhakuṭī, he opened the door of the Gandhakuṭī;
for this very reason it is said in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "having bowed to the Gandhakuṭī. "Withered flower-garland debris" (*milātamālākacavara*) means withered remains of flower garlands.
"Having placed them in their original position" means having placed them exactly where they were originally situated, without overstepping the place where they first stood.
"It performed every duty that ought to be done while the Blessed One was staying" refers to the duties to be performed regarding the dwelling-place (*senāsana*).
While performing these, at times such as when sweeping the bathhouse or preparing water for washing, he would go to the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) and say:
"Is it not true, Blessed One, that this is your time for bathing; this is your time for teaching the Dhamma; this is your time for giving exhortation to the bhikkhus?"
He performed [the duties] while lamenting in this manner: "This is the time for the lion’s posture; this is the time for washing the face," and so forth.
Then a certain deity exhorted him, saying: "Venerable Ānanda, if you lament in this way, how will you console others?
At her words, his heart was moved with agitation; steadying himself, he [approached] the Tathāgata.
From the time of the Parinibbāna onwards, he drank a milk-purgative in order to soothe his body, whose elements had become aggravated due to his frequent standing and sitting.
Now, showing this, the author said, "Then the Elder," and so forth.
"Usannadhātukan" means a body whose elements, such as phlegm (semha), have accumulated. "Samassāsetun" means to refresh or satisfy it. "On the second day" refers to...
"From the day he was moved by the deity," they say; "or on the second day after the day he entered the Jetavana monastery.
It is called *virecana* because one is purged by it; milk that has been processed with medicinal herbs is itself a purgative, hence it is called "milk-purgative.
"With reference to which" means with reference to which drink of medicine. It is beautiful because of the beauty of its constituent parts; thus it has received this name.
By the young Brahmin Subha. Regarding the phrase "the young Brahmin sent": having heard that "The Teacher has attained final Nibbāna;
it is said that the Elder Ānanda has come taking his bowl and robe, and the great multitude is approaching to see him," [Subha thought]:
"But if I go to the monastery in the midst of the great multitude, it will not be possible to easily exchange greetings or listen to a discourse on the Dhamma."
Thinking, "Having seen him as soon as he has arrived at my home, I shall offer him a hospitable welcome;
furthermore, I have a certain doubt, and I shall ask him about that," [the Blessed One spoke] to the young man sent by the youth Subha.
"He said this" refers to what the Elder Ānanda said, beginning with "It is not the right time. "It is not the right time" means that today is not the appropriate time to go.
Why is this? He says: "There is for me today," and so forth. "A small amount of medicine" (*bhesajjamattā*) means a trifling amount of medicine;
for the word *matta* here has the sense of "small," as in such expressions as "a small sacrifice of happiness" (*mattā sukhapariccāgā*).
"On the second day" refers to the second day after the day the milk-purgative was drunk. "By the Elder Cetakatthera" [refers to one] in the kingdom of Ceti.
By one named Cetaka because he was born thus. Questioned by the young man Subha:
having thought, "Those phenomena upon which the venerable Gotama established this world—have they perished after his passing, or do they still endure?
If they endure, Ānanda will know; come, let me ask him," [he asked] regarding those phenomena of which the venerable Gotama...

When asked by the young brahmin Subha, "In what things, Master Ānanda, did that Blessed One Gotama speak in praise? and so forth— beginning with where he exhorted, settled, and established this generation— the Elder, for him,
demonstrated the three Piṭakas by grouping them under the three aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
“Monk, that Blessed One speaks in praise of three aggregates,” with these words he spoke the Subha Sutta.
Referring to this, it was said: “In the Dīgha Nikāya, he spoke the tenth sutta, named the Subha Sutta.
Regarding the phrase “the repairing of what is broken and cracked”: here, *khaṇḍa* means what is cut; *phulla* means what is split. The repairing of these two [is meant].
"Restoring properly" means making it new again; that is what is meant. "Rājagaha" is a city of that name.
For it is called "Rājagaha" because it was presided over by Mandhātā, Mahāgovinda, and others.
"Thrown away, fallen, and filthy" means they had become thrown away, fallen, and filthy. This is what is meant: [this was] the place of the Blessed One’s final nibbāna.
Left behind by monks who were departing, they were abandoned; and because they were eaten by ants and other creatures, they fell here and there.
Due to the lack of sweeping, they became filthy, being covered with refuse.
To demonstrate this very point, he said, "Of the Blessed One," and so forth. It is called a *pariveṇa* because it is seen as being enclosed or surrounded.
"In those" means in those monasteries (*vihāra*). This is connected with the phrase "the repairing of what is broken and dilapidated.
"The first month" refers to the first month of the rainy season; this is the accusative case used to express continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

It is stated that "it was praised by the Blessed One... because the rules for lodgings (*senāsanavatta*) were laid down in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, and because many matters related to lodgings are mentioned therein.
"On the second day" means on the day following the one they had intended for "repairing what was broken and dilapidated.

This should be understood as the second day from the day of entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*). For those elders, having performed the Uposatha on the full moon of Āsāḷhī, assembled on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*), entered the rains residence, and then thought thus. [Ajātasattu...]
The king, having been born as one who was not born [as a human], became an enemy to his father; thus he received the designation “Ajātasattu.
It is said that while he was in her womb, such a craving arose in the queen: “O, would that I might drink blood from the right arm of the king!
Then, seeing her emaciated state and her pallid appearance, and because she was unable to speak of it, the king—

Having questioned him himself and understood the situation, he summoned physicians, had his arm incised with a golden blade, took the blood in a golden vessel, mixed it with water, and made him drink it.
When the fortune-tellers heard of this, they prophesied: "This fetus will become the king's enemy;
by him the king will be slain. Therefore, [he was known as] "the enemy of the king even before birth."
Because it was pointed out by the soothsayers, saying, “He will become [a king] named Ajātasattu,” he was born with that name.

*Kiṃ* is a particle used in the sense of asking for a reason; its meaning is “why. *Paṭivedesuṃ* means they informed or made known; the meaning is “they caused to be known. *Vissatthā* means those whose minds were free from apprehension. *Āṇācakkam*:

the very command itself is called a “wheel” (*cakkam*) in the sense of proceeding with unimpeded function; thus it is the “wheel of command” (*āṇācakkam*). *Sannisajjaṭṭhānam* means a place for sitting together.
Having assembled, [they went] to the place for sitting.
"The splendor of the royal palace" means the excellence of the royal residence. "As if mocking" means as if performing a derisive laugh.
"As if the abode of glory" means as if the dwelling place of majesty. And "as if a bathing-place for the birds that are the eyes of gods and humans."
Like birds gathering at a single watering place, the eyes of all people fell upon the pavilion alone;
thus, it was like a single bathing-place where the "birds" known as the eyes of gods and humans converge.
It was like the world's beauty gathered together—like the quality of loveliness found throughout the world concentrated in one spot and heaped up. If [this] exists in the world...
It is said that "it would be like all beauty brought together and condensed into one"; that is, it is like the essence stripped of its sapwood, or like something pure and free from dregs.
Regarding the phrase "the essence and purity among things to be seen," the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries on the three [texts] state:
"It is the essence and the pure state among those forms worthy of being seen—that is, those things which ought to be seen. *Daṭṭhabba* means "to be seen" (*dassanīya*).
"Daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍo" should be understood as "that which has the essence, the most excellent, the cream (maṇḍa), the adornment, the ornament (maṇḍana) as its substance";
thus, "maṇḍapa" is the meaning to be grasped here—this is our own preference, though one should accept what is more appropriate after careful investigation.
It is called "maṇḍapa" because it wards off the rays of the sun (maṇḍa). Regarding the phrase "various... beautiful canopy," the flower-garlands [are to be understood here].
"And those hanging [garlands]" means flower-garland hangings. Here, the inversion of the qualifier should be understood;

the meaning is "flower-garland hangings. That canopy (*vitāna*) is beautiful (*cāru*) and lovely (*sobhana*), as it emits, vomits, or brings forth (*viniggalanta*) various (*vividha*) and manifold kinds (*anekappakāra*) of these;
thus, it is "one where there is a beautiful canopy emitting various flower-garland hangings" (*vividhakusumadāmaolambakaviniggalantacāruvitāno*).

"One should connect [the phrase] 'having adorned that pavilion. 'Like a floor of a jeweled terrace variegated with gems' means: because the ground-work was so well-finished and made variegated with various flower offerings, it was like a floor of a jeweled terrace made variegated by various gems.

And here, the mention of 'variegated with gems' is an illustration of its being variegated by various flower offerings, while the mention of 'floor of a jeweled terrace' illustrates the excellence of the ground-preparation."
It should be understood as follows: *maṇikoṭṭimatalaṃ* means a floor produced by the polishing of gems, having been made smooth by the grinding of jewels;

*taṃ* refers to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); *pupphūpahāro* is an offering of flowers, that is, flower-worship; *uttarābhimukhaṃ* means facing the northern direction; *āsana-ārahaṃ* means worthy of a seat, fit for sitting upon;
*dantakhacitaṃ* means inlaid with ivory, which is to say, fashioned or constructed from ivory. *Ettha* (here) refers to...
"On the seat. "Venerable sir, my task is finished" means that what was to be done by me has been completed.
On that day, however, some monks said this concerning the Venerable Ānanda:
"In this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, there is one bhikkhu who wanders about emitting a foul odor. When the Elder heard this, [he thought]: "In this..."
"There is no other monk in the Saṅgha who wanders about emitting such a foul odor;
surely they are speaking of me," he thought, and he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Some said to him, "Friend, there is a gathering tomorrow," and so forth.
Now, showing that, he said: "The monks said to the Venerable Ānanda," and so on. *Tenā* means "therefore. *Āvajjesī* means...
He offered it. "Without clinging" (*anupādāya*) means: without grasping at any phenomenon by way of craving or views;
or, the meaning is, without grasping even a mere trace of those defilements from which one is liberated. "From the taints" (*āsavehi*) means:

from the defilements known as taints (*āsava*), which flow forth from existence up to the peak of existence, or from phenomena up to the stage of lineage (*gotrabhū*). And this is a term for their characteristic.
"From the taints" means that, because they are associated with them, the mind is indeed liberated from all defilements (kilesa) and all evil states (pāpadhamma).
"The mind was liberated" means that having been in the process of being liberated from the taints at the moment of the path of Arahantship, it was liberated at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship.
"By means of walking" refers to the act of walking back and forth (caṅkamana). That which serves as the necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya)...

"One who has performed merit" (*katapuñño*) means one by whom merit has been performed and accumulated; the meaning is that he has undertaken the necessary application for the attainment of *arahantship*.
"Devote yourself to exertion" (*padhānam anuyuñja*) means devote yourself to energy; the meaning is: "Apply yourself to the attainment of *arahantship*.

"There is no fault in the talk" means there is no offense against the discourse. "Over-exerted energy" (*accāraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ*) means energy that is excessively aroused. "For the sake of agitation" (*uddhaccāya*).

"For the sake of the state of agitation": "I shall apply equanimity of energy"—this means that because the energy of walking meditation was excessive, by means of abandoning that [excess] and bringing about a state of equal flavor through concentration, I apply equanimity of energy.
"On the second day" means on the day following the day the Elder attained Arahatship. "Assembled in the Dhamma Hall."

On the fifth day of the fortnight, they assembled. Desiring to make known his own attainment of *arahantship*, [the Elder] thought, "Although it is improper for one still in training (*sekha*) to participate in the Dhamma-recitation (*dhammasaṅgīti*), because of my great learning I shall take part.
To the Elders who were seated there, thinking, "Now he has attained *arahantship*," he gave the exhortation, "Be diligent! in order to arouse joy in them.

It should be understood that the Elder desired to make known his own attainment of Arahatship because the Blessed One had praised the "Exposition by Another" (*aññabyākaraṇa*) rather than the "Personal Application" (*attupanāyika*) for the purpose of illuminating its fruitfulness. "According to seniority" (*yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*) means without overstepping the order of age.
"Some" (*eke*) refers specifically to some among the Majjhima reciters (*majjhimabhāṇaka*); for indeed, everything previously mentioned belongs to the Majjhima reciters.
"It should be understood that they indeed say this. However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say here as follows:
'Then the Venerable Ānanda, though already an arahant, went to the assembly. How did he go?
Thinking, "Now I am worthy to enter the midst of the assembly," with a heart joyful and elated, he adjusted his robe over one shoulder and [released himself] from his bonds.'"

He proceeded as if announcing his own attainment of Arahatship with a face that was pure, radiant, luminous, and beautiful— like a ripe palm fruit fallen upon a white cloth, like a natural gem set upon a pale blanket, like the full moon risen in a cloudless sky,
and like a lotus whose interior is golden-hued from pollen opened by the touch of the morning sun.
Then, seeing him, it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: "How truly radiant is Ānanda, having attained arahantship!
If the Teacher were still living, he would surely grant his approval to Ānanda today.
Come now, I shall give this very approval that the Teacher ought to have given. And so, he gave his approval three times.

Regarding the statement, "Some say he came through the air and sat down," they say that apart from the fact that he arrived having been taken there in such and such a manner, there is no other specific reason for each of these separate accounts. However, the Elder Upatissa said:
"Because at times, after the Dhamma Council had been concluded seven months later, he arrived by sinking into the earth..."
"Having taken it up," some say; "because it sometimes comes through the air, having taken it up, some say so"—this is what they mean.
"Addressed the bhikkhus" means he spoke to the bhikkhus, he talked to them, he awakened them; this is the meaning here.
But elsewhere it also occurs in the sense of making known, as it is said: "I address you, bhikkhus; I make it known to you, bhikkhus."
It is also seen in the case of summoning (*pakkosanepi*). As it is said: "Come, bhikkhu, address Sāriputta in my name. "Āvuso" is an indication of the manner of addressing.
"Making whom the leader? means making whom the senior (*jeṭṭhaka*). "Is Ānanda not capable?"—this is a question posed by the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).
"Not capable" means he is not able. "This is the foremost" (*etadaggaṃ*) means this one is the best; [the word *agga*] is used with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
For this is the explanation. *Yadidaṃ* means "that which is this," or it should be construed as "that which is this: the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).
*Samanne* means he made it agreed upon. Regarding the phrase "he should question Upāli on the Vinaya," this is stated because the verbal root *pucch* (to ask) takes two objects.
Regarding "having taken a fan," it should be understood that taking up a fan here is the custom (*dhammatā*) of those who preach the Dhamma.
For even the Blessed One takes up a variegated fan solely for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of things to those who discourse on the Dhamma.
Otherwise, the orb of the moon-like face of the Buddhas—which is the ornament of the entire world and possesses the most excellent training and self-restraint—would not need to be concealed.
"Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense committed?"
Why was it said, “it was laid down”? Is it not the case that its status as the first [recitation] at the time of the previous council is not appropriate?
It is not inappropriate, because its status as the first is established by the sequence in which the Blessed One laid them down and the sequence in which the Pātimokkha is recited.
For, with the exception of a few cases, the three Piṭakas were recited in the very order they existed during the lifetime of the Blessed One.

In particular, it should be understood as referring to the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas. In the phrase "in what matter" (*kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ*) and "in sexual intercourse" (*methunadhamme*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause or occasion (*nimitta*).
The statement "he asked about the matter" (*vatthumpi pucchi*) and so forth includes both what has been shown by the phrase "where was it laid down" (*kattha paññattaṃ*) and what remains after that.
This was stated by way of inclusion for the purpose of showing [the offense]. But in this regard, was there anything in the Pāḷi of the first Pārājika that needed to be removed or added?
There is nothing whatsoever to be removed from what was spoken by the Blessed Buddha;
for the Tathāgatas do not utter even a single syllable in vain. However, regarding what was spoken by disciples or deities...
There were certain passages that ought to be removed, which the Elders who compiled the Dhamma removed;
however, there were also passages that ought to be inserted, and these exist throughout the entire work. Therefore, wherever it was appropriate to insert something, they inserted it right there.
But what is that? It is such expressions as “At that time,” or “Now at that time,” or “Then,” or “Thus.”
The mere introductory words such as "when it was said" or "he spoke this" were thus inserted where appropriate.
Having inserted what was suitable to be included, they established this as the first *pārājika*.

Once the first *pārājika* had been compiled into the collection, five hundred Arahants performed a communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*) according to the very method by which it had been brought into the collection. At that time...
And as soon as they began their recitation, saying, "The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā," the great earth, as far as the ocean's edge, shook as if giving its approval.
In this same manner, they compiled the remaining *pārājika* rules and established them as the "Pārājika Section.
Likewise, the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules [were established] as the "Thirteenfold" section, and so forth.
Having spoken thus, they proclaimed the two hundred and thirty training rules as the "Mahāvibhaṅga" and established them.
At the conclusion of the Mahāvibhaṅga, the great earth shook once more in the same manner as before.
Then, having stated the eight training rules in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga as the "Pārājika-khaṇḍa," and so forth, [they established] three hundred and four training rules.
Having recited the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*, they established it, saying: "This is called the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*, consisting of sixty-four *bhāṇavāras*.
At the conclusion of the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*, the earth shook again in the same manner described previously.
By this very method, having compiled the *Khandhaka* measuring eighty *bhāṇavāras* and the *Parivāra* measuring twenty-five *bhāṇavāras*, [they declared]: "This is the Vinaya Piṭaka."
They established [the title] as "Nāma. At the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka, an earthquake occurred in the same manner as previously described.
They entrusted that Venerable Elder Upāli with it, saying, "Friend, teach this to your pupils. In this way, even though not explicitly stated here, the specific detail should be understood.
Having thus compiled the Vinaya Piṭaka, they recited the Sutta Piṭaka. Now, showing that:
He said, "Having recited the Vinaya," and so forth. Regarding the statement that the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Ānanda about the Dhamma, this sequence should be understood:
when the Elder Ānanda had taken up a fan inlaid with ivory and was seated on the Dhamma-seat, the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa asked the bhikkhus, "Friends, which Piṭaka should we recite first?"
“The Sutta Piṭaka, venerable sir. “In the Sutta Piṭaka there are four collections; which of those is the first collection? “The Dīgha Saṅgīti, venerable sir.
“In the Dīgha Saṅgīti there are thirty-four suttas and three sections;
which of those is the first section? “The Sīlakkhandha Vagga, venerable sir. “In the Sīlakkhandha Vagga...”
“There are thirteen Suttantas. Among them, which Suttanta should be recited first? “Venerable sir, it is the one called the *Brahmajāla-sutta*.

It is adorned with the threefold morality, it destroys various kinds of wrong livelihood, hypocrisy, and flattery, it unravels the net of the sixty-two views, and it causes the ten-thousandfold world system to tremble.
Let us recite that first. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda.
“Friend Ānanda, where was the *Brahmajāla* spoken?
“Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, venerable sir. Here, the word *antara* is seen in the senses of cause, time, the middle of the mind, an opening, and so forth. For instance, as in:
“Who could know that interval (*tadantaraṃ*) other than the Tathāgata? and: “People, having gathered... [etc.]
In such passages as “What is the difference between ‘I’ and ‘that’? the word *antara* is used in the sense of a cause.
In such passages as “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me through a crack in the wall while she was washing a vessel,” it is used in the sense of a moment.

In such passages as “In whom there are no anger-spirits within,” it is used in the sense of the mind. In such passages as “He fell into despondency midway,” it is used in the sense of the middle. [And] “Moreover, this Tapodā...”
In such passages as, "He comes from the interval between two great hells," it refers to an opening or gap (*vivara*).
Here, however, it functions in the sense of an opening; therefore, the meaning should be understood as "in the opening between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā.
Because it is joined with the word *antara*, the accusative case is employed. And in such instances, grammarians [say]: "Between the village... [etc.]
And [the phrase] “he goes to the river”—thus they employ the single word *antarā* alone; it must also be construed with the second word (*nadi*).

If it were not so construed, the accusative case would not be reached, because when there is the possibility of a genitive case, the accusative is desired due to its connection with the word *antarā*.
But here it is stated having been so construed. Regarding the term *rājāgāre*: therein, of the king...
For the purpose of recreation, they built a residence variegated with beautiful paintings; that is called the Royal Residence (*rājāgāraka*), and it was in that [place].
"Ambalaṭṭhikā" is the king’s pleasure garden. It is said that near its gate there was a young mango tree (*amba-rukkha*), which they call "Ambalaṭṭhikā.
Because it was situated not far from that [tree], the garden itself is designated as "Ambalaṭṭhikā."
"Has gone," as in "to Varuṇanagara" and so forth.
Regarding "Suppiya the wanderer": here *Suppiya* is his name; *paribbājaka* refers to Channa the wanderer, a pupil of Sañjaya.
Regarding "Brahmadatta the young man": here *Brahmadatta* is his name; *māṇava* means...
One who is old is called "corrupt," and one who is young is also called "corrupt.
For it is said: "Those youths who, when exhorted by the messengers of the gods, remain heedless—those men, having entered a base body, grieve for a long time."
In such contexts as these, "māṇava" refers to a being. In passages such as, "They encounter māṇavas who have performed their duties and those who have not," it refers to a thief.
In passages such as, "The young man Ambaṭṭha, the young man Aṅgaka," it refers to a youth.
Here too, this very meaning is intended. What is meant is: "With reference to a young man named Brahmadatta. [The phrase] "in Jīvaka’s mango grove" [is used].
In Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove. Now, why was it said “with whom? instead of saying “concerning whom”?

It should be understood that this discourse was not spoken by the Blessed One alone; there is also something spoken by the King himself, beginning with the words, “How now are these various fields of craft...”;
therefore, it should be seen as having been spoken in this manner. “By the son of Vedehī” refers to the King of Kosala.
"Vedehiputta" does not mean "the son of the King of Videha"; rather, this is a designation for a wise person (*paṇḍita*).

"Veda" means that by which one knows; it is a designation for knowledge. One who strives, exerts effort, and endeavors by means of that knowledge is a "Vedehi. The son of a Vedehi is a "Vedehiputta"—by him [it was asked].
By this same method, the five Nikāyas were questioned; herein, this sequence should be understood. According to the stated method, [this applies] to the *Brahmajāla*.
At the conclusion of the answering of the questions, five hundred Arahants performed the recitation (*sañjhāya*). And in the same manner as previously described, there was a shaking of the earth.

Having thus chanted the *Brahmajāla*, they thereafter chanted thirteen discourses together with the *Brahmajāla* in the sequence of questions and answers, beginning with: "But, friend Ānanda, where was the *Sāmaññaphala* spoken? and so forth.
Having recited it, they established it, saying, “This is the section named the Sīlakkhandha-vagga. Immediately after that, the Mahāvagga, and after that, the Pāṭhika-vagga—
thus having chanted this textual tradition (tanti), which comprises three sections, is adorned with thirty-four discourses (suttantas),
and measures sixty-four recitation units (bhāṇavāras)— they declared, “This is the Dīgha-nikāya,” and entrusted it to the Venerable Elder Ānanda.

“Friend, teach this to your own pupils. Immediately thereafter, having recited the Majjhima Nikāya, which consists of eighty *bhāṇavāra*s, they entrusted it to the pupils of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, saying, “You must preserve this.
Following that, having recited the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which consists of one hundred *bhāṇavāra*s, [they entrusted it] to the Elder Mahākassapa...
They entrusted it [to him], saying, "Venerable sir, please teach this to those who rely on you.

Immediately thereafter, having recited the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which measures two hundred thousand recitation units (bhāṇavāra), they entrusted it to the Elder Anuruddha, saying, "Please teach this to those who rely on you.
Immediately thereafter—
“The *Dhammasaṅgaṇi*, the *Vibhaṅga*, the *Kathāvatthu*, the *Puggalapaññatti*, the *Dhātukathā*, the *Yamaka*, and the *Paṭṭhāna*—this is called the Abhidhamma.
Having thus chanted this textual tradition, which is the domain of subtle knowledge as described, [they declared]: “This is named the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.”
Having spoken thus, the five hundred arahants performed their recitation. Just as previously described, there was a trembling of the earth.

Thereafter, having chanted this body of scripture—consisting of the Jātaka, the Mahāniddesa, the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Apadāna, the Suttanipāta, the Khuddakapāṭha, the Dhammapada, the Udāna, the Itivuttaka, the Vimānavatthu, the Petavatthu, the Theragāthā, and the Therīgāthā—[they concluded].
The Dīgha-bhāṇakas say that after stating, “This is called the Khuddaka-gantha,” they included it within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself.
The Majjhima-bhāṇakas, however, say that all of that Khuddaka-gantha, together with the Cariyāpiṭaka and the Buddhavaṃsa, is contained within the Sutta Piṭaka. This is the intended meaning here:

It is appropriate to include the *Jātaka* and other works contained within the *Khuddakanikāya*—which for the most part consist of systematic expositions of the Dhamma—in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, but not in the Sutta Piṭaka such as the *Dīghanikāya* and others, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which consists of the exposition of formal rules (*paññatti*).

The Dīgha reciters (*Dīghabhāṇakā*) maintain that the *Jātaka* and other such works are included in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Furthermore, the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and the *Buddhavaṃsa* are also included here.

It is not included because it belongs to the *Jātaka* genre. However, the Majjhima reciters (Majjhimabhāṇakas) maintain that since the *Jātaka*s and other such texts were taught by way of specific occasions (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and lack the systematic, sequential teaching (*yathānuloma-desanā*) found in the Sutta Piṭaka, their inclusion in the Sutta Piṭaka is appropriate;

whereas their inclusion in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—which is a teaching according to the nature of phenomena (*yathādhamma-sāsana*) intended to describe the intrinsic characteristics of things—is not. Thus, they state that the *Jātaka*s and so forth are contained within the Sutta Piṭaka. In this regard:
One should accept [the teaching] after investigating whether it is appropriate.

Because the Khuddaka Nikāya is not as well-known as the other Nikāyas, he sets them aside and, demonstrating that the Khuddaka Nikāya is well-known, says: "In that regard, what is called the Khuddaka Nikāya," and so forth.
*Tattha* means among those Nikāyas; *tattha* means in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Having thus shown the First Great Council by way of its cause, purpose, time, place, agent, instrument, and manner, he now says, "All this," and so forth,
in order to show the various classifications— such as the singlefold and others— for the sake of proficiency in the Dhamma and Vinaya as they were established therein. In that context,
regarding the phrase "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ*), it has unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
The knowledge of the path and the knowledge of the path as its proximate cause—this unobstructed knowledge is called "perfect self-enlightenment" (sammāsambodhi).
The phrase "by one who reviews" refers to the states occurring by way of exultation (udāna) and so forth.

"The flavor of liberation" (vimuttirasa) means either the relish of the fruit of arahantship, or the attainment of liberation because it produces the supreme fruit, or the function of liberation because it effects the absolute liberation from defilements.

Although the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) is, without distinction, the Discipline (*vinaya*) because it disciplines the defilements (*kilesa*), and it is also the Dhamma because it sustains one from falling into the states of misery and so forth when practiced according to the instructions, nevertheless, in order to distinguish the specific Dhamma and Vinaya intended here, he said: "In that regard, the Vinaya Piṭaka," and so forth.
This is because it contains a preponderance of teachings on phenomena (*dhamma*) as actual entities (*sabhāva*) by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.

He said: "The remainder of the Buddha’s word is Dhamma. Alternatively, even though the Vinaya is indeed Dhamma because it possesses the nature of the scriptures (pariyatti) and so forth, nevertheless, when the word *dhamma* is employed in close proximity to the word *vinaya* as having a non-different substratum, it indicates a body of teaching distinct from the Vinaya tradition—just as in the expressions "the equipment of merit and knowledge" (*puññañāṇasambhāra*) or "the cow and the ox" (*gobalībadda*), and so on.

The verse, "Through many a birth in saṃsāra," was spoken by the Blessed One immediately after his nineteenth reviewing knowledge, as he reflected upon his attainment of Arahatship, which is the foundation for his omniscience. Therefore it is said:
"This is the first word of a Buddha. Indeed, this is the udāna never abandoned by any Buddha. This is its...
The summary meaning: Seeking the builder of this house of a personal existence—
that craving— for which knowledge it is possible to see him, I made a resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha for the sake of that knowledge of enlightenment (bodhiñāṇa),
and for so long a time, throughout many births and a cycle of existence numbering many hundreds of thousands of births, I wandered through the round of saṃsāra without finding [him].
Not having reached that knowledge, not having found it, and indeed not having obtained it, I have run on and wandered through saṃsāra.
Since this thing called birth—being mixed with old age, sickness, and death—is painful to undergo again and again, and since it does not cease as long as that [knowledge] is not seen, the meaning is:
"searching for that, I have run on."
"You have been seen" means: now, by me while penetrating the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), you have been seen. "Again, a house" means:

again, you shall not build, nor will you build, this house of mine known as this personal existence (*attabhāva*). All your comforts of the defilements (*kilesa*) without exception have been demolished by me.
The pinnacle of this house of personal existence built by you—the circular central pillar known as ignorance (*avijjā*)—[has been destroyed].
The unconditioned has been shattered. My mind has now gone to, that is, entered into, Nibbāna which is free from formations (*asaṅkhāra*), by way of making it its object.
And I have attained—that is, reached and acquired—the Path of Arahantship or the Fruit of Arahantship, which is known as the destruction of craving (*taṇhā-kkhaya*).
This is the meaning. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated: "‘Gone to the unconditioned’ refers to the mind itself..."
"Or he has attained, reached, and acquired the path of Arahatship or the fruit of Arahatship, which is designated as the destruction of craving"—this meaning is also stated.
This is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by means of the mind.

However, they say: "But 'When indeed phenomena become manifest'—this is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by means of speech. It is said that the Blessed One [spoke this] by way of internal reflection.
He said, “Through many births in saṃsāra,” and so forth.
“Some” refers to the reciters of the Khandhaka. However, it should be understood that the statement made first represents the intention of the reciters of the Dhammapada.
And here, the reciters of the Khandhaka say: “Because the verses of the reciters of the Dhammapada were taught mentally at that time...”
"It was not for the benefit of the great multitude of people; however, because our verses were recited as vocal utterances, they were beneficial to the devas and brahmas who heard them at that time.
Therefore, this alone is the first word of a Buddha. But the reciters of the *Dhammapada* say:
"The criterion [for being the first word] is not whether the teaching was beneficial or not to the people."
Some say, "This is the first word of the Buddha precisely because it was taught by the Blessed One with his mind (*manas*).
Therefore, it should be understood that neither of these two [positions] is mutually contradictory.
But if it was taught with the mind as "through the saṃsāra of many births," then why, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, is it said: "'Through the saṃsāra of many births'—this Dhamma teaching..."?
Is it not stated that the Teacher, while seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, uttered this as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), and later, when questioned by the Elder Ānanda, explained it?

In that case as well, the meaning should be understood as “having uttered it with the mind. Alternatively, if one asks what the reason is for taking it as “taught by the mind alone,” [the answer is: if it had been taught by means of vocal expression, then in the *Udāna-pāḷi*...

It would have been included [in the Udāna]; therefore, they say that the very fact of its not being included in the Udāna-pāḷi is the reason for its having been confessed mentally without vocal expression.
In the verse, "When indeed phenomena become manifest," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning.
By this, it includes the triad of verses beginning with: "For the ardent, meditating brahmin, all his doubts vanish; when he understands phenomena together with their causes."
“Udānagāthā,” however, is a singular form used for the sake of the meter;
it should be understood that this refers specifically to the first verse therein. Furthermore, whatever needs to be said on this point will be made clear in the Khandhaka.

Regarding the phrase “on the day of the first of the fortnight (pāṭipadadivase),” this should not be connected with the words “of one who has attained omniscience,” but rather with the words “arose while he was reflecting.”
This, however, must be connected [to the following]. For it was on the full moon day of Visākha, at the time of dawn, that the Blessed One attained omniscience.

"By means of knowledge associated with joy" means by means of knowledge conjoined with joy (*somanassa*). "I inform you" means I announce; the sense is that I awaken you. "Subject to decay" refers to the characteristics of suffering and non-self through the gateway of the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca*) regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
One contemplates [them] by way of the statement: “What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self.

It should be understood that by demonstrating insight with that as its object through this very method of contemplating the three characteristics, he reveals the practice leading to Nibbāna—unmistaken, the exclusive domain of the Buddhas, based on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, and inaccessible to all other sectarians. Now, regarding the correct practice therein:

He enjoins them, saying, "Accomplish [this] through diligence. Alternatively, having stirred their sense of urgency by means of the brief summary, "All conditioned phenomena are subject to decay," he shows the entirety of right practice in that same brief manner by saying, "Accomplish [this] through diligence.
For the term "diligence" stands encompassing the entire, complete teaching contained within the three trainings.
*Antareti* means "in the interval"; the sense is "in the middle.
Regarding *suttantapiṭaka*: here, just as *kamma* itself is *kammanta*, so too *sutta* itself is to be understood as *suttanta*.
*Asaṅgīta* refers to the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*, the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, and so forth. However, some maintain that even the *Subhasutta* was [recited] at the First Council (*paṭhamasaṅgīti*).
To say that it was "not recited" is incorrect. For the Venerable Elder Dhammapāla has stated:
"Indeed, even prior to the First Council, while residing at Jetavana, the Venerable Elder Ānanda taught it to the young Brahmin Subha.
Furthermore, the Subha Sutta begins: "Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was at Sāvatthī..."
It is recorded [in the texts] as: "He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna," and so forth.
In that context, the statement beginning with "Thus have I heard" would not be appropriate for the Venerable Ānanda Thera alone to have spoken at the First Council;
for it is not fitting that the Venerable Ānanda Thera, having himself taught the Subha Sutta, should then say, "Thus have I heard," and so on.
He says this. However, it might be stated thus: "Once, venerable sir, I was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Therefore, it appears that the Subha Sutta was included in the recitation by the compilers of the second and third councils by means of the formula beginning with "Thus have I heard. Now, such is the intention of the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla Thera.

It might be argued: "Even though the Subha Sutta was spoken by the Elder Ānanda himself, when the Elders Mahākassapa and others—who desired to include it in the First Council and establish the textual tradition—established its recitation, they did so using the standard formula 'Thus have I heard' and so forth, according to the method found in other suttas.
This would be logical if that were the case. Alternatively, even while the Venerable Elder Ānanda himself was teaching the Subha Sutta, as he did in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and others...

The intention should be understood as follows: because he taught by standing upon the method received in the presence of the Blessed One, teaching exactly according to the manner taught by the Blessed One, he said "Thus have I heard" and so forth, not attributing to himself the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One.
"Both Pātimokkhas" refers to the Pātimokkhas for monks and for nuns. "Two Vibhaṅgas" refers likewise to the Vibhaṅgas for monks and for nuns.
There are two Vibhaṅgas. Regarding the twenty-two Khandhakas: these are the twenty-two Khandhakas found in the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga.
Regarding the "sixteen Parivāras": it is called "having sixteen Parivāras" because it is characterized by sixteen Parivāras. For indeed, in the Parivāra-pāḷi it says:
"That which was [spoken] by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, first..."
The section on the formulation [of the rule] begins with "Where was the *pārājika* offense formulated? and so forth;
following that is the section on the offenses committed, beginning with "While engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur? and so forth;

then there is the section on failure, which is divided into such questions as "Of the four failures, how many failures do the offenses incurred by one engaging in sexual intercourse fall under? and so forth; [and finally,] "Sexual intercourse..."

The section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*) begins with: "For one who practices the *dhamma* [of sexual intercourse], how many of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) are those offenses included in?

The section on origination (*samuṭṭhānavāra*) begins with: "For one who practices the *dhamma* of sexual intercourse, from how many of the six origins of offenses (*āpattisamuṭṭhāna*) do those offenses originate? [And so forth, including: "Sexual intercourse..."

There are eight [sections]: first, the section on legal issues (*adhikaraṇavāra*), beginning with "For one who commits an offense while engaging in sexual intercourse, to which of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) does it belong?";

second, the section on principles for settling disputes (*samathavāra*), distinguished by such questions as "For one who commits an offense while engaging in sexual intercourse, by how many of the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*) are those offenses settled?";
and third, the section on compendium (*samuccayavāra*) immediately following that. These constitute the eight.

The [first] eight sections have been stated. Following that, in the manner beginning with "Where was the *pārājika* offense prescribed on account of engaging in sexual intercourse?", another set of eight sections is stated:

one section on the rule (*paññattivāra*) according to the specific condition, and based on that, seven further sections—the section on the commission of the offense (*katāpattivāra*), and so forth—which are exactly like the preceding ones.
Thus, these eight plus the previous eight make sixteen sections in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
Sixteen sections have been shown. Beyond that, by the same method, sixteen sections also appear in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.
Because it is characterized by these sixteen sections, it is called the *Soḷasaparivāra* (The Sixteen-Sectioned).
However, in some manuscripts only the word "Parivāra" is seen; yet in many manuscripts, as well as in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, [the full title is given].
Because it is stated exactly thus, "with a retinue of sixteen," this reading also cannot be rejected; therefore, its meaning has been explained.
It is called the *Brahmajālādicatuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaha* because thirty-four discourses, beginning with the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, are collected therein, or by means of it;
or alternatively, it refers to the collection of those discourses of the stated measure.
"Saṅgaho etassa" means it is a collection of thirty-three discourses, beginning with the *Brahmajāla*. The same should be understood for the others as well.
In explaining the meaning of this verse, he said "vividhā hi" and so forth, [meaning] "for they are manifold.

"For the purpose of strengthening and relaxing" means, respectively, the purpose of strengthening the training rules regarding what is forbidden by the world (*lokavajja*), and the purpose of relaxing the training rules regarding what is forbidden by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
It should be understood. "As the prevention of transgression" means that conduct which proceeds by exceeding the limit of restraint is *ajjhācāra*—that is, transgression;

the meaning is "as the prevention of that. "By that" refers to the reasons such as its possession of various methods (*nayatta*). "This" refers to the statement in the verse beginning with "Because it possesses various specific methods.
"Of this" refers to the Vinaya. "But the other," however, is the Sutta.
Now, explaining the meaning of the verse beginning with "By indicating the purpose," he said, "For that... and so forth. Regarding the distinction between one's own welfare and the welfare of others:
for one who recites, hears, speaks, reflects upon, or teaches that discourse, the purpose consisting of virtue and so forth—which is comprised within that discourse—belongs to him as well;
and because it is to be accomplished by him for the sake of another, it also belongs to the other. Thus, that discourse indicates both of these.
It illuminates. Likewise, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it includes meanings such as those pertaining to the present life and the future life, and those mundane and supramundane;
these are the various types of meanings. Furthermore, this word *attha* is a synonym for "benefit" (*hita*), not a term for "the meaning of what has been spoken.
If it were the latter, then since a discourse (*sutta*) indicates both its own expressed meaning and that of another, this [specific] sense would have been stated.

The meaning that is elucidated by the *sutta* belongs to that [sutta] alone; it does not indicate another’s purpose (*parattha*) by means of it. Therefore, because there is no other purpose to be indicated or to be set aside, the mention of "one's own" (*attagga-hana*) need not be made.

And because there is no meaning of what is spoken apart from one's own purpose and another's purpose, the mention of "beginning with" (*ādiggahaṇa*) need not be made. Thus, regarding the aforementioned synonym for "benefit" (*hitapariyāya*)...

Because the meaning [of the term *attha*] is not possible in the sense of a "sutta" (discourse), the benefit for oneself and the benefit for others are stated by way of the person who is the locus of the sutta.

Alternatively, disregarding the sutta, those classifications of meaning such as benefit for oneself and so forth—which were stated in the commentary (*niddesa*) on the phrase "There is no killing, there is no gain through praise"—are:
benefit for oneself, benefit for others, benefit for both, and benefit pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).

The meaning is to be understood as follows: "sutta" indicates these meanings—namely, the meaning pertaining to the future life, the manifest meaning, the profound meaning, the hidden meaning, the concealed meaning, the meaning that must be inferred, the explicit meaning, the blameless meaning, the stainless meaning, the purified meaning, and the ultimate meaning.
For indeed, although [terms such as] one's own welfare (*attattha*) and so forth may exist independently of a discourse (*sutta*), [it is the latter that indicates them].

They are called "meanings" because they have not been explicitly defined as being of the nature of the Sutta's meaning; yet, among them, not even a single variety of meaning exceeds the requirement of being illustrated by the Sutta.

Therefore, it is said that the Sutta "indicates" (sūceti) those meanings. And in this interpretation of the word *attha*, this term *attha* also functions as a synonym for "that which has been spoken.
For here, the first five varieties of meaning are synonyms for "benefit" (*hita*), and from that...
The former [types of meaning] are distinguished by their expressed meanings, while the latter possess both natures.

In this context, "profound" (*gambhīra*) refers to that which is unfathomable due to its difficulty of comprehension; "hidden" (*guḷha*) means not revealed, but concealed—obscured by the arrangement of syllables and so forth, like roots or water covered by soil.
That which must be made known by extracting [the underlying sense] is the "implicit" (*neyya*); that which is to be understood according to the literal expression is the "explicit" (*nīta*).
The "purification from faultless states" is stated by way of synonyms as the absence of fault and the cleansing away of defilements; or else, it refers to wholesome resultant and functional states.
The ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) is Nibbāna, or simply the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
Alternatively, "he himself is of few desires" refers to his own welfare, and "he is one who speaks to others about being of few desires" refers to the discourse on fewness of wishes for others.
It indicates the welfare of others. In this way, discourses such as “He himself abstains from taking life” and so forth are to be applied.

Furthermore, the meaning of the word *sutta* should be explained by distinguishing it from the *Vinaya* and the *Abhidhamma*. Therefore, because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*), self-benefit, benefit for others, and so forth, are most prominently manifested;
this is due to their being the primary focus, and not because the teaching proceeds by way of commands or the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
It is precisely because this indicates the meaning that it is called a *sutta*. And having established it thus,

one should understand that in such passages as "so much has come down as *sutta* and is included within the *sutta* of that Blessed One," and "there are five hundred *suttas* in our own tradition," the word *sutta* is used figuratively (*upacāra*).
In the Suttas, the commands, the Dhamma, and the intrinsic nature conform to the inclinations of those to be trained;

it is not as in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, where the inclinations of those to be trained conform to the commands, the Dhamma, and the intrinsic nature. Therefore, the teaching of the Suttantas leads to the attainment of absolute welfare for those to be trained;
thus it was said: "And herein, the meanings are well-spoken," and so forth. "Leading to the attainment of absolute welfare."

The phrase "the teaching of the Suttantas" is also stated with reference to the fact that the teaching of the Suttantas is primarily intended for the attainment of welfare for those to be trained (*veneyya*).

And this state of being primarily intended should be understood as conforming to the inclinations of those to be trained. For this very reason, he said: "because it was spoken in conformity with the inclinations of those to be trained.
Unlike the teaching of the Vinaya, which is not taught by way of establishing commands out of a sense of lordship, [it is taught] for those to be trained...
The meaning is: because it was spoken and taught in accordance with their inclinations (*adhyāśaya*) and in conformity with their conduct (*caryā*).
Showing that its accomplishment occurs at a later time by way of successive training (*anupūrva-śikṣā*), etc., he said, "like a crop, [it yields] fruit.
"Produces" (*pasavati*) means it bears fruit; the meaning is that it brings about accomplishment. He shows that accomplishment belongs only to those who possess the means (*upāya*).
He said, “Like milk from a cow. For even from a cow, milk is obtained only by those who possess the proper means.
Indeed, one who milks a cow that has not yet given birth to a calf because it is the wrong time, or who milks her even at the right time by grasping her horns, does not obtain any milk at all.
To clarify the meaning of the term *suttāṇā*, it was stated: “And it protects them well (*suṭṭhu ca ne tāyatī*).”
“Similar to a thread” (*suttasabhāga*) means resembling a thread. Showing precisely this similarity to a thread, he said, “Just as,” and so forth.
“The carpenters’ thread” refers to the black measuring line of builders. “It serves as a measure” because one carves according to it.
“In the same way, for the wise” means that just as when a black line is stretched out and a mark is made, what is to be grasped and what is to be discarded becomes evident; [so too is this].

Thus, when disputes have arisen, as soon as the discourse (sutta) is brought forward, the dispute is settled because it becomes clear to the wise that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected.
Therefore, the meaning is that this discourse also serves as an authority for the wise.
Now, showing the similarity to a discourse in another way, he says, "And just as," and so forth. Because it is an authority like a discourse...
And because it binds together [the meanings], it is called a "sutta" (thread), as if it were a thread itself.

In this context, one should apply the fact that the sutta serves as the authority for the exposition of one's own welfare and so forth, and that it acts as the binder of those very things—since the sutta has as its primary function the illumination of their meaning.

Furthermore, the distinction between this [Abhidhamma] and the Vinaya and Abhidhamma should be applied according to the method already stated previously. This refers to the [passage]: "Of the meanings..."
The phrase beginning with "sūcanato" is a statement of the meaning [of the word *abhidhamma*]. "Etassa" means of this sutta. "Yaṃ" means because.
"Ettha" means in the Abhidhamma. Regarding the word "abhikkamanti," since the prefix *abhi-* here indicates the state of increase or excess in the action of going, he said:
"In 'abhikkamanti' and so forth, it is used in the sense of increase. "Abhiññātā" means by means of the crescent moon and so on.
The meaning is that it is known, recognized, and made manifest by some sign (*saññāṇa*). For the state of being a half-moon and so forth serves as a sign by way of characterizing the night:
because the moon is half-full, it is the eighth day; because it is deficient, it is the fourteenth day; because it is full, it is the fifteenth day.
This same meaning should be understood here for the word "distinguished" (*abhilakkhitā*); it is a synonym for the word "signified" (*abhilakkhita*).
Regarding the word *abhiññāta*, it is said: "In [the phrase] ‘abhiññātā abhilakkhitā,’ etc., it occurs in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).

And here, because particles (*nipāta*) merely indicate the meaning of other expressive words when placed in their proximity, it is stated that the prefix *abhi-* occurs in the sense of a characteristic, as it indicates the meaning of the word *lakkhita*.
In the expression *rājābhirājā*, it means a king worthy of being honored by kings. *Pūjita* means worthy of honor.

*Abhidhamma* refers to those teachings (*dhamma*) that are free from confusion with the *Vinaya* formulations, such as the statement: "Even though there is no offense in the emission of semen during sleep, unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) is still present.
Some also say it refers to "teachings that are themselves free from mutual confusion because they lack internal contradictions between earlier and later parts.
And [it applies] to such passages as: "The taking of life is unwholesome," and so forth.
The volition that originates the action which severs the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) in one who intends death is unwholesome (*akusala*);

it is not the "taking of life" (*atipāta*), which is defined as the severance of the life-faculty designated as a living being. Likewise, the intimation (*viññatti*) consisting of the taking of what is not given—the property of another—is an indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomenon;
the volition of theft that originates that intimation is an unwholesome phenomenon. It is in this manner [that the distinction is made].
The meaning should be understood as "phenomena that are free from mutual confusion. Regarding the term *abhivinaya*:

here, one who says, "Gold and silver must not be accepted," is said to train in the *vinaya*. Furthermore, it is said that one who says, "For one who accepts [them] in this way, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
for one who accepts in that way, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*)," is said to train in the *abhivinaya*. Therefore, gold and silver...
For one who takes what belongs to another with a thieving mind, there is one of the following: a *pārājika*, a *thullaccaya*, or a *dukkaṭa*, according to the specific object;
for one who takes it under the pretext of being a storekeeper, there is a *pācittiya*; for one who takes it for one's own benefit, there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
For one who takes it merely out of greed, there is a *anāmāsa-dukkata*; however, there is no offense for one who has been appointed as the discarder of money.
Thus, the meaning should be understood as: "one who is capable of training [others] in the Vinaya that is free from mutual confusion.
Regarding the word *abhikkantena*, it is said "in the superior" (*adhike*), because the prefix *abhi-* indicates the superiority of the beauty (*kanti*).
But is it not the case that in the expression *abhikkamanti* (they go forth), the prefix *abhi-* indicates the state of increase or excess in the action of going?

In the phrase "well-known and well-characterized" (*abhiññātā abhilakkhitā*), the prefix *abhi-* indicates a distinction because the functions of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) are clearly manifest;
whereas in "by the excellent" (*abhikkantena*), it indicates the excellence or superiority of the desirability (*kanti*). This is indeed appropriate, as the prefix serves to qualify the action.
However, in the cases of "an eminent king" (*abhirājā*) and "an eminent discipline" (*abhivinayo*), the prefix *abhi-* [indicates] kings and discipline that are honored and distinguished.

If it is asked, "How is it appropriate that it occurs [in this way]?"—here too there is no fault, because it indicates the actions of honoring, delimiting, and so forth, and because those actions are connected with the *rājavinaya* (the King's Discipline).

Therefore, just as the word *ati-* in *atimāla* and other compounds expresses the action together with its instrument, the terms *abhirāja* and *abhivinaya* are established; likewise, it is in the term *abhidhamma*.
It should be understood that the meaning shown here is that the prefix *abhi-* indicates an action such as growth (*vuḍḍhi*) together with its accomplishment.
And in this context—namely, in the Abhidhamma—"develops" (*bhāveti*) refers to the expansion of the mind; "pervading" (*pharitvā*) refers to the expansion of the object.
Furthermore, it is stated that there are also phenomena possessing growth by way of the growth of development and pervasion.
Meaning: “By way of object and so forth” means by way of object, associated states, kamma, doors, path, and so on. “Because they are to be characterized” means because they are to be cognized.
Since only supramundane states are worthy of worship in an absolute sense, it is shown that only the supramundane are worshipped by such terms as “the states of those in training” (sekha-dhammā).
“Because they are delimited by their own intrinsic nature” means because they are delimited by their own specific characteristics, such as contact and so forth. Furthermore...
Regarding the phrase "the states are spoken of": here, because they are greater than those of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the sublime states (*mahaggata*) are also included as "additional";
thus, the additional states are spoken of along with them.
As for the phrase "that which is not distinguished here": among these three—namely, the Vinaya and so forth—which are mutually distinguished, that which is not distinguished [is meant].
"Samānaṃ" means that it is the word "piṭaka. For the three words beginning with "Vinaya" are called "distinguished" because they are not shared with one another;
however, the word "piṭaka" is said to be "undistinguished" because it is common to all three of them.
"Mā piṭakasampadānena" means "do not take [it] by way of the transmission of the text (pāḷi). "Kudālañca piṭakañca": a spade and a basket.
“Kudālapiṭakaṃ. In this compound, *ku* refers to the earth; because it digs (*dālanato*) or tears open (*vidālanato*) that earth, a particular iron instrument is called a *kudāla*.
A particular vessel made from palm leaves, cane, creepers, and so forth, is called a *piṭaka*. The meaning is: having taken that, having grasped it.
“In the manner already stated” means: in the way described by the passage beginning with “in this twofold sense,” and so on.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction between teaching (desanā), instruction (sāsana), and discourse (kathā)": herein, *desanā* is the imparting and awakening [of others] to the meanings to be spoken by means of the methods of command and so forth, dependent upon the teacher.
*Sāsana* is the instructing and disciplining of individuals to be instructed, according to their respective offenses and so forth, in accordance with the state of those to be instructed.
*Kathā* is the speaking of the meaning to be spoken, such as restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

The act of making [the teaching] dependent upon words is called "discourse" (*kathā*). Therefore, one should understand the distinction between these—teaching (*desanā*), instruction (*sāsana*), and discourse (*kathā*)—as follows:
it is "teaching" in relation to the Blessed One who teaches; it is "instruction" by way of the person to be instructed; and it is "discourse" by way of the meaning to be explained.
And here, although teaching and the others do not depend upon that which is to be taught and so forth, [they are designated thus for the sake of clarity].

They do not exist; however, since commands (*āṇā*) and so forth depend specifically on the teacher and other factors, the distinction between teaching and the rest is stated by way of their connection with those respective specific qualities.
For indeed, the formulation of a command depends specifically on one worthy of commanding, due to the application of skill therein.
Likewise, the formulations of conventional and ultimate truth depend on the formulator; thus, the dependence of the formulation of commands and so forth upon the teacher is stated.

The teaching is stated specifically with reference to the person to be instructed— just as it is said to be in accordance with the Dhamma, as if in accordance with the underlying intention regarding an offense— considering the individuals who are to be trained.

Since the explanation of the view that must be disentangled is like [the explanation] of restraint and non-restraint regarding name-and-form, it is said to be "specifically dependent" upon that [view], provided there is a basis for speech and not otherwise.
The discourse was spoken by way of the meaning (*attha*). The word "division" (*bheda*) should be joined individually [to each term]:

"one should clearly illustrate, as appropriate, the division of the teaching (*desanā*), the division of the dispensation (*sāsana*), and the division of the discourse (*kathā*). Furthermore, "division" (*bheda*) means "variety" (*nānatta*).

Among those Piṭakas, the training (*sikkhā*), the abandonments (*pahāna*), and the profundity (*gambhīrabhāva*) constitute the "profundity of the training and abandonments" (*sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāva*); and that, as appropriate...
The meaning is "to illuminate. The connection is "and to discern the divisions of the scriptures" (*pariyatti*).
"Divisions of the scriptures" means "divisions of mastery. "In which" refers to whichever Piṭaka, such as the Vinaya. The connection is:
"and whatever success (*sampatti*) and failure (*vipatti*) one attains, all that too one should discern. Now...

Or rather, it should be connected thus: "He should also analyze all that—both the divisions of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and both prosperity and adversity—as well as where and how one attains them.
Here, "as" (*yathā*) refers to the various modes such as the mastery of causes for censure and so forth;
[it includes] the mastery of causes for censuring, escaping, protecting the Dhamma-treasury, right practice, and wrong practice.
"By these modes" is what is meant. "Illustration and manifestation" is stated in accordance with what was said previously; however, in terms of meaning, they are one and the same.
"Worthy of command" (*āṇāraho*): he is worthy of establishing an injunction, thus he is "worthy of command," the Blessed One. For, by virtue of his perfect enlightenment and his great compassion...
And because his words are authoritative due to his state as a teacher of unerring benefit, he is worthy to issue a command (*ājñā*);
since both conventional and ultimate meanings are possible, he says, "due to the abundance of commands. This same method applies to what follows.
"The first" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Those who frequently commit offenses" refers to the Elder Seyyasaka and others; for they, due to an abundance of faults...
“They are called ‘those with frequent offenses. Those for whom there are many (pacura), numerous, and abundant (bahula) offenses—faults and transgressions—are ‘those with frequent offenses.

Regarding the phrases beginning with ‘those with various underlying tendencies’ (anekajjhāsaya): an underlying tendency (ajjhāsaya) is simply a latent disposition (āsaya). In terms of its meaning, it consists of view and knowledge; as for its classification, however, it is fourfold.
For instance, by way of past conduct, [one becomes] worthy of arising in the future when conditions are present.”

The wrong view known as eternalism and annihilationism, and the right view known as the knowledge that accords with truth and the knowledge that deeds are one's own property, are called the "underlying tendency" (*āsaya*). For it has been said:
"The views of eternalism and annihilationism, and the inclination (*khanti*) that accords [with truth];"
"And that knowledge which is according to reality—this is designated as 'disposition' (āsaya).

Furthermore, this is called "disposition" because beings dwell therein; thus it is a fourfold disposition. There are seven underlying tendencies (anusaya): by way of sensual lust, lust for existence, views, aversion, doubt, conceit, and ignorance.
Future defilements that are ready to arise when they encounter their conditions are like the poison of a rat; [this includes] those of the past and the present.
And they are spoken of in exactly that way; for there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena due to a difference in time.

"Conduct" (*cariyā*) refers to the six root types of conduct, beginning with lustful conduct (*rāgacariyā*); these are of many kinds according to internal subdivisions, but by way of association (*saṃsagga*), they become sixty-three.
Alternatively, "conduct" means "behavior" (*carita*); it is twofold by way of good conduct (*sucarita*) and bad conduct (*duccarita*). "Resolve" (*adhimutti*) means "this very day... [and so forth].
