"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated: 'It is the resolution proceeding with a leaning toward that [goal], such as: "I shall go forth; this very day I shall attain Arahatship. However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated: 'It is the inclination [of beings] resulting from their past conduct (*pubbacariyā*).
That [inclination] is twofold, distinguished as inferior and superior. 'In accordance' (*yathānuloma*) means suitable to one's disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) and so forth. I...
"Perceiving 'mine'" means those who perceive "I" and "mine" by way of views, conceit, and craving.

"In accordance with the nature of phenomena" (yathādhammaṃ) means that here there is no self or anything belonging to a self, but only a mere phenomenon; thus, it means in conformity with the true nature of phenomena.
Regarding "restraint and non-restraint" (saṃvarāsaṃvara): here, restraint (saṃvara) is the act of restraining; it is the non-transgression [of precepts] by body and speech. Great restraint...
Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). This prefix *a-* has the sense of increase (*vuḍḍhi*), as in the expression “the qualities of one beyond training” (*asekkhā dhammā*);
therefore, the meaning is that it is a restraint (*saṃvara*) that is small and great. “The unraveling of views” (*diṭṭhiviniveṭhana*) means the liberation from views.

The classification of the trainings in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth will be made clear later in the commentary on the first *pārājika*. In the Sutta-pāḷi, [it is said] beginning with “quite secluded from sensual pleasures,” etc.
Because of the abundance of teachings on concentration (*samādhi*), it is said in the Suttanta Piṭaka that "the training in higher mind" (*adhicittasikkhā*) [is taught there].

The abandoning of transgressions regarding the defilements means the abandoning of any transgression through the doors of body and speech committed by the defilements of corruption (*saṃkilesadhamma*) or by karma and the defilements themselves.

Defilements that persist within the continuum by way of latent tendencies (*anusaya*) may, upon finding the necessary conditions, become manifest (*pariyuṭṭhita*) and lead to the breach of virtue (*sīlabheda*).
"They do not obtain the opportunity to transgress" means he said, "because virtue is the opposite of transgression.
Regarding "the abandoning of the obsessions": an obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) is the arising of defilements that, by way of providing an opening, exhausts the occurrence of the wholesome in the mind;
the abandoning of that is called "the abandoning of the obsession of defilements" in the sense of their non-arising within the mental continuum.

"Abandoning the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Regarding this: underlying tendencies are so called because, while not yet abandoned, they lie down (*sayana*) repeatedly (*anu anu*) within the continuum; they are factors that are ready to arise when they encounter their appropriate conditions.
These are the seven defilements, such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), which have become firmly rooted and are ready to arise upon obtaining their corresponding conditions.
The abandoning of these is "abandoning the underlying tendencies. And these are abandoned entirely by means of the wisdom of the Noble Path.
He said: "Because wisdom is the antidote to the underlying tendencies (anusaya).

"Abandonment by way of a specific factor" (tadaṅgappahāna) refers to the abandoning of this or that unwholesome factor by means of this or that wholesome factor—such as the bases for meritorious action like giving—which is like the dispelling of darkness by the light of a lamp. But here, by means of this or that...
The abandoning of each respective factor of immorality by means of a corresponding factor of virtue should be understood as "abandoning by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

Regarding the abandonings of suppression, equanimity, and eradication: here, the abandoning of those various hindering states (*nīvaraṇa*) by means of concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—through the prevention of their occurrence, like the suppression of seaweed on the surface of water by striking it with a pot, is "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).

The abandonment by way of absolute non-occurrence—known as "abandonment by cutting off"—of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination within the continuum of one who possesses each respective noble path, due to the cultivation of the four noble paths, is "abandonment by cutting off" (*samucchedappahāna*). Regarding the phrase "the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct":
misconduct (*duccarita*) refers to bad conduct such as bodily misconduct, or it is conduct that has been corrupted by defilements.
That very thing which, having arisen, thoroughly defiles, afflicts, and torments that continuum is "corruption" (*saṃkileso*);
its abandonment is what is meant by the phrase "abandonment through substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgavasena*) regarding the corruption proceeding by way of bodily and verbal misconduct.
Because concentration is the direct opposite of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), [it serves as the antidote] to the corruption of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkileso*) in the Suttanta Piṭaka.

Abandonment has been stated. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the abandonment of the defilement of views is stated because it elucidates phenomena whose intrinsic nature is distinct from a self and so forth.
"In each one of these" means that this should be understood as referring to each individual Piṭaka among these three. Regarding the phrase "the Dhamma is the Pāḷi":

here, it is called *dhamma* because it makes known (*bodhana*) the preeminent and exalted meanings such as virtue (*sīla*), and because it possesses the state of being a natural expression (*nirutti*).
Because it is spoken by the Buddha and others, the *pāḷi* is the series of words that have been brought forth (*pakaṭṭha-vacanappabandha*); it is the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).

Regarding the statement, "The Dhamma is the *pāḷi*," it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada* [commentaries] that "in this context, the word itself which illuminates both the meaning and the conventional expression spoken by the Blessed One is called *pāḷi*.
This is stated in the Sinhalese *Gaṇṭhipada* written for the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*.

However, this has been stated: the conceptualization (*paṭṭhāna*) determined by the Blessed One through the mind, in accordance with the actual nature (*sabhāva*) and the conventional expression (*vohāra*) of that nature, is called the "text" (*pāḷi*).
If the word itself were the text, there would have to be a difference between the text and the teaching.
And apart from the mere act of producing vocal utterance, there is nothing other than the text determined by the mind.

There is no difference between the teaching and the text. For when the one who presents the teaching gives that teaching, it is stated as non-different from the text, even without the mere act of vocalizing the text that has been determined by the mind.
And likewise, because it is stated later that "the teaching is a designation," the status of the text as a designation exists through its identity with the teaching.
It has been stated. Furthermore, if the teaching were something other than the text, one would have to say, "the realization of the text, the meaning of the text, and the teaching as they truly are";
however, since it was not said thus, but rather "the realization of the text and the meaning of the text as they truly are," it is shown that the text and the teaching are non-different. And so...

Having stated this, by subsequently showing that "teaching" (*desanā*) is indeed a "designation" (*paññatti*), it is already implied that the Canon (*pāḷi*) possesses the nature of a designation, because teaching is not something other than that.

And here, if one asks: "If the position is that 'the word itself is what is called the Canon,' then since the Dhamma also has the intrinsic nature of sound, what is the distinction between the Dhamma and its teaching?
[The answer is: It is known as such by virtue of making those various meanings understood, and by way of being grasped and so forth, previously...

It should be understood that the *dhamma* is the established continuity of sounds, while the *desanā* (teaching) is the sound subsequently uttered for the purpose of making it known to others, which illuminates its meaning.
Alternatively, the *desanā* is the mental state (*cittuppāda*) that originates the aforementioned sounds, based on the derivation:

"that by which the sound is taught—that is, originated"—just as in the case of false speech (*musāvāda*) and so forth. For in those cases as well, it is the mental state that originates false speech and the rest [which constitutes the action].
Volition (*cetanā*) is expressed by such terms as "false speech" (*musāvāda*).
Regarding the phrase "in these three, there are the penetration of the meaning of the Dhamma, the teaching, and the text":

here, the subject matter of the texts consists of these three—the meaning of the text, the teaching of the text, and the penetration of the meaning of the text—referring to the teaching and the penetration of the meaning of the *Vinayapiṭaka* and so forth.
If it is asked: "The status of being a support (ādhārabhāva) is appropriate for the *piṭakas*, but since the *piṭakas* are themselves the *pāḷi*, how could they be the support for the Dhamma?
It is because the collection (*samudāya*) of the *pāḷi* is the support for its constituent parts (*avayava-pāḷi*).
For a whole is called the support of its parts, just as one says, "the branch is in the tree. And here, because the Dhamma and so forth are difficult to fathom...
Since the Vinaya and so forth are profound by virtue of those [qualities] such as the Dhamma, the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and so forth has indeed already been stated.

Therefore, one should not object that "only the Dhamma and so forth are profound because they are difficult to fathom, but not the Vinaya and so forth," for this objection is invalid because the profundity of the Vinaya and so forth has been stated both directly and by way of their respective objects. For the Dhamma consists of the Vinaya and the rest.

The meaning is their domain, and the penetration of the teaching has the meaning of the Dhamma as its domain. In this context, because penetration is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of penetrating the Dhamma and its meaning should be understood;
and because the knowledge of the teaching is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of plunging into the teaching should be understood.
Furthermore, because penetration cannot be produced, and because the arising of the knowledge that has that [penetration] as its object is difficult to achieve—
It should be understood as being difficult to fathom. They are "difficult to fathom" (dukkhogāhā) because they are plunged into with difficulty.
He said, "and it is impossible to find a foothold," because even those of dull intellect who plunge into it only partially are unable to gain a firm footing.
"In each one" means in each individual Piṭaka. "Therein" refers to within these Piṭakas; this is a locative case used in the sense of selection.
Now, demonstrating the profound nature [of the Dhamma] by way of cause, fruit of the cause, and so forth, he says, "Another method," and so on.
"Cause" (*hetu*) means condition (*paccaya*). For that which holds its own fruit, brings it about, is called a "dhamma.
To show how the word *dhamma* is understood here as a synonym for "cause," he says, "For this has been said," and so on. But is it not the case that... [in the context of] "the cause"?
If it is asked, "How is the causal nature of the Dhamma understood by this statement, 'Knowledge [of the cause] is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma'?"— it is because,
when the meaning of the component words of the compound term *dhammapaṭisambhidā* is shown, it is stated as "knowledge regarding the cause" (*hetumhi ñāṇaṃ*).
For in the phrase "analytical knowledge regarding the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma" (*dhamme paṭisambhidā dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the word "regarding the Dhamma" (*dhamme*)...
By showing the meaning of this [term "cause"], it is said "in the cause"; by showing the meaning of "analytical knowledge" (*paṭisambhidā*), it is said "knowledge.

Therefore, by stating that the words *hetu* (cause) and *dhamma* (phenomenon) are synonymous, and that the words *ñāṇa* (knowledge) and *paṭisambhidā* (analytical knowledge) are synonymous, the fact that a phenomenon possesses the nature of being a cause is established. This is established by the statement: "Knowledge regarding the cause and its fruit is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)."
The relationship between cause and fruit regarding the goal (attha) should be understood in exactly this way. "Cause-fruit" (hetuphala) means the fruit of a cause.
And because that [fruit] is sought after, attained, and reached by following the cause, it is therefore called the "goal.
In the phrase "according to the Dhamma" (yathādhamma), the word *dhamma* here encompasses both the cause and the cause-fruit in their entirety; it is a term denoting intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

This word *dhamma* does not denote the state of being a cause for the scriptures (*pariyatti*); therefore, "according to the *dhamma*" (*yathādhamma*) means "in each respective case," referring to whichever *dhamma* there may be, such as ignorance (*avijjā*) or the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*).
Alternatively, "according to the *dhamma*" means "in conformity with the *dhamma*" (*dhammānurūpa*).
For the teaching, like direct realization (*paṭivedha*), proceeds in conformity with the *dhamma* because it reveals the object without error; and for that very reason, it is an unerring expression.
It is called "expression of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhilāpa*). This refers to an expression that conveys both the meaning and the phrasing, and which is non-erroneous.

Furthermore, in this context, "expression" (*abhilāpa*) is said to mean "sound," because it is expressed (*abhilappati*). By this, he demonstrates the "linguistic expression of the Dhamma" (*dhammanirutti*) mentioned in the passage: "Knowledge regarding that linguistic expression of the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*)," since the teaching has the nature of sound. For indeed, [this is] the analytical knowledge of language.
The state of having a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga-pāḷi*.

Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, its status as having sound as its object is shown by the passage beginning, "having made that word, which is the conventional expression of its own nature, the object. For it is thus:

having determined the relationship between a word and its referent in the sense of "this word is the designator of this meaning," [the knowledge] proceeds by way of elucidating the specific meaning of each respective word.
"Sound" is what is called "teaching" (*desanā*). By the word "intention" (*adhippāya*), he shows the intended meaning of this statement:

"'Teaching' is a designation" (*paññatti*) is said with reference to the verbal expression of the linguistic formulation of the Dhamma (*dhammaniruttābhilāpa*), and not with reference to a designation that is separate from that.

For it is called "teaching" because the meaning is taught by means of it; or it is called "designation" because it makes known [the object] in a specific manner, or because it makes known [it] by way of a specific manner.
“The expression of the linguistic formulation of phenomena (dhammaniruttābhilāpa)” is what is meant. Thus, in this position that “teaching (desanā) is sound,” this meaning should be understood.
However, regarding the statement “teaching is a designation (paññatti),” those who maintain the doctrine of designation (paññattivādino) speak as follows:
although in the phrase “expression of phenomena” the word *abhilāpa*—meaning that which is expressed—is said to be sound and not a designation, nevertheless...
When the word "sound" (sadda) is spoken, one grasps the conventional expression corresponding to it;

because one understands the meaning expressed by that conventional expression, when the sound is mentioned, the designation (paññatti) corresponding to it is also effectively mentioned through the metaphorical application of the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*).

Alternatively, since it was stated, "The meaning is 'the utterance of phenomena' (dhammābhilāpo)," rather than saying "the meaning is 'the utterance of phenomena'," it is thereby demonstrated that what is called "teaching" (desanā) is not the sound itself.
Now, pointing out penetration (*paṭivedha*), he said: "Penetration is realization (*abhisamaya*).
That which penetrates is knowledge; thus it is called penetration. Or, that by which one penetrates is penetration. One realizes (*abhisameti*) through this, thus it is realization;
or, that by which they realize is realization. Now, [he explains] according to the divisions of realization and the modes of realization...
In order to make it clear both by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*) and by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), he said:

"And that is mundane and supramundane," and so forth. The connection is: "understanding (*avabodha*) by way of its object and by way of non-delusion. Therein, "understanding by way of its object" refers to mundane understanding whose objects are phenomena (*dhamma*) such as ignorance, whose objects are meanings (*attha*) such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and whose objects are the designation of both of those.

Awakening (*avabodha*). Furthermore, awakening to phenomena and so forth in accordance with their meaning and other aspects through non-delusion—being associated with the Path, having Nibbāna as its object, and destroying delusion regarding the aforementioned phenomena, meanings, and designations—is supramundane realization (*abhisamaya*).
For it is by way of taking as an object [the understanding]: "This is the cause, this is its fruit, and this is the conventional expression corresponding to both."

Mundane knowledge penetrates by way of the object (*visaya*), whereas supramundane knowledge penetrates through non-delusion, because delusion regarding cause, cause-and-effect, and so forth, has been eradicated by the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).

"In accordance with the meaning, among phenomena" means that ignorance is the cause and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are what arise from the cause; likewise, "in accordance with the effect, among causes" means that ignorance produces volitional formations.

The meaning [of *attha*]. Alternatively, among the three formations—meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), demeritorious formation (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*)—the ignorance associated with the demeritorious formation is the condition for that [formation], while for the others it is according to their respective suitability; thus, the meaning is "penetration into causes in accordance with their effects.

Regarding "meanings in accordance with phenomena" (*dhammānurūpaṃ atthesu*), this refers to [the penetration] into effects in accordance with their causes, as in "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.

The meaning is "understanding. "In accordance with the path of designation, within designations" means that understanding occurs within the designations in conformity with the phenomena being designated; this is the meaning.
To demonstrate the profound nature of the Piṭakas by means of the aforementioned phenomena and so forth, he said: "Now, because in these Piṭakas... and so on.
“*Dhammajātaṃ*” refers either to a classification of causes or to the cause itself. “*Atthajātaṃ*” refers either to a classification of effects or to the effect itself.

This is to be connected with the phrase “and this teaching. “*Yo cettha*” means that which is the penetration (*paṭivedha*) among these various teachings on the *dhamma*, the *attha*, and the instruction found within each respective Piṭaka.
“*Dukkhogāhaṃ*” is used here because ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth—the *dhammas* and *atthas*—are difficult to penetrate.

"Difficult to fathom" (*dukkhogāhatā*): It should be understood that it is difficult to fathom because it is difficult to establish for them, and because it is impossible to produce or to take as an object the penetration (*paṭivedha*)—which consists of both teaching and realization. "In this way also" (*evampi*):
the word *pi* (also) includes another aspect mentioned previously. "In this" (*ettha*): in these three Piṭakas. "The meaning has been stated" (*vuttatthā*): the meaning has been stated.
"Vuttatthā" means that the meaning has been fully described (*saṃvaṇṇita*).

Regarding the phrase "in the three Piṭakas," it should be understood here—either by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*) or by way of the specific treatises (*pakaraṇa*)—that this refers to each one individually.
"Pariyattibheda" [means]: mastery (*pariyāpuṇana*) is *pariyatti*. Here, the word *pariyatti* denotes the act of mastering, not the sense of the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "The manner of mastery for each of the three Piṭakas is to be seen and known.
For this very reason, it is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipadas* that "the *pariyatti*s are the modes of mastery.
Alternatively, the texts themselves are called *pariyatti* because they are to be mastered in three ways; and for this very reason, [it is said]:
“*Pariyattiyo* [are] *pāḷikkamā*” (the scriptures in their proper order)—this is stated in the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada*, which was written as a commentary on the Abhidhamma.
For in this way, because of the application of the method of mastering the *Alagaddūpama-sutta*, one can also say that the *pāḷi* itself is the “*pariyatti* called *Alagaddūpama*.
And having done so, the explanatory statement later on—“The *Alagaddūpama* has been mastered for the sake of finding fault and so forth, but it was wrongly grasped”—is also consistent.
This is appropriate. For in that case, it is fitting to say that the text itself has been wrongly grasped and mastered.
Regarding the phrase "alagaddūpamā": an *alagadda* is a water-snake; that which has the seizing of a water-snake as its simile is called "alagaddūpamā.
It should be understood that here, by the word "alagadda," the seizing of the water-snake is intended. In the term "āpūpiko," by the word *apūpa*, the eating of cakes is meant.
The learning that has been acquired is compared to the seizing of a water-snake (*alagadda*), but not to the snake itself.

Or, although one should say "the simile of seizing a water-snake" (*alagaddaggahaṇūpamā*), the middle term is elided and it is called "the water-snake simile" (*alagaddūpamā*), as in the case of "lip-mouth" (*oṭṭhamukha*) and so forth.
Here, "water-snake" (*alagadda*) refers to a venomous serpent. For *gada* is the name for poison, and that [poison] is its *alaṃ*, meaning full or complete.

It exists; therefore, because it is "alaṃ" (sufficient) and "pariyatto" (adequate), and because its "gado" (poison) is "paripuṇṇo" (complete), by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) and adding the letter *d*, it is called "alagaddo.
Alternatively, it is an "alagaddo" because it is "alaṃ" (capable) of taking away life and has "gado" (poison).
"Nissaraṇatthā" means that which has the purpose or aim of escaping from the suffering of saṃsāra. "Bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti" means...
Here, "bhaṇḍāgārika" refers to one appointed to the storehouse; like a storekeeper, he is a *bhaṇḍāgārika*, a guardian of the treasure of the Dhamma.
The "storehouse-study" (*bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti*) is the study undertaken solely for the sake of being a storekeeper, without regard for any other purpose.
"Ill-learned" (*duggahitā*) means wrongly grasped. Elucidating the state of being ill-learned, he says: "Memorized for the sake of criticism and so forth."
The meaning is that these [teachings] were learned for the purpose of finding fault with others and for the sake of escaping from such disputes.
It should be understood that even the mastery [of the texts] for the sake of gain, honor, and so forth is included herein. For this has been stated in the *Alagaddasutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
“For one who [studies] the Buddha’s word thinking, ‘In this way I shall obtain robes and other requisites,’ or ‘They will recognize me in the midst of the four assemblies’...”
If one masters [the teachings] for the sake of gain, honor, and so forth, that mastery is called "the mastery of a poisonous snake.
For it is better to fall asleep without having mastered the Buddha’s word than to master it in such a manner.
But is it not the case that mastery which is comparable to seizing a poisonous snake is called "likened to a poisonous snake"? And if that is so, even if it is well-mastered...

It is appropriate to say that the *pariyatti* (the textual doctrine) is like a poisonous snake (*alagadda*), because even in that context, it is spoken of in the Canon by way of being a simile for seizing a poisonous snake. For this has been said:
"Just as if, monks, a man needing a poisonous snake, seeking a poisonous snake, searching for a poisonous snake..."
While walking, he might see a large water-snake;
he would seize it very firmly with a forked stick, and having seized it very firmly with the forked stick, he would grasp it well by the neck.
Even though, monks, that water-snake might bite the hand or the arm or some other part of that man’s body...
One might wrap one's limbs and members with snakes, yet one would not thereby incur death or death-like suffering on that account.
Why is that? Because, monks, the snake was well-grasped.
In the same way, monks, here some sons of good family master the Dhamma—the discourses (*sutta*), the mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), and so forth.

Therefore, from what source is this distinction known—that the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) when wrongly grasped here is like a venomous snake (*alagaddūpamā*), such that it is said to be like a venomous snake because it is swallowed for the sake of criticism and so forth when wrongly grasped? This is true;
however, it should be understood as stated by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*). For indeed, [the scriptures] are [otherwise] the storehouse-keeper’s study for the purpose of deliverance.
Because it is grasped separately by way of elimination (*pārisesato*), the study that is like the wrong grasping of a snake is understood as the "snake-like study.
For study that is like a correct grasp is either for the purpose of deliverance (*nissaraṇattha*) or is the "treasury-steward study" (*bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti*); therefore, this is well said:
"The snake-like [study] is that which, being wrongly grasped, is swallowed up for the sake of finding fault and so forth. With reference to this...
This refers to the wrong grasp of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "It was said" means it was said in the *Alagaddasutta*.

"One who desires a snake" (*alagaddatthika*) means one who desires a venomous serpent (*āsīvisa*). "One who seeks a snake" (*alagaddagavesī*) means one whose habit is to search for and seek out a snake.
"Wandering in search of a snake" (*alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno*) means wandering for the purpose of searching for a snake. "In its coils" (*bhoge*) means in its body.

Regarding the phrase "in the hand or in the arm": here, from the wrist to the tips of the nails, it should be understood as the "hand" (*hattha*); together with the upper arm, the remainder is the "arm" (*bāhā*).
However, in some places, it is said that "from the elbow (*kappara*) up to the tips of the nails is the hand.
Excluding both the hand and the arm, which are defined by the characteristic mentioned in the phrase "in any other limb or member" (*aññatarasmiṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅge*), [the rest is intended].
The remainder of the body should be understood as "limbs and members" (*aṅgapaccaṅga*). "Tatonidānaṃ" means "having that as its source" (*taṃnidānaṃ*);
it is said to mean "having that as its cause. For in the first word, the case ending has been elided;

thus, while it should be called *taṃnidānaṃ*—meaning "that which has the stinging on the hands and so forth as its source or cause"—it is expressed as *tatonidānaṃ* by treating the first word as a relative pronoun (*paccatta*).
This is an exposition made by using the ablative case while not eliding the suffix *tassa*. As for the question "For what reason? (*taṃ kissa hetu*):
if it is asked why the biting on the hands and so forth, and the resulting encounter with death and other calamities, occur—by what cause or reason?

"Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching. "Certain empty persons" (*ekacce moghapurisā*) refers to certain hollow men. "The Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ*) refers to the Dhamma of the canonical scriptures (*pāḷidhamma*).
"To master" means to learn; it is said that they recite, bring to the lips, and retain [the words].
"The meaning" refers to both the meaning as it was spoken according to reality and the purposeful meaning.
"They do not examine" means they do not grasp or investigate. This is what is meant: "In this place, virtue was taught..."

"Here concentration is taught, here wisdom is taught, and we shall fulfill that"—thus they do not grasp the meaning of what was spoken and the purpose of it by way of such statements as "virtue is the cause of concentration, concentration is the cause of insight," and so forth.
"Not examining" means for those who do not examine. "They do not endure contemplation" means they do not tolerate the wisdom of contemplation; having contemplated...
The intention is that they are not to be grasped after having seen and approved them with wisdom. By this he illuminates the following meaning:
"For those who do not examine the matter with wisdom, those phenomena do not appear;
they are unable to know, 'In this place virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, the round of existence, or the turning away from the round was taught.'"
"And these advantages of refutation" means that they master the teachings by way of the advantage of attributing faults to the doctrines of others.
"And the advantage of escaping from such assertions" means that through this mastery of the teaching,
they master the Dhamma for the purpose of escaping— that is, of being released from the censure and defeat of an assertion leveled against themselves by others.
The meaning is as follows: this is what is intended—“we shall release ourselves from this and that fault in such and such a manner” when faults have been attributed to our own doctrine by others;
for this reason, they master [the texts]. Alternatively, *itivāda* refers to each respective doctrine; *itivādappamokkha* is the release from such doctrines;

those for whom the release from such doctrines (*itivādappamokkhānisaṃsa*)—that is, the benefit of being released from various doctrines—is their aim, are called “those who possess the benefit of release from such doctrines.”

This is the meaning. "For whatever purpose they master the Dhamma" means: for the sake of fulfilling virtue and so forth, or for the sake of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna, noble sons in this dispensation master the Dhamma. "And they do not experience that purpose" means:
these people who grasp it incorrectly do not experience, do not find, that purpose of the Dhamma known as the fulfillment of virtue and so forth.
Alternatively, for the sake of some criticism or for the sake of escaping from such a statement, those foolish men who have mastered the Dhamma are unable—
because they have grasped it wrongly— to establish that very point when others say, "This is not the meaning"; thus,
their own doctrines are neither capable of mounting a critique against the opponent's argument nor of liberating themselves from it.
The meaning should be understood thus: even though they are unable [to do so], they certainly do not experience that benefit.

"They lead to harm and suffering for a long time" means that because those phenomena have been wrongly grasped, they lead to harm and suffering for a long time by way of being causes for blame, pride, intoxication, malice, and harshness. For in this context, the term for the effect is used for the cause: "those phenomena..."
It is said: "They lead to what is harmful and to suffering.

For although those teachings do not actually lead to harm or suffering, nevertheless, for those who master them in the manner described, there exists the possibility of the arising of many unwholesome states—such as censuring and so forth—rooted in that [learning] at the time of recitation and at the time of debate;
therefore, "those teachings lead to what is harmful and to suffering."

The phrase "they lead to" is stated by using the terminology of the effect for the cause. Regarding the question "For what reason?", the word *tan* (that) refers to the failure to achieve the aforementioned goal and the resulting tendency of those qualities to lead to harm and suffering.
In the expression "only the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be understood as including concentration, insight, and so forth.
For indeed, when one who has mastered the Buddha’s word masters it with the thought: "In the place where morality is required, I shall fulfill morality;
in the place where concentration is required, I shall ensure the womb of concentration is conceived; in the place where insight is required, I shall establish insight;
and in the place where the paths and fruits are required, I shall develop the path and realize the fruit"—for him alone does that mastery of the scriptures become truly effective.
It is called "for the sake of escape. Regarding that which was said: this refers to the thorough mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) as stated in the *Alagaddūpama Sutta*.

"Leading to welfare and happiness for a long time" means that at the places where virtue (*sīla*) and so forth are mentioned, even those fulfilling virtue and the other perfections attain *arahantship*;
and having attained it, they teach the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly, and from those inspired by their teaching of the Dhamma, four [requisites] are brought forth.
Even for those who utilize the requisites, or who raise objections against the doctrines of others in accordance with the Dhamma,

or who remove flaws from their own position, these things lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. For it is not only through well-mastered scripture that one attains the development of the Path,
the realization of the Fruits, and so forth, but also through the refutation of opposing views and the establishment of one's own position.
They succeed. And so it has been said: “Having thoroughly refuted with reasoned doctrine any arisen opposing view,” and so forth.

One who has fully understood the aggregates (*pariññātakkhandho*) is one who has fully understood the aggregates through the full comprehension of suffering (*dukkhaparijānana*). One who has abandoned the defilements (*pahīnakileso*) is one who has abandoned the defilements through the abandonment of the origin (*samudayappahāna*).
One who has penetrated the unshakable (*paṭividdhākuppo*) is one who has penetrated the fruit of arahantship. It is called “unshakable” (*akuppa*) because it does not shake.

This is the name for the fruit of arahantship. For although the four paths and the four fruits share the same unshakable nature, the paths and fruits of the seven trainees (sekkha) are not called "unshakable" because they attain successive different names by relinquishing their respective individual names as they progress upward.
However, an arahant is always simply an arahant; therefore, his fruit alone is called "unshakable."
Thus it was said. And by this he shows the following meaning: “The mastery of the scriptures belonging only to one whose taints are destroyed is called ‘the mastery of the storekeeper.
For him, there is nothing that is not fully understood, not abandoned, not developed, or not realized;
therefore, while mastering the word of the Buddha, he learns it as one who maintains the thread, preserves the tradition, and protects the lineage. For this very reason, he said:
“‘For the sake of preserving the lineage,’ and so forth. In this context, ‘lineage’ (*paveṇī*) means the continuity of the Dhamma; the meaning is the uninterrupted occurrence of the Dhamma.
‘For the sake of protecting the lineage’ means for the sake of protecting the lineage of the Blessed Buddha.
It should be understood that its lineage, in terms of meaning, is indeed the same as the lineage.”

But surely, if the mastery of the Buddha’s word for the sake of preserving the lineage is the "storehouse-learning" (*koṭṭhāgārika-pariyatti*), why was it stated specifically as "one whose taints are exhausted" (*khīṇāsava*)? For this method applies even to certain worldlings (*puthujjana*).
Indeed, there may be a certain bhikkhu who, during times of famine, fear, and so forth, is unable to dwell in one place while those who bear the texts are scattered.
If one masters the teaching with the thought, "May I not grow weary through wandering for alms; may the exceedingly sweet word of the Buddha not be lost;
I shall uphold the tradition, establish the lineage, and preserve the succession," why then is his mastery not called the "storehouse mastery"?
It is said in reply: even though this is so, the mastery of an ordinary person (puthujjana) is indeed storehouse mastery.

It is not so called. For although an ordinary person (puthujjana) masters the texts with the intention, "I shall preserve the tradition," because he has not yet crossed over the wilderness of existence himself, his mastery is called "mastery for the sake of escape" (nissaraṇa-pariyatti).
Therefore, for an ordinary person, mastery is either like the simile of the water-snake or is for the purpose of escape; [but it is not so] for the seven types of trainees (sekkha).
It should be understood that for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), this is merely the mastery of the storekeeper’s duty for the sake of deliverance.
And because he resembles a storekeeper, the one whose taints are destroyed is called a "storekeeper.
For just as a storekeeper, having put away his ornaments, brings forth the appropriate ornaments at the time of adornment and presents them to the king so that he may be adorned; so too...

In the same way, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), having received the treasure of the Dharma-jewel and seeing beings who are capable of attaining liberation and possess the necessary causes,

increases his teaching of the Dharma accordingly and adorns them with the supramundane ornaments known as the factors of the path and the factors of enlightenment; thus, he is called a "treasurer" (bhaṇḍāgārika).

Having thus analyzed the three types of mastery (*pariyatti*), he now says, "But in the Vinaya," and so forth, in order to demonstrate in detail the success (*sampatti*) and failure (*vipatti*) appropriate to each of the three Piṭakas.
In such passages as "By relying on the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*), one attains the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*)," it is because virtue,

while being purified through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) and the power of the knowledge of action as one's own property (*kammassakataññāṇa*), [is freed] from the stains of defilement (*saṃkilesamala*).

It becomes purified and reaches fulfillment; therefore, when the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) is being accomplished, it establishes the power of mindfulness (*satibala*) and the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) by way of its nature as a supporting condition (*upanissaya*).
Thus, its status as a supporting condition for the three types of true knowledge (*vijjā*) should be understood through its provision of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).

For, by means of the power of mindfulness, the true knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-vijjā*) is accomplished, and through clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), there is the cultivation of performing all tasks with thorough vision.

The accomplishment of the second true knowledge (vijjā) follows from the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, due to the presence of the abandonment of defilements through the absence of transgression.

The accomplishment of the third true knowledge occurs by way of the purity of intention (ajjhāsaya), which serves as a necessary condition for the turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).

The fact that virtue (sīla) serves as a necessary condition for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa)—even without the full perfection of previously accomplished concentration and wisdom—should be illustrated by the case of those who have destroyed the taints through bare insight (sukkha-vipassaka-khīṇāsava).
Because of the statement, “One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are,” the perfection of concentration is the decisive support for the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

Because of the statement, “From yoga, indeed, wisdom is born,” the excellence of wisdom—cultivated through prior application, living with a teacher, proficiency in the local dialect, learning, and interrogation—is the decisive support for the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). And here, [regarding] the perfection of virtue...

Because it is stated [in the text], "by depending on," for one in whom the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), which are the manifestations of concentration, do not succeed in their entirety, there is no perfection of concentration according to the highest limit;

thus, although the higher knowledges are partial aspects of the true knowledges (*vijjā*), only those three true knowledges that have arisen from the attainment of virtue (*sīlasampatti*) are included. For just as the four [bases of psychic power] have arisen from the attainment of wisdom (*paññāsampatti*)...
The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) succeed through the path alone for one endowed with the decisive support (*upanissaya*), because they are to be acquired at the very moment of the path.

Thus, the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) brought about by the perfection of virtue, and the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*) brought about by the perfection of concentration, succeed through the path alone for one endowed with the decisive support;
therefore, their attainment should be understood as occurring precisely through the realization of the path.

For these specific attainments of these noble ones are indeed similar to the Paccekabuddhas and Sammāsambuddhas in their realization of the Dhamma of Pacceka-enlightenment and Perfect Enlightenment respectively.

And regarding the phrase "and the designation of their specific distinctions therein," the term "of those very [attainments]" (*tāsaṃyeva*) functions as a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) upon what is to be understood.
This was said with reference to the absence of a detailed exposition of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*) in the Vinaya;

for in the Verañjakaṇḍa, only the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) are analyzed. In the second [case], the restriction "of those very same" is made in relation to the four analytical insights, not the three true knowledges; for since those are included within the six direct knowledges, they are indeed analyzed in the Sutta.
In the phrase "and of these," the word "and" (ca) indicates that the remaining [qualities] also exist there.
For in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā), the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), and the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā) are indeed taught.

Desiring to show that while there is no detailed explanation of the analytical insights elsewhere, they are correctly analyzed in that very place, [the author] proceeds according to the method stated below.
Without making a restriction [to the first part], he changed "tattheva" (right there) and placed the restriction [on the latter part].

Now, showing that "one who practices wrongly regarding the Vinaya reaches a failure of virtue by not seeing the fault in transgressing sexual misconduct, thinking: 'Like the touch of soft coverings and such, even contact with women is permissible,'" he said: "In the Vinaya..."
"But one who has practiced wrongly," and so forth. In this context, "those with pleasant contact" (*sukhasamphassāni*) refers to things such as rugs and coverlets.
"Contact that is grasped" (*upādinnaphasso*) is "contact pertaining to women" (*itthiphasso*), which is to say, sexual intercourse. For it was said by him;
that is, it was spoken by the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha. He was indeed a learned expounder of the Dhamma, [who spoke] by way of action, defilement, result, slander, and transgression of the rules.

Among the five kinds of obstacles, he recognized those that are obstacles other than [the five sensual pleasures], but because he was unskilled in the Vinaya, he did not recognize those obstacles consisting of the transgression of formal rules (paṇṇatti). Therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought thus:

"These householders, while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, are even stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. Even monks [who enjoy] pleasing objects cognizable by the eye..."
“They see forms… they touch tangibles cognizable by the body; they enjoy soft coverlets, robes, and so forth—all this is permissible.
Why then are only the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of women impermissible? These too are permissible.
[This statement] compares the flavor of enjoying the sensual qualities (kāmaguṇa), which are blameworthy, with the flavor of enjoying requisites (paccaya) that are blameless.
Having combined both the enjoyment characterized by desire and lust and the enjoyment devoid of desire and lust into one—
like one attempting to join extremely fine thread with coarse hemp, or like one comparing Mount Sineru to a mustard seed—
he gave rise to an evil view and asked: "What was the purpose of the Blessed One, who acted as if he were binding the great ocean?"
“By his own exertion, the first *pārājika* was established;

there is no fault here”—thus, contradicting the knowledge of omniscience, obstructing the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*), and casting stumps and thorns into the Noble Path, he struck a blow at the Wheel of the Victor’s command by saying, “There is no fault in sexual intercourse. Therefore he said: “Thus by the Blessed One...”
“I understand the Dhamma as it has been taught,” and so forth.

In that context, “obstacles” (*antarāyikā*) means: they are called obstacles (*antarāya*) because they come (*eti*), that is, they approach, into the midst (*antara*) or middle of the mental continuum of beings by way of obstructing various forms of success;
they are misfortunes pertaining to the present life and so on. In the sense of being impossible to transcend, within that obstacle—

They are called *antarāyika* because they either deserve an obstacle to the fruit (*phala*), or because they have the habit of creating an obstacle; what is meant is that they create obstacles to heaven (*sagga*) and liberation (*mokkha*).
These are fivefold by way of action (*kamma*), defilement (*kilesa*), result (*vipāka*), slander (*upavāda*), and transgression of an injunction (*āṇāvītikkama*).
A detailed discussion of them will appear later in the Ariṭṭha training rule (*sikkhāpada*). This, however, is the connection between the words here.
"Those things which have been spoken of, taught, and prescribed by the Blessed One as obstructive and creating obstacles—
if, for one who indulges in those things, they do not become capable or sufficient to act as an obstruction for the sake of obstructing heaven and liberation in such a manner or by such a way,
then in that manner and by that way, I [declare] what has been taught by the Blessed One..."
"I understand the Dhamma. Thereby he reaches a state of immorality; that is, because of that perception of blamelessness, having transgressed, he reaches a state of immorality.
[This is shown] by the passage beginning, "These four, monks... and so forth.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? One who is practicing for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others;
one who is practicing for the welfare of others but not for his own welfare; one who is practicing neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others;
and one who is practicing both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.”
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), he indicates the scriptural texts (suttanta-pāḷi) associated with the teaching on persons (puggala).

"Not knowing the intended meaning" means not knowing the Blessed One’s intention in this way: "This teaching on persons is by way of conventional designation (vohāra), not from the standpoint of ultimate reality (paramattha).
For the teaching of the Blessed Buddha is twofold: the teaching of conventional designation and the teaching of ultimate reality. Therein...
“Person, being, woman, man, kshatriya, brahmin, deva, Māra”—such is a teaching by way of conventional designation (*sammutidesanā*).
“Impermanent, suffering, non-self; the aggregates, elements, bases, foundations of mindfulness”—such is a teaching by way of ultimate truth (*paramatthadesanā*).
In this regard, those who, having heard the teaching by way of convention, have penetrated its meaning and abandoned delusion, are able to attain distinction.

To those who are capable, he teaches the teaching by way of conventional designation (*sammutidesanā*). But to those who, having heard the teaching by way of the ultimate sense (*paramatthavasena*), have penetrated its meaning, abandoned delusion, and are capable of attaining distinction, he teaches the teaching by way of the ultimate sense (*paramatthadesanā*).
In this regard, there is this simile: just as a teacher who is skilled in local dialects and is a commentator on the meaning of the three Vedas...

To those who understand the meaning when it is spoken in the Tamil language, he explains it in the Tamil language; to those [who understand] in one of the Andhaka languages and so forth, he explains it in that language.
Thus, having approached a teacher who is clever and proficient, those young men quickly master the craft.
In this context, the Blessed Buddha is like the teacher, and the three Vedas are like the subject matter to be explained.
The three Piṭakas stand like proficiency in the local language; the proficiency regarding the conventional and the ultimate (sammuti-paramattha) is like young students of various regional dialects;
and the beings to be trained, capable of penetrating [the truth] by way of the conventional and the ultimate, are like those students.

Just as a teacher explains in Tamil and other languages, so too should the Blessed One’s teaching be understood as being given by way of both the conventional and the ultimate. And it is said in this regard:
“The Perfectly Awakened One, the best among speakers, has proclaimed two truths:
the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.
The conventional expression is true by reason of worldly convention.”
“The ultimate meaning is the truth, for it is the actual cause of phenomena.
Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World,
who is skilled in conventional usage, no false speech arises when he employs conventional designations.”

Furthermore, for eight reasons the Blessed One speaks on the discourse concerning the person (*puggala*): for the purpose of illustrating moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*); for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one’s own karma (*kammassakatā*);

for the purpose of illustrating individual personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*); for the purpose of illustrating deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*); for the purpose of illustrating the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*); for the purpose of illustrating past lives (*pubbenivāsa*); for the purpose of illustrating the purification of offerings (*dakkhiṇā-visuddhi*);
and for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention (*lokasammuti*). “Aggregates, elements, and sense-bases...”
When it is said, "They feel shame and dread of wrongdoing," the great mass of people does not understand; they fall into confusion and become resistant, thinking, "What is this?
Are the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases said to feel shame and dread of wrongdoing? But when it is said, "A woman feels shame and dread of wrongdoing;
a man, a kshatriya, a brahmin, a deva, or Māra [feels shame and dread of wrongdoing]," the great mass of people understands and does not fall into confusion.

One does not become an adversary; therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). The same principle applies when it is said: "The aggregates (khandhā) are the owners of karma;

the elements (dhātuyo) and the sense bases (āyatanāni) [are the instruments]. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one's own karma. And when it is said:
"The great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were caused to be built by means of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases."

The same principle applies even when [the aggregates] are spoken of. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (*puggala*) for the purpose of illustrating individual human effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*). The same principle applies even when it is said:
"The aggregates murder the mother, murder the father, murder an *arahant*, commit the shedding of blood, and cause a schism in the Saṅgha;
the elements (*dhātu*) are the sense bases (*āyatana*). Therefore, the Blessed One [speaks of the person] for the purpose of illustrating the immediate offenses (*ānantariya*).
He speaks in terms of a person.

Even when it is said, "The aggregates feel loving-kindness; the elements and the sense-bases [feel it]," the principle is the same. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of a person for the purpose of illustrating the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Even when it is said, "The aggregates recollect past lives; the elements and the sense-bases [recollect them]," the principle is the same.
The same principle applies here. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of a person (*puggala*) for the purpose of illustrating his previous births.

Even when it is said, "The aggregates (*khandhā*) receive the gift; the elements (*dhātuyo*) and the sense-bases (*āyatanāni* [receive it])," the great mass of people does not understand, falls into confusion, and becomes resistant, wondering, "What is this that you call 'the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases receiving [the gift]'? [He says,] "Persons..."
But when it is said, “The virtuous ones of beautiful character accept [it],” one knows this;
one does not fall into confusion, nor does one become an adversary. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating the purification of the offering.
And the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention; they employ worldly designations, worldly terminology, and worldly expressions.
They teach the Dhamma while remaining [within the conventional]. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of a "person" (puggala) even for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention;

thus, it is said that he who does not understand this intention—that the Blessed One’s teaching of a person is by way of this intention and not a teaching of the ultimate truth (paramattha)—is one who lacks such understanding.

“He grasps wrongly” means that he grasps having made a wrong grasp by thinking, “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the cycle of existence, and not another,” and so forth; what is meant is that he grasps it perversely.
For “wrongly grasped” (*duggahita*) is a neuter abstract noun. “With reference to which” means with reference to that...
This refers to grasping what has been wrongly grasped. It should be understood that there is an ellipsis for the words "by means of a doctrine wrongly grasped by oneself.
Alternatively, *duggahitaṃ* is the state of wrong grasping (*duggahaṇaṃ*). In the word *attanā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive;
therefore, it means "by one's own wrong grasping" or "by a perverted apprehension. The phrase "he slanders us as well" means he slanders us too.
He does it. "He digs up himself" means that by digging up his own roots of merit, he is said to dig up himself.
"Reflection on the Dhamma" is the discernment of the intrinsic nature of phenomena. "Running too far" means not remaining within the proper boundary, [thinking]:
"A gift is accomplished merely by the arising of the thought; the mind itself becomes its own object; every mind..."
"An object consisting of non-existent phenomena"—thus he runs too far, proceeding by overstepping [the bounds].

"Four" refers to the four known as the domain of the Buddhas, the domain of psychic power (*iddhi*), the domain of karmic fruition (*kamma-vipāka*), and the domain of the world. For this has been said:
"Monks, these four are inconceivable and should not be contemplated; one who contemplates them will fall into madness and distress..."
One would partake [of madness and frustration]. Which four? Monks, the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable; it is not to be thought about.
One who thinks about it would partake of madness and frustration. Monks, the domain of one in meditative absorption is inconceivable;
it is not to be thought about... Monks, the ripening of kamma is inconceivable; it is not to be thought about... Monks, worldly speculation...
“Unthinkable things are not to be thought about... These, monks, are the four unthinkable things that are not to be thought about;
one who thinks about them would partake of madness and frustration.
In this context, “unthinkable things” is an indication of their intrinsic nature, while “not to be thought about” is an indication of what should be done regarding them.
In this context, "inconceivable" (*acinteyya*) means that which is impossible to conceive; the meaning is that they are not of a nature that ought to be conceived.

Precisely because they are inconceivable, they should not be thought about. Granted, even the six inconceivable things, such as the unique qualities (*asādhāraṇa*), may be reflected upon because they serve as causes for the arising of wholesome states in one who recollects them; however, these [other matters] are not so, because they are fruitless.
The intended meaning is that they should not be reflected upon. For this very reason he said: "One who reflects upon them would partake of madness and distress.
"Of those" means of those Piṭakas.
"This" refers to this word of the Buddha. "Comprising three sections" means by way of what are known as the Sīlakkhandhavagga, Mahāvagga, and Pāthikavagga.
"Those which have a compendium by way of three groups are 'compendia consisting of three groups' (*tivaggasaṅgahāni*).

Regarding the verse 'There are exactly thirty-four suttantas,' the construction of the meaning should be understood as follows: in that collection (*nikāya*), from the count of its suttas, there are exactly thirty-four suttantas;
and because it has a compendium of three groups by way of its grouping, it is a 'three-group compendium. This first collection is the Dīghanikāya; thus it is concordant [with the definition]."
“Not contrary” means that it is called a name according to its meaning (*anvatthanāma*) because it conforms to the sense.

Because it conforms to the sense, it is “conformable” (*anulomika*); and in order to clarify this very state of being conformable, he said, “But why? and so forth. “Even a single group” (*ekanikāyam-pi*) means even a single collection.
“Thus variegated” (*evaṃ cittaṃ*) means thus diverse. “Just as these” (*yathayidaṃ*) means just as these [are]. “Sloping” (*poṇikā*) and “muddy” (*cikkhallikā*).
And the Kṣatriyas; their dwelling is called the Poṇika group and the Cikkhallika group.

Such examples as these—both from the teaching (sāsana) and from common worldly usage—are the proofs and authorities establishing that the word *nikāya* denotes both a "collection" (*samūha*) and a "dwelling" (*nivāsa*). Herein, the first example is: [The text continues with the explanation of the first example.]
It should be understood that the first [classification] is by way of the teaching (*sāsana*), while the second is by way of the world (*loka*).
"Comprising fifteen chapters" means those whose compilation consists of fifteen chapters, beginning with the *Mūlapariyāya-vagga*.
"One hundred and fifty-two suttas" means one hundred and a half; "one and a half" (*diyaḍḍha*) is [formed] with the addition of a half (*aḍḍha*) to the second [hundred].
The meaning is: one hundred and fifty discourses (*sutta*). "In which" means in whichever *nikāya*.
"Comprising fifteen chapters" means it is encompassed and collected by fifteen chapters.
Regarding the reading "seven thousand and seven hundred discourses," [the meaning is] seven thousand and seven hundred discourses.
"And seven hundred" should also be supplied [to the previous phrase]. However, in some places the reading is "seven thousand and seven hundred suttas.
"The Compendium of the Saṃyutta" means the compendium of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
"Shown previously" means shown in the exposition of the Suttanta Piṭaka. What was already stated is here summarized by way of a different method of presentation.
In order to show this, it was said: "the remainder of the Buddha’s word, excluding the four Nikāyas.

For what was already indicated by the passage beginning with "the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," etc., is here stated again in a condensed manner through this alternative formulation. Therefore he said: "excluding these four," and so forth.
"Other than those" (tadaññaṃ) means other than those four Nikāyas; that is to say, the remainder.
"Sabbameva hidaṃ" means "all this indeed. Regarding the phrase "navappabhedaṃ" (ninefold division):
how, then, does this become ninefold? For it must be established by way of nine factors that are free from mutual confusion;
and if that were the case, then the *geyya*-factor and the others would either lack the nature of *sutta*, or else they would possess the nature of *sutta* alone.
If [the Sutta Piṭaka] were to consist of the Geyya and other factors in this way, then the "Sutta" would not exist as a separate Sutta-aṅga at all;

such being the case, it would follow that the Dispensation consists of eight factors. Furthermore, it is stated in the Commentary: "A Sutta with verses is Geyya; a Sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa.
Thus, a so-called Sutta may be either with verses or without verses, and therefore [it is included] within these two factors alone.
Since both of those [categories] are included therein, there is no discourse (sutta) apart from those two that lacks the specific designations such as Udāna and so forth,

which could constitute the *sutta-aṅga*. Furthermore, even if some discourse were somehow to exist separately as a *sutta-aṅga*, then either the *maṅgala-sutta* and others would not be included in the *sutta-aṅga* due to their being in verse (*gāthābhāva*),
like the *Dhammapada* and other such works, or they would instead be included in the *geyya-aṅga* because they contain verses (*sagāthakattā*).
Is it like the Sagāthaka-vagga, or likewise the sections containing verses found in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other texts? It is said:
"Sutta" is a general rule, while others are specific rules;
they are established with their own defining characteristics because of conventional usage, and not through association with anything else.
There is no room for the aforementioned fault here;
therefore, the ninefold teaching of the Teacher is indeed free from confusion.
For "discourse" (*sutta*) is the general designation for all the Buddha’s word. Thus it is said: "This much of his..."

Because of such statements as, "That which has come down in the Suttas of the Blessed One, is included in the Suttas, [found] in the Sutta-vibhaṅga at Sāvatthī, and in our own school (sakavāda) there are five hundred suttas," the designation "sutta" is seen even in the specific categories of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
For this very reason, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the *Nettippakaraṇa*: "The investigation of the ninefold suttanta. Therein:
Indeed, the search for, the seeking out of, and the investigation of the meaning of the ninefold teaching by way of the Sutta and the other divisions is called "the search for the ninefold Suttanta.
Among its parts, however, specific types such as the Geyya are established by their respective characteristics.
For instance, the fact that the Geyya contains verses (*sagāthakatva*) is its defining characteristic; for even in the world, that which is accompanied by verses is called *sagāthaka*.

Or they call the *cuṇṇiyagandha* (the prose collection) "Geyya. However, when it is devoid of verses, the state of providing an answer after having posed a question is the defining characteristic of *Veyyākaraṇa*.
For the answering of a question is called "byākaraṇa" (explanation). *Veyyākaraṇa* is simply an elaboration (*veyyākaraṇa*) of that explanation.
This being so, [it applies] even to those works such as the *Sagāthaka*, which proceed by way of posing questions and providing answers.
Does it attain the status of a *veyyākaraṇa* (expository prose)? It does not.

Because there is no occasion for the designations of *geyya* and so forth, and because the rule for what lacks an occasion is stronger than that which has an occasion, and also because of the specific qualification "when there is an absence of verses.

For instance, in the *Dhammapada* and other such works, even though they consist entirely of verse compositions (*sagāthaka*), and even when joined with verses consisting of joy and knowledge, and connected with statements such as "For this was said," [they are not considered *veyyākaraṇa*].

And regarding specific discourses associated with marvelous phenomena (*abbhutadhamma*), the designations "verse" (*gāthā*), "inspired utterance" (*udāna*), "thus-it-was-said" (*itivuttaka*), and "marvelous phenomenon" (*abbhutadhamma*) are established according to their respective order.

For here, even though there is the application of other designating causes, the designations such as "verse" are established solely by virtue of the predominance of the designation of non-occasion (*anokāsa*).
Likewise, even though they possess the nature of being composed in verse, those [discourses] that proclaim the power of the conduct of the Blessed One in his past births—
The designation *jātaka* is established because the perception of "birth stories" (*jātaka*) is firmly fixed;

and the designation *vedalla* is established because it causes the Veda to be obtained in certain Suttantas, despite their having the nature of question-and-answer and containing verses (*sagāthaka*).

Thus, by such respective characteristics as containing verses and so forth, the designations *geyya* and the rest are established for those specific Suttantas; therefore, *geyya* and the others are particular modes belonging to the category of Sutta.

However, that which is here devoid of the characteristics of the *geyya* factor and so forth is the *sutta* factor, because it proceeds by means of a general designation (*sāmañña-saññā*) through the avoidance of specific designations (*visesa-saññā*).

But is it not the case that even if this were so, the objection remains in force—that the *sutta* factor is impossible—given that "a sutta with verses is *geyya*, while a sutta without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*"?

No, that objection does not hold, because [the definition] has been clarified. For it has been clarified: [...]* (The text continues with the clarification of the definitions. *Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence regarding the clarification.*
Previously, when there was an absence of verses, the state of posing questions and providing answers was the defining characteristic of a *veyyākaraṇa*;

that [characteristic] is the cause for its being so designated. As for what was said—"Because of the absence of verses, the *Maṅgalasutta* and other such texts would not be included among the *sutta*-limbs"—that is not so, because the designation is conventional (*nirūḷha*).
For the status of being a *sutta* is conventionally established for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others; they are not like the *Dhammapada*, the *Buddhavaṃsa*, and so forth.
They are not renowned as being in the form of verses (*gāthā*), but rather precisely as being in the form of discourses (*sutta*).

For that very reason, the name "discourse" (*suttanāmaka*) was assigned to them in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As for what was said—"Because it contains verses, it might be included in the *geyya* division"—that too is not the case, because it is accompanied by something else.
For "being accompanied" (*sahabhāva*) exists in meaning through another; thus, [it means] "together with verses."

And [the term] *sagāthaka*. There is no portion of a sutta in the *Maṅgalasutta* and other such texts that is devoid of verses (*gāthā*) such that it could be called "together with verses" (*saha gāthāhi*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that a collection of verses is something other than the individual verses, and thus, by virtue of that [collection], it is possible to say "together with verses" (*saha gāthāhi*) as *sagāthaka*? [Response: That is not so; for [a collection] is not separate from its constituent parts.

There is no such thing as a "composite" (samudāya) that exists as a distinct entity. As for what was said—that "portions containing verses from the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth might be included within the *Geyya* factor"—that too is not the case.

For those verses are indeed different, being comprised within the *Jātaka* and other categories. Furthermore, it is not by virtue of those verses that the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth possess the status of being *Geyya*.
Thus, one should understand the absence of mutual confusion among the factors, such as the *Sutta* and the rest.

Now, having analyzed the ninefold division beginning with the Sutta, he says: "In that regard, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, and Parivāra," and so forth. Therein, the Niddesa is as follows in the Suttanipāta:
"When one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them, he surely becomes joyful in mind, having gained what a mortal man wishes for."
Of the Aṭṭhaka-vagga, which begins with:
“By what is the world shut in? (Thus asked the Venerable Ajita;
By what does it not shine forth?”
"Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi,
kiṃsu tassa mahabbhayan?"—
with these words begins the Pārāyanavagga as it has come down to us.
“Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
and not harming even one among them,
he would desire neither a son, much less a friend.”
The *Mahāniddesa* and the *Cūḷaniddesa* are so called because they were composed by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta— the General of the Dhamma, who was like the Teacher himself—
as an exposition analyzing the meaning of the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta*, which begins with the words: “Let one wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
Thus, it should be understood that the inclusion of the Sutta-aṅga within the Niddesa was shown by the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa.
Furthermore, in all other places, such as the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and others, the inclusion of the Sutta-aṅga within the Niddesa is shown precisely as:
"The two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra. This was also stated by the Elder Teacher Dhammapāla in his commentary on the *Nettipakaraṇa*.

Thus, the inclusion of this [text] within the *sutta* factor has been explained. However, some maintain that it is included within two of the factors of the *niddesa*: the verses (*gāthā*) and the prose exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*).

For this was stated by the Elder Upasena in the *Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā*: “This Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka—among these three Piṭakas, it is comprised within the Suttanta Piṭaka.”
Among the five great collections— the Dīghanikāya, Majjhimanikāya, Saṃyuttanikāya, Aṅguttaranikāya, and Khuddakanikāya—

it is included within the Khuddaka Mahānikāya; and among the nine factors of the Teacher’s dispensation— sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla— it belongs to these as appropriate.
"...is included within the two factors of Gāthā and Veyyākaraṇa.
Here, while it may be appropriate that a portion of the Niddesa is included in the Veyyākaraṇa factor because its nature consists of questions and answers, one must investigate this:
how could its inclusion in the Gāthā factor be justified? [This applies to] the *Dhammapada* and so forth...
For the mere fact of being composed in verse is the cause for the designation "verse" (*gāthaṅga*) in that sense.

Indeed, the conventional term "verse" is established only for those works consisting solely of verse compositions, such as the *Dhammapada*; moreover, no portion consisting solely of verse composition is found in the *Niddesa*.
This is because [the term applies] only to those verses spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One and included within the *Aṭṭhakavagga* and other such collections.

The Dhammasenāpati has provided merely a commentary (*niddesa*). For even those root verses included in the *Aṭṭhakavagga* and so forth, though brought here for the purpose of analyzing the meaning, do not count as "commentary" because they are distinct from it due to being contained within the *Suttanipāta*.
Likewise, verses contained in the *Jātaka* and other collections do not receive that designation, even though they appear in such works as the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*.
Like the verses, therefore another reason must be sought here, or a more appropriate [explanation] should be accepted.

Regarding the *Nālakasutta* and the *Tuvaṭṭakasutta*: here, the *Nālakasutta* refers to [the account of] one who, having seen a disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara practicing the way of moneyya (monkhood), and desiring that same goal, from then on for a hundred thousand eons...
On the seventh day after the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the Venerable Nālaka Thera— the nephew of the seer Asita who had come having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs)—
asked the Blessed One about the practice of the noble way (moneyyapaṭipadā) with the two verses beginning, “This has been understood. In response,
the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Nālaka Thera the discourse beginning with, “I shall explain the noble way to you,” which elucidates the practice of the noble way.
The Sutta. As for the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta, after the Buddha had caused himself to be questioned by the Emanated Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) with the words,

"I ask you, O Kinsman of the Sun," in order to clarify that matter for certain deities who had gathered during the teaching of the Mahāsamaya Suttanta and whose minds were wondering, "What indeed is the practice for attaining Arahatship?"—

The discourse beginning with “The root of conceptual proliferation (*papañcasaṅkhā*)” has been cited. Thus, the inclusion of the discourses within the Sutta-aṅga for those such as the *Maṅgalasutta* found here in the *Sutta Nipāta* has been shown;
now he will show the inclusion of the Gāthā-aṅga for the pure verses (*suddhikagāthā*) that appear in that very same collection but do not bear the name of a discourse (*asuttanāmikā*).
This being so, at the commencement of the commentary on the *Sutta Nipāta*:
“If it is filled with hundreds of verses (*gāthā*) and marked by *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa*,
why has it come to be designated as the ‘Sutta Nipāta’?”—
Why is it objected that the entire Sutta Nipāta is included within the *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa* divisions [of the Khuddaka Nikāya]? This is not a contradiction.

For in that context, one should understand that the "Coda" (Exhortation) consists merely of the exhortation itself, having taken from it only the fact of being with verses (*sagāthaka*) and, in some instances, mere questions and answers.
Otherwise, since there would be no sutta at all in the Sutta Nipāta that is without verses (*niggāthaka*), its inclusion within the *Veyyākaraṇa* division would not be tenable.
Thus, the section containing verses (*Sagāthāvagga*) should be connected with the term *geyya*. [End of] "By eight..."
"Included among the [other] factors (aṅga) are the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and so forth"—this is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, some maintain that the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* is included within the two factors of *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa*. For it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Among the nine factors of the Teacher’s dispensation, it is included within the two factors of *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa* as far as possible."

“Nosuttanāmikā” means those whose names do not appear in the Suttas. Regarding the statement, “The ‘pure verses’ (suddhikagāthā) are the narrative verses (vatthugāthā),” this is stated in three commentaries (gaṇṭhipada). Therein, the narrative verses are:
“The Kosalan king, formerly of delightful city, went to the Southern Land, Desiring the state of nothingness, a brahmin who had mastered the mantras.”

The fifty-six verses spoken by the Venerable Elder Ānanda at the time of the Council while introducing the introduction to the *Pārāyana-vagga*, as well as those spoken by the Elder Ānanda himself at the time of the Council while introducing the introduction to the *Nālaka-sutta*:
“When the host of the Thirty-three had assembled and approached,
and when Sakka the Lord and the gods in their bright raiment [were present]...”
“Taking up a cloth, they were praising him exceedingly;
the seer Asita saw them during his midday rest.

These and about twenty other verses are recited. Regarding this, it is stated in the Commentary: “The introductory verses of the Nālaka Sutta are counted as part of the Nālaka Sutta itself. For this is said in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*:
But when the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, while conducting the communal recitation (saṅgīti),
questioned the Venerable Ānanda regarding that very practice of the noble way (moneyyapaṭipadā).
Desiring to make manifest everything— including how and when he exhorted Nālaka and what Nālaka asked the Blessed One— he spoke the twenty introductory verses beginning with “Ānandajāte.”
He spoke; all of that is called the Nālaka Sutta.

Therefore, since the introductory verses (vatthugāthā) of the Nālaka Sutta are included by the very mention of the Nālaka Sutta, it should be understood that the introductory verses of the Pārāyanavagga are what are meant here by "pure verses" (suddhikagāthā).
Furthermore, therein, in the Pārāyanavagga itself, [the verses] of Ajita Māṇavaka and the others...
