It is also appropriate to say that the sixteen questions of the brahmins and the Blessed One’s verses in response to them are here called "pure verses" (*suddhikagāthā*).

For it is fitting to call them "pure verses" not named after specific suttas, because they appear in the Canon under names such as "The Questions of the Young Brahmin Ajita" and "The Questions of the Young Brahmin Tissametteyya," and because they are unmixed with the prose commentaries (*cuṇṇiyagantha*).
Now, defining the *udāna* according to its specific nature, he said: "Connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge," and so forth.
In what sense, however, is this called an "inspired utterance" (*udāna*)? In the sense of being "uttered" (*udānana*). What is this thing called an *udāna*?
It is an expression brought forth by the surge of rapture (*pīti*). For just as when a substance to be measured, such as oil, cannot be contained within a measuring vessel, it overflows—
That which flows and is called "an irrigation stream" (avaseka), and that water which is unable to enter a pond but flows over it,
is called "a great flood" (mahogha); even so, when the expansion of applied thought (vitakkavipphāra) produced by the surge of joy is unable to be contained within the heart,
it becomes excessive and, instead of settling inside, issues out through the door of speech.
An utterance that has issued forth, independent of a recipient, is called an *udāna*.
This form is indeed found even by way of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*). It occurs in some instances as verse composition and in others as prose. For example:
"Now at that time, the Blessed One was instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna..."
He incites, inspires, and gladdens them. Those monks, having made it their bone, having applied their minds, having focused their whole hearts, and lending an attentive ear, listen to the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance: “There is, bhikkhus, that sphere where there is neither earth nor water.”
In these cases, it occurs by way of speech arising from joy and knowledge.

But is it not true that what is called an *udāna* is an utterance produced by rapture and joy, or produced by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding the Dhamma, and is independent of any recipient of the teaching;
and since this is how it is recorded everywhere, why does the Blessed One here address the bhikkhus while uttering an *udāna*?
It was for the purpose of instructing those bhikkhus.

For after the Blessed One had taught those bhikkhus the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), prompted by the joy and gladness arisen through recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna:
"In this world, every conditioned phenomenon (sabhāvadhamma) except for Nibbāna is found to exist solely in dependence upon conditions; it does not exist independently of conditions."
"But how is this dhamma of Nibbāna apprehended as being without a cause?"—perceiving the reflection in the minds of those bhikkhus and wishing to inform them, he said:
"There is, bhikkhus, that sphere," and so forth. It should not be understood that he addressed these words solely to those who were recipients [of his teaching].
"If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you..."
"Do not commit an evil deed, whether openly or in secret"—
this and similar passages should be understood as *udāna* (inspired utterances) that arise through the power of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*).
"He who harms with a stick beings who desire happiness..."
"Seeking his own happiness, he does not find happiness after death"—this too they call an *udāna* arising from a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*).
For at one time, a large number of cowherds were striking a snake with sticks between Sāvatthī and Jetavana. At that same time...
As the Blessed One was going to Sāvatthī for alms, he saw those boys on the way striking the snake with a stick.
Having asked, "Why, young men, do you strike this snake with a stick?

and being told, "Out of fear of its bite, venerable sir," he said, "These boys, striking it while thinking 'we shall bring ourselves happiness,' will experience suffering in the place where they are reborn."
"Ah, the skill in drawing near to ignorance! Thus he gave rise to a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*).

And by that very same spiritual urgency, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*). It should be understood that these [utterances] occur in some cases by way of verse composition, in some cases by way of prose sentences, in some cases by way of joy, and in some cases by way of spiritual urgency. Therefore, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)...
Regarding the definition of an *udāna* stated as "connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge," it should be understood that this is stated by way of the majority.

For, generally speaking, an *udāna* is spoken in verse form and is originated by rapture and joy. This [type of utterance] is threefold: that spoken by an omniscient Buddha, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha, and that spoken by a disciple. Among these, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha—
“Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
not harming even one among them”—
this and more is found in the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta*. There are also verses spoken by disciples:
“All passion has been abandoned by me; all hatred has been uprooted;
all delusion has been dispelled by me; I have become cool and am extinguished.
Thus it is said in the *Theragāthā*.
“I was restrained in body, and likewise in speech and mind;
having uprooted craving with its very root, I have become cooled and extinguished.
These verses are found in the *Therīgāthā*. There are also other words spoken by deities such as Sakka: “O, what a gift! A supreme gift!”

There are indeed *udānas* such as "Well-established in Kassapa" and those spoken by people such as the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, beginning with "Homage to that Blessed One," which were included in the three councils; however, those are not what is intended here.
Rather, it refers to those which were spoken directly by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself and constitute the word of the Victor (*jinavacana*).
And these very [verses] were compiled by the Dhamma-recorders as the "Udāna.
It is with reference to these that it was stated, by one who was reciting the Blessed One’s Pariyatti-dhamma after dividing it into nine categories, that they constitute the Udāna.
As for the verses beginning with "Through many a birth in saṃsāra," which were uttered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the manner of an Udāna—
These [verses] were utterances (*udāna*) of many hundreds of thousands of Perfectly Enlightened Ones;

because they were later taught by the Blessed One to the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda), the compilers of the Dharma did not include them in the *Udāna-pāḷi*, but instead included them in the *Dhammapada*.
Furthermore, as for the utterance "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! which [resounded] throughout the ten-thousandfold world system...
The proclamation uttered by the Blessed One, which resounded with a resonance capable of being heard by gods and humans,
was likewise at the conclusion of the teaching of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* during his first awakening; it was caused by all the bhikkhus reflecting upon their correct practice,
similar to the statement beginning, "Indeed, on one occasion the bhikkhus have pleased me."
Because the Elder was the very first among his disciples to realize that portion of the Dhamma he himself had attained— the Noble Path as it was taught—
this utterance, born of rapture and gladness due to reflecting on the fruitfulness of his own exertion, is merely a formal expression;
it is not like the statement beginning with "When indeed phenomena become manifest," which concerns both their arising and their cessation.
Or, "it was not proclaimed" should be understood as meaning it was not included in the *Udāna* collection by the compilers of the Dhamma.

And in the *Udāna* collection, in the eight chapters beginning with the Bodhivagga, exactly eighty suttas were recited, ten being grouped together in each chapter. For this very reason, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*:
"There are exactly eighty suttas; in brief, there are eight chapters."
And ninety-five verses have been proclaimed in the Udāna.
As for its measure, it consists of eight and a half recitation-sections (*bhāṇavāra*);
likewise, there are eighty-one thematic transitions (*anusandhi*) in the Udāna.
“The wise one should point out that twenty-one thousand and seven hundred verses have been calculated as the total number of lines for this Udāna.”—
Furthermore, according to the verse-quarter:
“There are eight thousand and four hundred introductory verses (padāna),
and twenty-three [hundred] explanatory verses (udāna).
There are six thousand seven hundred syllables.”
“And likewise, eighty-three [sections] have been proclaimed for the Udāna.
But here it is stated, “eighty-two suttantas,” which does not agree; therefore, the reading should be “eighty suttantas.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “‘Thus have I heard, spoken by the Arahant: Bhikkhus, abandon one thing...’”
“I am your guarantor for non-returning. What is that one dhamma? Abandon greed, monks; I am your guarantor for non-returning.
In this way, the one hundred and twelve discourses compiled in the *Itivuttaka* Piṭaka according to the categories of single, pairs, triads, and tetrads are known as the *Itivuttaka*.
Pointing this out, he said, “For it has been said,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “one hundred and ten suttantas,” there must also be a reading here as “one hundred and twelve suttantas.

For indeed, in the *Itivuttaka* collection, there are twenty-seven suttantas in the Ekaka-nipāta (Single Chapter), twenty-two in the Duka-nipāta (Pair Chapter), fifty in the Tika-nipāta (Triplet Chapter), and thirteen in the Catukka-nipāta (Quadriplet Chapter); thus, there are exactly one hundred and twelve suttantas in the *Itivuttaka* canon.
They have arrived. And for that very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi:
“Greed, hatred, and delusion, anger, with malice as the fifth;”
Pride and all [other] pride;
greed with hatred makes thirteen.
Delusion, anger, and then hypocrisy;
The hindrances and craving as the fifth;
the two types of trainees and concord;
with the corrupt hell, there are thirteen.
“‘Pasannā ekamābhāyi’—the fifth person by way of the past;
thus, twenty-seven types of merit pertaining to the acquisitions (opadhika) have been proclaimed.
By such summary verses (uddānagāthā), one hundred and twelve suttas are shown after being counted. For that very reason, it is also stated in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā):

It is stated: “In the Suttanta, there is a collection of one hundred and twelve suttas—namely, twenty-seven in the Ekakanipāta (Single Chapter), twenty-two in the Dukanipāta (Pair Chapter), fifty in the Tikanipāta (Triplet Chapter), and thirteen in the Catukkanipāta (Quadriplet Chapter).
Granted, in this context, a slight deficiency or excess in the count does not affect the total;
thus, just as one would say “eighty khandhaka-vattas” when it should be said “eighty-two khandhaka-vattas,” so too [one may say] “one hundred and twelve suttantas.”
Although it could be said that "one hundred and ten suttas" might have been stated, nevertheless,
when one intends to show the measure in such a context, it must be presented by specifying it exactly as it is; therefore, the reading should be "one hundred and twelve suttas."

It is called a *jātaka* because it makes known (*kāyati*), tells (*katheti*), and reveals (*pakāseti*) the past conduct of the Blessed One—what was born, what came to be, and what occurred in former times.
“Monks, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda. What are the four?
Monks, if a company of monks approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him, they are satisfied even by the sight of him. In that regard...”
When Ānanda speaks on the Dhamma, she is pleased by what he says, yet, monks, the assembly of bhikkhunīs remains unsatisfied;
then Ānanda falls silent. If an assembly of bhikkhunīs... [and so on] ...if an assembly of laymen...
[and so on] ...or an assembly of laywomen approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him, they are pleased by the mere sight of him. If, in that situation, Ānanda—
"He speaks the Dhamma, and even though he has spoken, that assembly of female lay followers remains delighted and still unsatisfied;
then Ānanda falls silent. These, monks, are the four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda.
All discourses (suttantas) occurring in this manner, connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, [should be understood in the same way].
Showing what is meant by "a marvelous phenomenon" (*abbhutadhamma*), he said, "These four, monks," and so forth.

It should be understood that the discourse spoken by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā when questioned by the lay follower named Visākha in the *Cūḷavedalla* and other texts is the *Cūḷavedalla*. As for the *Mahāvedalla*, it was [spoken] by the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika...
The *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta* was spoken by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta when he was questioned by the bhikkhus;

it is included in the *Majjhima Nikāya*. However, the *Sakkapañha-sutta* was spoken by the Blessed One when he was questioned by Sakka, and it should be understood as being included in the *Dīgha Nikāya*. The *Mahāpuṇṇama-sutta* is also [included therein].
On the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon, when asked by a certain bhikkhu, this was spoken by the Blessed One;
it should be understood as being included in the Majjhima Nikāya. "Veda" means knowledge.

"Tuṭṭhi" (joy) refers to the state of exultant appreciation that arises through such expressions as "Excellent, Noble Lady! or "Excellent, Friend! upon understanding the Dhamma teaching as it was spoken.
“Joy and gladness. *Laddhā laddhā* means having obtained, having obtained; it is said to mean having obtained again and again.
Having thus analyzed the entire word of the Buddha by way of its factors (*aṅga*), he now says, “How [is it] by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*)?
and so forth, desiring to explain it by analyzing it according to the aggregates of the Dhamma. Therein, “by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma” means:
By way of the mass of the Dhamma. "I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, and two thousand from the bhikkhus"—this is the connection.
Therein, "from the Buddha" means I learned from the Perfectly Enlightened One;
the meaning is that I acquired eighty-two thousand more than two thousand aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*) in the presence of the Teacher. "Two thousand from the bhikkhus" means...
"I learned two thousand sections of the Dhamma from the Bhikkhus; I acquired them from such Bhikkhus as the Dhammasenāpati and others.
For it is on account of the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta* and other discourses spoken by the Elder Sāriputta and others that it is said, "two thousand from the Bhikkhus.
As for the "eighty-four thousand," this is the total when those two figures are combined, amounting to four thousand in excess [of eighty thousand].

Eighty thousand. "Those teachings that proceed for me" means those teachings which proceed for me—being well-mastered, present on the tip of the tongue, and revolving upon the tongue—are what is meant by the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).
Some, however, making the word-division "ye ime," [interpret it as] "those which are these teachings of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and of the monks..."

"Those that were current, those propagated by them; from among these, I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha and two thousand from the Bhikkhus—thus there are eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma. This is how they explain the connection here.
And herein, the Subha-sutta and the Gopakamoggallāna-sutta were [recited] by the Elder Ānanda after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna.
Because it has been spoken, is it included within the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma, or is it not? Regarding this, first, in the *Paṭisambhidāgaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"It should be understood that he spoke thus after having summarized the aggregates of Dhamma spoken by himself as they were received from the Bhikkhu.
However, because it was spoken while standing upon the method given by the Blessed One, even those aggregates of Dhamma spoken by himself [are included].
Regarding the phrase “he took from the Buddha,” it appears more appropriate here to say that this was spoken after having been compiled;
for disciples teach the Dhamma by abiding within the method bestowed by the Blessed One himself.
It is for this very reason that even the *Kathāvatthu* treatise, though spoken by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa during the Third Council, came to be known as "spoken by the Buddha."
And for that very reason, when the Venerable Ānanda Thera was compiling the Saṅgīti, he stated "Thus have I heard" even regarding the Subha Sutta and others spoken by himself.
Thus, by way of the categories of Dhamma thus elucidated, the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna said: "You are one of great learning..."

When asked, "How many Dhammas spoken by the Teacher have been retained by you, who are well-known in the Buddha’s dispensation? the Venerable Ānanda Thera gave this reply by way of the aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) thus: "I received eighty-two from the Buddha," and so forth. Because it proceeds by way of explaining the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) starting from the passage, “This, bhikkhus, is the one-way path for the purification of beings,” etc., it is called “having a single connection” (*ekānusandhika*).
That which has multiple connections (*anekānusandhika*) is that which has various connections, such as the *Parinibbāna Sutta* and others.
For the *Parinibbāna Sutta* consists of various teachings on the Dhamma in different locations.
Because it proceeds by way of [various] sections, it is called "having many connections. Regarding the posing of questions within the metrical compositions (gāthābandha):
"How many should one cut off? How many should one abandon? How many should one cultivate further?
How many bonds has the bhikkhu transcended that he is called 'one who has crossed the flood'?"—thus [it is asked].
The meaning is that the posing of questions according to such a method as this constitutes one aggregate of the Dhamma.
“Cut off five, abandon five, develop five further;
the bhikkhu who has transcended five is called ‘one who has crossed the flood. — [Dhp 255]

It should be understood that the response proceeds in this manner and other similar ways. The *Tikadukabhājana* (the Exposition of Triplets and Couplets) should be understood by way of the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* (Section on Enumeration) and the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* (Section on the Commentary).
Therefore: "Wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states;
states associated with pleasant feeling, states associated with painful feeling, states associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling..."
In the *Nikkhepakanda*, in the context of analyzing the "Wholesome Triplet" among such triads as "associated states," it is stated:
"Which states are wholesome? The three wholesome roots: non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*);
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with them; and bodily action and verbal action originated by them."
mental action. These states are wholesome. “What states are unwholesome?

The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion; the defilements associated with them; the aggregate of feeling associated with them... [and so on] ...mental action. These states are unwholesome.
“What states are indeterminate? The results of wholesome and unwholesome states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.”

“The aggregate of feeling that is not included [in the mundane], …pe… the aggregate of consciousness; those states which are functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not the result of kamma;
all form (rūpa); and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). These states are indeterminate (abyākata).
This is one aggregate of dhamma. In this way, it should be understood that for each of the remaining triads as well, the analysis of each individual triad constitutes one aggregate of dhamma.
Likewise, regarding the pairs (duka) such as "states that are roots" and so forth, that which was stated by way of analyzing each individual pair—namely, "Which states are roots?

Three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and three indeterminate roots," and so on—in that context too, the analysis of each individual pair constitutes a single aggregate of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha). Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*—
“Which phenomena are wholesome? Wholesome states in the four planes. These phenomena are wholesome. Which phenomena are unwholesome?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. These phenomena are unwholesome. Which phenomena are indeterminate?
Resultant states in the four planes, functional-indeterminate states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna. These phenomena are indeterminate.”

In this way, among the "triplet-classifiers" (tikabhājana) that proceed by means of classifying the wholesome triad and so forth, each classifier for a single triplet constitutes one aggregate of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha). Likewise, among the "dyad-classifiers" (dukabhājana) that proceed according to such methods as:
"Which phenomena are roots? The three wholesome roots, the three unwholesome roots, and the three indeterminate roots," each individual dyad-classifier constitutes one aggregate of the Dhamma.
Thus, the classification of the aggregates of the Dhamma should be understood here by way of these triplet and dyad classifiers.
Regarding the phrase "each single section of the exposition of consciousness":

here, in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (Section on the Arising of Consciousness), which proceeds according to the method beginning with, "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen that is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and has a visible form as its object... at that time there is contact...
up to... there is non-distraction," each single section of the exposition of consciousness constitutes a single category of the Dhamma.

It should be understood. Regarding the phrase "one category of the Dhamma" (*eko dhammakkhandho*): since it has been stated that "the classification into ones, twos, and threes is the classification of each individual mental cycle," the meaning should be understood as "each single category of the Dhamma.

For even if the word "each" (*ekeko*) were not explicitly mentioned, this meaning would be understood from the context; thus, it is expressed as "one category of the Dhamma. In passages such as "there is a basis" (*atthi vatthu*), the term *vatthu* [refers to]...

The section on the triads (*tikapariccheda*)—which proceeds according to such methods as "if one is in doubt, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and expiation (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*); if ten days have elapsed and one perceives them as not having elapsed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and expiation"—is divided into categories such as the triads of offenses entailing expiation and the triads of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Now, this [section] is, in its undivided form, of a single type by way of its flavor (*rasa*), and so forth: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya... [etc.]..."

By the community of masters headed by Mahākassapa, who chanted together after defining the word of the Buddha according to its divisions such as the Dhamma and the Vinaya— saying, "These are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma"—
the nature of this Piṭaka as the Vinaya and its status as the Middle Word of the Buddha and so forth were established, adorned as that council was by the manifestation of many wonders.

[The author] shows this. He says, "And not only this," and so forth, in order to show that it was not only this [work] that was chanted after having been established according to its aforementioned divisions, but that there is another as well.

Therein, the *uddānasaṅgaha* (summary of headings) was spoken by the compilers of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgāhakā*) by way of showing a concise collection of the introductory narratives (*vinītavatthu*) and other matters found in the first *pārājika* and subsequent sections.
“Makkaṭī, Vajjiputtā, and Gihī; Naggā and the Tīrthikas;
Dārikā and Uppalavaṇṇā; and two others by way of their characteristics”—these are the initial verses.

The grouping by way of the Sīlakkhandha-vagga, Mūlapariyāya-vagga, and so forth, is the Grouping by Chapter (Vaggasaṅgaha). The determination [of the sequence] by way of the series on superhuman states (Uttarimanussadhamma-peyyāla), the series on the blue wheel (Nīlacakkapeyyāla), and so forth—

The compendium of *peyyāla* (repetitive formulas). The compendium of the *Ekakanipāta* and so forth in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* and other collections. The compendium of the *Saṃyutta* in the *Saṃyuttanikāya* by way of the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and so forth.
The compendium of the *Paṇṇāsaka* in the *Majjhimanikāya* and other collections by way of the *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka* and so forth.
The connection [of the text] is: "As if giving a cry of approval (*sādhukāra*) at the conclusion of the recitation (*saṅgīti*) of this word of the Buddha. "It shook" (*saṅkampīti*).
"Going upwards, it shook violently. "It shook all around" means that going upwards and downwards, it shook completely.

"It quivered" means that going in the four directions, it quivered intensely. "Marvels" (*acchariya*) are those worthy of being struck with wonder, such as the rain of flowers, the tossing of garments, and so forth.
That which was the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*), performed by the compilers of the Dhamma, Mahākassapa and the others...
It is called "Pañcasatā" because it was compiled and chanted by five hundred [monks], and thus she (the collection) possesses those five hundred;
and it is called "Therikā" in the world because it was composed by elders (*thera*), such as Mahākassapa and others, and thus she possesses those elders.
This is the connection: "this is named the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*)."

Having thus shown the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti), [the author], in order to demonstrate the purpose for which it was presented here, spoke the words beginning with “imissā” as a conclusion.
By the Venerable Elder Upāli, the entire introductory narrative (nidānavacana) to be spoken below, beginning with “tena samayena,” was stated, saying that it was “spoken by.
But for what purpose is this being told while the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being discussed?
The introductory statement (*nidānavacana*) has been spoken; but should not the compilation consist only of the words actually uttered by the Blessed One? It is said:
for the purpose of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, credibility, and acceptability of the teaching.

For a teaching established by being bound together with specific indications of time, place, teacher, and audience becomes long-lasting, non-confusable, and credible; [these are] by way of the place, time, agent, cause, and sign.
The determination of the legal procedure is like a formal binding.

And for that very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions such as, "Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* rule laid down?", the Elder Upāli, providing the answers to those questions, spoke the introduction (*nidāna*) of the first *pārājika* beginning with the words, "At that time... and so forth.
Furthermore, the introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation (sāsana).
For the Blessed One, whose every action is embraced by wisdom and compassion, there is no practice devoid of purpose, nor is there any for his own benefit alone;
therefore, every deed of body, speech, and mind performed by the Perfectly Enlightened One—who acts solely for the benefit of others—exactly as it occurred, [is included here].
Being spoken, it is called the *sāsana* (teaching) in the sense of instructing beings as appropriate through the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;

it is not a mere literary composition. This [teaching], composed by the Teacher, is manifested in its various places together with the introductory narratives (*nidāna*) according to the requirements of time, place, teacher, and assembly.
Furthermore, the introductory statement (nidāna-vacana) is intended to demonstrate the authoritative status of the Teaching by way of demonstrating the authoritative status of the Teacher.
And that demonstration of its authoritative status should be understood as being elucidated by these two phrases, "The Buddha, the Blessed One.
For by the word "Buddha," there is the illumination of the Tathāgata’s possession of specific, pre-eminently pure qualities such as knowledge, which are not shared by others.
And by this term "Bhagavā," through the illumination of the abandonment of all stains of defilement, misconduct, and faults such as lust,
hatred, and delusion— and precisely because of that, through the illumination of the state of being the supreme among all beings— this meaning is explained in every respect; thus,
this is merely a demonstration of the primary purpose of the introductory statement here.
In this regard, "this succession of teachers" means this lineage, tradition, and sequence of teachers in that Jambudīpa.
Among those such as Upāli and Dāsaka, the Elder Upāli is indeed well known; however, the Elders Dāsaka and the others should be understood as follows.
It is said that in Vesālī there was a brahmin youth named Dāsaka, who was the senior pupil among three hundred pupils.
Having offered [oblations] and learning the craft in the presence of his teacher, he became a master of the three Vedas at the age of twelve alone.
One day, surrounded by his pupils, after reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya,
he approached the Venerable Elder Upāli, who was residing in the Vālikārāma, and [explained] to the Elder all the difficult points in his own Vedas.
He questioned him. The Elder, having answered everything, himself also asked a question, referring to a name, and posed this question:
"Young man, there is one state that follows after all states;
all states, young man, converge upon one state. What, young man, is that one state? And that young man—
Not understanding the meaning of the question, he asked, "What is this, sir, for those who have gone forth? [The other replied,] "This is a Buddha-mantra, young man.
"But can it be given to me as well, sir? "It can, young man; it can be given to one who has received the going-forth from us.
"Very well, sir, for those who have gone forth," the young man accepted and [went to inform] his mother and father.
Having obtained permission from his teacher, he went forth in the presence of the Elder together with three hundred disciples.
When he had reached the full age of twenty and received full ordination, he attained Arahatship.
The Elder, making him his primary assistant, taught the Tipiṭaka to a thousand monks whose taints were exhausted.
Soṇaka, however, was the co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Dāsaka. It is said that he was the son of a merchant in Kāsī;
when he was fifteen years old, he once went with his parents to Giribbaja for the sake of trade.
From there, having gone to Veḷuvana together with fifty-five other boys, he [beheld] the Elder Dāsaka and his retinue there.

Having seen this, he was filled with exceeding faith; having requested ordination and been told by the Elder, "Go forth," after obtaining his parents' permission, he went before his mother and father. When they were unwilling, he cut off his food;
only then did he obtain their permission, and together with fifty-five children, he went forth in the presence of the Elder.
Having received full ordination, he attained arahantship. The Elder caused him to master the entire word of the Buddha.
He, too, having become a leader of a group, taught the Dhamma and Vinaya to many.
The Elder Siggava, however, was the co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Soṇaka. It is said that Siggava [lived] in Pāṭaliputta.
Having become the son of a minister, while enjoying prosperity in three palaces suited to the three seasons,
one day he went with his friend Caṇḍavajjī, the son of a merchant, and their retinue to the Kukkuṭārāma. There,
seeing the Elder Soṇaka seated having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he paid homage to him.
Realizing that he was not speaking with her, she went and asked the Saṅgha of bhikkhus about the reason for this.
When the bhikkhus told her, "She is not speaking because she has entered a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)," she asked again, "Venerable sirs, how does one emerge from such an attainment?
They replied, "Upon being summoned by both the Teacher and the Saṅgha, [she emerges] after the time previously determined..."

Having said, "And she emerged from the attainment at the exhaustion of her life-span," and having seen that the Elder Soṇaka had been brought out of cessation by the word of the Saṅgha after perceiving the underlying potential (upanissaya) of the prince and his retinue,
[the king] asked, "Venerable sir, why did you not speak with me? When the Elder replied, "Prince, we have finished eating what was to be eaten," [the king asked], "Venerable sir, is it possible..."
Having asked, "May you also feed us," and being told, "It is possible, Prince,
provided you treat those like us as equals," he informed his parents of this matter. With their permission,
together with his own companion Caṇḍavajjī and five hundred men, he went forth under the Elder Soṇaka and received full ordination.
Therein, Siggava and Caṇḍavajjī, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of their preceptor alone, later attained the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā).

As for the successive account of Tissa Moggaliputta, it will be made clear further on. They are called "the Victorious Ones" because they have conquered all adversaries in the form of the defilements (kilesa).
"Victorious ones. "Successively" means in regular order, in due sequence; this is what is meant. "Named Jambuśrī" means having a name like the *jambu* tree;
it is meant that [the island] is named *Jambu*. For because it is distinguished by a great *jambu* tree, the island itself is called "Jambu.
"Making it uninterrupted" means making it imperishable.
By the three terms beginning with *vinayavaṃsa*, only the Vinaya Piṭaka is spoken of, because they are synonymous expressions.
*Pakataññutaṃ* means proficiency; it is said to be a state of cleverness. *Dhuraggāho ahosi* means he was one who took up the burden;
it is said that he took it up having become the leader of all. *Bhikkhusamudāyo* is a collection or assembly of monks; the meaning is a group of recluses (*samaṇagaṇa*).
Thus ends the commentary on the First Great Council in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya commentary.
Now follows the commentary on the Second Council.
The connection is: “When they were extinguished. And having illuminated everywhere—that is, having made that very True Dhamma manifest in all places.
Where it should have been said “possessing radiance” (*jutimanto*), it is stated as “*jutīmanto*” due to the requirements of the verse meter;
the meaning is “endowed with the light of wisdom,” or “possessing splendor,” which is to say, “of great power. “They were extinguished” means by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue.
They attained final Nibbāna. Because all defilements have been abandoned, they have no attachment (*ālaya*)—that is, craving—anywhere;

thus they are "without attachment" (*anālayā*), meaning they are free from lust. "When the Blessed One had been parinibbānized for a hundred years" means: he whose parinibbāna occurred one hundred years ago is "one who has been parinibbānized for a hundred years."
"Lord," it is said, refers to when one hundred years had passed since his final nibbāna. "Vesālikans" means those residing in Vesālī.
"Vajjiputtakas" means sons of families in Vesālī within the Vajjī country.
"The practice of carrying salt in a horn is allowable" means that it is allowable to carry salt in a horn and eat it repeatedly together with saltless alms-food; it is not [allowable] to store it.

The intended meaning is "it makes. "The two-finger-breadth allowance" (*dvaṅgulakappa*) means that it is permissible to eat a meal at an improper time when the shadow has exceeded [the prescribed length] by two finger-breadths.

"The village-boundary allowance" (*gāmantarakappa*) means that for one who has invited others with the thought, "I will go to another village," it is permissible to eat food that is not considered leftover. "The residence allowance" (*āvāsakappa*) refers to [staying within] a single boundary...
The meaning is that it is permissible to perform sangha formal acts, such as the Uposatha, separately in various places and on separate seats.

Regarding "the procedure by way of consent" (*anumatikappa*): it is permissible to perform a formal act with an incomplete assembly while those [monks] have not yet arrived, thinking, "I shall obtain their consent when they arrive," and to obtain their consent afterwards;
the intention is that this does not constitute an invalid (incomplete) formal act.
"Is it allowable? It is allowable by way of customary practice (*āciṇṇakappa*). This means that what has been practiced by teachers and preceptors is allowable.

Furthermore, it should be understood that some such practices are allowable and lawful (*dhammika*), while others are not allowable and unlawful (*adhammika*). "It is allowable as unchurned milk (*amathitakappa*)" refers to milk that has lost its state as milk but has not yet reached the state of curds;
this may be eaten by one who has finished his meal and refused further food, provided it is not considered leftover (*anatiritta*).
The meaning is that it is allowable to eat. Regarding the phrase "it is allowable to drink fermented liquor" (*jalogi*): here, "fermented liquor" (*jalogi*) refers to fresh beer.
The intention is that it is permissible to drink that which consists of fermented ingredients but has not yet reached the state of being intoxicating liquor (*majja*).
Regarding "gold and silver" (*jātarūparajata*): it is called "born" (*jāta*) because, without undergoing any transformation from its original essence, it remains always simply "born form" (*rūpa*).
"Jātarūpa" means that which has form as its nature; it is gold. It is called "rajata" because it shines (rājati) due to its white nature;
it is silver. "Susunāgaputta" means the son of Susunāga.
"Kākaṇḍakaputta" means the son of the brahmin Kākaṇḍaka. "In the Vajjīs" is expressed in the plural because it refers to a country.
It is said. For even a single district is expressed by the plural number due to its being a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*).
"He went to where Vesālī was" means that he went toward whichever direction Vesālī was to be reached, or he arrived at that place where Vesālī is located;
such is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall": here, "Great Wood" (*mahāvana*) refers to a self-grown, uncultivated area with defined boundaries.
"A great forest" (*mahāvana*): Now, the Great Forest (*Mahāvana*) in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu was continuous with the Himalayas, being without boundaries and extending as far as the great ocean;
this [forest] was not like that, so it is called "Great Forest" because it was a large forest with defined boundaries.
As for the Gabled Hall (*kūṭāgārasālā*), it was built within a monastery established adjacent to the Great Forest, with the gabled hall situated inside and covered by a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* roof.
It was fashioned in the shape of a circle of swans.
Regarding the phrase *tadahuposathe*: here, *tadahū* means "on that day" or "on that particular day. It is called *uposatha* because they dwell (*upavasanti*) therein;
it is the day upon which one should dwell. And "they dwell" refers to dwelling by means of virtue, or by means of the total abstention from food.
The meaning is that they dwell having become endowed with fasting, or with the drinking of milk, honey, and so forth.
Furthermore, this day is threefold, being divided into the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth.

Now, the word *uposatha* occurs in reference to the Pātimokkha, to virtue (*sīla*), to the observance (*upavāsa*), and even to the formal proclamation (*paññatti*). For instance, it is said: "Come, friend Kappina, let us observe the *uposatha*..."

In such passages as "We shall go," it occurs in reference to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In such passages as "Thus, Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with eight factors is observed," it occurs in reference to virtue (sīla).
In such passages as "For one who is pure, there is always softwood; for one who is pure, there is always the Uposatha," it occurs in reference to the observance (upavāsa).

And in such passages as "The Uposatha is the name of a king of nāgas," it occurs in reference to a conventional designation (paññatti). Therein, because one must dwell having approached [the precepts], it is called *uposatha*.

*Uposatha* is the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*. It is called *uposatha* because it is to be dwelt in by one who has approached and is endowed [with the precepts], or because it is to be made to dwell within one’s own continuum;
thus, it refers to moral virtue (*sīla*). Alternatively, it is called *uposatha*—meaning "fasting" (*upavāsa*)—because they dwell having approached the restraint of sitting and other such practices.
In the case of specific elephants or horses, it is called *uposatha* merely as a conventional designation; this is a mere description (*paññatti*). However, here [in the rule]: "Monks, do not..."
In such passages as “on that very Uposatha day, from the monasteries containing bhikkhus,” the Uposatha day is intended; therefore, "on that very Uposatha day" means on that Uposatha day.
"A bronze bowl" (kaṃsapāti) means a golden bowl. Regarding "even a kahāpaṇa," and so forth: a half (aḍḍha) is an equal portion of a kahāpaṇa;
a quarter (pāda) is a fourth part. A māsaka is simply a coin of the māsaka type. All of this, first of all, should be explained.
This shows that the entire text (pāḷi) contained in the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka* should be brought here and recited.
To the question, "From where should it be recited? he says: "As far as this Council of the Vinaya (*vinayasaṅgīti*), etc. The connection is: "They recited exactly as it had been recited [previously].
"Based on what was done previously" means based on the First Council (*paṭhamasaṅgīti*) which was performed previously. The connection is: "And this is that Council."
"Among them" means among those elders who were the compilers of the Council. "Renowned" means famous because of their leadership of groups, well-known everywhere.
For in that assembly there were eight great elders who were leaders of groups;
among them, two elders—Vāsabhagāmī and Sumanā—were the co-residents (*saddhivihārikā*) of the elder Anuruddha, while the remaining six were co-residents of the elder Ānanda.
Moreover, all these eight great elders had previously seen the Blessed One. Now, showing those elders according to their individual forms, he said, "Sabbakāmī," and so forth.
"Sāṇasambhūta" refers to the Elder Sambhūta, an inhabitant of the region of Sāṇa. "The second Saṅgha" is the connection [of the verse].
"Pannabhārā" means those who have laid down the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*). As it is said: "The burdens are indeed the five aggregates."

For it has been said: "One who has done what was to be done" (*kata-kicca*) means that one has completed the sixteenfold task—consisting of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing—which is to be accomplished through the four paths regarding the four truths;

thus, they are "one who has done what was to be done. They call a calamity "a swelling" (*abbuda*); even the work of thieves [is so called], having subverted the word of the Blessed One to establish their own doctrine...
“Because it illuminates. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated: “*Abbuda* is a tumor (*gaṇḍo*).
“This” is a demonstrative pointing toward what is about to be explained. “Face-to-face” means appearing directly before one’s eyes.

“The path developed for rebirth in the higher Brahma-world” means the jhāna produced for the sake of rebirth in the higher Brahma-world. For jhāna is here called the “path” because it serves as the means for rebirth there.

For "means" (*upāya*) is called the "path" (*magga*). As for the etymological meaning here, it should be understood thus: it is called a "path" because it seeks out, searches for, produces, and brings about various rebirths.
In terms of its actual nature, this so-called path consists of both volition (*cetanā*) and the mental factors associated with volition;
indeed, it is both of these. "Sāriputta, I know hell, and I know that which leads to hell..."
For here, volition is what is called the "path.
"Faith, moral shame, and wholesome giving—
these qualities are followed by the virtuous."
"For this they call the divine path;
by this one goes to the world of the devas.
Here, the factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) are what is called the "path. As stated in such suttas as the *Saṅkhārūpapatti-sutta*: "This, monks, is the path; this is the way."
Both volition and the states associated with volition are called the "path. Since it is *jhāna* that is intended here, the states associated with volition should be understood.
"Of the brahmin Moggallāna" refers to the brahmin named Moggallāna, who was renowned in the world and childless. But how is this so?
It was stated [in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*] that “he will take rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggallī.
Does rebirth in the sense-sphere realm occur even for those who have attained meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) in the higher realms? It does occur.

And it should be understood that this occurs through the power of a mental aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) on the part of those of great merit who have performed meritorious deeds, but not for everyone. Now, as for sublime (*mahaggata*) weighty karma...
How does a limited (paritta) kamma, having set aside its own maturation (vipāka), create an opportunity for its own result?

Regarding this, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "One falls away from jhāna precisely through the power of attachment (*nikanti*); then, having fallen away from that jhāna, one is reborn.
However, some, having investigated the falling away from jhāna through an attachment that exists even in the state free from hindrances (*anīvaraṇa*), [state as follows:]...
Having said, "It should be accepted," they state the reason for this as follows: "Even though there is no minor karma capable of obstructing the ripening of a sublime (mahaggata) kamma,

because of the statement, 'Bhikkhus, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds due to its purity,' the mental aspiration regarding the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) obstructs the ripening of the sublime kamma and [leads to] the minor kamma..."
"He makes room for the fruition.
Regarding the phrase "Excellent, good man" (*sādhu sappurisa*): here, *sādhu* is a particle used in the sense of a request; the meaning is "we entreat you.

"Exultant and overjoyed" (*haṭṭhapahaṭṭho*) means satisfied again and again through the gladdening of the mind. "Elevated and uplifted" (*udaggudaggo*) refers to the state of rapture produced by a physical transformation.
"Exultantly exultant. For a person who possesses joy is called "exultant" because of the loftiness and elevation of his body and mind.
"Having assented with 'Very well'" means having given the reply, "Very well. "Having concluded" means having brought it to a close.
"They returned again" means they came back once more. "Now at that time" refers to the time when they held the Second Council.
The meaning is "at the time of the agreement. To clarify the same point already stated, it is said "the junior bhikkhus.
"They did not reach that legal issue" means they did not arrive or come to adjudicate that legal issue raised by the Vajjiputtakas.
This connects with the words "they did not become [present]. "This is the disciplinary action" is what must now be explained.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). The connection is: "Having remained for the full span of their lives, they attained final Nibbāna. The meaning is: having remained for as long as the measure of their respective lifespans lasted, they attained final Nibbāna.
But what did those elders do before they attained final Nibbāna? He says: "Having performed the second compilation," and so forth. Also in the future...
The connection is: "They have attained final nibbāna, having made the growth of the true Dhamma their cause.

Now, in order to inspire a sense of urgency by saying, "If even those elders of such great power have fallen under the sway of impermanence, how much more so others?", he spoke the words beginning with "those whose taints are destroyed" while giving this exhortation.
"Under the sway of impermanence" (*aniccatāvasa*) means being subject to impermanence, being dependent on impermanence, or being subservient to impermanence.
"It exists. The connection is: "Having thus understood impermanence—which is base, wretched, difficult to reach, unconquerable, and impossible to transcend.
However, some take the meaning of "durabhisambhava" here to be "impossible to attain," and [interpret it as]:
"The wise person should strive to attain that state which is difficult to reach, eternal, and deathless."
They speak of the connection. "In every way" means that nothing whatsoever that ought to be said has been left out;
the intention is that [the Vinaya] was expounded at the Second Council.
Thus, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā...
The commentary on the account of the Second Council is completed.
Now, for the commentary on the account of the Third Council: those ten thousand Vajjiputtakas were expelled by the Theras who compiled the Dhamma at this [Third] Council.
The monks, seeking a faction, obtained a weak faction suitable for themselves and established it as a separate teacher-lineage called the Mahāsāṅghika.
Having split from that, two other teacher-lineages arose: the Gokulika and the Ekavyāvahārika.
From the Gokulika school, having split further, two other teacher-lineages [arose].
The Paṇṇattivādins and the Bāhulikas arose; "Bahussutikas" is also another name for those very same [groups].

Furthermore, other teacher-lineages called the Antarā-Cetiyavādins arose among them. Thus, in the second century [after the Parinibbāna], five teacher-lineages arose from the Mahāsāṅghika school; together with the Mahāsāṅghikas, there are six.
In that very second century, having split from the Theravāda, two teacher-traditions (ācariyavāda) arose:
the Mahīṃsāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas. Therein, having split from the Vajjiputtaka tradition, four other teacher-traditions arose:
the Dhammuttarikas, the Bhaddayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitiyas. Again, in that very same [second century]...
After one hundred years, having split from the Mahīśāsaka school, two teacher-traditions arose: the Sabbatthivāda and the Dhammaguttika.
Again, having split from the Sabbatthivāda lineage, the Kassapika school was born; when the Kassapikas also split, another school named Saṅkantika was born;
and when the Saṅkantikas split, the Suttavāda school was born—thus [it is said] from the Theravāda perspective.
Having split apart, these eleven teacher-teachings (ācariyavāda) arose; together with the Theravāda, they become twelve.
Thus, these twelve and the six teacher-teachings of the Mahāsāṅghikas—altogether eighteen teacher-teachings—arose in the second century [after the Parinibbāna].
They are known as the "eighteen schools" (nikāya) or the "eighteen teacher-lineages" (ācariyakula); it is precisely these that are meant.
This is the name [of the school]. Among these, it should be understood that seventeen schools are split, while the Theravāda alone is unsplit.
And this has been said in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
“The Vajjiputtakas, those wicked monks, were expelled by the Elders.”
Having gained another faction, many people who spoke what was not the Dhamma assembled in ten thousand and performed the compilation of the Dhamma;
therefore, this recitation of the Dhamma is called the Great Recitation (Mahāsaṅgīti).
“The monks of the Great Council acted contrary to the Teaching;
having split the original compilation, they made another compilation.
They placed the discourses compiled in one place into another.”
They split both the meaning and the Dhamma within the Vinaya and the five Nikāyas.
Not understanding what was taught by way of a method (*pariyāya*) and what was taught without a method (*nippariyāya*),
nor what was of direct meaning (*nītattha*) and what was of indirect meaning (*neyyattha*), the bhikkhus [disagreed].
“Intending one thing they spoke, yet they established another meaning;
through the mere shadow of the phrasing, those monks have destroyed much of the true meaning.
Having discarded a portion of the profound Sutta and Vinaya,”
They composed the *Suttavibhaṅga* and the *Khandhaka*,
as well as other [works] such as the *Parivāra*, the *Aṭṭhuddhāra*, the *Abhidhamma*, the six *Pakaraṇas*,
the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the *Niddesa*, and a portion of the *Jātaka*.
Having relinquished that much, they made others [of themselves]:
"The name, the gender, the requisites, and the modes of deportment—
they abandoned their natural state and made it otherwise."
“The makers of the Great Recitation were the first to have differing doctrines;
following their example, many differing doctrines arose.
Then, at a later time, a schism occurred therein.”
The Gokulikas split into two, O monks, as solitary practitioners.
Later on, two further schisms among the Gokulikas arose:
the Bahussutikas and the Paññattis; thus the monks split into two.
Furthermore, there were those who spoke of cetiyas and those who caused the schism of the Great Council;
all these five proponents are rooted in the Great Council.
They divided both the meaning and the doctrine, as well as a portion of the compilation.
Having discarded a portion of the texts, they composed others.
Abandoning their names, gender, requisites, modes of dress, and natural state,
they made those things into something else.
“In the doctrine of the Elder Visuddha, a further schism arose;
the monks split into two groups: the Mahīśāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas.
In the doctrine of the Vajjiputtakas, a fourfold schism arose.”
The Dhammuttarikas, the Bhaddayānikas, and the Channāgārikas—this was the assembly.
In a later time, two divisions arose among the Mahīśāsakas;
the Sabbatthivādins and the Dhammaguttas—the monks split into two.
“From the Sabbatthivādins came the Kassapikas; from the Kassapikas, the Saṅkantikas.
From the Saṅkantikas arose the Suttavādins, and thus they split in succession.
These eleven schools branched off from the Theravāda.”
They split the meaning and the Dhamma, and compiled only a portion;
having discarded a portion of the texts, they composed something else.
They [altered] the names, the gender, the requisites, and the modes of conduct.
Having abandoned their original nature, they made it something else.
The seventeen schools of schism and the one school that was not schismatic—
all together with that schismatic school, they become eighteen.
Like a great banyan tree, the Elder’s Teaching is supreme.
Without deficiency and without excess, it is the complete teaching of the Victor;
all other doctrines have grown forth from it like thorns upon a tree.
“In the first century there were none;
in the interval of the second century, seventeen schools split off and arose within the teaching of the Victor.
Furthermore, [the schools] are the Haimavatas, Rājagirikas, Siddhatthikas, Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, and Vājīriyas.
Furthermore, six other teachers’ doctrines arose. While the Dispensation was proceeding by way of those previous eighteen teachers’ doctrines,
King Asoka, having gained faith, gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day for the worship of the Buddha,
one hundred thousand for the worship of the Dhamma, one hundred thousand for the worship of the Saṅgha, and [one hundred thousand] for his own teacher, the Elder Nigrodha.
Giving five hundred thousand [pieces of gold]— one hundred thousand for each of the four gates as medicine—

he caused great gain and honor to circulate within the Dispensation. At that time, having purified the manifold stains of the Dispensation raised by the heretics who had lost their own gain and honor,
the Elder Moggaliputtatissa [convened the council] for those who upheld the study of the Tipiṭaka.

Taking one thousand bhikkhus who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he held a council exactly as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa had recited the Dhamma and the Vinaya; thus, while conducting the recitation, he performed the Third Council.
Now, explaining that Third Council in detail from its very beginning, he said: "Then the Great Brahmā Tissa..."
“Having passed away from the Brahmā world, he took rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggallī,” and so forth.
In that context, “he took rebirth in the house” means that he took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin’s wife within the house of the brahmin Moggallī.
However, because the house is the support for that [rebirth], by way of designating the supported by the name of its support, it is said: “he took rebirth in the house.”
“He took [them],” as it is said in such expressions as “the beds cry out” or “the whole village has arrived.
“For seven years” is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). “Aticchatha” means “go beyond and desire”;
the intention is: “Alms are not obtained here; go elsewhere from here and seek alms. “O, you who have gone forth,” and so forth.
The brahmin, not desiring to receive almsfood in his own home, said: "From the prepared meal" means from the meal that has been prepared and set aside.

"Worthy of that" means corresponding to that. "Having seen tranquility" means having repeatedly seen the tranquility of the elder’s body and mind; the meaning is "having known. For by demonstrating the tranquility of the postures, [he demonstrates] that which is bound to it...
The subsiding of the mind through its wise application is also understood. "Having become even more confident" means having become confident again and again, specifically and to a greater degree.
"For the purpose of dismissing the meal" means for the purpose of performing the meal-rite.
"Having consented" means having accepted.
"Designated as sixteen years old" (*soḷasavassuddesika*) means that he is to be designated or spoken of as "sixteen years old";

thus, he is one "designated as sixteen years old. Alternatively, he is one "designated as sixteen years old" because he is worthy of being designated as "sixteen years old," or because he has sixteen years to be designated, or because his designation is "sixteen years old."
"One who has it" (*assa atthīti*) means one who is sixteen years of age; in terms of meaning, however, it is said to be "one who is sixteen years old.

"One who has reached the further shore of the three Vedas" (*tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragūti*): he is a "pāragū" because he has gone to the further shore (*pāraṃ gata*) by way of making the three Vedas—namely, the *Iruveda*, *Yajuveda*, and *Sāmaveda*—thoroughly mastered.

Furthermore, in this context, the term "pāragū" should be understood as a compound beginning with a noun that possesses a constant requirement for a complement (*niccasāpekkhatāya*). "Having hung [it]" (*laggetvā*)...
"Having hung [it]. In the phrase "not even any," the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that not even any talk arises.
"Pallaṅka" refers to a seat upon which one should sit. Regarding the phrase "will arise," here too the word "talk" (*kathā*) must be supplied and connected.
"Angry and displeased" means angry through anger and displeased through dejection (*domanassa*). For a person who possesses dejection is...

"One who is not pleased with joy and happiness, whose mind is not his own," is called *anattamano*. Or, he is *anattamano* because he is not satisfied, since his mind does not abide under his own control.
"The state of ferocity" (*caṇḍikkabhāva*): a person who is fierce and stubborn is called *caṇḍiko*; his state is *caṇḍikkaṃ*, which is the state of being stubborn.

The meaning [of *attha*] here is as follows. Since it is stated as "in the state of ferocity" (*caṇḍikkabhāve*), one should understand that "ferocity" (*caṇḍikka*) itself is what is meant by "the state of ferocity" (*caṇḍikkabhāva*);
therefore, in this context, "the state of ferocity" should be understood to mean "the state of rigidity" (*thaddhabhāva*). "Some spell" (*kiñci mantaṃ*) means some Veda.
"Who else will know? implies that no one at all will know. "It is possible to know by asking" refers to oneself...

Because he was established in partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*), the Elder spoke thus. For only the omniscient Buddhas offer the invitation of omniscience—unique to them and not shared with Paccekabuddhas and others—by saying, "Ask, young man, whatever you desire," and so forth.
Disciples, however, being established in partial knowledge, say, "We shall know after hearing," or "It is possible to know after asking."
Regarding the phrase "in the three Vedas" and so forth: the three Vedas are exactly as described by the method previously stated.
"Nighaṇḍu" refers to the science that elucidates synonyms, such as for names and trees; the meaning of "elucidating synonyms" is "indicating words used in various ways.
What is meant is that it reveals multiple synonymous expressions for each single meaning. This is merely an illustration.
This treatise was composed also by way of elucidating how many meanings are expressed by a single word.
It is called *nighaṇḍu* because it digs up (*nikhaṇḍeti*), breaks open, and shows by analyzing the meaning and the word through their relationship as signifier and signified;
here, the letter *kha* has been changed to *gha*, thus it is called *nighaṇḍu*. *Keṭubha* refers to the various forms of ritual action and prosody.

The *kiriyākappavikappa* is a manual for the assistance of poets. Herein, "kiriyākappavikappa" refers to that by which action—characterized by verbal expression and the like—is fashioned (*kappīyati*) and varied (*vikappīyati*);
furthermore, because it possesses many variations through the analysis of phonemes, word-arrangements, word-meanings, and so forth, it is called the *kiriyākappavikappa*.
This [definition] is stated with reference to the root text of the *Kiriyākappa*.
It has been stated. For that [work] consists of a treatise comprising a hundred thousand measures, such as the *Naya* and the *Cariyā*. As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*):

it is called *keṭubha* because it "drives" (*kiṭati*) or "leads" (*gameti") to the classification of verbal roots and so forth, or because it "fills" (*pūreti*) by bringing them to completion without remainder;

thus it is said to be *keṭubha*. Together with the *nighaṇḍu* and the *keṭubha*, they are "with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*" (*sanighaṇḍukeṭubha*). These are the three Vedas. Among those, [it refers to] "among those with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*."

That by which syllables (*akkhara*) are analyzed according to the divisions of *ṭhāna* (place of articulation), *karaṇa* (organ of articulation), and so forth, as well as according to the divisions of etymological derivation (*nibbacana*), is "the analysis of syllables" (*akkharappabheda*).
This refers to both *Sikkhā* (phonetics) and *Nirutti* (etymology). Together with the analysis of syllables is "that which possesses the analysis of syllables" (*sākkharappabheda*).

Among those [scriptures] that possess the analysis of syllables, the phrase "with history as the fifth" (*itihāsapañcamesu*) means that, having made the *Athabbana-veda* the fourth, it is associated with such expressions as "thus indeed it was" (*itiha āsa itiha āsā*).

The "five, with history as the fifth" (*itihāsapañcamā*) means that the Purāṇas, known as *itihāsa*, constitute the fifth among these; thus there are three Vedas. "In those five, with history as the fifth.
"He does not see for himself" means he does not see by his own power; the sense is that he does not know.
"Ask, and I shall explain"—he spoke thus, perceiving that "all questions are indeed contained within the Vedas."
The two questions beginning with "Whose mind... are stated with reference to the moment of arising of the death-consciousness of an arahant (khīṇāsava) who possesses that death-consciousness.
Therein, in the first question, "it arises" means it arises by virtue of being at the moment of arising;
"it does not cease" means it does not cease because it has not yet reached the moment of cessation. "His mind" refers to the mind of that person.
From that point on, he asks: "Will consciousness cease and not arise? Regarding the second question, beginning with "Or for whom...":
"Will it cease" means for whom consciousness, having reached the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), will cease.
"Will it not arise" means that after the moment of dissolution, either that [consciousness] itself or another will not arise; [this refers to] that person.
He asks: "Does consciousness arise and not cease? Now, among these questions, the first question is one to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīya*).

Therefore, when asked: "For whom does consciousness arise and not cease, will that person's consciousness cease or will it not arise?", this question should be answered as follows: "At the moment of the arising of the final consciousness..."
“Their consciousness arises and does not cease; it will cease and will not arise.
In the case of others, at the moment of the arising of consciousness, their consciousness arises and does not cease; it both will cease and will arise.
For those whose round of existence has been delimited and whose taints are exhausted, this refers to the final death-consciousness (cuticitta).
At the moment of arising, that very death-consciousness of theirs will cease but not arise.
It is said to "arise" because it has reached the state of arising; it does not "cease" because it has not yet reached dissolution.

However, once it reaches dissolution, that consciousness of theirs will cease, and because there is no further rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*), nothing else will arise. This is with the exception of one who possesses the final consciousness and whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

In the case of others—namely, those in training (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), and worldlings (puthujjana)—the consciousness that possesses the moment of arising is said to "arise" because it has reached the state of arising;
it does not cease because it has not yet reached the moment of dissolution. However, once it reaches dissolution, it will certainly cease;
furthermore, in either this or another existence, it will both arise and cease. As for the second [type of consciousness]...
Because this question is restricted to the arising moment of the death-consciousness of an Arahant, it is to be answered categorically;
therefore, when asked, "Is it the case that for one whose consciousness will cease but not arise, his consciousness arises but does not cease?
one should reply, "Yes. For the death-consciousness of an Arahant, occurring at the moment of arising, is already in a state of dissolution.
"Having reached [the present], it will indeed cease; beyond that, it will not arise again.
However, by virtue of being possessed of the moment of arising, it is said that "it both arises and does not cease because it has not yet reached dissolution.
But this young man, being unable to answer these questions in this way, fell into distress; therefore it was said:
“Unable to move the youth either upward or downward,” and so forth.
In that context, “unable to move either upward or downward” means being unable to mentally attend to the upper part of the body while in the lower part, or the lower part while in the upper part;
it means being unable to determine the meaning of the question by connecting what precedes with what follows.
It has been said. First, he explained the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects, beginning with "In this body," saying, "This is the preliminary stage of the mantra.

He said, "Now, one is incapable of falling away from the teaching" because for those who have entered the stream, there is no falling away from the virtue they have undertaken due to their perfection of moral conduct.
"Having returned. "Having expanded" means having expanded the meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths.
"He should be unconcerned about learning the Buddha’s word" is said with the underlying intention that he has already performed what was to be done for the attainment of Arahatship.
To demonstrate his proficiency in the conventions of social discourse, he said, "Venerable sir, my preceptor sent me to you," and so forth.
"He provided water and a tooth-stick" means that he prepared and set out both water and a tooth-stick for the purpose of use.
It is called a *dantapona* because by it one cleanses (*punanti*) or purifies the teeth; thus, it refers to a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*).
Because those possessing virtues are worthy of being supported, the Elder [did this] in order to make manifest for the novice the qualities such as patience, energy, and serviceability.
Without relying on supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*), but investigating by his own nature, he again performed the sweeping and other duties.
Some also say, "He did this for the purpose of taming the novice's mind. "He established the Buddha-word" means he began to have him learn the Buddha-word.
Regarding the phrase "excepting the Vinaya Piṭaka," it is because "the study of the Vinaya is not the proper conduct for novices."
"Excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka, he caused him to master the remainder of the Buddha’s word"—this is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipadas*.
"Though he was still a mere novice" means that from the time of his full ordination (*upasampadā*), he was less than one year in seniority; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, although the Buddha’s word was established in the heart of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, it was [attributed] to him by way of conventional designation (*vohāra*).
It is said, "having placed it in his hand," meaning that they placed the entire word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) in the hand [of Moggaliputtatissa].

Having remained for the full span of their lives, they attained final Nibbāna; that is, by establishing the entire dispensation (Sāsana) in the hands of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, they were freed from the disciplinary penalty (daṇḍakamma) imposed for convening the Second Council, and having remained for the full span of their lives, they attained final Nibbāna.
Regarding the statement "King Bindusāra had one hundred sons": here, the one named Bindusāra was born into the Śākya clan as the son of King Candragupta.

For it was thus that Prince Candragupta, born of a Kṣatriya family, became king in Pāṭaliputra after having been raised in the city of Moriya, which was built by the Śākyan princes who had departed from Kapilavatthu during the battle with Viḍūḍabha.
His son, the prince named Bindusāra, having become king upon the passing of his father, became the father of one hundred and one sons.
"One hundred and one" (*ekasata*) means one and a hundred; the meaning is "a hundred plus one. "Of a single mother" (*ekamātika*) means having the same mother;
it is said that they were born of his own womb. Yet, he had not yet established a unified kingdom.

He said: "Having exercised sovereignty even without being consecrated. "The consecration for sole sovereignty" refers to the consecration performed by way of supreme lordship over the entire Jambudīpa.

Although royal powers are to be attained through the radiance of merit, they—like the remaining distinctions such as the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) which come through the path of Arahatship—arose here specifically through the majesty of the consecration, being the result of perfected application.
He said: "And by the power of his consecration, these royal supernormal powers (rājiddhi) came to him.
In this context, "royal supernormal powers" refers to the majesty inherent in his status as a king. "From which" means from the sixteen-year-old water-pot.

"One who has conceived faith in the Dispensation" means one who has acquired faith in the Buddha's teaching. "Asandhimittā" is her very name. It is said that in her body there were no joints (sandhayo).
They were not recognized, and therefore they say, "A girl named so-and-so was born. The connection is that deities themselves brought [the food] day after day.
*Devasikaṃ* means day by day. *Agadāmalakaṃ* refers to a medicinal myrobalan (*osadhāmalaka*) capable of cleansing the body and removing all impurities with only a small amount.
*Agadaharītakaṃ* is likewise a myrobalan (*harītaka*) of the same kind. Regarding those two...
He enjoys one of the two as he wishes. "From the Chaddanta Lake" means from a celestial mansion situated near the Chaddanta Lake, or from a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*).
Some say, "There are such special trees at the Chaddanta Lake; they bring [the food] from there.
"Divine drink" refers to a drink made from the juice of divine fruits. "Not made of thread" is because it is a divine cloth produced from a wish-fulfilling tree.
"Not made by threads" means not consisting of thread (*asuttamayika*).

"A cloth of *sumana* flowers" means that because it is everywhere fine and possesses flowers that have risen upward, it became known as a "cloth of *sumana* flowers. "Of standing rice" refers to rice that grows spontaneously;
here the singular number is used with reference to the collective whole, meaning "of the rice. "Nine thousand loads": herein, "four handfuls make one *kuḍuva*."
It is stated in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries that: "four *kuḍuva*s make one *pattha*; four *pattha*s make one *āḷhaka*;
four *āḷhaka*s make one *doṇa*; four *doṇa*s make one *mānikā*; four *mānikā*s make one *khārī*;
twenty *khārī*s make one *vāha*, which is the same as one cart (*sakaṭa*). However, in this [text], it is said: "two carts make one *vāha*."
They say: "They make [the sound] while free from husks and chaff" means they make it when devoid of rice-husks and bran. "They make honey" means having come, they make honey in the vicinity.

"They perform an offering" means that, like the inhabitants of the kingdom who perform offerings everywhere, they utter sweet sounds and present the offering. "Having come, making a sound in the sky itself... [they reveal themselves].
“They go without having informed [him],” they say.
A “golden chain bond” (*suvaṇṇasaṅkhalikabandhana*) is a bond consisting of a golden chain.
“Of the four Buddhas” refers to the four Buddhas beginning with Kakusandha. “Having obtained the sight of forms” means having acquired the vision of forms.
It is said that because he was destined to live for an eon (*kappa*), he personally witnessed the physical excellence of all four Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "having had the Naga king named Kāḷa brought," it should be understood that the Naga king came having gone along the Ganges, perceiving that his own feet were touching a golden chain placed there. But is this not the command of King Asoka?
It moves above one *yojana* from below, and this [Nāga]’s palace is established below the limit of one *yojana*;

therefore, how did this Nāga king come at the King’s command? Even though his own palace is established below the limit of one *yojana*, nevertheless, because it is connected as a single unit with the place where the King’s command operates, [he is subject to] his command.
He did so. For just as people living on the border between two kingdoms, being oppressed by their respective kings, act according to the commands of each, they say this is exactly like that.
"Make it appear" means make it manifest before you; the meaning is "make it your object. By that, the form of the Buddha was fashioned.
The connection is with the word "passanto" (seeing). To the question, "Of what kind is that form of the Buddha?", he says: "scattered over the entire body," and so forth.

Therein, the mention of "produced by the radiance of merit" applies also to the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana) and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) fashioned by him, because they too are produced by the radiance of the Blessed One’s merit, such as his eighty minor marks and so on.
It should be understood that it was created by the presence of beings (*saddhisattā*).

For it cannot be said that the Buddha-form, complete in its manifold aspects, was produced at that time through the power of the Blessed One’s merit alone. [The eighty minor marks] include the copper-colored nails, the prominent nose, and so forth.
[The thirty-two marks of a Great Man] include the well-placed feet and so forth. "The blossomed... [down to] the surface of the water" refers to [the lotuses] being touched by the rays of the sun.

It was like the surface of the water, adorned and arrayed on all sides with red lotuses—known as *kamala* because they "beautify what" (*kaṃ alaṅkaroti*) by blooming and reaching full expansion—and with various kinds of blue water-lilies (*nīluppalādi*) and white lotuses known as *puṇḍarīka*.
It was like the expanse of the sky (*gaganatala*) where the hosts of stars (*tārāgaṇa*)... [are] scattered everywhere.

It was like the surface of the sky, shining with a radiance and luster that spread forth and blazed brightly from a mass of rays as pure as a net; it was like the peak of the Golden Mountain (Sumeru),
encircled and surrounded on all sides by rainbows and flashes of lightning, colored by the glow arising at twilight.
Like the peak of a golden mountain. Regarding the phrase *vimalaketumālā*:
here they say, "A *ketumālā* is a mass of rays seen emerging from the head and forming a cluster above the crown.
"It is also said to be a raised area appearing in the middle of the head," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. Furthermore, because King Asoka was a Dhamma-king...

With joy and gladness arisen, remaining without food for seven days, he gazed incessantly at the form of the Buddha with eyes full of serene confidence, his mind undistracted while remaining exactly as he was;
