therefore, it is said that "eye-worship" was performed, meaning that worship was offered through the eyes by means of presenting such a desirable object to them.
Alternatively, [it refers to] the presentation of such a desirable object to the eyes.
It is said that "the eyes have been honored," which is expressed as "he performed an eye-worship.
This story was told in connection with the section on the manifestation of psychic power (iddhi), not according to the sequential order.
For this is the sequence here: King Asoka, looking through the lion-window in the manner that will be explained below, [saw] the novice Nigrodha.
Having seen him endowed with perfect deportment, drawing the eyes of the city folk as he looked ahead only the distance of a yoke,
the king was inspired with faith; filled with affection and great respect, he invited him, seated him upon a lion-throne beneath a white parasol, and after feeding him,
beheld the Dhamma-body of the Ten-Powered One reflected in the mirror at the novice’s word, and thus gained confidence in the Triple Gem.
Together with his retinue, having established himself in the refuges and precepts, from that time forth his faith increased.
He dismissed the sixty thousand heretics who had previously been fed, and instead provided for sixty thousand bhikkhus a meal prepared from rice harvested by hand.
He offered them water brought by deities from Lake Anotatta and tooth-sticks made of *nāgalatā* vines, and thus maintained constant attendance upon the Saṅgha.
One day, while performing his duties, he released his golden chain and summoned the Naga king Kāḷa;
beholding the image of the Buddha fashioned by him, endowed with such excellence of beauty and majesty as previously described,
he performed an offering of eyes for seven days with the radiance of his long, wide, and steady gaze.

Now, however, connecting the sequence as it follows, he spoke the words beginning with “The king, it is said, having attained consecration,” etc., in order to show the gradual entry into that teaching.
“An external heresy” (*bāhiraka-pāsaṇḍa*) refers to the doctrinal discourse proclaimed by outsiders.
For the doctrinal discourses proclaimed by outsiders ensnare and cast the net of craving and the net of views over sentient beings.
“They are called ‘heretics. He “grasped” means that, while investigating, he took hold [of them]. Bindusāra was devoted to the brahmins;
that is, from the time of his father Candagutta, he had been well-disposed toward the brahmins.
It is said that, incited by a brahmin named Candaka, Prince Candagutta, following the method given by him, throughout the whole of Jambudīpa...

He ruled for one reign; therefore, out of great respect for that brahmin, from the time of Candagutta onwards, about sixty thousand individuals of the brahmin caste became permanent recipients of alms at that royal court.

The phrase "of the brahmins" indicates those who had entered the state of wandering mendicants such as the Paṇḍaraṅgas and others; and the Paṇḍaraṅga wanderers and the rest were indeed of the brahmin caste.

He said, "Of the heretics belonging to the brahmin caste. Here, however, it is the Paṇḍaraṅgas and others who are called "heretics" (pāsaṇḍā) because they cast out (oḍḍanato) the snares of wrong views and so forth.
"In the lion-window" means in the great air-vent. "With that which is outside of tranquility" means outside of tranquility;
the meaning is "devoid of tranquility. "Bring him to the inner palace" means cause him to enter the inner palace; "bring him here" is what is meant.
They are called *amaccā* because they exist together (*saha*) with [the king] in his affairs; they are those who bring the royal duties to completion. They address the king as "deities" (*devā*).

For kings "shine" (*dibbanti*) by means of the strands of sensual pleasure, they "sport" (*kīḷanti*), or they "dwell" (*viharanti*) among them by virtue of their capacity for victory, desiring to conquer adversaries.
Or they exercise authority, status, and so forth, performing the giving and receiving of honors, or providing instruction on various matters.
They are called "deities" (*devā*) because they speak in common parlance, or because they shine with a radiance attained through the power of merit.

Likewise, they are called "kings" (*rājāno*) because, while delighting the people through the four bases of sympathy, they themselves rule, shine, and are resplendent with the aforementioned special qualities.
Regarding the term "Nigaṇṭhas and others": here, a "Nigaṇṭha" is one whose "bond" (*gaṇṭhana*)—that is, the defilement—is [absent].

The heretics who have acquired the name "Nigaṇṭhas" because they profess, "In saṃsāra there is no defilement such as lust that acts as an obstacle, nor is there any object such as fields, lands, sons, or wives;
we are free from the knots of defilement. The term "uccāvacāni" means both high and low, both great and small, or alternatively, distinguished.
"And even lowly ones" is the meaning. "On the Bhaddapīṭhaka seats" means on seats made of cane. "Essence" (sāra) refers to the essence of virtues such as moral discipline (sīla).

"By the royal courtyard" (rājaṅgaṇena) means by the open space at the gate of the royal residence. For in some contexts, "courtyard" (aṅgaṇa) refers to defilements (kilesa), as in "passion is a courtyard" (rāgo aṅgaṇaṃ) and so forth;
for passion and the like are called "courtyards" because by means of them, persons possessing them fall into a state of degradation.

They are called *aṅgaṇāni* because they "go" (*gacchanti*). In some instances, it refers to dirt or mud, as in such passages as: "He exerts himself for the sake of abandoning that very dust or *aṅgaṇa*" (*tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamatī*).
For *aṅgaṇaṃ* means that which "smeared" (*añjati*) or defiles, namely dirt and the like. In other instances, it refers to an open space of that kind, as in such passages as:
"the *aṅgaṇa* of the cetiya," "the *aṅgaṇa* of the Bodhi tree," and so forth. One "smeared" (*añjati*) [one's mind] there because of its extreme beauty.
For it is called *aṅgaṇa* because it manifests [faults]; it is an open space on the ground. Here too, that very same meaning is intended.

Regarding the terms "tamed" (*danta*) and so forth: it is "tamed" due to the mind being free from the agitation of the defilements; it is "guarded" (*gutta*) due to the protection of constant mindfulness ever-present;
it is "with senses at peace" (*santindriya*) due to the tranquility of the eye and other faculties; and it is [so called] because of being endowed with a pleasing deportment.
[He was] perfected in the postures (*īryāpatha*). Now, desiring to clarify who the novice Nigrodha was in terms of his actual identity, [the author] said:
"But who is this one named Nigrodha?
and so forth. Regarding that, the "graduated narrative" (*anupubbikathā*) is as follows: it is said that among the hundred sons of Bindusāra, there was Dhammādevī, born of the Moriya lineage...
Between his two sons named Asoka and Tissa, the elder, Prince Asoka,

was ruling the province of Avanti. Sent by his father, he reached the city named Veṭhadīpa— the residence of the Sākyans who had fled from fear of Viḍūḍabha at a distance of fifty yojanas from Pāṭaliputta—
and having taken there the daughter of a merchant named Veṭhā, he proceeded to the capital city of Ujjain.
While ruling the kingdom, having obtained a prince named Mahinda and a princess named Saṅghamittā, and enjoying the pleasures of sovereignty with them, he heard of his father’s illness;
leaving Ujjenī, he quickly went to Pāṭaliputta, attended upon his father, and after the latter’s passing, assumed the kingship. Hearing this, the crown prince—

Having become enraged, the one named Sumanā, surrounded by ninety-eight brothers, approached [Asoka], overwhelming him like a mass of water waves in the Saṃvaṭṭa ocean, thinking, "Today let there be either my death or the kingdom.
Then Asoka, the King of Ujjainī, having entered the battle and crushed his enemies, seized the prince named Sumanā and had him executed.

Therefore it was said: “It is said that while King Bindusāra was still weak, Prince Asoka abandoned the kingdom of Ujjenī which he had obtained for himself, came [to Pāṭaliputta], brought the entire city under his own control, and seized a prince named Sumana.
*Paripuṇṇagabbhā* means one whose pregnancy has reached maturity. *Ekaṃ sālaṃ* means a single palace, completely enclosed on all sides. “By a deity...”
However, they say that by his supernatural power, he dwelt in that palace while remaining invisible to the great multitude.

"A fixed routine" (*nibaddhavatta*) refers to a practice established by determining a specific amount for a single day. "Perfection of causes" (*hetusampadā*) refers to the perfection of merit that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for attaining Arahatship.
"Right at the razor's edge" (*khuraggeyeva*) means right at the conclusion of the shaving; [this refers to] the meditation subject of the five layers of skin.
It is said that having taken it up and grasping it, at the very moment he shaved off his final lock of hair (*kesavaṭṭi*), he attained *arahatta*.
"Having groomed his body" means having performed bodily care through such acts as chewing tooth-sticks and rinsing the mouth.
"He walks back and forth near the lion-window" means he paces to and fro in the vicinity of the lion-window. "At that very moment" means at that same instant.
"At that very moment. "This person" refers to the people he sees walking about in the royal courtyard as he speaks.

"Resembling a startled deer" means he is like a startled deer because of his instability and his fickle physical movements. "He shines exceedingly"—this is the connection. Regarding "looking ahead and looking around":
here, "looking ahead" (*ālokita*) means gazing forward; for gazing directly toward something in front is indeed called "looking ahead."
It is said. "Looking about" (*vilokita*) means looking toward the intermediate directions; the meaning is that it is looking toward the direction following upon whichever direction one is facing.
"Contracting" (*samiñjana*) is the contraction of the joints. "Stretching" (*pasāraṇa*) is the extension of those very same [joints].
"Supramundane state" (*lokuttaradhamma*) is a distinguished state not found among ordinary people. "Affection settled" (*pemaṃ saṇṭhahi*) means affection was established; it arose.
"Meaning": "He was a honey-merchant" means he was a seller of honey.
It is said that in the past there were three brothers who were honey-merchants. Among them, the youngest sold the honey, while the others brought it from the forest.
At that time, one *paccekabuddha* was afflicted with jaundice (*paṇḍukaroga*). However, another *paccekabuddha*...
For that purpose, he entered the city while wandering for alms of honey.
As he had entered, a certain slave-girl carrying a water-jar, who was going to the bathing place to fetch water, saw him. Having seen him, she asked him his reason for coming;
and having learned it, she said, "Venerable sir, honey-merchants live here; go there," and extending her hand, she pointed out the honey-shop.

He sent word, and he went there. Seeing him, the younger brother, the honey-merchant, was filled with joy and gladness; he asked, "From where have you come, venerable sir? Having understood the matter, he took the bowl, filled it with honey, and offered it. But seeing the honey filling the bowl overflow from his mouth and fall upon the ground, [he thought: [The Buddha said: "Monks, this honey-merchant, by means of this gift of honey, will enjoy celestial bliss for eighty-four thousand aeons. Having passed away from there, he will be reborn in a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. There, he will become a great merchant, possessing vast wealth and great resources. He will give alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. After his death, he will be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, he will become the son of Sakka, the king of the gods, named Jayampati. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, what was the cause, what was the reason, for the honey-merchant’s bowl being filled with honey, overflowing from his mouth, and falling upon the ground? "Ānanda, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, this honey-merchant was a monk who lived in the forest. While he was dwelling there, a certain monk came to that forest monastery seeking almsfood. Seeing him, the forest-dwelling monk was filled with joy and gladness and thought: 'It would be well if this venerable one were to eat my portion of almsfood. Then, having taken his own portion of almsfood, he gave it to that monk. Because of that deed, Ānanda, this honey-merchant’s bowl became filled with honey, overflowed from his mouth, and fell upon the ground."
With a serene mind, he made this aspiration: "Venerable sir, by this meritorious deed may I exercise sole sovereignty over Jambudīpa;
and may my command prevail throughout the sky and over an area of one yojana upon the earth.
The Paccekabuddha replied, "So be it, lay follower," and having gone to Gandhamādana, he prepared medicine for the Paccekabuddha.
But the youngest, the honey-merchant, having given the honey, sat in his house; seeing the others returning from the forest, he said to them, "Your brothers have calmed their minds;
they took honey both from me and from you, filled the bowl of such a Paccekabuddha, and gave it to him. Among them, the eldest became angry and said, "Even outcasts..."
“They are dwellers in saffron robes; surely that outcaste who went away after receiving honey from your hand must be one!
But Majjhima, becoming angry, said, “Take your Private Buddha and throw him into the great ocean!
Later, however, those two brothers [listened] to the discourse concerning the benefits of giving as it was being spoken by the youngest brother.
Having heard it, they indeed rejoiced. And that slave-girl Kumbhadāsī made a wish, thinking, "May I become the chief queen of that giver of honey.
Among them, the youngest became King Asoka Dhammarāja, and that slave-girl Kumbhadāsī, having attained the very pinnacle of physical beauty, became his chief queen by the name of Asandhimittā.
But the middle one, Parasamuddavādī, [remained] in this very place.
In the island of Tambapaṇṇi, there was a king of great power named Devānaṃpiyatissa.
But the elder brother, who had been born in a village of Caṇḍālas due to his occupation as a Caṇḍāla, became a novice monk named Nigrodha. Therefore it is said:
"Indeed, in former times, when he was performing meritorious deeds, this elder brother of the king was a merchant."
Regarding the phrase *pubbe va sannivāsena*: it should be understood that the shortening of the vowel in the word *vā* is for the sake of metrical composition;
thus, it means "by previous association" (*pubbe sannivāsena*). In this context, *pubbe* refers to a past birth. *Sannivāsena* means by living together.
For this prefix *saṃ-* has the sense of the word *saha* (together). Regarding the phrase *paccuppannahitena vā*: this refers to the present, the currently existing existence.
Or by acting for one's welfare. Thus, through these two causes, affection—known as endearment—is born and arises.
This is what is meant: this affection is produced by both causes;
having been one’s mother, father, daughter, son, brother, sister, husband, wife, companion, or friend in a previous existence...
When someone has previously lived in one place together with another, that affection does not abandon its continuity even in another existence because of that former cohabitation;
or, it arises through the benefit performed in this present life.
Thus, by these two causes, that which is called "love" (pema) is born. To the question "Like what?", he said: "Like a lotus..."

"In water" (*yathodake*). Here too, it should be understood that the shortening of the vowel *vā* has been made according to the method already stated. And here, the particle *vā* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned;
by this, it includes the lotus (*paduma*) and so forth. The word "just as" (*yathā*) is used for the sake of comparison. This is what is meant:
just as the blue lotus (*uppala*), and the rest—the lotus and so forth—when growing in water, grow depending upon two causes, namely, the water itself and...
And because of the *kalala* (embryo), affection arises through these two causes.
"In the king's hand" means in the hand of the king who has approached [him].

"Worthy of the king" means that, because ninety-nine brothers had been killed and because he was established in the kingdom despite his fierce nature, [the king], thinking "this man lives in negligence," [acted] in a manner appropriate to that.
He began to teach the Chapter on Heedfulness (*Appamādavagga*) in the *Dhammapada*. Therein, "heedfulness" (*appamāda*) is the non-separation from mindfulness;
it is a designation for mindfulness that is constantly established. "The deathless state" (*amatapada*): the "deathless" (*amata*) is said to be Nibbāna.
For because it is unborn, it does not age and it does not die; therefore, it is called "the deathless. The "state" (*pada*) of the deathless is the "deathless state."
It is said that it is the means for the attainment of the Deathless (*amata*). "Heedlessness" (*pamāda*) is the state of being negligent;
it is a name for the relinquishing of mindfulness, which is characterized by forgetfulness. "Of death" (*maccuno*) means of dying. "Footstep" (*pada*) means a means or a path.
For one who is heedless does not transcend birth; and once born, one both decays and dies. Thus, heedlessness is called the "footstep of death."
"It leads to death"—this is what is meant.

By the words "I have understood, dear father; please conclude [the teaching]," he shows his desire to practice that Dhamma himself, thinking: "I have understood this much alone: that one must always live with heedfulness; you may now finish your discourse on the Dhamma."
By illuminating [the meaning] and bringing the teaching of the Dhamma to its conclusion, he generates enthusiasm for the recitation. However, some say:
"Regarding the word *abhāsī* (he spoke), the meaning is taken as 'I shall speak' or 'I shall reflect'; because he had resolved, 'I shall speak the entire Appamādavagga,' it is said that he 'spoke.
But the King, having heard only half a verse, said: 'Understood, dear father; please finish it.'"
Because it was so stated, they say, "He did not speak further. However, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* (commentaries), it is stated that "this is not correct.
*Dhuvabhattāni* means regular meals. Regarding the term *upajjhāya*, it is said that one is called an *upajjhāya* because he contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless;

thus it says, "one who, having seen what is blameworthy and what is blameless, reproves and reminds. In this context, "what is blameworthy and what is blameless" refers to both minor and major offenses.
*Vajjaṃ*: "One who reproves" means one who reproves by saying, "This is an evil deed (*dukkaṭa*) committed by you," or "This is a wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*)," and so forth.
"One who reminds" means one who arouses mindfulness in one who has forgotten their own fault, or one who reminds [another] of right practice; the meaning is "one who causes it to proceed.
[This is done] by saying, "The word of the Buddha should be recited by you in this way," "You should step forward in this way," "You should step back in this way," and so forth.
He said, "One is called an *ācariya* because he trains in proper conduct (*ācāra*)," meaning "one who establishes [others] in the things that are to be trained in within this Dispensation.
In this context, "the things to be trained in" refers to the entirety of the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) as well as the qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
The phrase "both going-forth and full ordination" is stated according to what is currently available. By the expression "of the preceptor and the teacher," going-forth is indicated.
Furthermore, full ordination (*upasampadā*) should be connected [with the Sangha], while by the phrase "and for me," only going forth (*pabbajjā*) is intended.
However, since Nigrodha was then still standing on the level of a novice (*sāmaṇera*), both [going forth and full ordination] should be connected with reference to his future full ordination.

Because going forth is accomplished by means of taking refuge, it should be understood that the Saṅgha of monks also serves as the support for going forth. This is also evident from the act of shaving the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*).

It should be understood that the state of dependence is indeed obtained. "Increasing it day by day" means increasing it day after day by doubling it from its original amount according to the method already described.
"By way of the ordinary person" (*pothujjanika*) means in accordance with the nature of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Because this section concerns the praise of the power of the Elder Nigrodha, what was stated previously and what is to be stated later are combined here.
He said: "Furthermore, having caused the great monastery named Asokārāma to be built," and so forth. Regarding the term *cetiyapaṭimaṇḍitāni*:
here, a *cetiya* is that which is to be piled up or worshipped; or, it is a *cetiya* because it is heaped (*cita*) with bricks and the like.
Those adorned or embellished by *cetiya*s are called *cetiyapaṭimaṇḍitāni*. *Dhammena* means in accordance with the Dhamma, not departing from the Dhamma.
Explaining this same matter in detail, he said, “It is said that one day,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “having given a great almsgiving in the Asokārāma”:
the expression “in the Asokārāma” is stated with reference to the conventional designation of the name established by the king who later had it constructed.
However, some say that on that very day, the king [gave it] right in his own house... [all].
They say: "Having had the community of bhikkhus seated and fed, he asked this question. Regarding the phrase "having given a great gift":
it means having fed them and given a great gift by way of bestowing all types of requisites. For this has been stated in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
"Having ushered him into the residence and having had him seated upon a throne..."
She gave rice-gruel, various kinds of hard foods, and costly meals,
with hands purified, as much as was needed and according to their desire.
When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had finished eating and had put away their bowls and washed their hands—
To each individual monk, he gave a pair of garments.
He also gave oil for anointing the feet, a parasol, and sandals;
indeed, he gave all requisites for a recluse, as well as molasses and honey.
Having paid homage, Asoka Dhamma, the lord of the earth, sat down.
Once seated, the king offered the requisites to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
“As many bhikkhus as there are who desire them, I shall give whatever they wish.”
"Having satisfied him with requisites and having provided him with the necessary conditions, he then questioned him regarding the profound and well-expounded mass of Dhamma.
They say, O Great King, that this passage beginning with "Nine factors," and so forth, was spoken by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa. [The section on] the supervisor of new construction.
Thinking, "She is no longer a slave," he gave her away, appointing her as the supervisor and organizer of the new construction work to be carried out in the eighty-four thousand monasteries.
It is said that on a single day, letters arrived from all the cities;
for it appears that in all the monasteries, having begun the new construction on the very day Rāhu eclipsed the moon, they resumed the work again on the very day Rāhu eclipsed the moon once more.
They completed it; therefore, they say that the leaves arrived on that very same day. "The eight factors of virtue" (*aṭṭha sīlaṅgāni*) refers to the eight precepts of the Uposatha.
The phrase "adorned with all ornaments" is stated with reference to those who have not undertaken the Uposatha factors.
"In the royal capital Amarāvatī" means in the city of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. "Adorned and prepared" means fully equipped by way of decorative arrangement.
*Adhikaṃ kāraṃ* means *adhikāraṃ*; it is said to mean "an extraordinary deed. Regarding the phrase "they performed the miracle called the 'Opening of the World'":
here, the miracle that effects the opening of the world-space, which consists of many thousands of worlds, and the world of sentient beings who dwell therein, is called the "Opening of the World.
When one possessing supernormal power (*iddhimā*) performs this, they turn darkness into light or reveal what is concealed.
Or he makes what is covered uncovered, or what is not within range come within range. How?

For just as one’s own self or another person is seen even when concealed or standing at a distance, so too, desiring to make oneself or another manifest, one emerges from the basic jhāna and resolves:
"Let this place of darkness become filled with light," or "Let this which is covered become uncovered."
Having adverted [to the object] with the thought, "Let it be so," or "Let this which is not within range become within range," he enters the foundational jhāna again, emerges, and resolves.
Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes exactly as resolved. Others standing at a distance see it;
and he himself, if he wishes to see, sees it—just as the Blessed One did when descending from the world of the gods (devorohaṇa). For the Blessed One, in the world of the gods...
Having concluded the teaching on the Abhidhamma, as he was descending toward the city of Saṅkassa, he stood upon the summit of Sineru and surveyed the eastern world-system.
Many thousands of world-spheres appeared as if opened up, manifesting as a single open space.
And just as it was in the east, so too it was in the west, in the north, and in the south.
He saw everything laid bare. From below as far as the Avīci hell, and from above as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, he saw all.
Humans saw the gods, and the gods saw humans. Therein, neither did the humans look upward, nor did the gods look downward;
everyone saw one another face-to-face. That day was known as the "Opening of the World."
Furthermore, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Taḷaṅgara, performed this miracle.
It is said that one day, while sitting in the courtyard of the Cetiya at the Mahāvihāra of Tissa, he was preaching the Apaṇṇaka Sutta, beginning with:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities is practicing the unerring way," and as he spoke, [the earth] turned face downwards.
He fanned [the ground] until it became a single level expanse as far down as the Avīci hell; then he fanned it upwards until it became a single level expanse as high as the Brahma-world.
The Elder, having exhorted them with the fear of hell and enticed them with the bliss of heaven, taught the Dhamma.
Some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; thus, on that very day—
It was named the "Opening of the World. Now, these monks made this resolve:

"Just as King Asoka, the Dhamma-king, standing in the Asokārāma and looking toward the four quarters, beholds the whole of Jambudīpa bounded by the ocean, and the eighty-four thousand monasteries shining with magnificent and great festivals for the monasteries; even so shall we behold the Opening of the World."
They performed a miracle known by that name.
Regarding "the festival of the monastery's great offering" (*vihāramahapūjā*): it refers to the offering designated as the "great festival of the monastery. "Prosperity" (*vibhūti*) means excellence.
"Such joy and gladness" (*evarūpaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ*) refers to the joy and gladness rooted in such renunciation. "He made the burden [fall] upon the Elder Moggaliputtatissa" means to the Elder...

Because of his great majesty, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, thinking, "If there is anything further to be said, he alone will say it," placed the burden of answering the questions asked by the king upon the Elder. "I am an heir to the Dispensation" means:
I am a kinsman of the Dispensation, an insider; I am not [merely] one who has gone forth in the Dispensation. Those who have gone forth in the Dispensation...
Thinking of this matter—that sons and daughters do not exist, and that they do not take upon themselves the burden of performing the duties required by the Teaching—the Elder spoke thus:
"Great King, it is not merely by this much that one becomes an heir to the Teaching.
Regarding the phrase "But how then, venerable sir, does one become an heir to the Teaching?"—here, the particle *carahi* indicates impatience (or a sense of challenge).
This is what is meant: if one does not become an heir to the Dispensation even after making such a sacrifice, what else could one possibly do to become so?
"From the time Prince Tissa went forth" means from the moment Prince Tissa had gone forth, and for whatever reason...

"Having gone forth"—all of this will be explained further in detail. "You will be able" (*sakkhasi*) means you will be capable. "Born of gladness" (*pāmojjajāto*) means one in whom gladness has arisen.

Regarding the phrase "having obtained the consent of his children": here it should be understood that daughters (*puttī*) are also expressed by the word "children" (*putta*) through its general application;
or rather, it should be seen as stated thus by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), whereby both son and daughter are referred to as "children."
For those learned in the science of grammar (saddasatthavidū) say that when used together with the word *dhītā* ("daughter"), only the word *putta* ("son") remains and the word *dhītā* ceases.
"They established them in the training" means by granting the formal authorization for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) within that very boundary (*sīmamaṇḍala*),
through the process of enjoining them to the six precepts beginning with abstention from taking life and ending with abstention from eating at improper times.

They established her in the training. For even a novice nun who is sixty years old must indeed train by undertaking the six precepts, beginning with: "I undertake the observance of abstaining from taking life for two years, without transgression.
Indeed, one may not confer full ordination upon a novice nun who has not trained in these six rules of training for two years.

It is permissible. "Six-year consecration" (chabbassābhiseka) means one who has six years [of seniority] for the consecration; what is meant is that more than six years have passed since the consecration.

"The entire Theravāda" should be understood here as the Pāḷi itself recorded in the two councils, which is called "Theravāda" because it is the doctrine (vāda) of the Great Elders such as Mahākassapa and others. The Elder Kontaputtatissa...

In this context, the *kontasakuṇi* are a species of *kinnara*. Regarding them, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "The Elder named Kontaputtatissa, who was of human birth, lay within the womb of one of them and was raised by the king. This is also stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
"Formerly, from Pāṭaliputta, wandering as a forest-dweller in the forest..."
It is said that he entered into a household life with a *kinnarī*.
Through that cohabitation, she gave birth to two sons:
the elder was named Tissa, and the younger was known by the name Sumitta.
“At the time of the Elder Mahāvaruṇa, they both went forth in his presence and attained arahantship, endowed with the sixfold direct knowledge.
However, some say this: “There was a daughter of the king named Kontā, born in the lineage of King Kaṭṭhavāhana. Her...”
A certain forest-dweller, having brought her from the wilderness by means of a *garuḷa* vehicle, lived in cohabitation with her.
She gave birth to two sons for him; there, this eldest one was born under the name Kontaputta, after his mother’s name.
It is said that in the city of King Kaṭṭhavāhana, all those endowed with great wealth possessed a machine resembling a *garuḷa* bird for river and mountain sports and other diversions.
Having had [the palace] constructed, he wandered about on a Garuḷa-vehicle like King Kaṭṭhavāhana.
While wandering for alms according to the practice of a mendicant for the sake of treating his illness, he did not obtain even a *pasata* measure of ghee;
it is said that at that time, a stomach ailment arose in the Elder Jeṭṭha Koṇḍaññatissa Thera. Due to that intense painful sensation—
Seeing him afflicted, the elder named Sumitta asked, "Venerable sir, what is it that needs to be obtained here?
The elder Tissa replied, "Friend, a mere *pasata* of ghee needs to be obtained.
Having thus informed the king and declined his subsequent visit for the sake of medicine after the meal, he said, "At the very time for the alms-round..."
"If you are able to obtain anything while wandering for alms, go about in this manner and bring back whatever you have received," he said.
The younger brother also went out to wander for alms according to the prescribed rules of conduct, but he did not obtain even a single measure of ghee.
However, his abdominal wind became so much more intense that it could not be pacified even by a hundred jars of ghee. The Elder—

He passed away by the very power of that illness. However, some say: "The Elder was bitten by a spider—a type of insect—and afflicted by the force of its venom with extreme painful sensations, he attained final Nibbāna because, despite his efforts, he could not obtain even a spoonful of ghee as prescribed for its pacification. For this is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“The eldest was bitten on the foot by a poisonous insect and was in great pain.
When questioned by his younger brother, he said: ‘A handful of ghee is the remedy.
The elder brother informed the king, as well as [the need for] requisites for the sick.”
“Practice for the sake of the true goal and refuse food after the meal.
Thus did that Elder Tissa speak to the supreme Elder Sumitta: “If, while wandering for alms, you obtain ghee, bring it back to me.”
“While wandering for alms, he did not receive even a handful of ghee;
yet, despite a hundred jars of clarified butter, a disease arose that was incurable.
Because of that very disease, the Elder reached the end of his lifespan.”
Having exhorted [them] not to be negligent, he caused his mind to attain Nibbāna.
Sitting in the sky, by means of the fire element,
he resolved according to his wish and attained final Nibbāna of the body.
“Having emerged from the lattice-work chamber, he burned the fleshless skin;
he burned the entire body of the Elder, yet he did not burn the bones.
Having exhorted them with heedfulness: “Even for those like us, such requisites are difficult to obtain; while you are receiving these requisites…”
"Practice the duty of a recluse with diligence"—having thus exhorted them with regard to heedfulness. "In the cross-legged posture" means by sitting with the thighs bound all around.

This word for the instrument (the locative case) is used here in the sense of a characteristic of the state attained. "Having entered the fire-element attainment" means having entered the jhāna that has the fire-element kasiṇa as its object.
"Having performed an offering to the Elder" means having performed an offering to the relics of the Elder.
"Having had lotus ponds constructed at the four gates and having had them filled with medicinal herbs.
This means that having had four lotus ponds constructed at one gate, he filled one pond with ghee, one with honey, one with molasses, and one with sugar.
They say that he had them constructed in the same manner at the remaining gates as well.
"In the assembly hall" means in the hall of justice in the center of the city;
by this, he indicates the revenue arising from the entire city. "Five hundred thousand arise for the king" is said excluding the revenue arising from the kingdom.
"From that" means from the aforementioned five hundred thousand. [This was given] daily to the Elder Nigrodha.
"He sent a hundred thousand [pieces of cloth]"—but how did he send a hundred thousand to the Elder? It is said that the king would change his robes three times a day;
whenever he asked, "Has the robe for the Elder been taken? and heard the reply, "Yes, it has been taken," he would immediately change them.
The Elder, too, changed his triple-robe (ticīvara) three times a day. For it was his habit...

The triple robe was brought early in the morning, as well as at midday and in the evening, placed upon the neck of an elephant together with five hundred caskets of perfumes and five hundred caskets of garlands. The Elder did not tie them into bundles and store them away;
rather, he gave them to his fellow celibates as they arrived. At that time, it is said, for the most part among the community of monks in Jambudīpa...
The robe belonged to the Elder Nigrodha alone. Thus, he sent a hundred thousand [pieces of money] to the Elder day after day.
Regarding the phrase "excellent gain and honor" (*ulāro lābhasakkāro*): here, *lābha* means that which is obtained or acquired; it is a designation for the four requisites (*paccaya*).
That which should be performed with respect and given is *sakkāra*; these are likewise the four requisites. It is simply the requisites.
For indeed, those things which have been prepared and made very refined and very beautiful are called "hospitality" (*sakkāra*).
Alternatively, hospitality is the performance of respectful service to be done by others, or worship with flowers and so forth.

Regarding the term "views" (*diṭṭhigatāni*): here, view itself is "view-position" (*diṭṭhigata*), as in such expressions as "a position of excrement," "a position of urine," or "a position of formations."
Or, because there is nothing further to be gone toward, it is "gone" (*gata*) merely by way of view;
thus, *diṭṭhigata* means "merely the grasping of a view. Alternatively, *diṭṭhigata* is a "mode of view"; what is meant is a "division of views.
For worldly people accept that the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *ppakāra* are synonymous. However, it is not possible for one living among these people to bring them to peace, for...
Because he was living among them, being included within their midst, his words were not to be accepted; therefore, he thought in this way.
Since there was no dwelling in comfort for one living in that place at that time, having abandoned it and taken up merely the dwelling in comfort he desired, it is said:
"desiring to dwell in personal ease. "Ahogaṅga Mountain" refers to the mountain of that name.
"A mountain. Regarding the phrase "by means of the Dhamma, by means of the Vinaya, by means of the Teacher’s instruction": here, *dhamma* refers to the factual basis (*vatthu*).

*Vinaya* refers to the formal charge (*codanā*) and the reminder (*sāraṇā*). *Satthusāsana* (the Teacher’s instruction) refers to the perfection of the motion (*ñatti-sampadā*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvana-sampadā*).

Therefore, having charged [the person] with the factual basis and reminded them, one proceeds by way of formal acts such as suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) through the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation.
"Even while being suppressed," this is what is meant. "A tumor" (*abbuda*) is so called in the sense of swelling;

"dirt" (*mala*) in the sense of making something dirty; "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) in the sense of piercing. "Worshiping the fire" means they honor the fire like those who maintain the *aggihutta* sacrifice.
"Tormenting themselves in the five fires" means they place fires in four directions and stand in the middle, tormented by the heat of the sun. [The word] *ādicca*.
"Anuparivattantī" means that from the time of sunrise, while gazing at the sun, they revolve facing the sun until its setting.
"Vobhindissāmāti paggaṇhiṃsū" means they exerted themselves with the thought, "We shall dispel [the darkness]. "Avisahanto" means being unable.
"Sattadivasena rajjaṃ sampaṭiccha" means: first experience the bliss of sovereignty for seven days. Regarding that matter:
“Made him understand” means he awakened him to the matter of his remorse. How did he make him understand? He said, “It is said that he,” and so forth.
“Cittarūpaṃ” means conforming to the mind; it is equivalent to saying “according to one’s desire. “Kissa” means for what reason.
“Are tvaṃ nāma paricchinnamaraṇaṃ” means you whose death was delimited by seven days. “Vissattho” means with a mind free from apprehension, devoid of fear regarding death.
"Free from fear" is what is meant. "Beholding death bound up with inhalation and exhalation" means:
"O, may I live for that interval during which, having inhaled, I exhale, or having exhaled, I inhale;
may I attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would be accomplished by me"—thus, because of his devotion to the mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*).
They perceive death as being bound to the time of the occurrence of inhalation and exhalation. In this context, "inhalation" (assāsa) is the breath that goes out;
"exhalation" (passāsa) is the breath that enters within. They also speak according to the reverse of what has been stated.
"Having gone forth for the hunt" means having gone forth with the intent to kill deer, thinking, "I shall go wandering in search of deer in the forest."
In this context, "deer-hunt" (*migava*) refers to that which has received the conventional designation "deer-hunt" because it involves the hunting, seeking out, and afflicting of deer.
"The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita the Yonaka" refers to the great elder named Dhammarakkhita, who was born in the Yonaka region and went forth into homelessness after coming here.
"By the elephant-king" means by a great elephant; for they say that the word *nāga* is also a synonym for "great."
Or rather, it is stated as "by the elephant-nāga" for the purpose of specification from [other] nāgas such as the *ahināga*.
"His intention" (*tassāsayaṃ*) means his underlying purpose. "Even as he was looking on" uses the genitive case in the sense of disregard; the meaning is "even while he was looking on.

Regarding the phrase "having leaped up into the air," this is not a power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*); thus, he displayed this miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) even to a householder. For that—
“Having abandoned his natural form, he displays the form of a youth or the form of a nāga;

he displays various military arrays as well”—thus, the psychic power (iddhi) described in this way is called *vikubbaṇā-iddhi* because it proceeds by means of the transformation (*vikāra*) of abandoning one's natural form (*pakativaṇṇa*).
However, there is no denial of *adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*. And so he will say in the commentary on the *Khuddakavatthu-khandhaka*:

“Regarding ‘the miracle of psychic power’ (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), it should be understood that here the miracle of transformation (*vikubbaniddhipāṭihāriya*) is excluded, whereas the miracle of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is not excluded.
“Having hung [it] up” means having spread out his waist-band in the air and hung his robe there.
“A festive costume” (*chaṇavessa*) means a dress that produces joy; the meaning is “a festival costume. “They prepared” means that at the time of arrival, robes and so forth...
Thinking, “Seeking [alms] is burdensome,” they first prepared their bowls and robes.
A “dwelling for striving” (*padhānaghara*) is a secluded lodging suitable for the exertion of energy through application to meditation. “He too” refers to the king’s nephew.
“Having gone forth in succession” means he went forth after being followed by a multitude of nobles of great wealth. “Having gone” means by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*).

"Having gone. "With a wholesome intention" means having a pleasant disposition. "Fallen into doubt" means having fallen into uncertainty, thinking, "These bhikkhus are not speaking along the same path.
"Each with a retinue of a thousand bhikkhus" means each one having a retinue of bhikkhus limited to one thousand.
Even when told, "Go and bring them," [he thought], "He is capable of upholding the Dispensation."
Because it had been so stated, the elder monks went along, thinking it was a "Dhamma-act" (*dhammakamma*). In such instances, one should not feel remorse;
for this is a permissible message (*kappiyasāsana*) and not connected with household affairs.
Although it is proper to come for the sake of a Dhamma-act even when told "the king summons you," yet even though he was sent for twice, the elder did not come.

"He has not come, it seems. For the Elder had not come because he was highly esteemed for his renown everywhere, and since one who is so esteemed must have his further duties accomplished, he did not come under the pretext of some unsuitable business.
"Is the Elder venerable sir an old man? Although the king had previously seen the Elder, he was unable to recognize his name.

They say it was asked in this way. *Vayha*: they say a *vayha* is a particular kind of cart made with a covering like a pavilion on top, covered with planks, or entirely enclosed. "Having lashed together a boat-raft":
here, "boat" (*nāvā*) means a vessel (*pota*). For it is called a *pota* because it goes, crossing from this shore to the other; and it is called a *nāvā* because it carries beings across.
A boat joined together on one side is a "boat-hull" (*nāvā-saṅghāṭa*); the meaning is that it was bound in such a manner.
He said, "having provided protection," because of the great number of enemies of the Dispensation. The word "yaṃ" means "because" or "for which reason.
According to the statement, "One who does not commit an offense (*āga*) is a *nāga*," a monk is called a *nāga* here because of his absence of committing evil deeds.
Thinking thus, they prophesied: "O Great King, that single elephant among ascetics will take you by the right hand.
"They dragged him" means they pulled him along. They say: "Why was this objection raised—that the king’s taking of his hand seemed as if done in sport?
"From the outside" means from the exterior of the park. It appears to be exceedingly difficult for those who witness it.
He said, "Causing even a portion of the earth to tremble is difficult. However, in this case, there is no difficulty whatsoever in the act of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"Having stepped within the boundary" means having stepped inside the boundary, into the interior of the boundary.

"The basis for direct knowledge" means that which serves as the foundation for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Since the power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) was specifically excluded, he resolved upon the trembling of the earth.
Regarding the statement, "The foot standing within the boundary of the chariot moves," here "foot" refers to the chariot wheel.
For, because it performs the function of moving the chariot and is thus similar to a foot, it is called "foot" in this context.
"Is able" means "will be able. "This matter" refers to the point that evil is impossible without volition (*cetanā*). "Of volition" means...
Here, the word division should be made as “*cetanaṃ ahan*” (I killed the intention). “Having intended” (*cetayitvā*) means having set the intention in motion.

“The lamp-quail” (*dīpakatittira*) is a quail so named because it indicates its own state of being seated; it is the quail that a fowler, having led it into the forest, captures whenever other quails come and go upon hearing its sound.
"He questioned the ascetic": it is said that in the past, in a certain frontier village, a fowler caught a wild partridge, trained it thoroughly, and kept it in a cage.
He would take it into the forest and catch whatever partridges came by the sound of its cry. The partridge thought, "Because of me, many of my kinsmen are being destroyed."
"May this evil be mine," he thought, and became silent. Knowing his silence, the fowler struck him on the head with a bamboo splinter.

The partridge, overcome by pain, cried out. In this way, that fowler relied upon him to catch other partridges and made his living. Then that partridge thought: "It was my intention that these should die."
"It is not that I do nothing; rather, it is because of my past karma that it touches me.
For when I do not make a sound, they do not come; only when I do make one do they come. Once they have arrived, he seizes them and brings them to the end of their life.
Is there any evil in this for me, or is there none? From then on, he thought, "Who indeed might cut through this doubt of mine?"

He lived observing such a wise man. Then one day, that fowler, having caught many partridges and filled his basket, thinking, "I shall drink water," went to the hermitage of the Bodhisatta who had gone forth into the ascetic life, had developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal powers, and was dwelling in the forest; there he [placed] that cage before the Bodhisatta.
Having placed it nearby, he drank some water and, lying down on the sandy ground, fell asleep.
The partridge, perceiving that he had fallen asleep, thought while sitting in the cage: "I will ask this ascetic about my doubt; if he knows, he will explain it to me.
Thus he remained seated in the cage—
“Thinking, ‘A relative of ours is sitting here,’ many people have come;
they experience the results of their own actions, and my mind is apprehensive regarding them.
Thus she questioned the ascetic. The meaning of this is: “Venerable sir, if I were not to make a sound, these partridge folk...”

If he were not to come, yet because I am making a sound, this great multitude would arrive thinking, "A relative of ours is sitting here," and as each person arrives, the hunter would seize them and bring them to their death;

thus, by depending on me and relying on me, he would commit, incur, and acquire this kamma of taking life. Regarding that evil committed in dependence upon me, [the hunter might wonder]: "Is this evil mine?"
"In this way my mind shrinks back, recoils, and falls into remorse.
However, the meaning of the verse spoken by the ascetic beginning with "One does not touch the fruit because of karma" is as follows:
if your mind does not become corrupted by evil deeds, and does not incline toward or lean toward them—this being so, even if you were a hunter... [he would not be stained].
Even a wicked deed committed through dependence does not touch you, nor does it adhere to you.

For, since you are one who is diligent in avoiding evil, free from worldly attachment, auspicious, and pure, and because there is an absence in you of the volition for taking life, that evil does not smear you;
it does not adhere to your mind.
"Caused him to learn the agreement" means he caused him to learn the doctrine (laddhi) of his own Perfectly Enlightened One. "Having had it enclosed with a screen-wall" (*sāṇipākāra*):
here, *sāṇipākāraṃ* is in the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is that he had himself and the Elder enclosed on all sides by a screen-wall so that those monks would not see them—or [alternatively], a screen-wall.
"Having had it enclosed on all sides"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Within the wattle-and-daub wall" means inside the wattle-and-daub wall.
"Of one who holds the same view" means one who shares the same doctrine. "What does he say by way of his nature?"—thus he is a "proponent of what" (*kiṃvādī*).

Alternatively, "what is his doctrine?"—thus it is a "doctrine of what" (*kiṃvāda*); since he possesses that, he is a "proponent of what" (*kiṃvādī*). They proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.
"They describe [it] by means of virtue" refers to the eternalists (*sassatavādin*). Alternatively, it is called a "doctrine" (*vāda*) because they speak by means of it;
this is a designation for a view. An eternal doctrine is an "eternalist doctrine" (*sassatavāda*); those who possess that are "eternalists," meaning those with the eternalist view.
Now, why is it said that "an eternal doctrine exists for them"? For it is intended that their self and the world are eternal.

"Is it not the case that they do not hold a doctrine? This is true. However, because it is associated with eternalism, even the doctrine is called "eternalism," just as one says, "the spears are walking.
Alternatively, the word *iti* should be understood as having been elided in the phrase "those whose doctrine is eternalism" (*sassato vādo etesaṃ*).

Those who, having grasped any one of the aggregates such as form and so forth as the self and the world, proclaim it to be eternal, unchanging, permanent, and stable, are the Eternalists (*sassatavādino*).
This should be understood. For it is said in the *Niddesa* and in the *Paṭisambhidā*:

“They proclaim both self and world as ‘form is self and the world, and it is eternal. They proclaim both self and world as ‘feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is self and the world, and it is eternal.
And this meaning is expressed by: “One regards form as self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self.”
This is stated by way of the fivefold *sakkāyadiṭṭhi* (personality-belief) beginning with “he regards [the self] as possessing form.

However, by way of the fifteenfold *sakkāyadiṭṭhi* beginning with “the self as possessing form,” there is also this further meaning to be understood: that they describe the world as something other than the self, having grasped four aggregates each as the “self. Likewise, having grasped one aggregate as the “self,”...

The meaning here should be understood as follows: they designate the world as something else that serves as their own object of enjoyment; or, having grasped the aggregates that fall within their own continuity as "self," they designate the world as something other than that.
Thus it is "partial-eternalism" (*ekaccasassata*), meaning that for this [view], some things are eternal.
It is the doctrine of partial-eternalism. Those who possess this [doctrine] are the "partial-eternalists," the proponents of the doctrine of partial-eternalism.
They are of two kinds: those who hold that some beings are eternal and those who hold that some conditioned phenomena are eternal. In this regard, those whose doctrine proceeds thus:
"The Lord (Issara) is eternal, but other beings are impermanent," such as the proponents of the Lord (Issaravāda), are those who hold that some beings are eternal.
It should be understood that those whose doctrine proceeds thus: "Brahmā is eternal, but other beings are impermanent," are likewise those who hold that some beings are eternal.

Those who maintain the doctrine that "atoms are eternal, while dyads and so forth are impermanent" are eternalists regarding some conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-ekaccasassatikā*), such as the followers of Kaṇāda and others.
Likewise, those who assert that "the eye and other [faculties] are impermanent, but consciousness is eternal" should also be understood as eternalists regarding some conditioned phenomena.
Is it not the case that in this doctrine—"some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal"—there is a determination of the non-eternality of the eye and the rest?

If it is simply the realization of things according to their true nature, how can this be wrong view? Who indeed says that "the determination of the non-eternality of the eye and so forth is wrong view"?
Rather, here wrong view is the adherence to the notion of eternality regarding certain phenomena that are actually non-eternal.
However, by that [adherence] occurring even for a single moment, [one regards] the eye and so forth...
The realization of impermanence (*asassatabhāva*) is defiled by association;
like clarified butter mixed with poison, it is incapable of performing its own function and thus does not deserve to be placed on the side of right view.

Or rather, even though the eye and so forth are determined to be impermanent, they are grasped by those holding wrong views as having the nature of a soul (*jīva*) superimposed upon them; therefore, regarding that realization—

The state of wrong view cannot be prevented. And having accepted this, the objection that "the Vibhajjavāda—which asserts, according to the unconditioned and conditioned elements respectively, that some phenomena are eternal and some are non-eternal—thereby falls into the position of Ekaccasassatavāda (the doctrine of partial eternity)" finds no ground;
for it correctly apprehends the true nature of phenomena without distortion.
In this context, while it is indeed a particularly wrong view to grasp impermanent phenomena as permanent even within the first eternalist doctrine,
the apprehension of what is actually permanent as permanent is not a wrong view, because it is an apprehension in accordance with their true nature (*yathāsabhāva*).
However, among those very impermanent phenomena, there is a specific occurrence of differentiation when certain phenomena alone are grasped as permanent.

The fact that this doctrine is a distinct position has been stated. And it cannot be said here that the apprehension of eternalism with limitations—the partial aspect being included within the whole—coincides with the apprehension of eternalism without limitations, because these two doctrines function according to the specific distinctions in their respective objects of discourse.
For other proponents of views are indeed attached to the notion that "all phenomena are eternal."
The view that "some things are eternal" is clearly understood as two distinct doctrines: the complete exhaustion of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) and the grasping of only a portion of them.
Regarding the term *antānantikā*: here, *anta* (end) refers to that which one reaches or arrives at; it is the limit where the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) terminates.

By its negation, there is *ananta* (infinite). To what, then, does this "end" or "infinity" belong? It belongs to the world (*loka*), which is scrutinized by those holding views who seek escape from *saṃsāra*.

Or, it is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are experienced (*lokīyati*) therein; thus, it refers to one's own nature, which consists of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) and so forth, that has come to be designated as "the world.

The term "finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, and neither finite nor infinite" is a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*), or [a compound] by the principle of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*), as in such expressions as "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition. Alternatively, it is a discourse associated with the finite and the infinite.
"Finite and infinite" is, for example, as in "the spears are moving. Or, it refers to that which is dependent upon the finite and the infinite, as in "the beds are shouting.
Those who possess these [views] are the *antānantikā*, the proponents of the finite and infinite [doctrine].
Thus: "This world is finite; this world is infinite; this world is both finite and infinite; this world is neither finite nor infinite. In this way...
The meaning is: those who propound doctrines concerning whether [the world] is finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite.

For there are four kinds of proponents of views on finitude and infinity: the proponent of finitude, the proponent of infinity, the proponent of both finitude and infinity, and the proponent of neither finitude nor infinity.
Thus, for instance, someone might take a counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) that has not been expanded to the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa), and grasping it as "the world,"...
One perceives the world as finite. However, when expanding [the meditation object] up to the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) by means of the expanded kasiṇa, one perceives it as infinite.
But when not expanding upwards or downwards, yet expanding across, one perceives it as finite above and below, and infinite across.
Furthermore, because some have seen with their own eyes that the self—designated as "the world"—is at times infinite by great seers who have attained specific distinctions...

Because he has heard that it is finite, he does not perceive it as finite; yet because he has also heard that at certain times those very same beings were seen to be finite, he does not perceive it as infinite.
Thus, regarding the world, he is one who perceives neither as finite nor as infinite. However, some say:
"If this self were finite, then the accomplishment of functions such as the recollection of rebirths in distant places would be impossible. If, on the other hand, it were infinite..."
For one situated here, there might even be the experience of pleasure and pain in the deva-worlds, the hells, and so forth.
However, if [the self] were both finite and infinite, there would be the conjunction of the faults associated with negating both [possibilities].
Therefore, they explain that by means of such reasoning, one does not perceive the self as "neither finite nor infinite," because it is undeclared whether the self is finite or infinite.

And here, it is indeed appropriate that the first three proponents possess the quality of being "extremists" (*antānantika*), since their doctrines proceed by taking as their object the finite, the infinite, and both the finite and the infinite.
But how can the last one be considered an extremist, given that his doctrine proceeds by way of negating both of those?
Precisely because his doctrine proceeds by way of negating both the finite and the infinite; for even the doctrine that negates the finite and the infinite [is an extremist position].
It has precisely the finite and the infinite as its object, because it proceeds by taking those as its basis.
Indeed, it was stated below that they are called "proponents who proceed by taking this as their basis" for this very reason.

Even so, while it is appropriate for the latter two views to be classified as "finite-and-infinite-ists" (antānantika) because their doctrine has both the finite and the infinite as its object, how can the former two views individually be considered "finite-and-infinite-ists"?

By way of figurative application (*upacāravutti*). For the term "eternalist" (*antānantika*), when applied to the doctrines of finitude and infinity taken together, occurs even with respect to each individual eternalist because of its established usage therein—

just as the designation "eight liberations" (*aṭṭhavimokkha*) applies to each of the formless attainments (*arūpajjhāna*) individually, and just as in the world the term "a hundred spears" (*sattisaya*) is used for each individual spear.
Regarding the term *amarāvikkhepikā*: here, it does not die and is not cut off, thus it is *amara*. What is that?

It is both the view and the speech of one who holds a dogmatic position (*diṭṭhigatika*), which is without limit due to the mode of expression occurring as follows: “It is not so for me; it is not otherwise for me; it is not in another way for me; it is not for me; nor is it not for me. By such means as “It is not so for me,” it is manifold.
*Amarāvikkhepa* is the tossing about, the throwing about, the evasion of opponents in various ways; or, it is the evasion through the doctrine of immortality (*amarā*) or through speech;
those who possess this are *amarāvikkhepikā*. Alternatively, they are called *amarāvikkhepino* because they evade by means of the doctrine of immortality or by speech;
*amarāvikkhepikā* is simply another term for *amarāvikkhepino*. Or else, *amara*...
There is a species of fish called the *amarā*; as it darts hither and thither in the water by way of surfacing and diving, it cannot be caught.
In the same way, this doctrine also runs hither and thither because it does not abide in a single nature;
since it does not come to a graspable conclusion, it is called "eel-wriggling" (*amarāvikkhepa*), like the wriggling of an eel. For this one is indeed an eel-wriggler.
When asked whether "this is wholesome" or "this is unwholesome," he does not give any answer.
When asked, "Is this wholesome? he says, "It is not so for me. Then, when asked, "What is unwholesome? he says, "It is not so for me either.
When asked, "Is it otherwise than both? he says, "It is not otherwise for me either. Then, [regarding] the threefold...
When it was asked, "Is it not so? What is your doctrine? he replied, "It is neither so nor not so for me.
Then, when it was asked, "Is it not not so? What is your doctrine? he replied, "It is neither not so nor not not so for me. Thus he resorts to mere evasion; he does not stand by any single position.
Consequently, even when questioned whether "there is another world" and so forth, he likewise evades the issue and does not settle upon any one [view].
He stands on one side. Since this aforementioned form of "eel-wriggling" (amarāvikkhepa) exists among these [people], they are called "eel-wrigglers" (amarāvikkhepikā).

Now, surely all such eel-wrigglers—failing to understand as it really is wholesome states and so forth, as well as those who seek the next world and so on—merely resort to evasive wriggling when questioned on various points; of such a person...

How is it that he is one who holds a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*)? For is it not the case that being a holder of a wrong view is not appropriate for one who merely evades the question—like someone who does not wish to speak—simply because he does not know the answer?
It is said: His status as a holder of a wrong view is certainly not due to his mere evasion of the question;
rather, it is due to his adherence to eternalism (*sassata*) by way of a false conviction (*micchābhinivesa*). It is precisely because he is falsely convinced [of this]...

For indeed, a person—due to dullness of intellect, failing to correctly comprehend wholesome states and such matters as the pursuit of the welfare of the next world, and because of the inability to make another understand a meaning that one has not oneself understood, as well as through fear of false speech and the like—falls into equivocation.
And thus it has been said: "There are exactly seven views of annihilationism; the rest are views of eternalism."

Alternatively, it should be understood that this is a distinct view—arising in one who, through lack of understanding and lack of faith regarding merit, demerit, and their respective results, develops an inclination and preference for the position that "it is better to create confusion by evading a question concerning those matters"—just like the "sevenfold negation" (sattabhaṅga) view. For this very reason, it is said: "without limits."
“For one who follows a wrong view, it is both the view and the speech.
Regarding the term *adhiccasamuppannikā*: here, *adhicca* means “by chance”; the view that the self and the world have arisen without any cause whatsoever—whatever that may be—is *adhiccasamuppanna*.
For this refers to the objective support consisting in the mode of spontaneous arising of the aggregates designated as “self” and “world.”

Because it occurs by depending on that aspect [of consciousness] and because it is concomitant with that aspect, "view" (dassana) is called "fortuitously arisen" (adhiccasamuppanna), just as one says, "the beds cry out" or "the spears are walking. Those who possess this [view] are the Adhiccasamuppannikas. As for the Saññīvādins:
because they possess a doctrine of perception (saññī vādo), they are Saññīvādins, just as one says, "he possesses awakening (buddhaṃ), therefore he is a Buddha."
Alternatively, the term "proponents of consciousness" (*saññīvāda*) refers to those for whom the doctrine proceeds by way of association with consciousness;
that is, they are "proponents of consciousness. They proclaim: "The self is possessed of form and is unimpaired after death, and they describe it as conscious;
or the self is formless; or the self is both possessed of form and formless; or the self is neither possessed of form nor formless. Or the self is finite; or the self is infinite."
The self exists; the self is finite; the self is both finite and infinite; the self is neither finite nor infinite. The self possesses the perception of unity;
the self possesses the perception of diversity. The self possesses limited perception; the self possesses immeasurable perception.
The self is exclusively happy; the self is exclusively suffering; the self experiences both happiness and suffering; the self experiences neither-suffering-nor-happiness.
“The self exists, healthy after death, and is percipient”—this is the designation for those who maintain doctrines analyzed in sixteen ways.

The doctrines of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*) and neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) should be understood by the same method as that stated for the doctrine of perception (*saññīvāda*).

For the doctrines of perception were stated with reference to those who grasp the view, “The self is percipient,” while [the others] are [stated] as “non-percipient” and “neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.”

It should be understood that the doctrines of non-percipient existence (*asaññīvāda*) and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are stated by way of those who hold them.
In this context, the proponents of non-percipient existence declare: "The self is possessed of form and is healthy after death; they describe it as non-percipient. Or the self is formless;
or the self is both possessed of form and formless; or the self is neither possessed of form nor formless. Or the self is finite; or the self is infinite."
“The self exists; the self is finite; the self is both finite and infinite; the self is neither finite nor infinite, being healthy after death and non-percipient”—thus they describe it in eight ways.
The proponents of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self also describe it in exactly the same way, beginning with:
“The self is material, being healthy after death, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient,” and so forth.
It should be understood as analyzed in eight ways. Regarding "annihilationist views" (*ucchedavāda*):
annihilation is the view of annihilation that proceeds according to such methods as, "This self is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father;
with the breakup of the body, it is cut off and destroyed, and does not exist after death."

By way of association: those for whom there is a doctrine of annihilation are "annihilationists" (*ucchedavāda*); or, they are "annihilationists" because the doctrine of annihilation exists within them;
or, they are "annihilationists" because they advocate for annihilation.

Regarding the term "those who advocate for Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*): here, "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the phenomena (*dhamma*) apprehended by knowledge that functions as seeing.
The meaning is "a directly perceived phenomenon" (*paccakkhadhamma*). This is a designation for the specific state of existence obtained here and there.
"Nirvana in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means nirvana in the present phenomena; the meaning is the subsiding of suffering in this very selfhood.

Those who speak of that are the "proponents of nirvana in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā*). They, moreover, [say]: "When, sir, this self, by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure..."

“Endowed with and possessed of these, he enjoys them; it is in this way, sir, that this self attains the supreme Nibbāna in this very life”—in such a manner they proclaim Nibbāna in this visible world.
For they [proclaim it] regarding human sensual pleasures, which are similar to those of King Mandhātu, and divine sensual pleasures, which are similar to those of the deva-king Paranimmitavasavatti.
They declare that for those who have approached [the teaching], there is the attainment of *nibbāna* in this very life.

He is called a "proponent of analysis" (*vibhajjavādī*) because, according to the method presented in the *Verañjakaṇḍa*, he speaks by analyzing the state of being a "remover of defilements" (*venayika*) and so forth.
For therein the Blessed One, having said, "Brahmin, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of passion," and so on—

Furthermore, he is called a Vibhajjavādī because he explains, by way of analysis, the state of being to-be-cultivated and not-to-be-cultivated regarding joy and so forth, as well as robes and so forth—as in the passage beginning, “But it is not with reference to what you say.
Alternatively, he is a Vibhajjavādī because he speaks by distinguishing between the doctrines of eternalism and annihilationism, saying, “It is eternal... [and so on].
The Blessed One is a proponent of analysis (vibhajjavādī) because he sets aside those questions to be set aside, such as "Is the self and the world [eternal]?

He is a proponent of analysis because he speaks of eternalism, which is the persistence of lust and so forth, and of annihilationism, which is the destruction of lust and so forth, as well as bodily misconduct and the like.

He is a proponent of analysis because, without falling into either of the two extremes consisting of eternalism and annihilationism, he teaches dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which constitutes the Middle Way.
"Crushing the doctrines of others" refers to the controversies that arose at the time of the Third Council,

as well as those that would arise in the future until the disappearance of the True Dhamma; for it was with reference to all such matters— both those that had arisen at that assembly and those that would arise in the future— that this Elder [said].
In order to repel them, by means of the method given by the Teacher himself, the Tathāgata analyzed the matrix (mātikā) he had established; thus,
having brought forth five hundred suttas for his own position and five [hundred] for the positions of others— totaling one thousand suttas— he crushed the doctrines that arose at that time,
and because it has the characteristic of preventing the arising of future doctrines, it is called "the crushing of the doctrines of others."
He composed the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, which has the characteristic of prohibiting [wrong views] for the future.
Thus ends the commentary on the Third Council in the *Sāratthadīpanī*,
a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.
In the commentary on the account of the lineage of teachers (*ācariyaparamparakathā*),
while answering the question "By whom was it brought?", the lineage of teachers in Jambudīpa up until the Third Council has first been shown;
now, in order to show the lineage of teachers in the island of Sīhaḷa, [the text begins] with "But after the Third Council," and so forth.
"Initiated": this refers to this island, Tambapaṇṇidīpa. "At some time": at a certain period. "The ancient ones": the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās.
"Named Bhadda": the Thera Bhaddasāla; for usage by even a single part of a name is seen, as in "Devadatta" for "Datta.
"They do not cause harm": thus they are *nāgas*. "They recited the Vinaya Piṭaka": this is the connection [of the sentence].
*Tambapaṇṇiya* is a locative expression. "They taught the five Nikāyas" means they taught the five Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīghanikāya, excluding the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma.
"And the seven treatises (*pakaraṇa*)" means they taught the seven Abhidhamma treatises, beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and the *Vibhaṅga*.
It is called *medhā* because it grinds (*medhati*) or destroys defilements like a thunderbolt striking a mountain; it is [also] swift...
Or, *medhā* (intelligence) is so called in the sense of grasping and retaining; one who possesses this is *medhāvī*. *Tipeṭaka*: because he possesses the three *piṭakas*, he is *tipeṭaka*;
what is meant is *tepiṭaka*, which signifies one who upholds the study (*pariyatti*) of the three *piṭakas*.
*Tārakānaṃ rājā*: the king of stars, the moon. *Atirocatha*: he shone exceedingly. *Pupphanāmo*: [he whose] name was "Flower."
Mahāpaduma Thera. "Skilled in the lineage of the True Dhamma" means skilled in the tradition of the True Dhamma. "Flower-name" refers to Sumana Thera.

"Established in Jambudīpa": it is said that at one time, when the Dispensation was declining in the island of Sīhaḷa, Sumana Thera went to Jambudīpa, mastered [the teachings], and while protecting the Dispensation, he remained established right there. "Skilled in the path."
"Skilled in the paths to heaven and the path to liberation.
"Making them his burden" means making the teaching of those various bhikkhus his burden; the meaning is that he made them dependent [upon it].
Expanding upon this very point which was stated in brief—namely, "He dispatched those various bhikkhus here and there"—[the author] shows it as follows:
He said: “He sent the Elder Majjhantika to the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra,” and so forth. They call the Mahiṃsaka region the Andhaka kingdom.
Vanavāsi refers to the Vanavāsi kingdom. “With themselves as the fifth” means those for whom they themselves constitute the fifth;
what is meant is that five monks each went to their respective directions.

Now, wishing to show the power of the deeds performed by the elders who had gone here and there, [the author], first demonstrating the deed performed at the place where the Elder Majjhantika went, said: "At that time, in the kingdom of Kasmīra-Gandhāra," and so forth.

"A rain of hailstones" (*karaka-vassa*) means a rain that causes a falling of snow. "Having carried away" means having carried away by a flood of water. "On the surface of the Aravāḷa lake" (*aravāḷa-daha-piṭṭhiyaṃ*).
On the surface of the water of the Aravāḷa Lake. "Wearing tattered and torn robes" (*chinnabhinnapaṭadhara*):
he wears robes that have been cut with a knife and torn—having undergone a change of color through dyeing—thus he is one who wears tattered and torn robes.

Alternatively, he is called one who wears tattered and torn robes because he wears saffron-colored garments (*kāṣāya*) that are different from householders' clothes and have been cut with a knife. "A beggar" (*bhaṇḍu*).
"Shaven-headed one. "Clad in saffron robes" means dressed in garments of saffron cloth.

"Unable to endure malice" means being unable to endure, sustain, overcome, or pacify the malice characterized by the concealing of others' virtues that had arisen within his own continuum on account of the Elder. "Terrifying" means objects of a fearful nature. To demonstrate these:
He said, beginning with, “From here and there fierce winds blow. “Fierce winds” means powerful winds capable of shattering trees and toppling mountain peaks.
“Lightning bolts flash” means the lightning bolts break apart; it is said that they fall.
“Showers of weapons” refers to showers of various kinds of missiles. “Drive them out” means seize them and remove them. “Terrifying” refers to the nāga king.

The connection is: "May he not be, may he not become, capable of producing in me a physical or vocal disturbance caused by fear. In this context, "fear and terror" (*bhayabherava*) refers to minor and trivial fears.
Alternatively, "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of mental trepidation; it is a synonym for the fear of aversion (*paṭighabhaya*).
This is a designation. "Terrifying" means an object that produces fear.
