"Even if you were to lift up the entire earth, O Great Naga—along with the oceans, together with the oceans, and along with the mountains, together with the mountains—and hurl it over me, upon my head"—this is the meaning.
"You would not be able to produce in me any fear or terror."

The connection [is as follows]: "Aññadatthu" means "certainly. "Tavevassa vighāto uragādhipā" means that for you alone, O Lord of Serpents—king of the *uragas* or *nāgas*—there would be affliction, suffering, and injury; this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrases "having instructed with a discourse on the Dhamma," and so forth, it refers to a teaching of the Dhamma appropriate to that moment, concerning both the present life and the future life.
The meaning is: having pointed out the goal, having encouraged him toward wholesome states, having caused him to grasp them, and having inspired him therein by making him zealous;
and then, because of that zeal and by means of other existing virtues, having gladdened and satisfied him.
Showing the instruction to the Naga given by the Elder, he said, beginning with "Then the Venerable One... In this regard, from here upwards...
"As before" means: just as you previously, when you were devoid of the arising of hearing the True Dhamma, gave rise to anger toward others;
from now on, henceforth and into the future, do not produce anger.
Do not sever the affection even for your own born children—that which is the root of total ruin and the destroyer of crops. This is the meaning. "Those who desire happiness."
In the phrase *hi pāṇino*, the word *hi* indicates a reason; because all beings desire happiness, it is therefore said:
"Do not destroy the crops, which cause the cutting off of welfare and happiness.
*Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ* means whatever has been instructed; or, *yathānusiṭṭhaṃ* means not transgressing what has been instructed.

"Without overstepping the instruction given by the Elder"—this is what is meant. "There was a breakthrough in the Dhamma" means, they say, there was the attainment of the first path and fruit (*magga-phala*).
"A hundred thousand families"—by this he indicates a hundred thousand men. "The inhabitants of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra" refers to those dwelling in the kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra.
"Radiant with the saffron robes" refers to the monks by virtue of the saffron-colored garments they wear as lower and upper robes.

Illuminated. "Fanned by the breezes from the sages" means they were fanned on all sides by the wind from the monks' undergarments and upper robes, as well as by the wind from the movement of their hands and feet. "Corrupted" means agitated. "From the bonds" means from the bonds of *saṃsāra*.
"The eye of Dhamma" refers to the knowledge of the three lower paths. However, some here say, "They obtained the knowledge of the first path itself."

They say: "Having been urged by the messengers of the gods" means that, according to the teaching of the *Devadūta Sutta*, having been urged and exhorted by these five messengers of the gods—the young boy, the aged person, the sick person, the criminal being punished, and the dead person—and having thus produced a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
For it is the young boy and the others who are called "messengers of the gods" in that context.
For indeed, a young child speaks thus in substance: "Look, sirs, I too have hands and feet just like yours;
yet I am mired in my own urine and excrement. By my very nature, I am unable to stand up and bathe. I cannot even say, 'I am dirty; wash me,' for I am born so."
"Because of being not yet liberated, one is thus born; and it is not only I who am thus, for you too are indeed not yet liberated from birth.
Just as it has come to me, so will birth come to you as well; therefore, before it arrives, perform what is wholesome.
Thus he became known as the "Messenger of the Gods."
Even a being worn out by old age speaks thus in substance: "Behold, sirs, I too was once young like you, endowed with strength of thighs, strength of arms, and speed;
those perfections of strength and speed have now vanished from me. My hands and feet no longer perform the functions of hands and feet.
I have become such as this because I am not exempt from old age; yet it is not I alone."
"You too are certainly not exempt from old age. For just as it has come to me, so will old age come to you as well;
therefore, before its arrival, perform what is wholesome. It is for this reason that he is known as the "Divine Messenger" (*devadūta*).
A being who is ill also speaks thus in terms of the meaning: "Behold, sirs, I too was once free from disease, just like you."
"I am now struck down by disease, lying smeared in my own urine and excrement; I am not even able to rise up.
Although my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the functions of hands and feet. I have become like this because I am afflicted by sickness and have not been liberated from it.
But it is not only I who am thus; you too are indeed afflicted by sickness and have not been liberated from it. For just as it is with me..."
"In this way, illness will come to you as well; therefore, before it arrives, perform what is wholesome.
For this reason, he is known as the "Messenger of the Gods" (*devadūta*).
It should be understood that the executioner, or those who carry out the execution, constitute the fourth messenger of the gods. Regarding that, in the context of the executioners:
In substance, these thirty-two instruments of torture say this: "When we are produced, we are not produced upon trees or stones;
we are produced within the bodies of those such as yourselves. Therefore, while we are still being produced, perform wholesome deeds.
For this reason, they are called "divine messengers" (*devadūta*). In substance, the torturers also speak thus.
They say, “When we carry out the thirty-two tortures, we do not inflict them upon trees and such, but only upon beings like yourselves;
therefore, since we have previously inflicted these tortures upon you, you should now perform what is auspicious for us. For this reason, they are called “divine messengers” (devadūta).
A dead being also speaks thus in substance: “Behold me, sirs, cast away in the raw charnel ground, in the state of bloatedness and so forth!”
"I have become such as this because I am not yet liberated from death; it is not only I, however, who am not liberated from death—you too are certainly not liberated from death.
For just as it will come to me, so too will death come to you. Therefore, before its arrival, perform what is wholesome.
Because of this, he became known as "the Messenger of the Gods" (*devadūta*). Therefore, young children and others...
Here, they should be understood as "messengers of the gods.

*Anamataggiya* refers to the *Anamatagga Saṃyutta*. "He gave to drink the nectar of the Dhamma" means he caused them to obtain the drink that is the supramundane Dhamma-nectar by way of bestowing it upon them.
*Samadhikāni* means together with the additional; for here the prefix *sa-* has the sense of "together with."
“Resounding. One is called an *isi* because one has sought, searched for, and pursued the aggregates of the Dhamma, such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).

“The five kingdoms” refers to the five kinds of Chinese kingdoms. It should be connected thus: having gone to the Himalayas, while proclaiming the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, he gladdened the host of *yakkhas*.
"And at that time" means at that moment, prior to their departure.
"It will be obtained" means it will be obtained from the presence of Vessavaṇa. "Swiftly" means with speed.
"He established a guard all around" means he established a guard on every side by means of a formal resolve (adhiṭṭhāna), thinking, "From now on, let no one enter. Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni...
“Three thousand and five hundred” means three thousand and more than five hundred; it is said that this is “three thousand less half of a fourth,” which is three thousand seven hundred and fifty.
“One thousand five hundred” means one thousand and more than five hundred;
the meaning is one thousand and a half. “Soṇa and Uttara” means Soṇa and Uttara. “Having driven out” means having caused them to flee. “They proclaimed” means they made it known.
*Ajjhiṭṭho* means "commanded. Regarding *puna dāni*: here *dāni* is merely a particle; the meaning is "perhaps we might come again, or perhaps not.

*Rājagahanagaraparivattakena* means either by way of avoiding the city of Rājagaha and going by the path that circumambulates it from the outside, or by way of traveling [along its perimeter]. Now, as for the reason why the Elder’s mother resided in the city of Veṭasī:
In order to show that this city was the birthplace of that [Thera] and to demonstrate the origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*) of the Elder, he said, "Asoka, it is said, in his youth," and so forth.
Herein, this is the sequential narrative (*anupubbikathā*): Formerly, it is said, there was a king named Candagutta, born in the Moriya lineage...
The son named Prince Bindusāra became king in the city of Pāṭaliputta upon the passing of his father.
He had two sons born of the same mother, and they had ninety-nine half-brothers.
The king, however, having granted the position of viceroy and the province of Avantī to Asoka Kumāra, the eldest of them all, then one day—
Seeing that he had come to attend upon him, [the king] commanded: "Dear son, Uparāja, go to your own kingdom and dwell there in the city of Ujjenī.
Following his father’s word, as he was traveling toward that Ujjenī, he took up residence in the house of a merchant named Veṭṭisa in the city of Veṭṭisagiri along the way;
there, [he saw] the merchant’s daughter, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
Having seen a maiden named Veṭisagiri who had reached the prime of youth, his heart became bound to her;
after he had consulted with her parents and obtained her from them, he entered into a life of cohabitation with her.
Having conceived a child through that union, she was led from there to Ujjenī, where she gave birth to Prince Mahinda. Then, when two years had passed, [she gave birth to] Saṅghamittā.
Having obtained his daughter, he lived there together with the viceroy.
However, Bindusāra, the father of the viceroy, while lying on his deathbed, remembered Prince Asoka and dispatched messengers to Ujjain to summon him.
Those messengers went from there to Ujjain and reported the news to Asoka. At their word, he...
Traveling with great haste to his father’s presence, he left his wife and children behind at the city of Veṭṭhigiri on the way.
Having gone to his father’s domain, the city of Pāṭaliputta, immediately upon his arrival, he had the funeral rites performed for his father who had passed away.
Then, having caused ninety-nine half-brothers to be slain, he cleared away all thorns from his path and remained there.

Having raised the parasol, he received the consecration. At that time as well, the Elder’s mother sent the children into the presence of the king, while she herself remained right there in the city of Veḷigiri.
Therefore it is said: “At that time, his mother was living in her relatives’ home. *Āropesi* means he presented [them].
“The duty we had to perform here is finished”—this refers to the fact that the visit to the mother had been accomplished.

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). The detailed account regarding the sending of the consecration (*abhiseka*) and so forth—beginning with the words "Let my father’s sent consecration first be experienced"—will be made clear further on.

"For the sake of a festival" (*chaṇatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of a festival; the sense is "for the cause of a festival," which implies that he himself did not wish to engage in the festival games.
At that time, it is said, Devānampiyatissa [was born] on the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla.
Having had the auspicious day proclaimed and having commanded his ministers, "Hold a water-sport festival," he himself, desiring to go hunting, went to Mount Missaka.
It is called Mount Missaka because it is composed of a mixture of earth and stone.
"One who has seen the Truth" means one who has penetrated the Truth by means of the path of the Non-returner; it is said that he had attained the fruit of Non-returning.
He did. It is said that after hearing the Dhamma taught by the Elder to his own mother-queen, he realized the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*);

furthermore, it should be understood that he was the Elder’s nephew. For the Elder’s mother-queen’s sister was her [the queen’s] daughter, and this man was her son. Indeed, this is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“The queen’s sister’s daughter had a son named Bhaṇḍuka;
having heard the Dhamma taught by the Elder to the queen,
he attained the fruit of non-returning and lived in the Elder’s presence.”
And as for the fact that you were prophesied by the Fully Enlightened One: while at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, the Fully Enlightened One surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye;

seeing the island of Tambapaṇṇi and perceiving its future prosperity, he prophesied of you, saying, "In the future, a monk named Mahinda will bring faith to the island of Tambapaṇṇi. In this context, "the island of Tambapaṇṇi" refers to...

The inhabitants of the island were addressed. The knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of their underlying tendencies and dispositions (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*) are called the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*).

Since it is impossible to see anything else without [knowing] the degrees of others' faculties and so forth, the text says "having looked around" (*voloketvā*) rather than "while looking around" (*volokento*).
"This matter" (*etamatthaṃ*) refers to this meaning: "In the future, a monk named Mahinda will convert the island of Tambapaṇṇi."
"At Veṭṭhisagiri in Rājagaha" refers to the monastery built by the queen. "It was time for their departure; let us go to the supreme island"—this is how it should be construed.
This is an illustration of their reflection. "Into the sky" means they leaped into the air. "In the firmament" means in the sky.
Having thus leaped into the sky, what did they do? Showing that they alighted on Cetiyapabbata, [the text says: "they descended upon the mountain."

He said: "Thus having flown up, the elders descended upon the best of mountains. Now, in order to show the location where that mountain stands and the place where the elders descended there, he spoke the verse beginning with "In front of the best of cities" (*purato puraseṭṭhassa*).
"In front" (*purato*) means in the eastern direction. "Of the best of cities" (*puraseṭṭhassa*) refers to the preeminent city known as Anurādhapura. "Resembling a cloud" (*meghasannibhe*)...
Because they were blue in color all over, they resembled great blue clouds. "On the Peak of Virtue" (Sīlakūṭa) means on a mountain peak of that name.
"Like swans upon the mountain summit" means like swans on the top of the mountain.
Regarding when he established himself there, he said: "Thus, together with Iṭṭiya and the others," and so forth. "From the time of his final Nibbāna."
The meaning to be understood is that it was in the thirty-sixth year beyond two hundred years after the year of his *parinibbāna*, excluding that [year] as the limit.
To explain how this is to be known, he says, "For Ajātasattu," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in that very year": here, it refers to whichever year and whichever day the Blessed One passed away (*parinibbuto*).
It is said that on that very year and on that very day, Prince Vijaya arrived at this island. For it has been stated:
“In Laṅkā, a prince named Vijaya, firm in his resolve, landed upon the island of Tambapaṇṇi.”
“On the day the Tathāgata lay down to pass away between the twin Sāl trees.
Regarding the phrase “the son of Prince Sīha”: here, the prince born to Sīha from the womb of the daughter of the King of Kāliṅga is called Prince Sīha.
It should be understood that he said, "he made it a human habitation," because previously it had been an abode of non-humans (*amanussa*).
Regarding the phrase "in the fourteenth year": this refers to when the fourteenth year had arrived.
"Here Vijaya passed away" means that in this island of Tambapaṇṇi, Prince Vijaya, having reigned for thirty-eight years, passed away. For instance, King Ajātasattu [reigned] thirty-two...
He reigned for sixteen years; Udayabhadda [reigned] for sixteen years.

Therefore, by reckoning the eighth year of Ajātasattu as the first year of Vijaya, twenty-four years elapsed for Ajātasattu and fourteen years for Udayabhadda thereafter, thus completing thirty-eight years for Vijaya. And so it has been said:
“Vijaya, having arrived at Laṅkā on the day of the Teacher’s parinibbāna,
ruled the kingdom for thirty-eight years as the subduer of the yakkhas.
“In the fifteenth year of Udayabhadda’s reign, the one named Paṇḍuvāsudeva attained sovereignty over this island.”
Because it was stated [by Udayabhadda], it should be understood that during the single year counted as the fourteenth [of his reign],
between Vijaya and Paṇḍuvāsudeva, the island of Siṃhala remained without a king. For in that year, the ministers of King Vijaya,
having appointed a minister named Upatissa as their chief, [dwelt] in the village of Upatissagāma, which was named after him.
The Vāsantas ruled the kingdom without a king. For it is said:
“When he had died, those ministers, looking toward the arrival of a kṣatriya, remained in the village of Upatissa and governed the realm.”
“O King Vijayarāja, before the arrival of the kṣatriyas, this island of Laṅkā remained without a king for one year. Regarding the word *tattha* (there), it means in Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the phrase *idha Paṇḍuvāsudevo kālamakāsi*, it means that Paṇḍuvāsudeva passed away here in this Sihaḷa island.

Having ruled the kingdom for thirty years, he passed away. For indeed, immediately after Udayabhadda, Anuruddha and Muṇḍa ruled the kingdom for eight years; after them, Nāgadāsaka ruled for twenty-four years.
Therefore, together with the fifteenth and sixteenth years of Udayabhadda, [the total for] Anuruddha and Muṇḍa...
Eight years for Caṇḍavajji and twenty out of the twenty-four years for Nāgadāsaka—thus thirty years were completed for King Paṇḍuvāsudeva.
Therefore it is said: "Then Paṇḍuvāsudeva ruled the kingdom for thirty years."
*Therein* means in Jambudīpa. *In the seventeenth year* means when the seventeenth year had arrived.
For Susunāga reigned for eighteen years immediately after Nāgadāsaka;
therefore, having set aside twenty years out of the twenty-four years of Nāgadāsaka’s reign, [the period] together with the remaining four years is added to the eighteen years of Susunāga’s reign.
"Sixteen years"—here, twenty years of King Abhaya’s reign were fulfilled. For it is said:
"Abhaya ruled the kingdom of Laṅkā for twenty years.
A *dāmarika* is a robber who engages in combat. Furthermore, Paṇḍukābhaya was indeed the king who was the nephew of Abhaya, not [the other].
He is called a "bandit" (*dāmarika*) because he seized the kingdom by force.
It is said that "he took the kingdom" because he took a portion of it; for in the twentieth year of Abhaya’s reign, he had not yet taken the entire kingdom.
Thus, from the twentieth year onwards, Abhaya [killed] his nine brothers, who were his maternal uncles, here and there.
Seventeen years passed while he was slaying those who opposed him after engaging in battle, even though he had not yet been formally consecrated;
for that very reason, those years are known as the "vacancy of kings. And so it is said:
"Between King Paṇḍukābhaya and Abhaya..."
“Seventeen years passed as empty of kings. Therein means in Jambudīpa.
Of Paṇḍuka means of Paṇḍukābhaya; for a designation may be made by way of a single part, just as one says “Datta” for Devadatta.
“The seventeen years were fulfilled” means they were fulfilled even while he was not yet consecrated. Here—
Excluding the sixteenth year of Kāḷāsoka, fifteen years are to be counted from below;
taking two—the seventeenth and eighteenth years of Susunāga—and adding them to the seventeen years, they become eighteen when combined with the single year mentioned below.
Thus, those seventeen years of royal vacancy are situated between the kings Vijaya and Paṇḍuvāsudeva.
Together with one year without a king, these constitute what are known as the eighteen years of royal vacancy.
It was in the fourteenth year of Candagutta that Paṇḍukābhaya passed away here;
thus, in the fourteenth year of Candagutta, King Paṇḍukābhaya, having ruled over this island of Tambapaṇṇi for seventy years, [died].
He passed away. For thus Susunāga’s son, Kālāsoka, reigned for twenty-eight years.
After him, his ten brothers reigned for twenty-two years; after them, the nine Nandas reigned for twenty-two years;
and Candagutta reigned for twenty-four years. In that regard, concerning Kālāsoka—
Of the twenty-eight years, fifteen years were taken from the preceding period;

setting those aside, the remaining thirteen years—twenty-two for the ten brothers, likewise twenty-two for the nine Nandas, and thirteen years after setting aside the fourteenth year of Candagutta—thus fulfilled seventy years for Paṇḍukābhaya. And so it has been said:
“King Paṇḍukābhaya was seventy years old. Regarding this: in the seventeenth year of King Asoka Dhamma, King Muṭasiva passed away here;
thus, in the seventeenth year of King Asoka Dhamma in Jambudīpa, the king named Muṭasiva [reigned] sixty years here.
Having ruled the kingdom, he passed away. For thus Bindusāra, the son of Candagutta, reigned for twenty-eight years;
after him, his son King Asoka-dhamma attained the throne.
Therefore, of the twenty-four years mentioned prior to Candagutta, thirteen years have already been accounted for; setting those aside, the remaining eleven—
Twenty-eight years for Bindusāra, four years for Asoka before his consecration, and seventeen years after his consecration—thus sixty years were fulfilled here by Muṭasīva. And so it has been said:
"Muṭasīva exercised sovereignty over Laṅkā for sixty years."
"Devānaṃpiyatissa attained the kingship" means he attained it in the eighteenth year of King Aśoka Dhamma.

Now, showing that thirty-six years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One—calculated by counting the years of Ajātasattu and the others together—two hundred years had passed, he said: "And when the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained Parinibbāna," and so forth.
In that context, regarding Ajātasattu, the number twenty-four is stated excluding the eighth year, which is reckoned as the year of his Parinibbāna.
Regarding Asoka’s ten sons, the "ten brother-kings" refers to these ten:
Bhaddasena, Koraṇḍavaṇṇa, Maṅkura, Sabbañjaha, Jālika, Ubhaka, Sañcaya, Korabya, Nandivaḍḍhana, and Pañcamaka—the sons of Kāḷāsoka.

They should be understood as the "brother-kings. Uggasena-nanda, Paṇḍuka-nanda, Paṇḍugati-nanda, Bhūtapāla-nanda, Raṭṭhapāla-nanda, Govisāṇaka-nanda, Saviddhaka-nanda, Kevaṭṭaka-nanda, and Dhana-nanda—these nine should be understood as the "Nandas.
"By this lineage of kings" means by this lineage of the kings dwelling in Jambudīpa.
The meaning is that this should be understood.
Furthermore, the calculation for those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi should be understood according to their kings as follows:
having taken the first year of Vijaya here to be the year of the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha, and having set that aside from the year of the Parinibbāna...
Thirty-seven years after Vijaya, then one year without a king,
thirty years for Paṇḍuvāsudeva, twenty years for Abhaya, seventeen years before the consecration of Paṇḍukābhaya,
seventy years after his consecration, sixty years for Muṭasīva, and first for Devānampiyatissa.
"Rain falls" means that it should be understood as thirty-six years after two hundred years from the Parinibbāna.
Since the full moon of the month of Jeṭṭha coincides with either the Jeṭṭha or Mūla lunar mansion, he said, "it is called the Jeṭṭha-Mūla lunar mansion.
Furthermore, the festival to be performed under that lunar mansion receives that same name because it depends upon it.
It should be understood as follows: "Migava" (the hunt) is so named because it is the hunting, the seeking, and the afflicting of deer.
"Rohitamigarūpaṃ" means having the appearance of a red deer (*rohitamiga*), resembling a *gokaṇṇa* deer. "Jiyā" refers to the bowstring. "Anubandhanto" means pursuing on foot.
Regarding the phrase "May the King see me alone," [it implies that] even though many of us have been seen, the King—[prefers]...
It should be understood that by saying, "He will be afraid," he resolved, "Let him see me alone," in order to reveal himself for this very reason.
Having said, "He thought," the text says, "Born on this island," and so forth, showing the manner of his reflection.
The Elder, knowing his reflection and wishing to comfort him by declaring his own true nature, [said]: "The recluses..."
He said, "We are [monks], O Great King," and so forth. The meaning is: "O Great King, we are indeed called recluses; do not harbor such thoughts.
"Out of compassion for you alone" means the intention is that they have come solely for the sake of showing compassion toward you, and not for the sake of turning their faces away from you.
Why did the Elder say, "We are recluses, O Great King," to one who did not know, "These are indeed called recluses"?
If it is asked, "Why does he say this?"—it was said thus in order to remind [the king] of the recognition of him as a monk previously received through the very message sent by King Aśoka-dhamma.
To clarify this point, the passage beginning with "At that time" (*tena ca samayena*) was stated.
"Friends who had not seen each other" (*adiṭṭhā hutvā sahāyakā*) means those who, without having seen one another, entered into a state of friendship.
It is said: "At the foot of Mount Chāta" means at the foot of the mountain named Chātavāha.
It is said that this mountain stands about two yojanas to the south-east of Anurādhapura.
Later, a great king named Saddhātissa built a monastery in that place, which came to be known as the "Chāta Monastery."
“‘The size of a chariot-pole’ means that in length and circumference it is equal to a chariot goad,” so it is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
It is also stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“At the foot of Mount Chāta, there were three bamboo poles;”
“They were born equal in size to the chariot-goad.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated: “‘Of the measure of a chariot-pole’ means of the measure of the flag-pole of a chariot.
“They arose” means they arose at the very moment of his consecration. In this same way, the manifestation of the wonders that will be described hereafter [should be understood].
It should be understood thus. And so it is said in the Mahāvaṃsa:
“Upon the passing of his father, Devānampiyatissa became king;
at the same time as his consecration, many wonders occurred.”
"One creeper-staff" means there was a single staff that had received this name because it was adorned with golden creepers.
"A creeper arisen having adorned it" means a creeper that arose right there, as if fashioned by painting, after having adorned that silver-colored staff.
"Appears" means it is seen. "Filaments" means the stamens. And these [are found] upon the flower-staff.
It should be understood that blue flowers and so forth, as well as various kinds of birds and wild animals, appear right there as if they were fashioned in a painting (*cittakamma*).
"A white silver-staff" means a single staff of white color, like one made of silver.
"Creeper" refers to a creeper appearing right there as if it were fashioned in a painting. "Blue and so forth" refers to whatever [colors] they may be.
"Whatever kind of flowers there are in the world, such as blue and others, they appear upon the flower-stalk"—this is the meaning.

"Various kinds of jewels arose" means that various sorts of jewels, having themselves ascended from the ocean to the shore, arose upon the beach like a natural boundary-wall produced by the force of the waves; the meaning is that they rose up and remained there. [In] Tambapaṇṇi...

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, eight pearls appeared," it should be understood that here too, eight pearls of that species arose spontaneously from the ocean in Tambapaṇṇi and remained on the shore of the sea in the manner already described. For this is stated in the Mahāvaṃsa:
"In the entirety of the island of Laṅkā, treasures and jewels;..."
Emerging from within, they ascended to the surface of the earth.
Having arrived on a broken ship near the island of Laṅkā,
as well as those born there, the jewels ascended onto dry land.
“Horse-shaped, elephant-shaped, chariot-shaped, and pure lotus-shaped;
bracelet-shaped, finger-ring-shaped, *kakudha*-fruit-shaped, and natural [stone-shaped]—these are the eight types by birth.
Pearls, having emerged from the ocean, remain on the shore like a ring.”
"This is the manifestation of all the merit of Devānaṃpiyatissa.
"Horse-muktās" are those shaped like horses; "elephant-muktās" are those shaped like elephants.
In this way, throughout all cases, the varieties of muktā should be understood according to their respective shapes. "Finger-ring muktās" are those shaped like rings.
“Shaped like grapes” means that. “Pearls shaped like *kakudha* fruits” refers to many non-oceanic pearls in the form of *kakudha* tree fruits.
“Royal insignia” means articles worthy of a king, the highest regalia. Showing these in their actual form, he said, “The parasol, the chowrie,” and so forth.
The connection is: “He sent various other kinds of gifts as well. “Conch” refers to the vessel used for the consecration sprinkling.
A sea conch shell, spiraling to the right. The water of Lake Anotatta itself is referred to as "Ganges water.
*Vaḍḍhamāna* refers to cosmetic powder; some say it means "bath powder. *Vaṭaṃsaka* means an ear-ornament; that is what is meant.
Some also say, "A *vaṭaṃsaka* is a hanging ornament worn on the upper part of the ear. *Bhiṅgāra* means a golden vessel.
A large water-pot (*mahābhiṅgāra*). Some also say it is a type of vessel fashioned in the shape of a makara’s mouth for the purpose of performing offerings and other rites.
A *nandiyāvaṭṭa* is a type of golden vessel fashioned in the shape of a crow’s foot for the sake of auspiciousness.

A “maiden” (*kaññā*) refers to a daughter of a noble family (*khattiya*). A pair of lower garments (*adhovimaṃ dussayugaṃ*) [is so called because] as soon as they become soiled, they are thrown into the fire.
A pair of lower garments (*adhovima*) made of pure cloth; a hand-wiping cloth (*hatthapuñchana*)—that is, a costly yellow-colored hand-wiping cloth;
yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*)—meaning sandalwood of golden hue—or red sandalwood, meaning *gosīta* sandalwood. It is said that when boiled oil was placed on the hearth...
Even a mere drop of oil, when combined with sandalwood capable of extinguishing a fire, is called "goṣītacandana.
For by the word *go* water is meant; sandalwood that is as white as that is *goṣītacandana*. [It is also] clay from the abode of the nāgas, the color of dawn.
*Harītaka* and *āmalaka* refer to the *agada-harītaka* (the antidote myrobalan) and *agada-āmalaka* (the antidote emblic myrobalan). That [remedy] very quickly...
It is capable of performing such tasks as cleansing the impurities of the body.
*Uṇhīsa* means a turban-cloth. *Veṭhana* means a head-wrap. *Sārapāmaṅga* means an excellent jewel-garland thread.
*Vatthakoṭika* refers simply to a pair of garments. *Nāgamāhaṭa* means brought by the *nāgas*. The letter *m* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
*Amatosadha*: This is a type of medicinal pill; it is so called because its function is like that of the Deathless (*amata*).
It is said to be a pill prepared by rolling together various antidotal medicinal ingredients that dispel obstacles and bring success in all matters.
At the conclusion of their baths, kings have this brought to them with great ceremony to cleanse their mouths. By means of it, they...

They apply what is called "body-ointment" (*aṅgarāga*); and while applying it, one should understand that they prepare the body—namely the forehead, the tops of the shoulders, the chest, and the middle of the torso—with two or three medicinal marks (*tilaka*) of non-poisonous herbs as appropriate, and thus apply the body-ointment.
Furthermore, that pill (*guḷikā*) destroys the poison even of snakes, scorpions, and the like; for that reason also, it is called "the medicine of immortality" (*amatosadha*).

In the passage beginning with "I [saw] the Buddha," the term *Buddha* refers to the Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), who has awakened to and fully realized all phenomena (*dhammā*) exactly as they are;

and the term *Dhamma* refers to the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) together with the scriptural teaching (*pariyatti*), which is designated as *Dhamma* because it sustains those who have attained the path and realized cessation, and who practice according to the instructions so that they do not fall into the states of misery (*apāya*).
Because they are united by the commonality of view and virtue, it has attained the designation "Saṅgha";
and I have gone for refuge to that Saṅgha of noble disciples, having approached it as my ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*)—the meaning is that I have cultivated and served it.

Alternatively, [it is called *saṅgha*] because it destroys (*hiṃsati*) the defilements of those who have gone for refuge through the act of going for refuge itself, by means of a mental state that arises in the form of taking them as its ultimate resort, accompanied by the honoring and cherishing of them.
It is called a *saraṇa* (refuge) because it strikes down, destroys, and eliminates fear, terror, suffering, miserable rebirths, and affliction;

this is a designation for the Triple Gem. Furthermore, the Fully Enlightened One is called a refuge because he harms the fear of sentient beings by promoting their welfare and turning them away from what is harmful.
The Dhamma as well [is a refuge] because it delivers one from the wilderness of existence and bestows consolation.

And because it destroys the fear of beings, it is called a "refuge" (*saraṇa*). The Saṅgha, too, is called a "refuge" because it destroys the fear of beings by bringing about the attainment of vast fruits even from small deeds.

In this sense, the Triple Gem, which has become a refuge, is "gone to" (*gata*) as a refuge for that very reason; the meaning is that one has understood or known it. "He declared his status as a lay follower" means [he declared his taking refuge in] the Triple Gem.
The meaning is: "He who worships is a lay follower (*upāsaka*); having thus manifested the state of being a lay follower—which was established within me—he proclaimed it with his speech.
What is meant is that he announced his status as a lay follower by saying, "I am a lay follower; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I have gone for refuge.
In the phrase "in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans" (*sakyaputtassa sāsaneti*), the Blessed One is the "Son of the Sakyans" because he is the son of Sakyamuni Suddhodana.
The meaning is: "in the teaching of that Son of the Sakyas. *Saddhā* means "with faith";
here, the elision of the letter *y* should be understood as in such expressions as *sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*.
*Upehī* means "approach. *Asokaraññā pesitena abhisekena* means "by the consecration equipment sent by King Asoka. For when...
The Great King Devānampiyatissa sent from here to his friend, King Dhammāsoka, costly gifts such as bamboo staffs and other items.
Upon seeing them, the latter was inspired with faith and became exceedingly joyful, thinking, "What more precious gift than these could I send to my friend? Having consulted with his ministers, he—
Having inquired about the procedure for the consecration on the island of Laṅkā,
and having heard that "there is no such procedure for consecration there," he said, "It would be well indeed if I were to send the procedure for my companion's consecration.
He then took three kinds of shells— namely, those from the ocean— and the water of the Gaṅgā, as well as clay the color of dawn, and eight each of Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, and Gahapati maidens.
He sent eight jars made of gold, silver, iron, and clay, along with eight families of ministers from the eight guilds of merchants;

thus he sent what is known here as the "Eightfold Set," saying, "With these, perform the consecration for my friend once again," and he also sent many other gifts for the sake of the consecration. Therefore it was said: "Sent by King Asoka..."
“By means of consecration. One who has been consecrated for one month is “one-month-consecrated. But how is it known that he was then one-month-consecrated?

To this he says: “For they performed his consecration on the full moon of Visākha,” referring to the fact that even though he had previously received consecration, on the full moon of Visākha he again [received it] with priceless honors sent by King Asoka.
The meaning is that they performed the consecration. For this is said in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
"On the day the sun rose in the month of Migasira, the ministers, devoted to their lord, consecrated the Lord of Laṅkā."
“Having heard the words of Dhammāsoka, those who delight in their own welfare,
and who take pleasure in the well-being and happiness of Laṅkā, consecrated him once again.
This is also stated in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
"On the twelfth day of the month of Visākha, [the throne] came here from Jambudīpa;
the consecration, together with its retinue, was sent by Asokadhamma.
They consecrated for the second time the king Devānampiya."
“He was consecrated with the second consecration on the Uposatha day of the month of Visākha.
Then, after a month had passed, on the Uposatha day of the month of Jeṭṭha,
Mahinda, having become the seventh [member of the mission], came here from Jambudīpa.”

However, because the consecration of that king was performed on the full moon day of Visākha, from that time until the present day, it has become customary to perform the consecration specifically on the full moon day of Visākha.
The procedure for the consecration should be understood as follows:
inside a decorated and prepared pavilion, a pavilion made of *udumbara* branches has been constructed for the sake of the auspicious consecration ceremony.
Having seated the noble Kṣatriya, worthy of consecration, upon a magnificent Udumbara throne firmly established in the center,
first of all, a high-born Kṣatriya maiden, adorned with auspicious ornaments,
carefully took with both hands a conch shell from the southern ocean filled with Ganges water, raised it above his head, and [poured] it over him.
He sprinkles the consecration water upon his head and speaks thus:
"Your Majesty, all these groups of kṣatriyas perform this consecration to make you a consecrated Great King for the sake of protecting themselves;
established in the duties of kingship, rule the kingdom with righteousness and impartiality, out of affection and compassion for these groups of kṣatriyas as if they were your own sons."

“Be of a unified mind, and be one whose mind is characterized by benevolence, equanimity, and loving-kindness; thus, through their protection, defense, and guardianship, may you yourself be protected.

Then the chaplain once again, having adorned himself and prepared himself with ornaments appropriate for his office as chaplain, carefully took a silver conch filled with water from the Ganges in both hands, held it aloft above his head, and with that—

They pour consecration water upon his head and speak thus: "Your Majesty, all these hosts of brahmins, for the sake of their own protection, make you a consecrated great king by means of this consecration.
Standing firm in the duties of a king, rule the kingdom with righteousness and impartiality; toward these brahmins, maintain a heart filled with the affection and compassion due to a son."
"And be one whose mind is equal in friendliness toward all; be protected by guarding, shielding, and defending them.

Then the merchant, adorned with ornaments befitting his status as a merchant, respectfully took a jeweled conch filled with water from the Ganges in both hands, raised it above the other's head, and poured the consecration water upon his head.
He sprinkles [the water] and speaks thus: "Sire, all these groups of householders, for the sake of their own protection, have made you a consecrated Great King by means of this consecration.
You, remaining established in the duties of a king, should rule with righteousness and impartiality;
toward these groups of householders, you should be possessed of a heart joined with the affection of a father's love, and a heart of equal benevolence and loving-kindness."
"And you, O King, be protected, shielded, and guarded by them.

But as they spoke thus to him, they pronounced this curse upon the king: "If you rule the kingdom in accordance with our word, that is well; if you do not so rule, may your head split into seven pieces!"

This should be understood as it has been explained. However, regarding this island, they say that the very princess sent here by Dhammāsoka for the head of Devānaṃpiyatissa was consecrated with the water of the Anotatta lake using a right-spiraling conch shell from the ocean.
And this aforementioned procedure for consecration is found in the Majjhima Nikāya.

In the *Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā* commentary on the *Cūḷasīhanādasutta*, it is stated: "First of all, for kings receiving consecration, it is necessary to obtain three types of conchs made of gold and so forth, water from the Ganges, and a kṣatriya maiden," and so on; thus they say.

Regarding the phrase "engaging in friendly conversation": it is because it generates friendliness (*sammoda*), which consists of joy (*pīti*) and gladness (*pāmojja*), and because it is appropriate for such mutual delight.
And while exchanging greetings with such words as, "Venerable sir, I hope you are well, I hope you are comfortable, I hope you are free from affliction, free from illness, light in body, strong,
and living at ease," he showed the six people who had come with the king,
so that they might recognize them, saying, "These are not *yakkhas*, these are human beings," to the lay follower Bhaṇḍuka.
Because he had brought them, he showed six people together with him.

"Possessors of the three knowledges" (*tevijjā*) means endowed with the three types of knowledge consisting of the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). "Attained to psychic powers" (*iddhippatta*) means having attained the knowledge of the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*).

"Skilled in reading the minds of others" (*cetopariyakovida*) means expert in the mental conduct of others. Thus, five of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are stated here by their specific names, while the divine ear (*dibbasota*), however—

It is precisely by virtue of them that [the number] has come about. "Many" means many such disciples of the Buddha possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), exceeding the path of calculation, wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, making it radiant with the saffron robe.

However, some say: "Having connected 'those possessing the three knowledges (*tevijjā*) and those who have attained psychic power (*iddhippatta*), as well as those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) and those skilled in reading the minds of others (*cetopariyakovida*), and separately [connecting] 'some whose taints are destroyed,' the term 'Arahants' refers here to those who practice dry-insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*)."
“Clarity of wisdom” (*paññāveyyattiya*) means proficiency in wisdom; the meaning is the sharp and keen state of wisdom. “Nearby” (*āsanna*) means standing near.
“Excellent, Great King, you are wise” is a praise of the king. Examining him further, he said, “But do you have, Great King,” and so forth.
He related the *Cūḷahatthipadopama-sutta* (The Short Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint), [thinking], “This king—‘these ascetics...’”
Thinking, “He does not know that their names are such-and-such, nor that their practice of virtue and so forth is such-and-such;

come now, I shall make him understand both the attainment of the state of a recluse and the practice of a recluse by means of this teaching of the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta,” he first delivered the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. For therein—
“In the same way, brahmin, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct...
[he] proclaims the holy life, which is entirely complete and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma...”
Having heard [the teaching], he gains faith in the Tathāgata; endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
“Household life is crowded and dusty, while going forth is open air;
it is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life (brahmacariya) in its complete perfection, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell. What if I were now...”
“Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a great mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or a great circle of kinsmen, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life;
laying aside the rod and the weapon, being modest and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
“Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft and pure.

By such passages as these, the attainment of faith in the Teaching is proclaimed, as well as the going forth for those who have attained faith, and the factors of the Dhamma—beginning with the aggregate of virtue—that are to be practiced by those who have gone forth.
Even while merely listening to the Sutta, the King understood: “He abstains from the destruction of seeds and living plants...”
Because it is stated in that sutta thus, “He eats but one meal a day, refrains from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times,” he understood it even as he was hearing it.
He did not say, “I shall dwell right here,” because the night had not yet arrived.
He said, “One who has attained the fruit,” referring to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); the meaning is, “one who has reached the fruit of non-returning. And for that very reason—
"Viññātasāsano" (one who has understood the teaching) means that he has specifically understood the Teacher’s dispensation without error.
He spoke thus because the duty brought about by his lay appearance—namely, "He will now go forth"—had been fulfilled. "Not long after the king had departed" means when the king had recently departed.
"Having resolved" means having resolved, "Let those gathered within the island of Tambapaṇṇi hear!"
"By way of a carpet spread upon the ground" means in the manner of a ground-covering. "Readers of portents" refers to those who read signs;

the meaning is "interpreters of omens. "Now this earth has been taken by these [seats]"—they spoke thus because the seats were laid out upon the earth. Regarding the phrase "thinking that it will be established":
here, because there was no establishment of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) for that reason, [the thought arises] regarding that which will inevitably be established.
"It is a foretoken of the Dispensation"—thus it should be understood that he perceived it as such by way of being a foretoken.

"With excellent" means with the most superior. "With his own hand" means having satisfied them with his own hand; the meaning is: having thoroughly satisfied them, making them full, well-fed, and as much as they required. He spoke the *Petavatthu*, the *Vimānavatthu*, and the *Saccasaṃyutta*.
The Elder, skilled in the methods of instruction, first recounted a story of the departed spirits (*petavatthu*) to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the people.
Immediately thereafter, he recounted the stories of celestial mansions (*vimānavatthu*) by way of a discourse on heaven (*saggakathā*) to comfort those who had become spiritually urgent.
Then, for those who had found such comfort, he said: "Do not find gratification in this; apart from Nibbāna, there is nothing else among conditioned things (*saṅkhāra*) [worth desiring]."

It should be understood that, at the end, he spoke the *Saccasaṃyutta* (Connected Discourses on Truth), generating enthusiasm for the penetration of truth by saying: "There is indeed the Permanent; therefore, strive to attain Nibbāna, which is the ultimate consolation.
"Having heard from them" means having heard the discourse on the virtues of those elders. "Having made it known to the king" means to the king...
"Having made a report" means having informed the king. "Enough, let us go" was said by way of rejection, because [the place] was too close to the city and thus not appropriate.
"The park called Meghavana" refers to the Mahāmeghavana garden.
It is said that on the day the ground for that garden was being taken, an untimely great rain-cloud arose, and all the tanks and lotus-pools...

Filling [the air], he rained down as if out of compassion for the trees, creepers, and other plants scorched by the summer heat; for that reason, it became known as the Mahāmeghavana (Great Cloud Forest) park.
Indeed, this is stated in the Mahāvaṃsa:
"When the site for the park was being selected, a great cloud appeared out of season..."
“By that [rain] he rained upon the park; it became like a great cloud-forest.
Having asked about the state of his comfortable rest—asking thus, “Venerable sir, did you sleep comfortably here?
Is your dwelling here pleasant?”—the Elder then replied, “I slept comfortably, Great King.”

When it was said, "This park is for the comfort of the bhikkhus," he thought, "If that is so, I shall give this park to you," and asked, "Venerable sir, is a monastery allowable for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?

This is the Sutta spoken regarding the acceptance of the Veḷuvana Monastery. "Water" refers to the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*). He gave the Mahāmeghavana Park, saying, "This Mahāmeghavana Park..."
Having said, "I give this to the Saṅgha," he gave it on the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha.
Although [the gift] was established together with the pouring of the consecratory water for the Mahāvihāra, the construction work for that monastery had not yet been finished;
therefore, he said, "And this shall be the first site for a vihāra. "On the following day as well" means on the very second day of the dark fortnight.
"Of eight thousand five hundred beings" means of eight thousand five hundred beings; the meaning is of eight thousand plus five hundred.
"The place of the manifestation of light" means the place where the light of knowledge manifests.
"The *Appamāda-sutta*" refers to the *Mahā-appamāda-sutta* in the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*; it is stated that this is the *Rāja-ovāda-sutta*.
*Mahaccā* is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "by means of great royal majesty.
The connection is with the phrase "you know the matter. "The minister named Ariṭṭha" refers to the minister named Ariṭṭha, who was the king's nephew.

Regarding the expression *pañcapaññāsāya*, it should have been stated as *catupaṇṇāsāya*. For if that were the case, then the statement "sixty-two arahants" mentioned further below would be consistent.
The statement is consistent. For that very reason, it is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, written in the Sinhalese language: "together with fifty-four.

"The royal family crowded with ten brothers" means the royal family was filled with ten brothers, such as Abhaya, Devānaṃpiyatissa, Mahānāga, Uttiya, Mattābhaya, Sūratissa, and others, who were the sons of Muṭasiva.

“They spent the rains retreat at Cetiyagiri” means that on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī, having accepted the monastery offered by the king, they entered the rains retreat on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada).
“Having performed the invitation ceremony” means having performed the Great Invitation ceremony (mahāpavāraṇā).

“On the full moon of Kattika” refers to the later full moon of Kattika; for the Elder Mahāmahinda, having entered the earlier rains retreat and completed it, [performed] the Great Invitation ceremony...
Having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony and then passed one month, on the full-moon day of the fourth month, he went to the royal palace surrounded by a company of noble ones.
At the conclusion of the meal, he spoke these words: "Great King, it has been a long time since we have seen the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth.
Having acted in this way, he will later say: "On the full-moon day of the fourth month, the Great Hero came here. As for that which was said here by someone...
It is said: “‘Having completed the rains and performed the *pavāraṇā*’ means having performed the *pavāraṇā* at the end of the four months;
or, having performed the first *pavāraṇā*, he stayed right there for one month and spoke on the full moon of Kattika.

Otherwise, it could not be accepted because it is stated: ‘On the full moon, the Great Hero. In this context, “having performed the *pavāraṇā* at the end of the four months” is an alternative interpretation of the meaning.
This is not tenable. For those who have entered the rains residence during the first period do not perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) at the end of the four months.

One should understand that [the statement] was made thus by applying the designation of the whole to its parts—thinking, "The Perfectly Enlightened One has long been seen," and considering that even a limb of the Teacher’s body is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One himself—just as one says, "The ocean has been seen."

Setting aside even the reason for going mentioned by the Elder, and desiring to prevent the departure by demonstrating the purpose for staying here, he said, "Venerable sir, I [shall attend] upon you," and so forth.
Regarding acts such as salutation: when one sees the teacher, the act of performing a salutation is called *abhivādana*.
Or, having bowed facing toward whichever direction the teacher dwells while performing his postures, [one should attend].
To go [to him], to stand after having paid homage, to sit down after having paid homage, or to lie down after having paid homage—this is called "salutation" (*abhivādana*).
Furthermore, upon seeing the teacher from afar, rising and going forward to meet him is called "rising" (*paccuṭṭhāna*).

Moreover, upon seeing the teacher, raising one's joined palms and placing them on the head while paying reverence to the teacher in whichever direction he may be—this is [called] "reverence" (*namassana*).
Whether he is staying, or facing [the object of veneration], or even while walking, standing, or sitting, he pays homage with palms joined;
this is called the act of *añjalikamma*. Furthermore, performing what is appropriate is called *sāmīcikamma* (service).
For when giving robes and other requisites, one does not give just anything, but rather something of great value.
He gives even that which is worth one hundred root-coins, or five hundred root-coins, or even one hundred thousand root-coins.

The same principle applies to alms-food and other such things. This is called "performing respectful service" (sāmīcikaraṇa). "Relics of the body" (sarīradhātu) means parts of the body. "Known" (aññātaṃ) means known;
the meaning is "understood by me. "From where shall we obtain? means "from where will we receive it? "Consult with Sumanā."
It should be understood that he spoke thus either because it had already been told to the novice, or because [the Buddha] knew, "He understands our intention.
"Be unconcerned, O Great King" means: O Great King, do not exert yourself regarding the recovery of the relics; do not be preoccupied with that matter;
perform instead whatever else is to be done by you—this is the intended meaning. Now, that very same [instruction] was given by the King...
Showing what must be done, he said, “having had the streets cleared,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “having had all the musical instruments (tāḷāvacara) set out”:

that which moves within (avacarati) the bronze cymbals and other percussion instruments is called *tāḷāvacara*; thus, it refers to the entire collection of musical equipment, such as stringed and percussion instruments.
For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Parinibbāna Sutta*, it says: “‘And let all the musical instruments be assembled’—here, ‘all’ [refers to...]”
“*Tāḷāvacaraṃ* means ‘all musical instruments,’ so it is said. Here, however, by the principle of association (*sahacaraṇanaya*), the players of all the musical instruments may also be included;
thus, it is meant that they were all summoned and assembled. “*Lacchasi*” means “you will obtain.
“The elders went to Cetiyagiri itself” means that after departing from the royal residence, they returned once more to Cetiyagiri itself.
"At that very moment" means at that precise instant. "At the gate of Pāṭaliputta" means at the city gate of the town of Pāṭaliputta.
"Venerable Sir, why do you wander about, Sumana?"—he asks this, meaning, "Sumana, why do you roam about without practicing the duty of a recluse?
"Having established it right there on Cetiyagiri"—this is because later on, it was desired that a monastery should be built right there on Cetiyagiri.
"Having established [it]. "When the shadow was lengthening" means after the meal;
for it is precisely after the meal that the shadow grows longer. "Then this thought occurred to him": having seen the reliquary casket, he thought thus.
"'Let the sunshade be lowered'": the meaning is, "let this white sunshade itself lower down from above my head, facing toward the reliquary casket."
"May it rest upon my head": this means that the relic casket, having come from the Elder's hand together with the relic, [should] rest upon my head.

"A rain of lotuses" (pokkharavassa) refers to a great rain that arises in the midst of clouds, reaching the size of a lotus leaf, and which, while wishing to moisten by gradually spreading, actually moistens as it becomes vast.
It rains. "Mahāvīra" means one of great prowess. And here, because they are parts of the Great Hero, the relics themselves are designated by the term "Teacher.
For this verse was spoken with reference to the arrival of the relic-body;
it says that he departed while facing toward the western direction, meaning he went back step by step, facing toward the western direction.

"Having sacrificed, he retreats" means "he goes. Although he does not look toward the western direction, nevertheless, because he goes with reference to the western direction, it is said, "facing the western direction.
Regarding the phrase "having entered the city by the eastern gate," [it means] having come right behind him along the back, and when reaching the gate, having turned around.

It should be understood that he entered the city by a direct route. "The site named Mahejava" should be understood as a certain divine abode occupied by a *yakkha* named Maheja. Regarding "the site of a *paribhoga-cetiya*":
a *cetiya* constructed there by enshrining articles used [by the Buddha] is to be regarded as a *paribhoga-cetiya*. For they speak of three kinds of *cetiya*.
[There are] the *paribhoga-cetiya*, the *dhātu-cetiya*, and the *dhamma-cetiya*. Among these, the *paribhoga-cetiya* is exactly as previously described.

The *dhātu-cetiya*, however, is one constructed after enshrining relics (*dhātu*). That which is constructed after enshrining a manuscript containing [texts such as] the *Paṭiccasamuppāda* and so forth is called a *dhamma-cetiya*.
Furthermore, it is also divided into three types: the bodily relic (*sārīrika*), the object used by the Buddha (*paribhogika*), and the dedicated relic (*uddissaka*).
They call it a *cetiya*. Furthermore, this classification is even more appropriately applied since even the form of an image is included within the category of *uddissaka-cetiya* (dedicated shrines).
But how did this place become a site for the *paribhoga-cetiya* (shrines of use) of the three Buddhas? To this he said: "In the past..."
"Kirā," etc. Here, "pajjaraka" refers to a disease. It should be understood that this arose through the power of a *yakkha*.

At that time, it is said, a *yakkha* named Puṇṇakāla, by his own supernatural power, caused a disease called *pajjaraka* to break out even in the bodies of human beings. For this is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“Among the people here, a plague caused by *rakkhasas* arose”;
this is also stated in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
“Many *rakkhasas* and *pajjaras* arose there.”
“Many beings perish through hunger in this most excellent island.
Here, *anaya* means lack of progress (*avaḍḍhi*). That which destroys (*byasati*), scatters, and ruins physical and mental happiness is called *byasana*;
it refers to suffering (*dukkha*). Although it was said, “surveying the world with the Buddha-eye,”...

Although this has been stated, nevertheless, because of the expression "seeing those beings falling into ruin and disaster," it should be understood that he first surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and subsequently,
while surveying the world with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),

saw those beings falling into ruin and disaster. For those beings falling into ruin and disaster were not [visible] to the Buddha-eye regarding their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) and latent dispositions (*anusaya*).
They are seen. "Bad rain" (*dubbuṭṭhikā*) refers specifically to rain that is spoiled and unsightly due to irregularity in its falling;

the intended meaning is that there is no "right rain" (*sammā vuṭṭhi*) there—that is, no rain which serves as the cause for the growth of crops, which is conducive to the arising of physical well-being, and which is beneficial to sentient beings.
For this very reason, it is said: "famine and poor harvests. This means the absence of alms-food, or its being difficult to obtain.
"Or famine" means that alms-food was not easily obtainable there. "Drought" refers to the absence or the failure to ripen of crops.
"The god" is a name for the cloud. "He bestowed a proper shower" means he released a stream of water properly;
it is said that he rained down properly.
“*Mahāvivādo hotīti*”: it is said that at that time, a great war broke out on this island between the Great King Jayanta and his younger brother, the viceroy named Prince Samiddha.
Therefore it was said: “At that time, there was a great conflict in Maṇḍadīpa. *Hoti* is a verb.

The use of the present tense is employed here with reference to time; however, the fact that the dispute belongs to the past is understood precisely by the phrase "at that time" (*tena kho pana samayena*).
For in this context, the comprehension of the past tense occurs through the proximity of other words, just as in the expression "he speaks and prospers then.
Thus, in all such instances, the use of the present tense should be understood in this manner. [They were] "engaged in strife and contention."
In this context, "quarrel" (*kalaha*) refers to both physical quarrels and verbal quarrels that have reached their peak.

Therein, a quarrel to be performed by means of the body—such as through grasping with the hands—is a physical quarrel (*kāyakalaha*). A quarrel to be performed by means of speech—such as through striking at vital points—is a verbal quarrel (*vācākalaha*).
"Dispute" (*vigga*) is the taking up of an opposing position; it is the mutual, contradictory grasping that arises prior to a quarrel. Now...
Or "quarrel" (*kalaha*) means a quarrel of words. "Strife" (*viggaha*) is the grasping of one another in a distorted or hostile manner by means of seizing hands and so forth;

it is a physical quarrel. Those in whom such a quarrel and strife as described have arisen—that is, have been produced—are called "those for whom quarrel and strife have arisen" (*kalahaviggahajātā*);
the meaning is "those in whom quarrel and strife have been produced."

"They will perish through the disappearance of the Dispensation" means that when the threefold Dispensation—consisting of the study (pariyatti), realization (paṭivedha), and practice (paṭipatti)—disappears upon the final nirvana of the relics (dhātuparinibbāna), those shrines (cetiyas) will perish. For there are three kinds of final nirvana:

the final nirvana of the defilements (kilesaparinibbāna), the final nirvana of the aggregates (khandhaparinibbāna), and the final nirvana of the relics (dhātuparinibbāna). Now, these [three] belong to our Blessed One...

They should be understood according to this sequence: for his *parinibbāna* of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) occurred at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), his *parinibbāna* of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*) occurred at Kusinārā, and his *parinibbāna* of the relics (*dhātuparinibbāna*) will take place in the future.
It is said that when the Dispensation (*sāsana*) declines, the relics will gather together in this island of Tambapaṇṇi and proceed to the Mahācetiya; from the Mahācetiya, they will go to Nāgadīpa.
From the Rājāyatana Cetiya they will go to the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka;

even from the abode of the Nāgas, from the world of the gods, and from the Brahma-world, the relics will go only to the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka, and not even a relic the size of a mustard seed will perish along the way.
All the relics, having become a single heap at the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka, will be as one solid mass like a block of gold.
Having offered it, they will emit six-colored rays that will pervade the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*).
Then, the deities in the ten-thousandfold universe (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*) will assemble and say: "Today the Teacher attains final Nibbāna; today the Dispensation declines;
this is now our last sight of him. Thus, on the day of the Tenth-Powered One’s (*Dasabala*) final Nibbāna, [they will perform] a [celebration] even greater than [usual].
They will show compassion; with the exception of those non-returners whose taints are destroyed, the rest will not be able to remain in their own natural state.
Among the relics, the fire element will arise and rise up as far as the Brahma-world;
as long as there is even a relic the size of a mustard seed, it will be a single flame, but when the relics have been consumed, it will be extinguished. Thus great...
When his majesty has been displayed and the relics have disappeared, it is said that the Dispensation (sāsana) is considered to have disappeared.

They say that while he stands by day at the site of the Bodhi tree in the elephant stable, making an opportunity for the selection of the site, he takes a relic from there, places it in a jar, and remains standing together with that relic. For this is stated in the Mahāvaṃsa:
“By night the Naga wanders around that site containing the relics;
by day he stands at the Bodhi-tree shrine in the hall, together with the relics.
Regarding the phrase “he wanders around the ground where the stupa was established”: having placed the relic there from the top [of the tree], he remains together with the relic.
It traversed the site where the stupa was to be established during the night; the meaning is that it moved about on all sides.
"The height of a man" refers to the height of the location for the flowers, for they say the lower part of the stupa, below its dome, is the "jaṅghā.

"For the purpose of depositing the relics" means for the purpose of lowering the relic casket from the elephant's forehead. "The entire city and the countryside" refers to the inhabitants of the city.
And those dwelling in the countryside are expressed by the terms "city" and "countryside" without distinction, as in such examples as "the whole village has arrived" or "the beds are making a shout.
"A great multitude of people" (*mahājanakāya*) means a collection of many people; here, the word *kāya* is used in the sense of a "group.

The miracle that occurred as a pair (*yamaka*), proceeding by way of the simultaneous emission of fire and water from each individual part of his body, is called a "pair-miracle" (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
"The Twin Miracle" (*yamakapāṭihāriya*). The connection should be made as "rays of six colors. Some here state that the connection should be "streams of water of six colors.

To show that even after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, such a miracle occurred through his power, he spoke the verse beginning with "Thus inconceivable. Here, "Buddha-qualities" (*buddhadhammā*) refers to the virtues of the Buddha.

"He came three times even during his lifetime" means that, it is said, in the ninth month after his full enlightenment, on the full-moon day of the month of Phussa, the Blessed One approached Laṅkādvīpa, the abode of yakkhas.
Standing in the sky above the Mahānāgavana garden— which was situated in the center of Laṅkā, extending three yojanas in length and one yojana in width— at a great assembly of yakkhas,
he [addressed them] with rain and wind no different from those that arise at the time of the world's dissolution.
And having produced fear and terror in the *yakkhas* by means of a mass of dreadful darkness resembling the gloom of the Lokantara hells,
by an intense cold indistinguishable from that of the cold hells, and by a sky-shattering roar like the thundering of clouds agitated by the winds arising at the time of world-destruction,
he said to them when they had requested his protection: "Give me, all together, a place to sit."
Having said this, when they replied, "We give you the entire island; grant us safety, O Noble One," he caused all that calamity to vanish.
He spread out his leather mat upon the ground given by the *yakkhas*, sat down there, and extended the leather mat so that it blazed all around.
[He thus saved] those who were overcome by a burning heat like the fire at the end of an eon and were terrified of the waters of the ocean.
Having shown Mount Giridīpa to the yakkhas who were wandering all around the coastal region, and once they had settled there,
he placed it back in its original position; then, folding up his leather mat and sitting down amidst the vast assembly of many deities who had gathered,
he taught the Dhamma and brought about the realization of the Truth for many tens of millions of beings, including Mahāsumana, the king of the gods dwelling on Sumanakūṭa.

Having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), he was honored by being requested [to give relics]; having touched his head and given him a handful of dark-blue hair-relics, he departed for Jambudīpa.
In the fifth year after his second full enlightenment, [he went] to Cūḷodara and Mahodara, who dwell in water and on land...
Having witnessed the great destruction of the nāgas in a great battle that had arisen near the jeweled throne of his maternal uncle and nephew,
the two Nāga kings, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Cittamāsa,
the tree-deity named Samiddhasumana fashioned a royal parasol and held it aloft. Having arrived at Nāgadīpa, he stood in the midst of the battlefield.
Seated cross-legged in the air, he terrified the nāgas with a terrible darkness and then reassured them by showing them light.
Having taught the Dhamma conducive to harmony to the nāgas who had approached him with joy and gladness, he was honored by the two nāga kings, Mātula and Bhāgineyya;
then, seated upon a jeweled couch on the surface of the earth, he was served by the nāgas with divine food and drink.
Having satisfied the eighty million nāgas dwelling in the waters and on land, and having established them in the refuges and the precepts,
he set up his throne and the Rājāyatana tree there for them to pay homage,
and then departed for Jambudīpa. For the third time, in the eighth year after his full enlightenment, he was requested by his maternal uncle, the Nāga King Maṇiakkhika, who had a large belly.
On the full moon day of Visākha, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, he approached the palace of Maṇiakkhika at Kalyāṇīpada.

There, seated upon a beautiful and excellent couch within a pavilion constructed of exquisite jewels, he was entertained with divine food and drink by the Nāga king and honored with celestial garlands, perfumes, and other offerings by a host of Nāga maidens; there he preached the Dhamma.

Having taught [the Dhamma] and risen from his seat, he left a footprint on Sumanakūṭa. Having spent the day’s rest at the foot of the mountain, he sat down together with his disciples at the site of the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, at the site of the Mucalinda Cetiya, at the site of the Kalyāṇī Cetiya, at the site of the Mahābodhi, at the site of the Thūpārāma, and at the site of the Mahācetiya;
there, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), he remained at the very site of the Silācetiya.
Having stayed there and instructed the devas and nāgas, he went to Jambudīpa. Thus, it should be understood that even while the Blessed One was still living, he came to this island three times.
Now, explaining briefly that very same threefold visit, he said: "The first was for the purpose of subduing the yakkhas," and so forth.
"Providing protection" means providing protection so that the *yakkhas* do not enter again.
"Went about" means he wandered all around. "Of the maternal uncle and nephew" refers to Cūḷodara and Mahodara.
Here, although the Blessed One had arrived together with the son of a deity named Samiddhasumana, nevertheless, he was even accompanied by a single monk as his attendant.
Because he had not yet arrived, it is said, “having come all alone. Because the obstacles corresponding to that [arrival] had been destroyed, it is said, “having calmed the fever.
“The king’s brother” means the king’s younger brother. “Abhaya” refers to Mattābhaya.
“Queen Anulā” refers to Queen Anulā, the wife of the king’s elder brother. Of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones...
"Established in enlightenment" means that when the Blessed One named Kakusandha, seeing the humans on this island overcome by epidemics and falling into ruin and calamity,
came to this island with a heart stirred by compassion, he then pacified that fear of disease and,
while teaching the Dhamma to those assembled, brought about the realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings.
Having done so, at the time of evening, he went to the place worthy of becoming the site of enlightenment; there, having entered into meditative attainment and emerged from it, he made this resolve:
"Let the bhikkhunī Rucānandā come here, taking with her the great southern branch from my Sirīsa Great Bodhi tree.
Knowing the Teacher’s intention, she took King Khema from the royal capital of Khemavatī at that very moment.
Having approached the Great Bodhi tree, and having had Khemarāja cause an inscription of mind-made stone to be made on the great southern branch, she herself cut that branch and,
taking the Bodhi branch which was placed in a golden bowl, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhunīs and deities,
brought it here by means of psychic power and placed it in the outstretched right hand of the Tathāgata together with the golden bowl.
He established the Mahābodhi. The Tathāgata, having given it to the king named Abhaya, had it installed at that time in the Mahāmeghavana garden, known as "Mahātitthavana.
And the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, seeing the inhabitants of the island oppressed by drought, came to this island; [he dispelled] that fear.
Having brought [the assembly] to peace and teaching the Dhamma, he established eighty-four thousand beings in the fruits of the Path.

Then, going to the site of his previous enlightenment, at the conclusion of a meditative attainment, he thought: "Let the bhikkhunī Karakanattā come here, taking a great southern branch from my Udumbara Great Bodhi tree.
Understanding the Blessed One’s intention, she, at that very moment, [arrived].
Taking King Soba from the capital city of Soba and approaching the Great Bodhi tree, she had King Soba cause an inscription of mind-made stone to be made on the great southern branch;
then, having herself cut that branch and taken it as it rested in a golden basin, she— surrounded by a host of deities and accompanied by five hundred bhikkhunīs—
brought it here by means of her psychic power and placed the golden-basin branch upon the outstretched right palm of the Teacher.

He established the Great Bodhi tree. The Tathāgata, having given it to King Samiddha, had the Great Bodhi planted at that time in the Mahāmeghavana garden—which was then known as the "Great Nāga Forest.
And the Blessed One Kassapa, seeing the destruction of living beings through the war between the incumbent king and his rival, was impelled by compassion.
Having come to this island and pacified that quarrel, while teaching the Dhamma, he enabled eighty-four thousand beings to attain the fruits of the Path.
Then, having gone to the site of the Great Bodhi tree, he entered a meditative attainment there; emerging from it, he said:
"Let the bhikkhunī Sudhammā come here, taking a great southern branch from my Great Bodhi tree at Nigrodha."

She made a formal resolve. Having understood the Blessed One’s intention, at that very moment she took King Brahmadatta from the royal capital of Bārāṇasī, approached the Great Bodhi tree, and had Brahmadatta cause an inscription of mind-made stone to be placed on the great southern branch.
She herself cut that branch and, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhunīs and a host of deities, took the Bodhi branch which was resting in a golden vessel.
Having brought it here by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), he placed the Great Bodhi tree, together with its golden basin, upon the outstretched palm of the Lord of Sages’ right hand.

The Blessed One gave it to King Jayanta, who at that time established the Great Bodhi tree in the Mahāmeghavana garden, which was then known as the "Mahāsāla Grove. Thus, in this island, for the three former...

He established the Bodhi trees of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones. With reference to this, he said: "And in this island, O Great King, the Bodhi trees of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were established.
By "emitting a network of rays of nectar" is meant that, due to its smoothness, it emits a fresh network of rays that is flavorful and full of vital essence (*ojas*).
"By emitting. Alternatively, "by emitting a web of rays that was full of essence, full of life, as if living, due to wandering here and there through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Or alternatively, "by emitting a web of rays like the Buddha while in the period of his vitality, during the time he was still living"—thus they explain the meaning here.
The connection is: "he went in a single day. "With five hundred maidens."
