"With her own five hundred female attendants. "Having had a residence built" means having had a nunnery (bhikkhunupassaya) built. "He sent" means he dispatched a written message.
"And he spoke thus" means that after sending the king's message, he spoke as follows while requesting the Elder’s oral instructions. "He looks toward" means he regards or yearns for.
"Like one with a severed hand" means like one who possesses a severed hand.
"One whose hands are severed" (*chinnahattha*) should be understood as a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound). "Intent on going forth" means facing toward the going forth;
it means having developed a longing for the going forth, having fallen into a state of eager anticipation, thinking, "When indeed shall I go forth? "He honors me" means...
"He gazes at me. "One who does not deserve death by the blade" means one who is not fit to be slain with a weapon.
"The interior of a cloud filled with snow" means the interior of a cloud full of snow. They also say that the snow itself, produced by way of a miracle, is called the "interior of a cloud.
"Measuring a doṇa" means the measure of sixteen nāḷis according to the Magadha standard.

"Road" means a road seven yojanas in length. "Having had it tended" means having had it cleared, having had stumps, thorns, and so forth removed, and having had thick, abundant sand sprinkled over it;
this is what is meant. "The color of a smith" means the color of the king’s ordinary goldsmith.
"Nine-cubit circumference" means that which has a circumference measuring nine cubits.
"By its circumference" means it is stated to be nine cubits in measure.
In such passages as "five cubits high," the meaning should be understood by this same method. "Three cubits wide" means having an extent of three cubits in breadth.

"With flags and banners raised" means with various flags and banners, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, hoisted up. "Variegated with diverse jewels" means [adorned] with various jewels set here and there.
"Beautifully adorned": it was decorated with various ornaments such as hand-fans and the like, which are honored by people of faith. "Strewn with various kinds of flowers":
it was covered with diverse types of water and land flowers, endowed with excellent color and fragrance, brought there as offerings.
"Resounding with many musical instruments": it was filled with the sounds of fivefold musical ensembles, including those that are struck, blown, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the remainder went out of sight": here they say that, as if saying, "Come now, Great King, this branch is for you to grasp;
this trunk is its support, but we are not for you to grasp," the remaining branches went out of sight through the Teacher's splendor.
The term *gavakkhajālasadisaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*).

The meaning is: "having made it like a lattice-window. "Hundreds of thousands of cloth-throws occurred" means that hundreds of thousands of throws of the upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*)—the cloths—of those various people occurred as they were whirling above their heads.
"By a hundred roots" means by a hundred roots that emerged ten by ten from each of the ten lines. Ten...
"Great roots" refers to the ten great roots that emerge from the first line.
"The divine drums resounded" means the divine drums thundered. And here, by "divine drum" no ordinary kettledrum is intended;
rather, it is the sound of a resonance occurring in the sky due to its nature as a portent. For "deva" here means a cloud.

For that sound, which issues forth from the radiance of the god who is crystal-clear and sky-colored, and which resembles the roar of a dry thundercloud, is conventionally designated as "divine drum" (*devadundubhi*);
therefore, the phrase "divine drums resounded" means that the god roared with a dry thunder.
"By the dances of the mountains" refers to the mountains whirling here and there due to the earthquake.
"By dances. "By the *hiṅkāra* sounds of the *yakkhas*" means by the sounds of *hiṅkāra* uttered to manifest the wonder of the *yakkhas* who have become filled with wonder;
for when the *yakkhas* are filled with wonder, they utter the sound "hiṃ hiṃ. "By hymns of praise" means by words of commendation.
"By the clapping of the hands of the *brahmās*" means by the striking of the arms of the *brahmās* who have become filled with joy and gladness.
By clapping their hands. For when the Brahmās are filled with rapture and joy, they bend their left arms and strike their own upper arm with the right hand.
"A single clamor" means a clamor occurring from one side. "A single roar" means a sound occurring from one side.
The six-colored rays issuing from his body rise straight up, then incline and strike the rim of the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
"Standing having struck [the earth]" means "making the entire Cakkavāḷa appear as if covered with jeweled rafters.

And "from that moment onwards" refers to the time from when the Great Bodhi tree, having been established in the golden basin according to the method already described, began to emit its six-colored rays.
"He entered and stood within the womb of the Himalayan cloud" means...
Having ascended together with the golden basin, it entered and remained within a cloud-filled womb full of snow-water.

For the Bodhi tree, having first established itself upon the golden basin, subsequently became adorned with the aforementioned wonders and entered and remained within the snowy cloud-womb. Therefore, he will say: "First, upon the golden basin..."
She took root; then, after spending seven days within the womb of the snow and seven days under the ritual sprinkling, and so forth.
And for this very reason it is said in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
"Thus, with a hundred roots, she [took root] there in that fragrant mud."
The Great Bodhi tree took root, inspiring faith in the great multitude.
Its trunk was ten cubits high, and its five branches were delightful;
each branch was four cubits long and adorned with fifty fruits.
“There were a thousand twigs, and on those twigs were buds;
thus was the Great Bodhi tree, charming like a sirindhara bird.
At the very moment the Great Bodhi was established in its basin, the earth—”
Various miracles occurred and there were many wonders.
There was the sound of musical instruments played spontaneously among the gods and humans, along with the sounds of "well done! from the hosts of devas and brahmās.
“From the cries of clouds, of beasts and birds, and of yakkhas and others,
and from the sounds accompanying the earthquake, there arose a single tumultuous roar.
From the fruits and leaves of the Bodhi tree, beautiful rays of six colors shone forth.”
Having emerged, they adorned the entire world-system.
The Great Bodhi tree, having risen from its chariot-stand into the sky,
remained within the womb of the clouds for seven days, invisible to sight.

Therefore, it should be understood that as soon as the Bodhi tree was established upon the golden basin, it rose up together with the basin itself, entered the womb of a snow-white cloud, and remained there.
However, regarding what was stated below by way of showing the sequence of the Blessed One’s resolve:
"The Blessed One, it is said, while reclining on the bed of his Great Parinibbāna, [resolved] for the sake of establishing the Great Bodhi in the island of Laṅkā..."

King Aśoka resolved: "When the Great King Aśoka goes for the purpose of taking the Great Bodhi tree, may a southern branch of the Great Bodhi tree break off of its own accord and settle in the golden basin.
This was the first resolution. Furthermore, at the time of its settling there, he resolved:
"May the Great Bodhi enter the womb of the Himavat cloud and remain there. This was the second resolution.

“On the seventh day, having descended from the womb of the Himavalāhaka cloud and standing upon a golden basin, may he emit six-colored rays through his hands and his fruit—thus he made this resolve; this is the third resolve.

This does not agree with the following account: for in that case, he first enters the womb of the Himavalāhaka cloud, and subsequently, on the seventh day, after descending from the womb of the Himavalāhaka cloud, there is the emission of the six-colored rays and the standing upon the golden basin.
Thus it has been stated; therefore, the sequence in the commentary does not agree with what follows.

In the *Mahāvaṃsa*, however, even regarding the resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), the first thing mentioned is the settling [of the relics] in the golden casket, followed by the emission of the six-colored rays and the entry into the womb of the Himālaya cloud. For this is said:
"By the Conqueror, while reclining upon the bed of his final passing..."
The great resolution was made: "When the southern branch of the Great Bodhi tree is being taken by Aśoka,
let it break off of its own accord and settle itself within the vessel."
“Having taken firm root, may that beautiful branch with its six-colored rays,
illuminating all directions, release its fruits and leaves. Having risen up,
beautiful with its golden bowl, may it be enchanting.”
"Remaining invisible for seven days, let it stay within the womb of the snow.

This same sequence of resolutions (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is also stated in the *Bodhivaṃsa*; therefore, the sequence of resolutions stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* should be accepted after investigating how it does not contradict what precedes and follows.
And the snow and the six-colored rays, having turned back, entered the Great Bodhi tree itself—thus, having concealed the Great Bodhi...
The snow and the six-colored rays that had issued from the Bodhi tree turned back, circled to the right, and entered the Bodhi tree itself;

it is said that they vanished as if having entered the Bodhi tree. In this context, however, the reading "the snow and the rays" (himañca raṃsiyo ca) is found only in the ancient manuscript considered to have been corrected a hundred times, while it is absent from all other manuscripts.
It is seen. This is also stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
"In the past, during those seven days, all the snow-clouds and all those rays of light entered into the Great Bodhi tree."
However, as for what some have said— having imagined a reading of "five rays" (pañca raṃsiyo)— namely, "because five rays revolve from all directions,

they are 'five' because they issue forth from the five fruits, and those [rays] are six-colored," that should be regarded as nothing more than the manifestation of their own delusion. [The tree is described as] "adorned with the five fruits and with full trunks, branches, and twigs."
"Adorned with full trunks, branches, and twigs, as well as five fruits" means it was decorated on all sides.

"Having given the consecration" means having given the consecration with the water of Anotatta. "He remained right at the site of the Great Bodhi" means he dwelt in the immediate vicinity of the Bodhi tree.
"On the day of the *pavāraṇā* of the former *kattika*" means on the full moon of the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja.

Because the *uposatha* falls every two weeks due to the fourteen-day *uposatha* cycle, he said, "on the *uposatha* day of the dark fortnight," meaning on the fourteen-day *uposatha* of the dark fortnight of the month of Assayuja.
"He placed it at the foot of the eastern Great Sāla tree" means in the eastern direction of the city.
Having had a pavilion constructed beneath a newly grown great *sāla* tree, he placed [the Bodhi sapling] there.
"On the seventeenth day" means on the second day after the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).

"He saw the Kattika festival offering" means that the novice Sumana saw the offering being made for the Bodhi tree by way of the Kattika festival; having seen it, he returned and reported all those proceedings.
It was with reference to this very matter that the Elder sent [messengers] for the purpose of bringing the Bodhi tree.
Regarding the phrase "the eighteen families of deities," the connection is that he gave the families of deities—such as the nāgas and yakṣas—who stood surrounding the Great Bodhi tree.
He gave the families of ministers for the sake of deliberating on what should be done for the Bodhi tree, and the families of brahmins because they were esteemed by the world.
He gave [them] for the purpose of sprinkling water; he gave families of householders for the purpose of guarding the requisites for the worship to be performed for the Bodhi tree.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*: "The *gopaka* families are royal officials, and likewise the *taraccha* families. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it says:
"The *gopaka* families [were given] for the purpose of sprinkling the Bodhi tree, and the *taraccha* families and the *kāliṅga* families for the purpose of tending the milk-cows."
“It is said: ‘The clans of human beings who strive are trustworthy.

Regarding the phrase ‘clans of the Kaliṅgas,’ it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* that ‘the Kaliṅgas are those who dive into water and so forth. Some say: ‘A clan of noble birth born in the kingdom of Kaliṅga is a “Kaliṅga clan.
The expression ‘with this retinue’ is used in the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment; that is, ‘together with this aforementioned kind of retinue.’”

The meaning is as follows: "Having crossed the Viñjhāṭavi forest" means that the King himself, proceeding by land-path surrounded by his military forces, went forth to meet the Great Bodhi tree and, having passed beyond the forest named Viñjhāṭavi, reached the port named Tāmalitti.
"This was his third [arrival]" refers to the Great Bodhi tree when it was established in the golden cauldron.

This was said with reference to the bestowal of his own kingdom. Prior to that, however, he had already once honored the Great Bodhi tree with the sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa by means of his faith;
therefore, this present bestowal of his kingdom constitutes the fourth such instance alongside that one.
Furthermore, on whichever day he honored the Great Bodhi tree with his sovereignty, on that very day [he would relinquish] the sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa.
Having taken the revenue that had arisen, he performed a great worship of the Bodhi tree.
"Of the month of Māgasira" means of the month of Migasira. "On the first day of the waxing moon" means on the first day of the bright fortnight (*sukkapakkha*).
For that is called "the first day of the waxing moon" in relation to the first day of the dark fortnight (*kaṇhapakkha*). And this—
This is stated by adopting the conventional usage current in this island (Jambudīpa).

However, since the conventional usage there proceeds such that one month consists of the period from one full moon until the next full moon, according to that usage it would have to be called "the second first-day-of-the-month.
For in that system, the first day of the dark fortnight is called the "first first-day-of-the-month" (*paṭhamapāṭipada*).
"Having lifted up" means they say it was lifted up together with sixteen clans of noble birth who had been given [the task] at the foot of the great *sāla* tree.
"He goes, he descends"—here *areti* is used in the sense of exhaustion (*kheda*). For this very reason he says "having wept";
the meaning is that, unable to endure not seeing the Bodhi tree, he wept and lamented. Regarding the phrase "a mass of shimmering rays," here the method is exactly as stated below.

The meaning should be understood as follows: "mounted upon the Great Enlightenment" means mounted by means of the Great Enlightenment. "Of one seeing, seeing" is a genitive used in the sense of disregard; the meaning is "even while seeing.
"Leapt onto the surface of the great ocean" means she leapt onto the water-surface of the great ocean.
"For a league all around" means in a region measuring one league on each side. [This indicates] continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
This is a term used for application (*upayoga-vacana*). "The waves were stilled" means that the waves did not rise; it is said that they did not exist.

"They set forth" means they cried out; the sense is that they uttered a roar. Regarding the phrase "those residing in trees and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes deities residing in mountains and other such places.

"By means of the form of a supaṇṇa" means by means of a form resembling a supaṇṇa. "He terrified the families of nāgas" means he terrified the families of nāgas who had come for the purpose of seizing the Great Bodhi;
it is said that he caused them fear and made them flee.
For at that time, the nāgas dwelling in the ocean performed a great display of psychic power through wind, rain, darkness, and so forth, in order to seize the Great Bodhi.
They did so. Then the Elder Saṅghamittā assumed the form of a Garuḍa;

filling the sky with that Garuḍa-form, she made the heavens pitch black with a mass of crest-rays, churned the great ocean with the wind from the flapping of her wings, and terrified the Nāgas as if piercing their hearts with a roar like the crashing of the waters at the end of an aeon, thereby driving the Nāgas away.
"And those terrified nāgas, having come back"—meaning those nāgas who had been frightened in the manner previously described came once more.
"That splendor" (taṃ vibhūtiṃ) refers to that manifestation known as a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*); it is what is meant by "that marvel. "Having entreated the Elder Nun" means:
"Noble Lady, our Blessed One [used] the coils of the nāga king Mucalinda for his own fragrant cell (*gandhakuṭi*)."

Having done so, he provided him with hospitality for seven days. On the day of his full enlightenment, on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, he offered his own bowl, which had been used for leftovers, to the Great Black Nāga.
Disregarding the poisonous smoke and fire produced by the Nāga of Uruvelā, he bestowed upon him the ornaments of refuge and virtue.
Then, having dispatched the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, [he converted] the Nāga kings Nanda and Upananda.
Having subdued it, he rendered it harmless. Thus that Leader of the World was our benefactor;
you too, disregarding our offense, release the Great Bodhi tree for a moment and provide the path to heaven and liberation for the world of the Nāgas. Having thus entreated him, [the text continues:
“Afflicted by separation from the Great Bodhi” means suffering due to the separation from the Great Bodhi, with mental anguish having arisen. “Having wept” means...
"Having wept" is merely a figurative expression for this; the meaning is: having wept again and again by way of praising his virtues, or having uttered lamentations.

"From the northern gate" means from the northern gate of Anurādhapura. "Having had the road cleared" means having had the road cleared by removing stumps, thorns, and so forth. "Having had it adorned" means by scattering sand and other such materials.
Having prepared [it]. "In the site of the Ocean-Hall" means in the location that served as the site for the hall near the ocean.
It is said that because the ocean was visible to those standing in that place, a hall was built there to manifest that wonder;
it became well known by the name "the Hall Near the Ocean. For this has been stated:
“Standing in a hall near the ocean,
he beheld with great psychic power the Great Bodhi tree approaching across the vast sea.
To proclaim that miracle, a hall was built in that very spot.”
‘The Hall near the Sea’—it was well known by that name.
“By that splendor” means by that aforementioned excellence of offerings, honors, and so forth. “Of the Elder” refers to the Elder Mahāmahinda.
It is said that on both sides of the road, at intervals, there were flower-stūpas (pupphacetiyāni) shaped like gabled chambers (kūṭāgāra) made of flowers.
He had it made. With reference to that, it was said: "placing flower-offerings here and there.
"Āgato vatare" means "it has come"; here *are* is used in the sense of praise, meaning "how excellent!
"By sixteen families of noble birth" means by eight families of ministers and eight families of brahmins—thus, by sixteen families of noble birth.
"Having placed the Mahābodhi on the seashore" means having placed the Mahābodhi in a delightful pavilion, beautifully adorned and prepared, situated on the edge of the ocean tide.
Having done this, and having worshipped the Mahābodhi with the entirety of the sovereignty over Tambapaṇṇi and handed over the kingship to the sixteen clans,
he himself stood in the position of doorkeeper and performed various kinds of worship for three days.
He had it built. Showing that, he said, "For three days," and so forth. "He administered the kingdom" means he entrusted the administration of the kingdom [to others];
or the meaning is that he had the kingdom administered by sixteen families of noble birth.
"On the fourth day" refers to the tenth day of the waxing moon of the month of Migasira. "Gradually arrived at Anurādhapura" means on the tenth day...
Having placed the Great Bodhi tree upon a decorated and prepared chariot and performing magnificent worship, he brought it to the site where the monastery on the eastern side was to be established.

There, after providing a morning meal for the Saṅgha, he heard the Elder Mahinda recounting the taming of the Nāga performed by the One of Ten Powers at Nāgadīpa. [He reflected: "By the Perfectly Enlightened One, through sitting and other such acts..."
Thinking, “I shall pay honor with stūpas and other monuments at the places where [the relics] were used,” he had a sign made;

then, having brought [the relics] from there and placed them at the gate of the village of the Tavakka Brāhmaṇa, he paid homage. Having thus performed worship at each respective place in this sequence, he eventually arrived at Anurādhapura.
On the fourteenth day means on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Migasira.
"At the time when the shadow is lengthening" means at the time when the shadow is increasing;

that is to say, during the evening. "Attainment" refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Having become a tilaka" means having become an ornament. "At the place of the royal park's gate-tower" means at the location of the gate-tower of the royal garden.
They say: "Because the entire kingdom had previously been given to the Great Bodhisatta, the king assumed the guise of a gatekeeper for the sake of formal protocol."
"Successive insight" (*anupubbavipassanā*) refers to successive insight beginning with arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*). "Having established" means having commenced.

Regarding the phrase "simultaneously with the establishment of enlightenment," although one should have said "simultaneously with the establishment of enlightenment" (*saha bodhipatiṭṭhānena*), the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) "simultaneously with the establishment of enlightenment" (*saha bodhipatiṭṭhānā*) was used by changing the grammatical case-ending.
For when used in conjunction with the word "together" (*saha*), the instrumental case must be employed. "The great earth shook."
And this was merely a manifestation of a fraction of his power; indeed, many other wonders also occurred.
For instance, simultaneously with his establishment in enlightenment, the great earth, bounded by the waters, shook;
those roots, having emerged from the rim of the basin's mouth, descended to the surface of the earth while encircling that basin; and divine flowers rained down on all sides.
Divine musical instruments resounded in the sky; a great cloud arose and released a stream of rain;
regions of the sky thundered, and flashes of lightning burst forth. Deities offered shouts of "Well done!";

all the inhabitants of the island gathered together and honored [the Buddha] with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings; gentle breezes blew laden with nectar; and thick, cool, snow-white clouds gathered on every side.

They covered the Great Enlightenment Tree. Thus, having established itself upon the earth of enlightenment and having sat within the womb of snow, it remained invisible to the world for seven days. "Sat within the womb of snow" means it stood inside the womb of snow.
"Streaming forth" means streaming and wandering here and there. "Issued forth" means they emerged. "Appeared" means...
They appeared. "All the island-dwellers" means all those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
"One fruit from the northern branch" means one fruit situated on the northern branch; some say, "one fruit from the eastern branch.
"In the place of the great seat" means in the place established by the great stone seat on the eastern side. "In the monastery of Issaranimmāna" means in that which is designated as Issaranimmāna.

In the Kassapa Hill Monastery (*Kassapagirivihāra*). For it was spoken [earlier] by way of ancient convention as the "Monastery of the Creator" (*Issaranimmānavihāra*), but now that monastery is known as "Kassapa Hill. Some also read "in the Īśvara-Śramaṇa Garden" (*Issarasamaṇārāma*). And thus it has been said:
"In Tavakkabrāhmaṇagāma, and likewise in Thūpārāma..."
"In the Issarasamaṇārāma, at the first shrine courtyard.
Regarding "in the monasteries within a league": this refers to the monasteries established within a league’s radius all around Anurādhapura.
This connects with the phrase "the Great Bodhi tree established all around. Thus, in the vicinity of Anurādhapura, through the succession of sons and grandsons, [he established] the Great Bodhi tree.
The meaning is "established. "He worshipped the site of the Lohapāsāda" means he worshipped the place where the Lohapāsāda was to be built.

Regarding this, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipadas*: "Although it was King Devānampiyatissa himself who would cause the Lohapāsāda to be built, nevertheless, because it did not exist at that time, it is said to be 'in the future. However, some [commentators] say: "By Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya alone..."

"the Lohapāsāda was caused to be built," they say. By the phrase "but its roots have not yet gone deep," it is shown, O Great King, that in this island the Teacher’s Dispensation had only just been established;

it was not yet well-established. The meaning here should be understood as: "but the roots of this Teacher’s Dispensation have not yet descended. Regarding the word *otaranti*: [it means "they descend"].
For here, a present tense verb is used in the sense of the past. It is for this very reason that he said: "But when, venerable sir, will the roots have gone down?
The statement "the monk Mahā-Ariṭṭha" refers to that minister who went forth at Cetiya-giri together with his forty-five elder and younger brothers.
[The phrase] "at the site of the cell of the minister Meghavaṇṇābhaya" [is used].
At the site intended for a monastery cell to be built by the minister of King Meghavaṇṇābhaya. "In the form of a pavilion" (maṇḍapappakāraṃ) means resembling a pavilion;

for they explain that the word *pakāra* can also have the sense of similarity. By the phrase "I shall see the roots of the Dispensation taking root," he indicates that he will see the manner in which the Dispensation is firmly established.
Because it resounded like the stainless sky when it is devoid of clouds, it is said: “The sky roared with a great roar.
“By the individual leaders of the groups” means by the teachers of separate groups. They are called “individual leaders of the groups” (paccekagaṇino) because each of them has their own group.
Just as a physician, out of compassion for the sick, places the act of healing alone before him and is free from desire and aversion toward things that are loathsome...
Just as one treats wounds and secret places with medicinal ointments and the like, so too the Blessed One,
out of compassion for beings afflicted by the disease of the defilements and desiring to liberate those beings from the suffering of the disease of the defilements,
speaks— even while addressing improper matters concerning secret places that ought not to be spoken of— regarding the defilement-disease of beings through the formulation of the Vinaya.
It heals. Therefore it is said: “illuminating the quality of the Teacher’s compassion.
“Of those who provide instruction” means of those who carry out the instruction; the meaning is: of those who practice the Blessed One’s instruction correctly.

“For the removal of the agitation of bodily and verbal action” means that which effects the removal of the agitation of the defilements occurring through transgression at the doors of body and speech.
*Rājinoti* is a genitive case used in the sense of the dative; the meaning is "instructing the king. *Ālokan* means the light of knowledge (*ñāṇāloka*).
Regarding the phrase *nibbāyiṃsu mahesayo*: here, the Great Elder Mahinda arrived in the island of Tambapaṇṇi when he was twelve years old;
having resided there for two years, he established the Vinaya. When he was sixty-two years old...
"They say he has attained final nibbāna.
"The pupils of those elders" means the pupils of those elders headed by the Elder Mahāmahinda.
As for Tissadatta and the others, they were pupils of the Elder Mahāariṭṭha; therefore, [the phrase refers to] Tissadatta, Kāḷasumana, Dīghasumana, and so forth.
It should be construed as "and the pupils of the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha.
"Pupils of the pupils" refers to the pupils of both types of pupils mentioned previously. Regarding those described in the manner stated before:
"Then Mahinda, Iṭṭhiya, Uttiya, and likewise Sambala..."
And the wise one named Bhadda.
These Nāgas of great wisdom came here from Jambudīpa;
they taught the Vinaya, the Piṭaka, in Tambapaṇṇi.
“They recited the five Nikāyas and the seven treatises (pakaraṇa);
then the wise Ariṭṭha and the learned Tissa-datta;
the confident Kāḷasumana and the elder named Dīgha.”
In this manner, the lineage of teachers of the type previously described has been explained.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the lineage of teachers is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discourse concerning the benefits of the Vinaya.
Having thus analyzed in detail the question, "By whom was it brought?", he now spoke the words beginning with "Where is it established?
in order to answer the question, "Where is it established?". In that context, "like oil" means like lion’s fat.
Regarding the phrase "in mindfulness, movement, wisdom, and mantras": here, "mindfulness" refers to the mindfulness of one who has mastered and retained the Buddha’s word.
"Gati" means the process of learning. "Dhiti" means the wisdom that grasps after having reached a definitive conclusion. Alternatively, "gati" refers to the course of wisdom (*paññā*).
"Dhiti" refers to the energy for learning the Buddha’s word, the energy for reciting it, and the energy for retaining it.
"In those who are conscientious" means in those endowed with the sense of shame (*lajjā*) characterized by a loathing of evil. "In those who are scrupulous" means regarding even the slightest faults.
Regarding those who, out of a sense of seeing danger, are scrupulous concerning what is allowable and what is not allowable:
"those desiring training" refers to those who, longing for the three trainings—namely, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom—train with affection.

They are said to be "in the place of mother and father" because they restrain one from what should not be done and establish one in what should be done. "Skillfulness in conduct and resort" (ācāra-gocara-kusalatā):
By completely abandoning improper conduct through the non-practice of wrong livelihood such as giving bamboo,

as well as bodily insolence and so forth, and by avoiding the improper resort of prostitutes and the like through the attainment of the conduct befitting a bhikkhu— described as "non-transgression of body" and "non-transgression of speech"—
one should resort to a proper resort consisting of those places suitable for approaching for the sake of alms-food and other necessities.
And there is proficiency in the conduct and the range of a recluse due to its perfection. Furthermore, that bhikkhu who is respectful and deferential toward the Teacher,
respectful and deferential toward his fellow celibates, endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing,
well-clad and well-robed, and graceful in his advancing, retreating, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, and stretching;
One who dwells with downcast eyes, perfected in deportment, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness,
endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, few in desires, contented, energetic, secluded, unassociated with the crowd,
performing duties regarding higher conduct with diligence, and full of reverence and respect— this is called "conduct" (ācāra).

The resort (*gocara*), however, is threefold: the resort as a decisive support (*upanissaya-gocara*), the resort as protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the resort as a basis for anchoring the mind (*upanibandha-gocara*).

In this context, a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) is one endowed with the qualities of the ten bases of talk (*dasakathāvatthu*); depending upon whom one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one's view, and gains confidence in the mind;
or, by training under whom one increases in faith, virtue, and so forth.
One increases through learning, generosity, and wisdom; this is the resort of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-gocara*).
Furthermore, that bhikkhu who has entered among the houses and is walking along the street goes with downcast eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, restrained;
he does not look at an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a foot soldier, nor a woman, nor a man, nor upwards.
He goes looking ahead, not looking down, nor glancing about in various directions; this is the range of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*).
The range of anchoring (*upanibandha-gocara*), however, consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), wherein a bhikkhu anchors his own mind.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, bhikkhus, is the bhikkhu’s own range, his ancestral domain?"
Namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. This is the range of the tethering. Thus, because one is endowed with both this conduct and this range, there is "skill in conduct and range.

Having thus avoided improper conduct and improper ranges, the state of skill in the aforementioned conduct and ranges for those who have gone forth out of faith depends upon those who uphold the Vinaya; this is the benefit.
It should be understood that he is shown [to be so] by means of the mastery of the Vinaya.
"In dependence on the mastery of the Vinaya" means in dependence on the thorough mastery of the Vinaya.
How is his own aggregate of virtue well-guarded and well-protected? For, regarding an offense—

One commits an offense in six ways: through lack of shame, through ignorance, through being overcome by remorse, through the perception of what is improper as proper, through the perception of what is proper as improper, and through forgetfulness.
One who is a bearer of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), however, does not commit an offense in these six ways.
How does he not commit one through lack of shame? For he thinks: "Look, sirs, this person knows very well what is proper and what is improper..."

Even while protecting himself from the reproach of others, saying, “He commits a transgression of the rules,” he does not commit a transgression by disregarding the fact that it is unallowable, precisely because he knows its unallowable nature.

Thus, through his lack of shamelessness, he does not fall into an offense. Even if he should inadvertently incur an offense, having confessed one that requires confession and emerged from one that requires formal rehabilitation, he establishes himself in the state of purity; thereafter—
“He does not intentionally commit an offense; he does not conceal an offense;
and he does not go upon a wrong path—it is such a person who is called ‘one possessed of shame.
Thus, he is indeed established in this state of shame.

How does he not fall into ignorance? For he knows what is allowable and what is unallowable; therefore, he performs only what is allowable and does not perform what is unallowable. Thus he does not fall into ignorance. How does he not fall into being overcome by remorse?

When remorse arises concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, he examines the basis [of the action], looks at the rules, the word-commentary, the intermediate offenses, and the non-offenses; and if it is allowable, he performs it.
If something is improper, he does not do it. Furthermore, having arisen from remorse, he does not transgress by suppressing it with the thought "it is permissible" before having resolved the matter.
Thus, through being governed by remorse, he does not fall into wrongdoing.
How does he avoid falling into wrongdoing through such things as perceiving what is improper as proper? For he knows what is proper and what is improper; therefore...
He does not perceive what is unallowable as allowable, nor does he perceive what is allowable as unallowable; his mindfulness is well-established;
he determines what must be determined, and he designates what must be designated. Thus, by these six ways, he does not incur an offense;
not incurring an offense, he possesses unbroken virtue and perfectly pure virtue. Such is his case.
One’s own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected.
"For those overcome by remorse" means for those overwhelmed by remorse arising on account of what is permissible and what is impermissible.
But how is one a refuge for those overcome by remorse? It is for those who have arisen with remorse in foreign kingdoms and foreign districts.
Thinking, "A master of the Vinaya dwells in such-and-such a monastery," monks come into his presence even from afar to ask about their remorse.
Having examined the basis of the action committed by them, and having discerned whether it was an offense or no offense, heavy or light, and so forth,
he causes them to confess what requires confession and rehabilitates them through that which requires rehabilitation, thereby establishing them in purity.
Thus it is a refuge for those overcome by remorse.
"He speaks confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha": one whose *sārajjā*—that is, fear—is gone is "confident" (*visārado*);
the meaning is that he is fearless. For fear and timidity descend upon one who is not a master of the Vinaya when speaking in the midst of the Saṅgha, but not upon one who is a master of the Vinaya.
That does not exist. Why? Because one speaks having known: "In speaking thus there is fault; in speaking thus there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "he refutes adversaries with the Dhamma, refuting them thoroughly," here there are two kinds of adversaries:
adversaries of oneself and adversaries of the Teaching. Among these, the Mettiya-Bhummajaka monks and Vaḍḍha...
And those Licchavis who accused [the monks] with a groundless charge concerning a matter involving defeat—these are called "enemies of themselves.
Furthermore, others who are immoral and of evil character are all enemies of themselves.

However, those such as the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, the Vesālika Vajjiputtakas, the Mahāsaṅghikas, and so forth—who, possessing perverted views, claim that what is not the Buddha’s teaching is the "Buddha’s teaching" and exert themselves for its sake—are enemies of the Teaching.
By name. He refutes them all with words that possess the true Dhamma and its logical reasons, having thoroughly subdued them so that they are unable to establish that which is not the true Dhamma.

Regarding the phrase "he is practicing for the stability of the true Dhamma," here the true Dhamma is threefold by way of the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*).
In this context, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas is called the True Dhamma of the Teaching (pariyatti-saddhamma).
The thirteen ascetic virtues (dhutaṅga), the fourteen rules of conduct for the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two major rules—this is called the True Dhamma of Practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma).
The four paths and the four fruits—this is called the True Dhamma of Realization (adhigama-saddhamma). Regarding this, some elders [say]: "O Ānanda, whatever..."
By this sutta, "The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been taught and laid down by me;

they shall be your teacher after my passing," they say that "the study of the scriptures (pariyatti) is the root of the Dispensation. Some elders say that "the practice (paṭipatti) is the root of the Dispensation" by means of this sutta: "If these monks, Subhadda, were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants."
Having said this, they declared: “As long as five monks who practice rightly exist, so long does the Dispensation endure.
But the other elders said: “When the scriptures have disappeared, there is no realization of the Dhamma even for one who practices well.
Even if there were five monks who observe the four Pārājika rules, [the Dispensation would not endure].

Having caused those faithful sons of good family to go forth and having conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon them in the border regions, they will complete a quorum of ten members and confer full ordination even in the Middle Country.

By this means, having completed a Saṅgha of twenty members and having performed their own act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), they will cause the Teaching to reach growth and expansion. Thus, this master of the Vinaya...
"He practices for the long endurance of the Triple Gem. Thus it should be understood that this bearer of the Vinaya obtains these five benefits.
Regarding the passage beginning "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," "Vinaya" refers to the mastery of the Vinaya, or alternatively, "Vinaya" refers to the formal codification of the Vinaya.
Thus it has been said; therefore, the entire formulation of the Vinaya, or the mastery of the Vinaya, is for the purpose of restraining the doors of body and speech—this is the meaning.
What is meant is that it serves as the decisive supporting condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for virtue (*sīla*) culminating in purity of livelihood.
"Non-remorse" (*avippaṭisāra*) refers to the absence of mental remorse (*citta-vippaṭisāra*) arising from the state of not grieving over evil deeds done or good deeds left undone.
*Pāmojja* is weak, fresh joy (*pīti*). *Pīti* is powerful joy. *Passaddhi* is the subsiding of the agitation of body and mind.
*Sukha* is bodily and mental happiness; for both these kinds of happiness serve as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for concentration.
*Samādhi* is one-pointedness of mind. *Yathābhūtañāṇadassana* is the discernment of name-and-form together with their conditions.

“Disenchantment” (*nibbidā*) refers to insight (*vipassanā*). Alternatively, it is the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*), which is the designation for nascent insight;
for one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) serves as the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*) for nascent insight.

“Disenchantment” also refers to powerful insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminibalavavipassanā*) when it has reached its culmination. “Fading away” (*virāga*) is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). “Liberation” (*vimutti*) is the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*).
For even the fourfold Noble Path is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for Arahantship.

"Knowledge and vision of liberation" refers to the knowledge of reviewing. "For the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging" means for the sake of final Nibbāna by not grasping at any phenomenon whatsoever, leaving nothing behind;
that is to say, for the sake of final Nibbāna without conditions. For [this leads to] final Nibbāna without conditions...
The knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is a condition because, once it has arisen, one must necessarily attain final Nibbāna;
and there is no intermediate final Nibbāna before the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) has arisen.
"This is the purpose of the talk" means that this talk on the Vinaya is for this purpose—that is, for the purpose of final Nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādāparinibbāna*). This is the meaning.
The same applies in all cases. *Mantana* refers specifically to the deliberation on the Vinaya—the consultation concerning the Vinaya regarding whether "we shall do it thus" or "we shall not do it.
The term *upanisā* has this meaning: it is called *upanisā* because the fruit rests (*upanisīdati*) therein due to its dependence upon that; thus, it is said to be the cause or the condition.
The meaning is that the sequence of causes, beginning with "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," has this as its purpose.
"For this purpose, the application of the ear": the application of the ear to this discourse on the chain of dependent conditions is for this purpose;
and the knowledge that arises from hearing this discourse is also for this purpose. "Namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging":
*yadidaṃ* is a particle (*nipāta*). It remains the same in all genders, cases, and numbers, and should be adapted according to the sense in each respective instance.

Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: this liberation of the mind known as the fruit of arahantship, which does not cling by means of the four kinds of clinging, is for that very purpose—for the sake of final nibbāna through non-clinging;
thus the connection here should be understood. This path, known as the liberation of the mind through non-clinging, which was mentioned above—
"All of this is for this very purpose. This being so, it should be understood that by this [statement], the necessary application to be accomplished through great effort is shown;
whereas by the preceding statement, "Dispassion... for the sake of Nibbāna," the fruit consisting of the obtainable benefits is shown.
"Application" (āyoga) means repeated exertion by way of grasping, reflecting, and so forth.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Benefits of the Vinaya is concluded.
Thus ends the commentary on the External Introduction in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Commentary on the Verañja Chapter:

1. *Seyyathidaṃ* means "what is that? or "how is that? It is a term used as an indefinite description. It is called "indefinite" (*aniyama*) because there is no fixed restriction (*niyama*) regarding it;
it is called "description" (*niddesa*) because meaning is described (*niddisīyati*) by means of it; and it is called "expression" (*vacana*) because it is spoken (*vuccati*) by means of it.
“Niddesavacanaṃ” means a statement of exposition (niddesa). “Aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ” means a statement of exposition that is unrestricted (aniyama);
the meaning is: a statement of exposition for a time (samaya) that was not previously restricted. Some also say:

“Because it is stated as ‘tena’ instead of ‘yena,’ it is a statement of exposition that has been pointed out by making it unrestricted; thus it is called ‘aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ. [This refers to] the words “yaṃ” and “taṃ.”
Because of their state of constant connection, he says: “Even though its own form has not been stated,” and so forth. Therein, “its” (*tassa*) refers to “by that” (*tena*).
“Even though its own form has not been stated” means even though it has not been stated in the text by way of its own form as “by which” (*yena*).
“Established by way of meaning” means established by way of the meaning consisting of the reflection arising in the Elder Sāriputta at a subsequent time.
For when the reflection (*parivitakka*) is established, the statement "at which time the reflection arose" is already established by implication.
Therefore it was said: "Subsequently, the reflection of the Venerable Sāriputta, which became the cause for requesting the formulation of the Vinaya, was established," and so forth.
Having stated "by that," the phrase "by which" is then used to express that same meaning through its underlying sense (*atthato*).
“*Yena*” (by which) has become a reference (*paṭiniddesa*) for “*tena*” (thereby). “Reference” means an explanatory elaboration (*vitthāraniddesa*).
In the phrase “*aparabhāge hi*,” the particle *hi* denotes a cause; it means “because. It means: “Because it was the cause for requesting the formulation of the Vinaya:
‘Bhagavā, this is the time; Sugata, this is the time for the Bhagavā to lay down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) for the disciples.’”

The meaning is that it is the cause for the request for the formulation of the Vinaya as it proceeded thus: "One should recite the Pātimokkha, so that this holy life (brahmacariya) may endure for a long time and remain stable. "Reflection" (parivitakka) means:
"Of which Blessed Buddhas was the holy life not long-enduring? Of which Buddhas..."
“The holy life of the Blessed Ones has long endured”—such was the reflection that arose.
Because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* have a constant connection, he said, “Therefore, by which occasion,” and so forth. By that which is established in meaning either before or after means:
by that which is established through the meaning arisen either previously or subsequently. The further specification (*paṭiniddesa*) must be made; for this [the word] “namely” (*yadidaṃ*) [is used].

This is the connection. Regarding the phrase “a detailed exposition (paṭiniddesa) should be made”: the meaning is that this method (vidhāna) which has been stated is the principle applicable to the entire Vinaya.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase “a detailed exposition should be made”: the meaning is that this principle which has been stated is the principle applicable to the entire Vinaya.
“Herein, this is a mere indication of the opening”: this is an indication of the opening for the purpose of illustrating the reasoning already stated;
the meaning is that it is an indication of a mere means (*upāya*). For “opening,” “door,” and “means” are one in meaning.
Having shown the canonical text (pāḷi), “Therefore, monks, I shall lay down a training rule for the bhikkhus,” he provides a further explanation therein: “by which...”

[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "Sudinno. Regarding the word "tena" (by that), because it is used in the instrumental case in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), its correlative (*paṭiniddesa*) is likewise of the same nature;
thus he says, "because he was a consumer. "Established by the meaning previously" means established by the meaning consisting of the prior occurrence of the consumption of sexual intercourse.
"Established by the meaning subsequently" refers to the subsequent occurrence of taking wood not given by the king.
By the word *siddha*. The word *samaya* is connected with the verb "is seen.
In the phrase *samavāye*, it means in the collection of conditions; the sense is "in the convergence of causes. In the phrase *khaṇe*, it means in an opportunity. The connection is:
"of this," that is, of this word *samaya*, "the meaning is 'convergence' (*samavāya*). [And] "perhaps even tomorrow we might approach, and [find] the time..."

Regarding the phrase "and having taken into account the time and the occasion" (*samayañca upādāya*): here, "time" (*kāla*) refers to the appropriate and suitable moment for approaching [the teacher].

"Occasion" (*samaya*) refers to the convergence of conditions for that very act; in terms of its actual meaning, it consists of bodily strength commensurate with that task, as well as the absence of obstacles related to those conditions.

"Taking into account" (*upādāna*) means grasping and discerning these by means of wisdom. Therefore, one should [approach] by means of wisdom, having taken into account both the time and the occasion.
"Having taken up" means "having reflected. This is what is meant:

if tomorrow will be the appropriate time for our departure, if strength shall suffuse the body, and if there shall be no other discomfort on account of the journey, then, having reflected upon this time and the occasion consisting of the convergence of the causes for going—even so...
"May we indeed come to our own [home].
*Khaṇo* means opportunity (*okāsa*). For the appearance of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions;
thus, the *khaṇa* itself is the *samaya*. The meaning is that what is called both *khaṇa* and *samaya* is one and the same. *Mahāsamayo*...
A great multitude. A grown forest is a *pavana*; in that *pavana*, the meaning is "in a grove.
"Even this occasion (*samaya*), Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you"—here, "occasion" refers to the cause for fulfilling the training rule.
"Bhaddāli" is the name of that bhikkhu. This is what is meant: "Bhaddāli, this is something suitable for you to penetrate."
There is a reason for this, yet you have neither penetrated nor observed it. What is that reason? He says: "The Blessed One," and so forth.
Regarding the terms "Uggāhamāna" and the rest: *māna* is the personal name of that wanderer;
however, because of his ability to grasp various things, people know him as "Uggāhamāna" (the Grasper), and thus he is called by that name. [He was the son] of Samaṇamuṇḍikā.
The son was Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta. He, it is said, was an attendant of Devadatta.
One who propounds a doctrine (samaya) here is called a *samayappavādaka*; in that context, the meaning is "one who propounds views" (*diṭṭhippavādaka*).
It is said that in that place there were brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, as well as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, Paribbājakas, and others.

And because wandering ascetics (paribbājaka) gathered there, each proclaiming, discussing, and expounding their own respective doctrines (samaya) and views (diṭṭhi), that monastery was called “Samayappavādaka.
And because it was surrounded by a row of *timbaru* trees known as the *tindukācīra*, it was called “Tindukācīra.
It is called “Ekasālaka” because there is a single hall (*sālā*) there. Furthermore, because here—
Originally, there was only one hall built; later, many halls were constructed through the support of the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, who possessed great merit.
Therefore, it is called "Ekasālaka" (The Single-Hall) based on that original hall and the name thus acquired.
Furthermore, because that park was covered with flowers and fruits and served as a pleasure garden for Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi, it was designated as such.
It became known as "Mallikā’s Park. At that time, he was dwelling in Mallikā’s Park, which had a single sal tree and a tinduka grove used for public discourse.
"Dwells" means he lives there with a sense of ease and comfort.

"In this very life" (diṭṭhe dhamme) refers to the immediately present personal existence. "Welfare" (attha) means progress. "Pertaining to the future life" (samparāyika) refers to [the results] by way of karma and defilements.
*Samparāya* means that which is to be reached or attained; it is the world beyond (*paraloka*). That which pertains to this is *samparāyika*, meaning for the sake of the world beyond.
"The realization of the goal" (*atthābhisamaya*) refers to the attainment of welfare consisting of both goals as previously described.
For even the welfare pertaining to the world beyond is said to be "attained" because the cause has been brought to fruition; thus, these two goals are treated as one.
“It is said: ‘the realization of the goal. One who grasps by means of the mind—that is, by wisdom—is wise (*dhīra*). Alternatively, one who possesses wisdom (*dhī*) is wise (*dhīra*).
‘The complete realization of conceit’ means through the complete abandoning of conceit. By the word ‘complete,’ it refers to the knowledge of the supreme path regarding conceit.”

"Abandonment by eradication" has been stated. Regarding "the sense of oppression of suffering," and so forth: the oppression of the truth of suffering is the harming of one who possesses it, the making of it non-expansive;
"the sense of oppression" (*pīḷanaṭṭho*) is simply the meaning of oppression (*pīḷana*), stated by changing the letter *t* to *ṭ*.

The same applies to the remaining [terms]. The sense of being conditioned (*saṅkhataṭṭho*) is the state of being produced by conditions through their coming together. "Torment" (*santāpo*) refers to the state of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth.
“Tormenting” means burning. “Transformation” refers to the state of being subject to transformation in two ways:
by aging and by death. “Abhisamaya” means that which is to be fully understood and penetrated; thus, *abhisamaya* itself is the meaning, the sense of *abhisamaya*.

[The terms] “affliction” (*pīḷana*) and so forth are stated as “the sense of *abhisamaya*” because they are brought into a single unity by virtue of their being what must be fully understood (*abhisametabba*). This is because of the full understanding (*abhisamaya*).
Alternatively, the meaning that constitutes the object of penetration is the sense of "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*);
thus, those very factors—affliction and so forth—are spoken of as a unity because they share the commonality of becoming the objects of clear realization.
And here, since prefixes are merely indicators, the word *samaya* alone is the designator of each respective meaning.

Even in the extraction of the meaning of the word *samaya*, the term *abhisamaya* is stated with its prefix. Therein, it is a *samaya*—a conjunction—in the sense that it comes together (*sameti*) or assembles (*samaveti*) through the presence of cooperative causes.
It is a *samaya*—an occasion—in the sense that the noble life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*) comes together (*sameti*) or meets (*samāgacchati*) here with the persons who are its support.
It is a *samaya*—a meeting—in the sense that phenomena come together (*samenti*) here, or by means of this, they conjoin with co-nascent phenomena.

"Samaya" means time (*kāla*), in the sense of arising and so forth. For although time does not exist as a substantial entity (*attha*) apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*), it is nevertheless conventionally expressed by a form established through mere conceptualization (*parikappanā-matta*) as if it were the locus or the cause for the occurrence of phenomena.

"Samaya" also means the coming together, simultaneous movement, or persistence of parts; it is a collection (*samūha*), just as in the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*). [It is formed] with a part [representing the whole].

A collection is indeed the very state of co-existence. It is called a "condition" (*samaya*) because the fruit comes (*eti*) from it, or because the fruit arises and proceeds from it—just as a cause is called "origination" (*samudaya*).

It is called a "bond" (*samyoga*) because it comes together through the state of being a fetter, or because beings come (*ayanti*) and proceed within their own domain due to its state of firm grasping, according to their respective inclinations.

By this [term] "samaya" is meant view (*diṭṭhi*). For it is by the fetter of views that beings are bound exceedingly tight. *Samaya* means meeting, gathering, or coming together; it means acquisition.
Or, *samaya* means the vehicle (*yāna*) to cessation (*sama*), or the correct (*sammā*) vehicle, the departure, the non-arising;
it means abandoning. *Abhisamaya* means that which is to be approached, correctly attained, or realized directly through knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

The intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena (*dhammā*) is their non-erroneous state. It is called "realization" (*abhisamaya*) because one approaches (*eti*), goes toward (*gacchati*), and awakens (*bujjhati*) by way of being directed toward (*abhimukha*);
it is the awakening to the true nature of phenomena as they actually are. In this manner, the application of the term *samaya* should be understood according to each specific meaning.
But is it not the case that words adhere to a mere object, and that multiple meanings are not expressed by a single word?
This is true when there is a dependence on a specific word. For when a specific word is being depended upon, it is not possible for a single word to express multiple meanings.
Indeed, that which is the word *samaya* in the sense of "time" does not itself denote the sense of "collection" and so forth.

However, in this context, the multiplicity of meanings of the word *samaya* is established by taking into account the commonality of the word *samaya* as the designator of those various respective meanings.
Thus, in all instances, the intended meaning (adhippāya) should be understood from the extraction of the sense (atthuddhāra).
Here, however, "time" (kāla) is the meaning of this word *samaya*, because other meanings such as "assemblage" (*samavāya*) and so forth are impossible here,
and because time— like the place, the teacher, and other factors— is to be cited as the causal basis (*nidāna*).

Having provided the exposition by means of the locative case (*bhummavacana*) and the instrumental case (*upayogavacana*), he—desiring to determine the purpose of the exposition here by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*)—raises an objection through another person with the words, "In this regard, it is said," and so forth.

Here, the meaning is that the caviler (*vitaṇḍavādī*) speaks at this point [with the words] "at that time" (*tena samayena*). The word "then" (*atha*) indicates the desire to raise the objection; "is it not? (*nanu*)...

This has the same meaning [as the previous]. The connection is: "Why was the description made using the instrumental case? It should be construed as: "The description was made using the locative case.
Here too, the word "just as" (*yathā*) must be supplied and connected. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in those two—the Suttas and the Abhidhamma.

"Thus" (*tathā*) means by means of the accusative and locative cases. "Here" (*idha*) means in this Vinaya. "Otherwise" (*aññathā*) means by means of the instrumental case. "Entirely" (*accantam eva*).
The meaning is: from the very beginning until the conclusion of the teaching, it is absolutely and continuously so.
"By abiding in compassion" means by the abiding in compassion characterized as the practice for the welfare of others.

For it is because the teaching has compassion as its source that the practice for the welfare of others is here called "abiding in compassion," and not the abiding in the attainment of the meditative absorption of compassion (*karuṇā-samāpatti*).

For it is not possible for the knowledge of teaching—which has as its object the phenomena to be taught—to arise simultaneously with great compassion—which has sentient beings as its object—because their objects are distinct.

Therefore, the dwelling here termed "abiding in compassion" should be understood as the state consisting in the attainment of the welfare of others that proceeds by way of compassion. The phrase "for the purpose of indicating its meaning" is for the purpose of demonstrating the sense of absolute conjunction.
The instruction on usage has been given, as in the example: "He studies for a month.

The sense of locus (*adhikaraṇattha*) means the sense of support (*ādhārattha*). "State" (*bhāva*) refers to an action; the characterization of one action by another action is "the characterization of state by state" (*bhāvena-bhāvalakkhaṇa*), and that very sense is the sense of the characterization of state by state.
But how is it possible for the two aforementioned senses to occur in the Abhidhamma?
He said: “For it is a ‘subject matter’ (adhikaraṇa),” and so forth. Therein, the meaning reckoned as time is the “time-meaning” (kālattha);

the meaning reckoned as a collection is the “collection-meaning” (samūhattha). Alternatively, the meaning of the word *kāla* is the “time-meaning,” and the meaning of the word *samūha* is the “collection-meaning.
What is that? It is the “occasion” (samaya). This is what is meant: the occasion possesses both the time-meaning and the collection-meaning therein, in the Abhidhamma.
The "basis" (*adhikaraṇa*) or "support" (*ādhāra*) refers to that collection of phenomena (*dhamma-puñja*) in which the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen;
for at that very same time, contact and the other factors are also present within that collection—this is the meaning here.

But surely this time and this collection are merely conceptually designated (*paññatta*) based on [the constituent moments] and are mere conventional designations (*vohāramattaka*); how then can they be the support there?

[Is it not the case that] "of the phenomena already stated"? This is no fault. For just as time—though itself non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) and defined by the phenomena of its own nature—is designated as a support [for events], because of the absence [of those events] prior to and after them at the moment they occur, as in such expressions as "born in the forenoon, he goes in the afternoon";
and just as a collection (*samūha*), though non-existent apart from its constituent parts, [is likewise designated].

It is designated as the locus of its parts by way of mere conceptual construction, as in such cases as "the branch on the tree" or "grown in a heap of grain," and it should be understood that the same applies here.

Having shown the possibility of the sense of locus (*ādhāra*) in the Abhidhamma, he now shows the possibility of the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa*):

He said: "Of that which is reckoned as the cause of the coincidence of moments," and so forth. Therein, "moment" (khaṇa) refers to the ninth moment, distinct from the eight [inauspicious] moments, known as the arising of a Buddha;
or else it refers to those [factors] mentioned here: "Monks, there are these four wheels by which the fourfold wheel of gods and humans revolves":
dwelling in a suitable locality, relying upon a true person, [hearing the true Dhamma, and practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma]."
The four wheels have been taught as: right disposition of oneself (*attasammāpaṇidhi*) and merit performed in the past (*pubbe ca katapuññatā*).
These, taken together, should be understood as the "occasion" (*khaṇa*) in the sense of being the scope (*okāsa*). For these indeed constitute the scope for the arising of the wholesome.

As for "conjunction" (*samavāya*), it is defined by such passages as, "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," because it produces the common fruit known as eye-consciousness and so forth.
The collection of conditions, such as the eye and visible forms, is established.
For the eye, visible forms, and so forth, have as their common fruit the eye-consciousness and its like. "Cause" (*hetu*) means a productive cause.

Because of the existence (*bhāva*)—that is, the being present—of that occasion (*samaya*), which is reckoned by the aforementioned moment, and which is reckoned as a conjunction and reckoned as a cause, the existence (*sattā*) of those phenomena such as contact is characterized and made known.
The meaning is as follows: Just as in the expression, "He went while the cows were being milked;

he returned when they had been milked," the act of going is characterized by the act of milking, so too here, when it is said "at whatever time, at that time," the sense of "being present" (sati) is understood precisely because there is no connection with any other action, and thus the state of the word-meaning lacks an absence of existence.
The activity of the arising of consciousness and the activity of the manifestation of contact and so forth are characterized as the activity of the being of the moment.
This is the meaning therein: at whatever aforementioned moment, when the collection of conditions and the cause exist, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen;
at that very same moment, when the collection of conditions and the cause exist, contact and the other factors also [arise].

“*Hontīti*”: for the purpose of illustrating that meaning—that is, for the purpose of demonstrating the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa*).
“*Idha pana*”: here, in this Vinaya. The sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are both possible;

the sense of cause is as in examples such as “he dwells because of food” (*annena vasati*) or “he dwells because of knowledge” (*vijjāya vasati*), while the sense of instrument is as in examples such as “he cuts with an axe” (*pharasunā chindati*) or “he digs with a spade” (*kudālena khaṇati*).
And the sense of the instrumental case is also possible. To explain how it is possible, he says, "For that which... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by that occasion as cause and as instrument," here the very transgression of the respective basis is both the cause and the instrument for the promulgation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
For instance, when the Blessed One, at the very first [instance] of the promulgation of a training rule, [perceived] their...

When he dwells observing the transgression that served as the cause for the promulgation of this or that training rule (sikkhāpada) in various instances, then—having observed those respective transgressions—he dwells for that purpose;

thus, the causality of the transgression of the object (vatthu-vītikkama) is established, just as in such expressions as "he dwells because of food," meaning "he dwells having regard for food and for its sake. At the time of the promulgation of the training rules...
However, because he prescribes the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) on account of that very transgression already established,

the transgression itself is established as the instrument (*karaṇa-bhāva*) due to its being the most effective means for the prescription of the training rule— just as in expressions such as "he cuts with a sword.
Yet, depending upon the transgression, he dwells together with it, taking into account also the period of time during which it was relied upon.

Here, the causal status of time is also stated; for when laying down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), one does so at the very time of a particular transgression without having bypassed it, and thus the status of time as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the basis of the transgression is also stated.
Therefore, by this method, the causal status and the instrumental status of time are both obtained.
It is said: "By that occasion, acting as the cause and acting as the instrument. However, in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), it is the transgression itself that is the cause and the instrument.
For at the moment of the transgression it becomes the cause, and subsequently, when the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is being promulgated, it also becomes the instrument.
"While promulgating the training rules" means: having asked about the transgression and having convened the Saṅgha of monks, [he deals with] the matter that has arisen.
Having questioned the individual and having rebuked him, he laid down the training rules at the very time when each respective matter had occurred and was not yet passed over,

using that very time as the occasion for their enactment. And "having regard for the cause of the laying down of the training rules" means having regard for those respective matters which served as the causes for the laying down of the training rules,
such as in the case of the third *pārājika* and others, at the moment of the transgression.
The meaning is that at that time, by means of that which had become the cause, the Blessed One dwelt here and there.
Although it could have been stated as "at that time, by means of that which had become the instrument and the cause," based on the statement,

"Laying down the training rules while having regard for the reason for laying down the training rules," the initial expression "by means of that which had become the cause" is used here to indicate the sense of cause (*hetu*).

It was stated because it was intended [to be so]. For it is said in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā, he dwelt at that time by virtue of that occasion which was the cause for the Elder’s request for the promulgation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), having regard for the moment of reflection that had become the cause.
But what is the point of investigating the logic here? There is no desire on the part of the Teacher here to arrange the words in a specific sequence; thus it stands.

It should be accepted as such. For that very reason, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* as well, this same sequence was stated in the passage beginning, “by that which had become a cause, by that which had become an instrument,” and so forth.

Indeed, the statement “by that which had become a cause” at the beginning there was not uttered for the purpose of indicating that the sense of cause is intended here in the phrase “at that time he was dwelling at Verañjā.”

“They say that the connection here should be made thus: ‘While laying down the training rules, he dwelt by way of a cause and by way of an instrument; and looking toward the cause for the laying down of the training rules, he dwelt by way of a cause.
It is for the purpose of illustrating that meaning—that is, for the purpose of showing the sense of cause or the sense of instrument. ‘Here’ means in this Vinaya.”
"‘There is here’: in this place, this verse exists by way of including the meanings as they have been stated. ‘Elsewhere’: in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma. ‘The ancient ones’:
the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). ‘A difference in mere expression’: a distinction consisting merely of words.
By this, he shows that a change of case-ending has been made in the Suttas and the Vinaya. ‘We shall explain the meaning further on’ refers to the passage beginning with ‘Thus indeed...’"
We shall explain [the term] in the places where it occurs, such as in the passage beginning with "The Blessed One. Regarding *Verañjā*:
because there was no oppression of the people due to the collection of taxes (*balikara*), it is "Verañjā" in the sense that "dust (*raja*) has departed (*vigata*) from it";

or, because in the *Serivāṇija Jātaka* a place for the arising of enmity (*vera*) toward Devadatta was established there, it is "Verañjā" in the sense that "enmity (*vera*) is born (*jāta*) here"; and because of the frequent entry of actors, theatrical troupes, and the like...
Some explain it thus: "It is Verañjā because it delights with various requisites such as hard food, soft food, ornaments, and so forth;
or it is Verañjā because it was born after overcoming opposition, having overcome *vera*;
or it is Verañjā because it was established on the site of the hermitage of the seer named Verañja. What is the use of this?
Showing that this is merely a name for that city, he said: "‘Verañjā’ is a designation for a certain city.
The locative case is used in the sense of proximity, as in examples such as "cows graze on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyaṃ*) or "the Gagga family lives by the well" (*kūpe*). "Without distinction" means:
"He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; having attained the first jhāna..."
...he dwells. He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.

He dwells having entered the signless concentration of mind by not attending to any signs"—as in such passages, [the meaning is understood] without the qualification implied by the proximity of other words.
Alternatively, "without distinction" means not by way of a specific distinction, but by way of the commonality of the state of dwelling (*vihāra*).

"In the modes of conduct... in the abidings" means: among these four abidings, namely, the abiding in conduct (*iriyāpatha-vihāra*), the divine abiding (*dibba-vihāra*), the sublime abiding (*brahma-vihāra*), and the noble abiding (*ariya-vihāra*).
Therein, "conduct" (*iriyā*) is movement or proceeding; it is bodily effort, bodily activity.

Because they are the means for the occurrence of that [activity], standing, sitting, and so forth, are called "modes of conduct" (*iriyāpatha*), as they are the paths (*patha*) for conduct. For it is not by standing, sitting, and so forth alone—

It is not possible to perform any bodily action without postures. For one who possesses the posture of standing might do something with the body, or one who possesses any other [posture] such as walking and so forth.
"Vihāra" means dwelling, or that by which one dwells; thus it is the posture itself that is the "vihāra.
And this, in its actual sense, is merely a continuity of the fourfold material phenomena (rūpa-santati) proceeding in the modes of standing, sitting, and so on.
“Divine” (*dibba*) means existing in the heavens; the meaning is that it is an existence in the divine worlds, such as those of the Brahma-parisajja gods, due to its frequent occurrence there.
Alternatively, it is “divine” because it conduces to divine power (*anubhāva*); or it is “divine” because it possesses a great range through the application of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
It is a “divine abiding” (*dibbavihāra*) because it is both divine and an abiding, or because it is an abiding that brings about a divine state.
The sublime jhānas. For even the formless attainments (ārūppasamāpatti) are included right here. However, in the *Nettippakaraṇa*, it is stated:

"The four formless attainments are the imperturbable abodes" (*āneñjavihāra*). This was said with reference to their specific nature as meditative developments, just as the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are designated for the jhānas of loving-kindness and so forth.
In the commentaries, however, they are [classified separately] because they generally bring about a divine state.
These too are called "divine abidings" (*dibbavihāra*). They are "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*) because they are the abidings of Brahmas, or because they are abidings that are themselves Brahmic;
the meaning is that they are abidings that have become sublime (*brahma*) or excellent due to their occurrence by way of bestowing welfare and so forth.

They are the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*), beginning with the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*). They are "noble abidings" (*ariyavihāra*) because they are noble or supreme abidings, owing to their being not shared by others.
The "abodes of the noble ones" (ariyavihāra) are the noble dwellings; they are the four attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Specifically, however, the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*), and the attainment of fruition belonging to the fourth jhāna constitute the divine, brahma, and noble abodes of the Blessed One. "Indicating possession of one or another abode" means indicating the state of being possessed of one or another of the aforementioned abodes.
For when the world is overwhelmed by greed, hatred, and delusion, the Blessed One enters and dwells in the divine abodes (*dibba-brahma-vihāra*) for the sake of training it through his own practice.

Thus, it is said that whenever beings act perversely toward sense pleasures, the Blessed One dwells in the divine abode for the purpose of generating the wholesome root of non-greed in them, thinking: "Perhaps they might [adopt] this practice..."
