"Having seen this, may they develop a preference for it and become dispassionate toward sensual pleasures.
But when they act wrongly toward beings for the sake of power, he then dwells in the divine abode (brahmavihāra) in order to arouse the root of non-hatred in them, thinking:
"Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a preference for it, they might pacify their hatred through non-hatred."
But when those who have gone forth dispute over matters pertaining to the Dhamma, he dwells in the noble abode for the purpose of generating the wholesome root of non-delusion in them, thinking:

"Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it, they might pacify their delusion through non-delusion. And by acting thus, through these divine, brahma, and noble abodes, he [benefits] sentient beings.
Because it carries away, brings, leads toward, produces, and generates various kinds of welfare and happiness, it is called "dwelling" (*viharati*).
However, one never fails to dwell by means of the dwelling in postures (*iriyāpatha-vihāra*), since without that, there would be no maintenance of the physical body.
For this very reason, the dwelling in postures is common to the divine dwellings (*dibba-vihāra*) and so forth as well; thus he said, "But here," and so on.

"An exposition of the conjunction of the postures" is stated because there is no specific term to expound the conjunction of other modes of dwelling, and because the purpose of expounding the conjunction of the postures is thereby accomplished.
In this alternative view, however, in the phrase "he dwells" (*viharati*), the prefix *vi-* indicates separation;
"he carries" (*harati*) means he leads or maintains [the posture], having separated [it from others].
"It takes away" is what is meant. In that regard, with reference to the internal objection—"Of what is there a severance by what? And how does it proceed for whom?"—he says "He indeed," and so forth.

"He" refers to the Blessed One. Even though the Blessed One is capable of maintaining his physical existence for a very long time through even a single posture (*iriyāpatha*), nevertheless, this is the inherent nature of a body that has been grasped by clinging (*upādinnaka*).
To demonstrate this, it was said: "a single obstruction to the postures," and so forth. "Aparipatantaṃ" means not falling.

Furthermore, because the Blessed One dwells wherever he may be, teaching the Dhamma to those to be trained and spending his time in various meditative attainments (samāpatti), he brings and leads toward manifold welfare and happiness for both sentient beings and himself.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "he moves about in various ways" (*vividhaṃ harati*); thus he "dwells" (*viharati*).
Regarding the phrase "at the foot of the Naḷeru-pucimanda tree," they explain it thus:
*Naḷeru* is a designation for the *yakkha* inhabiting that tree; therefore, the *pucimanda* tree inhabited by him is called "the Naḷeru-pucimanda."
It is called *naḷeru*. Alternatively, it is *naḷeru* because it grows (*ruhattā*) or is born (*jātattā*) in a reed (*naḷe*).
Here, the word "reed" (*naḷa*) refers to a hollow; therefore, because it is born within the hollow of a tree, it is called *naḷeru-pucimanda*, meaning both a *naḷeru* and a *pucimanda*.
Or, it is *naḷeru* because it grows or is born in a reed forest (*naḷavane*). It is said that this *pucimanda* tree was born in a reed forest. [The term] *urunāḷo pucimando* [is used].
*Naḷerupucimanda*: here, the word *urū* is a synonym for "great," and the word *naḷa* is a synonym for "hollow";
therefore, a *pucimanda* tree possessed of a great hollow is called a *naḷerupucimanda*. However, the Teacher, thinking, "What is the use of much talk on this matter?
and wishing to show only one meaning, said: "*Naḷeru* is the name of a *yakkha*," and so forth.
Showing that the word *mūla* (root) is intended here in the sense of "proximity" and not as it occurs in terms such as *mūlamūla* (root of the root), he says:

"*Mūlan ti samīpan*" (The root means proximity), and so forth. In its primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), the word *mūla*, which refers to a specific part functioning to establish the firm standing of a composite whole possessing branches and so on, [is applied] by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) to similar things and to the location upon which they depend.
It occurs by way of a figurative method (pariyāya); therefore, in the phrase "one should uproot the roots," it is the literal root that is intended.
To specify this with one word "root," he said, "it is seen as 'root-of-roots,'" just as in the cases of "suffering-of-suffering" and "form-of-form.
In the phrase "in the uncommon cause" (asādhāraṇahetu), it means in the uncommon condition. For greed is [the cause] only of unwholesome states of consciousness accompanied by greed.
Because it is a cause that is not common [to all unwholesome states], the meaning is:

those specific conditioning factors which, in the sense of being roots, assist by establishing the state of being well-founded exclusively for the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobha*).

Alternatively, while non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth are common to both the wholesome and the indeterminate, greed and so forth are not so; rather, they are common only to the unwholesome. Thus, they are uncommon causes. Now...
Regarding the phrase "or beginning with," here the word "beginning" (ādi) should be understood as including the wholesome and indeterminate roots such as non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth.
For among those, the wholesome root of non-greed and so forth is an uncommon cause because it is not shared with the unwholesome or indeterminate [roots];

likewise, the indeterminate root of non-greed and so forth is also an uncommon cause because it is not shared with the other two [types of roots]. "In a windless place" means in a location free from wind.
Or in the absence of wind. "Falling" means they descend; or this reading, *nipatanti*, is the very same. "Delightful" (*ramaṇīyo*) means agreeable.
"Pleasing" (*pāsādiko*) means inspiring confidence; the meaning is "one that generates confidence. The connection is with the phrase "as if exercising lordship. Regarding the word "there" (*tattha*):
"At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru-fig tree."
Regarding what was stated there: *siyā* means that someone might have such a reflection, or that they might at some time raise an objection in the manner about to be described.
In the passage beginning with "If, first of all, [it were] the Blessed One," the intention of the objector is this:
if there were a locative of location (*adhikaraṇādhikaraṇa*), as in expressions such as "he dwells in a palace in Pāṭaliputta," then [the phrase would mean] "he dwells in Verañjā."
The designation of two locations would be appropriate [if it were said], "at the foot of the Naleru and Pucimanda trees";
however, because these two are situated in different places, the designation of both together is not appropriate. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he dwelt there":
if he dwelt at the foot of the Naleru and Pucimanda trees, one should not say "at that time," because Verañjā and the foot of the Naleru and Pucimanda trees are distinct locations.
And this is the intended meaning because it has been so stated. Now, the objector clarifies his own intention with the words beginning "for it is not possible," and so forth.

Indeed, it is not possible for [the Buddha] to dwell in both places at that same time, precisely because the locations—the grounds at Verañjā and at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree—are distinct;
yet, it is stated that he dwelt "in both places at that same time."
It should be understood that dwelling at various times is not prohibited.
Showing that the other [position] was stated by you because you do not know this entire matter without error, he said, "But this is not to be viewed in this way," and so forth.
In that context, "this" refers to the statement: "He dwells at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree."
This is the statement. Regarding the word "thus" (*evaṃ*): that which was questioned by you starting with "If, first of all, the Blessed One...
should not be understood in that sense; rather, the meaning is that it is not for the purpose of showing two monasteries simultaneously, neither before nor after.
Now, [the author] states his own intended, unerring meaning, and the fact that he had already expressed it in anticipation of this.
And demonstrating that this has not been understood by others, he said: "Have we not stated that the locative case is used in the sense of proximity?
and so forth. "Herds of cattle" (*goyūthāni*) means circles of cows. Even so, one should simply say "he dwells at the foot of the Naleru and Pucimanda trees," and not "in Verañjā.

Therefore, one might raise the objection in one's mind: "What is the purpose of stating the introduction in both ways, [once] for the sake of the location in the sense of proximity and [once] otherwise?"
Having set this down, he said: "For the purpose of indicating the village of the alms-round," and so forth. "Of him" refers to the Blessed One.
And here, the naming of the village of the alms-round must certainly be performed.

For just as the naming of Naḷeru’s Pucimanda tree had many purposes—such as providing assistance to those who have gone forth—likewise, the naming of the village of the alms-round also has various purposes, such as providing assistance to householders.
Showing this, he said, "By the praise of Verañjā," and so forth. Therein, "rendering assistance to householders" means:

by providing them with the opportunity to receive requisites there, by granting them the chance to approach and pay their respects, by establishing them in the refuges and the precepts, and by bringing about the attainment of higher distinctions according to their respective spiritual potential, [the Buddha] assists householders.

“Rendering assistance”: regarding “rendering assistance to those who have gone forth,” this refers here to rendering assistance to those who have gone forth by providing them with suitable clothing, dwellings, and places for study, as well as by means of instruction, questioning, and application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Because the enjoyment of requisites is established through the very act of receiving them, he says: “In the same way, by the former... [omission] ...by avoidance.”
In this context, "by the former" refers to the mention of Verañjā. That wherein the conceit of "I" (ahaṃ-māna) is placed is the self (attā), that is, the personal existence (attabhāva).
The exhaustion of that, its state of being exhausted, is "exhaustion of self" (attakilamatha); what is meant is the affliction of the self or the suffering of the self.

The pursuit or practice of that is "the pursuit of the exhaustion of self" (attakilamathānuyoga), which is the production of suffering for oneself through such means as fasting and sleeping on beds of thorns.
This has been stated. The avoidance of that is the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification.

Since for those living within a village, even if they do not wish it, there is the possibility of seeing objects such as disagreeable forms and so forth, whereas for those living outside the village in a suitable location, that does not occur, he says:
"By the latter, through the abandoning of sensual objects," and so on. Therein, "by the latter" means—

By means of the words regarding the roots of the *naḷeru* and *pucimanda* trees. Because they serve as the basis for the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*), the five strands of sensual pleasure—form and so forth—are "sensual desire as a basis" (*vatthukāma*).

The abandoning of that is the "abandoning of sensual desire as a basis" (*vatthukāmappahāna*). "Showing the means for avoiding devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukhallikānuyogavivajjanupāyadassana*) means:

devotion (*yoga*), pursuit (*anuyoga*), and experience (*anubhava*) of the pleasure associated with the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) toward those objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*); it is the showing of the means for avoiding that.
Having himself approached the village within his range of activity, he perceives those individuals capable of hearing the Dhamma according to their own disposition;
thus, it is understood that the time for teaching the Dhamma has arrived, and so his application to the teaching of the Dhamma is made known. Therefore, he says:

"And by the former, there is application to the teaching of the Dhamma. Application to the teaching of the Dhamma (*dhammadesanābhiyoga*) is the state of being energetic (*saussāha*) in the teaching of the Dhamma.
Because one who dwells in a secluded place outside the village is free from crowded habitation, their inclination toward and tendency toward physical seclusion and the like are made known;
thus it is said, "by the latter, there is inclination toward seclusion.
Compassion and wisdom, which are themselves the causes for both the application to teaching the Dhamma and the inclination toward seclusion, [constitute] the approach to the teaching of the Dhamma.
Therefore, he says, "The approach through compassion by means of the former," and so forth, because these two serve as the causes for the subsequent departure.
For it is precisely compassion and wisdom that are the causes for the following pair of verses. By this, he clarifies the absence of defilement in both the approach and the departure:
that the approach through compassion is not motivated by gain and the like, and that the departure through wisdom is not motivated by opposition and the like.
It should be seen. "Inclination" means the state of being directed toward that. "Unstained" means unstained by attachment, not clinging.
"On account of not abandoning righteous happiness": here, "righteous happiness" (dhammikasukha) means blameless happiness.
For that is called "righteous happiness" because it arises in dependence upon righteous gain (dhammika-lābha). It is on account of the application to superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma).
The connection is with "living in comfort. "Abundance of benefit for human beings" refers to the abundance of benefit by way of receiving requisites, teaching the Dhamma, and so forth.
"Abundance of benefit for deities" is due to being secluded from people; for deities consider a place secluded from common folk to be worthy of their approach.
"Having grown up in the world" refers to the state of having been nurtured by the enjoyment of material things.

Regarding the phrase "one person" (*ekapuggalo*): here, "one" (*eko*) has the sense of excluding a second or more, and refers to a numerical limit. "Person" (*puggalo*) is a conventional expression (*sammuti-kathā*), not an expression of ultimate truth (*paramattha-kathā*).
For the Blessed Buddha’s teaching is twofold: the conventional teaching and the ultimate teaching.
This matter, however, has already been explained in detail below, so it is not stated here. Thus, "one" (*eko*) and "that person" (*puggalo*) [constitute the term].
The One Person. In what sense is he the One Person? In the sense of being peerless, in the sense of being distinguished by his qualities, and in the sense of being unequaled.

For he is the One Person in the sense of being peerless because, beginning with the mental advertence toward the ten perfections in their proper sequence, he is peerless among the rest of the world both in terms of the qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment and in terms of the Buddha-qualities themselves. And those which are his...
His qualities are also superior to the qualities of other beings; thus, he is the "one person" in the sense of being distinguished by his qualities.
The previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were unequal to all beings, yet he alone is equal to them in both the qualities of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the qualities of the name-body (*nāmakāya*);
thus, he is the "one person" in the sense of being equal to the unequaled. "In the world" means in the world of beings (*sattaloka*).
Furthermore, both [phrases] "arising, it arises" and "it arises while arising" are indeed incomplete expressions.
However, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "While arising, it arises for the benefit and welfare of many people, and not for any other reason.
And such a characteristic cannot be refuted by any other grammatical rule (*saddalakkhaṇa*). Moreover, that which is called "arising" (uppajjamāna) is what "arises" (uppajjati).
The distinction here should be understood as follows: "named" (*nāma*) and "arisen" (*uppanna*).

For he—who received the prophecy at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha—while seeking the qualities that make one a Buddha, saw the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and made the resolution: "These qualities must be fulfilled by me.

Thus, even while fulfilling the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), he is said to be "arising"; likewise for the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*)... [and so on] ...up to the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramitā*).

Even while fulfilling these ten perfections (*pāramī*), even while fulfilling the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), he is said to be "arising. Even while fulfilling the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*), he is said to be "arising.
Even while relinquishing the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*), he is said to be "arising.

Even while fulfilling the conduct for the sake of knowledge (*ñātatthacariyā*), the conduct for the sake of the world (*lokatthacariyā*), and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood (*buddhatthacariyā*), he is said to be "arising."
Even while reaching the pinnacle of the qualities that produce a Buddha over four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand kappas, he is said to be "arising.
Even while remaining in the Tusita heaven after relinquishing the Vessantara existence for seventy-five million years plus six million, he is said to be "arising.
When requested by the deities, he performs the five great observations (*pañca mahāvilokanāni*).
Even while taking rebirth in the womb of Queen Māyā, and even while dwelling in the womb for exactly ten months, he is said to be "arising.
Even while remaining in the midst of the household life for twenty-nine years, he is said to be "arising.
Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, on the very day Rāhula Bhadda was born, accompanied by Channa—

Even while departing after mounting Kaṇḍaka, the noble horse, he is said to be "arising. Even while crossing the three kingdoms and going forth on the bank of the Anoma River, he is said to be "arising.
Even while performing the Great Struggle for six years, he is said to be "arising.
Even while consuming coarse food once his knowledge had reached maturity, he is said to be "arising. At the time of evening...
On the full moon day of Visākha, having ascended the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) and shattered the host of Māra, he recollects his past lives during the first watch of the night,
purifies his divine eye during the middle watch, and immediately following the final watch,

contemplates the twelve-fold dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and reverse order; thus, even while penetrating the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), he arises [in this world].
It is called "arising" at the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, at the moment of the fruit of once-returning, and at the moment of the fruit of non-returning.
However, it is called "arising" at the moment of the path of arahantship, and "having arisen" at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
For in the case of Buddhas, the various powers such as the knowledge of supernormal feats (iddhividha-ñāṇa) do not arise sequentially as they do for disciples; rather, they arise all at once.

By means of the path of arahantship, the entire mass of qualities such as omniscience and so forth is indeed said to have arrived; therefore, because all its functions have been accomplished, it is said to have "arisen" at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
In this sutta as well, the phrase "it arises" is stated with reference specifically to the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
"It has arisen" (uppanno hoti) is precisely the meaning here.
"For the welfare of many" means it arises for the benefit of the great multitude. "For the happiness of many" means it arises for the well-being of the great multitude.
"Out of compassion for the world" means it arises out of compassion for the world of sentient beings.
Which world of sentient beings? That which, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, drank the drink of the Deathless and [embraced] the Dhamma...

He penetrated it. For after the Blessed One had spent seven weeks at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) and then returned from the Seat of Enlightenment to Isipatana, he taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, beginning with the words, "Bhikkhus, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.
At that time, together with the Venerable Aññā Koṇḍañña Thera, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās drank the drink of the Deathless (amatapāna).
[They] drank; [this radiance] arose out of compassion for this world of beings.
On the fifth day, at the conclusion of the *Anattalakkhaṇa-sutta*, the five bhikkhus of the group attained *arahatship*; this too arose out of compassion for this world of beings.
Thereafter, he established fifty-five men, headed by the youth Yasa, in *arahatship*; then, in the Kappāsika grove...
He established the thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group in the three paths and their fruits; he arose out of compassion for this world of beings.
At Gayāsīsa, at the conclusion of the discourse on the "Blazing," he established a thousand matted-hair ascetics in Arahatship.
Then, in the Laṭṭhivana grove, eleven million brahmins and householders, headed by Bimbisāra, [listened to] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Having heard [the teaching], they were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*); ten million were established in the refuges (*saraṇa*).

At the conclusion of the *Tirokuṭṭa-anumodanā*, the drink of the Deathless (*amata-pāna*) was drunk by eighty-four thousand beings. In the assembly of the garland-maker Sumanā, [it was drunk] by eighty-four thousand;
in the assembly of Dhanapāla, by ten thousand beings; and in the assembly of the *Khadiranga-jātaka*, by eighty-four thousand beings.

At the meeting with the Jambuka Ājīvaka, eighty-four thousand [beings] drank the drink of the Deathless; at the meeting with the merchant Ānanda, eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
On the day of the discourse on the Pārāyana Sutta at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, fourteen koṭis drank the drink of the Deathless.
On the day of the Twin Miracle, twenty koṭis of beings [drank it], as did those in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven upon the Paṇḍukambala stone.
While he was seated and teaching the Abhidhamma consisting of the seven treatises, having made his mother a bodily witness, eighty koṭis of beings drank the drink of the Deathless;
at the Descent of the Gods, thirty koṭis of beings did so; and in the Sakkapañha Sutta, eighty thousand deities drank the drink of the Deathless.
Furthermore, in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda, and the Samacittapaṭipadā—these [discourses]...
There is no limit to the number of beings who have attained clear realization (abhisamaya) in these four stages;

this [compassion] has arisen out of sympathy for this very world of beings. Furthermore, this meaning should be understood even with reference to those who, from this day forward and in the future, will establish themselves on the path to heaven and liberation by relying upon this teaching.
"Of gods and humans" means that he has arisen not only for the sake of gods and humans, but also for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the rest—the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth.

However, this was said specifically to show those persons capable of realizing the paths and fruits who possess the necessary causes for rebirth. Therefore, it is for the sake of the welfare, benefit, and happiness of these as well.
"It has arisen" is how it should be understood.
"Which single person? is a question arising from a desire to explain. Now, elucidating the single person asked about by that question, he says:
"The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. "The accomplishment of that purpose" means the accomplishment of the welfare of the world.
The meaning is "the accomplishment of the Buddha’s duties. First in the Lumbinī grove, second on the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa):
he was born with the physical body (rūpakāya) in the Lumbinī grove, and with the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) on the seat of enlightenment.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "and so forth," it shows that by praising Verañjā, the favoring of the physical body is indicated, and by praising the foot of the Naḷeru pucimanda tree, the favoring of the Dhamma-body is indicated. Likewise...
By the first [verse], there is the performance of an action dependent on others; by the second, the performance of an action independent of oneself.

Or alternatively, by the first there is the function of compassion (*karuṇā*), and by the other, the function of wisdom (*paññā*); by the first, one is endowed with supreme sympathy, and by the latter, one is endowed with supreme equanimity (*upekkhā*). In this way, it includes such points as these.
“Last” (*pacchima*) means “the final one” (*pacchimaka*) by virtue of its quality; this was said with reference to the Elder Ānanda.

“Also by number” (*saṅkhyāyapi*) means even by way of counting. To clarify the meaning that it is called a “Saṅgha” because of being a collection due to the commonality of view and virtue, he said: “by the group of recluses designated as a ‘Saṅgha’ through the commonality of view and virtue.
Herein, [it refers to] “this noble view which is emancipating, which leads the one who practices it toward [liberation] rightly...”
Regarding the view thus described as "he dwells having attained conformity of view through such a view for the destruction of suffering," [it is said]:

"He dwells having attained conformity of virtue through such virtues— virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration."

And because those virtues thus described are gathered together—being "assembled" (*saṅghaṭita*) and "united" (*sameta*) by what is called their commonality (*sāmañña*)—it is called a "gathering" (*saṅghāta*) by way of the commonality of view and virtue;
that is, the community of recluses (*samaṇagaṇa*). What is meant is that it is "collected" (*saṃhata*) through the commonality of view and virtue. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should intentionally deprive a living being of life; such a thing is not possible."

Because of such statements as "it exists," and because view and virtue possess a fixed nature, even stream-enterers are united with one another through the commonality of their views and virtues, let alone once-returners and the rest.
For noble persons, even when standing far apart in any place, remain united by the harmony of their own qualities.
"He dwells having attained conformity of view with such a view; in such [persons]..."

Because of the statement, "He dwells having attained commonality of virtue with regard to virtues," even ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) possess a state of being united by the commonality of view and virtue;
however, in this context, only the Noble Saṅgha is intended, because of the statement, "Whosoever there is the last among them, he is a stream-enterer.
By this means—that is, by the expression "with about five hundred bhikkhus"—of that [Saṅgha] consisting of about five hundred...
Of a hundred bhikkhus. The meaning of the terms *nirabbuda* and so forth will be explained later on.
Regarding the word *assosi* (he heard): here, "hearing" (*savana*) means "obtaining" (*upalabbha*). Thus he said, "‘Assosi’ means ‘he heard,’ that is, he obtained"; the sense is that he knew.
And since this obtaining occurs precisely by way of hearing, showing this point he said: "By following the sound of the words that reached the door of the ear..."
"Did you understand? Because the application of a word has the function of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), every sentence contains an implicit restriction;
thus he says: "The word *kho* is a particle used merely for the purpose of completing the metrical line.

By the phrase "in the sense of restriction," however, he shows that even in a sentence where restriction is already implicit, the word *kho* is employed to indicate the specific restriction intended by the speaker. That very intended restriction—
Showing this, he said: “In that context, ‘by way of the sense of restriction,’ and so forth. Then, as to what the purpose of the word *kho* is when used for the sake of completing the meter, he said:
“But by the completion of the meter, there is merely the smoothness of the phonetic expression (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*).

For when the word *assosi* (he heard) is taken together with the word *kho*, it becomes as if blossomed, adorned, and embellished; thus it is said to be “completed,” and thereby the preceding and following phrases—
They are smooth; since [the meaning] is not grasped when that [word] is omitted, the purpose is merely the smoothness of the phrasing (*byañjana*) through the filling of the metrical foot.
Here, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding a qualification (*visesanivatti*); by this, it shows that it indicates nothing other than that [smoothness].
Furthermore, by the word *eva*, it shows the exclusivity of the smoothness of the phrasing.
Regarding "Verañjā," showing the meaning here according to the rules of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*), he said: "Born in Verañjā," and so forth.
In the phrase "he breathes the *brahma*," the word *brahma* refers to the Veda; moreover, that [Veda] is threefold, according to the divisions of *manta*, *brahmakappa*, and *vasa*.
Among these, the *mantas* alone are set forth by Aṭṭhakā and others because they constitute the primary root, while the other two exist by depending upon them.
Because he was born [from that], only "striving" (padhāna) is grasped [by the term]. "He recites mantras" means he recites the body of mantras such as the *Iruveda* and so forth;
for the *Iruveda* and others are called "mantras" because they must be spoken with restraint (*gutta*).

By the restrictive particle "this very," he rejects the etymological derivation (nirutti) such as "born from Brahmā. By the phrase "of the birth-Brahmins" (*jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ*), other types of Brahmins are also [implied].

He shows that [they] exist. For there are two kinds of brahmins: birth-brahmins and purity-brahmins. Now, showing the etymological derivation (*nirutti*) for the purity-brahmins therein, he says, "But the noble ones," and so forth.

"Because evil has been stilled" means because evil has been stilled completely, without remainder, along with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*). For it is in this way that they differ from the external ascetics who have not abandoned passion, and from the trainees (*sekkha*) and non-trainees (*asekkha*) who have merely stilled evil.
The Blessed One’s definition of a "wicked ascetic" (pāpasamaṇa) is thus distinguished. Explaining this very point by means of an illustration, he says, “For this has been said,” and so forth.

Regarding this, they say: “‘One who has banished evil is a brahmin; one is called an ascetic (samaṇa) because of having stilled evil’—this is stated by taking two phrases from two different verses and combining them. This is indeed stated in all three *gaṇṭhipadas*: “Because of having stilled evils...”
Taking up the statement, "He is called a *samaṇa*," it was said: "Because he has stilled [the defilements], he is called a *samaṇa*.
However, the phrase "one who has banished evil is a *brāhmaṇa*" is a statement found in another metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
Since particles have multiple meanings, he said, "The particle *khalu* is used here in the sense of 'reporting' (*anussavana*)."
“Accomplished by birth” means arrived at through birth; it is said to be established by birth. “Merely a form of address” means merely a word of affectionate address.
For these are terms of endearment: “Sir,” “Venerable One,” or “Devānampiya.

“He is called one who addresses others as ‘Bho’” means that he who wanders about addressing people with “Bho, Bho! in greetings and the like is called a *bhovādī*. “Possessing something” (*sakiñcana*)... [text ends]

One who possesses the "possessions" (kiñcana) such as lust and the rest is called "one with possessions. For lust and the rest are called "possessions" because they possess, crush, and entangle beings.
It is said that when people have oxen tread out a threshing floor, they say, "Tread it out, Kapila! Tread it out, Kālaka!
Therefore, the sense of "crushing" (maddana) should be understood as the sense of "possession" (kiñcana).

Regarding the term *gotavaśena*: here, that which protects (*tāyati*) the lineage (*gaṃ*) is called *gotta*. In this context, by the word "cow" (*go*), both the designation (*abhidhāna*) and the cognition (*buddhi*) are meant;

therefore, the meaning should be understood in this way. The designation and the cognition occurring as "Gotama" is called *gotta* because it protects (*tāyati*) and guards them by virtue of having a single-pointed object.
For just as cognition does not function without an object that serves as its referent, [so too the name protects the lineage].

Thus, the designation [is explained] by means of that which constitutes its referent; therefore, it is said that this meaning, termed a "clan" (*gotra*), protects (*tāti*) or guards those designations of the intellect.

Furthermore, it should be understood as a common form belonging to that clan, originating from the first ancestor of that family, which is unique to that lineage and not shared with other lineages. Herein—
By the term *samaṇa*, the Blessed One’s state of being highly esteemed by his peers is shown, because it signifies that he has stilled evil;
by the term *Gotama*, his descent from a noble lineage is indicated for the sake of worldly people. He is the son of the Great King Suddhodana of the Sakya clan, thus a *Sakyaputta*.
And by this, his birth into a most exalted and vast Kshatriya family is revealed; hence it is said: "This, however—"

"...as an illustration of the Blessed One’s high birth. For from the Great King Mahāsammata, the very first of all Kṣatriyas, down to the present, the Śākya royal family has remained of the most exalted and undiminished lineage.
"Unconquered by any loss" means it is not overcome, nor overtaken, by any kind of decline such as the loss of kinsmen or the loss of wealth.
For thus, at the birth of the Lord of the World, there was no loss whatsoever for that family; rather, there was only increase.

And upon his Great Renunciation, his state of being most prosperous in the world became manifest and renowned. Therefore, the statement "he went forth from the Sakyan clan" was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating that the Blessed One had gone forth out of faith, despite leaving behind a vast circle of kinsmen.
Because of the accomplishment of his state as one who has gone forth after abandoning a great mass of wealth. "Thereafter" refers to the passage beginning with “He was staying at Verañjā.
Regarding the term *itthambhūtākhyāna* (the expression of a state attained): one who has become (*bhūta*) or reached (*āpanna*) this manner or mode is *itthambhūta*;
the expression of such a person is *itthambhūtākhyāna*, and that itself is the meaning of *itthambhūtākhyānattha*. Alternatively, *itthaṃ*...
The meaning of "having become such a one" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*) is the sense of describing how someone has come to be;

the term *tasmiṃ* (in that) refers to the accusative case used in this sense. Here, in the word *abbhuggato*, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the sense of "having become such," because it illuminates the manner of rising after having overcome [obstacles].
Due to its connection with that [prefix], the phrase "that venerable Gotama... [is used].
The use of the accusative case is the same even when [the word] has a possessive sense (*sāmī-attha*), because it serves to indicate a description of a state as it is (*itthambhūta-ākhyāna*);
therefore, it is stated as "in the sense of a description of a state as it is. For this very reason, he said: "The meaning is 'of that venerable Gotama'. This is what is meant:
just as in the phrase "Devadatta is kind toward his mother," the accusative case is used for a description of a state as it is due to its connection with the prefix *abhi*.

It has been stated thus; likewise here, in the phrase "But this good report of the venerable Gotama has arisen concerning him" (*taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ abhi evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo uggato*), because of its connection with *abhi*, it is used in the accusative case to express a state of being so characterized (*itthambhūtākhyāna*).
For in the example "Devadatta is kind toward his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi*), [the word *mātaram*] is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇatthe*) as follows:
"Devadatta is kind toward his mother (*mātaramabhi*), that is, in respect to his mother (*mātari visaye*), or toward his mother (*mātuyā*)."

In this context, where there is a connection with either a locative case, a genitive case, or a nominative case, the accusative case is employed in conjunction with the prefix *abhi*, which indicates the sense of "having reached such a state.

Just as here the meaning is understood to be: "Devadatta has attained a state of excellence within the sphere of his mother, or is related to his mother," so too here [the meaning is]: "related to the venerable Gotama."
The meaning understood here is: "The sound of fame has arisen, having surpassed [all others] and reached the state of rising up.
For in that context, the mention of Devadatta is like the mention of the "sound of fame" here;
likewise, the statement "his mother" there is like the statement "that venerable Gotama" here; and the mention of the word "good" there...
Here, the grasping of the word "arisen" (uggata) should be understood as being like [the grasping of] "excellent" (kalyāṇa).
"Excellent" means auspicious. Its state of being excellent consists in its having excellent qualities as its object; thus he said, "endowed with excellent qualities. The meaning is:
endowed with excellent qualities, it is joined with them by virtue of having them as its object. For here, "endowment" (samannāgama) consists in having those [qualities] as its object.
The intention is that it is "dependent on that" because its object consists of excellent qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*). The same principle applies here to the word "excellent" (*seṭṭha*).
For the excellence of the word "fame" (*kittisadda*) is due solely to its having excellent qualities as its object, as in such passages as, "The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent.

Because he recites the qualities through the formula "The Blessed One is an Arahant," and because it is something to be praised (*saddanīya*), it is called "fame"; thus he says, "Fame is simply renown (*kitti*)."
Indeed, it is *vaṇṇa* (beauty/quality) itself that is called *sadda* (sound) because it is to be praised (*kittetabba*) and because it is worthy of being celebrated (*kittisaddanīya*).

For the word *sadda* is a synonym for *kitti* (fame/glory), as in the passage: “The sages, possessing virtues and practicing austerities, have a sublime sound (*uḷārasaddā*). Sound that proceeds by way of praise is *thutighosa* (the sound of praise), which is the utterance of praise.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *abbhuggata* is not shown in the Commentary; therefore, its meaning should be understood as follows:
*abbhuggato* means "risen up having overcome," which is to say, it has arisen pervading the world with its devas because it proceeds by way of qualities that are not shared by others.
To the question "In what way? he said: "It is thus (*itipi so*)."

“‘The Blessed One,’ and so forth. From here on, however, in such instances where the meaning of the scriptural passage (pāḷi) ought to be stated, we shall state it there, saying “But in the text (pāḷiyaṃ panā),” and then show the meaning. Now, showing the meaning preceded by the word-arrangement (padayojanā), he said:
“In ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One,’ and so forth, this first of all is the arrangement,” and so on. “He is the Blessed One.”

He who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the Lord of the World—who received the name "Bhagavā" for reasons such as his blessedness (*bhāgyavantatā*) and so forth:
he is the Blessed One. For "Bhagavā" is this designation of the Teacher's name.
Therefore, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said: “‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother,” and so forth.

But what follows is merely a recitation of his qualities. Just as one who practices meditation (kammatthānika) recollects the Buddha’s qualities by joining the word *itipi* to each of the nine epithets beginning with “Arahan,” so too does one who recites the Buddha’s qualities; showing this, he says:
He said: “Thus indeed is the Arahant; thus indeed is the Perfectly Enlightened One... [and so on] ...thus indeed is the Blessed One.

For this being so, by means of these nine terms beginning with “Arahant,” those qualities of a Buddha that are exceedingly well-known and renowned throughout the world including the devas are analyzed in their various aspects.
Indeed, here the word *iti* is used in the same way as in such expressions as “Thus indeed this is real; thus indeed this is true.”
The particle *pi* has the sense of being near or manifest, and it has the sense of inclusion;

by this, the multiplicity of those qualities is indicated. Furthermore, since those causes for perceiving the qualities are manifest to wise persons endowed with faith, a wise person reciting them should do so having brought them directly before the mind, as if they were present.
He said, "It is meant that [the meaning] is shown by this and that reason.
Since it was stated below, "Explaining the meaning of the words of the Suttas in accordance with the Suttas," he states the purpose here for wishing to show in detail once again—
even though it has already been commented upon in every way in the *Visuddhimagga*— the meaning that was treated there.
“Now, for those who uphold the Vinaya,” and so forth. In that context, “for the purpose of gladdening the mind” means for the purpose of satisfying the mind;

it is said to be for the purpose of generating confidence in the mind. Regarding the phrases beginning with “because of being far away”: “because of being far away” (ārakattā) means because of being very distant.

“Of enemies” (arīnaṃ) refers to the enemies that are the defilements. “Of spokes” (arānaṃ) refers to the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. “Because of being struck down” (hatattā) means because of having been destroyed.
“Of the requisites, etc. refers both to the requisites such as robes and to specific forms of worship.
Now, in order to clarify the meaning just stated, he says: “For he is far away,” and so forth.
Since distance is spoken of in relation to what is near, he shows the state of being at the ultimate limit of distance by saying: “Very far, far away.”
He said, "Standing," meaning that he stands far away by virtue of being very remote indeed.

To show that his state of standing far from defilements (*kilesa*) is not merely due to physical location, but rather because they have been entirely abandoned, he said, "Because the defilements have been shattered by the Path.
[An objection is raised: "But have those [defilements] not already been abandoned by other *khīṇāsavas* (those whose taints are destroyed) as well? To this inquiry...

Having taken this into account, it is said: "together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). For indeed, apart from the Blessed One, no others are able to abandon defilements along with their latent tendencies.
By this, it is shown that the state of *arahantship* of the Blessed One is not shared by others.
What, then, is this so-called "latent tendency"? It is the cause for an application similar to that of one who has abandoned defilements, even though [the defilements] have not been abandoned.
A specific capacity based on defilements is like the Vāseṭṭha’s mode of address toward the Venerable Pilindavaccha.
But how is the meaning "from defilements" obtained when the word "far from" (ārakā) is used?

Because it settles upon a specific sense through a general inquiry, and because a specific term must be supplied by one seeking that specific sense, [it is understood that] "evil things are far from him."
Sutta passages such as “unwholesome states” (akusalā dhammā) should be cited here as examples.

Furthermore, in this term, the vowel *ā* is shortened to *a*, and the consonant *k* is changed to *h* with an anusvāra according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*); thus, the formation of the word “Arahant” should be understood.
To facilitate the easy comprehension of the meaning already explained, the following is said here:
“Thus, he is called ‘distant’ (āraka) because he is devoid of those things;
and since the Lord is devoid of faults, he is therefore considered ‘Worthy’ (Araha).

Because the defilements themselves are the enemies due to their harmful conduct, they are called “enemies of the defilements” (kilesārayo). Although it should be said that he is an “Ariha” (one who has slain the enemies) because he has slain the enemies, it is expressed as “Araha” according to the rules of etymological derivation (niruttinaya). Here too, for the sake of easily grasping the meaning already stated, this should be understood:
“Because all enemies, reckoned as lust and the rest, have been slain by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason too he is considered an Arahant.
This is the connection with the phrase “this wheel of saṃsāra. Like the nave of a chariot wheel, it is the constituent part that serves as the root within.

And it is said that outside [the wheel] the two—ignorance (*avijjā*) and the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*)—are firmly established, as in the phrase "the hub consisting of ignorance and the craving for existence.

Connected to the hub and the rim like spokes are the formative forces of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable, which are linked to ignorance, craving, aging, and death as their conditions and fruits;
thus it is said, "the spokes consisting of the formative forces of merit and so forth."
In various states of existence, aging and death are manifest as the limit; making that the rim, he says, "the rim of aging and death.
Just as the axle is the primary cause for the turning of a chariot wheel, so too the origin of the taints (*āsava*) is the cause for the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra;
thus he says, "having pierced it with the axle consisting of the origin of the taints. The taints themselves [are the spokes] of ignorance and the rest...
The origin of the taints (*āsava*) is due to their being the cause. As it is said: "With the origin of the taints, there is the origin of ignorance.
The threefold existence (*tibhava*), consisting of the realms of sense-desire and so forth—which is differentiated as resultant form, kamma-form, and non-material form—is itself the chariot;

[the cycle] is "fully yoked" (*samāyojita*) because it has been yoked from the very beginning, either equally through its own conditions or in its entirety. It is "occurring from time immemorial" (*anādikālappavatta*) because it proceeds throughout a time that is without beginning.
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.

Thus, the very saṃsāra described in this way is the wheel of saṃsāra (*saṃsāracakka*). By him—by the Blessed One—at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), that which is designated as enlightenment...

At the place or time when knowledge has reached its state of culmination (*maṇḍa*). "Bodhi" means wisdom (*paññā*); because that wisdom has here become culminated and clarified, it is called the "seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

"With the feet of energy" means he proceeds in two ways—with his own feet known as energy—by means of their function of suppressing and establishing [the mind] regarding the factors conducive to defilement and purification respectively. "On the earth of virtue" means in the sense of being firmly established.
"Virtue itself is the earth": in that [earth]. "Having established oneself" means having stood firm by way of its accomplishment. "With the hand of faith":
because it is the means for taking up blameless phenomena, faith itself is the hand; by that [hand]. "Bringing about the destruction of karma":

because it brings about the destruction of all karma, including the divisions of bodily action and so forth, it is "the destroyer of karma. "The axe of wisdom" [is applied] upon the rock of concentration.
Having taken up the well-sharpened axe of the knowledge of the Path,

and having thus provided the interpretation of the meaning by taking what was stated here as "because the spokes have been destroyed"— namely, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) known as the "spokes" (ara)— and regarding it as a "wheel" (cakra) because it is like a wheel—
he now says "Or else," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that same point according to the sequence of the teaching on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

It has been stated. Therein, "the cycle of saṃsāra whose beginning is not known" (*anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭa*) refers to the wheel of saṃsāra whose end is not reached and whose starting point has never been cognized before.

"The remaining ten phenomena" refers to the ten phenomena beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and ending with birth (*jāti*). To the question, "In what way do those [phenomena] beginning with volitional formations have the nature of a root?
he says: "Because they are rooted in ignorance (*avijjā*) and because they terminate in aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Therein, ignorance is the root.
Those formations and so forth for which exertion is the cause are rooted in ignorance; their state is "having ignorance as their root" (*avijjāmūlakattaṃ*).
Those for which aging-and-death is the limit—that is, the finality—are "ending in aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇapariyantā*);

these are the ten factors beginning with formations. Their state is "ending in aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇapariyantattaṃ*). [This refers to] the ten factors beginning with formations and ending with birth.
The meaning is: "because it has ignorance as its root" and "because it ends in aging and death.

The intention is that because ignorance is not overcome from its very root, and because it connects the formative forces (saṅkhāra) and so forth to aging and death—which acts like a rim—at their conclusion.

"Regarding suffering and so forth" means regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. "Ignorance" refers to delusion (moha), which is called ignorance because it is the opposite of knowledge (ñāṇa).

But it is neither something other than knowledge, nor is it a mere absence of knowledge. In this context, ignorance regarding suffering and so forth functions solely by way of concealing those [truths], because it fails to provide penetration into their true nature.

For although ignorance arises here even with respect to objects in all remaining cases—setting aside the two supramundane truths—even so, it is intended here specifically in its capacity as a concealer.
For once arisen, it remains concealing the noble truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), not allowing one to penetrate its true essential characteristic;
likewise, it conceals the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
And here, by "suffering," the noble truth of suffering is intended, which is divided into three types according to the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth.

Likewise, having divided ignorance—which conceals that [suffering]—into three types, he says, “And ignorance in the sensual existence,” and so forth, showing the sequence of formations and the other conditions starting with ignorance within the three existences.
Therein, “ignorance in the sensual existence” means ignorance that conceals the danger in the sensual existence.
Regarding “ignorance in the fine-material existence” and “ignorance in the immaterial existence,” it is the same here as well.

The same method applies here. "Volitional formations in the sense-sphere existence" means volitional formations—both meritorious and demeritorious—comprised within the plane of sense-sphere existence;

or, it means those meritorious and demeritorious volitional formations that are to be produced in the sense-sphere existence. The sense is: "of those volitional formations that bring about rebirth in the sense-sphere existence.
And here, "volitional formations" should be understood as mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*). "Is a condition" refers to [the condition] for the meritorious volitional formations.
Thus, it acts as a condition in two ways: by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and by way of decisive-support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

Among meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), for those that arise simultaneously, it is a condition by way of the simultaneous [condition] and so forth; for those that do not arise simultaneously, it is a condition by way of the immediate (anantara) and proximate-immediate (samanantara) conditions and so forth.
However, for those that are not immediate, it is a condition by way of object and by way of decisive support. This applies to volitional formations in the immaterial realm (arūpabhava).
“Of immovable formations” (*āneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ*). “Is a condition” means by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) alone.

Furthermore, if this matter were to be explained here in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it here. “In the others” refers to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpabhava*).
“Of three bases” refers to the eye, ear, and mind bases, because the triad beginning with the nose is impossible there. “Of one” refers to...
Because the other [bases] are impossible therein for the mind-base (*manāyatana*). By this method, the meaning should also be understood in the cases of "of the three contacts," and so forth.

"Of the sixfold contact" means by way of eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. "Of the six feelings" means feeling born of eye-contact, and likewise...
"Of these six kinds of feeling": namely, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.

"Of the six classes of craving": namely, craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena—of these six classes of craving. In each respective case...
"Each such craving" refers to the craving that arises here and there in the realms of sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, distinguished as craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*) and the rest.

Since the discourse beginning with "that craving" is extremely concise, the passage beginning with "How [does it arise]? was stated in order to show it by analyzing and expanding upon both clinging (*upādāna*) and existence (*bhava*).
Therein, by the phrase "I shall enjoy sense-pleasures," he expresses the occurrence of craving for sense-desires (*kāmataṇhā*).
Likewise, [it arises] through such thoughts as, "I shall experience the attainment of heaven," and so forth.
Since that craving, when it proceeds by way of intense grasping, becomes what is called *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sense pleasures), it is therefore said: "conditioned by *kāmupādāna*.

"In the same way" means precisely conditioned by *kāmupādāna*. "The attainment of the Brahma-world" refers to the attainment in the fine-material (*rūpa*) Brahma-world. "All those belonging to the three planes..."

Because of the statement, "Phenomena are called 'desires' (kāma) in the sense of being desirable," attachment to existence (bhavarāga) is also considered to be simply clinging to sense-desire (kāmupādāna);

thus it is said, "One develops loving-kindness (mettā) precisely with clinging to sense-desire as its condition," and so forth. In this context, "develops loving-kindness" means that which is moistened (mijjati) and made smooth (siniyhati) is loving-kindness;
the meaning is that one develops—that is, increases—it. Alternatively, that which possesses loving-kindness is "loving" (mettaṃ), namely the mind associated with it.
The meaning is that one develops, increases, or arouses that jhāna. The meaning in such passages as "he develops compassion" should also be understood according to this same method.

Regarding the phrase "also in those rooted in the remaining types of clinging," this refers to the applications rooted in the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
The meaning is: "The same method applies. Herein, this is the application: here someone adopts the nihilistic view, thinking, "There is no other world";
he engages in misconduct by body, etc., conditioned by that clinging to views—the rest should be applied according to the method already stated.
Another adopts the annihilationist view, thinking, "In such-and-such a state of prosperity, the self is annihilated"; for the sake of rebirth there...

“He practices good conduct with the body,” and so forth, should be applied according to the method already stated. Another [type of person] develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, thinking, “Having become possessed of form and mind-made, the self will be annihilated”; all this is to be understood according to the method already stated.
Yet another develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm, thinking, “Having arisen in a formless existence, the self will be annihilated.”
"Develops for the fulfillment of development"—all this should be understood according to the method already stated.

It should be seen that by these very [terms], the application based on the root of the clinging to a self (attavādupādāna) has also been explained. In this way, the application should also be understood by way of the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda).
Another person, misapprehending an impure path as "the pure path," [clings] thinking, "Purification comes through virtue; purification comes through conduct."
"Due to clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), one engages in misconduct with the body"—all such passages are to be applied according to the method already stated.

Now, as for this demonstration of the wheel of saṃsāra, wherein the state of being a condition for ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) was shown by the statement, "In the sensual existence, ignorance is the condition for volitional formations," and so on;
and the state of being the result produced by those conditions for the volitional formations and so forth—
Bringing forward that very *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text as a conclusion, he says, "In this way," and so forth.

Therein, just as formations (*saṅkhārā*) are produced by causes, so too ignorance (*avijjā*) has causes such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*); thus he says, "Both of these are arisen from causes.
Regarding the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggahe*), [this refers to] the conditions for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), namely ignorance and the rest.
*Paricchijja gahaṇe*: the locative case is used in the sense of that which is to be accomplished.

*Paññā* is the knowledge (*jānanā*) by way of the prefix *pa-* (thoroughly), characterized as the purification by overcoming doubt. *Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ*: it is called *ṭhiti* because the phenomena of the fruit abide therein, their existence being dependent upon it;
thus, *ṭhiti* means the cause. The abiding of phenomena is *dhammaṭṭhiti*; the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena is *dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ*.
The meaning is "knowledge of conditions"; what is meant is "the realization of dependent origination.

Granted that here the wisdom consisting in the discernment of conditions is itself the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), nevertheless, as long as the formations (*saṅkhāra*) have not been seen, it is impossible to see the state of being a condition for those formations by way of ignorance;
therefore, the inclusion of the conditioned phenomena themselves—namely, that "formations are produced from a cause"—is also made.
This should be understood. The statement, "Both of these are arisen from causes," is said with the intention of showing that both possess the state of being dependently arisen.

And because this knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) occurs by way of crossing over the stain of doubt regarding the three periods of time, it is therefore said, "The past period as well," and so forth. In this manner, all the phrases should be expanded in detail.

By this method, all the terms beginning with “formations are the cause, consciousness is cause-arisen,” etc., should be expanded in the same manner as was stated for ignorance in the passage beginning “ignorance is the cause.

It is called a “summary” (saṅkhepa) because ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are summarized herein; that is, the cause and the result. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]
It is called "concise" (*saṅkhepa*) because it is summarized as "cause and result. This refers to ignorance and the rest [as the cause], and consciousness and the rest [as the result].
It should be understood that the singular number is used here due to the commonality of their state as being concise.

These concises, when divided by way of time, become fourfold: the cause in the past, the result in the present; the cause in the present, and the result in the future. Therefore, he said: "The former concise..."
And here, “the past time,” and so forth, is the connection with “the present time. Craving, clinging, and existence are indeed already included;
for here, by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), craving and clinging are included because they share the common nature of being defilements (*kilesa*);

and by the mention of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), existence is included because it shares the common nature of being kamma. Furthermore, this is because ignorance and volitional formations cannot perform their own functions without those [latter factors].
Craving, clinging, and becoming are thereby included. Alternatively, the ignorant person is agitated;
being agitated, he clings; with clinging as condition, there is becoming. Therefore, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included. And so it has been said:

"In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance, the exertion is volitional formations, the attachment is craving, the approaching is clinging, and the intention is becoming; thus these five states in the previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking here."
In that context, "in the previous kamma-existence" (*purimakammabhava*) means in the prior kamma-existence, that is, while the kamma-existence of a past birth was being performed;
this is the meaning. "Delusion is ignorance" (*moho avijjā*): that delusion regarding suffering and so forth at that time, by which one who is deluded performs kamma—that is ignorance.
"Accumulation is volitional formations" (*āyūhanā saṅkhārā*): those prior volitions of one performing that kamma, such as the thought, "I shall give a gift."
The volitions that have arisen while one is preparing the requisites for giving for even a month or a year are called "volitional formations as accumulation" (*āyūhana-saṅkhāra*);
however, the volition of one who places the offering into the hands of the recipients is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Alternatively, among the six impulsive moments (*javana*) of a single cognitive process, the volitions are called "volitional formations as accumulation," and the seventh is "existence. Or, any volition whatsoever [is so classified].
Existence (*bhava*) refers to the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) associated with the act of accumulating [kamma]. Craving (*taṇhā*) is attachment;
it is that longing and aspiration for the fruit of one’s actions in the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). Grasping (*upādāna*) is the approaching [of that fruit];

it is that which serves as the condition for the existence of kamma, such as thinking, "Having done this, I shall enjoy sensual pleasures in such-and-such a place," or "I shall cut off [the world]," and so forth.
Approaching, grasping, and clutching that which proceeds by way of this method is called "clinging" (upādāna).

Regarding "volition is becoming" (cetanā bhavo): among the three alternative meanings explained below starting with "the volitions prior to one performing that action," that which was stated as "volition is becoming"—that volition is what should be understood here as "becoming."
Now, wishing to show how all these phenomena, beginning with ignorance, are comprised within the two rounds (*vaṭṭa*), he said:
"These five phenomena are the round of kamma in the past. And here, in the primary sense, volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) and becoming (*bhava*) are kamma;
however, ignorance and the others are called "kamma" because they are companions to kamma, similar to it, and supportive of it. [Regarding] ignorance and the others...

Indeed, by virtue of their nature as phenomena subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhammatā*), they are similar to karma; they assist karma both through the mode of co-nascence (*sahajātakoṭi*) and the mode of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭi*).
And karma itself, being mutually connected, constitutes the "wheel of karma" (*kammavaṭṭa*) in the sense of revolving again and again.
"The five beginning with consciousness" refers to the five starting from consciousness and ending with feeling, which [exist] now, at this present time.
"In this selfhood" is what is meant. Regarding the statement "ignorance and formations are indeed included":
here too, as before, ignorance should be understood as being included by the mention of craving and clinging due to their common nature as defilements and karma;

and formations should be understood as being included by the mention of existence (*bhava*). Alternatively, when existence is mentioned, the formations that precede it or are associated with it [are included].

They are indeed included; for by the inclusion of craving (*taṇhā*) and clinging (*upādāna*), those factors associated with them are also included. And since it is through that [craving] by which one, being deluded, performs karma, that very ignorance (*avijjā*) is included as well.
Thus, by the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming (*bhava*), ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are indeed included.

Therefore it was said: "Here, due to the ripening of the sense bases (*āyatana*), there is delusion, which is ignorance; the exertion is volitional formations; the attachment is craving; the approaching is..."
“Clinging, volition, and becoming—these five factors here are conditions for rebirth-linking in the future.

In this context, by the phrase “because the sense bases have matured here,” the delusion of one with matured sense bases at the time of performing the kamma is shown. The rest is exactly as explained below.
It is stated that the states of birth, aging, and dissolution of consciousness, name-and-form, the sixfold sense base, contact, and feeling constitute birth, aging, and death.
Since the states possessing the phases are already included by the mention of the phases themselves due to their inseparability, he says:

"Because consciousness and the rest have been indicated by way of birth, aging, and death. "By way of" (apadesena) means by the mention of birth, aging, and death. "These" refers to consciousness and the rest.
"The round of future fruition" is said because those things yet to come in the future are included by virtue of their present causes. "Those" refers to ignorance and the rest.

"By way of aspect (*ākāra*)" means: although not explicitly stated as such in their individual groupings, they are "scattered" (*ākiriyyanti*) therein and are made manifest through the inclusion of ignorance, formations, and so forth;
thus they are called "aspects. Alternatively, aspects are the modes (*pakāra*) of past causes and so on. "From that, by way of aspect" means:
they become twentyfold by way of the fivefold division of past causes and so on.

In this context, there is one "link" (*sandhi*) between the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). Because of the state of uninterrupted occurrence from cause to fruit, there is one link that constitutes the connection between cause and fruit;
likewise, there is one between the various types of existence (*bhava-jāti*).

Furthermore, between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*taṇhā*), there is one link that constitutes the connection between fruit and cause, because of the state of uninterrupted occurrence from fruit to cause.
For even a phenomenon that has become a fruit (phalabhūta) serves as a condition for another phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is that of a cause.
The word "iti" is a reference to the manner already described. Therefore, he said: "the four compendia," and so forth.
"In all aspects" means by way of those [aspects] stated here and those not yet stated, including those found in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*, the *Anantanaya*, the *Paṭṭhāna*, and other such works.
"In all aspects. "He knows" means he understands. "He sees" means he sees directly with the eye of knowledge that has become vision.
"He cognizes" and "he penetrates" are synonyms for those same acts. "That" refers to that knowing.

"In the sense of having known" means in the sense of knowing according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāvato*). "In the sense of fully understanding" means in the sense of penetrating by way of such modes as impermanence and so forth.

Now, in order to show the purpose for which this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) has been brought forward here, the passage beginning with "By this" was stated. Therein, "those phenomena" refers to those phenomena beginning with ignorance.
"Having known them as they truly are" means having understood them according to reality by means of the great thunderbolt-like knowledge (*mahāvajirañāṇa*).
"Becoming disenchanted" means becoming disenchanted through powerful insight (*vipassanā*). "Becoming dispassionate and being liberated" [occurs] by means of the noble paths (*ariyamagga*).

“Becoming dispassionate, one is liberated. The connection is with the word “he destroys” (*hanī*). In that context, when the Blessed One becomes dispassionate and is liberated, at that time he is said to “destroy the spokes” (*arā hanti*).
However, what follows—namely, “He destroyed, he utterly destroyed, he demolished”—is stated by taking the moment of his full enlightenment (*abhisambuddha-kkhaṇa*) as the reference point.
Thus, because the spokes have been destroyed, they are called *arahant*; in this manner, according to this explanation, [the term applies] to the aforementioned wheel of saṃsāra.
He is an Arahant because he has destroyed the spokes and so forth [of the wheel of existence]. Regarding this, it is said:
“Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by the sword of knowledge by the Lord of the World, for that reason he is called ‘Arahant.’”

"Because he is the foremost object of offerings" means because of his state as the supreme recipient of offerings. To show that when the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) of a universal monarch (cakkavatti) appears—even though it is insentient—the world offers worship right there, and elsewhere distinctions of worship are cut off; how much more so when a Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha) has appeared, he said:
"When the Tathāgata has appeared," and so forth. "Each aggregate of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) by means of each dwelling..."
Even though it was said, "I shall worship," the words "referring to the Blessed One" and so forth were spoken because [the offering] was made specifically for the Teacher.
But what need is there to mention other special forms of worship?

What indeed can be said regarding the worthiness of other special forms of worship—those not very sublime, performed by gods and humans of no great power—as distinguished from those already mentioned? Also, because he is worthy of requisites and so forth...

They are "Arahant" also because they are worthy (anucchavika) by virtue of being the foremost recipients of offerings (aggadakkhiṇeyya) for the specific kinds of requisites such as robes already mentioned, as well as for special forms of worship.
To facilitate the easy comprehension of this meaning, the following is said:
“[They are worthy] of special worship together with the requisites...”
"Since this Lord of the World is worthy (araha), and in the world they call one 'worthy' (araha) for being in accordance with the goal,
therefore the Victor is worthy of this name."
“Out of fear of ill-repute” means out of fear of dispraise; it is said to mean out of fear of infamy and out of fear of censure.
“Committing evil in secret” means they commit evil in private, thinking, “Let no one know of it.

“In this way he never does so” means that the Blessed One, because the causes of evil were utterly abandoned even at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), never at any time acts in such a manner. And on this point there is a verse:
“Because for such a one there is no secrecy whatsoever regarding evil deeds,
he is renowned as ‘Arahant’ (Worthy) precisely because of that absence of secrecy.
Now, in order to facilitate easy comprehension, [the author] says “it exists,” presenting all the aforementioned points in a summarized form.

"Thus he is," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the Sage (muni) who has slain the enemies that are the defilements (kilesa)," here the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) should be understood for the sake of metrical convenience;

the meaning is "because the enemies that are the defilements have been slain. Regarding the phrase "one who has abandoned the wandering through conditions and so forth," here too the elision of the *niggahīta* should be understood in the same manner as stated above.
Regarding the term "Arahant," another method of interpretation should be seen here: one is an "Arahant" because of being "far away" (*āraka*), that is, by virtue of being very remote [from evil].

This is the meaning. But from what [distance] is it very far away? It is very far away from those who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom;

who, for that very reason, have not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion; who are unskilled in the Noble Dhamma, undisciplined in the Noble Dhamma, do not see the Noble Dhamma, have not entered upon the practice, and have practiced wrongly. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to follow closely behind me, step for step, grasping the corner of my outer robe,
yet he were covetous, with intense lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt intentions, muddled mindfulness,
lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties— then he would indeed be far away.”
“...is mine, and I am his. Why is that? Because, monks, that monk does not see the Dhamma;
not seeing the Dhamma, he does not see me.
For even if the persons mentioned above were to remain constantly in the presence of the Teacher day and night, they would not [attain it] by that alone.

“He is from the presence of the Teacher”—thus it should be said; likewise, the Teacher is also from their presence. Thus, because he is far away and remote from those who are not true men (asappurisa), he is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ). Therefore, this is said:
“Those men of inferior aspiration who do not practice rightly;”
“The Blessed One is far from those; therefore, he is considered an Arahant.
Likewise, he is an Arahant because he is “far” (*āraka*); the meaning is that he is near (*āsannabhāva*). But from what is he near?

From those who have cultivated the body, cultivated virtue, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom—it is from them, precisely because they have abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, that he is near to the Noble Dhamma.
They are experts in the noble Dhamma, well-trained in the noble Dhamma, seers of the noble Dhamma, and practitioners of the right way, because they are in close proximity to it.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to dwell a hundred yojanas away from me, yet he is one who is free from covetousness for sensual pleasures..."

"One who is not intensely lustful, whose mind is without ill will, whose intention is not corrupt, who is established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and with sense faculties restrained—he is indeed near to me, and I am near to him. For what reason?
Because, monks, that bhikkhu sees the Dhamma; seeing the Dhamma, he sees me."

For such individuals, even if they are separated from the Teacher by an interval of a hundred yojanas, they cannot be said to "wander far from the Teacher," nor can the Teacher be said to wander far from them. Thus, because he is neither distant nor near to true persons (sappurisa), he is *arahaṃ*. Therefore, this is said:
“Those who practice rightly, whose resolve is well-guided— He is neither distant nor near to them;
for that reason, the Conqueror is *arahaṃ*.”
Those evil states such as lust and the rest, which arise within a particular continuum, bring about harm both in this present life and in future lives;
they are also, in every respect, direct adversaries to the path leading to Nibbāna.
Therefore, by the virtuous who practice rightly in order to fulfill their own welfare and the welfare of others, these states must be shunned from afar.

Those things which must be surrendered and abandoned are called *rāga* (lusts). And since these were entirely abandoned and thoroughly eradicated by the Blessed One at the very foot of the Bodhi tree through the Noble Path—as it is said:
