"Brahmin, lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, hatred has been abandoned, delusion has been abandoned; all evil unwholesome states have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future."

Therefore, although it should be called *arahā* in the sense that "there are no defilements (*raha*) for him in every respect," by applying the substitution of the vowel *a* with the nasalized *ā* for the vowel *o*, it is stated as "*arahaṃ*. Regarding this, it is said:
"Evil qualities are called *raha* because they are to be abandoned by the virtuous;
because the Blessed One has utterly abandoned them, he is considered *arahaṃ*."
Those who are Arahants with taints destroyed— having fully understood all aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, and realized cessation—
and those who are trainees whose minds have not yet reached their goal but dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage,
and those individuals whose application is pure, whose disposition is noble, and who are endowed with qualities such as faith, virtue, and learning; by these [persons].
He is not to be separated from nor abandoned by those [disciples], and he is so for the Blessed One; thus he is *Arahan*.

For likewise, noble persons (*ariya-puggala*), because they have made the Dhamma of the Teacher manifest to themselves, are never separated from the Teacher’s Dhamma-body. As the Venerable Piṅgiya said:
"I see him with my mind as if with my own eye..."
Day and night, O Brahmin, being diligent,
I spend the night paying homage;
by that very act, I consider myself never separated [from him].
“Faith, rapture, mind, and mindfulness—
these do not depart from the teaching of Gotama;
in whichever direction the one of vast wisdom goes,”
“I am led by that very [teaching],” he says.
And for that very reason, they do not point to another teacher. As it is said:
“It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should point to another teacher; such a case does not exist.”
Even virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇaputhujjana) are for the most part possessed of unwavering faith in the Teacher.
Thus, because he is never separated from these distinguished persons who have practiced well, and because they are never separated from him, there are no "separators" (raha) who abandon him;
or, there is no one worthy of being abandoned by the good. Therefore, he is "Arahant. Regarding this, it is said:
“The Noble Ones who have realized the true Dhamma, whose range is pure— The Protector is not separated from them;
therefore he is considered ‘Arahant.
And *raha* is said to mean wandering; for the Blessed One, [there is no longer] the wandering through various destinies within *saṃsāra*.

There is no going by means of the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of karma, because at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, the entire cycle of karma along with its constituent factors has been utterly demolished. As it is said:
"By which [path] one is reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird..."
“Those taints by which one might go to the state of a *yakkha* or fall back into the human state—those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.
Thus, because there is no secret going for him into those destinies or rebirths, he is also called an *arahant*. Therefore, this is said:
“He for whom there is no going anywhere at all in the cycle of existence, who has abandoned birth and death—he is considered an Arahant, a Sugata.
Or, the Blessed One is an Arahant because he is worthy of praise; for etymologists explain the word *arahat* as signifying praise.
And the Blessed One’s state of being praiseworthy is well-established in the world with its devas, having been attained through qualities that are true to reality and not shared by others.
For in this way, he is peerless in unsurpassed virtue, unsurpassed concentration, unsurpassed wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation;
thus, he is unequaled, equal to the unequaled, matchless, incomparable, and without a counterpart among persons. In this manner, regarding him—
When those qualities are being analyzed and described by wise men, or even by devas, Brahmas, or the Blessed One himself, they are such that it is impossible to reach their end.
Thus, because he is praiseworthy, the Blessed One is an Arahant. Therefore, this is said:
“There is no one equal to him in qualities, Since he exists in the world together with its devas.”
"Therefore, because he is worthy of being seen, he is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ), the supreme among bipeds.
Furthermore, by way of encompassing all [qualities]:
"He is far removed from those of dull intellect, and far removed even from those who understand;"
Because of the thorough abandonment of taints (*raha*), because of the destruction of what is unworthy (*arahayya*),
and because of the absence of taints regarding states of existence (*bhava*), he is praised as the Worthy One (*Arahan*),
the Victor (*Jina*). To this extent, the meaning of the term "Arahan" has been analyzed in its entirety.
Now, having analyzed the meaning of the term *sammāsambuddho*, he says: "Sammā sāmañca," and so forth.
Therein, *sammā* means "unerringly" (*aviparītaṃ*). *Sāmaṃ* means "by himself alone"; the sense is that he is not led by another.
For here, in the word *sambuddho*, the prefix *saṃ-* should be understood as signifying the sense of "awakening" (*sayanti etassa atthassa bodhako*). [The phrase continues with] *sabbadhammānaṃ*.
Of all the phenomena that are to be known (*neyyadhamma*). But how, in this context, is the distinction "all phenomena" obtained?

Because there is no mention of a partiality. For when there is no mention of a specific portion, the fact that what is to be grasped is without remainder is understood, just as in the expression, "The initiated one does not give.
And by doing so, the word *buddha* is established for the agent alone, in view of the specific meaning.
It should be understood that this is because there is no desire for a formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*).

For here, only so much as "He is perfectly and personally awakened, therefore he is the Perfectly Awakened One" (*sammāsambuddho*) is obtained from the literal expression; however, the phrase "of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānaṃ*) has been stated by taking what is obtained through the sense.
Indeed, the act of awakening cannot logically be without an object.
Now, in order to show by analysis the scope of that [knowledge], which was stated in general terms as "all phenomena" (*sabbadhamme*), it is said:

"phenomena to be directly known" (*abhiññeyye dhamme*), and so forth. Therein, "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) means those phenomena of the Four Truths that are to be known by means of distinguished knowledge regarding their characteristics such as impermanence, and their functions and so forth.
"A Buddha because of what is to be directly known" (*abhiññeyyato buddho*) means he awakened (*bujjhi*) by virtue of the state of being that which is to be directly known.

The meaning is that he "knew" (aññāsi) by means of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) and so forth during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), by means of path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) at the moment of attainment, and subsequently by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) and so forth.
This same method applies to the subsequent [passages] as well. Regarding the phrase "phenomena to be fully understood" (*pariññeyye dhamme*):

he refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering, which is to be thoroughly known by way of impermanence and so forth. "To be abandoned" (*pahātabbe*) refers to those things belonging to the side of the origin (*samudaya*). "To be realized" (*sacchikātabbe*) he says with reference to Nibbāna.
Furthermore, the use of the plural number here is made with reference to the distinctions established by way of synonyms, such as "with residue remaining" (*sopādisesa*) and so forth;
or else, this is a mere enumeration (*uddesa*) of the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. For he will say later: "The eye is the truth of suffering," and so on.
And an enumeration is made by way of a phenomenon whose specific definition has not yet been determined. For, regarding those things being enumerated by means of an enumeration—

"Existence-merely" (atthitāmatta) is spoken of, not "delimitation"; thus it is expressed by a plural number without delimitation, as in "states without conditions" (appaccayā dhammā) or "unconditioned states" (asaṅkhatā dhammā).
Or, regarding the term "to be realized," the inclusion of both the fruits and the liberations is intended, rather than Nibbāna alone;
hence the designation in the plural is made. And likewise, in the phrase "to be developed," the inclusion of the meditative absorptions (jhānas) should also be understood.
And for this very reason, he spoke thus while establishing his own state as a Buddha to the Brahmin Sela.

But does the Blessed One establish his own status as a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) by himself? He establishes it out of great compassion, because [that status] is not within the domain of others.
In that regard, there are such passages as: "I am the one, the Perfectly Enlightened One; I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all."
These very words of the Sutta, beginning with “to be directly known” (*abhiññeyya*), are the proof for this meaning.
Therein, by the term “to be directly known,” he refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); by “to be developed” (*bhāvetabba*), he refers to the truth of the path (*maggasacca*).

Furthermore, the word “and” (*ca*) here has the sense of an inclusive conjunction of what is not explicitly stated; by it, the inclusion of that which is to be realized (*sacchikātabba*) should be understood. Alternatively, “to be directly known”...

By this very method of exclusion (*pārisesa*), he shows both the phenomena to be fully understood (*pariññeyya-dhamma*) and the phenomena to be realized (*sacchikātabba-dhamma*). Therefore, regarding "I am a Buddha":
because the Four Truths have been awakened to by me, and because there is no object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) whatsoever apart from the Truths, I am a Buddha with respect to all objects of knowledge;
the meaning is that I have directly known them all (*abbhaññāsiṃ*). However, in the *Sela Sutta Aṭṭhakathā*, this is stated as follows:

“‘To be directly known’ refers to both true knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*). ‘To be developed’ is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). ‘To be abandoned’ is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
Furthermore, because the fruit is established by the mention of its cause, their fruits—the truths of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) and suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—are also implicitly stated.
Thus, that which is ‘to be realized’ and has been ‘realized,’ and that which is ‘to be fully understood’ and has been ‘fully understood,’ are likewise included herein.”
"By demonstrating the cultivation of the Four Truths and the liberation that is the fruit of such cultivation, he establishes his state of Buddhahood through the appropriate reason:
'Having awakened to what was to be awakened to, I have become a Buddha.

In this context, "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the clear knowledge of the Path (*magga-vijjā*), expressed in its most exalted sense. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the liberation of the Fruit (*phala-vimutti*). And here, of course—

The knowledge of the path (*maggavijjā*) is also included by virtue of its being something to be developed; however, since all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), the state of being directly knowable through direct knowledge (*vijjā*) has been stated.
It should be understood that by this very method, the state of being directly knowable for all [phenomena] has likewise been stated.
It should be understood that because the status of being a cause cannot exist without its fruit, the establishment of the fruit is stated by means of the mention of the cause.
For the path is the cause [of cessation] by way of bringing about its attainment, and craving is the origin [of suffering] by way of producing it.

Thus, having stated the matter in general terms according to the Truths, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) is commenced in order to demonstrate that same matter according to the Truths by analyzing it in terms of the doors and objects, as well as the mental states occurring at the doors, such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. By way of being the root cause...
Even though other causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) exist, [craving is mentioned] because it is the fundamental cause even for those others.

For craving is the primary cause for the diversity of suffering, both because it is the cause for the variety of kamma and because it enters into the state of being its companion. "Originator" (*samuṭṭhāpikā*) means producer.
"Prior craving" (*purimataṇhā*) is craving established in a previous existence. "Of both" refers to the eye and its origin.

“Non-occurrence” (*appavatti*) means the sign of non-occurrence. “Penetrating cessation” (*nirodhappaṭivedha*) means the piercing through of cessation by way of the clear realization of actualization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).
“By drawing out each individual term” means by the extraction of each section, such as “the eye, the origin of the eye, the cessation of the eye,” and so forth.
This is because craving (*taṇhā*), too, possesses the state of being fully understood (*pariññeyya*), owing to its inclusion within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).

In order to show that craving is included within the truth of suffering because it is of the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), it is said: "The six groups of craving, beginning with craving for form.
Therefore, in the present existence, craving is the truth of suffering because it is comprised within the aggregates and because it is of the nature of the suffering of formations.
Furthermore, as the fundamental cause of whichever personal existence (*attabhāva*) it arises in, [craving is the truth of suffering].
The craving established in previous existences which gives rise [to suffering] should be understood as the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).
"Kasiṇas" refers to the jhānas having the kasiṇas as their object. "The thirty-two aspects" refers to the thirty-two parts and the jhānas having them as their objects.

"The nine existences" are: existence in the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*), existence in the fine-material sphere (*rūpabhava*), existence in the immaterial sphere (*arūpabhava*), existence with perception (*saññībhava*), existence without perception (*asaññībhava*), and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññībhava*).

There are nine types of existence (*bhava*): existence with one aggregate (*ekavokāra*), existence with four aggregates (*catuvokāra*), and existence with five aggregates (*pañcavokāra*). In this context, "existence" (*bhava*) means that which comes to be.

Existence associated with sensual desire (*kāma*), which is defined as craving for sense-pleasures, is "sensual existence" (*kāmabhava*); this refers to the eleven planes of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-bhūmi*).

Having abandoned sensual desires, existence associated with form (*rūpa*), which is defined as craving for form, is "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*); or rather, existence itself defined as form is form-existence.

The sixteen planes of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-bhūmi*). And having abandoned both desire and form, existence associated with the "formless" (i.e., craving for the formless) is "formless existence" (*arūpa-bhava*), which consists of the four planes of the formless.
Existence of those possessing perception is "perceptual existence" (*saññī-bhava*);
or, because perception exists in this existence, it is "perceptual existence. This includes the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) excluding the non-perceptual existence (*asaññī-bhava*).
The form existence (*rūpabhava*) is that which is free from the neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*), and there is also the formless existence (*arūpabhava*).

It is not the perception existence (*saññībhava*), nor is it the non-perception existence (*asaññībhava*); rather, it is a portion of the form existence. Because of the absence of grossness, it is "neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*); because of the presence of subtlety, it is "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*);
thus, the existence associated with that is the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence" (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*). Alternatively, [it is so called] because of the gross perception...

Because it is a state consisting of subtle non-existence and existence, neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called "the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*); this is a portion of the formless existence (*arūpabhava*). Because that existence is mixed with one aggregate of form, or because there is a single division (*vokāra*) within that existence, it is "single-aggregate existence" (*ekavokārabhava*); this is the non-percipient existence (*asaññībhava*). Because that existence is mixed with the four formless aggregates, or because there are four divisions within it— ... [text continues] ...it is "four-aggregate existence" (*catuvokārabhava*). Because that existence is mixed with the five aggregates, or because there are five divisions within it, it is "five-aggregate existence" (*pañcavokārabhava*); this is sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*). Because that existence is mixed with the six bases, or because there are six divisions within it, it is "six-base existence" (*saḷāyatanabhava*); this is the aforementioned threefold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the seven stations of consciousness, or because there are seven divisions within it, it is "seven-consciousness-station existence" (*sattaviññāṇaṭṭhānabhava*); this is the aforementioned fourfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the nine abodes of beings, or because there are nine divisions within it, it is "nine-abode existence" (*navasattāvāsabhava*); this is the aforementioned fivefold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the ten bases, or because there are ten divisions within it, it is "ten-base existence" (*dasāyatanabhava*); this is the aforementioned sixfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twelve bases, or because there are twelve divisions within it, it is "twelve-base existence" (*dvādasāyatanabhava*); this is the aforementioned sevenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the eighteen elements, or because there are eighteen divisions within it, it is "eighteen-element existence" (*aṭṭhārasadhātubhava*); this is the aforementioned eightfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-two faculties, or because there are twenty-two divisions within it, it is "twenty-two-faculty existence" (*bāvīsatindriyabhava*); this is the aforementioned ninefold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the three realms, or because there are three divisions within it, it is "three-realm existence" (*tirattabhava*); this is the aforementioned tenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the four nutriments, or because there are four divisions within it, it is "four-nutriment existence" (*caturāhārabhava*); this is the aforementioned elevenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the five aggregates, or because there are five divisions within it, it is "five-aggregate existence" (*pañcakkhandhabhava*); this is the aforementioned twelvefold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the six internal bases, or because there are six divisions within it, it is "six-internal-base existence" (*chaajjhattāyatanabhava*); this is the aforementioned thirteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the six external bases, or because there are six divisions within it, it is "six-external-base existence" (*cha bāhirāyatanabhava*); this is the aforementioned fourteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the seven types of craving, or because there are seven divisions within it, it is "seven-craving-type existence" (*sattataṇhākāyabhava*); this is the aforementioned fifteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the eight worldly conditions, or because there are eight divisions within it, it is "eight-worldly-condition existence" (*aṭṭhalokadhammabhava*); this is the aforementioned sixteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the nine fetters, or because there are nine divisions within it, it is "nine-fetter existence" (*navasaṃyojanabhava*); this is the aforementioned seventeenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the ten courses of wholesome action, or because there are ten divisions within it, it is "ten-wholesome-action-course existence" (*dasakusalakammapathabhava*); this is the aforementioned eighteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the eleven types of perception, or because there are eleven divisions within it, it is "eleven-perception-type existence" (*ekādasasaññākāyabhava*); this is the aforementioned nineteenfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twelve links of dependent origination, or because there are twelve divisions within it, it is "twelve-link-dependent-origination existence" (*dvādasapaccayākārabhava*); this is the aforementioned twentyfold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the thirteen types of defilement, or because there are thirteen divisions within it, it is "thirteen-defilement-type existence" (*terasakilesakāyabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-one-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the fourteen types of latent tendencies, or because there are fourteen divisions within it, it is "fourteen-latent-tendency existence" (*cuddasānusayabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-two-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the fifteen types of views, or because there are fifteen divisions within it, it is "fifteen-view-type existence" (*pañcadasadiṭṭhikāyabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-three-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the sixteen types of conceits, or because there are sixteen divisions within it, it is "sixteen-conceit-type existence" (*soḷasamānabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-four-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the seventeen types of mental states, or because there are seventeen divisions within it, it is "seventeen-mental-state existence" (*sattarasacittuppādabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-five-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the eighteen types of craving, or because there are eighteen divisions within it, it is "eighteen-craving-type existence" (*aṭṭhārasataṇhākāyabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-six-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the nineteen types of formations, or because there are nineteen divisions within it, it is "nineteen-formation-type existence" (*ekonaviṃsatikharaṇabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-seven-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty types of clinging, or because there are twenty divisions within it, it is "twenty-clinging-type existence" (*viṃsatupādānabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-eight-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-one types of ignorance, or because there are twenty-one divisions within it, it is "twenty-one-ignorance-type existence" (*ekavīsatiajānanabhava*); this is the aforementioned twenty-nine-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-two types of doubt, or because there are twenty-two divisions within it, it is "twenty-two-doubt-type existence" (*bāvīsatikaṅkhābhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-three types of delusion, or because there are twenty-three divisions within it, it is "twenty-three-delusion-type existence" (*tevīsatimohabhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-one-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-four types of agitation, or because there are twenty-four divisions within it, it is "twenty-four-agitation-type existence" (*caturvīsatibhantabhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-two-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-five types of restlessness, or because there are twenty-five divisions within it, it is "twenty-five-restlessness-type existence" (*pañcavīsatiummaggabhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-three-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-six types of unwholesome roots, or because there are twenty-six divisions within it, it is "twenty-six-unwholesome-root existence" (*chavīsatiakusalamūlabhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-four-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-seven types of wrong paths, or because there are twenty-seven divisions within it, it is "twenty-seven-wrong-path existence" (*sattavīsatiamagga-bhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-five-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-eight types of evil destinies, or because there are twenty-eight divisions within it, it is "twenty-eight-evil-destiny existence" (*aṭṭhavīsatiduggatibhava*); this is the aforementioned thirty-six-fold existence. Because that existence is mixed with the twenty-nine
"Of that existence": this refers to fourfold existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), which is exclusively immaterial existence (*arūpa-bhava*).

"Fivefold existence" (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) means an existence mixed with five aggregates, or an existence of which there are five modalities (*vokāra*); this consists of sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and a portion of fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*).
Alternatively, "modality" (*vokāra*) is a designation for the aggregates; therefore, it is an existence of which there is one modality.
The meaning here should be understood through such terms as "one-constituent existence" (*ekavokāra-bhava*) and so forth.
"The four jhānas" refers to the four fine-material-sphere jhānas (*rūpāvacara-jhāna*), without specifying their particular objects.

Alternatively, this is a reference to the resultant jhānas (*vipāka-jhāna*). And herein, craving that gives rise to [subsequent] craving should be understood as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for wholesome states; however, for functional states (*kiriyadhamma*), it is where—
Those active phenomena arise; craving is the cause of that personal existence (*attabhāva*). Regarding the term "in accordance" (*anulomato*):
here it should be applied according to this sequence: "volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are the truth of suffering, and ignorance (*avijjā*) is the truth of origin.
"Awakened in accordance" (*anubuddho*) means awakened in conformity with the phenomena that are to be awakened to. "By that" (*tena*) means because, both in general and in particular...

And because he has awakened to all phenomena by grasping each one individually, it was said. To the question "What was said?", he replied: "Because of having awakened to all phenomena correctly and personally.
The meaning is: because he himself has fully awakened to the entirety of all that is to be known (ñeyya) in every aspect, without error.
By this, [he refers to] his capacity to comprehend all phenomena in every aspect, independent of instruction from others.
The attainment of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), which is designated as unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa) because its functioning is bound to one’s wish, has been demonstrated.
But is not unobstructed knowledge different from omniscient knowledge? Otherwise, the statement that "the six unique knowledges are the Buddha-knowledges" would be contradicted.
It is not contradicted; for it is intended to show that [omniscience] is unique among others by way of the distinction in its objective domain and its mode of occurrence.

Because that single knowledge is described in two ways. For that very same knowledge is called "omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) because its object is the entirety of conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception;
and it is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) by way of its unimpeded movement due to the absence of any obscuration therein.
As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "It is omniscience because it knows all the conditioned and the unconditioned without remainder."

"In that regard, there is no obstruction; thus it is 'unobstructed knowledge' (anāvaraṇañāṇa)," and so forth. Therefore, there is no difference between them in meaning, and this must certainly be accepted as such.
Otherwise, the omniscience and the unobstructed knowledge would result in being identical and having all phenomena as their object alike.
For there is not even the slightest obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge, [and this applies] to the unobstructed knowledge.
If it were not an object for all things (*asabbadhammārammaṇa*), then wherever it does not occur, there would be no state of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇabhāva*) due to the presence of an obstruction.
Alternatively, let there be a different kind of "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) than the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);

however, in this context, it is precisely the knowledge of omniscience that is intended by the term "unobstructed knowledge," because its operation is unimpeded everywhere. And through the attainment of that—
The Blessed One is called the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, and the Perfectly Enlightened One not merely because of his awakening to all phenomena at once.

Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "This designation 'Buddha' is a realization-based appellation pertaining to the final liberation of the Blessed Buddhas, co-arising with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree. This is due to the acquisition of the knowledge capable of awakening to all phenomena.
For indeed, there was in the Blessed One’s continuum the capacity to penetrate all phenomena without exception.
Here it may be asked: when this knowledge arises, does it proceed toward its entire object all at once, or rather successively? What is the point here?
If, first of all, it proceeds toward the entire object all at once, [then consider] those things divided by distinctions such as past, future, present, internal, external, and so forth...
If conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) and the conventionally designated unconditioned phenomena (*asaṅkhata-sammuti-dhammā*) were to appear together as one,

there would be no distinct comprehension of them, like someone looking at a cloth from a distance; if that were the case, then for those practicing insight (*vipassanā*) with the thought "all phenomena are non-self," all phenomena would be objects of the Blessed One’s knowledge in an undifferentiated form, just as they appear under the aspect of non-self.

[They] fall into [the error] that [the Buddha] possesses [such knowledge]. As for those who say: "The Buddhas' knowledge operates at all times regarding the characteristic of stability (ṭhitalakkhaṇa) of all knowable phenomena, being free from conceptual construction; it is because of this that they are called 'all-knowers.
And having accepted this, the statement, 'The Naga is concentrated while walking, and he is concentrated while standing,' is also well-spoken"—for them too, the aforementioned faults apply.

Because it has the characteristic of being established as its object, and because past and future conventional phenomena lack that [present] existence, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have only a partial range;
therefore, it is not tenable to say that knowledge occurs all at once.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that knowledge occurs sequentially across the entire range of objects, even this is not tenable. For [knowledge does not arise] by way of genus, plane, nature, and so forth...

And when the objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*), which are divided into many categories according to direction, place, time, and so forth, are grasped in succession, it is possible to comprehend them without remainder, because the objects of knowledge are boundless.
However, as for those who say: "The Blessed One is omniscient because he does not deceive regarding the meaning;
having made one portion of the objects of knowledge directly perceived, he resolves that it is likewise in the remainder, and establishes this through such determination."
And that knowledge is not inferential knowledge because it is free from doubt. For they say, "In the world, inferential knowledge is bound up with doubt," but even for them, that is not correct.

For if everything were beyond direct perception, it would be impossible to determine anything else by resolving that "it is so" based on having made one part of the knowable object directly perceived through non-deception regarding its meaning.
For that which remains is not directly perceived (*appaccakkha*).
If even that were directly perceived, would its status as "the remainder" not cease to exist? All of this is irrelevant. Why?
Because it concerns an investigation into what is not an object [of such perception]. For this was said by the Blessed One: "The domain of the Buddhas, monks, is inconceivable."
"It should not be thought about; whoever should think about it would partake of madness and frustration. This, however, is the definitive conclusion here:

whatever the Blessed One desires to know—whether in its entirety or in part—his knowledge proceeds directly with unimpeded functioning in each instance, and his concentration is constant due to the absence of distraction. And of that which he desires to know...
If it were not the object of all [knowledges], its functioning would not be dependent upon his will; for this must necessarily be accepted, based on the statement:
"All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, dependent upon the will, dependent upon the attention, and dependent upon the arising of consciousness of the Blessed Buddha.
Furthermore, even regarding objects past and future, the Blessed One’s knowledge is indeed direct perception (*paccakkha*), because it is devoid of inference, scripture, or conceptual reasoning.

But surely, even in this position, when one wishes to know everything, then the Blessed One’s knowledge would have to proceed all at once toward its entire object in an undifferentiated form; thus, does it not still fail to avoid the aforementioned fault?

No, because that has been cleared away. For that domain of the Buddha has been established as inconceivable. Otherwise, by having a mode of operation identical to the knowledge of ordinary people, [the Buddha's knowledge] would be limited.
The inconceivability of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas would not exist;

therefore, although that knowledge has all phenomena as its object, it proceeds by making those phenomena well-defined as if they were the object of a single phenomenon—this is what is inconceivable here:
"As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable."
"Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit.

Thus, because he has perfectly and personally awakened to all phenomena—whether collectively, individually, simultaneously, or sequentially, according to his wish—he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha).

Regarding the term *vijjā*: here, it is called *vijjā* because one finds (*vindati*) what is to be found (*vindiya*); the meaning is that it is apprehended exactly as it is. Or else, [it refers to] one's own...
*Vijjā* (clear vision) is so called in the sense of piercing the opposite [of ignorance]; the meaning is that it shatters the mass of darkness and so forth.
For that very reason, it is also *vijjā* in the sense of making its own object known. *Sampannattā* means because of being endowed with or because of being fulfilled;
the meaning is "without deficiency. *Tatra* refers to the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Regarding the phrase *manomayiddhiyā*, here: "In this case, a bhikkhu..."

The supernormal power (iddhi) described by the method beginning, "From this body he creates another body, material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, not lacking any faculties," is called *manomayiddhi* (mind-made power) because it proceeds by way of creating a mind-made body produced by means of jhāna within one's own physical body.
The six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) [begin] with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*).

Together with these are the five supernormal powers (abhiññā), beginning with the power of psychic transformation (iddhividha). It should be understood that the mention of three and eight types of clear knowledge (vijjā) in various suttas is done according to the inclinations of those to be trained (veneyya).

The seven true qualities (saddhamma) are faith (saddhā), moral shame (hirī), moral dread (ottappa), erudition (bāhusacca), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā). With reference to these, it was said: "Here, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith..."
“He is virtuous, possessed of shame, possessed of fear of wrongdoing, learned, energetic, established in mindfulness, and wise.
Regarding the phrase “the four jhānas,” this refers to whatever four fine-material-sphere jhānas there may be.
Anticipating the objection as to why only these fifteen factors—beginning with virtue—are called “conduct” (*caraṇa*) here, he says: “These very [factors]...”
“Hī” and so forth. By this, he states that these [three trainings], being comprised within the three trainings, are the definitive means for attaining Nibbāna.

Now, showing the scripture (āgama) that establishes this meaning, he says “As it has been said,” and so forth. The passage beginning with “The Blessed One,” etc., is stated by way of a conclusion to the very same point already explained.
[Objection: But is not this perfection of true knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampadā) also found among the disciples (sāvaka)? [Reply: Even though that is so...
To show that it is not attained in the same way as it was by the Blessed One, the passage beginning with “therein, the perfection of true knowledge (vijjāsampadā)” was stated.

Because the state of omniscience is established through the true knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayavijjā), he said: “The Blessed One’s perfection of true knowledge stands having fulfilled omniscience.
Since the sublime abiding of compassion (karuṇābrahmavihāra) is included within the four meditative absorptions (jhāna) and is thus comprised within the factors of conduct (caraṇadhamma)...
Since this unique quality is found in the Blessed One by way of his attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), according to what is appropriate, it is said:
"The perfection of conduct stands having fulfilled the state of being a Greatly Compassionate One.

Just as the guidance of beings toward their welfare while avoiding what is harmful does not occur without wisdom, so too the Teacher’s knowledge of what is beneficial and what is harmful for them arises through compassion.
Since neither exists without the other, both would each perform their respective functions in both cases.
However, in order to show which one holds the primary status in each instance, it was said: "He [does so] for the sake of omniscience," and so forth.

Just as in the phrase "one endowed with true knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*), the particle *taṃ* is merely a grammatical filler; the meaning is: "just as another person endowed with true knowledge and conduct would direct, so does he."
This shows that this practice is unique to one who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*).

Furthermore, in order to show that this perfection of true knowledge and conduct in the Teacher is the absolute cause for the disciples' right practice through the liberating nature of the Dispensation, it was said:

"Therefore, for him... and so forth. Therein, by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "those who torment themselves, etc.," those who torment others and those who torment both are included. The rest is easy to understand.

And herein, by the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*), the greatness of the Teacher’s wisdom (*paññā*) is revealed; by the perfection of conduct (*caraṇa*), the greatness of his compassion (*karuṇā*) is revealed.
Of these two, through wisdom the Blessed One attained sovereignty over the Dhamma, and through compassion he shared that Dhamma with others.

Through wisdom there is revulsion toward the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and through compassion there is the endurance of the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Through wisdom there is full understanding of the suffering of others, and through compassion there is the undertaking of efforts to remedy the suffering of others.
Through wisdom there is the state of being oriented toward final Nibbāna; through compassion, the attainment thereof. Through wisdom there is one’s own crossing over;
through compassion, the crossing over of others. Through wisdom there is the accomplishment of the state of a Buddha; through compassion, the accomplishment of the Buddha-activity.
Or else, through compassion there is the state of being oriented toward saṃsāra while on the stage of a Bodhisattva; through wisdom, a lack of delight therein; likewise through compassion.
Not causing harm to others, and by means of wisdom, not fearing others oneself. Protecting another through compassion, one protects oneself;
protecting oneself through wisdom, one protects another. Thus, through compassion one does not torment others, and through wisdom one does not torment oneself.
Therefore, among the four types of persons—those practicing for their own welfare and so forth—one becomes the fourth type of person.

He is perfected. Likewise, through compassion he is a lord of the world, and through wisdom he is a lord of himself. Through compassion he possesses the quality of being inclined [toward others], and through wisdom he possesses the quality of not being uplifted [by worldly things].
Similarly, through compassion he generates assistance for all beings, yet because it is accompanied by wisdom, his mind is not dispassionate toward anything;
through wisdom he is dispassionate toward all phenomena, yet because it is accompanied by compassion, [he does not abandon them].

And it is not that it does not proceed for the benefit of all beings. For just as the Blessed One’s compassion is devoid of affection and sorrow, so too his wisdom is free from the notions of "I" and "mine";
thus, these mutually purified and supremely pure distinguished qualities should be understood as being manifested through the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampad*).
Now, in order to show the meaning of the term *sugata*, he said, “Because of his beautiful gait,” and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with “whether walking or standing,” since even the act of going is called “gone,” he said, “for the act of going is indeed called ‘gone. *Sobhana* means *subha*;
its state of being beautiful (*subhabhāva*) consists in purity, and purity consists in the removal of faults. Therefore, he said, “perfectly pure and blameless.”
Since there are many kinds of "going," the author says "the Noble Path" to show the specific kind of going intended here.
For that [Path] is called "going" because it is the reaching or the attainment of Nibbāna.
Now, to show the reason for that very going, he says "for by that... and so forth. "The secure place" refers to Nibbāna. "Without clinging" means...
Because there was an absence of obstacles, he did not cling—that is, he did not form attachments—even when proceeding toward a happy destination, much less in other circumstances.
Alternatively, having sat upon a single seat, by means of swift direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*), he attained all four paths;
thus he "went" without clinging or being obstructed. This going, while he was going, brought about the purpose of all going, and it was the supreme of all.

It brings about prosperity; that alone is what is called "beautiful" (*sobhana*). And because the Blessed One has gone by means of that, it is said: "Thus, by virtue of his beautiful going, he is the Sugata.
This is done by taking the word *su* to have the sense of "beautiful.
Because of the absence of unpleasant sufferings and the occurrences of conditioned formations, it is absolutely beautiful due to its state of ultimate bliss.
He said, "This is the unconditioned element," meaning, "He has gone to that beautiful place, the deathless Nibbāna.
Therefore the Blessed One said, "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. "Samma" means "well. Well-going, moreover, is the going of one who is not overcome by opposites;
thus he said, "not returning again to the defilements already abandoned," by way of the non-recurrence of those defilements once they have been abandoned.
"Not returning. Having shown the scriptural authority for this very meaning and elucidating it, he said, "And this has been stated," and so forth.
"This" refers to the non-returning of defilements abandoned by each respective path; and this is the culmination of right progress (*sammāgamana*).
That path of practice by which this is accomplished is also indeed right progress. Thus, the Blessed One [has spoken].

To show that he is a "Sugata," it is said, "He has come rightly," and so forth. "By means of right practice" means by means of the unerring practice that leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

By the phrase "bringing about only the welfare and happiness of the entire world," he shows that the path to great enlightenment proceeds precisely as a source of welfare and happiness for all beings at all times, without distinction.
By the phrase "going without falling into these extremes—eternalism and annihilationism"—he shows the course of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
By the phrase "going without falling into these—sensual pleasure and self-mortification"—he shows the course of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

In that context, the locative case is used in the sense of speaking appropriately to one who is appropriate for the place; it is a locative used in the sense of what is to be accomplished or achieved. "It was not" (*abhūtaṃ*)...
It is what is untrue. For the truth or untruth of speech is determined by way of its meaning. "Atacca" is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Anatthasaṃhitaṃ" means connected with harm, whether pertaining to the present life or the future life;
it brings about harm. "Anattha" means not-benefit; it is the opposite of benefit and its absence. That which is connected with this is "anatthasaṃhita," namely, malicious speech.
The meaning is "frivolous chatter. In this way, the inclusion of all fourfold types of verbal misconduct should be understood here.
Furthermore, the first type of speech should be seen as applying to one who speaks of a virtuous person as "immoral," or of one who is not a caṇḍāla and so forth as a "caṇḍāla" and so forth.
The second type applies to one who addresses an immoral person as "immoral," or a caṇḍāla and so forth as a "caṇḍāla" and so forth, without restraint.
Of that which appears. The third is the discourse that elucidates the state of being a denizen of hell and so forth for one who is a denizen of hell and so forth, such as:
“Devadatta is destined for ruin; he is a denizen of hell,” and so on. The fourth is the discourse that deludes the world, such as:

“The performance of killing and other acts according to the sacrificial rites prescribed in the Vedas brings about a happy rebirth. The fifth is the discourse involving the instigation of malicious talebearing toward a living being.
The sixth [meaning] should be understood as discourse on giving, virtue, and so forth, occurring in a suitable context. Thus, because he speaks rightly (*sammā gadatto*):

having avoided what was previously mentioned, such as the unreal and so forth, and because he speaks what is real, true, beneficial, pleasant, and agreeable—and for that very reason speaks rightly and well—he is the "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*).
For even if something is unpleasant to someone, it does not become so to the Blessed One by the mere fact of entering his range of perception.
His speech is indeed pleasant and agreeable because it brings about the accomplishment of welfare and confers benefit and happiness upon the world.
In this context, however, it should be understood that the term "Sugata" is spoken by changing the letter *da* to the letter *ta*.
Another method: he whose going—his movement—is beautiful is the Sugata. For the Blessed One’s approach to those who are to be trained...
It is beautiful and auspicious because it exclusively accomplishes their welfare and happiness.

Likewise, due to his physical body being adorned with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), his bodily movement and his movement of knowledge—free from the defects of haste, slowness, stumbling, dragging, pressing down, contraction, crookedness, and confusion—are like the gait of a graceful royal swan, a bull, an elephant, or a lion king;
and through his resolve, they are endowed with the excellence of qualities such as vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, and energy.
It is indeed beautiful because it leads to great enlightenment, to blamelessness, and to the welfare and happiness of beings.

Alternatively, he is the "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*) because, through his self-born knowledge, he has fully understood the entire world by means of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*), and thus has rightly gone and understood it.
Likewise, he is the Well-Gone One because, by means of the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), he has abandoned the origin of the world and brought it to a state of non-arising.
He has gone beyond, thus he is the Sugata. He has rightly gone to and attained the cessation of the world, which is Nibbāna, by way of the clear realization through direct experience;
thus he is the Sugata. He has rightly gone upon and entered the path leading to the cessation of the world by way of the clear realization through cultivation;
thus he is the Sugata. Likewise, whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, or attained in this world with its devas...
That which was sought, known, and investigated by the mind—all that has come to be perfectly evident to him through direct realization, like an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of the hand;
thus he is the Sugata. Now, in order to clarify the meaning of the term "Lokavidū" (Knower of the World), he said: "Because the world is known in every way," and so forth. Therein:

"In every way" (*sabbathā*) means in every manner; the meaning is: in whatever manner each world is to be known, in that very manner. To demonstrate those modes, it was said, "by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*), and so forth.
Therein, "by way of intrinsic nature" means by way of the intrinsic nature of suffering (*dukkhasabhāva*).
For the entire world has the intrinsic nature of suffering. As it is said: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering."

"From its origin" means from that [source] from which it arises, namely, from craving and so forth. "From its cessation" means from that [state] wherein it ceases, namely, from the state beyond formations (*visaṅkhāra*).
"From the means to its cessation" means from that noble path by which that cessation is to be attained, because there is no other way besides this.
Thus, having stated "he knew the world in every respect," [the author] provides the following to establish that meaning:
Showing this sutta, he said, “Friend, where indeed...,” and so forth.

And this sutta was spoken by the Blessed One when he was asked by the deva-son Rohitassa, with reference to the destination of the world of space: “Venerable sir, where, venerable sir, one is not born... [as in the full passage] ...does not undergo rebirth; is it possible, venerable sir, by going to know, or to see, or to reach the end of the world?”
The Blessed One spoke. Therein, by the words beginning with "is not born," he directly negates birth and the other [stages];
then, by the two phrases "does not pass away" and "does not reappear," he negates successive death and rebirth. However, some say:
"The passage beginning with 'is not born' refers to those born from a womb and so forth, while the other refers to those of spontaneous birth (opapātika). That...
It is devoid of birth and so forth. "By going" means by going on foot. "The end of the world" refers to Nibbāna, which is the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"To be known" means it is to be understood. "To be seen" means it is to be beheld. "To be attained" means it is to be reached. Alternatively, there is the reading:
"This has been known, this has been seen, this has been attained. In that case, by going, the end of the world has been known; this [end] has been seen.
The meaning of "I do not say that this one has reached" is as follows: "this one" refers to the seeker of Nibbāna.
Granted, it is impossible to go, know, see, or reach the end of the world by traveling on foot;
nevertheless, showing that he points out and reveals it within a limited and defined place, he says "but yet," and so forth. In that regard:
"In a body the size of a fathom" means in a personal existence measuring one fathom. By this, he shows the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

"In that which possesses perception" means accompanied by perception. By this, under the heading of perception, he shows the other three aggregates—feeling and so forth—precisely because they are accompanied by perception.
"In that which has mind" means in that which has consciousness. By this, he shows the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*); however, in that which lacks consciousness...
The intention is that it is not possible to define [Nibbāna] as merely a collection of material phenomena arising from a cause.
"The world" (loka) refers to the world of the aggregates and so forth. "The cessation of the world" (lokanirodha) is either the ceasing of that world, or indeed Nibbāna itself;
for even Nibbāna is defined within the body alone, since it is defined in dependence upon the aggregates. Even though it has no location, it is [defined] by way of those whose cessation it is.
It is also described by way of proximity, as it is said: "The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
"By going" means by ordinary going. "The end of the world" means the end of the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka), that which serves as the cause for the making of an end.

Nirvana. "At any time" (*kudācana*) means even at some time. "Without reaching" (*appatvā*) means without having attained by means of the supreme path. "Liberation" (*pamocana*) means release or escape.
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because there is no liberation from the suffering of the round of existence without reaching the end of the world; therefore. "Hava" is a mere particle.
"Knower of the world" (*lokavidū*) means one who understands the entire world through its intrinsic nature and so forth. "Sumedha" means one of beautiful wisdom.

One who has gone to the end of the world: having understood the world through the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*), one has gone to the end of the world through the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*).
Because the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Path has been brought to completion, one is "one who has lived the holy life" (*vusitabrahmacariya*).

Because all defilements have been stilled, or because the Dhamma of the Four Truths has been realized, one is "one who has attained peace" (*samitāvī*). "He does not wish" means he does not aspire; as he does not aspire for this world, so too for the other world.
He does not seek a world, because he is without rebirth.

Thus, although the knowledge of the world has been shown in its entirety by way of its intrinsic nature and so forth, since the world was only mentioned partially, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, there are three worlds" was stated in order to show it without remainder. Therein, for those bound by the sense-faculties...

The world of beings (*sattaloka*) is the collection and the continuum of the aggregates (*khandha*). It is called "being" (*satta*) because it is attached to and bound by form and the other [aggregates].

It is called "world" (*loka*) because herein wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] and their result are perceived (*lokīyati*). The world of space (*okāsaloka*) is the collection and the continuum of form and so forth that are not bound to the sense faculties;
it is so called because mobile and stationary beings are perceived therein, and because it serves as the locus for them. This is due to its being the support for those [beings].

This is also called the "receptacle world" (*bhājanaloka*). Both types of aggregates are the "world of formations" (*saṅkhāraloka*) because they are formed by conditions, and they break up, fall apart, and disintegrate.
"Sustained by nutriment" (*āhāraṭṭhitika*) means sustained by conditions; the meaning is that their existence is dependent upon conditions.
Here, the word "nutriment" (*āhāra*) has the sense of "condition," as in such passages as: "This nutriment leads to the arising of unarisen sensual desire."

Thus, by the phrase "all beings," even non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) are included. Now, this state of being sustained by nutriment is, in the ultimate sense, a conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhāradhamma), not a phenomenon pertaining to a sentient being (sattadhamma).

Therefore, he said: "In the places where it is stated 'sustained by nutriment,' it should be understood as the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). If that is so, how is it that [the text] says "all beings"?
This is not a fault, for it is a teaching based on the designation of a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna-desanā). Why?
But as for the Blessed One, does he teach the Dhamma by taking a person as the basis in some instances, and teach the Dhamma by taking the Dhamma itself as the basis in others?
It is due to his skill in teaching and the inclinations of those to be trained.
For the Blessed Buddhas have attained such skill in teaching that, according to their preference, they may in some instances take a person as the basis and in others take the Dhamma as the basis.

They teach the Dhamma having made [the distinction]. Furthermore, for those who are to be trained (*veneyya*) and have not yet entered the sequence of the Dispensation (*sāsana-kkama*), they give a teaching based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

For those who have entered it, they give a teaching based on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). A teaching based on the person has conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*) as its domain; the other has ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) as its domain.
The former is conducive to compassion (*karuṇā*); the latter is conducive to wisdom (*paññā*). [This applies] to those of the lineage of the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī-gotta*).
Or else, the former [discourses] are based on individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), for they take persons as their measure;

the latter are based on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), belonging to those of the lineage of followers by Dhamma (*dhammānusārīgotta*). Alternatively, due to the predominance of faith (*saddhācaritatā*), they are based on individuals by way of those who have mastery over the world;

due to the predominance of wisdom (*paññācaritatā*), they are based on the Dhamma by way of those who have mastery over the Dhamma. Furthermore, the former are of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), while the latter are of definitive meaning (*nītattha*). Thus, the Blessed One [taught] each respective distinction.
It should be understood that he teaches there a twofold teaching by taking those respective points into account.

For the speculative theorists, the conceptualization of "self and world" by way of eternalism and so forth generally concerns the realm of sentient beings (*satta*), not the realm of formations (*saṅkhāra*);
thus he says: "In the passages where it is said 'the world is eternal' or 'the world is non-eternal,' [it refers to] the world of sentient beings."
"It should be understood. "As far as the moon and sun revolve" means in whatever extent of space the moon and sun turn and circulate.
"The quarters shine, radiant" means that by their very circulation, those respective quarters become luminous and shine forth.
Alternatively, *disā* is the accusative plural; therefore, it refers to the moon and sun themselves shining.
"However many directions there are that shine, beautify, and illuminate"—this is the meaning.
"A world-system of a thousandfold extent" means a spatial world consisting of a thousand such units in measure; the meaning is "a thousandfold world-system.
Alternatively, the reading is *tāvasahassavā*, which means "possessing a thousand of that extent. "Therein" refers to the world designated as a thousandfold world-system.
"Tampī" means the threefold world. "Sabbathā avedī" means he penetrated it in every way.
To explain how he penetrated it, he says, "For thus," and so forth. The phrase "tathā hissa" is connected with "sabbathā vidito.
"Assa" refers to this Blessed One. "One world: all beings subsist by nutriment"—this is according to that discourse which is expressed in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
It is stated that all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) exist in dependence upon conditions; by this, the entire world of formations is of a single kind, because there is no other mode of existence.
The meaning in such passages as "two worlds" and so forth should also be understood according to this same method.

Furthermore, in this context, *nibbāna* is not included under the term "name" (*nāma*), because its intrinsic nature is not that of light. But is it not said [elsewhere] that "it is sustained by nutriment"? [End of fragment]
Does it follow that even the states of the Path and its Fruits (maggaphala-dhammā) possess the quality of being "worldly" (lokatā) because they exist in dependence on conditions? It does not follow;
for here, the term "the world" (loka) is intended to refer to those phenomena belonging to the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) which are to be fully understood (pariññeyya).

Alternatively, since "the world" is defined as that which is taken up and which, once grasped, does not remain as it is—neither decaying nor perishing—there is no quality of being "worldly" for the supramundane (lokuttara) states, which are devoid of such grasping.
"Three feelings" refers to pleasure, pain, and equanimity. "Four nutriments" refers to the four nutriments:

edible food, contact as nutriment, mental volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment. Among these, edible food is called a nutriment because it nourishes the material form consisting of the eightfold nutrient essence (*ojā-aṭṭhamaka-rūpa*).
Contact is called a nutriment because it nourishes the three feelings. Mental volition [is a nutriment] with respect to the three realms of existence...

It is called nutriment (*āhāra*) because it brings about rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Consciousness is called nutriment because at the moment of rebirth-linking it brings about name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The aggregates that serve as the objective support for the clingings are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*). The six internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) are those beginning with the eye-base and ending with the mind-base.

The seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) are: those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; those with diverse bodies and uniform perceptions; those with uniform bodies... [and so forth].

Those with diverse perceptions and a single body who have a single perception, and the three lower formless attainments—these seven are called "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) because "consciousness stands there.
In this context, they are "those with diverse bodies" (*nānattakāyā*) because diversity is their body, or because their body is diverse;
they are "those with diverse perceptions" (*nānattasaññino*) because they possess diverse perceptions. By this same method...
The meaning should be understood in the remaining sections as well.

All human beings and the gods of the six sense-sphere realms (*kāmāvacara*), along with certain beings in the states of deprivation (*vinipātika*), are called "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions.
For, within the immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there are immeasurable humans who differ in terms of complexion, shape, and so forth.

Even twins are not exactly alike. Even those who are twins—whether by complexion or by physical form—are nonetheless distinguished by their ways of looking forward and looking around, by their speech, laughter, walking, standing, and so forth.
Furthermore, their rebirth-consciousness may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless; therefore, all human beings possess diversity of body (*nānattakāya*).
Those with diverse perceptions: among the gods of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), the bodies of some are blue, while those of others are yellow or other colors;
and their rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-saññā*) may be either two-rooted or three-rooted. Therefore, they too are "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions.

Furthermore, certain beings in the states of misery (*vinipātika*) who are excluded from the four lower realms—such as the female spirits (*yakkhinī*) Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, and Dhammaguttā—[are also included].

These and others should be understood in this way. For their bodies differ according to whether they have white, black, mottled, or golden-brown skin, and according to whether they are emaciated, stout, short, or tall;
and like humans, their rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-saññā) varies according to whether it is triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless.
However, unlike those gods, they are not of great power; like wretched humans, they are of little power and find food and clothing difficult to obtain.
They dwell oppressed by suffering; some are afflicted during the dark fortnight and become happy during the bright fortnight.

Therefore, because they have fallen from a high state of happiness, it is said that they are "fallen" (*vinipātika*) since they possess a fall from that high state of happiness, even though they possess the status of a deva due to the absence of divine success (*dibbasampatti*).
Furthermore, for those among them who possess three roots (*tihetuka*), there is also the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*).
It happened thus: At the time of dawn, the yakkhinī Piyaṅkaramātā, having heard the Elder Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma, said:
"Make no sound, Piyaṅkara! The bhikkhu is reciting verses of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, having understood a verse of the Dhamma, let us practice so that it may be for our welfare."
“Let us restrain ourselves from taking life; let us not speak falsehood knowingly.
Let us train ourselves in our own good conduct, so that we may even be released from the womb of a *pisāca*.
Having thus exhorted her son, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) on that very day. But as for Uttara’s mother, [she approached] the Blessed One...

Having heard the Dhamma, they became stream-enterers. Thus, these too, due to the diversity of their bodies and the diversity of their rebirth-consciousnesses, are reckoned as "diverse in body and diverse in perception.
However, those known as the Retinue of Brahmā, the Ministers of Brahmā, and the Great Brahmās—[who are distinguished] by the division into inferior, middling, and superior...
Those beings born through the first jhāna— the Brahmakāyika devas and the beings in the four lower realms—
are called "diverse in body and uniform in perception. Among these, the bodies of the Brahmapurohita devas are larger in measure than those of the Brahmapārisajja devas,
and the bodies of the Mahābrahmās are even larger in measure than those of the Brahmapurohitas.
Granted that their bodies are increasingly more sublime than those below them by virtue of their radiance, that factor is not the defining criterion here.
For even though there is a degree of radiance in the bodies of the Parittābhas and the Parittasubhas, they are defined solely on the basis of unity;
thus, they are called "of uniform body" (*ekattakāya*). In this way, these are the Brahmakāyikas.
However, because of the diversity of bodies and the unity of the perception at rebirth-linking due to the result of the first jhāna, they are "those with diverse bodies and a single perception.
And as they are, so too are the beings in the four states of misery.
For in the hells, the personal existence (attabhāva) of some is a quarter-league, of some half a league, and of some a full league; but that of Devadatta was a hundred leagues long.
They are born [there]. Among the animals, some are small and some are large; in the realm of the *petas* (hungry ghosts), some are sixty cubits tall and some are eighty cubits tall;
some are beautiful and some are ugly, as are the *kālakañjika* asuras. Furthermore, among them, those known as the long-backed *petas* can even be sixty *yojanas* in height;
however, the perception at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is the same for all of them.
They are exclusively unwholesome-resultant and rootless. Thus, even those belonging to the states of deprivation are reckoned as "diverse in body and uniform in perception.
However, those belonging to the plane of the second jhāna—the Parittābhas, Appamāṇābhas, and Ābhassarās—are called "uniform in body and diverse in perception.
For the bodies of all these beings are of one and the same measure; it is only their rebirth-perception that is diverse, owing to the resultants of the second and third jhānas.
The Parittasubhas, Appamāṇasubhas, and Subhakiṇhas, however, belong to the plane of the third jhāna; they are uniform in body and uniform in perception.
According to the method already stated, this is because of the uniformity of both the body and the rebirth-linking perception due to the fruition of the fourth jhāna.
The Vehapphalas also belong to this same fourth station of consciousness, because of the uniformity of both the body and the perception due to the fruition of the fifth jhāna.

And because the perception of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-saññā) is of a single nature. However, the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) belong to the side of turning away from existence (vivaṭṭa-pakkha) due to their non-returning;
they are not present at all times. They do not arise even for a hundred thousand eons or an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) eon when the world is empty of Buddhas;
they arise only within the interval of sixteen thousand eons while Buddhas are actually appearing, specifically during the period of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakkappavatti).
“They are like the encampment of the Blessed One’s army; therefore, they do not partake of a station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) nor of an abode of beings (*sattāvāsa*),” they say.

However, the Elder Mahāsīva [cited] this: “Indeed, Sāriputta, such an abode is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas. By this—
By means of the Sutta, it is stated that “the Suddhāvāsa deities also belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings”;

because this cannot be contradicted by the Sutta, it is accepted. Therefore, excluding the non-percipient beings, beings in the nine planes beginning with the Parittasubha and ending with the Akaniṭṭha should be understood as “having a single form and a single perception.”
However, non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) do not fall within this classification because of the absence of consciousness.

For instance, when a Buddha has not yet appeared, those who have gone forth in a heretical order perform preliminary work on the wind-kasiṇa, attain the fourth jhāna, and upon emerging from it, think:
"Shame on the mind! Shame on the mind! The mere absence of mind is indeed better. For, depending on the mind..."
Having developed a conviction and preference, thinking, "Suffering arises conditioned by killing, binding, and so forth;

it would not exist if the mind did not exist," they pass away without falling away from jhāna and are reborn in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-bhava*) by way of a material rebirth-linking (*rūpa-patisandhi*).
Whichever posture was adopted by each person in the human world, they are reborn in that same posture for five hundred eons.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, consciousness does not arise there for them by way of the development of dispassion toward the mind;

thus, due to the absence of consciousness, they do not partake in the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*). However, because the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) is as subtle in its perception as it is in its consciousness, it is not included among the stations of consciousness.
For just as with perception, because consciousness has reached a state of extreme subtlety due to the remaining residual formations, it lacks the manifest function of consciousness;

thus, it is neither consciousness nor entirely non-consciousness. Therefore, it is "neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness" (*neva-viññāṇā-nāviññāṇā*), and for this reason, it is not included among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) which possess the function of clear consciousness.
Consequently, the six classes of sense-sphere devas, together with those in the states of deprivation, [are excluded].
These are: humans with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; beings of the plane of the first jhāna and those in the woeful states with diverse bodies and uniform perceptions;
beings of the plane of the second jhāna with uniform bodies and diverse perceptions;
and—excluding the non-percipient beings—beings of the plane of the third jhāna and those of the plane of the fourth jhāna, who have uniform bodies and uniform perceptions. These are they.

The four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo), excluding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) and including the three lower immaterial bases beginning with the base of infinite space, should be understood as the "seven stations of consciousness.
The eight worldly conditions (aṭṭha lokadhammā) are these eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
They are called "worldly phenomena" (*lokadhammā*) because they belong to the world. For these are phenomena that inevitably occur within the world of sentient beings;
therefore, there is no sentient being whatsoever who is entirely free from them. Indeed, these sometimes pursue the world from one instance to another, and sometimes the world pursues them.
And this has been said: "Monks, these eight worldly phenomena revolve around the world."
“And the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions. Here, “gain” (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of food, clothing, and so forth, or the very fact that these are obtained.
The absence of these is “loss” (*alābha*). By the mention of “gain,” attachment toward its object is implied; by the mention of “loss,” aversion is implied.
In the same way, it should be understood that for “fame” (*yasa*) and the others as well, the inclusion of attachment and aversion toward their respective objects is intended.
But when gain has arrived, loss has indeed already arrived; thus both gain and loss are mentioned.

The same principle applies to fame and the rest as well. And likewise, just as pus exists when there is blood by way of its corruption, so too when there is attachment to gain and the rest, aversion toward loss and the rest finds its opportunity.
The "nine abodes of beings" (*nava sattāvāsā*) refers to the seven stations of consciousness mentioned above, together with the non-percipient beings and the fourth formless realm.
They are called "abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*) because beings dwell within them;

they are categories of beings distinguished by such features as diversity of body and diversity of perception. Indeed, those categories of beings [are so called] because of the very fact that the beings included therein are comprised within them.
They deserve to be called a "basis" (ādhāra) by virtue of being the basis for a collection, just as one says, "the branch is on the tree.
The reason why the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) are also included in the enumeration of the "abodes of beings" has already been explained above.

Regarding the phrase "ten bases" (dasāyatanāni): this refers to all bases except for the mind-base (manāyatana), which is immaterial by nature, and the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana), which is a mixture of material and immaterial factors.
The ten bases—the five beginning with the eye-base and the five beginning with the visible-object-base—are spoken of solely by way of material phenomena.
However, when these same [ten] are together with the mind-base and the mental-object-base, they are spoken of as the "twelve bases.

But why are the eye and the others here called "bases" (*āyatana*)? Because of their being a place of arrival (*āyatanato*), or because of the stretching out (*tananato*) of what has arrived (*āyatassa*).

And they are bases (*āyatana*) by way of leading forth (*nayanato*). For, in the case of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, the states of consciousness and mental factors—by means of their respective functions such as experiencing—lead forth (*āyanti*), arise, strive, and exert themselves toward those various doors and objects.

Furthermore, these [bases] stretch out (*tanonti*) and expand those states that have become the "leadings" (*āya*). And this [process] has proceeded throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
They are called "bases" (*āyatanāni*) because they lead and cause one to proceed through the long suffering of *saṃsāra* as long as it does not cease.
Furthermore, they are bases in the sense of being a dwelling place, a source, a meeting point, a region of birth, and a cause.
For instance, in common usage, in expressions such as "the abode of Īśvara" or "the abode of Vāsudeva," the term refers to a dwelling place.
It is called an *āyatana*. In such expressions as "the gold mine (*suvaṇṇāyatana*)" or "the silver mine (*rajatāyatana*"), it means a source.

In the Teaching (*sāsana*), however, in such passages as "In delightful *āyatana*s, birds frequent them," it means a place of assembly. In such passages as "The southern region (*dakkhiṇāpatho*) is the *āyatana* of cattle," it means a place of origin.
In such passages as "He attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is a corresponding *āyatana*," it means a cause.
