It is called an "āyatana" (base). Because those various mental states and mental factors dwell within the eye and the other [senses] due to their dependence upon them, the eye and so forth are the dwelling places for them.
Furthermore, because they are crowded within the eye and so forth—being supported by them and having them as their object—the eye and so forth are their source (*ākara*).
This is because they converge in each respective instance by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*), the door (*dvāra*), and the object (*ārammaṇa*).
The eye and so forth are their place of convergence. Because they arise right there by virtue of having those as their support and object, the eye and so forth are their place of birth.
Because they do not exist in the absence of the eye and so forth, the eye and so forth are their cause.
In the sense thus described, it is both the eye and a base (*āyatana*), hence "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*). The same applies to the rest.
Furthermore, these same twelve bases (āyatana), together with the six consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, are called "elements" (dhātu) because they provide a basis in eighteen ways.

For each individual phenomenon among the eye and the rest is called an "element" because it, as the case may be, provides a basis (vidahati), is held (dhīyate), is a basis (vidhānaṃ), is that by which something is held (vidhīyate), or that in which something is held (ettha vā dhīyati). Indeed, mundane elements...

Having become established as causes, they produce manifold suffering in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)—just as gold, silver, and other ores produce gold, silver, and so forth—and they are borne and carried by sentient beings like a load by load-carriers;
for these [aggregates] are merely the manifestation of suffering, since they do not admit of mastery over them. And through these things acting as causes, the suffering of the cycle of existence...
They are followed by sentient beings, and being so established, they are placed and fixed within these very [aggregates]; therefore, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, just as the so-called "self" of the non-Buddhist sectarians does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, these [elements] are not like that;

rather, they are called "elements" because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). And just as in the world there are various mineral constituents such as yellow orpiment and red arsenic, [so too are these].
They are called "elements" (*dhātu*); thus these too are elements because they are like elements.

Or, just as the designation "element" is applied to the constituents of a body—such as lymph, blood, and so forth—which are parts of the whole known as the body and are demarcated by their mutually distinct and dissimilar characteristics, so too the designation "element" is applied to these parts of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) known as the five aggregates.
They are to be understood as such. For these, beginning with the eye, are demarcated by their mutual dissimilar characteristics.

Furthermore, "element" (*dhātu*) is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a soul (*nijjīva*). Indeed, the Blessed One, in such passages as "This person, bhikkhus, consists of six elements," taught the elements for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a soul.
Therefore, they are called "elements" also in the sense of being soulless.
And here, by the statement "subsisting on nutriment," which expresses the dependence of formations (*saṅkhārā*) upon conditions, their impermanence is revealed;
and through that, by the statement "what is impermanent is suffering, what is suffering is non-self," their suffering and non-self nature are also revealed.
Thus, all three universal characteristics are included. "Name" refers to the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*), and these...
In terms of their actual meaning, these are contact and so forth. "Form" refers to the primary elements (bhūta) and derived form (upādāyarūpa);

and since these, in their actual meaning, are the earth element and so on, they are included as formations (saṅkhāra) by way of their specific characteristics without distinction. By including those, those which are distinguished as wholesome and so forth, as well as the causes and so forth, are also indeed included;
thus he said: "In this way, this world of formations is also known in every respect."
Having thus shown the state of having understood the world of formations in every respect, he now said, beginning with "But because this...
in order to show the state of having understood the world of beings in every respect as well. Therein, "he knows the abode" (*āsaya*):

it is called an "abode" (*āsaya*) because the mind lies down (*seti*) there after coming back, just like the abode of deer. Just as a deer, having gone out for grazing and returned, remains right there—
He dwells in the forest-thicket, thus that is his abode (*āsaya*); likewise, even though it functions otherwise, wherever the mind comes to rest, that is called its abode.
That, moreover, is fourfold by way of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) and so forth. And it is said:
"The eternalist and annihilationist views, and the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*);..."
"And that knowledge which is according to reality—this is called 'the underlying tendency' (āsaya).
In this context, because all views are subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism, all beings who follow views are dependent upon these two very views.
As it is said: "Kaccāna, for the most part, this world is dependent upon a duality."
"Both existence and non-existence. For "existence" is intended here as the grasping at eternalism (*sassataggāha*), and "non-existence" as the grasping at annihilationism (*ucchedaggāha*).

This, first of all, is the disposition (*āsaya*) of worldlings (*puthujjana*) who rely on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); however, for pure beings who rely on the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), there are two kinds of dispositions:
conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*) and knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*). Among these, "conformable acceptance" refers to insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*).
"Knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūtañāṇa), however, is path-knowledge (maggañāṇa)"—this is stated in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Sammohavinodanī*.

That [knowledge], though fourfold, knows the dispositions of beings; and in knowing them, it knows even at the moment when those wrong views and those types of knowledge do not yet occur. For this has been said:

“He knows one who indulges in sensual pleasures as ‘this person is heavy with sensual pleasures, inclined toward sensual pleasures, intent upon sensual pleasures,’ and he knows one who indulges in sensual pleasures as ‘this person is heavy with renunciation, inclined toward renunciation, intent upon renunciation,’” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “he knows the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*”) : they are called *anusaya* because they lie down (*sayanti*) little by little (*anu anu*). The meaning is that they arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause. By this, he shows their fitness to arise when a cause is obtained. For when defilements have not been abandoned, [they arise] upon obtaining a cause...
They arise when there is [a basis]. But what are they? They are the seven future defilements, beginning with sensual lust;
those of the past and present are likewise so called because they possess that same nature. For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena due to a difference in time.
He knows that sevenfold underlying tendency (*anusaya*) as it occurs in the mental continuum of each respective being in a successive sequence.

Regarding the phrase "he knows the temperament" (*caritaṃ jānāti*): here, "temperament" (*carita*) refers to good conduct and bad conduct (*sucarita-duccarita*), for that is what is explained in the *Vibhaṅga* under the exposition of temperament.
Alternatively, "temperament" should be understood as "conduct" (*cariyā*).

These consist of six root types of conduct based on greed, hatred, delusion, faith, wisdom, and thought; their internal subdivisions are limitless, while their subdivisions by way of association are sixty-threefold. That...
One knows conduct by way of its intrinsic nature, its defilement, its purification, its origination, its fruit, and its outflow, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "one knows the disposition" (*adhimutti*): here, "disposition" refers to the element of inclination. That is twofold:

inferior disposition and superior disposition. By means of which, beings of inferior disposition associate only with those of inferior disposition, and those of superior disposition [associate] with those of superior disposition.
It is just so. For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous while the co-residents are virtuous, they do not even approach their own teachers and preceptors;
they approach only those bhikkhus who are like themselves and worthy.
If the teachers and preceptors are worthy bhikkhus while the others are unworthy, they likewise do not approach their teachers and preceptors.
They approach only those who are similar to themselves in disposition and inferior inclinations.
It is said that when the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya was traveling to Nāgadīpa for the worship of the cetiya accompanied by five hundred bhikkhus, he was invited by people in a certain village;
there was one unsuitable bhikkhu with the Elder, and there was also one unsuitable bhikkhu in the head monastery.

When the Bhikkhu Saṅghas were descending upon the village, although those two groups of people had never before seen either a visitor by a resident or a resident by a visitor, nevertheless they stood together, laughing repeatedly as they conversed.
Seeing this, the Elder said: "The Perfectly Enlightened One, having known this, spoke the *Dhātusaṃyutta*. Thus it was.

The element of inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*), the state of inclination (*ajjhāsayabhāva*), which determines the mutual association and so forth of those with inferior inclinations and others, is called "inclination" (*adhimutti*);
he knows that inclination. He penetrates it thus: "This one's inclination is inferior, this one's is sublime;
even therein, this one's is mild, this one's is milder, this one's is mildest," and so forth. Furthermore, [he knows] the sharpness, mildness, and other qualities of that inclination.
It is to be understood by way of the sharpness, dullness, and so forth, of the faculties.

Regarding the term *apparajakkha*: those who have little (*appa*) or limited (*paritta*) dust (*raja*)—namely passion, hatred, and delusion—in their eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya-akkhi*) are *apparajakkha*;
or alternatively, those beings whose dust of passion and so forth is slight are *apparajakkha*. These are the *apparajakkha*.
"Those with great defilement" (*mahārajakkha*): the same method applies here as well; those whose dust of passion and so forth is excessive are "those with great defilement. "He knows":
he knows those with little defilement and so forth by way of such [distinctions] as, "For this one the dust of passion is slight;

for this one the dust of hatred is slight," and so on. "Those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriya*): those endowed with the sharp faculties of faith and the rest. "Those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*): those with dull [faculties].
"Endowed with the faculties beginning with faith": in both instances, the faculties that serve as decisive supports (upanissaya) are intended.
"Of good disposition" (svākāra) means of beautiful disposition, of noble character, or having a tendency toward the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭajjhāsaya).

Alternatively, those whose dispositions (āsaya), etc., and modes (ākāra)—that is, their constituent parts—are beautiful, are "of good disposition. The opposite are "of two-fold disposition" (dvākāra). "Easy to instruct" (suviññāpaye) refers to one who has entered the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma).
Those who are easy to convince are those who possess faith and wisdom, or those who perceive the reason that has been stated;

they can be easily convinced and are thus "easy to instruct" (*suviññāpayā*). The opposite are "difficult to instruct" (*duviññāpayā*). Regarding the terms "capable" (*bhabbe*) and "incapable" (*abhabbe*):

here, those who are suitable for the penetration of the Noble Path, who possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), and who are free from the obstructions of karma, defilements, and karmic results, [are the capable].

They are capable; those who are the opposite are incapable. Therefore, because the Blessed One knows immeasurable beings without exception—starting from their underlying tendencies—the world of beings is known by that Blessed One in every respect.
But is it not the case that even a measure among beings must be known? Yes, there is; however, the knowledge of that [measure] does not lead to disenchantment.

The phrases "for the sake of dispassion" and "for the sake of cessation" are not included here; however, the Blessed One certainly understood and well-established them as well, yet they did not enter into the teaching because there was no purpose [in mentioning them]. Therefore it was said:
"Then the Blessed One, having placed a small amount of dust on the tip of his fingernail, addressed the bhikkhus: 'That...'"
“What do you think, monks? Which is more: this small amount of dust I have placed on the tip of my fingernail, or this great earth? and so forth.
Having thus shown that the world of sentient beings is known in its entirety, he now likewise shows that the world of space is known in the same way.
Showing this, he said, “And as the world of beings,” and so forth. The connection is that the world of space (*okāsaloka*) is also known in its entirety.
“Cakkavāḷa” means a world-system (*lokadhātu*). For it is called a “cakkavāḷa” because it is completely encircled by the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, which resembles the rim of a wheel.
“Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni” means three hundred and fifty—that is, three-quarters.
Meaning: "Nahutāni" means ten thousand. "Saṅkhatā" means spoken of. Since this earth is indeed unbounded across its breadth, therefore, the limit stated is only in terms of its thickness, as in:
"This Vasundharā is spoken of as being so much in thickness. [Objection:
But is not each individual world-sphere earth bounded by the Cakkavāḷa mountains? [Reply: No.

This is because the earth of other world-systems is joined together as one. For there is no earth in the intervals between the three sets of three world-systems—just as there is no space between three bowls placed side by side—due to the existence of the Lokantara hells;

however, at the places where the Cakkavāḷa mountains are connected with the gaps between those mountains, the earth is indeed joined as one, even when it is being formed during the period of world-expansion.
The earth stands as a single solid mass, just as the earth is naturally situated.
"Situated" (*saṇṭhitī*) means its stability in every respect, both below and above. "Thus situated" (*evaṃ saṇṭhite*) means thus established.

"Therein" (*ettha*) refers to the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "Plunged down" (*ajjhogāḷho*) means standing after having plunged into and entered within it. "Protruded upwards by that same amount" (*accuggato tāvadeva*) means [protruded] by exactly that much.
It rises exactly eight million four hundred thousand yojanas. Not only is its height such, but its length and breadth are also that great.
For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and eighty-four thousand yojanas in breadth."
"Sineru, the supreme of mountains" means it is the best among mountains; or, it is a mountain that is itself supreme, thus "supreme mountain.
"Sineru, the supreme mountain" means the supreme mountain known as Sineru; what is meant is "the king of mountains, Sineru.
Its eastern face is made of silver; therefore, by its radiance flooding over it, the water of the ocean in the eastern direction becomes like milk.
It appears as such. However, the southern side is made of sapphire (indanīlamaṇi);
therefore, the ocean water in the southern direction appears for the most part blue in color, and likewise the sky. The western side is made of crystal (phalika).
The northern side is made of gold. The four oceans are also demarcated by the very rays of Sineru. Likewise...
Indeed, the rays of silver and gems issuing from the eastern and southern sides join together, travel across the surface of the great ocean, and remain striking against the Cakkavāḷa mountain;
those issuing from the southern and western sides are rays of gems and crystal;
those issuing from the western and northern sides are rays of crystal and gold; and those issuing from the northern and eastern sides—
The rays of gold and silver, having come together, travel across the surface of the great ocean and stand striking against the Cakkavāḷa mountain; between those rays are the four great oceans.
"From there" means from below and above Sineru according to the stated measurement. "By half and half" means by one half and another half.
This is what is meant: the Yugandhara mountain plunges forty-two thousand yojanas into the ocean and rises an equal distance above it;
the Īsadhara mountain plunges twenty-one thousand yojanas into the great ocean and rises an equal distance above it.
In this manner, the successive mountains should be understood to be half the size of each preceding one.

Just as the great ocean slopes gradually down to the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, so too, from the base of Sineru downwards, Mount Yugandhara—even though it is half the size of Sineru—is firmly established on the earth;
the same should be understood for Īsadharā and the other mountains. For this has been said: "The great ocean, bhikkhus, slopes gradually..."
“Sloping gradually, inclining gradually. Between Mount Sineru, Yugandhara, and the others, there are what are called the Sīda intermediate oceans.
It is said that in those waters, even a tiny object the size of a peacock feather cannot remain standing; it simply sinks.
Therefore, they are called the Sīda oceans. As for their width, they correspond respectively to the widths of Mount Sineru and the other mountains.
They say they are equal in measure to their respective heights above [the water]. "Submerged and risen" means both submerged and risen. "Brahā" means great.
"All around Sineru" means standing all around Sineru by way of encircling it. Yugandhara stands having first encircled Sineru;
Īsadharo stands having encircled that. Thus, each one stands having encircled the preceding one.
They are said to be "situated all around Sineru. However, in some places another sequence has been handed down, stating:
"Having encircled Sineru, the mountain named Assakaṇṇa is established; having encircled that, the mountain named Vinataka [is established].
For instance, in the Nimijātaka—
“Mounted upon a divine vehicle drawn by a thousand horses, the Great King, while traveling along, saw mountains within the ocean.
Having seen them, he asked his charioteer: ‘What are these mountains called?’”
Thus was it spoken by the divine son Mātali when questioned by King Nimi:
“Sudassana, Karavīka, Īsadharo, Yugandharo;
Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the lofty mountain.”
“O King, these mountains you see, rising up in succession from within the waters, are the abodes of the Great Kings.
Thus it was said.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
"Great King, this is the mountain named Sudassana, which is the outermost of all these;
next to it is the one named Karavīka, which is higher than Sudassana. Between those two, however, lies the great ocean known as Sīdantara."
Adjacent to Karavīka is the mountain named Īṣādhara; it is higher than Karavīka. Between those two as well is one great ocean of salt water.
Adjacent to Īṣādhara is the mountain named Yugandhara; it is higher than Īṣādhara. Between those two as well is one great ocean of salt water.
Adjacent to Yugandhara is the mountain named Nemindhara; it is higher than Yugandhara.

Between those two is one Great Ocean of Sīdantara. Immediately adjacent to Nemindhara is the mountain named Vinataka, which is higher than Nemindhara. Between those two is one Great Ocean of Sīdantara.
Immediately adjacent to Vinataka is the mountain named Assakaṇṇa, which is higher than Vinataka. Between those two is one Great Ocean of Sīdantara.
"These seven mountains rise up in succession within the great ocean between the Sīda [continents], standing like a flight of stairs.
"The Himavat mountain is five hundred yojanas high"—the meaning is that the Himavat mountain is five hundred yojanas in height;
"height" being the sense. Therein, it is called "Himavat" because during the season of snowfall, it is possessed of snow; that is, "it has snow (hima)," thus it is Himavat.
It is called Himavā because it vomits forth snow (*hima*) during the summer season. "Mountain" (*pabbata*) means a rock (*sela*).

For a rock is called a "mountain" (*pabbata*) because it is composed of joints (*pabba*); and it is also called a "hill" (*giri*) because it swallows (*giraṇa*) water and the sources of medicinal herbs and other substances that constitute its essence through the process of oozing and so forth. It is three thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
The meaning is that it is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth; thus, it is said to be three thousand yojanas both in length and in breadth.
It is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, such as the Sudassana peak, the Citra peak, and others—meaning with eighty-four thousand peaks.
"Adorned" means "beautified. Furthermore, this further distinction should be understood even though it was not explicitly stated:
this mountain named Himavā is variegated by five hundred rivers flowing from all sides;
there, the Anotatta Lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, as well as in depth, and measures one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.
Seven great lakes are established there: Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake, Rathakāra Lake, Chaddanta Lake, Kuṇāla Lake, Mandākinī Lake, and Siṅhapapāta Lake.
Among them, Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citrakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak. Therein, Sudassana Peak is made of gold.
Two hundred yojanas in height, curved within and shaped like a crow’s beak, it stands covering that very lake.
Citrakūṭa is composed entirely of jewels. Kāḷakūṭa is composed of collyrium. Gandhamādana-peak is composed of sandalwood;

its interior has the color of green gram, and it possesses the fragrance of roots such as kāḷānusāri, the fragrance of heartwood such as sandalwood, the fragrance of softwood such as sarala, and the fragrance of bark such as cloves.

It is rich with these ten kinds of scents: the scent of the bark of *kapittha* and other trees, the scent of the sap of *sajja* and others, the scent of the leaves of *tāmāla* and others, the scent of the flowers of *nāgakuṅkuma* and others, and the scent of the fruits of *jātiphala* and others;

because it possesses the nature of fragrance in every way, it is called "fragrant-scented. Covered with various medicinal herbs, on the uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a glowing ember.
In that very place is a mountain cave named Nandamūlaka, a dwelling-place for Paccekabuddhas. There are three caves:
the Golden Cave, the Jewel Cave, and the Silver Cave. At the entrance of the Jewel Cave stands a tree called Mañjūsaka, one *yojana* in height and one *yojana* in breadth;
it blooms with all kinds of flowers, whether they grow in water or on land, especially so.
On the day of the arrival of the Paccekabuddhas, there was a pavilion made of all kinds of gems above that place.
There, a sweeping wind cast away the refuse; a leveling wind made the sand consisting of all kinds of gems even;
a sprinkling wind brought water from Lake Anotatta and sprinkled it; and a perfuming wind [brought] the scents of all fragrant trees.
The wind called "Bringer of Fragrance" blows, gathering flowers and causing them to fall; the wind called "Spreader" spreads them everywhere, and seats are always already prepared there.
It is the custom that on the day a Paccekabuddha attains enlightenment and on Uposatha days, all the Paccekabuddhas assemble and sit upon these seats.
This is the established order there. [Then] the Paccekabuddha who has attained full enlightenment...
Having gone there, he sits on the prepared seat. Then, if at that time other paccekabuddhas are present, they too gather at that moment and sit on the prepared seats;
having sat down, they enter some meditative attainment (samāpatti) and emerge from it.
Thereafter, the senior elder of the community [addresses] the newly arrived paccekabuddha for the purpose of giving thanks for the meal for everyone.
When [the Buddha] asks, “How was it attained? he is inquiring about the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); at that time, the [paccekabuddha] recites his own verse of inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Thus, it should be understood that this Peak of Gandhamādana is the dwelling place of the paccekabuddhas.
Furthermore, the Peak of Kelāsa is made of silver. All these, such as Citrakūṭa and the others, are equal to Sudassana in height and configuration.
They stand covering that very lake. It is said that they are all fifty yojanas in width, and two hundred yojanas in length as well as in height.
All of them remain there through the power of the devas and the power of the nāgas; rivers flow into them, and all that water enters only the Anotatta [Lake].
When the moon and sun travel to the south or the north, they cast their radiance upon it through the intervening mountain range;
when traveling directly overhead, they do not. For this reason, the designation "Anotatta" (Unheated) arose for it.

Therein are bathing pools with delightful stone terraces and stairways made of jewels, free from fish and turtles, with water as pure as crystal, intended for the enjoyment of the beings who frequent them.

By the power of common karma alone, these [pools] are well-prepared and beautifully situated, wherein Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants whose taints are destroyed, as well as powerful seers, bathe;
and where gods, yakkhas, and others enjoy themselves with park-sports.
On its four sides are four faces: a lion’s face, an elephant’s face, a horse’s face, and an ox’s face.
There are [four mouths] from which the four rivers flow. On the banks of the river issuing from the lion’s mouth, lions are more numerous;
from the elephant’s mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls [issue].
The river issuing from the eastern direction circles Anotatta three times clockwise and, without reaching the other three rivers, follows the path of non-humans through the eastern Himalayas.

Having reached it, they enter the great ocean. The rivers issuing from the western and northern directions likewise circumambulate it to the right, pass through the non-human territories of the western and northern Himalayas respectively, and enter the great ocean.
However, the river issuing from the southern direction circumambulates it three times.
Having turned to the right and traveled sixty *yojanas* in a straight line along the surface of the rock, it struck the mountain and rose up;
becoming a stream of water sixty *gāvutas* in circumference, it traveled sixty *yojanas* through the air and fell upon the rock named Tiyaggaḷa.
The rock was split by the force of the stream of water. Therein, [a lake] measuring fifty *yojanas*—
A great lotus pond named Tiyaggaḷā came into being; having broken through the bank of the great lotus pond and entered the rock,
it traveled sixty yojanas, then, having broken through the solid earth, it went sixty yojanas through a subterranean passage,
struck the transverse mountain named Viñjha, and [emerged as] five streams like the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
Having been offered, it flows forth. Having made three circumambulations of Anotatta Lake from left to right, it is called the "Whirlpool Gaṅgā" at the place where it has gone;

the "Black Gaṅgā" at the place where it has gone straight for sixty yojanas over the surface of the rocks; the "Sky Gaṅgā" at the place where it has gone through the air for sixty yojanas; and it stands upon the Tiyaṅgaḷa Rock in a space of fifty yojanas.
Regarding "the Tiyaggaḷa lotus pond": where it has broken through the bank and entered the rock, having traveled sixty yojanas, it is called the "Bahalagaṅgā";
where it has traveled sixty yojanas by way of a subterranean passage (umaṅga), it is called the "Umaṅgagaṅgā.
However, at the place where it strikes the mountain named Viñjha and flows forth in five streams, it is [known as] the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
The Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—thus they are reckoned as five. In this way, these five great rivers originate from the Himālayas.
Furthermore, in the center of the Chaddanta Lake, in a place measuring twelve *yojanas*, there is neither moss nor aquatic plants;
only water, with the color of a mass of jewels, remains still. Immediately adjacent to that is a forest of pure white lotuses (*kalahāra*) extending for one *yojana* in width.
Surrounding that water stands a grove of pure blue lotuses (*nīluppalavana*) exactly one *yojana* wide;

surrounding that, there stand groves of red lotuses (*rattuppalavana*), white lotuses (*setuppala*), red lotuses (*rattapadumavana*), white lotuses (*setapadumavana*), and white water-lilies (*kumudavana*), each exactly one *yojana* wide, standing one after the other in succession.
Following these seven groves, for all of them—
By way of the *kallahāra* (blue lotuses) and other such flowers, there is a mixed grove one *yojana* in extent, situated surrounding those [forests].
Immediately after that, in water reaching the depth of a nāga’s waist, there is a grove of red rice (*rattasāli*) one *yojana* in extent.
Following that, at the edge of the water, there is a grove of small shrubs strewn with blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, and delicate flowers.
These ten forests were each exactly one *yojana* in extent. Following those were the forests of small beans (*khuddakaramāsa*), black gram (*rājamāsa*), and mung beans (*mugga*);
immediately after that, the forests of *tipu*, *saeḷā*, eggplants (*alābu*), bottle gourds (*kumbhaṇḍa*), and creepers (*vallī*);

then a sugarcane forest as large as a *pūga* tree; then a plantain forest with fruit the size of an elephant’s tusk; then a *sāla* forest; and immediately following that, [a forest] with fruit the size of a *cāṭi*.

Then there is the Panasavana, then the Ambavana of sweet fruit, then the Ciñcavana, then the Kapiṭṭhavana, then the great mixed forest grove, and then the Veṇuvana. Surrounding the Veṇuvana stand seven mountains;
starting from their outer edge, the first is named Cūḷakāḷapabbata, and the second is Mahākāḷapabbata.
Next is the mountain named Udakapassapabbata; next, the mountain named Candapassapabbata;
next, the mountain named Sūriyapassapabbata; next, the mountain named Maṇipassapabbata; and the seventh is the mountain named Suvaṇṇapassapabbata.
It is seven yojanas in height and stands encircling the Chaddanta Lake like the rim of a vessel. Of that—
Seeing the inner mountain, which is gold-colored, the Chaddanta Lake, illuminated by the radiance emerging from it,
appears like the rising sun. As for the outer mountains, one is six yojanas in height,
one five, one four, one three, one two, and one one yojana.
Thus, on the northeastern corner of that lake, which is encircled by seven mountain ranges, at a place where the wind from the water strikes, there is a great banyan tree.
Its trunk is five yojanas in circumference and seven yojanas in height.
In the four directions, its four branches extend six yojanas each, and the branch that rises upward is likewise six yojanas long.
Thus, from its base upwards it stands thirteen *yojanas* in height; from the near side of its branches to the far side, it is twelve *yojanas* wide;
adorned with eight thousand shoots, it stands shimmering like a mountain of polished gems.
Furthermore, on the golden mountain in the western quarter of the Chaddanta Lake, there is [a tree] twelve *yojanas* in size.
The Golden Cave. The Naga king Chaddanta dwells in the Golden Cave during the rainy season, surrounded by eight thousand nagas;
in the summer, seeking shelter from the wind and rain, he stands amidst the sprouts at the foot of a great banyan tree.
Furthermore, for a distance of twenty-five yojanas in the middle of the Mandākinī River, there is neither moss nor algae.
The water there is crystal-colored; beyond that, however, in water reaching the depth of a nāga’s waist, there stands a forest of white lotuses, half a *yojana* in extent, surrounding that water.

There, the stalks are as large as the tip of a plowshare, and the bulbous roots are the size of great kettle-drums or *pokkhara* flowers. Within each interval between the leaves, there is [a flower] the measure of an *āḷhaka*.
It becomes milk. At the time when the lotuses are in bloom, the wind raises a mass of pollen and deposits it upon the lotus leaves;
there, drops of water fall, and after being cooked by the heat of the sun, it remains as "lotus honey" (pokkharamadhu), like a vessel of cooked curd.
Immediately following that is a vast grove of red lotuses of equal size, and immediately following that is a grove of red water-lilies (rattakumuda).
Immediately after that was a grove of white water-lilies; after that, a grove of blue lotuses; after that, a grove of red lotuses;
after that, a grove of fragrant rice; after that, sweet-tasting climbing fruits such as eḷāluka, alābu, and kumbhaṇḍa;
and after that, a sugar-cane grove exactly half a yojana in width, where [the stalks] were as thick as the trunks of betel-nut trees.
Sugarcane. Immediately after that was a grove of plantains, from which two [monks] grew weary while eating the ripe fruit.
After that was a grove of jackfruit trees with fruit the size of bowls, then a mango grove, a rose-apple grove, and a wood-apple grove;
in brief, it cannot be said that there was no fruit fit for eating in that lake. Thus.

It should be understood that in this Himavat, the Blessed One knew, understood, and fully penetrated every particular detail—such as the measurements and shapes—of the seven great lakes and so forth that exist there.
"With trunks and circumferences of three or five yojanas" means with trunks measuring fifteen yojanas in circumference; [this refers to] the trunk...
"Width" means it is stated to be fifteen yojanas in measure. "Named 'Naga'" means it is to be called by the word *naga*;
the meaning is that it is designated as a tree. For a tree is called *naga* because it does not move (*na gacchati*).
The phrase "the Jambū named Naga" is how it should be construed. "With a trunk and branches fifty yojanas [in extent]" means its trunk and branches have a height and span measuring fifty yojanas.
It is fifty yojanas in height and fifty yojanas in circumference. For that very reason, it is one hundred yojanas wide and rises to the same extent.
Indeed, from the root of the Jambu tree up to its branches and foliage, it extends for fifty yojanas;
beyond that, the trunk rises straight up for another fifty yojanas, and each branch extending outwards in every direction is likewise fifty [yojanas].
They increased by fifty *yojanas*. Into them flow very large rivers;
on both banks of those rivers, at the places where the *jambu* fruits fall, golden sprouts arise.
Being carried along by the river water, they gradually enter the great ocean. Because they are produced in the *Jambunadī*, it is called "Jambunada" (Gold of the Jambu River).
That is called gold.
"By whose power" means by the majesty of that [gold], which is its greatness manifested through its radiance lasting for an eon and so forth.
And this same measurement as the *jambu* tree is the measurement of the *cittapāṭali* tree of the asuras, of the *simbali* tree of the garuḍas, and in Aparagoyāna...
In Kadamba for Uttarakuru, the wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha) for Pubbavideha, the Sirīsa for Tāvatiṃsa, and the Pāricchattaka for the gods. Thus the ancients have said:
“The Pāṭali, the Simbalī, the Jambu, The Pāricchattaka of the gods, The Kadamba, the wish-fulfilling tree, And the Sirīsa is the seventh.”

Regarding the phrase "there the *sirisena* tree becomes the seventh": here, *sirisena* is used in the instrumental case in an absolute sense (*paccatte karaṇavacanaṃ*). The term "seventh" (*sattama*) is stated with a shift in gender; the meaning is that the *sirisena* tree becomes the seventh.
"The mountain-heap of the world-sphere" (*cakkavāḷasiluccaya*) refers to the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
"Having surrounded all this, it stands as the world-system" means that the mountain-heap of the world-sphere is established having surrounded everything mentioned below; this is one [world-system].
The meaning is "world-system" (*lokadhātu*). The letter *ma* has been inserted for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).

They explain the connection here as follows: "Having surrounded that entire world-system, this mountain range of the world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*) stands. Even when stated thus, it should be understood that the mountain of the world-sphere itself is indeed a world-system.
*“Therein”* means in that world-system. The moon’s disk is forty-nine *yojanas*: straight on, in length, breadth, and height, it is forty-nine *yojanas*;
but in circumference, it is one hundred and fifty *yojanas* less three *yojanas*.
The sun’s disk is fifty *yojanas*; here too, according to the same method stated for the moon’s disk, it is fifty *yojanas* straight on.
It should be understood that, in its circumference, it is one hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
Among them, the moon’s disk is below and the sun’s disk is above; between them there is an interval of one *yojana*.
From the lower limit of the moon to the upper limit of the sun, the distance is one hundred *yojanas*; the moon’s celestial palace is within [that space].
The palace made of jewels is encircled on the outside with silver; it is cool both inside and out.
The sun-palace is made of gold within and encircled by crystal on the outside; it is warm both inside and out.
The moon moves straight and slowly. For on the day of the new moon, as it travels together with the sun, day after day—
Lagging behind little by little, it falls half a day's journey behind on the full-moon night, yet it moves swiftly across the sky.
Thus, within a single month, it is sometimes seen to the south and sometimes to the north.
While the constellations and stars move on both sides of the moon, the moon approaches each constellation like a cow approaching her calf.
The lunar mansions (*nakkhattāni*), however, do not abandon their own positions; they move only along their own paths.

The sun’s direct course is swift, while its transverse course is slow. A "transverse course" means moving from the southern direction to the northern direction, or from the northern direction to the southern direction;
that is slow because it is accomplished over six months at a time.
On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, the sun travels together with the moon;

thereafter, on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada), because of its own swiftness of movement and the moon’s slowness, it proceeds leaving the lunar disk behind by one hundred thousand yojanas, so that the moon appears like a mere streak.
Thereafter, on the second day of the fortnight, [it leaves it behind] by another hundred thousand yojanas.
It departs from the moon’s disk. In this manner, day by day, until the Uposatha day of the bright fortnight, it departs by increments of one hundred thousand [yojanas] each;
then, the moon gradually increases in size until it becomes full on the Uposatha day.
Herein, its gradual increase is due to the light of the sun falling upon its upper surface, while its lower surface remains in shadow.
It should be understood that this is due to the sun’s distance; as its own shadow diminishes day by day in gradual succession, the region of the solar disc appears to increase in size accordingly.
Therefore, having increased as it were in gradual stages, on the Uposatha day of the full moon, it becomes a full orb.

It is seen. Then, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), the sun, having run a hundred thousand yojanas, again overtakes the moon’s disk because of the moon’s slow motion and its own swift motion;
likewise on the second day it runs another hundred thousand, and thus it continues to overtake it by running a hundred thousand yojanas each day until the Uposatha day. Then the moon, in due course—
Having diminished, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight it is no longer visible at all;
and here, the process of gradual diminution should be understood by the same method as the process of gradual increase previously described.
In that case, due to the diminishing of the shadow, the disk appears as if increasing; whereas here, due to the increasing of the shadow, the disk appears as if diminishing.
It appears as if it were diminishing; therefore, having gradually decreased, on the Uposatha day it is no longer visible at all.
With the moon below and the sun above, the lunar disk is covered like a small vessel placed inside a large bowl;
the shadow of the moon is not perceived, just as the shadow of a house is not seen at midday. Since that shadow is no longer perceived—
To those standing at a distance, it is not even visible by day, like a lamp.
Furthermore, these have three paths of movement: the horse-path, the elephant-path, and the cow-path.
Among them, water is repulsive to horses, pleasant to elephant-kings, and comfortable for cows due to the balance of cold and heat.
And likewise, when the sun travels along a particular path, the rain-cloud deities (*vassavalāhaka-devaputta*), heated by the sun’s glare,
do not emerge from their own celestial mansions (*vimāna*) nor wander about intent on play; at that time, it is said,
the sun’s mansion descends below its usual course and moves there, and by the very act of its descent, the moon’s mansion also descends.
Because it moves having gone down [into the water], that path— due to its lack of water and its resemblance to a goat—
is known by the conventional name "Ajavīthī" (Goat-path). Furthermore, when the sun travels along this path, the rain-cloud deities (vassavalāhakadevaputtā), being free from the sun's heat,
frequently emerge from their own celestial mansions and, intent on play, wander here and there.
At that time, it is said, the sun’s celestial mansion (sūriyavimāna) moves by ascending above its natural course;
and because it follows that same path, the moon’s celestial mansion (candavimāna) also ascends and moves above, as it shares that same trajectory.

This shared trajectory occurs because the celestial mansion is propelled by a circular wind (vātamaṇḍala); therefore, that path is characterized by an abundance of water, being suitable for the Nāgas.

It has acquired the designation "Nāgavīthī" (The Elephant’s Path). When the sun proceeds by its natural course, neither ascending upwards nor descending downwards, then the rain-clouds emerge from their celestial mansions at the proper time and according to their inclination, moving about with ease;
because it rains at the appropriate times due to that, there is seasonal harmony in the world, and with that seasonal harmony serving as the cause—
Because it follows the course of the moon and sun like that of a cow, it has acquired the designation "the Cow-path" (*govīthī*).
Therefore, when the moon and sun ascend the Horse-path (*ajavīthī*), not even a single drop of rain falls from the sky.
When they ascend the Naga-path (*nāgavīthī*), the sky pours down as if it were broken open. When they ascend the Cow-path, the regularity of the seasons is established.
But when kings become unrighteous, through their unrighteousness all the subordinate kings, generals, and so forth, as well as the gods and Brahmās, become unrighteous.

Then, through their unrighteousness, the moon and sun move irregularly. For at that time, there arises that aforementioned condition known as unrighteousness, which serves as the supporting cause for undesirable results such as the prevalence of disease and other afflictions.
By the power of common evil karma, the wind blows irregularly;
being driven by that wind, the moon and sun, though they circle Mount Sineru, revolve unevenly and do not proceed according to their proper course.
The wind does not blow along its proper path, but blows contrary to it; blowing contrary to its path, it agitates the celestial palaces situated in the sky.
When the celestial mansions are shaken, the minds of the deities do not incline toward their play;
when their minds do not incline, the seasonal weather—distinguished by cold and heat—does not occur at its proper time. When that does not occur, the rain does not fall properly:
sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; it rains in some places, and in others it does not. Even when it rains...

At the time of sowing, at the time of sprouting, at the time of the stalks, at the time of flowering, and at the times of milking and so forth, whenever the rain does not provide benefit to the crops, it rains and then ceases accordingly.
Because of that, the crops ripen unevenly and are deprived of their excellence in fragrance, flavor, and other qualities;
even in the case of rice grains placed in a single vessel, in one particular spot—
The rice becomes undercooked; in one part it is over-soggy, while in another it is evenly cooked.

When consumed, it is entirely undigested in the stomach, or only partially digested, or even well-digested—thus it is digested in only three ways, and it does not properly reach the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya). Because of this, beings become afflicted with many ailments and short-lived.
But in the time of righteous kings, by way of the reverse of what was stated [above], the moon and sun revolve evenly;

they proceed along their proper paths, and the regularity of the seasons is established. For six months the moon and sun go outside of Sineru, and for six months they move within it. Thus, they circumambulate it clockwise in the vicinity of Sineru.
Having done so, while traveling for six months, they emerge from that path of travel toward the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) by moving diagonally away from themselves.
Thus, by retreating moment by moment from Sineru over the course of six months, they depart from there and reach the vicinity of the world-system.
From there as well, they depart moment by moment over the course of six months by means of retreating.
Reaching the vicinity of Sineru, they move within it. For during the month of Āsāḷhī, they move near Sineru;
then, having emerged for two months, they move outside. In the first month of Kattika, they pass through the middle;
then, having gone toward the Cakkavāḷa and moved near the Cakkavāḷa for three months, they emerge again in the month of Citra.
Having traveled by way of the middle, they then leap toward Sineru for the next two months;

subsequently, in Āsāḷha, they move near Sineru. In this context, it should be understood that as they travel by way of the middle point between Sineru and the Cakkavāḷa, and specifically by way of the middle point of Sineru itself, they move near Sineru—not [merely] near Sineru [in general].
They are attached to the outer rim; by this same method, their movement near the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is also to be understood.
But when they go straight through the middle of Sineru and the world-system, then it should be understood that they move through the center.
Moving in this way, they produce light simultaneously in all three continents. In each direction, there are nine...
Having dispelled the darkness over nine hundred thousand *yojanas*, they reveal light. How so?
For when it is sunrise here on this island, it is midday in Pūrvavideha, sunset in Uttarakuru, and midnight in Aparagoyāna;
when it is sunrise in Pūrvavideha, it is midday in Uttarakuru, and [midnight] in Aparagoyāna.

It is the time of setting here; it is mid-night in Uttarakuru, sunrise in Aparagoyāna, mid-day here, mid-night in Pubbavideha, sunrise on the island of Aparagoyāna, mid-day here, sunset on the island of Pubbavideha, and mid-night in Uttarakuru. For in this [world-system]...

At the time of midday on the island of Jambudīpa, half of the solar disc appears as it sets to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha, while the other half appears as it rises to the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna. The same applies to the remaining islands.
Thus, it should be understood that in this very manner, the moon and sun simultaneously provide light across the three continents.
Otherwise, however, they display light simultaneously across two continents alone.
For on whichever continent half the solar disk appears by way of setting, once it has set there, it no longer appears and does not display light;
yet simultaneously across both [other] continents, both [the appearance and non-appearance] occur. In each direction, [it extends for] nine hundred thousand leagues.
The dispelling of darkness should also be understood by this same method.
For when it is midday for those situated on this island, the sun’s orb appears half-set to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha;
thus, having dispelled the darkness in the region of Pubbavideha, which measures nine hundred thousand yojanas, it displays light there, and likewise in Aparagoyāna.
Because even there, it is only half [of the day] that is discernible by way of the sun’s rising. However, for the inhabitants of Pubbavideha, it is not discernible when [the sun] has set;
thus, having dispelled darkness everywhere in both continents, it displays light.
Furthermore, when the sun has risen over Aparagoyāna as well, it dispels darkness everywhere.
When the moon and sun appear in the world, they appear together; yet of these two, the sun becomes manifest first.
For when the self-luminosity of the beings of the first eon had vanished, there was darkness.
Terrified and trembling, they thought, "How wonderful it would be if there were some other light! Then, for the great multitude...
The solar disc arose, generating a state of brilliance; for that very reason, its name became "Sūriya" (the Sun).
On that day, when it had made light and then set, darkness returned once more.
Terrified and trembling, they thought, "How wonderful it would be if another light were to arise! Then, as if knowing their desire, [he appeared].
The moon-disk arose, and for that very reason its name became "Canda" (the Moon).
Thus, when the moon and sun had appeared, the lunar mansions and the forms of the stars became manifest; from that time forth, nights and days were discerned.
Gradually, months, fortnights, seasons, and years came into being. On the very day the moon and sun appeared, however—
It should be understood that Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the Himavanta mountains, and the four continents manifest simultaneously;
they manifest neither before nor after, but specifically on the full-moon day of the month of Phagguna.
And herein, it should be known that one Cakkavāḷa is twelve hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
"Three thousand, four hundred, and fifty yojanas," as stated in the Aṭṭhakathā; therefore,
having excluded eighty-four thousand yojanas from the aforementioned measurement in the area where Sineru stands within this Cakkavāḷa,
and having also excluded the extent of the northern quarter up to the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, [this space] lies in the southern direction of this world-system—
The distance between Mount Sineru and the Cakkavāḷa mountains,
in terms of measurement, should be known as five hundred thousand [yojanas],
sixty thousand less one, seven hundred, and twenty-five more.
"Located in the middle" means that the sun is situated at the center there.
When it is positioned in the middle from the center up to Mount Meru and within the circle of the world-systems (cakkavāḷa), it is then "reached both ends."
From the center up to Mount Meru and the Cakkavāḷa mountains,
there are two hundred thousand and seventy-eight thousand [yojanas].
There are eight hundred and sixty-two yojanas and two gavutas.
Between the two ends of Mount Meru and the Cakkavāḷa mountains,
there are one hundred thousand, thirty-nine thousand,
nine hundred and thirty-one yojanas, and one gāvuta.
In measurement, the circular area surrounding the central road should be understood as being nineteen hundred thousand,
thirty-one thousand, one hundred and seventy-five [yojanas].
Furthermore, as the sun moves toward the south and the north,
it travels in a circular path according to the measure of the middle course;
and as it thus proceeds, it descends and ascends from below.
Ascending again and again upwards, wherever he always went,
by way of that very movement, it became for him a long distance.
In measure, it was three million yojanas.
Therefore, he travels around it, day after day, for exactly that distance:
one thousand, five hundred, forty-five yojanas;
three gavutas, thirteen usabhas, and thirty-three ratanas.
In one day, the sun travels eight finger-breadths across;
in one month, it travels thirty-four thousand six hundred and forty-three yojanas.
Ten thousand nine hundred and eighty-two,
and two *gāvutas* more, it travels in two months;
at this speed, from one street-end to the next street-end.
The sun travels to the vicinity of Sineru in six months, and in three months it reaches the middle of the path;
returning, it arrives at the center of this island in two months.
Therefore, from the center of the Island of Siṃhala to the [center of] Mount Meru,
the distance is two hundred thousand [yojanas],
plus two hundred and thirty-three thousand, eighteen, and three-quarters of a yojana.
The space between world-systems, like the interior of an island,
measures three hundred thousand,
twenty-six thousand, five hundred and one and a quarter yojanas.
In this regard, this distinction should also be understood.
Concerning the phrase "the Tāvatiṃsa realm is ten thousand yojanas": thirty-three persons who have performed meritorious deeds are reborn there;
thus, the place associated with them is called "Tettiṃsa. That very place is "Tāvatiṃsa," and those whose dwelling is there are the "Tāvatiṃsas."

O gods, their abode is the Tāvatiṃsa realm. For it is said that this designation for this divine world arose beginning from the thirty-three sons of the gods who were reborn there after Magha the youth passed away in the village of Macala.
Alternatively, because the six sense-sphere heavenly realms exist in other world-systems as well. As it is said:
This refers to "a thousand [deities] of the Cātumahārājika realm and a thousand of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

Therefore, it should be understood that this is merely a designation (nāmapaññatti) for that divine world. Furthermore, the statement "ten thousand yojanas" should be understood as referring specifically to Sakka’s city;
for among the gods belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa host, there are some who dwell on mountains and some who dwell in the sky.
Their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and likewise for those of the Cātumahārājika and Yāma heavens and so forth.
Indeed, within a single divine world-system, there is no lineage of devas that does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.
However, it should be understood that this Tāvatiṃsa realm is established upon the upper surface of Sineru at a place ten thousand yojanas in extent. Regarding its eastern and western gates:

The distance between the eastern and western gates was ten thousand yojanas, as was the distance between the southern and northern gates. That city was provided with one thousand gates and adorned with parks and lotus ponds.
In its center stood [the palace], made of the seven precious gems, seven hundred yojanas in height and adorned with banners three hundred yojanas high.
Sakka’s palace was named Vejayanta. There, upon golden poles there were jeweled banners;

upon jeweled poles, golden banners; upon coral poles, pearl banners; upon pearl poles, coral banners; and upon poles made of the seven precious gems, there were banners made of the seven precious gems.
The Vejayanta chariot is one hundred and fifty yojanas in length.
For its rear end is fifty yojanas, the central chariot-fender is fifty yojanas, and from the chariot-joints to the front of the chariot it is likewise fifty yojanas.
Some say that by doubling that very measurement, it is "three hundred yojanas in length. Within it is a couch one yojana long.
It remains in its actual sense. Therein, the white parasol is three *yojanas* in size, yoked to a single pole by a thousand thoroughbred steeds.
There is no limit to the measure of the other ornaments. Its banner, moreover, rises two hundred and fifty *yojanas* high;
when struck by the wind, it emits a sound like that of the fivefold musical ensemble.
Sakka’s elephant, named Erāvaṇa, is one hundred and fifty yojanas in height; he too is a son of the gods.

For there are no animals in the world of the gods; therefore, when departing for a pleasure excursion in the park, he discards his own form and becomes the elephant named Erāvaṇa, one hundred and fifty yojanas high. He creates thirty-three frontal globes.

Within an area of one and a half *yojanas* by means of his supernatural power (*āvaṭṭa*), he creates for the sake of Sakka a thirty-*yojana* high vessel named Sudassana in the midst of them all. Above it is a jeweled pavilion twelve *yojanas* high.
There, at intervals, banners made of the seven precious gems rise up to a height of one *yojana*. Around the perimeter is a network of tinkling bells.

They hang down, and from that which is stirred by a gentle breeze, a sound issues forth like the sound of divine song, resembling the music of the fivefold orchestra. In the center of the pavilion, a jeweled couch one *yojana* in length is prepared for Sakka;
there Sakka sits. Upon each of the thirty-three jars, he arranges seven tusks, and upon those—
Each one is fifty yojanas in length. On each tusk there are seven lotus ponds;
in each pond there are seven lotus thickets; in each thicket there are seven flowers;
on each flower there are seven petals; and on each petal seven celestial maidens dance.
Thus, within an area of fifty *yojanas* all around, there is a theatrical performance using only elephant tusks.
Furthermore, the lotus pond named Nandā is fifty *yojanas* in extent; some say it is five hundred *yojanas*.
The Cittalatā Grove, however, is sixty *yojanas* in extent; some say it is five hundred *yojanas*. It is adorned with a thousand celestial trees.

Likewise there are the Nandana and Phārusaka groves. Here, Sakka, surrounded by a host of apsarases, descends upon the sixty-yojana golden Great Road and wanders through the Nandana grove and other such places while sporting in the constellations.
The Pāricchattaka coral tree, however, is three hundred yojanas in circumference and fifteen yojanas in girth at its trunk.
It is one hundred yojanas in height. At its base is the Pandukambala stone, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high, with the color of a jayasumana flower.
Because of its softness, when Sakka sits upon it, half his body sinks into it;
when he rises, the depression is filled back up.
The divine assembly hall named Sudhammā is three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, nine hundred yojanas in circumference, and five hundred yojanas in height.
Its floor is made of crystal; its pillars, beams, and joints for the connection of the framework are made of gems set with images of beasts and the like;
the pillars are made of gold; the pillar-capitals and the framework are made of silver; and [the railings] are made of coral.
The forms of wild beasts, the rafters, the side-walls, and the cornices were made of the seven precious gems;
the roof was covered with sapphires, the roof-ornaments were made of gold, and the pinnacle was made of silver.
There is a certain creeper named Āsāvatī; thinking, "It will flower," the devas go to attend upon it for a thousand years.
When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, they go to attend upon it for one year.
From the time it begins to turn yellow and wither, they become joyful in mind. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas turns yellow..."
“Monks, at that time the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven are uplifted, thinking: ‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree is now pale-yellow;
before long it will become covered with green leaves,’ and so forth.
When the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree is in full bloom, its radiance extends for five hundred yojanas all around.”
It spreads; its fragrance travels a hundred leagues with the wind.
When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, there is no need for climbing, nor for using a hook to bend it down, nor for a ladder to gather the flowers.
A "shaking" wind arises and shakes the flowers from their stalks; a "receiving" wind receives them, and a "inserting" wind...
He causes [the assembly] to enter the Sudhamma Hall of the devas; the sweeping wind removes the withered flowers;
the carpeting wind spreads the carpet, arranging the edges of the cloth, the tassels, and the filaments; in the center is the Dhamma-throne, a jeweled couch measuring one *yojana* in size;
above it is held a white parasol three *yojanas* in height; immediately following that is [the throne] of Sakka.
A seat is prepared for the King of the Devas, then for the thirty-two sons of the gods, then for other high-ranking deities.
For other deities, however, a mere flower-pedestal serves as a seat. Having entered the divine assembly hall, the deities sit down.
Then, from the flowers, a cloud of pollen rises and falls, striking against the upper surface of the pedestal, covering the deities to the extent of three-quarters of a league (tigāvuta).
It makes one’s own body appear as if prepared with lac-dye; their sport lasts for four months.
Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One knew the Tāvatiṃsa realm in its entirety, endowed with these perfections.

Likewise, regarding "the realm of the asuras": here, they are called *asura* because, unlike the devas, they do not shine (*suranti*), they do not exercise sovereignty (*īsaranti*), and they do not radiate light (*virocanti*).
The *surās* are gods; they are called *asuras* because they are the adversaries of those [gods].

It is said that Sakka, having been a young brahmin named Magha in the village of Macala, took thirty-three men and, performing meritorious deeds and fulfilling seven conditions of conduct, was reborn in the world of the gods together with his retinue after passing away there. Then the former gods thought, "Visiting sons of the gods have arrived."
Having said, "Let us pay them honor," they offered celestial lotuses and invited him to share half their kingdom.
Sakka was not satisfied with half the kingdom; then the residents, thinking, "Let us pay honor to these visiting deva-sons," prepared fragrant drinks.
Sakka gave a signal to his own retinue: "Sirs, do not [accept] the fragrant drink."

"Drink! You must show at least the appearance of drinking. They did so. The resident deities, having drunk their fill of the fragrant drink served in golden goblets, became intoxicated; they fell here and there upon the golden ground and lay down.
Sakka said, "Seize those rogues! Take away those rogues! and had them seized by the feet at the base of Sineru.
He hurled it down. By the power of Sakka’s merit, all those who followed him also fell right there.

Then, by way of their own karma, a city of the Asuras—ten thousand yojanas in extent—arose at the base of Mount Sineru, brought forth by the seasonal conditions of that karma, and adorned with variegated *pāṭali* trees concealed by *pāricchattaka* blossoms. Sakka turned back from them...
He established a guard for the purpose of preventing their arrival. With reference to this, it is said:
“Between the two cities of Ayujjha, a fivefold protection was established:
the serpent, the skull-bearer, the one who carries the water-pot, the four Madana-yuta spirits, and the four Mahattha.”
In this context, "between the two cities that cannot be fought" means between the two cities of the gods and the asuras.
It is said that these two cities came to be known as "cities that cannot be fought" because they could not be captured by means of war.
For when the asuras were powerful, they would flee from the gods, enter the city of the gods, and close its gates; then the gods... [of the asuras].
Even a hundred thousand [gods] are unable to do anything. When the gods are powerful, they flee from the Asuras and enter the city of the Asuras;
once the gates are closed, even a hundred thousand Sakka-devas are unable to do anything.
Thus, these two cities are called "Impregnable Cities" (Ayujjhapura). Between them, at these five locations, such as the Uraga and others—
Sakka established a guard there. In this context, by the term "uraga," the *nāgas* are meant. They possess great power in the water;

therefore, their guard is stationed at the first terrace of Sineru. It is said that around Sineru, at a distance of five thousand yojanas in both thickness and breadth, there are four enclosures (*paribhaṇḍa*) for the protection of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
These are presided over by the nāgas, garuḷas, kumbhaṇḍas, and yakkhas. It is said that they occupy half of Sineru;
these very places are called the terraces (ālindāni) and the girdles (mekhalāni) of Sineru.
By the word "karoṭi," the supaṇṇas are included. It is said that their food and drink is called "karoṭi," and they received their name from that; [they dwell] on the second terrace.
Their protection: by the term *payassahārī*, the kumbhaṇḍas are included; they are said to be dānavas and rakkhasas, and their protection is in the third gallery.
By the term *madanayuta*, the yakkhas are included; they are said to be of erratic conduct and fond of battle, and their protection is in the fourth gallery.
And the "four of great power" refers to the four Great Kings (*mahārājāno*); for it is they who...

On each side of Sineru, including Yugandhara and the other mountains, they are called "of great purpose" (*mahatthā*) because they serve the great goal of instructing the inhabitants of the five hundred minor islands that surround the great continents. Their protection extends to the fifth terrace.
Furthermore, those asuras are equal to the Tāvatiṃsa devas in their excellence of lifespan, complexion, glory, and sovereignty; therefore, [they guard] themselves in the interval.
Not realizing that the *pāṭali* tree was in bloom, they thought, "This is not the city of the gods; there it is the *pāricchattaka* that blooms, but here it is the *cittapāṭali*.
We have been deceived by Old Sakka after he made us drink liquor, and he has seized our city of the gods.
Let us go and fight him! Having mounted elephants, horses, and chariots with seats of gold, silver, and jewels, [they set out].
Having taken up their positions and being ready for battle, they raise the asura drums and emerge, splitting the waters of the great ocean in two.
When the rain falls upon the devas, they begin to ascend Mount Sineru just as ants ascend an anthill.
Then, first of all, there is a battle between them and the nāgas. In that battle, however, no one...
Only the skin or hide is torn, and no blood flows;
it is merely a mutual terrifying of one another, like a wooden ram-fight among boys.
Even hundreds of millions or thousands of millions of nāgas, having fought with them, return after leading the asuras right back into their own city. But if the asuras are powerful, then—
The *nāgas*, having retreated, join together with the *supaṇṇas* in the second courtyard and fight. This same method applies to the *supaṇṇas* and the others as well.
But when the asuras crush those five positions, even those five forces, though gathered together, retreat.
Then the four Great Kings go and report the situation to Sakka. Sakka—
Having heard their words, he mounts the Vejayanta chariot, which is one and a half *yojanas* long, and either departs himself or sends one of his sons.
Having thus departed on a single day and attacked the Asuras in battle, he casts them into the ocean and sets up statues resembling himself at the four gates; therefore, the Asuras—
Even when the Nāgas and others have come after defeating [the gods], they flee upon seeing the likeness of Indra, thinking, "Sakka has emerged.
Thus, because they are the adversaries of the Suras, they are called Asuras—such as Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others—and their abode is the Asurabhavana.
To show that it is ten thousand yojanas in both length and breadth, it is stated: "Likewise, the Asurabhavana."
In the phrase "the great Avīci hell and Jambudīpa," the word *tathā* (likewise) should also be applied here;
the meaning is that the great Avīci hell and Jambudīpa are likewise exactly ten thousand *yojanas*.
Furthermore, in this context, the interior of the great Avīci hell is one hundred *yojanas* in both length and breadth; the iron ground, the iron roof, and each of the walls are nine *yojanas* thick.
It occurs thus: a flame rises from the eastern wall, reaches the western wall, pierces through it, and goes beyond for a hundred yojanas. The same method applies to the other directions as well.
Thus, in terms of length and breadth including the boundary of the net, it measures three hundred and eighteen yojanas; in circumference, nine hundred and fifty-four yojanas.
[It is] yojanas [in width]. However, including the surrounding protuberances, it is ten thousand yojanas.
Why, then, has this hell come to be designated as "Avīci"? "Vīci" means an interval;
and since there is no interval there—neither between the flames of fire, nor between beings, nor in the suffering—it has therefore come to be designated as "Avīci. From its eastern wall...
The flames, having risen up, travel a hundred yojanas while weaving together, then pierce through the wall and go another hundred yojanas beyond it.
This same principle applies to the other directions as well. Thus, because there is no interval between the flames, it is called Avīci (the Uninterrupted).
Within its space of a hundred yojanas, however, beings are packed without any gaps, like fine flour ground in a mill and filled into a tube. "In this..."
It cannot be said that "a being exists in this place" or "there is none in this place," for there is no space between those who are walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or being cooked;
those who are walking do not obstruct those who are standing, sitting, or lying down.
Thus, because there is no interval between beings, it is called Avīci (the Uninterrupted). Furthermore, in the door of the body, there are six [consciousnesses] accompanied by equanimity.
...consciousnesses arise; one is accompanied by suffering.

Even so, just as when six drops of honey are placed on the tip of the tongue and a single drop of molten copper is placed there, because of the intensity of its burning power, only that [drop] is perceived while the others become negligible, so too here, because of the intensity of its burning power, only suffering is continuous, while the others—
"Abbohārikāni" means that it is called "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted) because of the continuity of suffering.
They say, "And this great hell, Avīci, is situated beneath Jambudvīpa.
Now, Jambudvīpa measures ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; and therein, [the area] measuring four thousand yojanas...
A portion of that [ocean], submerged by water due to the exhaustion of the merit of the beings who enjoy it, came to be designated as the "sea.
It should be understood that humans dwell within an area measuring three thousand yojanas, and Mount Himavanta is established within an area measuring three thousand yojanas.
In the passages beginning with "Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas," the measurement is shown both in length and in breadth.
This should be understood. Therein, Jambudīpa is shaped like a cart;
it is endowed with ninety-six hundred thousand millions of ports, fifty-six hundred thousand palaces of jewels, ninety-nine hundred thousand market-towns, and three times sixty-three thousand cities.
It is said that from the beginning, there were exactly sixty-three thousand cities in Jambudīpa.
Thus for the second time, thus for the third time. When those are added together, they amount to one hundred and eighty-nine thousand.
"Doṇamukha" refers to the principal hall, which served as the site for the origin of the great city.
Aparagoyāna is mirror-shaped; Pubbavideha is half-moon shaped.
Uttarakuru is shaped like a seat (*pīṭha*). They say that the faces of the people dwelling there, as well as those of the inhabitants of the surrounding islands, are also shaped accordingly.
Furthermore, this particular distinction here should be understood as being accomplished through the power of the merit of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. Regarding that, it is said:

In various places, trees with branches and twigs densely covered by thick foliage—resembling gabled houses and delightful to behold—fulfill the function of dwellings for those people; there they live happily.

Furthermore, other well-grown trees stand there, their tips always in bloom. The reservoirs of water, too, are covered with blossoming lotuses, white lilies, *sogandhika* lilies, and other such flowers.
At all times they remain emitting a supreme fragrance from every side.
Their bodies, moreover, being free from the defect of excessive height and endowed with perfect proportions, are not overcome by old age;
thus, until the end of their lifespan, they remain devoid of defects such as wrinkles and grey hair, possessing undiminished speed, strength, prowess, and beauty.
It remains. Because they subsist on the fruit of non-exertion, they have no suffering arising from the search for food through such means as agriculture or commerce;

for that very reason, they have no possession of male or female slaves, laborers, and so forth. Nor is there any danger there from cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, creeping things, or poisonous creatures.
Just as, for instance, in the last month of summer, at the time of dawn, the temperature is perfectly temperate—neither cold nor hot—so it is there.
In the same way, at all times the temperature there remains perfectly balanced between cold and heat, and no affliction or distress arises for them.
They consume rice that grows without being cultivated—free from husks and powder, pure, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains—which they cook over a fire made of smokeless embers.
It is said that there are stones there called "flame-stones" (*jotika-pāsāṇa*); then, those three stones...
Setting aside [the vessel], they place it upon a pan; heat is generated by means of stones and cooks that [food].
There is no other curry or sauce, yet for those eating, its flavor is exactly to their liking.
Furthermore, as they eat it, no disease whatsoever arises among them, such as leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, cough, epilepsy, or old age.
They give to those who have arrived at that place; indeed, they possess no mind of stinginess.
Even Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others of great psychic power go there and receive almsfood.
Nor are they hunchbacked, dwarfish, one-eyed, club-footed, lame, crippled in their wings, deformed, or deficient in their faculties.
The women there are neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;

they possess forms of supreme beauty. For indeed, they have long fingers, copper-colored nails, prominent breasts, slender waists, faces like the full moon, large eyes, soft limbs, shapely thighs, white teeth, deep navels, slim calves, long, dark, curling hair, and broad, beautiful hips.
Neither excessively hairy nor hairless, they are fortunate, with bodies pleasant to touch according to the season;
soft-spoken and gentle in their speech, adorned with various ornaments, they move about appearing as if always sixteen years of age. Men likewise appear as if twenty-five years of age.
Sons do not feel lustful attachment toward their mothers and others; this is the natural law (dhammatā) therein.
There, men and women dwell in the delight of sensual pleasure for exactly seven days; thereafter, as if free from passion, they depart at their ease.
Therein, unlike here, there is no suffering rooted in conception, no suffering rooted in the protection of the womb, nor any suffering rooted in birth;
for children emerge from the mother’s womb like golden statues from a red cloth casing.
Unstained by phlegm and other such secretions, they emerge with ease; this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in that regard.
However, after giving birth to a son or a daughter, the mother places them in a place suitable for their movement and departs as she pleases, without looking back.
When men or women see them lying there, they offer their own fingers to them.
By the power of their karma, milk flows forth from them, and by that the children are sustained.
Growing in this way, within just a few days they acquire strength; the girls reach womanhood and the boys reach manhood.
Furthermore, garments and ornaments of various colors and patterns are produced for them right there from the wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha).
Indeed, fine garments with soft and pleasant textures hang here and there from the wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*).
And from the wish-fulfilling trees come golden ornaments, interlaced with various colored gems blazing with networks of diverse rays,
variegated with many kinds of floral designs, vine-patterns, and wall-decorations, and fashioned to fit the head, neck, waist, hands, and feet.

In that way, musical instruments such as lutes, drums, small drums, hand-clappers, conchs, flutes, cymbals, and their various accompaniments, as well as stringed instruments like the *vallakī*, hang down from it.
And there, many fruit trees bear fruits the size of jars;
they possess a sweet flavor, and by consuming them, those beings are not afflicted by hunger or thirst even for seven days.
There, too, flow rivers with very pure water, with excellent landing places, delightful, free from mud, with bottoms of sand, neither too cold nor too hot;
they are covered with fragrant water-born flowers, and at all times they flow while sweet-smelling breezes blow.
There are no thorny, harsh shrubs or creepers there; rather, they are entirely without thorns and are covered with flowers and fruits.
The sandalwood and agarwood trees exude their resin of their own accord.

When those wishing to bathe place their clothes and ornaments together at a river landing, descend into the river, bathe, and emerge, each person takes the uppermost garment or ornament as they come out;
it does not occur to them, "This is mine, this is another's. From that very fact...
Among them there is neither quarrel nor dispute; their play for sensual pleasure lasts only seven days, after which they wander about as if free from passion.
