Wherever they wish to sleep upon a tree, a bed is found right there.
When beings die, they do not weep or grieve, but having adorned the body, they lay it down. And for that long, such [beings] remain.

Birds approach and carry the dead to another island; therefore, there is no cemetery or place of impurity there, nor do the dead from that place arise in hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of hungry ghosts.
They say, "By the power of the five precepts established through natural law, they are reborn in the world of the devas. For only a thousand years...
Furthermore, it should be understood that their lifespan is not constant at all times; rather, all of this is established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā*), just like the five precepts.
"In the intervals between them" means in the spaces between those world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). "World-void hells" (*lokantarika-niraya*):
the interval or gap between worlds—that is, between world-spheres—is the "world-void" (*lokantara*); those existing therein are the "world-void [hells]. For when three cart wheels—
Between the three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) situated like the interstices between adjacent bowls placed close together, there is a single Lokantarika hell for each.
As for its measurement, it is eight thousand yojanas in extent;
it is perpetually open, being neither covered from below nor closed from above. For just as there is a covering of water below...
"There is no earth" means that the intermediate hells (*lokantarika-niraya*) are unenclosed;

likewise, because there are no celestial mansions (*devavimāna*) as there are in the world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) above, they are unenclosed and uncovered, and are possessed of darkness capable of obstructing the arising of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise therein due to the absence of light. [This occurs] simultaneously across the three continents.
Although the moon and sun are capable of producing light, they do not provide light there.
For, as they move through a portion of space equal in measure to Yugandhara, they pass through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain;
and having passed beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain, they reach the Lokantarika hells. Therefore, they do not provide light there—such is the case for eye-consciousness.
It does not arise. However, when the radiance arises for an omniscient Bodhisatta at the time of taking rebirth-linking and so forth, then eye-consciousness arises.
On that day, they see one another, thinking, "Indeed, there are other beings who have been born here.
Yet this radiance does not remain even for the duration of drinking a single bowl of gruel; it lasts only as long as the snap of a finger.
Like a flash of lightning, it issues forth and vanishes even as those who say, "What is this?
are still speaking. But what kind of karma must be performed for beings to be reborn there?

It is the grave, cruel, and heavy offense committed against one's mother and father, or against righteous recluses and brahmins, as well as other acts of violence, such as the killing of living beings, committed day after day.
They arise in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, such as the Abhaya-coras, Nāga-coras, and others.
Their bodies are three gavutas in height, and they have long claws like those of bats. Like bats clinging to trees, they cling to the base of the world-sphere with their claws;
when, while crawling about, they come within arm’s reach of one another, they think, "We have found our prey."
Thinking they are food, those who attempt to seize them turn over and fall into the water that sustains the world;
even when struck by the wind, they break off like honeycomb fruits and fall into the water.
As soon as they have fallen, because of its extreme cold and the absence of the heat of the sun, they dissolve like a lump of dough in extremely caustic water. This very state of extreme cold—

For it was with this intention that its extreme saltiness was stated. Indeed, that water which establishes the eon, poured down by the great clouds that bring prosperity, cannot possibly be as salty as the water that destroys the eon.
If it were so, even the earth would dissolve; or else, through the power of their evil karma, even for those *petas*, the natural water would turn into spittle.
It is said that "they dissolve like a lump of dough in water that has become utterly alkaline," because at that time the water acquires a state of extreme alkalinity.
"Infinite" means immeasurable; they cannot be measured by others as being "this many. And the Blessed One knew them with his infinite Buddha-knowledge, [realizing]:
"Space is infinite, the multitude of beings is infinite, and world-systems are infinite."
For even the threefold [knowledge] is delimited by the Buddha’s knowledge because it itself is infinite.

For as far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit.
Therefore it is said: “He knew by means of the infinite Buddha-knowledge,” and so forth. And its infinity is due precisely to its penetration of the infinite knowable.
It should be understood that therein [the world] is to be known because of his unimpeded movement. Now, concluding the matter as it has been stated, he said:
"Thus, even the world of space is known by him in every way.

Furthermore, here the fact that the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) and so forth are also known should be mentioned; therefore, the turning away and the rest should also be understood from the beginning in this manner.

It should be understood that there are four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) of the world-cycle: the period of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of remaining dissolved (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), the period of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*), and the period of remaining evolved (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).
In this context, "dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭa*) refers to the process of destruction; it is the incalculable eon during which the world is perishing. In actual fact, however, this is simply time;
its destruction should be understood in terms of the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) occurring at that time. The period following dissolution is the time of remaining dissolved.
The period of subsistence during the eon of expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). Expansion (*vivaṭṭa*) means the process of opening up, manifestation, or increasing;
it is the increasing *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*. That too, in its actual sense, is simply time; its increase should be understood by way of the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) occurring at that time.

The period of subsistence following expansion is the "subsistence during the eon of expansion" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). In that regard, there are three types of contractions (*saṃvaṭṭa*): contraction by fire, contraction by water, and [contraction by wind].
The wind-dissolution. There are three limits of dissolution: the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms.
When the aeon dissolves by means of fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames.
When it dissolves by means of water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved away by water. When it dissolves by means of wind, [everything] below the Vehapphala realm...
It is destroyed from below by wind.
In terms of its extent, however, during all three periods of contraction (*saṃvaṭṭakāla*), one Buddha-field (*buddhakkhetta*) is destroyed.
A Buddha-field is of three kinds: the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākkhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakkhetta*). Among these, the field of birth—
It extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*), which tremble when the Tathāgata undergoes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and other such events.

For to whatever extent the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge—beginning with the knowledge of rebirth-linking—is manifested by its own inherent force, intensified by the fruit of his merit, all that is called the field for the production of the Buddha-sprout; thus it is termed the "Buddha-field" (*buddhakhetta*).

It is said [thus]. As for the field of command (*āṇā-khetta*), however, it extends as far as a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), wherein the efficacy of these protective charms (*paritta*)—namely, the Ratana-sutta, the Khandha-paritta, the Dhajagga-paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya-paritta, and the Mora-paritta—is operative.
For one who possesses psychic power (*iddhimā*) and has attained mastery over the mind can, wherever within the field of command, [exercise that power].
Having stood within one world-system and performed a protective chant (paritta) for one's own sake, one remains as one who has performed the chant even when going to another world-system.

When a protective chant is performed for the sake of all beings while standing in a single world-system, the power of that protection indeed reaches all beings within the sphere of authority, because the deities must accept the protection there; therefore:
That is called the field of authority (*āṇā-khetta*). The field of range (*visaya-khetta*), however, is infinite and immeasurable.
For within the infinite and immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), whatever the Tathāgata desires to know, he knows it, because the Buddha’s knowledge functions in dependence upon his will.
Thus, among these three fields of a Buddha, one—the field of authority—perishes; in that [case]...
However, when it perishes, the field of birth has already perished. Even as it perishes, it perishes all at once;
even as it re-forms, it re-forms all at once. In this way, its destruction and its re-formation are to be understood.
At the time when the eon (*kappa*) is destroyed by fire, first of all, a great eon-destroying cloud arises throughout a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
One great rain falls; people, being delighted, bring out all their seeds and sow them.
But when the crops have grown only as far as they have been trampled by cattle, it thunders like the bray of a donkey and not even a single drop falls; at that time, the rain is utterly cut off.
It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said: "There comes a time, monks, when for many years..."
It is said: "For many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years, the rain does not fall.
Even beings who depend on rain, having passed away, are reborn in the Brahma-worlds such as Parittābha and others, as well as deities who subsist on flowers and fruits.
When such a long period has elapsed, the water in various places comes to exhaustion.
Then, in due course, even fish and turtles, having passed away, are reborn in the Brahma-world, as are beings from the hell realms.
Regarding this, some say that hell-beings perish upon the appearance of the seventh sun.
However, there is no rebirth in the Brahma-world without jhāna; and among these [beings], some are oppressed by famine, while others—
Since they are incapable of attaining meditative absorption (jhāna), how do they arise there? It is by virtue of the absorption they attained in the world of the gods.

For at that time, when it is known that "after the passing of one hundred thousand years, the emergence of the aeon will occur," the sense-sphere deities called Lokabyūhas—having disheveled hair, with their heads bare and their hair scattered, weeping-faced and wiping away tears with their hands, and clad in red garments—[arise].
Assuming extremely hideous disguises and wandering along the public highways, they proclaimed thus: "O sirs, O sirs!
After the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the dissolution of the eon will occur; this world will be destroyed.
Even the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be consumed by fire."
“They will perish; until the destruction of the world reaches as far as the Brahma-world, dear sirs, cultivate loving-kindness;
cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity, dear sirs; attend upon your mothers; attend upon your fathers;
be respectful toward the elders of the family. And because those deities arrange and gather together the world, they are called “world-arrangers” (lokabyūhā).

They are so called because, upon seeing them, people—whether standing or sitting anywhere—become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and, overcome by agitation, gather together in a place near them.
But how do they know of the emergence of a world-age (*kappa-vuṭṭhāna*)? "Impelled by the natural law (*dhammatā*)," say the teachers. "By the sight of such a sign," [others say].
Some say [they were sent] by the Brahma-devas; others say [by the devas].

Having heard their words, most humans and earth-devas (bhummadevatā) become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega); with hearts softened toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness (mettā) and are reborn in the world of the devas.
There, having partaken of divine ambrosia (sudhā), they then perform the preliminary work (parikamma) on the wind-kasina (vāyokasiṇa).
They attain the jhānas by means of this. It is said that for the devas, the jhānas on the wind-kasiṇa succeed with ease due to their grasping the wind-element, which possesses a pleasant touch.
Furthermore, other beings who are destined for the woeful states are reborn in the world of the devas through karma to be experienced in a subsequent life.
For indeed, a being wandering in saṃsāra who is devoid of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life [does not so arise].
There is none. They too attain jhāna there in that very same way. Thus, by virtue of the jhāna attained in the world of the devas, all are reborn in the Brahma-world.

And this is stated according to the general rule (*yebhuyyavasena*). However, some say: "Beings from the states of misery (*apāya*) are reborn in other world-systems when the world-systems are contracting; they are not [reborn in the Brahma-world]."

For it can be understood that all beings from the states of misery (*apāya*) are then reborn in the realms of form and formlessness, since it is impossible for those with long lifespans in the states of misery to be reborn in the divine worlds.
However, one who holds a fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhika*) is not released from hell even when the aeon (*kappa*) perishes;
therefore, instead of being reborn there, he is reborn on the back of the world-sphere (*piṭṭhicakkavāḷa*). This is due to his fixed wrong view.
For one possessed of that [defilement], there is indeed no emergence from existence. For one possessed of it, there is neither heaven nor the Path;
therefore, after being reborn in a hell elsewhere from a world-system undergoing dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭamāna-cakkavāḷa*), he is tormented.
But does the back of the world-system not burn? It does burn. Even while that is burning, he [remains] in the space on one side...
They say, "It cooks in that region.
But after the cessation of the rains, when a long period of time has passed, a second sun appears.
Once it has appeared, neither the demarcation of night nor the demarcation of day is discernible. [There is] one sun...
It rises; one [sun] sets, and the world becomes as if scorched by the uninterrupted heat of the sun.
And whereas there is a Sun-devaputta in the sun-mansion that appears before the time of the aeon’s dissolution, such is not the case for the sun that destroys the aeon.
However, at the time of the aeon’s dissolution, just like other devas of the sense-sphere realm, the Sun-devaputta also generates jhāna.
He is reborn in the Brahma-world. However, others maintain that the solar disc continues to revolve, becoming even more radiant and more majestic; that it vanishes and another arises in its place.
In that regard, while the ordinary sun is present, clouds and columns of smoke also exist in the sky, but when the sun that destroys the eon is present, [the sky] is free from smoke and clouds.
The sky becomes as stainless as the surface of a mirror. With the exception of the five great rivers, the water in all other small streams and such dries up.
After a long period has passed from that point, a third sun appears; with its appearance, even the great rivers dry up.
After a long period has passed from that point, a fourth sun appears; with its appearance, [the waters] in the Himavat...

The sources of the great rivers—the Sīhapapāta lake, the Mandākinī lake, the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa lake, the Rathakāra lake, the Anotatta lake, the Chaddanta lake, and the Kuṇāla lake—these seven great lakes dry up.
Furthermore, after the lapse of a long period, a fifth sun appears; with its appearance, even water sufficient to wet a finger-joint gradually ceases to remain in the great ocean.
After the passing of a further long period of time, a sixth sun appears;

with its appearance, the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) becomes a single mass of smoke, its moisture completely consumed by that smoke. For the water element (*āpodhātu*), which exists there by binding and consolidating the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) in various places, comes to total exhaustion through the appearance of the sixth sun.
And as it is with this [world-system], so it is with hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
After the passing of an even longer period than that, a seventh sun appears;

through its appearance, the entire world-system, together with hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems, becomes a single mass of flame, including the peaks of Mount Sineru which are divided into heights of one hundred *yojana*s and so forth.
Having dissolved away, they vanish right there in space. That mass of flames rises up and seizes the realm of the Four Great Kings.
Having burned the golden palaces, the jewel palaces, and the gem-studded palaces there, it seizes the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
By this same method, it seizes everything up to the plane of the first jhāna; having burned the three Brahmā worlds there as well, it reaches the Ābhassara realm.
It remains. As long as even the slightest trace of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) exists, it does not go out.
But with the total exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena, it goes out like the flame of a fire fed with ghee or oil, leaving not even soot behind.
Together with the lower space, the upper space becomes one vast darkness.
Thus, when the world-system has remained for one incalculable aeon as a single plain, the rain begins to fall from the sky for the purpose of establishing the world’s configuration;
at first it is like a fall of snow during the intermediate season.

Then, the streams of water become the size of grains, rice-grains, mung beans, black grams, jujubes, myrobalans, *eḷāluka* roots, pumpkins, and gourds, and gradually increase to the size of a *usabha*, two *usabhas*, half a *gāvuta*, a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, a *yojana*, two *yojanas*, and so forth...
Having become a hundred yojanas and then a thousand yojanas in extent, it fills the interior of a hundred thousand million world-systems as far as the unshaken Brahma-world and then vanishes.
That water, stirred up by winds from below and from the sides, becomes solidified into a mass,
like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
If it is asked, "How does it make that great mass of water solid? [The answer is: "By providing openings for the wind.
For it provides openings here and there for that wind. Thus, being compressed and consolidated by the wind and gradually diminishing, it sinks down step by step.
As the water sinks, in the place of the Brahmā-world, there is the Brahmā-world; and in the place of the four upper sense-sphere heavens (*kāmāvacara*), there are those heavens.
And the celestial worlds appear. However, because they are connected to the earth, the abodes of the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa devas do not yet appear.
When [the water] has descended to the previous level of the earth, powerful winds arise;
these hold it back, rendering it motionless like water standing in a covered cistern. It is sweet water.
As it undergoes total exhaustion, it brings forth a layer of "taste-earth" (*rasapathavī*) above; the earth solidifies like a lotus leaf upon the surface of water.
It is endowed with excellent color, as well as with fragrance and flavor, like a crust on top of thickened rice gruel that has no water.
Furthermore, among these, the site of the Great Enlightenment Seat (*mahābodhipallaṅka*) is the last to perish when the world is being destroyed.
It should be understood that when [the world] is stabilizing, it first stabilizes there.

At that time, beings who had previously been reborn in the Ābhassara Brahmā-world pass away from there—either through the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit—and being of spontaneous birth (opapātika), they arise here. They are self-luminous and move through the sky.
Having tasted that earth of flavor, overcome by craving, they set about making lumps of it to eat.
Then their own radiance vanished and darkness arose. Seeing the darkness, they were afraid.
Thereupon, to dispel their fear and produce courage in them, the solar disk appeared, fifty yojanas in diameter.
It became manifest. Seeing it, they were thrilled and delighted, thinking, "We have obtained light!
And because it arose dispelling the fear of those who were afraid and producing courage, they gave it the name "Sūriya" (the Sun).
Then, when the sun had made the day bright and had set, they thought, "Even that light which we obtained has vanished."
Again they become afraid. It occurs to them: "It would be well indeed if we could obtain another light.
As if knowing their minds, the lunar disk, measuring forty-nine *yojanas*, becomes manifest. Seeing it, they become even more exceedingly joyful and delighted, thinking:
"He has arisen as if knowing our desire; therefore, he is the Moon (*canda*)."
"Let him be named Canda," they say, and so they give him the name Canda.
Thus, when the moon and sun have appeared, the lunar mansions and the forms of the stars appear;
from that time forth, days and nights become known, and gradually months, fortnights, seasons, and years [are established] according to the moon and sun.
On the very day they become manifest, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the Himavanta mountains, and the islands and oceans appear.
And these all appear simultaneously, neither before nor after, on the full-moon day of the month of Phagguṇa.
How so? Just as when millet porridge is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once, and certain areas become heaped up.
Some are low-lying, some are level; even so, in the place of the mound-like elevations there are mountains, in the low-lying places there are oceans, and in the level places there are islands.
Then, as those beings were consuming the savory earth (*rasapathavī*), by way of their karma some became possessed of beauty.
Some become ugly. Thereupon, those who are beautiful despise those who are ugly;
because of that pride, even that savory earth disappears, and a crust of earth appears.
Then, by that same process, that too disappears, and then a creeping plant (padālatā) appears. By that same process, that too disappears.
Rice that ripens without being cultivated appears—free from husks and powder, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains. Then vessels appear for them.
Having placed the rice in a vessel, they set it upon a stone slab; a flame of fire spontaneously arises and cooks it.
That cooked rice becomes like jasmine or *jāti* flowers; it requires neither soup nor condiment.
Or whatever was to be done, whatever flavor they desired to eat, that very flavor it became.
As they were consuming that gross food, from that time forward urine and feces began to arise.
For indeed, the earth of flavors, the earth-lichen, and the "padālatā" (the creeping plant)—having dispelled hunger like the *sudhā* food when consumed—[were carried] by the flavor-carrying channels.
They remain merely augmenting the nutritive essence (*rasa*) by way of the subtlety of the substance, not as a secretion;

and by that very subtlety, there is only the fuel for grasping. But when boiled rice has been consumed, although it increases the nutritive essence, it releases a secretion by way of the grossness of the substance, thereby producing urine and feces.
Then, for the purpose of their emerging, the openings of the wounds burst open. The masculinity of the male and the femininity of the female become manifest.

For as long as the sensual lust within the mental continuums of beings has been suppressed by the force of the access-concentration (upacāra-jhāna) that occurred in previous existences, the faculties of femininity and masculinity—which serve as the proximate cause for intense sensual lust—do not yet appear.

They appeared. But when, due to its interruption, the intense passion for sensual pleasures found an opportunity, then, through that underlying tendency (*upanissaya*), those [passions] arose within the individual existences (*attabhāva*) of beings;
at that time, the woman gazed excessively upon the man, and the man likewise gazed excessively upon the woman.
Due to the condition of their excessive gazing, a fever of sensual desire (*kāmapariḷāha*) arose, and from that, sexual intercourse.

They practice what is contrary to the Dhamma. Because of practicing what is contrary to the Dhamma, being censured and harassed by the wise, they build houses for the sake of concealing that unrighteousness.
While living in those houses, gradually following the example of a certain indolent being, they begin to store up possessions. Then...
From that time on, even the husks and chaff began to envelop the grain, and it no longer sprouted in the places where it had been harvested.
Gathering together, they lamented: "Alas, friends, evil things have appeared among beings!
For formerly we were mind-made," as should be expanded upon according to the method stated in the Aggañña Sutta. Thereafter, they established boundaries.
Then a certain being took what was not given from another. After rebuking him twice, on the third occasion they struck him with hands, clods of earth, and sticks.
When theft, quarreling, false speech, and the taking of sticks had thus arisen, they gathered together and deliberated:
"What if we were to appoint one being who shall [act] rightly for us?"
“Let him who should censure be censured; let him who should revile be reviled; let him who should be expelled be expelled;
and we, moreover, shall provide him with a share of the fine rice.
When the beings had thus reached a consensus, during this very kappa, at that time, among those beings, this Blessed One himself, while still a bodhisatta, was the most handsome.
He was more worthy of being seen, possessed of greater authority, endowed with wisdom, and capable of exercising restraint and encouragement.
They approached him, requested his consent, and formally elected him. Because he was elected by that great multitude, he is called Mahāsammata (“Greatly Elected”);
because he is the lord of fields, he is called Kṣatriya (“Noble”); and because he delights others through righteousness and equity, he is called Rāja (“King”)—thus he is known by these three names.
It was thus manifested. For whatever is a place of wonder in the world, the Bodhisatta alone is the first person therein;
thus, with the Bodhisatta as the beginning, when the circle of Khattiyas had been established, the other castes, such as the Brahmins and so forth, gradually came into being.
In this context, from the great cloud that destroys the eon until the severing of the net [of life], this constitutes one incalculable aeon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*).

It is said: from the cessation of the net that destroys the eon until the great cloud of prosperity that fills a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems, this is called the second incalculable period, the "subsistence of the contraction" (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

From the great cloud of prosperity until the manifestation of the moon and sun, this is called the third incalculable period, the "expansion" (*vivaṭṭa*). From the manifestation of the moon and sun until the great cloud that once again destroys the eon—
This fourth incalculable aeon is called the period of expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). The period of expansion comprises sixty-four intermediate aeons (*antarakappa*);
some say it comprises twenty intermediate aeons. The remaining incalculable aeons are equal in measure to that in terms of time.
These four incalculable aeons constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*). Thus, first of all, the destruction by fire and the re-establishment [of the world] should be understood.

But at the time when a world-cycle (*kappa*) is destroyed by water, it should be explained in detail according to the method previously stated, beginning with: "First, a great cloud that destroys the world-cycle arises. However, this is the distinction:
whereas in that case there is a second sun, here a great cloud of corrosive water (*khārudaka*) that destroys the world-cycle arises. At first, it rains very fine rain.
Gradually, filling hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) with great torrents, it rains.
The earth, mountains, and other things, wherever they are touched by the caustic water (*khārudaka*), dissolve; the water is held up on all sides by the winds.
From the very bottom of the earth upwards as far as the plane of the second jhāna, the water takes hold. By that very caustic water, wherever [things] are touched...
Some say that the earth, mountains, and so forth simply dissolve like salt or sugar thrown into water;
therefore, they become one and the same water together with the water that supports the earth. Others, however, state:
"Having completely destroyed both the water that supports the earth and the mass of wind that supports it, [the fire] itself remains everywhere as a single, solid mass. This...
This is appropriate. However, having caused even the six higher Brahma-worlds to dissolve, it remains reaching as far as the Subhakiṇha realm;
as long as there exists even a minute amount of anything comprised within conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it does not subside.
But once it has overwhelmed all conditioned phenomena that follow upon the water, it suddenly subsides and vanishes. [Thus] the upper space merges with the lower space.
"One great darkness exists"—all this is just as previously stated. However, here the world reappears beginning with the Ābhassara Brahma-world.
Beings fall from the Subhakiṇha realm and are reborn in the stations of the Ābhassaras and so forth.

Therein, from the time of the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the "water for the funeral pyre" that destroys the aeon—this constitutes one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeya*).
From the cutting off of the water until the appearance of the great cloud of prosperity—this is the second incalculable eon.
From the great cloud of prosperity until the manifestation of the moon and sun—this is the third incalculable eon.
From the manifestation of the moon and sun until the great cloud that destroys the world-cycle (kalpa)—this is the fourth incalculable eon. These are the four incalculable eons.
There is one great aeon (*mahākappa*). In this way, the destruction by water and the re-establishment [of the world] are to be understood.

At the time when an aeon is destroyed by wind, it should be explained in detail according to the method previously stated, beginning with: "At the very outset, a great cloud that destroys the aeon arises.
However, this is the distinction: whereas there [in the case of destruction by fire], there was a second sun, here—
In this way, a wind arises here for the purpose of destroying the world-age (*kappa*). First, it stirs up coarse dust;
then, fine dust, fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, stones, and so forth—up to stones as large as gabled houses—and trees standing in uneven places.
These, having risen from the earth into the sky, do not fall back down again.
Right there, they are reduced to powder and dust and pass into non-existence.
Then, in due course, a wind arises from beneath the great earth, overturns the earth, turns its roots upward, and hurls it into the sky.
Even portions of the earth measuring a hundred yojanas, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas in extent, are likewise cast up.
Having burst apart and been tossed by the force of the wind, they are reduced to powder and dust right there in the sky and pass into non-existence.
The wind even lifts up the Cakkavāḷa mountains and the Sineru mountain and hurls them into the sky;
these strike one another, are reduced to powder and dust, and perish. In this very manner, it destroys the celestial mansions situated on the earth and those situated in the sky.
Having destroyed the world of the devas belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), it destroys hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
Therein, the world-systems collide with world-systems, the Himalayas with Himalayas, and Mount Sinerus with Mount Sinerus; having met one another, they are reduced to powder and destroyed.
The wind seizes everything from the earth up to the plane of the third *jhāna*, including the nine Brahma-worlds.
Having destroyed [the Vehapphala world], it remains having reached [the next level].

Thus, together with the water that supports the earth and the wind that supports that water, all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) are destroyed; and then it itself is destroyed because of the absence of any cause for its persistence.
Together with the lower space, the upper space becomes one, a great darkness; everything else is as previously described. However, here—
The world manifests beginning with the Subhakiṇha Brahmā-world. Beings pass away from the Vehapphala realm and are reborn in the Subhakiṇha abode and other such places.
Therein, from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the wind that destroys the aeon—this constitutes one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeya*).
From the cessation of the wind until the great cloud of prosperity—this is the second incalculable period, and so forth.
It is exactly as previously stated. In this way, both the destruction and the stabilization by wind should be understood.

Now, for what reason does the world thus undergo destruction? For although the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) through their own inherent nature is causeless due to the absence of a separate agent of destruction, there is no cessation of the continuity (*santāna*) that is devoid of a cause.
This is just as it is with the classes of beings; so it is also with the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*).
There must be a cause for destruction; therefore, what is the cause for such a dissolution of the world? The root of unwholesomeness is the cause.
For just as the world first expands there through the power of the merit of the beings born therein, so too does it contract through the power of their evil karma;
thus, when the roots of unwholesomeness have increased, the world is destroyed in this manner.
Just as, due to the predominance of lust, hatred, and delusion respectively, these three types of intermediate aeons—
the disease intermediate aeon, the weapon intermediate aeon, and the famine intermediate aeon— arise during an incalculable aeon while the world is in the process of expansion; so too,
these three aforementioned contractions occur precisely through the predominance of lust and the other defilements.
In that regard, when lust (*rāga*) is more predominant, one is destroyed by fire; when hatred (*dosa*) is more predominant, one is destroyed by water.
For when hatred is more predominant, destruction by sharp caustic liquid is appropriate, as if by excessive hatred itself.
Some, however, say: "When hatred is more predominant, [one is destroyed] by fire; when lust is [more predominant], by water. Their intended meaning (*adhippāya*), it is said, is as follows:
It is appropriate that hatred, which is like an overt enemy, is like fire;
and that lust, which is like a hidden enemy, is like poison and water. However, when delusion is predominant, it is destroyed by wind.
Even while being destroyed in this way, it is destroyed by fire for seven consecutive times, and on the eighth time by water; then again for seven times by fire, and on the eighth [time]...

"By water": thus, perishing in this manner every eighth turn, after being destroyed by water seven times, it is again destroyed by fire for seven turns. At this point, sixty-three *kappas* have passed.
During this interval, the wind—having found its opportunity by warding off even the turn for destruction by water that had arrived—[destroys it] during a lifespan of full sixty-four *kappas*.

Destroying the Subhakiṇha realm, it destroys the world. Here, however, because passion (rāga) prevails extensively among beings, the destruction of the world should be understood as occurring many times by way of fire.

Thus, in this manner, the Blessed One knew the spatial world—both that which is being destroyed by these causes and that which, having been destroyed, re-forms and remains—as it truly is; in this way, for him, the spatial world is [known] in every respect.
It should be understood as "having known.
Now, concluding what was stated below—that "he is a knower of the world because he has known the world in every way"—the text says:

"Thus, because he has known the world in every way, he is a knower of the world. In this context, "in every way" means according to its various classifications, such as by way of characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so forth.

The meaning is: "one who has understood the world in all its modes"—that is, the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*) by way of its divisions such as underlying tendencies (*āsaya*); the world of beings (*satta-loka*) by way of its divisions such as their dispositions; and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*) by way of its divisions such as its dimensions and shapes.
Now, in order to comment on the meaning of the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), he said: "But by his own qualities," and so forth. Therein—
*Attano* is a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "from himself. It is to be construed with the phrase "one who is more distinguished than himself by his qualities.
Here, the inclusion of the comparative suffix *-tara* is made because it serves to explain the meaning of the word *anuttaro*, not because there exists anyone actually superior to him.
Indeed, in the world including the devas, there is no one even comparable to the Tathāgata.
How could there be anyone equal to him? What need is there to speak of one who is superior? "Of anyone" means of anyone at all.

He "overcomes" because, from the very moment of his attainment through the excellence of the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*)—which arises from the pre-eminent development of shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), faith (*saddhā*), mindfulness (*sati*), energy (*vīriya*), and wisdom (*paññā*) as their specific supporting conditions—he is not shared by others, owing to the abandonment of their opposites along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).

The Teacher’s quality of virtue has reached the highest perfection; therefore, the Blessed One proceeds having utterly surpassed the world with its devas, and is not himself surpassed by anyone—this is the intended meaning.
The same should be stated, as appropriate, regarding the qualities of concentration and so forth.
These qualities, beginning with virtue, should be understood as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane; however, the knowledge and vision of liberation—
The mundane [knowledge] belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
If this is so, how does it surpass the world together with its devas? Because its power is incomparable;
for even that [mundane knowledge] is indeed superior in terms of its object, its mode of occurrence, and its manner of manifestation. For it is not shared by others.
It proceeds concerning the quality of liberation (vimutti-guṇa) of the Teacher; and as it proceeds, it does so having made that which is beyond the reach of reasoning,
supremely profound, subtle, delicate, and pre-eminent— due to the thorough abandonment of opposing states— well-evident and more manifest,
and because it brings about mastery in the right way and because the dwelling in the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is exceedingly brief.
"It occurs very quickly.

Having thus shown the absence of anyone superior to the Blessed One in qualities such as virtue, he now says "unequaled even in the quality of virtue" and so forth, in order to show the absence of even an equal.
In that context, "unequaled" (asama) means that at no time does there exist anyone [equal to him].

One who is equal or similar in virtue such as morality (*sīla*) and so forth is "unequaled" (*asama*). Likewise, one who is equal to the unequaled is "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*). Or, one for whom the unequaled are equal is "equal to the unequaled.
One for whom there is no counterpart in virtue such as morality and so forth is "without counterpart" (*appaṭima*). The same method applies to the remaining two terms as well.

In this context, it should be understood that a mere likeness is a "counterpart" (*paṭimā*), a similar likeness is a "counterpart-image" (*paṭibhāga*), and one who stands in a state of mutual comparison is a "counter-person" (*paṭipuggala*).
Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "But I do not perceive," O monks, although I see the entire world with my all-encompassing eye as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of my hand,
I do not perceive even a single person among this generation— including its devas—
who is more endowed with virtue (*sīlasampannatara*) or possesses more perfect virtue than myself; the intention is that such a person does not exist.
Regarding the *Aggappasāda-sutta* and others:
herein it is said—“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them.”
“The Tathāgata is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Those, bhikkhus, who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost.
For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
This is the *Aggappasāda Sutta*. By the word “etcetera” (ādi)—

“Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...in the world with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power; therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata.
Such sutta passages are to be understood. Regarding the opening verses:
“For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed Teacher;”
“I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One; I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
Tamed among those who tame, I am the best; peaceful among those who seek peace, I am the sage.
Liberated, I am the foremost of those who liberate; having crossed over, I am the most excellent of those who help others cross.”
“Neither in this world nor in the next,
there exists anyone equal to or superior to the Buddha;
he has reached the supreme state of those worthy of offerings.”
“For those seeking merit who desire abundant fruit”—thus these verses should be recited in detail.

Regarding the phrase “charioteer of men to be tamed” (*purisadammasārathī*) and so forth: they are called *dammā* because they are to be tamed (*damitabbā*), meaning they are of a nature fit to be tamed. And they are both men and those to be tamed.
...and thus [there are] those to be tamed by men. Here, the description is formed by placing the qualifier after the qualified; the meaning is "men to be tamed.
They say that although women are also capable of being tamed, the mention of "men" is for the purpose of establishing the highest limit.
To show the meaning of the word *sāreti*, he says "tames," and so forth. Therein, "tames" means to compose, by means of bodily composure and the rest.

The meaning is "he joins. Furthermore, that joining by means of bodily concentration and so forth consists in establishing [them] in the respective *tadaṅgavinaya* (restraint by substitution of opposites) and other methods;
thus he said, "it is meant that he disciplines. As for the term "the untamed," this was stated with reference to those persons to be tamed who have not attained taming in any respect whatsoever.
However, those whose state of being tamed is incomplete are those who must be tamed in every way...
Even those who have not transcended [the world] are indeed persons to be tamed, since the Teacher tames them.

For the Blessed One—by explaining the first jhāna to one of purified virtue, and the second jhāna to one who has attained the first jhāna, and so forth, proclaiming each successive higher distinction—tames even those who are only partially tamed.
Therefore it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "Moreover..."

"Thus the Blessed One, by teaching the first jhāna and so forth for those with purified virtue and the like, as well as the higher paths of practice for stream-enterers and others, tames even those already tamed.

Alternatively, it should be understood that here, by the very term "the untamed," those who are entirely untamed and those who are partially tamed are both included. "Fit to be tamed" means worthy of being tamed.
Regarding the term *tiracchānapurisā* (animals) and so forth: they are called *tiracchāna* because they do not move upward but have moved and extended horizontally;
the meaning is that, unlike gods, humans, and others, they are long horizontally rather than long upward. Humans (*manussa*) are simply animals (*tiracchāna*) who are persons (*purisa*).
They are called "humans" (*manussa*) due to the abundance of mind (*manas*), by virtue of qualities such as mindfulness, intelligence, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"With developed minds" means having minds characterized by superior qualities. Who, then, are they? They are the distinguished beings dwelling in Jambudīpa. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, in three respects the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Which three? They are brave, they possess mindfulness, and here there is the living of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
For likewise, the Blessed Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, Wheel-turning Monarchs, and others—

And beings of great power were born right there. However, some say that because they possessed the same physical form and other characteristics as those dwelling on the small island, the inhabitants of the other great islands were also designated as "human beings" (*manussa*). Others, however, say:
"Humans" (*manussa*) are so called because of the predominance of a mind accompanied by greed and its opposites, such as non-greed; for those beings who belong to the human species—
Among those, greed and its opposites—non-greed and so forth—are predominant. Due to the predominance of greed and the like, they fill out the path to the woeful states;
due to the predominance of non-greed and the like, they fill out the path to the happy destinies and the path leading to Nibbāna.

Therefore, because of the predominance of the mind accompanied by greed and its opposites, the specific classes of beings dwelling in the four great continents, together with those dwelling on the minor islands, [are distinguished].
They are called "human beings" (*manussa*). However, worldly people say, "They are human beings because they are the descendants of Manu.

Manu is the name for the first being of the eon, the originator of the world's social conventions, the one who ordains what is beneficial and harmful for sentient beings, and who stands in the place of a father;
he is the one who is called "Mahāsammatā" in the sacred teachings. [These beings] stand within his instructions and admonitions, both directly and through tradition.
Because they resemble his son, humans (*manussa*) are called *mānusā*. For that very reason, those youths are designated as *manujā*;
and since they are both humans and men, they are *manussapurisa*. Regarding the term *amanussapurisa*, here *amanussa* means "not human.
What is intended here is their similarity [to him]. By this, the mere state of being human is indicated.
"None other than those who are equal [to us]" refers to non-human beings such as *yakkhas* and so forth. It does not mean any others whatsoever distinct from humans;
likewise, the separate mention of animals is made, and only *yakkhas* and the like are specified. Apalāla dwells in the Himalayas;
Cūḷodara and Mahodara dwell on Nāgadīpa; Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha dwell on the island of Sīhaḷa.
They have been rendered seedless by the removal of the poison of hatred. Therefore it was said: "They were established in the refuges and in the precepts.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "Kūṭadanta and others," the inclusion of householders such as Ghoramukha and Upāli should be understood.
By the word "etcetera" in "Sakka and others," the inclusion of beings such as the yakkhas Ajakalāpa and Bakabrahma should be understood. Now, their taming—
It can be understood in each instance according to the method already stated; therefore, it is not mentioned here for fear of excessive prolixity.

Furthermore, this discourse should be expanded upon: this *Kesī-sutta* should be expanded upon in the sense of "disciplined by various means of discipline," because it illustrates discipline through appropriate means such as gentleness and so forth.

“*Atthapadaṃ*” means a word that makes the meaning manifest; this is the meaning of “*vākyaṃ*. For it is by means of a sentence (*vākya*) that the meaning is manifested, not by a mere word such as a noun (*nāma*) and so forth.
And by its being a single word, the Teacher’s unique quality as the charioteer of men to be tamed is shown.
Therefore he said, “The Blessed One indeed,” and so on. “Eight directions” refers to the eight attainments (*aṭṭha samāpattiyo*). For these [attainments] are mutually...
They are called *disā* because they are seen and pointed out as being distinct and unmixed, or because they are like the [cardinal] directions (*disā*).

"Not clinging" (*asajjamānā*) means not adhering; through having attained mastery, their movement is free from attachment. "Running" (*dhāvantī*) means they run due to the application of swift activity.
"He runs toward one direction alone" means that he does not turn his body around; however, those tamed by the Teacher [behave] thus.
The eight directions in which tamable persons run are traversed by means of a single course of action alone. Therefore he said, “seated in a single cross-legged posture.

The phrase “eight directions” is merely an illustration, for it refers to leaping into the direction of cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the direction of the Deathless (*amatadisa*), which have never been reached by worldly people.

Regarding the passage beginning with “by way of the visible, the future, and the ultimate truth,” the term “visible world” (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived individual existence (*attabhāva*).
"Connected with that" (*tattha niyutto*) means pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), having the welfare of this world as its purpose.

Because one must go through it due to kamma and defilements, and because it is to be properly traversed, it is "the future state" (*samparāya*), namely the next world. That which is connected with that is "pertaining to the future state" (*samparāyika*), having the welfare of the next world as its purpose.

The supreme, highest purpose is the "ultimate purpose" (*paramattha*), which is Nibbāna. By these—namely, by those pertaining to the present life, the future state, and the ultimate purpose—"as appropriate" (*yathārahaṃ*).
"Accordingly" (*yathānurūpaṃ*) means in accordance with whatever person is worthy of whatever specific matter among those various matters.
"He instructs" (*anusāsati*) means he disciplines them and establishes them in those respective matters. "A caravan" (*sattha*) is so called because it proceeds together with its purpose (*attha*);

it refers to a multitude of people traveling to another region for trade by means of merchandise and capital. It is that which is to be protected and guided by way of beneficial instruction and the like.

"He has this [burden]," thus, according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), he is a "Teacher" (*satthā*) and a "Caravan Leader" (*satthavāho*). Because the Blessed One is like him, it is said:
"He is a Teacher because he is like a teacher; the Blessed One is a Caravan Leader.
Now, in order to demonstrate that meaning according to the method of the Explanatory Text (*Niddesa-pāḷi*), the passage beginning with "Just as a caravan leader... was spoken. Therein:
*Satthā* means people traveling together in a caravan. A *kaṇṭāra* is a waterless region of the forest where they cross (*tārenti*) the water;
however, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), other forest regions are also called by that name.

A *corakaṇṭāra* is a wilderness inhabited by bandits; likewise, there is a *vāḷakaṇṭāra* (wild-beast wilderness). A *dubbhikkhakaṇṭāra* is a wilderness where alms-food is difficult to obtain. *Tāreti* means [he leads them] through a place that is not secure.

*Atikkāmeti*. The phrase beginning with *uttāreti* is stated by augmenting the word with a prefix. Alternatively, *uttāreti* means he carries across (*tāreti*) while leading [beings] to the ground of safety (*khemantabhūmi*).
*Nittāreti* means he carries across while leading [them] out from an unsafe place. *Patāreti* means he carries across after having encompassed [them];
the meaning is that he carries them across as if encompassing them with his hand. All of this—carrying across, leading across, and so forth—[is explained].
"Establishing in a place of safety" is what is meant by the phrase "he brings them to the land of security. "Beings" refers to those beings who are to be converted.
Because it is a great thicket, a source of great harm, and difficult to cross, birth itself is the wilderness of birth; that is the wilderness of birth.
"By way of the highest limit" means by way of the highest limit of beings; for gods and humans alone are the highest of beings.
"Not animals and so forth. "This" refers to the expression "of devas and humans.

"By way of delimiting the capable person" means by way of defining the individual who is fit for entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). "From the Blessed One" is a genitive of source (*nissakka*), as in the phrase "he learns from the preceptor.
The meaning is "in the presence of the Blessed One. "The perfection of the decisive support" (*upanissayasampatti*).
The rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with three roots and so forth is a powerful cause for the attainment of the paths and fruits.
"At Gaggarā" means at the lake named Gaggarā, belonging to the queen of King Gaggarā, or because it was caused to be made by her, it received the name "Gaggarā.

"He took the sign in the lake" means that he grasped the sign in the lake with the perception of "Dhamma," thinking, "This is called Dhamma"; and while grasping it, his mind was full of serene confidence.
He lay down at the edge of the assembly. "He stood having pressed [the stick] down" means that, not seeing the stick placed upon the frog's head, he stood there having forced the stick down upon it.
Even though the stick was placed and even though it was forced down, the frog passed away while making a loud cry, due to his faith directed toward the Dhamma.
This is the natural law (*dhammatā*) for beings reborn in the world of the gods.
The reflection was: “From where have I been reborn here, and what indeed did I do there?

Therefore, because he had seen his own previous existence, he said, “Ah, so I too have been reborn here! He prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet out of love, reverence, and great respect, which had increased through gratitude for what had been done for him.
"Knowing yet he asked": Desiring to make the fruit of karma and the power of the Buddhas manifest before the great multitude, the Blessed One asked with the verse, "Who is worshipping me?
In this context, *ko* means "who," referring to who among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth;
*katamo* has the same meaning. *Me* means "my. *Pādāni* means "the feet. *Iddhiyā* means "by means of such supernatural power as this. *Yasasā* means by this...
With such glory and such retinue, he was shining and radiant. "Abhikkantena" means with an exceedingly lovely, desirable, and beautiful [appearance].
"Vaṇṇena" refers to the color of the skin, the luster of the body's complexion.
"Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā" means illuminating all ten directions; the sense is that, like the moon and like the sun, he was making them one mass of light and one mass of radiance.
Thus, when questioned by the Blessed One, the son of the gods, declaring himself, spoke this verse: "In a former birth I was a frog.
Therein, "formerly" (*pure*) means in a previous birth. "In water" (*udake*) is an indication of the place of his own rebirth at that time.
By saying "a frog in the water," he excludes the frog on dry land, such as the *uddhumāyika* (the bloated) and others. Cows...
“Gocara” means that which they move within; it is a place where cattle seek fodder. Here, however, it is like a pasture, thus it is called “gocara.
One who has water as his pasture is a “vārigocara. For even some turtles and other creatures that move in water are not those whose pasture is water;
therefore, he is specifically described as a “vārigocara. [The phrase] “of you who listen to the Dhamma” refers to one with a Brahma-voice, as sweet as the song of the cuckoo.

While you were descending and listening to the Dhamma with the apprehension of a sign (*nimittaggāha*)—thinking, "This is what is called the Dhamma"—this genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*).
The meaning is: "The cowherd boy (*gopālaka-dāraka*), while guarding the calves, having approached me and stood leaning on his staff, struck my head with that staff and killed me."

“Having smiled” means: having become filled with rapture and joy, thinking, “Thus, even by the power of such a small amount of merit, such exceedingly sublime mundane and supramundane successes can be obtained,” he smiled, illuminating that region all the more intensely with the rows of rays from his brilliant, white, and flashing teeth. Indeed, it was through the influence of that rapture and joy that he—
“Behold for a moment the success and the glory that come from clarity of mind;
behold my power, behold my beauty and my radiance.
And those who, over the long course of time, have heard the Dhamma from Gotama—”
"Those are your secure places, having gone where you shall not grieve.
Having spoken these two verses, he departed.
As for the word *yaṃ* (whatever) in the phrase *yaṃ pana kiñci*, it is an indefinite term; likewise with *kiñci*. *Panā* is merely an ornamental particle.
Therefore, by the phrase "whatever," the exhaustive inclusion of all that is knowable has been made. Alternatively, *pana* is a particle indicating a specific distinction;
by means of it, the Teacher’s full awakening to the Four Noble Truths is stated both in brief and in detail through the term "Sammāsambuddho.

By the term "Buddho," however, the awakening to other objects of knowledge besides those [truths] is indicated. Or else, by the former [term], the power of the Teacher’s knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is expressed.

The power of the knowledge of teaching [is exercised] by way of the western direction. The specific distinction called "rapture" (*pīti*) will be explained further on. Regarding the phrase "by way of the knowledge belonging to the end of liberation":

here, "liberation" (*vimokkha*) is that from which one is completely liberated from all opposing factors; it is the supreme path (*aggamagga*). "The end of that" (*tassa anto*) is the fruit of the supreme path (*aggaphala*).

When that [fruit] is attained, because what is to be attained has been attained, that which exists therein is "belonging to the end of liberation" (*vimokkhantika*); this refers to the knowledge together with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
It is all Buddha-knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "thus it occurs":
"He is a Buddha because of omniscience; he is a Buddha because of all-seeingness; he is a Buddha because of being independent of others' guidance; he is a Buddha because of his expansive wisdom..."

He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened; he is called "Buddha" because his taints are exhausted; he is called "Buddha" because he is unstained; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from lust;
he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from hatred; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from delusion; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from defilements;
he is called "Buddha" because he has traveled the path that goes alone; he is called "Buddha" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
He is called "Buddha" because he is devoid of non-intelligence and has attained intelligence.

This name "Buddha" was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and colleagues, nor by kinsmen and blood relatives, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities; it is a designation pertaining to liberation belonging to the Buddhas.
“At the root of enlightenment, together with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge, the realization is designated as ‘Buddha’”—this is the method of the Niddesa commentary.

And because there is no difference here in the analysis of that Paṭisambhidāmagga text, the particle *vā* (or) is used in the sense of non-restriction, to show that the purpose is accomplished by either one of the two [methods].
In this regard, just as in the world one who understands is called “understood,” so too, one who has awakened to the truths is a “Buddha” by way of the simple agent (*suddhakattar*).
Just as winds that dry up leaves are called "leaf-dryers" (*paṇṇasosa*), so too he is called "Awakened" (*buddha*) because he awakens the world by way of being the causal agent;
here, the sense of "cause" is inherent within the term. He is "Awakened" by virtue of omniscience, meaning he is awakened by an intelligence capable of awakening to all phenomena.
He is "Awakened" by virtue of all-seeingness, meaning he is awakened by an intelligence capable of perceiving all phenomena.
The meaning [of "Buddha"]: He is called "Buddha" because he is not to be awakened by another; that is, because he has become enlightened by himself and not through another, he is "Buddha.
He is called "Buddha" because of his expansiveness; that is, because various qualities have blossomed forth from him like a lotus in the sense of opening, he is "Buddha.
He is called "Buddha" by way of being one whose taints are exhausted—by these six terms, [it is shown] through the abandoning of those states that cause the contraction of the mind.
It is said that he is "Buddha" because he has awakened from the sleep of all defilements (*kilesa*), just as a man awakens from the exhaustion of sleep.
In this context, since *saṅkhā* and *saṅkhāta* are identical in meaning, the word *saṅkhātena* means "by way of a portion.

He is designated as "unsmeared" (*nirupalepa*) due to the absence of the smearing of craving (*taṇhā*) and the smearing of views (*diṭṭhi*). [This refers to] all defilements together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).
Having distinguished [the Buddha] by means of the term "exclusively" because of his having abandoned [defilements], it is said: "one who is exclusively free from passion," and so forth.

"Exclusively free from defilement" (ekantanikkilesa) means one who is free from all defilements, including the remnants of passion, hatred, and delusion. Regarding the phrase "gone by the path traveled by only one" (ekāyanamaggaṃ gata):

just as the sense of "awakening" (buddhi) is understood in the word "Buddha"—which is derived from the root *budh* meaning "to awaken"—the sense of "going" (*gamana*) can also be understood in the sense of "awakening. Thus, because he has gone by the path traveled by only one, he is called "Buddha."
The meaning is that he is called "Buddha. One who has awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment is "Buddha";
he is not "Buddha" because he was awakened by others, but rather he is "Buddha" because he himself has awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment.
Because of the destruction of non-intelligence and the attainment of intelligence, he is "Buddha"; thus, *buddhi*, *buddha*, and *bodha* [are synonymous].

There is no other meaning [here]. In this regard, just as a cloth is called "red" because of its connection with the quality of redness, so too it is stated for the purpose of making known that he is a "Buddha" because of his connection with the qualities of a Buddha.

Following that, the passage beginning with "This 'Buddha' is not a name" and so forth is stated for the purpose of making it understood that this is a designation (paññatti) that conforms to the actual state of things (atthānugata).
Thus, for this reason as well, the Blessed One is to be understood as a Buddha.
Now, in order to show the meaning of the term *bhagavā*, he said: “*Bhagavā*—this, moreover, is his...
and so forth. Therein, *assa* means “of the Blessed One. It is a designation for one who is distinguished by qualities, who is supreme among all beings, and who is venerable;
it is a word spoken out of respect for him who is thus distinguished by all qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and is therefore the highest of all beings.
"O Blessed One! For indeed, the Lord of the World, by virtue of being endowed with the excellence of immeasurable and incomparable qualities such as splendor and virtue;
by his unsurpassed perfection of skillful means, which is preceded by the removal of all harm and is solely intent upon providing every benefit and happiness;
and by his state of being supremely beneficial to the generation of devas and humans throughout immeasurable world-systems—"
"He is the supreme object of reverence for immeasurable beings.
Regarding the word *Bhagavā*: it is called "speech" (*vacana*) because it is the best; it is said to be "best" because it is associated with best qualities.
Alternatively, that which is spoken is "speech," namely the meaning; therefore, he who is to be expressed by the word "Bhagavā" [is so called].
The meaning is that he is the best; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "the Blessed One is the supreme word," the same principle applies here as well.

"Worthy of reverence" (*gāravayutta*) means endowed with a state of weightiness due to his possession of weighty qualities. Alternatively, he is "worthy of reverence" because he deserves exceptional honor;
the meaning is that he is one who possesses reverence. "Teachers of crafts and the like are venerable, yet they are not worthy of reverence; however, he is not like them."
"Therefore, having said 'one who has respect,' it was said 'one who is possessed of respect,'" say some.

Desiring to analyze in detail the meaning briefly stated—that "Bhagavā" is the name of the Blessed One based on specific qualities—he first shows the name itself by way of extracting its meanings, beginning with the words: "For a name is fourfold," and so forth.
In this context, "pertaining to states" (*āvatthika*) means known by way of a state; it is designated and expressed in reference to various specific states.
Likewise, "pertaining to characteristics" (*liṅgika*) means expressed by way of various characteristics. "Pertaining to signs" (*nemittika*) means derived from a sign.

"Arising by chance" (*adhiccasamuppanna*) means occurring according to whim, coming about according to whim, or being arbitrary. Now, the names beginning with "pertaining to states" [will be explained] according to their literal form.
Showing this, he said: "In that regard, [the terms] ‘calf,’ ‘tame ox,’ and ‘bull,’ etc. Therein, by the first word “etc.,” he includes such terms as ‘child,’ ‘youth,’ and ‘old man’;
by the second, such as ‘shaven-headed’ and ‘wearing matted hair’; by the third, such as ‘learned,’ ‘preacher of the Dhamma,’ and ‘meditator’;
and by the fourth, he includes such as ‘the Teacher’s word which reveals the state of woe,’ and so forth.
The phrase "not of Mahāmāyā," and so forth, was stated in order to establish the aforementioned meaning by way of contrast (*byatireka*).
By the term "pertaining to liberation" (*vimokkhantika*), however, he shows that this name arose at the very moment of birth from a noble lineage.
If it pertains to liberation, then why is it not shared with other *khīṇāsava*s? To this he says: "Together with the knowledge of omniscience..."
"...by way of attainment. For when the fruit of arahantship is being realized for Buddhas, it is realized together with all the Buddha-qualities, beginning with omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Therefore it is said: "conducive to liberation" (*vimokkhantika*). "Manifestation as a description" (*sacchikā paññatti*) means a description that serves as the cause for the realization of all phenomena.
Alternatively, "manifestation as a description" means established through direct perception (*paccakkha*).

"Designation" (*paññatti*). For whatever qualities are the basis for that [designation], those qualities were directly perceived by the Teacher; thus, like those qualities themselves, that [designation] is indeed said to be "realized," not merely through the conventional usage of others—this is the intended meaning.
He uses the plural form "they say" (*vadanti*) out of respect for the Great Elder, or as a reference to the recitation performed by the compilers of the Council (*saṅgītikāra*).
*Sandhāya*. One who possesses a portion (*bhaga*) consisting of sovereignty and so forth is *bhagī*.

One who, by habit, frequents (*bhaji*) and serves (*sevi*) the jewels of the Noble Dhamma—such as the paths and fruits—as well as remote lodgings in forests and groves endowed with qualities such as being free from noise, is *bhajī*;
the meaning is "one whose nature is to frequent. Furthermore, one who possesses a share (*bhāgī*) of the four requisites, namely robes, almsfood, and so forth...
The meaning is that he is a partaker of the essence of liberation through the goal and the Dhamma, as well as of the higher virtue and so forth.

He is a "Vibhattavā" (one who has analyzed) because he analyzed and fully explained the jewel of the Dhamma. He is a "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One) because he has caused what is to be broken—namely, the evil states such as lust—to be broken; this is the meaning.
Since even those who are venerable are called "Bhagavā" in the world, he says "venerable" (*garu*); because he is venerable, for that reason too he is called "Bhagavā."
The word *iti* has the sense of "cause" (*hetu*). And where the word *iti* does not occur—as in "bhāgī" and so forth—it must be applied individually [to each term].

"Possessing fortune" (*bhāgyavā*) means "one who has fortune" (*bhāgyam assa atthi*). "By many methods" (*bahūhi ñāyehi*) refers to the numerous stages of cultivation, such as the development of the body (*kāyabhāvanā*) and so on.

"One whose self is well-cultivated" (*subhāvitattano*) refers to one whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) has been properly cultivated. Furthermore, this genitive case ending is used here in the sense of identity (*paccatte*).

"By him well-cultivated" is what is meant; the meaning is "one whose intrinsic nature is well-cultivated. In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated: "One who has well-cultivated the self is one who has well-cultivated the body.
"One who has gone to the end of existence" means one who has gone to *nibbāna*.
Regarding the phrase "in the manner stated in the *Niddesa*," this is the method of the *Niddesa*: [text follows].
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence. Furthermore, he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed lust;

he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed hatred; he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed delusion; he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed conceit; he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed wrong views;

he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed craving; he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed the defilements; and he is the Blessed One because he has enjoyed, analyzed, and thoroughly analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma.
The Blessed One is one who makes an end of existence; the Blessed One is one whose body is cultivated, whose virtue is cultivated, whose mind is cultivated, and whose wisdom is cultivated.
Or else, the Blessed One frequented remote forest groves and secluded lodgings—places with little sound, little noise, devoid of crowds, hidden from people, and suitable for seclusion;
thus he is "Bhagavā. Or else, the Blessed One is a possessor of portions... [bhāgī vā bhagavā].
"Because he possesses the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick," said the Blessed One.
Or, "The Blessed One is a possessor (bhāgī) of the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, and the flavor of liberation, as well as of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom;
thus he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā). Or, "The Blessed One is a possessor of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; thus he is the Blessed One."

The Blessed One (Bhagavā). Or, the Blessed One is so called because he possesses (bhāgī) the eight liberations (vimokkha), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (anupubbavihārasamāpatti).

Or, the Blessed One is so called because he possesses the ten developments of perception (saññābhāvanā), the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatisamādhi), and the attainment of the foul (asubhasamāpatti). Or, the Blessed One is so called because he possesses...
“Of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path,” said the Blessed One. Or alternatively,
the Blessed One is “Bhagavā” because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four...
“The Lord is the one who possesses the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and the six qualities of a Buddha,” said the Blessed One.
“Blessed One (*bhagavā*)”—this is not a mere name... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, ‘the Blessed One.
And here, although the phrases beginning with ‘a synonym for veneration’ are not explained according to the sequence of the words as they appear in the verse, [they are nonetheless included].”
However, they should be understood as explanations for all of them, each according to its appropriate application.

In this context, "a synonym for reverence" (*gāravādhivacana*) means a word expressing the state of being venerable toward those who are venerable. "He shared" (*bhajī*) means he spoke by way of division. Therefore, it is said:

"He analyzed and fully analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma. The "jewel of the Dhamma" (*dhammaratana*) is precisely the noble Dhamma, such as the paths and fruits. [The phrase] "he shared again" refers to this...

"Sevī" means one who serves. "Bhāgī" means one who possesses a share (*bhāga*). Again, "bhāgī" here means one whose nature is to partake (*bhajana-sīla*). "Of the taste of the meaning" (*attharasassa*) means of the taste that has the meaning as its support.

For when one preaches or listens to the Dhamma while standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*), the rapture and mental joy (*pīti-somanassa*) that arise with reference to that meaning is the "taste of the meaning. When [joy arises] with reference to the Dhamma itself, it is the "taste of the Dhamma."
It is with reference to this that it was said: "He gains knowledge of the meaning (atthaveda), he gains knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammaveda).
"The flavor of liberation" means the flavor of that which is liberation itself, or that which is dependent upon liberation.

"Of the developments of perception" refers to the ten developments of perception, beginning with the perception of impermanence. "Of the six qualities of a Buddha" refers to the six types of uncommon knowledge (asādhāraṇañāṇa).
It has been stated. In each instance, the derivation of the word *bhagavā* by the Blessed One is to be understood according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*).

Although the meaning expressed by such terms as "possessor of fortune" (*bhāgyavā*) and so forth is indeed included within the explanatory verse beginning with "one who possesses" (*bhagī*) and "one who partakes" (*bhajī*), nevertheless, the method of commentary—comprising the grammatical derivation of the word, the analysis of its meanings, and the application of those meanings—is of a different nature than that [verse].
It is said: "But this is another method. Regarding the phrase *vaṇṇavipariyāyo ti etaṃ*, the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*);

by this, it includes these three types of grammatical characteristics: change of letter (*vaṇṇavikāra*), elision of letter (*vaṇṇalopa*), and application according to the meaning of the root (*dhātuatthena niyojana*).

The phrase *saddanayena* means by the method of the grammatical characteristics of words (*saddalakkhaṇanaya*). It is stated [thus] because words such as *pisodara* belong to the class of derivative forms (*ākati-gaṇa*).
“Having taken the characteristic of throwing into the belly and so forth. Throwing in itself is the characteristic; for throwing in is the act of causing something to be included therein.
“Reached the ultimate” means having attained the highest excellence, having reached the state of a perfection (*pāramī*). “Fortune” (*bhāgya*) refers to wholesome merit (*kusala*).
Among these, wholesome merit pertaining to the Path produces supramundane happiness, while the other produces mundane happiness; and as for that other [merit], it too—
Or, by way of sequence, it may be a support for the turning away [from saṃsāra] that produces supramundane happiness.
Now, explaining the meaning of the term "Bhagavā," he said, "Because... and so forth. Therein, greed and the other [defilements] are taken as single units;
likewise, distorted attention is included because of its commonality with the nature of perversion (vipallāsa); and shamelessness and the others [are included]...
By way of the unwholesome roots. Therein, anger (*kodha*) has the characteristic of being angry; it arises from the nine grounds for resentment.
Enmity (*upanāha*) is the binding of the mind through repeated anger, such as thinking, "He abused me, he struck me," and so forth.
Both are simply aversion (*paṭigha*), though they are stated separately by way of their different modes of occurrence. Anger that arises once is simply anger.
