Beyond that is resentment (*upanāha*). And this has been said: "In the earlier time there is anger (*kodha*); in the later time there is resentment.

Slander (*makkha*) is the destruction of a well-performed deed, whether by a householder or one who has gone forth. For even a householder, being poor, might be placed in a high position by someone compassionate;
yet at a later time, [that benefactor] might think, "What have you done for me? and thus destroy the merit of that well-performed deed.

He causes [them] to perish. Even one who has gone forth into homelessness, from the time he was a novice, having been assisted by his teacher or preceptor with the four requisites and through instruction,
interrogation, and so forth, and having been trained in skill in the methods of Dharma-discourse and the treatises,
at a later time becomes honored and revered by kings, royal ministers, and others, yet is shown no respect by his own teacher or preceptor.

When being told, "This man was thus favored and raised by us from our very childhood, yet now he has become devoid of affection," he destroys their merit for having done good deeds by saying, "What have you ever done for me? Thus,
he is a destroyer of that quality characterized by former kindness, like a water-wiper [rubbing away] what clings to the body.
“Smeared” (*makkha*) refers to one who smears away [the truth] with water; for he is called “smeared” in the sense of smearing over the virtues of others.
“Spite” (*paḷāsa*) means he spits out; the meaning is that, having displayed the virtues of another, he makes them equal to his own virtues.
Furthermore, even toward a person of great learning, he overwhelms them, thinking: “The destiny of such a learned person is uncertain...”

“What difference is there between you and me?”—this is the grasping at equality (*yugaggāha*) that arises by overstepping those individuals who have long been ordained and are known for their seniority, thinking, “You too have gone forth in this dispensation, I too have gone forth; you too abide in mere virtue, I too [do so],” and so on.
For envy (*paḷāsa*) has the characteristic of grasping at equality.
*Issā* (envy) is the state of being consumed by resentment and feeling envious toward the honors and so forth received by others.
*Macchariya* (avarice) is the concealment of one’s own prosperity, being unable to endure its being shared with others. *Māyā* (deceit) consists of fraudulent conduct;

it is characterized by the concealment of one’s own faults. For indeed, because it conceals existing faults of one’s own, it is called "deceit" (*māyā*), as it is like an illusion that deludes the eye.
Sāṭheyya (deceit) has the characteristic of manifesting qualities that do not exist in oneself; it arises through the state of being a *kerāṭika* (a hypocrite).
For the display of non-existent qualities is called "the act of a *kerāṭika*. Indeed, a person who is a *kerāṭika* is like the *āyanamaccha* fish.
The *āyanamaccha* is a species of fish that dwells in the mouths of snakes. It is said that this fish shows its tail to the fish and [its head] to the snakes.

Just as one might place a head on [someone's feet] to make them know, "I am like you," even so, a person who is a flatterer (kerāṭika) approaches whichever person is a master of the Suttas or the Abhidhamma and says to them: "I am your pupil;
you have compassion for me; I will not let you go. In this way, they think, "This person has respect for us; he honors us."
They will think thus; such is the deceitfulness arising from that state of being a huckster.

Or, because of the total absence of softness, the state of rigidity—resembling a leather bag filled with wind, like a straight staff that does not bend, and characterized by holding the head high and living in an unrestrained manner—is *thambha* (rigidity). Exceeding that is *sārambha* (aggression). That...

It is acquired in two ways: by way of the unwholesome and by way of the wholesome. Therein, for a householder, it arises by making twice or even more than twice as much [ornaments and so forth] upon seeing what has been made by another;
and for one who is not a householder, it arises by way of pride, making twice or even more than twice as much as whatever another person masters or recites.
It is unwholesome. A person endowed with it performs double, then double that amount again.
Being a householder, when one has prepared one dwelling-place, another prepares two; another four, another eight, and another sixteen.
Being a homeless one, when one has taken up one Nikāya, [another thinks]: "I will not study less than this."
"I shall become [one who gives more]," thinking thus, one person takes two, another three, another four, and another five.
Indeed, it is not proper to take [more] out of a spirit of rivalry, for this is an unwholesome side, a path leading to hell.

However, when a householder sees another giving even a single *salākabhatta* (ticket-meal) and, desiring to give two or three for himself, [this desire] arises in him; as for one who is homeless (*anagāriya*), [it is likewise improper].

And when another person has been assigned to one *nikāya*, it is wholesome for one who—without relying on pride, but seeing only that [assignment] and overcoming one’s own laziness—arises with the desire to take two *nikāyas* oneself.

For according to the side of the wholesome, if another gives one *salākabhatta* to one person, it is proper to give two; if they give two, it is proper to give four. And likewise for a bhikkhu, when another...

When two Nikāyas have been mastered, it is permissible to master more than that in order to stand on the side of turning away (vivaṭṭa), thinking, "It is comfortable for me to recite having mastered two Nikāyas.
However, in this context, the act of making more than that—belonging to the side of the unwholesome—is called "aggression" (sārambha).
That which proceeds by way of uplifting through such conceits as "I am superior," based upon birth and so forth, [is what is meant].
*Māna* (conceit). *Atimāna* (excessive conceit) is that which proceeds by way of overestimation.

It should be understood as *atimāna* arising when one first regards oneself as equal to another and subsequently regards oneself as superior to them. *Mada* (intoxication) is the mode of self-exaltation based on birth and so forth;

in its actual meaning, it is also simply *māna*. Furthermore, it consists of intoxication with birth, intoxication with clan, intoxication with health, intoxication with youth, and intoxication with life.
The intoxication of gain, the intoxication of honor, the intoxication of respect, the intoxication of precedence, the intoxication of retinue, the intoxication of wealth, the intoxication of beauty,

the intoxication of learning, the intoxication of eloquence, the intoxication of seniority, the intoxication of being an alms-food eater, the intoxication of not being despised, the intoxication of deportment, the intoxication of psychic power,

the intoxication of fame, the intoxication of virtue, the intoxication of meditative absorption, the intoxication of craft, the intoxication of height, the intoxication of circumference, and the intoxication of shape.
"Bringing to fulfillment" is of many kinds.
Among these, pride that arises based on birth and manifests as a state of intoxication is "pride of birth";
it arises among all four castes, beginning with the khattiyas. For a khattiya endowed with noble birth thinks, "There is no one else like me; the rest..."
“Other Kṣatriyas are born [only] in between, but I am a Kṣatriya of a lineage that has reached its peak,” thus he conceives pride. The same principle applies to Brahmins and the other castes as well.
Pride that arises based on one’s clan (*gotra*), manifesting as a form of self-exaltation, is called *gotramada*;
this also arises among all four castes, including the Kṣatriyas. For even a Kṣatriya might think, “I am of the Koṇḍañña clan; I am of the Ādicca clan.”
One conceives pride. A brahmin also conceives pride, thinking, "I belong to the Kassapa clan; I belong to the Bhāradvāja clan.

A merchant and a laborer likewise conceive pride based on their respective family lineages. Regarding the intoxication of health and so forth, one conceives pride through self-exaltation, thinking, "I am healthy, while others are full of disease;
even a mere scratching does not constitute what is called 'illness' for me."
The conceit that has arisen is called the intoxication of health. The conceit that arises through the sense of pride, thinking, “I am young;
the physical forms of other beings are like trees standing on the edge of a precipice, whereas I stand in the prime of my life,” is the intoxication of youth. [The conceit arising from the thought:
“I have lived long, I live long, I shall live long; I have lived happily, I live happily, I shall live happily.”
Pride arising through intoxication with one’s life is called *jīvitamada*. Pride arising through intoxication with the thought, “I am a recipient of gains;
other beings have little gain, whereas for me there is no limit to my gains,” is called *lābhamada*.
Pride arising through the thought, “Other beings receive this or that [meager thing], but I receive requisites such as robes that are well-made and excellent,” is called *sukatakammamada*.
The conceit arising from the sense of "I am receiving" through the influence of intoxication is called the pride of honor (*sakkāramada*).
[One thinks: "People do not even pay homage to this ascetic when they walk by treading upon the heels of the remaining bhikkhus; yet, seeing me, they pay homage.
They regard me as heavy as a stone parasol and as difficult to approach as a mass of fire."

Conceit arisen through the inflation of self-importance is called *garukāramada* (the intoxication of being held in high esteem). Conceit arisen through the inflation of thinking, “The question that has arisen can be answered by my mouth alone;
even when going out for alms or returning, they go surrounding me and placing me at their head,” is called *purekkhāramada* (the intoxication of precedence).
First, regarding a householder who has a large retinue, [even if] a hundred men...
“Even a thousand men surround me!”—this is called the conceit of retinue (*parivāramada*), which arises from the intoxication of thinking:
“As for one who has gone forth, even a hundred ascetics or a thousand ascetics surround me; others have little retinue, whereas I have both a great retinue and a pure retinue.
[He thinks: “The rest of beings do not obtain even enough for their own consumption...”
"Furthermore, there is no limit to my wealth, as if it were a buried treasure"—this conceit arising from the state of intoxication is called *bhogamada* (the pride of wealth).

Likewise, thinking, "All other beings are ill-favored and ugly, whereas I am handsome and pleasing," or "All other beings are devoid of virtue and lack renown, whereas my fame and reputation are well-known among gods and humans: 'Thus indeed is the Elder... [and so on].
"‘He is indeed learned, he is indeed virtuous, he is indeed endowed with the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa)’—
pride arising through such self-delight based on the excellence of one’s physical appearance and the excellence of one’s virtues is called *vaṇṇamada*.
Pride arising through self-delight in the thought, ‘Other beings are of little learning, but I am learned,’ is *sutamada*."
“Other beings are lacking in eloquence, but for me there is no limit to my eloquence”—this conceit arising from such intoxication is called *paṭibhānamada*. “I am one who knows the ancient lore;

I know such-and-such a lineage of Buddhas, a lineage of kings, a lineage of provinces, a lineage of villages, the divisions of days and nights, and the conjunctions of constellations and moments”—this [conceit] arising from such intoxication...

Pride consisting in intoxication with one’s seniority is called *rattaññumada*. Pride that arises from the conceit, "The rest of the bhikkhus have become alms-food eaters only occasionally, but I am a regular alms-food eater," is called *piṇḍapātikamada*.
Pride that arises from the conceit, "The rest of beings are despised and held in contempt, but I am not held in contempt," is called *anavaññattimada*. [As for] "of the rest..."
The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, "The deportment of other beings is unpleasing,
but mine is pleasing," is called *iriyāpathamada*. Or, through the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking,
"All other beings are like crows with clipped wings, whereas I am of great psychic power and great majesty," or "Whatever action I perform, that succeeds," [is also such conceit].
Arrogance that has arisen is called "pride in psychic power" (*iddhimada*).
However, "pride in fame" (*yasamada*) can be illustrated by both the householder and the homeless renunciant.
For even a certain householder might be the head of one of the eighteen guilds; he thinks, "I appoint the rest of the men; I direct them."
Even a certain homeless one (*anagārika*) may be senior in some respect; the conceit that arises from the sense of self-importance, thinking, "The rest of the monks follow my instruction;

I am the senior," is called the intoxication of status (*yasamada*). The conceit that arises from the sense of self-importance, thinking, "The rest of beings are immoral, but I am virtuous," is called the intoxication of virtue (*sīlamada*). [Regarding] "the rest of beings..."
“Even at the time of drinking water, a cock lacks one-pointedness of mind, yet I am an attainer of access and absorption”—this conceit arising from such intoxication is called *jhānamada*.
“All other beings are unskilled, while I am skilled”—this conceit arising from such intoxication is called *sippamada*.
“All other beings are short, while I am tall”—this [conceit arising from such intoxication...]

Pride that has arisen [thinking] "I am tall" is called *ārohamada* (pride of height). Pride that has arisen through the conceit, "The rest of beings are short or tall, but I am well-proportioned like a banyan tree," is called *pariṇāhamada* (pride of circumference).
Pride that has arisen through the conceit, "The bodily configuration of the rest of beings is ugly and repulsive, but mine is pleasing and beautiful," is *saṇṭhānamada* (pride of shape).

“‘Pride of self-satisfaction’ (pāripūrimada) is the pride that arises through the mode of self-exaltation, thinking: ‘In the bodies of other beings there are many defects, but in my own body there is not even a hair’s breadth of fault.
Thus, all this pride—which proceeds by way of the mode of self-exaltation based on birth and so forth—is here called ‘intoxication’ (mada).
[The next term is] ‘the mind’s indulgence in the strands of sensual pleasure’ (kāmaguṇesu cittassa vossaggo).”

Heedlessness (*pamāda*) is the relinquishing of the mind by failing to restrain mindfulness with regard to the five strands of sensual pleasure; what is meant is that it is the absence of mindfulness.
Craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) are indeed already evident.
Furthermore, greed (*lobha*) and the others are included under the heading of the "threefold unwholesome roots. The word "threefold" (*tividha*) also applies to misconduct (*duccarita*) and so forth.
Each [term] should be applied individually. Therein, bodily misconduct and so forth are the three kinds of misconduct.
Craving-defilement and so forth are the three kinds of defilements. The stains of lust and so forth are the three kinds of stains because they cause a state of being stained;
for lust and the rest stain the mind and cause it to take on a stain, and therefore they are called "stains. "Lust is uneven, hatred..."
The three kinds of unevenness (*visama*) are: those spoken of as "lust is uneven, hatred is uneven, delusion is uneven," namely lust and the rest;
and those arrived at as "unevenness of body, unevenness of speech, unevenness of mind," namely bodily misconduct and the rest.

Since beings stumble because of both lust and the rest, as well as bodily misconduct and the rest, and having stumbled, they fall from the Teaching and from a happy rebirth, they are therefore called "unevenness" by virtue of being the cause of stumbling and falling.

They are called "uneven. The threefold perceptions—namely, perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), perception of ill will (*byāpādasaññā*), and perception of cruelty (*vihiṃsāsaññā*)—are the perceptions associated with sensual desire and so forth as they have come down in the texts.

Likewise, the threefold thoughts—namely, thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*), thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*), and thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*)—are the thoughts as they have come down in the texts.

The threefold proliferations (*papañca*) are the proliferation of craving (*taṇhāpapañca*), the proliferation of views (*diṭṭhipapañca*), and the proliferation of conceit (*mānapapañca*). [These occur] within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Beings proliferate" means that craving and the like are called "proliferations" (*papañca*).
Regarding the phrase "fourfold perversions" (*catubbidha-vipariyesa*) and so forth, the word "fourfold" (*catubbidha*) should be applied to each term individually.

In this context, they are called "perversions" (*vipariyesa*) because they seek objects such as the impermanent in a perverted manner, such as by regarding them as permanent. [For example: "The perversion of perception is regarding the impermanent as permanent."
There are twelve [types of perversions] as they have been handed down: perversion of mind and perversion of view regarding suffering as pleasure;
perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view regarding the foul as beautiful;
and perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view regarding the non-self as self.
The perversions (vipallāsā) are described as "fourfold misapprehensions" by way of the four bases, beginning with impermanence.

Herein, the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) should be understood as occurring when unwholesome perception—devoid of wrong view—exerts its own function with strength at a point where the function of consciousness is weak;
likewise, [the perversion of volition] occurs when unwholesome consciousness—devoid of wrong view—exerts its own function with strength.

There is perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), and in a consciousness associated with views, there is perversion of view (*diṭṭhi-vipallāsa*). Therefore, the perversion of perception is the weakest;
the perversion of consciousness is stronger than that; and the perversion of view is the strongest of all.

The perception is like a child who has not yet developed intelligence seeing a kahāpaṇa coin, because it merely grasps the mode of appearance of the object as it presents itself. As for the village-dweller...

The mind is like the sight of the kahāpaṇa coin, because it brings about the penetration of the characteristics [of the aggregates]. View is like the blacksmith’s grasping the iron with the large tongs, because of its adherence and misapprehension.
In this context, there are four perversions of view, which proceed by way of the notions "permanent" and so forth regarding what is impermanent and non-self;
and there are four perversions of perception and mind. These eight perversions are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.

They are abandoned. The perversion of perception and mind that takes the unattractive to be attractive becomes attenuated by the path of the once-returner and is abandoned by the path of the non-returner.
It should be understood that the perversions of perception and mind that take suffering to be pleasant are abandoned by the path of arahantship.

The four taints—namely, the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance—as they appear in such passages, refer to the four cravings beginning with craving for sensual pleasures.
They are called *āsava* because they flow and proceed from the eye and the other [sense bases].

Although there is also the proceeding of wholesome states and so forth from the eye and the others, it is only the *kāmāsava* (taint of sensual desire) and the rest that flow with the nature of impurity, like pus from a wound;
therefore, only these are called "taints" (*āsava*). For the word *āsava* is conventionally established in the sense of flowing impurity.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and go forth from the perspective of their intrinsic nature (*dhammata*) as far as the stage of lineage (*gotrabhū*), and from the perspective of their spatial range (*okāsato*) as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), by way of occurring with respect to objects.
The meaning is that they occur having included within themselves these phenomena and this spatial range. For the prefix *ā-* has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).
And a limit is twofold, distinguished as "exclusive" (*mariyādā*) and "inclusive" (*abhividhi*). Among these, [the former] excludes the action from the limit.
It occurs in the sense of "flowing toward," as in "the rain fell as far as Pāṭaliputta";
however, it occurs in the sense of pervading an action through its extension, as in "the fame of the Blessed One extends as far as the peak of existence.

And since this prefix *ā-* is taken here in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*), they are called "taints" (*āsava*) because they flow by way of making those phenomena and that space their object, having encompassed them within.
They are so called. Furthermore, they are called *āsava* (taints) because, in the sense of having fermented for a long time, they are like fermented liquors (*madira*) and the like.

For in the world, fermented liquors and such that have been kept for a long time are called "taints" (*āsava*). And if they are taints by virtue of having fermented for a long time, then these [defilements] alone ought to be so.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned; before this, ignorance did not exist," and so forth.

However, when other states such as conceit (māna) and so forth—which proceed by taking the aforementioned phenomena as their scope and object—are present, it is only these [four] that possess the quality of being "outflows" (āsava) through their pervasiveness by way of grasping at self and what belongs to self, and through their capacity to cause intoxication; this is not the case for others.
Thus, in both of these two senses of the term, the word *āsava* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) only for these.
It should be seen. Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and pour forth (*pasavanti*) the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Indeed, there is no suffering of *saṃsāra* whatsoever that could arise without the *āsava*s.
"Covetousness is a bodily tie; ill will is a bodily tie; adherence to rules and observances is a bodily tie; the dogmatic insistence ‘This alone is the truth’ is a bodily tie..."

The four factors beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*), which are presented as "the bodily tie" (*kāyagantha*) and so forth, are called "ties" (*gantha*) because they tie and bind one who possesses them to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by means of death and rebirth. The four factors beginning with craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*),
which are presented as "the flood of sensual desire" (*kāmogha*), "the flood of existence" (*bhavogha*), "the flood of views" (*diṭṭhogha*), and "the flood of ignorance" (*avijjogha*),
are called "floods" (*ogha*) because they carry away and cause one who possesses them to sink into the cycle of existence.

These very things are called "yokes" (*yoga*) because they yoke one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), as they are described as "the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
Because the Noble Ones (*ariya*) do not go by means of this, it is called "non-going" (*agati*); it is fourfold, consisting of desire (*chanda*) and so forth.
"Or, craving arises in a monk for the sake of robes; craving arises for the sake of almsfood, lodgings, and for the sake of becoming this or that."
The four origins of craving (*taṇhuppāda*) are presented thus: "Or, craving arises in a bhikkhu as it arises. In this context, *itibhavābhavahetu*:
here, *iti* is a particle used for illustration; the meaning is that just as there is a cause such as robes and so forth, so too there is a cause for existence and non-existence (*bhavābhava*).

Furthermore, by "existence and non-existence" (*bhavābhava*), superior and more superior things such as oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, are intended. The four types of clinging (*upādāna*) are sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*) and the rest.

Regarding the passage beginning with "five mental barrennesses" (*pañca cetokhilā*), there are five mental barrennesses mentioned as follows: "He doubts the Buddha, doubts the Dhamma, doubts the Saṅgha, doubts the training, and he is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, having become barren.

They are called "mental barrennesses" (*cetokhilā*) because by means of them the mind becomes barren, that is, it reaches a state of rigidity. The word "five" (*pañca*) also occurs in the context of the "five bondages" (*vinibandha*) and so forth.
Each [term] should be applied individually: “He is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from lust for the body, not free from lust for form;
having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness;
and he leads the holy life aspiring for one or another class of devas. Thus it is said, having bound the mind to these five.

They are called "mental bondages" (*cetovinibandhā*) because they grasp the mind as if seizing it with a clenched fist. For, due to the activity of craving, these [hindrances] obstruct the mind as if binding it, by way of not allowing an opportunity for the arising of the wholesome.

In terms of the etymology of the word, however, they are called "mental bondages" because the mind (*ceto*) is bound—that is, restrained—by them in an improper way (*virūpa*). [These are] the five beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
They are called *nīvaraṇāni* because they shut off and obstruct wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). There are five kinds of delight, beginning with delight in forms (*rūpābhinandanā*).
Regarding the "six roots of dispute" and so forth: anger, hypocrisy, envy, deceit, evil desire, and adherence to one's own views—these are the six roots of dispute.
For it is said that one who is angry, or through the influence of anger... [and so on] ...or one who adheres to their own views, through the adherence to their own views.
One falls into quarreling, strife, and dispute; therefore, anger and the rest are called "the six roots of dispute.
There are six groups of craving (*taṇhākāya*): craving for forms, craving for sounds, and so forth.

There are seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*): sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, lust for existence, conceit, and ignorance. They are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie dormant in the sense that they have become firmly established and have not been abandoned. There are eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*): wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
“Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision-making;
dependent on decision-making, there is desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust, there is attachment;
dependent on attachment, there is possessiveness; dependent on possessiveness, there is stinginess; dependent on stinginess, there is guarding; and based on guarding—”
“From the taking up of sticks and weapons, from quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and lying—many evil, unwholesome states arise.
Thus, the nine [states] beginning with seeking (pariyesanā) that have thus come down are rooted in craving (taṇhā).
Therein, “dependent on craving” means relying upon craving. “Seeking” is the seeking after objects such as forms; for that [seeking] occurs when craving exists. “Gain” (lābha) is...
The acquisition of objects such as visible forms. For that [acquisition] occurs when there is seeking (*pariyesanā*). "Discrimination" (*vinicchaya*) here refers to applied thought (*vitakka*).
For having obtained what is acquired, one discriminates with applied thought alone between the desirable and undesirable, the beautiful and the ugly:
"This much will be for the sake of my object of visible form; this much for the sake of objects such as sound; this much..."
“...there will be this much for me, that much for another; I will enjoy this much, I will store away this much. Therefore it is said:
“In dependence on gain, there is decision-making (vinicchaya). Regarding “lustful desire” (chandārāga):
when an object has been thought over by such unwholesome thinking, both weak lust and strong lust arise. For here, “desire” (chanda) is a designation for weak lust.
*Aj-jhosānaṃ* means a strong conviction of "I" and "mine. *Pariggaho* is the act of grasping by way of craving and views.
*Macchariyaṃ* is the inability to endure sharing with others. For this very reason, the ancients explain its meaning thus:
"Because it occurs with the thought, 'Let this wonder be mine alone; let it not be a wonder for another.'"
"It is called avarice. "Guarding" (ārakkha) means protecting thoroughly by means of locking doors, closing windows, and so forth.
"It causes to proceed" (adhikaroti) thus it is "proceeding" (adhikaraṇa); this is a name for a cause. "Proceeding from guarding" (ārakkhādhikaraṇa) is a neuter abstract noun;
the meaning is "on account of guarding. "Taking up the staff," etc.: taking up a staff for the purpose of restraining others is "taking up the staff" (daṇḍādāna).
The taking up of a weapon such as a one-edged blade is "taking up a weapon. A quarrel (*kalaha*) is both a quarrel of body and a quarrel of speech.
Each preceding instance is a conflict (*viggaha*), while each subsequent instance is a dispute (*vivāda*). "You! You! is a disrespectful expression; the meaning is "you" and "thee.
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
The ten courses of unwholesome action; the four eternalist views, the four partial-eternalist views,
the four views on finitude and infinity, the four eel-wrigglers, the two fortuitous-originationists, the sixteen views of those who maintain the existence of consciousness after death,

the eight views of those who maintain the non-existence of consciousness after death, the eight views of those who maintain neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness after death, the seven annihilationist views, and the five views of Nibbāna in the present life.

These are the sixty-two views. The six types of craving—beginning with craving for form—each become eighteen by way of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). For instance, craving that has form as its object, or craving *for* form, is "craving for form" (*rūpataṇhā*).

When that [craving] proceeds by way of relishing form through the state of sensual lust, it is "craving for sense-pleasures. When it proceeds through the state of lust accompanied by the eternalist view, thinking "form is permanent," [it is craving for existence].

Craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is that which proceeds by finding gratification in this way: "It is permanent, it is eternal. Craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*) is that which proceeds by finding gratification through the passion associated with the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*), thinking:
"Form is annihilated, it perishes; having passed away, it does not exist. Thus, it is threefold.
And just as there is craving for form, so too are there cravings for sound and the rest. These are the eighteen modes of the movement of craving (*taṇhā-vicariya*).
These [cravings] exist: eighteen regarding internal form and so forth, and eighteen regarding external form and so forth, making thirty-six;
thus, thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present, which constitute the one hundred and eight modes of craving (*taṇhā-vicari-tāni*).
This is the meaning of "one hundred and eight modes of craving. The word *pabheda* (division) should be connected with each [of the three time periods]. In this regard, it is as follows:

The structural analysis (*yojanā*) is as follows: “the classification by way of greed, the classification by way of hatred, and so on, up to the classification by way of the eight hundred types of craving-conduct.
“All the hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause distress and fever” means all the many hundreds of thousands of defilements that produce distress and fever for sentient beings.
For indeed, the defilements have infinite classifications according to the division of their objects and according to the division of the modes of their manifestation.

In brief, regarding the phrase "or" (*vā*) and so forth: because they bring harm to sentient beings both in the present and in the future, the defilements (*kilesa*) are called "Māra" in the sense of killing and in the sense of afflicting;
thus, they are the *kilesa-māra*. Because they are murderous, the aggregates (*khandha*) are called "Māra"; for it is said:

"One does not understand as it really is that 'form is murderous, form is murderous,'" and so forth. [They are also called Māra] because they give rise to the great calamities of birth, aging, and so on.
Volitional formation itself is Māra; thus, he is *abhisaṅkhāramāra*. Being the sign of defilement, he is like a son of the gods (*devaputta*) in the sense that he destroys virtues;
thus, he is *devaputtamāra*. Because he is a great affliction by causing the destruction of beings' life and the requisites for life, death itself is Māra;
thus, he is *maccumāra*. In this context, [it refers to] making them entirely non-existent through abandonment by means of total eradication.
He shattered—the meaning is that he broke—Kilesamāra (the Māra of defilement) by means of the full understanding that abandons its arising;

Khandhamāra (the Māra of the aggregates) by means of bringing about their absolute non-arising through the lack of any companionship; Abhisaṅkhāramāra (the Māra of volitional formations) by making them cease to function altogether;
and Devaputtamāra and Maccurāja (the Māras of the son of a god and death) by means of shattering their power and transcending their domain. "Of perils" (*parissayānaṃ*) means of calamities.
"Of him who bears the marks produced by a hundred merits" means: of him who bears the marks of a Great Man produced by many hundreds of meritorious deeds.

For in this regard, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā did not approve of the view that "each single mark is produced by merely a hundredfold meritorious deed," [arguing] that "if that were so, anyone at all could become a Buddha. Rather, [they held that it was produced] by infinite...

They accepted this meaning: that whatever meritorious deeds, such as giving, have been performed one hundred times by each and every being in all the world-systems, the Great Being has performed each single meritorious deed a hundredfold more than that.
Therefore, in this context, the word "hundred" (*sata*) is a synonym for a great number, not a term denoting a specific numerical value.

It should be understood [in this sense], as in such passages as "a hundredfold for gods and humans. The excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is thus illustrated, because it serves as the root and the foundation for the other perfections of the fruit. The phrase "is illustrated" should also be applied to the "perfection of the Dhamma-body" and so forth.
In that context, because the perfection of knowledge and the others are preceded by the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of the Dhamma-body is illustrated.
It should be understood that [this] occurs. Regarding the phrase "the state of being highly esteemed by worldly peers":

here, one should connect this as follows—the state of being highly esteemed by worldly people due to their good fortune, and the state of being highly esteemed by peers due to the destruction of their faults.
In this way, the application [of the commentary] for those that follow should also be understood according to the respective order.

Householders, such as kṣatriyas and others, approach one who possesses merit; those gone forth, such as ascetics and wanderers, approach one who has abandoned faults in order to train in the removal of faults by means of the teaching of the Dhamma. Thus it is said: "The state of being approachable by householders and those gone forth.
Furthermore, he is capable of removing the physical and mental suffering of those who have approached him through both the giving of material goods and the giving of the Dhamma.

It should be understood that because of the presence of assistance, he brings about the subsiding of the two kinds of suffering after seeing his material body with the eye of faith and his Dhamma-body with the eye of wisdom.
He gives the gift of material things to those who have approached him due to his good fortune, and he gives the gift of the Dhamma due to his destruction of faults;
thus it is said: "He is helpful through the gifts of material things and the gift of the Dhamma."

And by thus enjoining those who have arrived [at this state] toward right practice—saying, "In the past, through gifts of material goods and gifts of the Dhamma, I attained this preeminence in the world;
therefore, you too must practice in exactly the same way"—it is demonstrated that there is the capacity to yoke them with mundane and supramundane happiness.
Thus, the capacity to yoke them with mundane and supramundane happiness is demonstrated by means of enjoining them toward right practice.

Mastery over one’s own mind (*sakacitte issariya*) means precisely bringing one’s own mind under control; it is the accomplishment of dwelling with the perception of the non-repulsive toward what is repulsive, and so forth.

Even the various types of supernormal power (*iddhividha*), such as the power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*), are indeed mastery over the mind, because they succeed through having attained mastery in the cultivation of the mind.

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “the powers of *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and so forth,” [the following are included]: *mahimā* (magnification), *patti* (attainment), *pākamma* (efficacy), *īsitā* (lordship), *vasitā* (control), and *yatthakāmāvasāyitā* (fulfillment of every wish).
These six are also included therein. Among them: *aṇimā* is the making of the body minute.
*Laghimā* is lightness by virtue of being capable of traveling through space on foot and so forth. *Mahimā* is greatness, the bringing about of the body’s largeness.
*Patti* is reaching a desired place. *Pākamma* is the accomplishment of what is desired by means of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth. *Issarabhāva* is self-mastery.

Mastery (*īsitā*). Mastery (*vasitā*) is the state of being a master over the various modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*). It is the attainment of proficiency in going through the air or performing any other such feat, reaching one's goal wherever desired;
it is also called "the ability to manifest forms such as those of a youth.
Thus, this eightfold sovereignty is recognized as mundane. However, that [sovereignty] belonging to the Blessed One is included within his own supernormal powers and is not shared with others.
He said: "It exists in its entirety, complete in all its aspects. Thus, the connection is that the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma) exists.

In the same way, the word "exists" (atthi) should be applied to fame and the other qualities as well. For some, fame exists only partially and is impure because it relies upon qualities that do not correspond to reality; it is not so [in the case of the supramundane state].
To show that it belongs to the Tathāgata, it is said: "pervading the three worlds.

In this context, for those who have realized the qualities of the Teacher and have arisen in the formless realm (ārūpa), the glory of the Blessed One—beginning with the words "Thus indeed is the Blessed One"—becomes manifest; therefore, he says "pervading the three worlds.
"Attained through qualities as they truly are" means attained by means of qualities according to reality. "Extremely pure" is because it has been attained through qualities as they truly are.

Thus it is absolutely pure. "Complete in every aspect" means fulfilled in all ways through the perfection of all the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*). "The splendor of all limbs and members" refers to the beauty of every limb and member.
"Whatever was desired or longed for by him" refers to whatever was sought by this Lord of the World, beginning with the words, "Having crossed over, may he ferry others across."
"Desired by way of mental and verbal aspiration" means wished for by way of physical aspiration. "In that very same way" means exactly in accordance with that aspiration.

"Exertion" refers to what is termed right effort; it is the striving termed right effort that has reached the state of the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramitā*) and is included within the Noble Path.

"By way of divisions such as the wholesome" means by way of the various classifications such as the wholesome and so forth, which are comprised within all the triplets and dyads. "By [the factors] such as dependent origination" means...

By the word "etc. (ādi), it should be understood that not only the foundations of mindfulness and so forth found in the *Vibhaṅga* text are included, but rather that the aggregates and so forth, the liberations through occasion and so forth, the establishing [of mindfulness] and so forth, and the threefold *Paṭṭhāna* and so forth are also included.

Or, in such passages as "The noble truth of suffering is, in the sense of being afflicted, conditioned, burning, and subject to change," the sense of being afflicted refers to that which possesses those [characteristics].

The sense of harming (*hiṃsana*) is the making of a being non-expansive. The sense of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) is the state of being produced by conditions through coming together, meeting, and combining.

The sense of distress (*santāpa*) is the burning and scorching by means of the suffering of suffering and so forth. The sense of change (*vipariṇāma*) is the state of being subject to two kinds of transformation:
by way of aging and by way of death. The sense of accumulation (*āyūhana*) refers to the origin of suffering.

The sense of "origination" (*nidāna*) is the bringing together by way of rebirth. The sense of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is the binding together with the suffering of *saṃsāra*, as if pointing out, "This is that suffering.
The sense of "impediment" (*palibodha*) is the obstruction to the attainment of the Path.
The sense of "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) regarding cessation is the state of having escaped from it, because its intrinsic nature is the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Or, it is the state of being the sign of escape from that. The sense of seclusion is the state of being dissociated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

The sense of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) is the state of not being conditioned by any condition whatsoever. The sense of the deathless (*amata*) is the absence of death due to its eternal nature, or the state of being the cause for the absence of death for sentient beings.
The sense of the path’s departure (*niyyāna*) is the sense of exiting from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The sense of the cause (*hetu*) is the state of bringing about Nibbāna.
The meaning of seeing (*dassanaṭṭha*) is the realization of Nibbāna, which is absolutely subtle.

The meaning of predominance (*ādhipateyyaṭṭha*) is the exercise of sovereignty by the associated states over the vision of the Four Truths, or rather, it is the state of being a predominant object (*ārammaṇādhipati*), specifically because of the designation "predominance of the Path" (*magga-adhipati*).

For even though jhānas and so forth possess the status of being predominant objects, one does not say "states with jhāna as their predominance" (*jhānādhipatino dhammā*) and so on; [rather, one says "states with the Path as their predominance"].
It is said, “states dominated by the Path”; therefore, it is understood that “there is a distinction in the state of being a dominant object (ārammaṇādhipatibhāva) for the Path.
And these very [factors], such as oppression (pīḷana) and so forth, are called the sixteen aspects (soḷasākāra).
Regarding the terms “divine, brahma, and noble abidings” (dibba-brahma-ariya-vihāra), etc., the fine-material-sphere jhānas having kasiṇa and other objects are the divine abiding.
The jhānas beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*) are the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). The attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is the noble abode (*ariyavihāra*).

Physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is the state of being alone by way of having withdrawn the body from sensual pleasures. Mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is the state of the mind being secluded from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth by means of the first jhāna and the rest.

Seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*) is Nibbāna. And here, "substrata" (*upadhi*) refers to the four substrata: the substratum of sensual pleasure (*kāmupadhi*), the substratum of the aggregates (*khandhupadhi*), the substratum of defilements (*kilesupadhi*), and the substratum of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārupadhi*).

For sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are called "substrata" (*upadhī*) in the sense of the word "that wherein happiness is deposited," because they serve as the basis for the happiness and joy that arise dependent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure—of which it is said: "Whatever happiness and joy arise dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification (*assāda*) of sensual pleasures.
Likewise, the aggregates (*khandhā*) are [called substrata] because they serve as the basis for the suffering rooted in the aggregates, and so too are the defilements (*kilesā*).
Because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the states of deprivation, and because volitional formations also serve as the basis for the suffering of existence,

they are called "substrata" (*upadhi*) according to the method already stated. Nibbāna is called "seclusion from substrata" (*upadhiviveka*) because of its state of being secluded from these four substrata.
The noble path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the aspect of emptiness (suññatā) is the emptiness liberation (suññatā-vimokkha).
For it is called "empty" because it has arisen from the element of emptiness, and it is called "liberation" because it is freed from the defilements (kilesa).

By this same method, the path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the aspect of the wishless (appaṇihita) is the wishless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha). [Likewise,] through the aspect of the signless (animitta)...
The signless liberation is that which proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object.

Alternatively, the Noble Path attained by means of the contemplation of non-self—which is termed the contemplation of emptiness—is called the "emptiness liberation" from the perspective of its approach.
Likewise, [the path] attained by means of the contemplation of suffering—which is termed the contemplation of the wishless—...

The wishless liberation (*appaṇihitavimokkho*). That which is obtained by means of the contemplation of impermanence—which is termed the "contemplation of the signless" (*animittānupassanā*)—should be understood as the "signless liberation" (*animittavimokkho*). For this has been said:
"One who attends to [the object] as impermanent and is abundant in resolution obtains the signless liberation; [one who attends to it] as suffering..."

"By attending to [the mind] as peaceful, one who abounds in tranquility attains the wishless liberation; by attending to it as non-self, one who abounds in equanimity attains the emptiness liberation.
"Other" refers to mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth.
Wandering through the realms of existence by way of the formations of defilements is primarily driven by craving; thus, he said, "going, which is termed craving.
"Vanta" means that which has been vomited out by means of the Noble Path and discarded so as not to return again.

Showing that the Blessed One (Bhagavā) is so called according to the method of etymological derivation (nirutti), he said, "Just as in the world," and so forth. Just as in the world, by way of etymological derivation...
Taking one syllable from each word, it is said “mekhalā”; the meaning is that it is the same here as well.
*Mehanassa* means of the private parts. *Khassa* means of the opening. Another method:

he possesses fortune (*bhāga*), thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). He has nurtured (*bhatavā*), thus he is the Blessed One. He desires fortune (*bhāge vanī*), thus he is the Blessed One. He dwells in fortune (*bhage vanī*), thus he is the Blessed One. He has eaten (*bhattavā*), thus he is the Blessed One. He emits into fortune (*bhage vamī*), thus he is the Blessed One. He emits into fortune (*bhāge vamī*), thus he is the Blessed One.

The Victor is called "Bhagavā" because he has partaken (*bhajitavā*) of the portions (*bhāga*), and because he has conquered (*vanitavā*) fortune (*bhaga*); likewise, he has vomited out (*vamitavā*) misfortune (*abhaga*) and has vomited out portions (*bhāga*).
In this regard, how is he "Bhagavā"? Those aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and the rest, which are portions (*guṇa-koṭṭhāsa*) not shared with others—[he has partaken of these].
The incomparable qualities of the Tathāgata are indeed found. For his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
his moral shame and fear of wrongdoing; his faith and energy; his mindfulness and clear comprehension; his purification of virtue and purification of view;
his serenity and insight; the three roots of the wholesome; the three types of good conduct; and the three kinds of right thoughts—all these exist in him to an unsurpassed degree.
Three perceptions of blamelessness, three elements, four foundations of mindfulness,
four right endeavors, four bases of psychic power, four noble paths, four noble fruits, four analytical knowledges,
four types of knowledge delimiting the four modes of birth, four noble lineages, four grounds of self-confidence, and five factors of exertion.
The five-factored right concentration, the five-knowledge right concentration,
the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements leading to escape, the five knowledges of the bases of liberation, the five perceptions that ripen liberation,
the six bases of recollection, the six kinds of reverence, the six elements leading to escape, the six constant abidings, and the six...
The unsurpassed states; the six perceptions conducive to penetration; the six direct knowledges; the six unique knowledges; the seven qualities that prevent decline;
the seven noble treasures; the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven qualities of a true person;

the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements]; the seven perceptions; the teaching on the seven types of persons worthy of offerings; and the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed.
The teaching on the causes for attaining wisdom regarding the eightfold path; the eight rightnesses; the transcendence of the eight worldly conditions;
the eight grounds for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments; the eight thoughts of a great person; the teaching on the eight bases of mastery;
the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention; the nine factors of striving for purification; and the teaching on the nine abodes of beings.
Nine ways of removing malice, nine perceptions, nine diversities, nine successive dwellings,
ten qualities that make one a protector, ten kasiṇa bases, ten courses of wholesome action, ten rightnesses, ten noble abodes, ten qualities of one beyond training,
ten powers of a Tathāgata, eleven benefits of loving-kindness, and twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (buddhañāṇa), the fifteen states that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma),

the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), the sixteen states that burn away the future (aparantapanīya-dhamma), the eighteen Buddha-qualities (buddhadhamma), the nineteen knowledges of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa),
the forty-four bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu), the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa), the more-than-fifty wholesome states (kusaladhamma), and the seventy-seven...
There exist infinite and immeasurable varieties of unique, unsurpassed, and supreme portions and categories of qualities, such as the bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*);
the great adamantine knowledge that traverses four hundred and twenty-four million meditative attainments;

the knowledges of analysis, review, and teaching regarding the *Paṭṭhāna* with its infinite methods; and likewise, the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings in infinite world-systems.

Because these [qualities] are found, and because he possesses the aforementioned portions of qualities (*guṇabhāga*), he should be called *bhāgavā*; however, by shortening the vowel *ā* to *a*, he is called "Bhagavā.
Thus, first of all, he is Bhagavā in the sense of being "possessor of portions" (*bhāgavā*).
Furthermore, because all the portions of qualities, such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest, exist in him without exception—
Because these qualities exist in the Sugata, he is called "Bhagavā.

How is he "Bhagavā" by virtue of being "one who has become" (bhūta-vā)? Those [qualities] which must be fulfilled by the Mahābodhisattvas—who have made the great resolution for perfect enlightenment after combining the eight factors beginning with human birth and who have applied themselves with zeal for the welfare of the entire world—[are found in him].
The ten perfections (pāramīs)—namely, the perfection of giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity;
the ten secondary perfections (upapāramīs); and the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs)—make thirty perfections in total.

Furthermore, there are the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthūs), beginning with giving; the four determinations (adhiṭṭhānas); and the five kinds of self-sacrifice: the sacrifice of one's own body, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife.
The five great renunciations, the preliminary application, the preliminary conduct, the proclamation of the Dhamma, the conduct for the benefit of relatives,

the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood— these and others such as these, in brief, are the qualities that constitute the equipment of merit and the equipment of knowledge which produce a Buddha.
From the time of the Great Resolve onwards, throughout four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, they [were fulfilled] as follows:
They do not pertain to decline, nor to defilement, nor to stagnation; rather, they pertain exclusively to ever-higher distinction.
Thus, because he has "borne" (*bhata*)—that is, accumulated—these [qualities] with care, continuously, and without remainder, he is called *Bhagavā*.
According to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), the letter *ta* is changed to *ga*, thus forming *bhagavā*. Alternatively, *bhagavā* refers to those very [qualities] as previously described.

He "maintained" (bharati) the qualities that constitute a Buddha according to the method described; the meaning is that he fulfilled them. Thus also, he is the Blessed One (bhagavā) because he maintained (bhatavā).
Since the Protector (nātha) maintained all the requisites for full enlightenment, such as the perfection of giving and the rest, for that reason also he is considered the Blessed One (bhagavā).

Why is he called "Bhāge vanī" (the one who has chosen his portion)? Those portions consisting of the twenty-four hundred thousand meditative attainments that are practiced daily—he chose, avoided [non-attainments], cultivated, and frequently practiced them for the sake of the welfare of the world and for his own dwelling in happiness in this very life throughout all time;
thus, because he "chose his portion," he is called Bhāge vanī. Alternatively, regarding the phenomena to be directly known, such as the wholesome states and so forth...
And among the aggregates and so forth, there are those fourfold portions of clear realization categorized briefly as "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) and so on;

but in detail, there are numerous portions to be fully understood, such as: "The eye is to be fully understood, the ear is to be fully understood... [and so on]... aging-and-death is to be fully understood";
and likewise, "The arising of the eye is to be abandoned... [and so on]... the arising of aging-and-death is to be abandoned."

Dhammas belonging to the category of what is to be abandoned by means of the method [of insight], those belonging to the category of what is to be realized— such as "the cessation of the eye... the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized"— and those belonging to the category of what is to be developed,

which are of many kinds such as "the path leading to the cessation of the eye" and "the four foundations of mindfulness," all these he frequented according to their respective requirements through resorting to their objective spheres and through cultivation.
He served [them] by means of these. Thus, he is called "Bhagavā" because he has sought (*vanī*) the portions (*bhāga*).

Alternatively, those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, which are common to his disciples—those portions of qualities, those segments of excellence—he sought with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to establish them within the mental continuums of those to be trained;
and that aspiration of his brought about the fruit exactly as intended.
"Thus he has partaken of the portion," said the Blessed One.
Because the Tathāgata partook of and aspired for the portion of the qualities of the knowable attainments for the welfare of beings, he is therefore called "Bhagavā."

Why is he called "Bhagavā"? Briefly stated, those things which are shared (*bhajīyanti*) according to one's wealth by those who have performed merit and are endowed with skillful means are called *bhagā*;
these are mundane and supramundane attainments. In that regard, first concerning the mundane:

prior to his full enlightenment, while still a bodhisatta, the Tathāgata frequented (*bhaji*), cultivated (*sevi*), and dwelt (*vani*) in the most excellent attainments, established upon which he [later] attained them without remainder.

Endowed with the qualities that produce a Buddha, he brought the Buddha-qualities to full maturity. Having become a Buddha, however, he resorted to and cultivated the forest—which is blameless, associated with happiness, and unique, not shared by others—even though it is supramundane.
In detail, however, [he enjoyed] through the sovereignty of regional kingship, the prosperity of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), the attainment of the status of a king of gods, and so forth;

and through the higher human states such as the meditations (*jhāna*), liberations (*vimokkha*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), the development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*), the realization of the fruits (*phala-sacchikiriyā*), and so on.
And he enjoyed, frequented, and cultivated manifold blessings that were not shared by others. Thus, because he enjoyed blessings (*bhaga*), he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
Whatever prosperities there are in the world, and whatever supramundane ones there are in abundance—the Fully Awakened One enjoyed them all;
for that reason also, he is considered the Blessed One.
"How is he 'possessed of devotion' (bhattavā), O Blessed One? "He is possessed of devotion because he has many devoted followers who are firm in their devotion.

For the Tathāgata is the supreme among all beings by virtue of possessing immeasurable and incomparable distinctions of power and qualities such as great compassion and omniscience; and [he is so] because of his unsurpassed [activity], which is preceded by the removal of all harm for others and is intent upon providing every benefit and happiness."
Because of his perfect application of means, his state of being of ultimate benefit to the world with its devas and humans,
and because his physical body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and other unique qualities not shared by others;
and because of the vast and utterly pure [glory] proceeding in the manner of "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," etc., which has attained qualities as they truly are and pervades the three worlds.
Because he is endowed with the sound of "thuti" (praise), because he is well-established in such qualities as fewness of wishes and contentment which have reached the highest perfection,

and because he possesses the distinguished and unsurpassed qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence, he is one who has confidence in the form to the measure of the form,
confidence in the sound to the measure of the sound, confidence in the coarse to the measure of the coarse, and confidence in the Dhamma to the measure of the Dhamma.
Thus, in this world-system consisting of the four measures, because it is beautiful on all sides by virtue of its quality of inspiring confidence,
it is the supreme object of love and devotion for immeasurable beings, including gods and humans, as it serves as a source of esteem, high respect, and reverence.
And those who are established in his instruction and endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda) become unshakable by anyone.
"Faith is not to be shaken by an ascetic, or a brahmin, or a deva, or Māra, or Brahmā.
For even at the sacrifice of their own lives, they do not abandon their confidence therein, because of the firm nature of their devotion to his command. Therefore it was said:
"The wise one who is grateful and mindful of what has been done..."
“He is a friend of virtue and firm in devotion.

And: “Just as, monks, the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore, even so, monks, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, that my disciples do not transgress even for the sake of their lives.”

"Bhattavā" (one who has supporters), says the Blessed One, according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), by eliding one *ta*-kāra and changing the other *ta*-kāra to a *ga*-kāra.
Because many have become his supporters— the Teacher who is endowed with preeminent virtues and seeks the welfare of the world— he is therefore called "Bhagavā."

Why is the Blessed One called "Bhagavā"? Because even while he was a Bodhisattva in former births, fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*), the Tathāgata vomited up, disgorged, and cast away—without regard, like a globule of spittle—the glory, sovereignty, and fame designated as "bhaga.
For instance, this occurred during his time as Prince Somanassa, during his time as Prince Hatthipāla, and during his time as the wise Ayoghara.

In such instances as his time as the wise Mūgapakkha and his time as Cūḷasutasoma, there is no measure to the number of times he renounced his own person— possessing royal glory equal to that of the gods—
in order to fulfill the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*); even in his final existence, he renounced the sovereignty of a world-ruler (*cakkavatti*) already in his hands,
the lordship over the realm of the gods, and the dominion over the four continents, which was based on the excellence of a world-ruler and radiant with the seven treasures.

Because he has renounced and gone forth without regard even for fame, and having done so, has awakened to perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), he is therefore called the Blessed One (bhagavā) because he has cast away (vamati) these fortunes (bhaga) such as glory and the rest.
Alternatively, "bhaga" refers to the constellations; those things that move and proceed in accordance with them are called "bhaga.
[The Buddha is so called] because he is supported by the specific features of the receptacle world (bhājanaloka), such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and the Himavat mountains.

"Beauty" (*sobhā*) is so called because it endures for an eon (*kappa*); the Blessed One "vomited" even those [beauties] because he transcended the abode of beings where they reside, by abandoning the desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) bound to them.
Thus, too, he is the "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) because he vomited out the "privates" (*bhaga*).
Because he [vomited out] the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-siri*), as well as fame, sovereignty, and happiness...
The Sugata, the Blessed One, has abandoned the worldly mind;
therefore, how could the Blessed One vomit up his share? "Shares" (bhāgā) refers to portions of phenomena that possess common characteristics.

These are manifold, categorized by way of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), and even within those, by way of form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), and so forth, as well as by way of the past and so on. And all such conceptual proliferation (papañca), the Blessed One has abandoned.
Having utterly severed all bonds, all ties, and all fetters, he attained the deathless element;
he vomited it up, cast it out without regard, and did not return to it.
For in this way, he was entirely indifferent toward earth, water, fire, and air, as well as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and toward forms, sounds, odors, and tastes.
Regarding tangible objects: eye-consciousness... [and so on] ...mind-consciousness;
eye-contact... [and so on] ...mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...feeling born of mind-contact; perception born of eye-contact...
[and so on] ...perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...volition born of mind-contact.

He vomited up and disgorged all categories of phenomena without exception—craving for forms... and so on... craving for mental phenomena; thoughts about forms... and so on... thoughts about mental phenomena;
and investigations of forms... and so on... investigations of mental phenomena—by way of the analysis of phenomena as they arise in succession.
He abandoned them with a relinquishment free from longing. For this has been said: "That which, Ānanda, has been cast out, vomited up, released, abandoned, and relinquished..."
"It is impossible that the Tathāgata will ever return to that [existence] again. Thus he vomits out existence;

this is why he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). Alternatively, "he vomits out existence" means that by means of the gateway of noble path-knowledge, he has vomited up, disgorged, and cast away—without regard or attachment—all phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless, inferior or superior, dark or bright, which are in mutual opposition; and he has abandoned them for others so that they may likewise become such.
He taught the Dhamma. For it has also been said: “Bhikkhus, even states that are in accordance with the Dhamma are to be abandoned, how much more so those that are contrary to the Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma as a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping,” and so forth.
Thus, too, he vomited out (vamati) what was on one side; therefore, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
Since the Great Seer has vomited out the various categories of phenomena— such as the aggregates, bases, and elements—
both dark and bright, for that reason also he is considered "Bhagavā.
Therefore it was said:
“He has attained the portion (bhāga), he has partaken of the portion, he has won the fortune (bhaga);
he vomits out fortune and likewise the portion—thus the Conqueror, the Blessed One, is called Bhagavā.
And here, because the qualities of a Buddha are, in brief, twofold by way of the attainment of one’s own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others,
Among those, the accomplishment of one’s own welfare is twofold, distinguished by the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge;
for the perfection of power and the others are included therein as being inseparable from them. The practice for the welfare of others is twofold, distinguished by application and disposition.

Therein, by way of application, it is the teaching of the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering for one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and the like; by way of disposition, [it is the same].
Even toward those who are hostile, there is constant desire for their welfare; this is the practice of benefiting others, such as by the arrival of the time for the ripening of their knowledge.

Even through the acceptance of material gifts and so forth, there is indeed the practice of beneficial conduct and the accomplishment of the welfare of others. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrases “worthy” (araha) and so on in the Canon are included here in order to clarify these qualities as well.
In this context, by the word "Arahant," the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare is manifested by way of the perfection of abandonment;

and by these words, "Sammāsambuddho" (Perfectly Enlightened) and "Lokavidū" (Knower of the World), it is manifested by way of the perfection of knowledge. [Objection: But is not the state of being a Sammāsambuddha also manifested by the term "Lokavidū"?
[Response: True, it is manifested; however, there is a distinction [between the two]. By the term "Sammāsambuddho,"...

By this [term], the power of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is manifested; furthermore, by the term "knower of the world" (*lokavidū*), the power of the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth is also manifested.
By the term "perfect in true knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*), all of the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare is manifested.

By the term "one who has fared well" (*sugato*), however, the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others, starting from the time of his full realization, are manifested.

And [the Blessed One] has been made manifest. By these words, "The unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans," the Blessed One’s practice for the benefit of others is made manifest.
By the word "Buddha," both the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the benefit of others are made manifest.
And having done so, by stating "the Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddho), the subsequent statement "the Buddha" is justified.
Therefore it was said: "He awakened by himself, and he awakened other beings," and so forth.
By the term *Bhagavā*, all the perfections for his own benefit and the practice for the benefit of others have been manifested in the Blessed One from the very beginning of his attainment.
Another method: briefly, the qualities of a Buddha are threefold, according to cause, fruit, and service to beings. Among these, *Arahaṃ*...
By the phrases "the Perfectly Enlightened One," "endowed with knowledge and conduct," and "knower of the worlds," the qualities of a Buddha are manifested by way of the perfection of the fruit.
By the phrases "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed" and "the teacher of gods and humans," the qualities of a Buddha are proclaimed by way of his assistance to sentient beings.
By the term "Buddha," the qualities of a Buddha are manifested both by way of the fruit and by way of his assistance to sentient beings.
It should be understood that by these terms, "Sugata" and "Bhagavā," the qualities of the Buddha are manifested by way of cause, fruit, being, and beneficence.
Regarding the passage beginning with "He, this world," etc.: "He, the Blessed One" refers to the Blessed One whose qualities have been extolled by the description beginning with "Arahant.
"This world" is not said merely with reference to those present before the great multitude; rather, it is spoken so as to include everything without exception.
The phrase beginning with "together with the devas" (*sadevaka*) was stated in order to show this. Therefore he said: "He now points out what is to be said.

"Because they have been born" (*pajātattā*) means because they have arisen through their own respective kamma and defilements. It should be understood that by the expression "together with the devas," the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere devas (*pañcakāmāvacara-deva*) is intended according to the method of elimination (*pārisesa-naya*), since the others are already included by the other terms. And the term "together with the devas" refers to a specific part [of the whole].

The compound (*samāsa*) is a collection; this is the meaning of the compound. By the term "together with Māra" (*samāraka*), it should be understood that the inclusion of the devas of the sixth sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is by way of proximity.
For therein he was born and dwelt. By the term "together with Brahmā" (*sabrahmaka*), there is the inclusion of the devas of the Brahmā-world (*brahmakāyika*) and so forth;
here too the same principle applies. The mention of "enemies... [and] recluses and brahmins" is merely illustrative.
This is because [the world] is included by way of the statement of the recluses and brahmins, both those who have adversaries and those who have not yet subdued their evil.

Granted, it is understood that the word *loka* has "beings" as its referent on account of the qualifiers such as "together with devas," since these [qualifiers] share a common grammatical connection (*tulyayoga*);
however, this compound occurs even in cases of non-common connection (*atulyayoga*), as in the expressions "having hair" (*salomako*) and "having wings" (*sapakkhako*).
He said, "The term 'progeny' (pajā) is used because it shows deviation [from the literal sense]," explaining that "by the word 'progeny,' the world of beings (sattaloka) is grasped.

Since the phrase "together with devas" (sadevaka) and so forth includes the devas of rebirth (upapatti-deva), and the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins" (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī) includes the purified devas (visuddhi-deva), he said, "By the phrase 'together with devas and humans' (sadevamanussa), the conventional devas (sammuti-deva) and the remaining humans are grasped. In this context, the conventional devas are...
"Kings. "The inclusion of the remaining people" means the inclusion of the remaining people apart from the recluses and brahmins.
"By three terms" refers to the expressions "together with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas. "By two" refers to these two terms: "with its recluses and brahmins" and "together with devas and humans.
As for "devas," they receive this etymological derivation because formless beings, dwelling in their own state of imperturbability (*āneñja*), shine forth; thus they are called *devā*.
He said: "By the inclusion of 'together with the devas,' the world of the formless realm (arūpāvacara-loka) is included. For this very reason, the Blessed One said:

"To the companionship of the devas who have reached the base of infinite space," and so forth. Because the sixfold world of the sense-sphere devas (kāmāvacara-deva-loka) specifically falls under the power of Māra, he said:
"By the inclusion of 'together with Māra,' the sixfold world of the sense-sphere devas is meant. Since the world of the formless Brahmas (arūpī-brahmaloka) has been mentioned separately...

He said, “The Brahma-world is material. Regarding the phrase “by way of the four assemblies”: this refers to the eight assemblies—the assembly of khattiyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of recluses, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmas—namely, by way of the four assemblies beginning with the khattiyas. However, the other four assemblies are already included by the mention of Māra.
But how, in this context, is the human world included by way of the four assemblies? By the phrase “together with recluses and brahmins.”

The assembly of recluses (*samaṇa-parisā*) and the assembly of brahmins (*brāhmaṇa-parisā*) are included; by the phrase "together with gods and humans" (*sadevamanussa*), the assembly of nobles (*khattiya-parisā*) and the assembly of householders (*gahapati-parisā*) are included.
Furthermore, by the word "people" (*paja*), these same four assemblies are meant; what is stated is that "people" refers to the group consisting of the four assemblies.
But how is the world of humans (*manussaloka*) taken here together with conventional deities (*sammutideva*)? To this, [the text] says: "together with recluses and brahmins" (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi*).
By the phrase "ascetics and brahmins," these are included;
by the phrase "together with gods and humans," the kshatriyas known as conventional gods (sammutideva), as well as the remaining humans known as householders and suddas, are included.
Since there are no human beings other than these, it should be understood that by the word "progeny" (paja), these very same human beings existing in four ways are what are spoken of.

Thus, since in both of these two interpretations the term "people" (*pajā*) refers only to humans existing as the fourfold assembly, he now says, "or the entire world of remaining beings," wishing to include and show all other sentient beings by means of this term "remaining.
In that context, the "world of remaining beings" should be understood by way of *nāgas*, *garuḷas*, and so forth. Here too, by way of the fourfold assembly—
Or, it should be construed that the world of all remaining sentient beings is together with the conventional deities (*sammutideva*).

What is meant is that either the world of all remaining sentient beings—such as pure *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and denizens of hell—together with the four assemblies, or the world of all remaining sentient beings—such as *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and denizens of hell—together with humans existing in their fourfold division, is included.
Having thus demonstrated the application by taking the world in its parts (*bhāgaso*), [the text] now proceeds to do so without such division (*abhāgaso*) according to various specific distinctions.
