In order to demonstrate a *yojana* by taking the world as a measure, the passage beginning with “Furthermore, here” (*apicettha*) was stated. Therein, “by way of the supreme limit” (*ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato*) means by way of knowing the highest degree.
For among the five destinations (*gati*), only those included within the divine destination (*devagati*) are superior;

even there, the formless beings (*arūpin*) are most excellent because their defilements and suffering have been cast far away, because they possess a peaceful, sublime, and imperturbable dwelling, and because they possess an exceedingly long lifespan.
By such distinctions as these, it is exceedingly exalted. "Brahmā of great power" is said with reference to the Great Brahmā of the ten-thousandfold world system;
for it is stated: "In terms of the highest limit. "The unsurpassed" means the supreme nine supramundane states (*navalokuttara*).
"The sequence of the connection" refers to the order of the connection between both meanings and words. However, the ancients explain it here in this way:
“Together with the devas” means the rest of the world together with the devas. “Together with Māra” means the rest of the world together with Māra.
“Together with Brahmā” means the rest of the world together with the Brahmas.

Thus, having included all beings subject to the three realms of existence within the three categories denoted by the three terms beginning with “together with the devas”—namely, being accompanied by devas, Māras, and Brahmas—
Furthermore, encompassing it by means of two phrases, he said, "the generation together with its ascetics and brahmins, together with its devas and humans.
Thus, even by means of these five phrases, the threefold world (tedhātuka) itself is encompassed in various ways, such as "together with its devas" and so forth.
Regarding the term *abhiññā*, this is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *y*; its meaning here is "having directly known," as he said: "by direct knowledge (*abhiññāya*)."

"Having known by means of superior knowledge. The rejection of inference and so forth refers to the rejection of inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), postulation (*arthāpatti*), and the like, because [for the Buddha] there is only a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the Blessed Buddhas have direct perception (*paccakkha*) of all things due to the unimpeded range of their knowledge regarding everything.
"Supreme bliss of seclusion" refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). By means of that, even when the Blessed One was on his way...
Regarding the phrase "there is a teaching of the Dhamma": the inclusion of the word *api* (even) signifies "even having abandoned.

For when the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma, at the very moment the assembly utters an exclamation of approval (*sādhukāra*) or reflects upon the Dhamma as it has been heard, he delimits that moment by his prior resolve and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). And from that attainment, according to the limit of his resolve...
Having risen, he teaches the Dhamma starting from the very place where he stood. "Whether teaching little or much" means:

he teaches little for the sake of one who understands through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), or he teaches much for the sake of one who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) or one who is to be guided (*neyya*).
"He teaches in a manner that is good in the beginning, etc. means: he teaches having made it good, auspicious, and blameless at the beginning; likewise in the middle and at the end.
It is said that one teaches only after having made [the teaching] beautiful, auspicious, and entirely blameless.
For the beauty of the Dhamma consists in its being a vehicle for deliverance, and its being a vehicle for deliverance arises from its state of being entirely blameless.
"All-auspiciousness" (*samantabhaddakatā*) means being excellent in every respect. "Of the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*). Although...
In the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "collection" (samudāya) existing apart from its constituent parts (avayava).

However, when those constituent parts are regarded as a collection-form, they receive the conventional designation "verse" (gāthā). To demonstrate this by applying a metaphorical expression (*saṃsāmivohāra*) as if it were distinct from them, he says:
"By the first quarter, it is 'good in the beginning' (*ādikalyāṇā*)," and so forth. The term "having a single connection" (*ekānusandhika*) means that it does not have too many divisions.
This was stated with reference to that which possesses a single continuous connection (*ekānusandhika*) according to its sequence of composition.

However, for the other type [of discourse], the beginning, middle, and end portions are obtained through that very same classification of the phenomena to be taught. "By the introduction" (*nidāna*) means by the introductory section characterized by the pointing out of the time, place, teacher, assembly, and so forth, as established by the Elder Ānanda.
"By the conclusion" (*nigamana*) means by such passages as "This he said," and so on, up to "Thus, that which was spoken, this is dependent upon this."

Or, it is said "thus" by way of concluding the meaning as previously stated. For even though the introductory settings (*nidāna*) and conclusions were established by the compilers of the Council, they are included within the Teacher’s own teaching because they conform to it. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:
"In a sutta consisting of a single sequence of connection, the introduction is the beginning; 'Thus he spoke' is the end; that which lies between the two is the middle."

Having thus shown that the Dhamma is excellent in the beginning by way of the Suttanta Piṭaka, [the author] now says “the whole of it,” etc., in order to show that same quality by taking all three Piṭakas together. Therein, the Dhamma of the Dispensation is as follows:
“To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome, to purify one’s own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
The Dhamma of the scriptures is the expositor of the Teacher’s instruction thus spoken. Because the Dispensation is rooted in virtue, it is said to be "good in the beginning through virtue.
Since serenity and the other factors constitute the middle stage of the Dispensation’s perfection, it is said to be "good in the middle through serenity, insight, the path, and the fruit.
Because there is nothing further to be done beyond the attainment of Nibbāna, it is said to be "good in the end through Nibbāna."

In the Dispensation, what is called "right practice" arises through wisdom (*paññā*), and for that, virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are the roots; thus he said, "or it is good in the beginning by way of virtue and concentration.
Since wisdom is twofold—by way of initial awakening and by way of penetration—he said, "it is good in the middle by way of insight and the path," thereby including both.
Its function as the fruit of its accomplishment is the realization of Nibbāna.
Showing that there is nothing further to be done beyond this, he said: "It is beautiful in its conclusion through the fruits and Nibbāna.
By the mention of "fruits," he refers to Nibbāna with residue remaining; by the other term [Nibbāna], he refers to the other [Nibbāna without residue].
Thus, he said "it is beautiful in its conclusion through the fruits and Nibbāna" to indicate that both of these constitute the culmination of the excellence of the Dispensation.

Or, it is "good in the beginning" because of the Buddha’s excellent awakening (*subodhitā*); that is, the Buddha’s state of being perfectly awakened (*sammāsambuddhatā*), and because [the Dhamma] originates from him, it is good in the beginning.
The complete abandonment of all defilements and the fulfillment of purification constitute the "wellness of the Dhamma" (*dhammasudhammatā*);
because it has that as its essence, it is good in the middle. The practice in accordance with what was instructed by the Teacher is the "good practice of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasuppaṭipatti*).
By that [teaching], it is "beautiful in its conclusion" because of the well-established nature of the Dispensation (sāsana) in the world. "That" refers to the Dhamma of the Dispensation.
"For the sake of suchness" means for the sake of that which the Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One; for the sake of suchness, for the state of being thus.

Furthermore, that [awakening] is threefold—namely, perfect enlightenment (abhisambodhi), solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhi), and disciple-enlightenment (sāvakabodhi)—because there is no attainment of Nibbāna other than through these.
In this context, the first enlightenment is said to be "good in the beginning" because it is the foremost of all qualities and is the root of the other two enlightenments;

the second is "good in the middle" because its qualities occupy a middle position; and the third is "good in the end" because it represents both of those states and because it is the final consummation of the Dhamma of the Dispensation.

This is the Dhamma of the Dispensation. "By the suppression of the hindrances" means that for one who stands at the head of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) and listens to the True Dhamma, there is the actual presence of the suppression of the hindrances. For this has been said:

"In whatever way, friends, the Teacher or a certain venerable fellow-celibate teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, in that very way he gains inspiration from the meaning therein, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma."
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, at that time his five hindrances are abandoned,” and so forth.
“Because it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight” means because it leads to the attainment of the bliss of serenity (*samatha*) and the bliss of insight (*vipassanā*).
And this has also been said: “Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he dwells with applied thought and sustained thought...”
“the rapture and happiness born of seclusion,” and so forth; likewise:
“From whatever [aspect] one contemplates The arising and passing away of the aggregates, One gains rapture and gladness— That is the deathless for those who understand.”
“And there is superhuman delight for one who clearly sees the Dhamma rightly.

Thus, “practicing accordingly” means practicing the Dhamma of the Dispensation in such a way as to bring about the bliss of serenity and insight, or in accordance with what was instructed by the Teacher.
“Because it brings about the state of neutrality” refers to [equanimity] through the sixfold equanimity regarding desirable and other objects.

Because it brings about a state of being unstained by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). Regarding "having the Protector as its source" (*nāthappabhavatta*): that from which something originates is its "source" (*pabhava*), meaning its place of arising.
That which has the Protector alone as its source is "Protector-sourced" (*nāthappabhava*); the state of being such is "Protector-sourcedness" (*nāthappabhavatta*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the Dhamma of the Dispensation has the Protector as its cause. Regarding "beautiful in the middle for the sake of purity of meaning": because of its freedom from defilements (*nirupakkilesatā*).
The purity of purpose (*atthasuddhi*) consists in its leading to liberation; by that, it is "beautiful in the middle. It is "beautiful in the end" through the purity of function (*kiccasuddhi*);
that is, it is beautiful in the end through the purity of the function known as right practice, because the Dhamma of the Dispensation culminates in right practice.
Concluding the aforementioned meaning, he says "Therefore," and so forth.

In such passages as "the holy life of the Dispensation" (*sāsanabrahmacariya*), the three trainings and the entire body of the Dhamma in its continuity constitute the holy life of the Dispensation without distinction;
it is with reference to this that it was said: "Venerable sir, for which Buddhas, Blessed Ones, was the holy life not long-lasting?
and so forth. The Noble Eightfold Path is the holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*). It is with reference to this that...
It is said: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done. “According to what is appropriate” means according to what is fitting.

For the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*), which comprises the three trainings, is “possessed of meaning” (*sāttha*) by way of the attainment of its goal; so too is the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).
But the other—the holy life of the Dispensation consisting of the textual teachings (*tantidhamma*)—is “possessed of meaning” and “possessed of phrasing” (*sabyañjana*) in the sense already stated.
"By the perfection of meaning" means by the state of having a perfect meaning; for here the word *saha* has the sense of "perfection.

"By the perfection of phrasing"—here too the same principle applies. For one whose teaching is dependent on descriptions of things such as rice-gruel and meals, or men and women, does not teach with a true purpose (*sāttha*), because that teaching is devoid of the purpose of deliverance (*niyyāna*). But the Blessed One [taught] in such a manner...
Having set aside [other] teachings, he teaches a discourse based on the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth;
therefore, it is said that "he teaches what possesses the goal because of its perfection in meaning.

Furthermore, his teaching is "endowed with a single phoneme" and so forth, because among the phonemes distinguished as soft or hard and so on, his discourse is joined with phonemes of only one kind or two kinds—just like the Tamil language—or because of the opening of the vocal organs.
Because it must be uttered without touching the lips, its consonants are all labial, like the Kirāta language;
or because it is suitable for release in every respect, its consonants are all released, like the Yavana language;
or because it possesses aspiration in every respect, its consonants are all aspirated, like the Pādasika and other barbarian languages—thus, regarding the perfection of its phonemes...
Because it lacks [proper] phonemes, the teaching is called "without phonemes" (*abyañjanā*).
For all of this is called "without phonemes" on account of its being incomplete in its phonemes, since it proceeds only by way of a portion of the phonemes. However, the Blessed One said:
"The relaxed and the emphatic, the long and the short, the heavy and the light, and the nasalized (*niggahīta*);"
“The relationship is established and liberated; this is the tenfold classification according to the understanding of the phrasing.

Having thus spoken, he teaches the Dhamma without defiling the tenfold phrasing, but rather making it complete in its phrasing; therefore, it is said: “He teaches with excellence of phrasing, possessing phrasing.
Now, in order to show the meaning here in the phrase “with meaning and with phrasing” (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*) even by way of the *Netti* method, [it says]: “The announcing... pe...”

It is said, "with the phrasing. In that regard, although in the *Netti* the phrases concerning the phrasing were first listed—beginning with "the apprehension of the meaning of the phrasing occurs by means of the phrasing;

thus, the syllable, the word," and so on—here, because it has come down in the Pāḷi as "with the meaning and with the phrasing," the phrases concerning the meaning are shown first with the words "manifestation and elucidation," and so forth.
It has been said. Therein, in brief, *saṅkāsana* means illuminating or making manifest. And "illuminating" (*kāsanam*) has the sense of being illuminated, made manifest, or clarified.
Just as in such passages as, "Monk, one who conceives is bound by Māra;
one who does not conceive is freed," illumination in brief is called *saṅkāsana*. For by that much alone was it penetrated by that monk.
Therefore he said, "It is understood, Blessed One," and so forth. *Paṭhama* means manifesting (*pakāsana*).
In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, everything is ablaze," the manifestation of a meaning that is to be stated later by means of an earlier statement is called *pakāsana*.
For this prefix *pa-* is used in the sense of an initial action, as in "he makes known" (*paññapeti*) or "he establishes" (*paṭṭhapeti*). And these two words refer to those of keen faculties.
Because it is a summary statement. For one with keen faculties practices the meaning stated briefly and first.
An expanded explanation of what was concise, and a restatement of what was said once, constitute exposition and analysis;
for example, regarding the meaning stated briefly and only once as "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*), [the question is asked]: "Which states are wholesome? Those in which... [and so forth].

The repetition [of the statement] by way of detailed exposition and analysis, beginning with “at that time, wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere,” refers to these two terms in relation to the medium faculties because they constitute the mode of description (*niddesa*).
The further verbalization of what has been explained, the more extensive expression of what has been analyzed,
the making known through various modes, the gladdening of the minds of those to be trained, as well as the making plain and the establishing [of the teaching], [are the functions of this repetition].

Just as, for example, after the meaning has been explained in detail by such statements as "there is contact," there is a further clarification and exposition by means of questions such as: "What kind of contact is there at that time? It is the contact, the touching, the contacting that exists at that time.
These two phrases are intended for those of dull faculties, because they function as a detailed explanation (*paṭiniddesa*).

Alternatively, by making clear once again the meaning already illustrated first in the statement, “Bhikkhus, everything is on fire,” through the detailed explanation of what was previously stated in brief—by saying, for example, “And what, bhikkhus, is everything that is on fire? The eye, bhikkhus, is on fire;
visible forms are on fire”—and thus expanding upon it, [the Buddha] spoke again.
“Exposition” (desanā) means “unfolding” (vivaraṇaṃ). When the wholesome states (kusala-dhammā), which were set forth in brief as “What are the wholesome states?

At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere has arisen,” are unfolded by way of the detailed explanation (niddesa), the making of distinctions among those wholesome states—such as “at that time there is contact, there is feeling”—is called “analysis” (vibhajana).
It makes clear by means of an exposition that which has been opened up through detailed description, and by means of a simile that which has been analyzed.

Thus, regarding that which has been opened up, there is the further opening up of the meaning by stating: "What on that occasion is contact? It is that which on that occasion is contact, the act of contacting, the state of contacting.
Regarding that which has been analyzed, there is the analysis by way of illustration: "Just as, for example..."
“Monks, just as a cow is without its hide, even so, monks, should this nutriment of contact be regarded,” and such like telling of similes is called "making clear.
Furthermore, it is the production of joy through a teaching of the Dhamma that is varied and manifold for those listening to the Dhamma,
and the making of various kinds of knowledge sharp for those of keen intelligence.
"Designation" (*paññatti*) is so called because it is the act of making known (*paññāpana*) through the gladdening and the focusing of the minds of listeners; thus it is "designation.

It is "with meaning" (*sāttha*) due to its connection with the words of the meaning, because the meaning of the scripture consists in the form of the words of meaning such as "explaining" (*saṅkāsanā*) and so forth; thus, by virtue of its connection with the six aforementioned kinds of words of meaning, it is "with meaning.
For explaining, clarifying, and so on, are called "words of meaning" because they are modes of meaning. Meaning itself...
For it is by means of the phrasing (*byañjana-pada*) that [the meaning] is indicated, elucidated, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and defined.

Regarding the phrase "perfection of syllables, words, phrasing, modes, etymologies, and explanations": here, in cases such as "sixty thousand years" (*saṭṭhi vassasahassāni*), a syllable (*akkhara*) is a phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) at the time of pronunciation, even when the word is not yet finished, such as the *sa*-sound, the *du*-sound, or the *so*-sound, and so forth.
Because it does not shift by way of synonyms and because it is non-synonymous. For there exists no synonym for a phoneme (*vaṇṇa*).
Just as a word (*pada*), by virtue of having synonyms, moves as if it were shifting according to its meaning, so it is not with a phoneme, due to its lack of synonyms.
Or, a single phoneme is a "syllable" (*akkhara*), such as the syllables *mā* and so forth in expressions like "mā evaṃ kira taṃ."

...as it were. However, some say: "Because they do not leak (*akkharanti*), because they are non-synonymous (*avevacana*), and because they have not been spoken (*akathita*) by the words of the teaching set forth by the mind—which is the basis for purification through the state of pure application in the three doors—they are called 'syllables' (*akkhara*).
This refers to the questions mentally asked by the Brāhmaṇas of the *Pārāyana* while the Blessed One was seated in the Jewel House."
They say it should be understood by way of the *Mahāpakaraṇa* (Great Treatise) on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

A "word" (*pada*) is so called because it makes known the meaning through its analysis; for a word is that by which a meaning is reached (*pajjati*). It is fourfold: the noun-word (*nāmapada*), the verb-word (*ākhyātapada*), the prefix-word (*upasaggapada*), and the particle-word (*nipātapada*).
Among these, such terms as "contact," "feeling," and "consciousness" are primarily concerned with substantial entities (*dabbapadhāna*).
A noun-phrase (*nāmapada*). In noun-phrases, the substance (*dabba*) has a manifested form (*āvibhūtarūpa*), while the action (*kiriyā*) has an unmanifested form (*anāvibhūtarūpa*).

A verb-phrase (*ākhyātapada*) is primarily characterized by action, such as "he touches," "he feels," or "he cognizes. In verb-phrases, the action has a manifested form, while the substance has an unmanifested form.
For example, in the phrase "one who has long been away" (*cirappavāsī*), the prefix *pa-* [in *pavāsi*] qualifies the act of dwelling by its separation [from the subject].
It illuminates; thus, because it illuminates a specific action, it is a sign for the comprehension of a specific action. *Pa-* and so forth are prepositional words (*upasagga-pada*).
Words such as *evaṃ* (thus) and so forth are indeclinable particles (*nipāta-pada*), which serve as the cause for manifesting the specific nature of both the action and the object.
For instance, in passages such as "Pay attention in this way; do not pay attention in that way," [the particle] illuminates a specific action.
The word *evaṃ* indicates a particular action, as in such cases as “of such virtue, of such nature. It indicates a particular substance, as in “of such virtue, of such nature,” and so forth.

It is called *byañjana* (the manifestor) because it manifests the meaning expressed by the words when stated in brief; thus, it refers to the sentence. For example, regarding the meaning briefly stated as “the four bases of psychic power,” [it is expanded]: “Which four?
Here, monks, a monk possesses the concentration of desire together with the volitional formations of striving...”

Or, it may be said that the sentence itself is the "phrasing" (*byañjana*), as in the passage: “He develops a basis for psychic power; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through energy, concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation.
This, however, should be understood in meaning as a collection of words (*padasamudāya*). For they say:
“A sentence is a collection [of words] together with verbs, together with nouns, together with agents, or together with qualifiers. Is it not so?
And does it follow that because meaning is manifested even by a single word, the word itself must be considered a "manifestor" (byañjana)? That is not so.
For even when only a single word is heard, the comprehension of the meaning occurs only after connecting it with other words obtained through the context and so forth;
thus, it is the sentence alone that manifests the meaning.
*Ākāra* (aspect) is the analysis of a statement according to its constituent parts. In such passages as, “Therein, what is desire (*chanda*)?

It is desire, longing, and the wish to act,” the analysis of the very statement thus spoken in various ways is called *ākāra*. Etymological derivation (*nirutti*) is the explanation expressed by way of *ākāra*.
In such cases as “contact is feeling,” that which is stated by way of *ākāra*—namely, “it touches, therefore it is contact”—is etymological derivation.
"Feeling is so called because it feels"—having extracted [this definition], the detailed explanation is called *nirutti* (etymological interpretation).

"Nibbāna is sought (*maggati*), or it is sought by those seeking Nibbāna, or it goes while killing the defilements (*kilesa*)—thus it is the path (*magga*)"—such a detailed etymological analysis is called *niddesa* (exposition) because it is a teaching that leaves nothing out.
Alternatively, regarding the terms obtained through such etymologies as "feeling is so called because it feels," within the categories of pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings:

It is called *sukhā* because it makes one happy; *dukkhā* because it makes one suffer; and *adukkhamasukhā* because it neither makes one suffer nor makes one happy—this is the detailed exposition of the meaning (*atthavitthāra*).
Because these syllables and so forth, these phonetic words, are complete in their excellence, it is called "with phonetic perfection" (*sabyañjana*).
In this way, however, its conjunction of meaningful words (*atthapada*) and perfection of phrasing (*byañjanapada*) should be understood.

Therein, the Blessed One makes it known through syllables (*akkhara*), reveals it through phrases (*pada*), discloses it through phonemes (*byañjana*), analyzes it through modes (*ākāra*), clarifies it through etymologies (*nirutti*), and defines it through detailed explanations (*niddesa*). For thus, by means of grasping the components of a phrase, there is the grasping of the phrase itself.

Furthermore, since the comprehension of the meaning of a word occurs for one who has previously grasped the linguistic convention through that very word, the Blessed One indicates [the meaning] by means of syllables (*akkhara*).

However, because the meaning being indicated in brief by means of syllables is first revealed and illuminated by the word—since the sentence is not yet complete at the conclusion of the word—he indicates it by means of words (*pada*). At the conclusion of the sentence...
However, since that meaning has been disclosed, opened up, and made clear, he discloses it by means of *byañjana* (phonemes).
And because when sentence divisions are made through various modes (*pakāra*), that meaning becomes analyzed (*vibhatto*), he analyzes it by means of *ākāra* (modes).

Likewise, since that meaning becomes manifest when the etymological analysis (*nibbacana*) of each component of the sentence is performed, he makes it explicit by means of *nirutti* (etymologies). By means of those [meanings] whose etymological analysis has been performed...

Furthermore, because the teaching is presented exhaustively through the expansion of the constituent parts of the discourse, it brings satisfaction to the minds of those to be trained and sharpens their intelligence;
thus he makes it known through the *niddesas*. Moreover, the Blessed One guides those who understand through what is condensed (*ugghaṭitaññū*) by means of syllables and phrases;
he guides those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) by means of phonemes and modes.

Having led [the listener] by means of definitions (*nirutti*), one leads the one who is to be led (*neyya*) by means of explanations (*niddesa*). Thus, when this Dhamma is being summarized, it leads the one who understands through summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*);
when it is being elaborated, it leads the one who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*); and when it is being led [through reasoning], it leads the one who is to be led.

In this context, the summary is at the beginning, the elaboration is in the middle, and the leading is at the end. Thus, taught in three ways during these three times, it destroys the three faults and brings about the three qualities.

“Guiding those to be trained in three ways”: thus, this Dhamma is also to be understood as threefold in its excellence, being "with meaning and with phrasing" due to the perfection of both meaning (*attha*) and phrasing (*byañjana*). For this has been said in the *Nettippakaraṇa*:

“In that regard, the Blessed One makes it known through syllables (*akkhara*), clarifies it through phrases (*pada*), reveals it through phrasings (*byañjana*), and [illuminates it] through modes (*ākāra*).”
He analyzes, clarifies with etymological explanations (*nirutti*), and defines through detailed descriptions (*niddesa*).
In this regard, the Blessed One introduces [the teaching] through syllables and phrases, elaborates it through phonemes and modes, and expands upon it through etymologies and detailed descriptions.
Herein, introduction is the beginning, elaboration is the middle, and expansion is the conclusion. This is that—
“The Dhamma-Vinaya, when condensed, disciplines the person who gains knowledge through what is condensed; therefore it is called ‘beautiful in the beginning.
When it is explained in detail, it disciplines the person who gains knowledge through detailed explanation; therefore it is called ‘beautiful in the middle.
When it is expanded, it disciplines the person who is guided by what is led; therefore it is called ‘beautiful in the end.’”

Regarding "depth of meaning" and so forth: "meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the textual string (*tanti*). "Dharma" (*dhamma*) is the textual string itself. "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization of the textual string and its meaning exactly as they are.
"Teaching" (*desanā*) refers to the teaching of the textual string as it has been determined by the mind.
Now, these factors—meaning and the rest—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, just as the great ocean is for crocodiles and the like.
And therefore, it is profound. Alternatively, "meaning" (attha) refers to cause and fruit; "dharma" refers to the cause;

and "teaching" (desanā) refers to designation (paññatti), which is the verbal expression of dharmas according to their nature, or the exposition by way of direct order, reverse order, summary, detailed analysis, and so forth.

"Penetration" (paṭivedha) is realization (abhisamaya); it is the conformity to dharmas according to the meaning, the conformity to meanings according to the dharmas, and the conformity to the path of designation.
It is the awakening to designations; or it is the unerring intrinsic nature, characterized as the specific mark, which is to be penetrated regarding those various phenomena.

Furthermore, these meanings and so forth are profound because they are difficult to plunge into and provide no foothold for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit—just as the great ocean is for crocodiles. This is because penetration into them is also dependent upon the meaning.
It is said, "It is 'possessing the meaning' (sāttha) by way of profundity of meaning and profundity of penetration," because it illuminates the qualities of the meaning.
It is said, "It is 'possessing the phrasing' (sabyañjana) by way of profundity of Dhamma and profundity of teaching," because it illuminates the excellence of the phrasing of those Dhamma-teachings.
Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

The knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) of meaning, phenomena, and language is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).

Because this analytical knowledge also has meaning as its object, it is said: "It is 'possessing the meaning' (sāttha) because of being the object of the analytical knowledges of meaning and perspicuity.

This is because, in the absence of the perfection of meaning, that [perspicuity] would not exist. "Phenomenon" (dhamma) refers to the doctrine (tanti). "Language" (nirutti) refers to the analysis of the words of the doctrine.
This is the statement. Therein, the knowledges that have reached differentiation are called the "analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language" (*dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā*).

He says, "by way of the domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language, it is 'with its phonemes' (*sabyañjana*)," because in the absence of perfection in phonemes, those [knowledges] would not exist.
Regarding the phrase "inspiring confidence in discerning people," here the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For discerning people, who are seekers of what is wholesome...

It inspires confidence; therefore, it is meaningful (*sāttha*). It is "endowed with meaning" (*atthasampanna*) because one can infer the presence of the cause from the fruit, just as one infers rain upstream from the swelling of a river.

Its meaningfulness, moreover, should be understood through its being perceivable by the wise, and that [perceivability] is to be known from its state of being supremely profound, subtle, and delicate.
For this has been said: "Profound and hard to see," and so forth. It is "pleasing to worldly people" because it is well-phrased (*sabyañjana*).
Because it brings confidence to worldly people, it is "possessed of phrasing" (*sabyañjana*).

For worldly people are satisfied by the excellence of the phrasing. Here too, there is an inference of the cause from the effect. Its state of being "possessed of phrasing," moreover, is due to its trustworthiness; that [trustworthiness] is to be understood through its being "good in the beginning" and so forth.

Alternatively, because it is to be experienced by the wise, it is "meaningful" (*sāttha*); this refers to its perfection of meaning (*atthasampannatā*) by virtue of being the basis for wisdom (*paññā*).
He said: "Therefore, 'pleasing to discerning people' means being endowed with the phrasing (*byañjana*) because it inspires confidence and is credible, due to its status as a foundation for faith;

'pleasing to worldly people'—this is how the meaning should be understood here. 'Possessing the meaning' (*sāttha*) means being endowed with the purpose (*attha*) because its intention (*adhippāya*) is unfathomable and boundless, for otherwise that would not exist. [It is] 'clear in its words' (*uttānapada*)."

"With the phrasing" (*sabyañjanaṃ*) means it is endowed with phrasing because the words are easy to understand, since even the most profound meaning is rendered easily comprehensible for those to be trained.

All this should be regarded as an elaboration (*papañca*) of the two meanings already stated at the very beginning—that it "possesses the meaning" (*sātthaṃ*) due to the perfection of its meaning, and "possesses the phrasing" (*sabyañjanaṃ*) due to the perfection of its phrasing. And so it is in various places.
It has been thus described. For here, there is no inclusion of either an alternative (*vikappa*) or a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"Because of the absence of anything to be brought near" means because of the absence of any unstated purpose of purification (*vodāna*) to be inserted.

The word *kevala* is a synonym for "entirety," hence he says "by way of its being entirely complete," meaning by way of its perfection in all its parts. "Of that which is to be removed" refers to the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*).
Regarding the phrase "he proclaims the holy life" (*brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti*): here, this term *brahmacariya* is seen in the following senses:

generosity, service, the morality of the five precepts, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), abstention from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, energy, the factors of the Uposatha, the Noble Path, and the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
“What was your vow, and what indeed was your holy life?
Of what well-practiced deed is this the result:
this psychic power, radiance, strength, vigor, and rebirth?”
And this is your great Naga mansion.
"In the world of humans, both my wife and I were faithful patrons of giving."
My home was then like a well,
and ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.
That indeed was my vow, that was my holy life.
"This is the fruition of that well-performed deed:
psychic power, radiance, strength, heroism, and rebirth—
this, O wise one, is my great celestial mansion."
For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving is described as "the holy life" (brahmacariya):
"With what hand does one give desires? With what hand is there the flow of honey?
By what holy life of yours does merit succeed in the hand?"
“By that hand, the giver of desires; by that hand, the source of honey-sweetness;
by that holy life of mine, merit succeeds in the hand.
In this *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*, service is referred to as “holy life” (*brahmacariya*). “Thus indeed, monks...”
In this *Tittira Jātaka*, the virtue of the five training precepts (*pañcasikkhāpadasīla*) is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*): "There was a holy life called Tittiriya.
And in this *Mahāgovinda Sutta*: "But that holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, was not for the sake of disenchantment, nor for dispassion, nor for cessation, but only for rebirth in the Brahma-world."
The four immeasurables are called “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*). In this *Sallekha Sutta*, it is said:
“Others will be unchaste, but we shall be chaste here”; thus, abstention from sexual intercourse is called “the holy life.
[And: “We do not transgress against our wives...”
Our wives do not transgress us;
apart from them we lead the holy life.
Therefore, our young ones do not die.
In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one’s own wife is called “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*).
In the Lomahaṃsa Sutta, it is said: “I recall, Sāriputta, having lived the holy life endowed with four factors; indeed, I was an ascetic,” thus energy is called “the holy life.”
“By a low holy life one is reborn as a khattiya;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified.
Thus, in the Nimi Jātaka, the eightfold Uposatha performed for the purpose of self-taming is called “the holy life” (brahmacariya).
“Moreover, Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine is for the sake of utter disenchantment, for dispassion...
[and so on] ...it is this very Noble Eightfold Path”—thus, in the Mahāgovinda Sutta itself, the Noble Path is called the “holy life” (*brahmacariya*).
“And this holy life was successful, flourishing, widespread, popular, and far-reaching...”
In the *Pāsādika Sutta*, the entire teaching comprised of the three trainings is stated to be the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) with the words, "well-expounded by men.
In this instance as well, it is precisely this that is intended by the term "holy life," as indicated by the phrase, "because it is encompassed by the three trainings," and so forth.

It is "by the best ones" (*seṭṭhehi*), meaning by the best ones such as the Buddha. Or, the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is the conduct (*cariya*) that has become sublime (*brahma*) in the sense of being excellent.
"With a cause" (*sanidāna*) means having a cause according to the definition stated below. "With an origin" (*sauppattika*) means having an occasion for its arising.

"In accordance with those to be trained" (*veneyyānaṃ anurūpato*) means in conformity with the conduct and so forth of those to be trained. "Of the meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to the meaning being taught, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
"Endowed with reasons and examples" (*hetudāharaṇayuttato*) refers to [passages] such as "For what reason? Just as, monks... and so on, occurring here and there.
"By means of grasping the cause" means by way of being endowed with the cause and the illustration.

"By the acquisition of faith" refers to the acquisition of faith as stated in such passages as, "Having heard that Dhamma, they acquire faith in the Tathāgata. "By practice" means by right practice such as the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*);
the meaning is "by the sign of practice. "By proficiency in attainment" is because of the presence of proficiency in attainment through the penetration of the Truths (*saccappaṭivedha*).
It is "meaningful" because, unlike the doctrines of Kapila and others which are empty and useless, it is endowed with meaning (*atthasampanna*). It is "well-phrased" (*sabyañjana*) because,
through familiarity with the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), it possesses the clarity and precision of great learning (*bāhusacca*), generating no confusion—
as would occur in one who is merely making a study of poorly taught doctrines— due to its excellence of phrasing (*byañjanasampatti*).
For when this exists, there is mastery of the scriptures. "Endowed with the five aggregates of virtue and so forth" means being not devoid of the five categories of phenomena beginning with virtue.
"Entirely complete" means filled and fulfilled without remainder on all sides.

"Free from defilements" means due to the absence of defilements such as wrong view and conceit. "For the purpose of crossing over" means for the sake of escaping the suffering of saṃsāra. "Independent of worldly gain" means...
It is pure because it is independent of the dependence on craving in any way whatsoever. This is what is meant:
the teaching of one who teaches with the thought, "By relying on this Dhamma instruction, I shall obtain gain or honor," is impure.
But the Blessed One, being indifferent to worldly gain and possessing a heart softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness that radiates for the welfare of others—
He teaches with a mind established in the nature of uplifting; therefore, his teaching is perfectly pure.
The word *sādhu* is seen in the sense of a request, as in: "It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to teach the Dhamma to me in brief.
It is also seen in the sense of rejoicing and appreciation, as in: "‘Very well, venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words..."
In the sense of acceptance, as in “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! and so forth. In the sense of encouragement, as in “Therefore, brahmin, listen well,” and so forth.
And it is seen in the sense of firming up and in the sense of an injunction, as in:
“Excellent is King Dhammaruci; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom.”
"In 'It is good not to harm one's friends, and the non-doing of evil is happiness'—in such passages [the word *sādhu*] means 'beautiful.
Here too, it should be understood as meaning 'beautiful,' as he says: 'It is good indeed (*sādhu kho pana*)' means 'it is beautiful indeed (*sundaraṃ kho panā*).
In that context, "beautiful" (*sundara*) means "excellent" (*bhaddaka*). And its excellence is due to its being a bringer of welfare and happiness for the one who sees it.

He said: "It brings benefit, it brings happiness. In this context, "bringing benefit" means bringing welfare known as that pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
"Bringing happiness" means bringing the three kinds of happiness as previously described. "Of such a kind" means of such a nature.
Furthermore, by those qualities with which the Blessed One is endowed, he is worthy of absolute confidence at all times for the world comprising the fourfold measure.
Showing that these possess their true nature as it is, he said, "of such a form," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "truly existing...
[up to] an arahant," he demonstrates that both beings who are measured by their qualities (*dhamma*) and those measured by their coarseness (*lūkha*) bring about confidence in the Blessed One;
and by demonstrating that, the fact that others measured by their physical form (*rūpa*) and measured by their voice (*ghosa*) also bring about confidence is likewise shown.

"It should be understood that it ‘comes to pass’ because of its invariable concomitance [with the goal]. Regarding the phrase ‘he proclaims the holy life,’ the connection here is that ‘a reputation has arisen’;
thus he said, ‘having formed such an aspiration as: “even a mere sight [of him] is good,”’ and so forth.
In this context, regarding the statement ‘even a mere sight is good,’ the story of the Kosiya bird should be told."

2. As for the phrase "by whatever cause" (*yena vā kāraṇena*), this is an expression of the instrument (*karaṇa*) used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). For the meaning of a cause is the cause of an action, whereas the meaning of an instrument is not like that of an instrument [in the sense of a tool];

rather, it is the purpose of the action. Therefore, since the action of approaching here has the purpose of attaining various specific qualities, this instrumental expression is appropriate only in the sense of a cause—just as in expressions such as "he lives by means of food" (*annena vasati*)—and not in the sense of an instrument [as a tool].
Regarding the phrase "because it was inappropriate for him," it is said: "or by whatever reason.

For, because he possesses the fruit of the True Dhamma—which is constant, unsurpassed, sweet, abundant, and of the nature of nectar—the Blessed One is compared to a great tree perpetually bearing sweet fruit.

Indeed, by the very mention of the intention to enjoy the sweet fruit, the fact that the great tree bears sweet fruit is already implied. "Upasaṅkami" means while approaching. [This is] due to his desire for what is attained.
For when one goes to any place, by means of passing over various locations, one receives the designation "approached" (*upasaṅkami*) or "one who approaches" (*upasaṅkamanto*).

Therefore he said, "it is meant that he has gone," the meaning being "he has arrived. He said, "having approached" is a description of an action in the prior time, [intended] as an indication of the conclusion of the act of approaching.
"From there" refers to that place which he reached and is described as having approached.
"From that place where he had approached" means from a location closer [to him], a place where one would be able to ask questions or listen to the Dhamma.

"Just as when asking about well-being, etc. means that just as the Blessed One, when asking about well-being and so forth with the words, "I hope it is bearable for you, brahmin? I hope it is sustainable? and so on, shared in joy with that brahmin.
It happened thus. By imitating that which was previously spoken, the connection is that this brahmin also came to experience joy equal to that of the Blessed One.
To illustrate that state of equal joy through a simile, it is said, "like cool water," and so forth.
"Sammodita" means conjoined. "Ekībhāva" means the state of equality or uniformity resulting from the act of mutual greeting.

"Endurable" (*khamanīya*): He asks, "Is this body—possessing four wheels and nine doors—capable of being endured, given that by its very nature it is difficult to bear due to the abundance of suffering?
"Sustainable" (*yāpanīya*): He asks, "Is it capable of being sustained for the duration of what is called a long continuity, since its existence depends upon the requisite conditions?
This refers to the absence of afflictions such as diseases of the head and so forth.

"Is there little affliction?"—this means: by virtue of the absence of a miserable livelihood, is there little illness? By virtue of the ease of exertion in performing various duties, is there lightness of body?

By virtue of being endowed with strength appropriate thereto, is there physical power? By virtue of the possibility of dwelling in comfort, is there well-being? The meaning should be understood by applying the word "kacci" (I hope) in each respective instance. [She was] one who had attained strength.
*Pīti* is simply rapture (*pīti*). *Pāmojja* is fresh rapture. It is called *sammodanika* because it produces or creates gladness (*sammoda*);

that very thing is thus called *sammodanīya*. He said, "because it generates gladness," in order to show this meaning. Furthermore, he said, "because it is fit for gladness," showing the sense that it is *sammodanīya* because it is something with which one ought to be glad. "Because it is to be remembered" means because it is to be recollected.

Where "saraṇīya" should have been said, it is stated as "sāraṇīya" by lengthening the vowel. "From the pleasure of being heard" refers to its extreme sweetness upon first entering the range of hearing.

"From the pleasure of being recollected" refers to its delightful quality when reflected upon. "By the purity of the phrasing" refers to the eloquence of the speech in that discourse due to its natural expression.
"By the purity of the meaning" refers to the meaning's freedom from defilement.
"By many methods" means by many reasons.
By the rejection of "too far" and "too near," "not too far and not too near" is understood;
that, moreover, should be seen as at least the distance where the outstretched hands of both [persons] do not touch. "Having extended the neck" means by way of turning the neck.
“Having extended [the hand]. Since *meti* is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent, he said, “heard by me.

“A brahmin by birth” means a brahmin by birth, not one who has warded off evil; this is what is meant. “Reduced to a state of brokenness and so forth” means brought to a condition of broken teeth, grey hair, and the like.
“Reached the limit of old age” means having attained the boundary of aging, i.e., having reached the ultimate stage of aging.

This is what is meant. "By reason of being advanced in age" means by virtue of having reached an advanced state through birth. One who takes (lāti) or possesses greatness (mahattaṃ) is called *mahallaka*;
one who is advanced in age (*jāti*) rather than in worldly status (*vibhava*) and so forth is "advanced in age.

"A long period" (*addhānaṃ*) refers to a long duration of time. To the question, "How much is that? he says: "Two or three royal successions," meaning the sequence of the reigns of two or three kings.

The meaning is as follows. Having stated "in one who has reached [old age]," he says "having arrived at the final stage of life" to show how the mention of "decline" (vaya) refers to the concluding stage of life.
The "final third part" means that from the sixty-seventh year onwards is the division of the final stage of life.
In the second interpretation of the meaning, "worn out" does not refer merely to the stage of life, but rather to being ancient by way of the succession of generations.
He said: "‘Jiṇṇā’ means ancient,” and so forth. By this, he expresses the state of being ever-increasingly eminent according to the lineage of those brahmins.
With the phrase “having reached old age,” since the increase of birth will be explained later, and because the increase of virtue is even more distinguished than that, he says:
“‘Vuddhā’ means endowed with the increase of virtues such as moral conduct and behavior. Likewise, since the state of being advanced in years will also be explained by that same [term] later on.
By the word "mahallaka" (an elder), great wealth is implied. "One who has entered upon the path" means one who has undertaken the method of practice of the brahmins and does not deviate from it.
"The final stage of life" refers to the last period of life.
Regarding "rising up," he says "does not rise from his seat," meaning that he does not rise from the seat where he is sitting.
The meaning [is as follows]. And here, in the phrase "when he is old... having reached old age," the accusative case ending does not relate to the action of rising from the seat;
therefore, the meaning should be understood by supplying the words "having seen him when he is old... having reached old age.
Alternatively, the accusative case ending relates to the action of going to meet him; therefore, [the sense is] that he does not rise up. Rising up... [he does not go to meet him].
The meaning should be understood as "he does not go out to meet [the teacher]. For going out to meet is indeed called rising up;
for it has been said: "But seeing the teacher from afar, rising up and performing the act of going out to meet is what is called 'rising up'.
By the phrase "he emerges from his seat," however, this is shown merely as an illustration of the absence of going out to meet.
It should be seen. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of manifestation" (*vibhāvane nāma atthe*): it means in the sense known as the manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*pakativibhāvana*).
It is stated that one does not pay homage, or rather, one perceives that "it is not to be paid homage to.
That is ignorance, in the sense of not knowing: "This person is not of a nature worthy for me to perform acts such as paying homage."
“Prevailing ignorance” means ignorance that has arisen. “Looking” means looking with the eye of knowledge by way of such suttas as: “One who lacks respect and deference dwells in suffering;
what ascetic or brahmin, then, should I honor and revere?
“Worthy of prostration” means worthy of humble salutation. “Just born” means born for a moment; immediately upon being born.
This has been said. "Facing north" means facing toward the north, that is, facing toward the northern direction;
this is what is meant by "having gone seven steps with a stride, he surveyed the entire ten-thousandfold world-system. This is the natural law (*dhammatā*), monks:
as soon as he is born, the Bodhisatta stands firmly on both feet and proceeds seven steps facing north.

"Even while a white parasol was being held over him, he looked toward all directions and uttered a lion’s roar"—this was said because the Pāli describes the surveying of all directions as if it were performed immediately after the seven-step stride;
however, it should not be understood in this way, for the surveying of the directions had already been performed even before the seven-step stride. Thus spoke the Mahāsatta.
Having escaped from the hands of men, he looked toward the eastern direction; thousands of world-systems became a single open space.
There, gods and humans, worshipping him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said:
"Great Being, there is no one here equal to you, much less anyone superior. Thus it was in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions.
It should be understood that after surveying the ten directions—above and below—and seeing no one equal to himself, he proceeded with the seven-step stride, thinking, "This is the northern direction.

"He looked" means: when the miracle of the opening of the world occurred through the power of his merit, he looked with his very fleshly eye upon the thousandfold world-system that was thus becoming visible; this is the meaning.
A "Great Man" (mahāpurisa) is a great person by virtue of birth, clan, family, country, and so forth. "Foremost" (agga) means preeminent among all in terms of qualities.
"Eldest" (jeṭṭha) means, by virtue of qualities alone, the most senior among all; what is meant is that he is the most venerable in terms of qualities.
"Best" (seṭṭha) means, by virtue of qualities alone, the most praiseworthy among all. As for the meaning, however, the latter two are merely synonyms for the first.
It should be understood. *Tayā* is the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
*Uttaritaro* means more excellent. *Patimānesi* means he honored. *Āsabhiṃ* means supreme. *Mayhaṃ abhivādanādiraho puggalo* means a person worthy of my acts of homage and so forth;
that is, a person suitable for such actions as salutation toward me. Here, however, a compound should be seen due to the constant requirement of the genitive. *Tathāgata* means...
“From the Tathāgata, from the presence of the Tathāgata”—this is what is meant. “Of such a kind” refers to the nature of salutation and so forth.
“With bonds loosened by ripening” means that the bonds have been slackened through ripening. 3.
“That speech” refers to the words beginning with “I am not such a one, O Brahmin. “I am not of a tasteless nature, nor are those like me of a tasteless nature.”
If this were said, the brahmin might become stubborn. Therefore it is said: "for the purpose of producing pliancy of mind.
For this term *pariyāya* applies to teaching, sections, and reasons. In this context, it is a *pariyāya* because it makes known and awakens one to the meaning that is to be taught;
thus, it is a teaching (*desanā*). It is a *pariyāya* because it proceeds from one to another and turns around; thus, it is a section (*vāra*). It proceeds...
The term *pariyāya* means that [a phenomenon] proceeds by grasping its own fruit, or that it becomes the cause for that [fruit];

thus, the application of the word *pariyāya* should be understood as occurring in the senses of "method," "section of the teaching," and "cause. "One should stand firm through higher knowledge" (*aññāya saṇṭhaheyya*) means one should be established in Arahatship.
As for the phrase "But which one is it?": this is a masculine designation (*pulliṅga-niddesa*) dependent on the relative pronoun *katama*, [meaning] "which one is it? (*katamo so*).
"Pariyāya" means "in a manner" (or "method"). "By way of birth" means by way of birth as a kṣatriya and so forth. "By way of rebirth" means by way of rebirth among the devas.
By the word "api" (even), he shows that this applies even to those regarded as superior, let alone those not regarded as superior.

"Abhinandantānaṃ" means of those who rejoice through the influence of craving accompanied by delight. "Rajjantānaṃ" means of those who are impassioned through the influence of powerful passion. [This occurs] by means of the enjoyment of forms and so forth.

The feeling of joy associated with arisen craving, having been produced from form and because it satisfies the heart, is called "the taste of form" (*rūparasa*), just as the juices of mangoes and other fruits are so called. "Drawing toward" means pulling [toward oneself].

"In the combination of the basis, object, and so forth" means in the combination of causes such as the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the objective field (*ārammaṇa*). "Throwing down" refers to what was said by the brahmin by way of self-exaltation.
Not elevating or exalting oneself because of its unsuitable nature.
In this context, however, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, in the phrase "by him who has abandoned" (*jahitā*), it refers to the meaning of abandonment.

In the expression "of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatassa*), the genitive is used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "abandoned by the Tathāgata. "Root" (*mūla*) refers to the root of existence (*bhava*). "Made like a palm stump" (*tālavatthuvatthukatā*).
It should be said: just as in the case of "oṭṭhamukho" (lip-mouth) and so forth, by eliding the middle word and lengthening the vowel *a*, it is called "tālāvatthukatā.
Thus he says: "Their basis was made like the base of a palmyra tree; therefore they are 'tālāvatthukatā'. In that context, the base of a palmyra tree is "tālavatthu.
Just as a place that formerly served as the site for a monastery is called "ārāmavatthu" (monastery-site) when the monastery is no longer there, [so too here].

It is said thus: when a palm tree has been uprooted by its very roots and only the site remains, that place is called a "palm-tree site" (*tālavatthu*) because it was formerly the location of the palm tree.
"Of these" refers to visible forms, tastes, and so forth.

But how is their basis (*vatthu*) like a palm-tree site? To this he says, "Just as," and so on. [This refers to] the feeling of joy associated with craving that arises through the enjoyment of visible forms, tastes, and the rest.

It is said, "When the mere continuity of consciousness (cittasantāna) has been made into a basis by virtue of having previously arisen before them," because it serves as the foundation for the stream of mind. In that context, "previously" (pubbe) means earlier; it refers to the time when there was still lust.
They are called "made into a palm-tree stump" (tālāvatthukatā) because, by making their own basis like the stump of a palm tree, the visible forms, tastes, and so forth are rendered [unproductive].
...are so called. By this, the non-recurrence of abandoned defilements is shown.

"By way of having the nature of not growing" means by way of having the characteristic of not growing. A palm tree cut at the top is one that has become a non-substratum for leaves, fruit, and so forth;
thus he said, "made like a palm tree cut at the top. By this, it is meant: "made like a palm-tree stump."

The analysis (*viggaha*) "tālāvatthukatā" is thus shown. Here, however, it should be understood that although it ought to be expressed as *avatthutālākatā*—meaning "made like a palm tree which has become a foundation"—the word *avatthu*, being the qualifier, has been placed last, hence it is stated as "tālāvatthukatā.
By this meaning, it shows that by the term "states characterized by ripening" (*vipākadhammadhammā*), [it refers to] form, taste, and so forth.
Previously, the arisen wholesome and unwholesome states were grasped;

although they had arisen, because they were severed by the army of the Path—the craving and ignorance which are like the crown of a palm tree—they became incapable of producing resultant aggregates in the future that are like palm leaves.
Therefore, the visible forms, tastes, and so forth are said to be "rendered like the stump of a palm tree" (*tālāvatthukatā*). For in this sense:
By the phrase "of those who rejoice," they say that wholesome joy (*kusalasomanassa*) is also included.
Regarding the term *anabhāvaṅkatā*, the prefix *anu-* has the same meaning as the word *pacchā* (afterwards); thus he says, "so that there is no subsequent existence for them," and so forth.
*Anuabhāvaṅgatā* means having gone to non-existence by way of the state of not arising again afterwards; that is, having reached destruction.

The meaning is "abandoned. Regarding the phrase, "These verses, which are not wonderful (anacchariyā), occurred to me," he says, "Just as 'anu-acchariyā' means 'not wonderful,'" showing the word *anacchariya* by way of illustration.
Therein, *anu-acchariyā* means that which causes wonder more and more at the time of hearing.

And as for what you say—that there is no such method—meaning that the reason you cite, namely the absence of the flavor of harmony consisting in acts of homage and so forth, because of its lack of flavor, is not a valid reason;
the meaning is that such a reason does not exist, it is not found.
But did not the Brahmin, with reference to that very method consisting in the absence of the flavor of harmony such as homage and so forth, say: "Master Gotama is without flavor"?
He said: "When it is stated that 'there is no such method,' one falls into the undesirable consequence that the Blessed One performs acts of homage and so forth.
Demonstrating this undesirable consequence, he said, "But why did the Blessed One speak thus?
and so on. "In all methods" means in all instances. "Merely spoken with reference to" means that which the brahmin had in mind.

He said, "Master Gotama is one who abstains from enjoyment," and so forth; and as for that which the Blessed One intends when he allows for himself such things as the state of non-enjoyment, it is merely spoken with that specific intention in mind.
"Enjoyment through desire and lust" means enjoyment by way of desire and lust.
"Another method" means another reason.
5. *Kulasamudācārakammaṃ*: This refers to the action known as family custom; it is what is called "family conduct. *Akiriyaṃ* means the state of non-performance.
*Duccaritaṃ* is that which is badly conducted. Because it occurs frequently through the door of the body, misconduct that proceeds from the body is called "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccaritaṃ*).
Showing its specific nature, he says, "In this regard... and so forth. [It consists of] the volitions of killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
Regarding the phrase "should be understood": here, "living being" (*pāṇa*) is, in the ultimate sense, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), while in conventional usage, it is a sentient being (*satta*).

And in this context, the life-faculty should be understood according to its material and immaterial aspects; for when the material life-faculty is impaired, the other [the immaterial] also perishes due to its connection with it.

Furthermore, "sentient being" should be taken as the continuum of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*), for it is therein that the designation "being" (*satta-paññatti*) occurs. By way of its own essence alone...

*Atipāta* (over-killing) is the excessive killing of that which is already subject to falling, occurring even in the interval; the meaning is that it is a killing that occurs swiftly, not allowing [the being] to fall slowly.
Alternatively, *atipāta* is the killing by surpassing or overcoming [the victim] with weapons and the like. Thus, *pāṇātipāta* is the over-killing of a living being (*pāṇa*);
it is the killing of a living being (*pāṇaghāta*). As for its actual meaning, however, it is [the act of one who] perceives another living being as a living being...
The volition of killing is that which, arising through either the door of body or the door of speech, initiates the process that severs the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

For that volition, while it is occurring, causes such great primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—which arise conditioned by the great primary elements acting as the cause for inflicting injury—to not arise within the great primary elements that serve as the support for the life-faculty;
such a volition initiating that kind of process is the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
For beings that have already attained their respective modes of existence are not as distinct as other beings; thus, they do not serve as causes for those of the same class.
Here it may be asked: since conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) have the nature of ceasing moment by moment, who is the slayer and who is slain?
If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, then because it is formless, it is incapable of being disturbed by means of cutting, piercing, and so forth; nor...
It is subject to agitation. Now, as for the continuity of form (*rūpa-santāna*), because it is insentient, it is like a piece of wood or a log;
thus, no taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*) occurs therein through cutting and so forth, as is the case with a dead body.

Furthermore, the application (*payoga*) for taking life—such as striking or wounding—might occur in past, future, or present formations (*saṅkhāra*). Among these, it cannot first occur in the past or the future.

Because they do not exist [in the future], and because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) in the present are momentary—having by their very nature a disposition to cease and thus being already facing destruction—any effort [to kill] would be purposeless.
Furthermore, since destruction is devoid of a cause, death is not caused by such efforts as striking with a weapon;
and since conditioned phenomena are inactive, for whom would that effort be intended? This is because, due to their momentariness, they perish at the very same time as the intention to kill arises.
Whose is the action? And to whom does the bond of the kamma of taking life belong, given that [the victim] does not persist until the time of the conclusion?
It is said: The "slayer" is a mass of volitional formations termed a "being," accompanied by the aforementioned volition to kill.
On account of the murderous application set in motion by him, the vital faculty—devoid of consciousness—is the basis for the employment of the conventional expression "dead."
When the aforementioned application of killing is carried out, the aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena— which is liable to arise— is destroyed,

or else the entire continuum of mind and mental factors. Even though that [continuum] is not the direct object of the application of killing, because its existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*) is dependent upon the material continuum,

through the application employed by another to sever the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) within the material continuum, there occurs the arising of dissimilar matter that obstructs the production of that [life-sustaining matter].

When [the process] is destroyed, there is an interruption; thus, it is not the case that there is no possibility of the taking of life, nor is the taking of life causeless, nor is the preliminary effort (payoga) purposeless.

Because the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakalāpa) which ought to arise immediately after [the preceding moment] does not arise in that way due to the preliminary effort exerted upon the present formations, there is here the "momentary death" of momentary formations.
Because death in its ultimate sense is not intended here, and because the death of the continuity (saṃtati-maraṇa) possesses causes according to the method already stated,
there is no such thing as causeless death; nor is the act of taking life devoid of an agent, for even though the formations (saṅkhāra) are inactive,
the designation "agent" is established through the mere presence of those factors that assist by being determined to produce their respective appropriate results.
As it is said: "The lamp illuminates, as does the moon, the maker of night.

Nor should the act of taking life be attributed solely to the aggregate of mind and mental factors that coexist with the intention to kill; for it is admitted [by the opponent] that this occurs only in that which persists by way of a continuum.
And since purposeful activity is observed in things such as lamps that proceed by way of a continuum, there certainly exists [the factor of] taking life.
He is bound by karma. This analysis should also be applied, as far as possible, to the taking of what is not given and other such offenses.
Furthermore, that killing of living beings is less blameworthy when the beings are animals devoid of special qualities and are small, but more blameworthy when they are large.
Why? Because of the greatness of the effort involved, and even when the effort is equal, because of the greatness of the object.
Among humans and other beings, the offense is slight when the being possesses few virtues, and grave when they possess great virtues.

Furthermore, even when the physical qualities [of the victim] are equal, it should be understood that the offense is slight due to the mildness of the defilements and the means employed, whereas it is grave due to their intensity.

That which is not given by body or speech is "what is not given" (*adatta*); the property of another is "what is not given," and the taking of that is "taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*). It is the seizing of another's property.

"Stealing" (*theyya*) means "theft" (*corikā*). In terms of its essential meaning, however, it is the volition of theft (*theyyacetanā*) that arises through either the door of body or the door of speech, initiated by the act of taking, while perceiving another's possession as such.
It is less blameworthy when the property of another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior. Why? Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*).
When the object is equal, there is a greater offense in the case of one who possesses superior qualities;
depending on how much more excellent those respective qualities may be, there is a lesser offense in the case of one who possesses inferior qualities compared to them.
*Micchā-caraṇaṃ* means wrong conduct; it is reprehensible and base behavior among sexual practices. As for its characteristic:
It is the volition of transgressing against a place that should not be approached, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of an unrighteous state.

Furthermore, this misconduct is less blameworthy when the place that should not be approached is devoid of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), and it is more blameworthy when that place is endowed with virtues such as moral discipline.

Its four constituent factors are: the object that should not be approached; the mind of indulgence toward that object; the application of indulgence; and the acquiescence in the practice of the path upon what is not the path.
The single application is exclusively the manual (sāhatthika).
Regarding the door of speech, because it occurs predominantly through speech, misconduct that proceeds via speech is called "vocal misconduct" (vacīduccarita).
Demonstrating its specific nature, he said: "It should be understood as the volition of false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. Therein:
*Musā* means a matter that is non-existent and untrue. It is called *musāvāda* because one speaks (*vadīyati*) by means of it;
it is the volition that originates such a communication from one who wishes to make another understand an untrue matter as being true.
That [volition] is slight in its degree of fault when the matter it destroys is small, and grave when the matter is great. Furthermore, regarding householders, [it refers to] their own property...

That which proceeds in the manner of saying "there is none" out of a desire not to give is slightly blameworthy; however, that which is spoken by one acting as a witness for the purpose of destroying another's welfare is greatly blameworthy.

For those who have gone forth, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee, to speak according to the method of exaggeration with a motive of amusement, saying, "Today in the village it seems as if the river of oil is flowing," is slightly blameworthy—even though [the oil] was not actually seen.
However, for those who speak according to the method beginning with "having seen," it is a great offense (*mahāsāvajja*). It has four constituent factors (*sambhāra*):

a basis that is not as it appears, a mind intent on deception, the corresponding effort, and making the other person understand that meaning. There is a single mode of application (*payoga*), which is exclusively manual;
this occurs when one performs an act intended to deceive another, either by means of the body, by means of something connected to the body, or by means of speech.

It should be understood as follows: if another person understands that matter through such an action, this person is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that originated the action.

For just as one deceives another by means of body or body-connected speech, so too does one who commands, "Speak this to him," or who writes a letter and places it before the other; [this person is also bound]. "This..."

"The meaning should be understood thus," he said, even as he had it written down on walls and other surfaces. Therefore, in this context, the applications (*payoga*) of commanding, relinquishing, and the fixed rule (*thāvara*) are all applicable.
However, since these are not mentioned in the commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*), they should be accepted after careful investigation.

She splits (*pisatīti pisuṇā*); the meaning is that she causes beings who are in harmony—being like the parts of a whole—to become divided into factions. According to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*):

Or, it is "slanderous" (*pisuṇā*) because it creates a void of affection (*piyasuñña*). For that speech by which one creates a state of being beloved in the heart of the person to whom one speaks, while creating a state of being devoid of affection (*piyasuñña*) for another, is slanderous speech.

By way of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), however, it is that which, arising from a defiled mind, originates the application of body or speech either for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own popularity.
It is volition (*cetanā*) because one speaks maliciously by means of it; this is what constitutes malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*).

It is less blameworthy when the person whom one causes to be divided possesses few virtues, and more blameworthy when that person possesses great virtues. Its four constituent factors (*sambhāra*) are: another person who is to be divided;
the intention to divide, thinking, "In this way these two will become separate, they will become apart"; or the thought, "In this way I shall be dear..."
"May I be trustworthy"—this is either the desire for endearment (*piyakamyatā*), the corresponding effort, or the discernment of that purpose.
Furthermore, when others have not yet divided, there is no breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*); it occurs only when they have divided.
It is called "harsh" (*pharusā*) because it is speech; for by that speech, through a lack of affection, one makes both oneself and another harsh.

That which makes one coarse is harsh speech (*pharusavācā*). Alternatively, it is harsh speech because it is itself harsh, arising from mental distress (*domanassa*), and being rough by its very nature, it is neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart.

In this context, however, the term "harsh" is applied to speech due to its absolute cruelty in cutting through the vital points of others, both by way of its intrinsic nature and by way of figurative designation for its cause.

It should be seen. It is called harsh speech because one speaks harshly with it; it is an exclusively harsh volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal undertakings intended to cut another to the quick.

To illustrate this, there is the following story: A certain boy, it seems, was going into the forest without heeding his mother’s words. His mother, unable to turn him back, said, "May a fierce buffalo pursue you!"
He reviled her. Then, right there in the forest, a female buffalo rose up. The boy made a declaration of truth, saying: "May that which my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass;
may that which she thought in her heart come to pass. The buffalo stood right there as if bound fast.
Thus, even though the action was one that would have pierced the vital organs, it did not become harsh speech because of the gentleness of his mind.
For parents sometimes say to their children even this: “May thieves cut you into pieces!
and yet they do not wish even a lotus leaf to fall upon them. And teachers and preceptors sometimes say to those dependent on them:
