“What are these shameless and unscrupulous ones doing? Drive them out! and yet they [do not wish harm] to them.
They desire the perfection of scriptural learning and realization. Just as harsh speech does not occur due to gentleness of mind, so too non-harsh speech does not occur due to gentleness of speech.
For a person wishing to kill, the words "Lay this one down comfortably" are not non-harsh speech;
rather, because of the harshness of the mind, it is indeed harsh speech. This [non-harsh speech] exists because of the lack of proficiency in the one toward whom it is directed.
It is slightly blameworthy, yet highly blameworthy due to its great demerit. It has three constituent factors: another person who may be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling.

Because it brings forth (*samphalati*), spreads (*visarati*), and destroys (*vināseti*) what is pleasant and beneficial, it is called *sampha*. That which is useless to oneself and others is *sampha*;
that by which one prattles such *sampha* is *samphappalāpa*. It is the volitional activity of body and speech that originates from and gives rise to what communicates what is meaningless.

It is unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*). It is of slight blame due to the weakness of its repetition (*āsevanamandatā*), and of great blame due to the greatness of its repetition (*āsevanamahantatā*).
It has two constituent factors (*sambhāra*): the preoccupation with useless talk such as the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual speaking of such talk.

However, if others do not take up that talk, there is no breach of the course of action (*kammapathabhedo*); it constitutes the path of action only when another person takes up that idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).
Regarding "covetousness, ill will, and wrong view": here, covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is so called because it "meditates" (*jhāyati*) directly upon the prosperity of others;
it is greed for the possessions of others. Its characteristic is the coveting of another's goods, thinking, "O, may this be mine!
Like the taking of what is not given, it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy. It has two constituent factors: another's property and oneself.

And there is dedication (*pariṇāmana*). For even when greed arises with another's property as its object, there is no breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*) so long as one does not dedicate it to oneself, thinking, "O, may this indeed be mine!

Malice (*byāpāda*) is the intent to harm or destroy the welfare and happiness of others; it is aversion (*paṭigha*). It is characterized by mental corruption directed toward the destruction of others.
Thus, harsh speech is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy. It has two constituent factors: another being and the thought of their destruction.
For even when anger arises toward another being, there is no breach of the course of kamma so long as one does not think of their destruction, such as:
"Oh, that this person might perish! Oh, that they might be destroyed!"
It is wrong view because one sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are.
Its characteristic is a distorted perception, according to the method beginning with "there is no giving. Like frivolous speech, it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy.

Furthermore, it is slightly blameworthy when indeterminate, and greatly blameworthy when determinate. It has two constituent factors: the distortion of the mode in which the object is grasped, and [the lack of faith].

And just as one grasps it, so does it appear to one through its very mode of being. In this context, the breach of the courses of kamma occurs specifically through the views of nihilism, causelessness, and non-doership.
Even though there is the general statement, "of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states," the specific meaning is understood through the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).
He said, "having set aside those states," and so forth, meaning that the remaining unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) are to be understood.
The sense is: having set aside those unwholesome states such as the aforementioned bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*), etc. "Of many kinds" means of various types.
"This worldly tradition" refers to this worldly custom characterized by acts such as saluting those who are senior. [This applies] to non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Brahmās.

Since the arising of lust occurs through attachment to ornaments and such for non-returner bhikkhus, and through attachment to robes and such, it should be understood that the abandonment of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure occurs specifically by means of the path of non-returning;

thus he said, "of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Lust that arises toward the five strands of sensual pleasure—form and so forth—which are categories of objective sensual desire, is called "lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure."
It should be understood that here the word *guṇa* denotes a "component," as in such passages as "the qualities of age gradually decline.

"In two unwholesome states of consciousness" refers to the two unwholesome states of consciousness accompanied by grief (*domanassa*). He says "of all that arises from unwholesomeness" because delusion (*moha*) is common to all unwholesome states.
"Of the remainder" refers to personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth.

7. "He feels disgust, thinking 'I am well-born, handsome, and wise; how indeed could I perform such acts as salutation for others?'"—it is in this sense that I observe he feels as if he were feeling disgust, or he feels disgust.
"In the sense of being produced by lack of skill" means in the sense of being produced by ignorance. One who feels disgust toward unwholesome states feels disgust even toward their possession.
It is said: “the attainment of unwholesome states. *Samāpatti* is a synonym for this very term;

it means entering (*samāpajjana*) or being possessed of (*samaṅgibhāva*). *Maṇḍanakajātika* means having the nature of adornment; the meaning is one whose character is to adorn. *Jegucchita* means the state of having a character that feels disgust. 8. *Lokajeṭṭhakakamma*:
the deed to be performed by those who are the elders in the world, or the deed recognized as the most excellent in the world.
*Tatra* means in both of the two alternative meanings as previously stated. *Padattha* is the meaning expressed by a word; what is meant is that it is the meaning of the phrasing (*byañjanattha*).
Regarding the phrase "or it deserves discipline" (*vinayaṃ vā arahati*), here *vinaya* is the act of disciplining (*vinayana*);
the meaning is "restraining" (*niggaṇhana*). Therefore he said: "What is meant is that it deserves restraint. But surely, in both of the two alternative meanings stated first...

The *taddhita* suffix is seen according to the characteristics of grammar in the sense of "own" (*sakattha*) and in the sense of "worthy one" (*arahattha*), but not in this sense of "teaching the Dhamma for the sake of discipline" (*vinayāya*). Therefore, as to how there can be a *taddhita* suffix here, he says:
"For the application of *taddhita* suffixes is manifold. And this manifoldness should be understood from the perspective of worldly convention. For in whatever [context]...

The application of *taddhita* suffixes is for the sake of worldly usage; since the occurrence of *taddhita* suffixes in various instances is established by worldly convention, the application of *taddhita* suffixes is manifold.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that just as one who says, "Do not make a sound," is called "māsaddika" (one who makes no sound), so too one who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline (*vinaya*) is called "venayika" (one devoted to discipline).
9. "A miserable person" (*kapaṇapuriso*) refers to a wretched human being due to a lack of virtuous qualities.

"Without investigating the phonemes" means that one does not analyze the phoneme by considering, as in the case of words such as *tissadatta*, "this is the suffix for this specific meaning"; what is meant is that it is done by way of an unformed [phonetic] spelling. 10.
Having stated "by the attainment of the womb in the world of the gods," [this excludes] the terrestrial devas; among the remaining devas, there is no taking of a womb.

Having explained that it should be understood that "rebirth itself is here the attainment of a womb" by way of its absence, he says, "it leads to the acquisition of rebirth in the world of the gods," demonstrating that very point. "Assa" refers to respectful service such as salutation and so forth.
By showing the fault in taking rebirth in the mother's womb, he demonstrates the state of being impure with respect to the mother.

The intention is that even one who reviles by pointing out a fault in the Blessed One’s taking of rebirth in his mother’s womb—just as one might revile someone wishing to abuse them by pointing out the fault of being born from the womb of a slave girl, saying "son of a slave"—says this.
"From the womb" means from the rebirth-linking in the deva-world; for this very reason he said, "He is incapable of reaching rebirth in the deva-world."

Regarding the phrase "the intention (*adhippāyo*)," he spoke thus—"because of being excluded from the womb of the deva-world, one is destined to obtain a lowly womb in the future"—in order to show the intention of this analysis (*viggaha*) that "one who has no womb is *apagabbho*" by way of one method. The word *iti* here has the sense of a reason;
because one is destined to obtain a lowly womb even in the future, therefore [one is called] "one who has a lowly womb" (*hīno vā gabbho*).
"Assa" means "of him"; the intention is that he is one who has avoided the womb. Again, regarding that same analysis, by way of anger...
[omission] ...showing it, he said, "The intention is that his dwelling in the mother's womb was inferior," having applied this in accordance with the method explained below.
The word *gabbha* has the sense of the mother’s womb, as in such passages as “the youth dwells in the *gabbha*”;
it also has the sense of a being born within the mother’s womb, as in such passages as “at least including the causing of an abortion.

Therein, taking it in the sense of the mother’s womb and demonstrating the meaning, he said: “in the womb-bed in the future. A bed in the womb is a “womb-bed” (*gabbhaseyyā*). By means of the unsurpassed...
"By the path" means by the supreme path (*aggamagga*). He says "because of being destroyed by the path" because the kamma and defilements have been demolished by that path.
"The other three as well" refers to the egg-born, the moisture-born, and the spontaneously born.

And here, although only "the womb-state" (*gabbhaseyyā*) should be mentioned in accordance with the term "one who is not subject to rebirth in a womb" (*apagabbha*), it should be understood that the "production of renewed existence" (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) is also mentioned so that everything applicable may be included by way of context.
Now, demonstrating the variety of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) by means of the word *gabbha* in its sevenfold sense, he says "Moreover," and so forth.

Regarding this alternative analysis, some say that both "lying in the womb" (*gabbhaseyyā*) and "the production of renewed existence" (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) are stated specifically by way of lying in the womb.
But is it not the case that because it was said, "Lying in the womb in the future has been abandoned," [it refers to] the lying (*seyyā*) in the womb?
[He] said, "And just as... and so forth, meaning that while [the fetters] are thus abandoned, one does not yet enter a womb. Now, if one asks:
why is the term "renewed existence" (*punabbhava*) used instead of merely saying "arising" (*abhinibbatti*)? He said, "And what is called 'arising'... and so forth.
"Arising" refers to the manifestation of phenomena that occur moment by moment, which constitutes renewed existence.
11. *Dhammadhātu*: herein, it is called the "dharma-element" (*dhammadhātu*) because it holds all phenomena (*dhamma*) without exception, examining them as they truly are;
it is the nature of awakening to phenomena according to their true essence. This is a designation for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Having penetrated" means having realized;
the sense is "having obtained," meaning "for the purpose of obtaining. He has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching.
"Desanāvilāsa" (the grace of teaching) means the capacity to teach by turning [the subject] according to one's inclination; the meaning is that he has attained or acquired that.
"Karuṇāvipphāraṃ" (the expansion of compassion) means the pervading of all beings with great compassion.

Having further elucidated this very characteristic of his qualities through a simile, he said: "Pathavīsamacittataṃ" (the state of having a mind equal to the earth). Just as the earth, in the placing of the pure and the impure, or in cutting and breaking, etc., [remains equanimous].

It does not waver; it does not fall into favor or opposition. Thus, by abandoning favor and opposition toward the desirable and undesirable, gain and loss, and so forth, the meaning is "the earth-like stability of mind" due to the unwavering nature of the mind.

Regarding the phrase *akuppadhammataṃ*, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "the 'unshakable state' (*akuppadhammo*) refers to the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*). Furthermore, even when others are reviling him, his own...
"The meaning to be understood here is: 'having a mind characterized by equanimity like the earth' and 'having a nature of non-anger. This is our interpretation.

"Pervaded by old age" means enveloped by old age. "Become like a withered stump" means it has become like a stump of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), because it serves as a pillar characterized by the falling upon many misfortunes and calamities. "Death is near due to the Brahmin’s advanced age."
It was said, beginning with “having died today,” by way of anticipation. “With great exertion” means with such great exertion as has arisen, thinking:
“It is indeed good to see such Arahants. “An incomparable state of pre-existence” means a state of pre-existence not shared by others.
It is called “incomparable” (*appaṭisama*) because there is nothing equal to it; this refers to the state of pre-existence.
By saying "pi" instead of saying "apī," he shows that the word *pi* is also a separate particle.
In the sense of "possibility" (*sambhāvanattha*), the sense of possibility is the sense of alternative, as in "perhaps it might be so"; the word *pi* is used there because it indicates that sense.
In the sense of "euphony of speech" (*vacanasiliṭṭhatāya*), the meaning is for the sake of the sweetness of the expression, that is, for the sake of its softness. For thus—

"In the world, speech is well-connected": thus, without stating only a single enumeration, speech together with another enumeration becomes well-connected in the world, such as "two or three drops of water.
"Properly laid" means that she, without causing them any injury herself by her feet or other limbs, [placed them] for the purpose of warding off external dangers such as wind and so forth.
They were properly placed on top. Here, the word *adhi* has the sense of "on top.
"Causing them to take up heat" means causing them to take up heat by means of the warmth of her own body for the purpose of exhausting their raw moisture and oiliness. Therefore, he said, "made warm.
"Well-perfumed" means thoroughly perfumed in every way with the scent of a hen. Therefore, he said, "made to take on the smell of a hen."

And here, it should be understood that proper drying and proper seasoning are accomplished through the power of the accomplishment of proper storage. For by means of proper storage alone, the other two are perfected;
there is no separate performance of proper drying or proper seasoning apart from proper storage.
Since the other two also succeed only together with that [first one], it is said: "In this way, those eggs are nurtured in three ways.
*Nakhasikhā* means the tips of the nails. *Mukhatuṇḍaka* means the tip of the beak. Regarding the phrase "due to the thinness of the shell":
just as the thinness of the shell is the cause for light being perceived within, so too...
The thinness of the skull and the hardness of the claws, beaks, and snouts should be understood as the reasons for the exhaustion of moisture and oiliness.

Regarding the phrase "with contracted hands and feet," here "hands" refers to wings; for chickens have no so-called hand other than their wings. "Therein" means in the place of light. "Shaking their wings" means moving their wings.
"Nikkhamantānaṃ" (of those emerging) is a genitive case used for specification; the meaning is "among those emerging.
"So jeṭṭho iti assa vacanīyo" means that the chick which first emerged from the eggshell should be called the eldest;
the sense is that it would indeed be so designated. "Sampaṭipādentī" means correlating or comparing. [This applies even to] those included within the three planes of existence.
"Beings have entered the shell of ignorance" means they are enveloped by ignorance that has not been abandoned here and there;
thus he said, "among beings who have entered the shell of ignorance. "The eggshell" refers to the outer covering of the seed.

"In the world-dwelling": the world itself is the world-dwelling. Regarding "perfect self-enlightenment" (*sammāsambodhi*): here *samma* has the sense of non-perversion, while the prefix *saṃ* signifies "together with."
This explains the meaning; therefore, because one awakens to and penetrates the Four Truths by oneself in a correct and non-erroneous manner, the Path is called *sammāsambodhi*.
Hence he said: “*Sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ*,” which means “awakening correctly and by oneself.
Alternatively, *sammā* is a word signifying praise, and the prefix *sam-* is a word signifying excellence.
He said: "Alternatively, 'bodhi' means that which is praised and beautiful.
Having shown the manifold meanings of the word *bodhi*, and wishing to determine and demonstrate the meaning intended here, he said: "*Bodhi* means both a tree and a path," and so forth.

Therein, it is called a *bodhi*-tree because one awakens (*abujjhi*) upon it; it is called a path because one awakens by oneself (*sayaṃ bujjhati*), or because noble ones awaken by means of it (*bujjhanti vā tena ariyā*).
*Bodhi*: All-knowing wisdom (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is *bodhi* because it awakens to and penetrates all phenomena in all their aspects.

Nibbāna is *bodhi* because it is awakened to and realized. The second example, "and between the *bodhi*," is stated to show that the word *bodhi* applies to a tree even without the word "tree" being used.
"Possessing excellent and vast intelligence" means like the great earth...
The meaning is "one whose excellent wisdom is spread abroad. Regarding "because of not giving all virtues": it means because of not bestowing all virtues.

For one who does not give all virtues is called "a non-giver of all virtues"; this is an irregular compound (ayutta-samāsa) used for the sake of clarity, just as in the expression "faces that do not see the sun" (*asūriyaṃpassāni mukhāni*).

"The three knowledges" (*tisso vijjā*): for one possessing the necessary support (*upanissaya*), he bestows the three knowledges together with the fruit of Arhatship. But is it not the case here that...?

Since the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) is included within the path among the three true insights (*tisso vijjā*), how is it appropriate to say, "The path gives the three true insights"? This is not a fault.

Even though the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is included within the path, when the eightfold path exists, the three true insights become complete together with the knowledge of the path; thus, it is said, "The path gives the three true insights."

It is so called. Regarding "the six direct knowledges" (*cha abhiññā*), the method here is exactly the same. "The knowledge of the disciple's perfection" (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) refers to all mundane and supramundane knowledge that is to be acquired by the foremost disciples.
Regarding "the knowledge of private enlightenment" (*paccekabodhiñāṇa*), the meaning should be understood in this very same manner.
"He directly knew" (*abbhaññāsi*) means he understood. And since this understanding was not by way of hearsay or the like, he said, "he penetrated" (*paṭivijjhi*).
The meaning is: "I have made it manifest. Furthermore, this penetration is not like the penetration of characteristics by one standing at a distance;
thus he said, "I have attained," which means "I have reached. And this reaching is not by going there oneself;
thus he said, "I have acquired," which means "I have obtained by way of its arising within my own continuum."
"Applying the simile" means the correct application of the meaning of the simile to the subject of the simile.

"By way of the meaning" means by way of the meaning of the subject of the simile. Just as the performance of the threefold action upon the eggs by a hen is the primary cause for the chicks emerging from their shells, so too is the performance of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta.
He said, "The threefold practice of contemplation is the primary cause for emerging from the eggshell of ignorance," because it is like that hen... [etc.
...due to the mention of the "continuum" (*santāna*), the continuum is similar to the egg, and the Buddha-qualities are similar to the chick that has emerged from outside;
and as for "Buddha-qualities," in actual meaning they are the Buddha himself, as it is said: "This, Vāseṭṭha, is of the Tathāgata..."
Because of the statement, "The Dhammakāya is also a designation [for this].

"The thinning of the eggshell of ignorance" means the thinning of the eggshell of ignorance by way of powerful insight; and ignorance is similar to an eggshell due to their common characteristic of concealing.

Since even that which has become soft may still undergo a state of hardness, the phrase "the state of being stiff and hard" is stated in order to exclude that possibility. "The state of being sharp, hard, clear, and courageous."
Herein, when formations are being comprehended, the penetration of bliss by insight-knowledge through the power of the concentration faculty is its sharpness (*tikkhatā*).
Its unbluntedness and keenness (*akuṇṭhatā kharabhāvo*) consist in not overstepping [the object] even after having penetrated it, due to the power of the mindfulness faculty.
For some arrows, though sharp, become blunt upon hitting the target; this [insight] is not like that. And although there is keenness, it is by way of a subtle occurrence [of the mind].
The state of clarity by way of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is due to being free from the agitation of the manifestation of defilements (*kilesa*);

and even while there is this state of clarity, the state of heroism by way of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) should be understood as the thorough overcoming of the adversaries that are the defilements without wavering in the interim.
Thus, it should be seen that by these modes, it is precisely the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) that is included within insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*).
"The time of transformation" refers to the attainment of the state of leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*) within insight (*vipassanā*);
at that time, she is as if carrying the embryo of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*), which is why it is called "the time of conceiving the embryo.

"Having caused her to conceive the embryo" means having caused her to conceive the embryo immediately after equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) by way of the culmination of conformity-insight (*anuloma-vipassanā*) for the purpose of giving birth to the Path.

"Attained by successive stages" means attained through the sequence of the first path and so forth. "In the category of higher knowledge" (*abhiññā-pakkha*) refers to the mundane (*lokiya*) category of higher knowledge;

for it is the supramundane (*lokuttara*) higher knowledge that has shattered the eggshell of ignorance. However, one should understand that where some manuscripts write "in the category of the six higher knowledges" (*cha-abhiññā-pakkhe*), that is not the correct reading.
"Elder" (*jeṭṭha*) and "best" (*seṭṭha*): he is an elder because of his state of being most grown; [he is the best] because of all his virtues.
"Best" (seṭṭha) means most excellent because it is praised due to its supreme nature.
Now, showing the connection to the teaching beginning with "But, brahmin, energy has been aroused by me," he said, "Thus the Blessed One," and so forth.
Therein, "from the prior stage onwards" means from the commencement of the exertion of energy belonging to the preliminary stage of meditation.
"Starting from. "The mind has arisen thus" means the mind has arisen by way of the reflections that will be explained further on.
There is also a reading, "Only the mind has arisen," in which case the meaning is: "Only the mind has arisen; there is as yet no confidence in the Blessed One.
"With muddled mindfulness" means with ruined mindfulness, i.e., devoid of mindfulness. "With an agitated body" means...

With a noble body of chariots. "At the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) means at the place where the state of being the "essence" (*maṇḍa*) of the knowledge known as enlightenment has been attained.
For "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is said to be wisdom; since that [wisdom] has become the essence—clear and pure—here, that location is designated as the "seat of enlightenment.
"Endowed with the four factors" means: "Granted that only skin, sinews, and bone remain, let the body wither away..."
"Endowed with the four factors" refers to energy as it has been described.
In this context, it should be understood that skin is one factor, sinew is one factor, bone is one factor, and flesh and blood are one factor.
Furthermore, "skin is one factor" should be taken to mean the state of being independent of skin. For one who is devoted to the exertion...
For even when the body is dissolving, not falling into despondency because of that [dissolution] is one factor, one cause, of that energy.

The meaning should be understood in the same way for the remaining [factors] as well. "Exerted" means grasped by way of the state of exertion known as firm perseverance, without making the undertaking lax.
Therefore he said: "It is meant that it proceeds without laxity."
“Unshrunk” means uncontracted, not having fallen into contraction due to laziness (*kosajja*).
“Established” means having approached the object by way of a state of non-floating known as plunging; therefore he said, “by way of being directed toward the object.
It is “unmuddled” because it proceeds by way of destroying confusion; thus it is not forgotten. Although [this occurs] precisely through the tranquility of the mind...
The mind itself is tranquil, and by means of bodily tranquility, the body becomes tranquil;
nevertheless, because bodily tranquility arises only together with mental tranquility and not apart from it, it is said:
"by way of bodily and mental tranquility. This is because bodily tranquility brings about the calming of both bodies.
It is said: “The material body (rūpakāya) also becomes tranquil. And that very body—“vigatadaratha” means free from the distress of the defilements (kilesa).
For when the mental body (nāmakāya) is free from distress, the material body also has its distress and fever (pariḷāha) stilled.
“Well-placed” (sammā āhitaṃ) means having cut off the distraction (vikkhepa) characterized by running after various objects, [and instead] fixing it upon a single [object].
It has been properly applied and established by bringing about a state of non-distraction toward the object. Therefore he said, "well-established," and so forth.
The mind's lack of one-pointedness is its flickering due to distraction; since that does not occur when there is one-pointedness, he said, "one-pointed, immovable, and unwavering.
By this much—namely, by the passage beginning with "But energy... has been aroused"—[the four factors] of energy, mindfulness, tranquility, and concentration [are shown].
By way of demonstrating the accomplishment of the task.
But surely, the accomplishment of the task for faith and wisdom must also be desired as the preliminary practice for jhāna? True, it is to be desired;
however, because that [accomplishment] is established without being explicitly stated due to its immediate succession, it was not included. For in the absence of faith...

It should be understood that the non-arising of energy (vīriya) and the other factors is itself impossible; and in the absence of their being embraced by wisdom, there could be no state of undertaking the method (ñāya) and so forth.

Likewise, since non-slackness, non-confusion, and the rest apply to energy and the others, it should be seen that the accomplishment of the function of wisdom is already included here by the very mention of non-slackness and the rest.
Or rather, it is to show that in the development of jhāna, the function of concentration (samādhi) must be considered predominant.
It should be understood that the preliminary practice for jhāna has been explained up to the conclusion of concentration. Now, regarding the first jhāna,
the meaning stated in the Jhānavibhaṅga according to the sequence of the Pāḷi beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (vivicceva kāmehi) is as follows:

Desiring to comment according to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he stated, "But although there [in the Vibhaṅga], 'What are sensual pleasures? and so forth, in order to show the reason for not repeating what was already said in the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*.
Therein, weak greed that proceeds in the form of a longing is "chanda" in the sense of wishing;
stronger than that is "rāga" in the sense of coloring; and even stronger than that is "bahalarāga" (intense lust).
Sensual desire (*chandarāga*). It is called "intention" (*saṅkappa*) because one conceives by means of it; thus, it is greed proceeding in that manner.

Therein, "conceiving the sign" (*nimitta-saṅkappanā*) refers to the imagining of a sign for the successive arising of defilements, having combined the parts together and made them into a single whole, such as "woman" or "man.
"Conceiving the secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjana-saṅkappanā*), however, [refers to] "hands..."
"Beautiful, the feet are beautiful"—this is the application [of the term] after analyzing according to the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).

For the "secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjana*) refer to the limbs such as the hands and feet, because they serve as the conditions for the arising of the defilements (*kilesa*) through their successive manifestation (*anu-anu byañjana*), full manifestation (*paribyañjana*), and distinct appearance (*paribyatti*).
From that, passion (*rāga*) is strong in the sense of coloring; it proceeds precisely by way of intention (*saṅkappa*).
Even stronger than that is the passion of intention (*saṅkapparāga*).

This distinction should be understood as occurring within a single state of greed (*lobha*) through its different modes of manifestation and its different stages, just as [one and the same animal is called] "a calf," "an ox," or "a bullock. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to the sensual pleasures of the defilements;
they are called *kāma* because they desire, or because one desires by means of them.
*“Seyyathidaṃ”* means: “Of these, which one? or “In what way? *Viviccitvā* means having become separate.
Therefore he said, “having become apart and having moved away,” the meaning being: having departed by way of abandoning.
Regarding the phrase *“vivicceva kāmehi”* (quite secluded from sensual desires), here by the word *“vivicca”* (secluded), the mere absence of sensual desires at the moment of jhāna is stated.

But by the phrase "one should dwell apart" (*vivicceva*), which indicates that one must definitely separate oneself from sensual desires, it is shown that the jhāna is the opposite of those desires, that the abandoning of sensual desires is the means for attaining jhāna, and that this is the purpose [of the instruction]. To show this meaning, the words "the first jhāna," etc., are stated;
and then, in order to make that same meaning more evident, the words "how," etc., are spoken. It is like a lamp when there is darkness.
By this, he shows that just as darkness overcomes one at night due to the absence of a lamp, so too does sensual desire overcome the mental continuum due to the absence of jhāna.
The word "etena" (by this) is a restrictive term applying only to the preceding phrase; it should not, however, be understood as "only by sensual desires."

Because no definitive determination has been made. "As the escape from that" (*tannissaraṇato*): it is an "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because by means of this, or in this, they escape—that is, they go forth.
What goes forth? Sensual desires (*kāma*). The escape from those sensual desires, their abandonment, is "the escape from that" (*tannissaraṇa*);
thus the meaning is "as the escape from sensual desire. But how is it that, when the suppression [of defilements] is equal, this alone is the escape for sensual desires?

In order to establish through both reasoning and scripture that [this absorption] is not [accompanied] by ill-will and so forth, the passage beginning with "the sense-sphere realm" (kāmadhātu) was stated.
Therein, "by way of transcending the sense-sphere realm" means because it is the path for transcending the entire existence of the sense-sphere (kāmabhava).

By this, he states that this jhāna possesses the full comprehension of sense-desires (kāmapariññā). "By way of being the antidote to sensual lust" refers to [the definition] beginning with "sensual desire is longing" (chando kāmo).
Because the defilement of sensual desire, as previously analyzed, stands in the state of being its adversary.
By this, it is shown that just as loving-kindness is the direct opposite of ill-will and compassion is the direct opposite of cruelty, so too this jhāna is the direct opposite of sensual lust.

Furthermore, here it should be understood that the transcendence of the sense-sphere realm occurs through its fruition, and that it acts as an antidote to sensual lust at the very moment of its own occurrence. Thus, of itself...

Because its intrinsic nature is one of turning away from sensual lust and from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) regarding both the process of existence and the occurrence of kamma-result, this jhāna is specifically the escape from sensual pleasures alone;
and since this point is established by the text itself, he says, "As it has been said," and so forth.
"Renunciation" (nekkhamma) refers to the first jhāna.

Although the restriction was already applied in the first phrase to illustrate this meaning here, the words “in the latter phrase too” and so forth are stated to show that it must likewise be applied to the latter phrase as well, because such a meaning is possible there. “From this” means from sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
“This is to be seen” means this rule is to be understood. “By a term common to all” means by a term common to all forms of seclusion.
“Partial, suppression, eradication, subsiding, and escape seclusion” refers to partial seclusion and so forth. “Physical, mental, and material seclusion” refers to physical seclusion and so forth.

Only these three are to be understood here; that is, only these three are to be understood here in this discourse on *jhāna*, because eradication seclusion and the others are impossible [in this context].
“In the Exposition” means in the *Mahāniddesa*. For therein it says: “In brief, there are two kinds of sensual desire: sensual desire for objects and sensual desire for defilements.”

Having thus announced [the two kinds of desire], the sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*) are specified therein by the passage beginning, “What are sensual objects? Agreeable forms... agreeable tangibles,” and so forth.
Furthermore, they should be understood as *kāmā* (desires) because they are desired. “Therein itself” means in that very exposition (*niddesa*). “In the Vibhaṅga” means in the Jhāna-Vibhaṅga.
“This being so” means when there is such an inclusion of both types of desire. “Even by means of sensual objects” means...
The word *pi* (also) has the sense of adding another compatible meaning, namely that the phrase “secluded from sensual pleasures” (*vatthukāmehi vivicca*) is also appropriate;

it does not have the sense of adding the defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*). Why? Because in this context, seclusion from the defilements of sensual pleasure is already expressed by the second clause [“secluded from unwholesome mental states”].
By the word *tena*, physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is indicated, because it illustrates seclusion from the possession of children, wife, and so forth.
Physical seclusion has been mentioned.
"By the former" means by physical seclusion. "In this" refers to these two phrases: "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.

Or, when the two types of seclusion are distinguished from this [context], if the word "unwholesome" (*akusala*) refers to the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*), [then the meaning is as follows].

Alternatively, all unwholesome states are included; thus, it is said that "seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāma) has been stated in every respect," for which he says: "Because of the statement regarding seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire by means of the second [term].

And "by means of the second" means by means of the seclusion of the mind (cittaviveka). "Of these" refers to the two aforementioned terms; this is a genitive case used in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa).
The abandoning of the basis for the defilements such as craving is "the abandoning of the basis for defilement" (saṃkilesavatthuppahāna).
"Lolabhāva" (the state of longing) means the arising of craving for various objects such as forms and so forth; its cause should be understood as sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) themselves.
"The abandonment of the cause of the state of folly" is the connection [to be made]. "Bālabhāva" (the state of folly) means ignorance (*avijjā*), or thinking what should not be thought and so forth;
its causes are improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) or all unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). [This is] the cause for the attainment of the strands of sensual pleasure.
The purification of the application is demonstrated by distinguishing it from impure applications such as killing living beings.

The purification of the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*)—which is the nourishment of the disposition (*āsaya*)—is achieved through the cleansing of the defilement of craving and the strengthening of the supporting conditions for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

This "nourishment of the disposition" refers to the perfection of the underlying intention established through prior practice and other factors that serve as the conditions for the development of meditative absorption (*jhāna*); and that, moreover, is...

It comes about through the removal of the torment of craving. Therefore it was said: "by means of purifying the defilement of craving. "In regard to sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) is the locative case used for specification.

"Of many kinds" (*anekabheda*) means that it is manifoldly divided by way of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*), and so forth, as well as by way of craving for form (*rūpa-taṇhā*) and the rest.

"Sensual desire itself" (*kāmacchando yeva*) means that desire is of the very nature of sensual pleasure; it is neither the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) nor wholesome desire (*kusala-chanda*).

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Included among the unwholesome" (*akusalapariyāpanna*) means included among those unwholesome states mentioned here in the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states.
"Because it is an adversary to jhāna" means it is mentioned separately because it is an opposing factor to jhāna;

it is taken separately in its own form, rather than being subsumed under the general category of the unwholesome. If only sensual desire as a defilement (*kilesakāma*) was mentioned in the preceding word, how can that be expressed in the plural?

He said: "By way of many divisions," and so forth. "Of others too" refers to wrong view, conceit, lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and so on, as well as the contact and other mental factors associated with them.

"Because of showing the state of being an antidote to the opposites of the higher jhāna factors": the jhāna factors to be mentioned further on, such as "with applied thought (*savitakka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*)," are the "higher jhāna factors"; it is because this [passage] shows their state of being the antidotes to their own opposites.
This is a term for the hindrances that are opposed to those [factors]. There is also a reading: “Because it shows the state of being an opponent and an antidote to the higher jhāna-factors.

In this context, they explain the meaning of “because it shows the state of being an opponent and an antidote” as showing the state of being an antidote to the jhāna-factors about to be described above by way of their direct opposites. “Opposed to the jhāna-factors” means because they obstruct the occurrence of the jhāna-factors.

The factors of jhāna are the opposites [of their respective hindrances]. "Destructive" means obstructive. Concentration is the opposite of sensual desire because it is the direct antithesis to longing for passion;

since it steadies the mind that is wandering and being enticed by various objects, concentration is the opposite of sensual desire. Joy is the opposite of ill will because it shares the same security of practice as gladness.

Joy is the antidote to ill will. Applied thought (*vitakka*) is the antidote to sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*); because it proceeds with wide extension through the power of wise intention (*yoniso saṅkappana*), applied thought is the antidote to sloth and torpor. Pleasure (*sukha*) is the antidote to restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*);

because pleasure has a nature that is tranquil and cool, it is the antidote to restlessness and remorse, which have a nature of lack of tranquility and burning heat. Discernment (*vicāra*) is the antidote to doubt (*vicikicchā*).
Investigation (*vicāra*) is the antidote to doubt (*vicikicchā*), because its essential nature is a semblance of wisdom (*paññā*) through the mode of repeated reflection upon the object.
"In the *Peṭaka*" refers to the commentary on the Piṭakas taught by the Elder Mahākaccāyana; it is in that *Peṭaka*.

"Of the domain distinguished by the five strands of sensual pleasure" means of the domain distinguished by the five specific strands of sensual pleasure, beginning with visible forms. "Of those whose domains are the various bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), etc. [is the phrase].
By the expression "seclusion from ill-will" (*byāpādaviveka*), the seclusion-by-suppression of hatred—which has as its object the various bases for resentment such as "he has done me harm"—is stated.

By the expression "seclusion [from states] associated with delusion" (*mohādhika*) such as sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), the seclusion-by-suppression of delusion—which has as its object the concealment [of reality] and the various divisions of the past limit of suffering and so forth—is stated. And this [first jhāna] is the suppressor of sensual lust, ill-will, and their concomitants, such as sloth and torpor.

Because all wholesome states have the nature of being the opposite of all unwholesome states, although by that very nature they abandon all unwholesome states, they nonetheless possess the specific nature of suppressing sensual lust and so forth.

Therefore, without making a distinction, it is said that "seclusion through suppression" refers to the suppression of the hindrances, the unwholesome roots, and the like, because of that nature. Thus he spoke.

Since there is no exercise of mastery over intrinsic-nature phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma) as they proceed according to their respective conditions, the phrase "thinking is thought" (vitakkanaṃ vitakko) is stated for the purpose of precluding the state of having mastery. For "thinking" (vitakkana) refers to the act of thinking;
and since that act is merely the occurrence of thought by means of its own conditions, this description in terms of its activity serves to exclude the notion of mastery. This, then—
"Vitakkana" means the conceptualizing of an object as "it is like this"; thus he said, "it is called 'estimation' (ūhana).
Because the mind, through the power of vitakka, becomes as if it has actually ascended to the object, it is therefore described as having the characteristic of directing the mind toward the object.
For just as someone, by relying on a royal favorite who is either a kinsman or a friend, ascends and enters the royal palace;
In this way, by depending on initial application (vitakka), the mind ascends to the object. If this is so, how does a mind without initial application ascend to the object?

It is solely through the power of previous initial application. For just as that man, through familiarity, enters the royal palace without fear even without [the king's] presence, so too, through familiarity, the mind without initial application ascends to the object even without initial application.
"By familiarity" means by the familiarity consisting in the cultivation of thoughts occurring within the mental continuum.
For, through the force of thoughts frequently occurring in the continuum, the mind's mounting upon the object becomes well-practiced;
therefore, it sometimes proceeds there even without a thought. This is just as when [the mind] is accompanied by knowledge and proceeds by way of comprehension (*sammasana*).

Just as that which has been long practiced may sometimes proceed by way of comprehension even when devoid of knowledge, or just as that which proceeded accompanied by defilements may proceed entirely free from defilements due to the force of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) through long practice—this should be understood in the same way.
"The nature of striking and beating" means, first of all, striking directly; or, striking from all sides after having turned around.

Or it is "striking" (āhanana) and "repeated striking" (pariyāhanana). It should be understood that the occurrence [of the mind] as if striking and repeatedly striking, thinking "form is form," "earth is earth," is what is meant by striking and repeated striking.
For when the mind applies itself to an object, initial application (vitakka), making that object fit for apprehension, is like one who strikes it. If this is so, then as the Elder Nāgasena said...

“Initial application (vitakka) has the characteristic of striking. Great King, just as when a drum is struck and it subsequently reverberates and resounds, even so, Great King, initial application is to be seen as the striking;
and subsequent reverberation and resounding are to be seen as sustained application (vicāra). Why was the characteristic of striking stated for initial application? It is not [that]...
There is a contradiction. For the Elder has stated the definition by making it dependent upon function (*kicca*).
Indeed, there is no such thing as an activity or a mode of apprehension for phenomena that is divorced from their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Nevertheless, in accordance with those people who are to be enlightened, even a phenomenon that is a single unity in the ultimate sense is explained through many modes by means of figurative expressions, as if its nature were superimposed.

For in this way, it is well-explained. Regarding the phrase "manifested as bringing [the object]": here, "bringing" (*ānayana*) means the directing of the object toward the mind, or its drawing [toward it].
"Wandering along" (*anusañcaraṇa*) means moving around [it].
This particular distinction, being found within the continuum (*santāna*), is evident within that very continuum.
It should be understood as "it occurs. The same method applies to the remaining [mental factors] as well. "Anumajjana" (stroking) means the stroking of the mind upon the object;
the sense is "rubbing all around. For it has been said: "Vicāra is like a hand that strokes, like a hand that moves about. "Tattha" means "upon the object.
The application to co-nascent [factors] occurs precisely by way of the stroking defined as the repeated movement over the object.
It should be understood as follows. *Anuppabandhana* (continuous binding) is the occurrence of the mind upon an object as if uninterrupted.
For it is described as "the state of continuous binding. And for that very reason, it is said to be "like the resonance of a bell" and "like a whirling motion.
"In some places" refers to the first jhāna and in the arising of limited states of consciousness (*paritta-cittuppāda*). "In the sense of being gross" refers to [its relation] to *vicāra*.

In the sense of being gross. Just as the sound produced by striking a bell is the first impact, so too, in the sense of directing the mind toward the object, initial application (vitakka) is like the first impact of the mind; thus he said, "like the sound of striking a bell," and so forth.
Regarding the term "diffusive" (vipphāravā), here "diffusiveness" refers to the counteractive quality of initial application against sloth and torpor, and its lack of shrinking back from the object.
It is without contraction; however, with the intention that it is like a movement due to its nature of directing [the mind] toward an object, he says, "the state of quivering of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "as if wandering about," here it should be understood as wandering for the purpose of testing whether there are any dangers (*parissaya*).
In the commentary on the Second Book (*Dukanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*), however—
“Just as a great bird traveling through the air proceeds by catching the wind with both wings and settling them,
so is initial application (vitakka), which occurs by way of directing the mind onto the object;
and just as its travel proceeds while fluttering the wings for the sake of catching the wind, so is sustained application (vicāra), which occurs by way of continuous mental scrutiny.”

What was stated is appropriate in terms of its occurrence through continuous succession. For indeed, whether in access concentration or in absorption, during the course of the mental continuum, applied thought (*vitakka*) proceeds as if having entered the object after becoming steady;
it is not manifest at the very first moment of contact. Just as applied thought, which constitutes the first moment of contact with a previously unknown object, [is not evident].

It is expansive; it does not proceed with such continuous succession upon a single object as it does [in the higher stages], yet it is not overly expansive there because of its settled state. It is manifest in the first and second jhānas:

the specific mode of directed application (*abhiniropanākāra*) of applied thought (*vitakka*) is manifest in the first jhāna due to its grossness, and because that [grossness] is absent [in the second].
In the system of the five jhānas, in the second jhāna, the specific quality of *vicāra*—its mode of "anumānajjana" (repeatedly gliding over)—is clearly manifest.

Here, however, is another method: when one holds a bronze vessel soiled with stains firmly with one hand and rubs it with the other hand using a pad made of powder, oil, goat’s hair, and so forth, the hand that holds it firmly...
Applied thought (vitakka) is like the hand that shapes [the clay], and sustained thought (vicāra) is like the hand that smooths it.

Likewise, for a potter who has set the wheel spinning with a blow from his staff and is fashioning a vessel, applied thought is like the hand that presses down the lump of clay, and sustained thought is like the hand that moves it back and forth. Similarly, it is like drawing a circular line on bronze vessels and the like.

It should be understood that applied thought (*vitakka*) is like a thorn standing upright after being driven into the middle of something being worked upon, while sustained thought (*vicāra*) is like a thorn moving about on the outside.
Just as a tree— though non-existent apart from its constituent parts such as flowers, fruits, and branches— is nevertheless said to be "flowering" or "fruit-bearing," so too...

Just as [the term "tree" is used], it is said "like a tree" and so forth in order to show that even though jhāna does not exist apart from its factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), it is nevertheless conventionally designated as "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*). However, in the *Vibhaṅga* and other such texts, because the meditation on jhāna must be taught by way of the person (*puggala*), it is stated by way of reference to the person:
"Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... and so forth.

"The jhānas have been pointed out. Although in the *Vibhaṅga* the teaching was given by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), the meaning there in the *Vibhaṅga* should nevertheless be understood exactly as it is stated here by way of the phenomena (*dhammavasena*), such as "by this applied thought" and so forth;

for the intention is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), the person simply does not exist. Alternatively, [it is said] by showing that one who possesses the jhāna possesses applied thought and sustained thought.

Since it was stated that the state of being with applied thought (*savitakka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*) belongs to the jhāna itself, he said: "But the meaning there should also be understood in exactly this way.
With reference to the abstract derivation (*bhāvasādhana*) of the word *viveka*, he said: "Therefore, from seclusion" (*tasmā vivekā*). This is an ablative case used in the sense of a cause;
thus, the meaning is "because seclusion is the cause. Alternatively, one may take the word *viveka* as having an agentive derivation (*kattusādhana*) or an objective derivation (*kammassādhana*).
Having intended this, he said: “Or in that seclusion. For by the term “secluded,” both of the two methods of derivation are indeed included:

being separated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and being cleared away by them. “Pīnayati” means it satisfies or increases. It has the characteristic of gladdening (*sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā*), which is the characteristic of complete contentment.
It has the function of nourishing (*pīnanarasā*), which is the function of full development. It has the function of pervading (*pharaṇarasā*), [meaning] by means of sublime forms, of the body...
Its function is to pervade. Enthusiasm (*odagya*) is the state of being uplifted. It is called "pleasure" (*sukha*) because it pleases;

the meaning is that it causes the associated states to obtain satisfaction. This description in terms of an agent is obtained figuratively for the purpose of precluding any agent other than the dhamma itself;
however, in the primary sense, only the abstract noun derivation is applicable, thus it is said: "pleasure is the act of pleasing. Its characteristic is gratification (*sāta*).

Because it is of a desirable nature, it "satisfies" (sādeti) the person possessing it, or the associated mental states, within itself; thus it is called *sāta*, having changed the letter *da* to *ta*.
They say that *sāta* means "sweet. That which has *sāta* as its characteristic is *sātalakkhaṇa*.
In the phrase "having the function of nourishing" (*upabrūhanarasa*) and so forth, "nourishing" (*upabrūhana*) is the strengthening of the associated mental states, unlike suffering (*dukkha*).
Non-neglect (*anuggaha*) is the successive grasping [of the object] without letting go, as if it were neither painful nor pleasant, and without indifference; or it is helpfulness.
"In some cases" refers to the first jhāna and so forth. "Satisfaction at obtaining" is the satisfaction that arises by way of obtaining.
"Experiencing the flavor of what has been obtained" is the experiencing of the flavor of the object already obtained. By this, joy and pleasure [are explained].
These have been shown by way of their intrinsic nature after having been analyzed. Where there is *pīti* (rapture), there is *sukha* (pleasure);

this expresses the absolute conjunction of *pīti* with pleasure, just as *vitakka* (initial application) is with *vicāra* (sustained application). Where there is *sukha*, there is not necessarily *pīti*;
this expresses the non-absolute conjunction of *sukha* with *pīti*, just as *vicāra* is with *vitakka*. By this, [the distinction between] absolute and non-absolute conjunction is established.
This shows the distinction between rapture (*pīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).

A "desert" (*kaṇṭāra*) is so called because they cross over water (*kaṃ*) there; it is a waterless, arid place. "Forest-end" (*vananta*) is simply the forest itself. Regarding the phrase "bliss as if entering forest shade and enjoying water":
for example, suppose a man traveling along a great desert road were oppressed by the heat, exhausted, and parched with thirst.
Seeing a man on the opposite path, he might ask, "Where is there water?
and that man might say, "Having crossed the forest, there is a grove of naturally flowing springs; go there and you will find it.
Upon hearing his words, the traveler would become exceedingly joyful; then, as he proceeds, he sees lotus petals, stalks, leaves, and the like fallen upon the ground.
Having seen this, becoming even more delighted as he goes along, he might see men with wet clothes and wet hair;
he might hear the cries of wild cocks, peacocks, and the like; he might see a dark-blue forest thicket resembling a net of blue jewels grown at the edge of a fresh lake;
he might see blue, red, and white lotuses growing in the lake; and he might also see water that is clear and serene.
He would go forth, becoming increasingly joyful; having descended into the lake, he would bathe and drink as he pleased,
and with his fatigue and distress allayed, he would eat lotus roots, stalks, and lotuses, adorn himself with blue water-lilies and other flowers,
sling mandālava roots over his shoulders, emerge from the water, put on his wrap, and lay out his bathing cloth in the sun.
This should be understood as being just like a man who, lying down in cool shade while a gentle breeze blows, might exclaim, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!

For the rapture (*pīti*) that has the form of being thrilled and overjoyed regarding the preliminary object is like that man’s state of being thrilled and overjoyed from the moment he first sees the young forest thicket until the time he actually sees the water.
The bliss that consists in the manner of experiencing the flavor of the object when it has reached its full strength— like the time when one, having bathed and drunk,
lies down in cool shade as a gentle breeze blows, saying, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"—
"at each respective time" means at the time of obtaining a desirable object and at the time of experiencing the flavor of what has been obtained.
[This refers] to forest-shade and so forth, at the time of hearing and seeing them, and at the time of their enjoyment.

"By way of manifest state" means by way of the distinct manifestation (*vibhūta*) of joy and happiness respectively. Regarding the phrase "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*): here, in the first sense, "born of seclusion" refers to the jhāna.
And because this jhāna possesses a specific meaning derived from the words "joy and happiness," or [it is said] "in this jhāna."

Here, the letter *a* is to be understood as in the word *ariyasava*. In the second [compound], there is the compound *pītisukham eva vivekajam*, and the compound *vivekaja-pītisukham* is a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound) in which the suffix of the personal pronoun (*paccattaniddesa*) has been elided; or, when that elision occurs, the reading is *vivekaja-pītisukha*.
This is the distinction.
By the phrase "first, by way of numerical sequence," he indicates the order of the teaching.
There is also a reading, "the first, by way of numerical sequence" (*gaṇanānupubbatā paṭhamaṃ*); here too, the meaning is "by way of numerical sequence.

Alternatively, the meaning is that this statement, "the first," refers merely to the state of being first in numerical sequence. However, the definition "it is called 'first' because one attains it first" is not an absolute characteristic.

For one who has attained mastery and possesses the eight attainments is able to enter them starting from the beginning and reaching the peak, or starting from the peak and reaching the beginning, or entering them at intervals.
Thus, in the sense of its prior arising, it is called "first" because it arose first. For this very reason, in the *Visuddhimagga*...
It is stated only thus: “The first is by way of numerical sequence; it is also called ‘first’ because it arises first. It burns away contrary states (*paccanīkadhamme jhāpetīti*):
it consumes contrary states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the meaning is that it abandons them by means of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
Its range (*gocara*) is the object (*ālambana*), such as the kasiṇas. “That” (*taṃ*) refers to that range. It closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyati*): it sees. Together with access (*saha upacārena*).

Together with access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). "By closely contemplating the kasiṇa object" means by closely contemplating one's own object, such as the earth-kasiṇa, as if it were a visible form with the eye.

"By closely contemplating the characteristics" means by closely contemplating, as far as possible, the three characteristics of impermanence and so forth, as well as the characteristic of suchness in the element of Nibbāna.
For this very reason, he said, "For here," and so forth. By the abandoning of the perversions of permanence and so forth...

The path contemplates the characteristics of impermanence and so forth through non-delusion; thus it is called "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). Therefore, he said, "the function of contemplation by means of insight," and so on.

Regarding "the characteristic of suchness" (*tathalakkhaṇa*): because Nibbāna, which is of a nature not subject to destruction, does not become otherwise, its intrinsic nature is the "characteristic of suchness.
Alternatively, since the path has Nibbāna as its object, its status as "contemplation of the characteristic of suchness" should be applied [to the path].
Showing first the example of the poisonous snake (*visada*), he said: “Just as one who possesses wealth,” and so forth.

Another person is worthy of being designated (*apadesāraho*): that is, a man who, distinct from his wealth and retinue, yet possesses wealth and a retinue, is fit to be designated as “possessing wealth” (*sadhana*) and “possessing a retinue” (*saparijana*);
thus he is worthy of being designated, meaning he is one who may be pointed to [as such].
This has been stated. Regarding the phrase "the designation 'army' applies only to the components of an army":

although there is no such thing as an "army" apart from its components such as chariots, it is called "an army with chariots" (*sarathā*) and "an army with infantry" (*sapatti*) because it functions together with them; thus, the conventional term "army" refers specifically to the components like chariots and so forth.
Now, addressing the objection: "Why is one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), which was not included in the list of jhāna factors, included here? he says:
“Because it was not stated,” and so forth. “Only as thus stated” means that it was indeed stated in its own specific form within the *Vibhaṅga*.

Regarding the phrase “possessing one-pointedness of mind”: even though it was not stated here [in this specific context], the meaning is that although it was not stated in its own specific form in this particular recitation of the jhāna formula, it is nevertheless included by the general term “jhāna. For this very reason he said, “by which,” and so forth. This is what is meant:

In order to illuminate that phenomenon which must be discussed together with applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest, the Teacher formulated the summary (*uddesa*) as "with applied thought, with sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*), etc., with the intention of explaining it.

That very intention was made clear by the Blessed One in the *Vibhaṅga* when he defined it as "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittassekaggatā*). Therefore, one should not think that this [one-pointedness] is not included in the recitation of the jhānas.
Regarding the term *upasampajja*: here, the prefixes *upa* and *saṃ* are shown to be devoid of meaning—as in words such as *upalabbhati*—by stating "having approached" (*upagantvā*) and so forth;
then, to show that they do possess meaning, "having fully attained" (*upasampādayitvā*) and so forth is stated.
Therefore, in this context, *upasampajja* means "having reached" or "having accomplished. *Iriyanti* means "activity. *Vutti* and so forth...
These are its synonyms. It is the protection and preservation of one posture by means of another posture, which prevents the obstruction of that posture.
Only the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) is mentioned because it is the practice customary for all Buddhas; for they say that this was indeed the custom of all Buddhas.
The discussion on the first jhāna is finished.
The Discussion of the Second Jhāna.
“Calm” (*vūpasama*) means the cause of calm. Here, “calm” is intended in the sense of abandoning;

and that, in its actual meaning, is the surmounting of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), which is their non-arising at the moment of the second jhāna. Therefore he said, “by surmounting,” and so forth. Of what?
Here, the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought is intended; but is this [subsiding] of those belonging to the first jhāna, or rather of those belonging to the second jhāna?
What is the point here? If it were of those belonging to the first jhāna, there would be no such subsiding, for there is never a time when the first jhāna is devoid of applied and sustained thought.
If, on the other hand, it were of those belonging to the second jhāna, even so there would be no subsiding whatsoever in every respect.
With reference to the inquiry, "Because all of them are absent there," he said, "In that regard, although...

and so forth. For it is the state of being subject to non-arising at the moment of each respective jhāna that is intended by "subsiding" (vūpasamana) for one who has seen the danger [in the hindrances];

and it is only applied thought (vitakka) and the others that, having become factors of jhāna, are made to do so, and not the contact (phassa) and other mental states associated with them. Therefore...

The term "tranquillization" (*vūpasama*) occurs in the context of *jhāna* specifically with reference to applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other [factors]. However, since the Sutta also presents the vision of danger (*ādīnava*)— namely, that "this is grosser than that"—
with respect to the mental states associated with applied thought and the rest, just as it does for applied thought itself,

it follows that when one speaks of the tranquillization of applied thought and the rest along with their concomitants without distinction, mentioning only the tranquillization of applied thought and the rest constitutes an overstatement (*adhikavacana*).
Having established that it "awakens another meaning," he says, "But of the gross... and so forth, in order to show that it demonstrates a certain distinction.

This is the intended meaning here: the second jhāna is attained through the surmounting of those very applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) by which the first jhāna is characterized as gross;
it is not through the surmounting of contact (phassa) and the other factors, which are not gross in their intrinsic nature.
This meaning is illustrated by the phrase, "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*);
therefore, an objection such as, "Is the subsiding of the applied and sustained thought belonging to the first jhāna intended here, or rather that belonging to the second jhāna? has no place at all.

The same principle applies to the phrases "and with the fading away of rapture" (*pītiyā ca virāgā*) and so forth. Consequently, the statements regarding the surmounting of applied and sustained thought, rapture, and pleasure [are to be understood accordingly].

The statement regarding the surmounting of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*)— which constitutes a portion of those [phrases] that illustrate the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth—
is stated as an illustration by means of the method of characterizing the whole through its parts. For even though the statements such as "surmounting applied and sustained thought" stand separately,
when they are grasped as a collective whole by virtue of the commonality of being descriptions of factors to be abandoned, the phrase "stilling of applied and sustained thought" [is understood].

"It becomes a part of that. Alternatively, by the very mention of the "stilling of applied and sustained thought," which indicates the attainment of the second [jhāna] and so forth through the transcendence of those [states], it is shown that the mentions of "fading away of rapture" and so on indicate the attainment of the third [jhāna] and so forth through the transcendence of rapture and so on;
thus, its indication of that is stated. For in this way, without using a part to characterize the whole, by the mention of the "stilling of applied and sustained thought," [the rest is indicated].
It has been shown that the statements beginning with "fading away from zest" (pītivirāga) have an identical function regarding their respective objects.

By saying "internally" (ajjhatta), what is intended is one's own internal state (niyakajjhatta), not the "internal-of-the-internal" (ajjhattajjhatta) and so forth; thus he says, "‘Internally’ means one’s own internal state is intended.
He states the reason for this with the words, "But in the Vibhaṅga," and so on. The particle *pana* (but/however) also...
The meaning of the word *api* is "also" (*vibhaṅgepi*), which is the sense; or rather, this is the very reading [itself].
Because it is joined with the color blue, it is "like a blue cloth"; the intention is that because of its connection with blue, the cloth is blue.
And in this alternative interpretation of the meaning—namely, in this position that "it clarifies the mind"—the genitive case in the word *cetaso* is used in the sense of the accusative.
"In the former" refers to the position stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*]: "Because it possesses serenity (*sampasādana*), jhāna itself is also 'serene' (*sampasādana*).

The word "of" (*cetaso*) is used in the genitive case to indicate a relationship. Regarding the statement, "In the world, even the word for 'best' (*seṭṭha*) is seen in the form of the word 'one' (*eka*)," as in "until I have made others one-minded," he says:
"For in the world, even the best is called 'one'. Also, in such passages as "He was conquered by the solitary and the lowly," it has the sense of "without a companion" (*asahāya*).
The word "one" has been seen [in this sense], hence he said: "being one, that is, without a companion.

Although faith and the other factors are indeed conditions for associated states both by way of being common and by way of being uncommon, concentration, however, at the moment of jhāna is an especially predominant condition for associated states by performing the function of a lord (indatthakaraṇa) through its characteristic of non-distraction; showing this, he said: "associated states... [etc. ...a designation."
The two qualifying terms, “serenity of mind” (*sampasādanaṃ cetaso*) and “singleness” (*ekodibhāvaṃ*), are taken here according to the desire for a statement of the excellence of this jhāna.
To show this distinction—that such excellence as is found in this jhāna is not found in the first jhāna—it is said, “Is it not so?
and so forth. [This refers to] the manner of striking and rubbing against the object, and the manner of massaging and applying oneself to it.

And although the mental states that are occurring have abandoned the hindrances and the turbidity of the defilements has departed, they—as if causing some agitation to their associated factors—do not settle down together with them;
thus it is said: "By the agitation of applied and sustained thought... it is not well-purified.
In this context, "small waves" refers to ripples, and "large ones" to billows. Concentration (*samādhi*) is also not well...

"Manifest": even though there is equality of the faculties and equality of energy, because of that very turbidity and lack of serenity, concentration is not clearly manifest, like a fish in thick water.

Regarding the phrase "by the absence of the impediments of applied and sustained thought," here the aforementioned agitation itself is the impediment. "As it has been stated" refers to that faith by virtue of which there is serenity.

And by means of that one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) by virtue of which jhāna is described as "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*), there is this commentary on the meaning, given through the *Vibhaṅga* recitation—which explains the specific modes of its occurrence by way of the terms "faith" (*saddahanā*) and so forth—as follows:

"It is 'tranquillizing' (*sampasādana*) because it is associated with tranquillity, or because it is itself tranquillity. It 'develops singleness' (*ekodibhāvaṃ bhāveti*) because it develops the state of being unified."
This commentary on the meaning proceeds thus: "Jhāna has been explained. Indeed, it should be understood that this commentary both accords with and conforms to the text of the *Vibhaṅga*.
How does this commentary accord with and conform to that *Vibhaṅga* text?
For, having cited the term "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*) in the *Jhānavibhaṅga*, [the text] explains it as "that which is faith, the act of believing," and so forth.

It was stated that faith alone is intended; yet, having extracted the phrase "singleness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), a description of concentration itself is given through such terms as "the stability, steadiness, and steadfastness of the mind.

However, since the Commentary states that "tranquillity and singleness of mind" refers specifically to the jhāna, does this not result in a contradiction with the *Vibhaṅga* text in the Commentary? It does not result in a contradiction.
In the *Vibhaṅga* as well, since the exposition was composed with this very same intention, it is so:

for when that serenity (*sampasādana*) by which the jhāna is joined is called "serenity," then— since that serenity has been shown [in the text] by the words "the faith, the act of believing," and so forth—
the application of that term to the jhāna through its connection with it is demonstrated precisely by means of a grammatical construction of common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa-niddesa*).

Having extracted the word "ekodibhāvaṃ," when "ekodi" is shown, the fact that jhāna increases unification is already stated by the very use of the grammatical construction of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-niddesa*) as "jhāna is ekodibhāva.

With this intention, it is appropriate to maintain that there is no contradiction, because only the phenomenon (*dhammamatta*) itself has been defined, without engaging in an analysis of the literal expression.
However, as for what was stated by the commentators, such as the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla and others:

"If the inclusion of 'unified' (*ekodi*) were intended as a reference to concentration (*samādhi*), then after citing the term 'state of being unified' (*ekodibhāva*), there would have been no need to provide a further definition of concentration.
Therefore, the word *ekodibhāva* itself functions with respect to concentration, just as the word 'serenity' (*sampasādana*) functions with respect to the jhāna."
The phrase "it is appropriate" contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, it must be understood that this is a distinct alternative interpretation of the meaning, independent of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For this is their intended meaning: because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), it "rises as one," thus *ekodi*;
taking only the meditative consciousness (*jhānacitta*) associated with such concentration, the state of being "one-pointed" (*ekodissa*) [is established].
It can be said that "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*) is a designation for concentration (*samādhi*).

However, as for their insistence—that "if singleness is taken as a designation for concentration, then after extracting the term 'singleness,' it would be improper to provide a definition of concentration"—that is incorrect because it is inconclusive. For elsewhere too, without analyzing the phrasing, [the meaning alone]...
In the *Vibhaṅga*, the exposition is seen for the most part [in this way]:

"Peaceful" (*santā*) means they have gone to an equal cessation (*sama-nirodha*). "Tranquilized" (*samitā*) means they have been brought to an equal state through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and have been ceased.

"Calmed" (*vūpasantā*) means for that very reason they are thoroughly calmed. "Passed away" (*atthaṅgatā*) means they have gone to their end (*attha*), which is destruction. "Completely passed away" (*abbhatthaṅgatā*) [is so called] by means of the prefix (*upasaggena*).
This was stated by expanding the word. "Appitā" means led away, gone to destruction.
"Sosītā" means gone to a state of withering or dryness due to the absence of the continuity known as the process of existence (*pavatti*). "Byantīkatā" means made to have its end removed.

"This is the meaning" refers to the meaning characterized by the non-existence of applied thought and sustained thought because they have been abandoned through cultivation. [The opponent] stated the point raised by the challenger.
Having accepted [the opponent's position] for the sake of refuting it, he said, "This is so;
this matter is established," and then stated, "But not this," and so forth. In that context, "this" refers to the statement, "With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.
"Illuminating its meaning" means illuminating the meaning defined as the mere absence of applied and sustained thought. "Not of the turbidity of defilements... [and so on].
The meaning is that it is not "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*) because of the subsiding of the agitation of the defilements known as the hindrances, just as at the moment of access concentration.
