But why was this said, given that "even though it has already been stated previously, it must still be mentioned"? For [the phrase] illuminates the means for attaining the second jhāna and so forth;

it illuminates the cause by way of internal tranquillity and the unification of mind; and it illuminates the cause for the state of being without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*).

If the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is already indicated by the very mention of their "subsiding" (*vūpasama*), what is the purpose of further stating that they are "without applied thought and sustained thought"?
It is not so, because [the absence] has not yet been fully clarified. For the mention of their "subsiding" does not express the non-occurrence of applied and sustained thought.
Indeed, the "subsiding" of these two refers to the abandoning of craving (*taṇhā*) for them; it is expressed by way of their coarse factor (*oḷārika-aṅga*).
For the suppression of the respective craving for jhāna is demonstrated by such expressions as "the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicāra-vūpasama*).
Thus, while the expression "subsiding of applied and sustained thought" indicates a state of detachment regarding applied and sustained thought,
the occurrence of formations (*saṅkhāra*) takes place in those paths which effect the abandonment of craving for formations, as well as in the fruits where craving has been abandoned.

Likewise here, since the association of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) with the second jhāna—which has already suppressed applied and sustained thought and craving—would not have been excluded by the preceding [definition], it was stated as "without applied thought, without sustained thought" (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*). This was said both to exclude that [association] and to show the subsiding of those [factors] through the transcendence of the desire to advert and so forth. The first jhāna serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the second jhāna.
"It is a condition" is why he said, "from the concentration of the first jhāna. "The first as well" means the first jhāna too.

"By way of numerical sequence," and so forth, should be understood according to the method already stated below. Here too, it is certainly permissible to say, "the second is called 'second' because it arises second.
To establish this very point by means of the text of the Vibhaṅga, he said, "As it has been said," and so forth.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*: “Jhāna is confidence, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind,” that was said figuratively in order to show jhāna together with its requisites.

For confidence is a requisite of jhāna, like a white woolen rug for a chariot, and not a factor of jhāna itself; thus he says, “This is merely a figurative expression. But in the non-figurative sense:
Because it possesses only three factors by way of those factors that have reached the characteristic of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*), he said,
"But setting aside serenity," and so forth.
The discussion of the second jhāna is concluded.
The Discussion of the Third Jhāna:
*Virajjana* means fading away (*virāga*). To show that this fading away is either a loathing by way of disenchantment or the abandoning of the lust bound up with it, it is said:
"the disgust for that rapture or the surmounting of it. "Between the two" means—
"Between these two phrases, 'with the fading away of rapture' (*pītiyā virāgā*) and 'in the middle' (*majjhe*) is the meaning. 'Conjunction' (*sampiṇḍana*) means a collection.
'Path' (*magga*) means a means. For, without the attainment of the second jhāna, there is no realization of the third jhāna;

thus, the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo*) is the means for the realization of the third jhāna. 'For the sake of its attainment' (*tadadhigamāya*) means for the sake of attaining the third path."

Regarding "by way of arising": because it functions by making even the equanimity of jhāna well-composed and internalized through its state of being thoroughly composed, he says, "he sees with evenness.
Regarding "clear": because it is distinct due to the departure of defilement. Regarding "vast":
because it has attained an exceedingly sublime state, it is great. Regarding "firm": because of the disappearance of rapture...
"Because it has attained a state of steadiness. If it is asked: "But surely no feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā) is possible here;

therefore, how can this possessor of the third jhāna be called 'equanimous' (upekkhako) on account of being endowed with equanimity? [The answer is: Equanimity is not called "equanimity" solely as a feeling of equanimity;
rather, there exists another kind of equanimity as well. Showing this, he says: "Equanimity, moreover, is tenfold."
"...becomes," and so forth. In that context, "Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad;

he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending"—this equanimity (upekkhā), which has been described thus, belongs to one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and consists in the state of not abandoning his naturally pure disposition when encountering the sixfold range of desirable and undesirable objects at the six sense-doors. This is called the "six-factored equanimity" (chaḷaṅgupekkhā).

However, that equanimity which consists in the mode of neutrality toward beings, as it occurs in the passage: “He dwells, having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity,” is called the divine abiding (brahmavihāra) of equanimity.

That equanimity which consists in the mode of neutrality toward co-nascent states, as it occurs in the passage: “He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is dependent on seclusion,” is called the enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga) of equanimity.

Furthermore, that equanimity described as "he attends to the sign of equanimity from time to time," which consists of energy that is neither over-exerted nor too lax, is called equanimity of energy (*vīriyupekkhā*). As for the question:
"How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight?"—[this refers to the following:]
Do they arise? Eight equanimities regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) arise by way of serenity (*samatha*); ten equanimities regarding formations arise by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
“Which eight equanimities regarding formations arise by way of serenity?

The wisdom that is reflective discernment and stability regarding the hindrances for the sake of attaining the first jhāna is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations; [the wisdom] for the sake of attaining the second jhāna...”
Wisdom as the reflective settling upon applied thought and sustained thought is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations;
wisdom as the reflective settling upon rapture for the sake of attaining the third jhāna is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations;

wisdom as the reflective settling upon pleasure and pain for the sake of attaining the fourth jhāna is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations; [and wisdom as the reflective settling] for the sake of attaining the base of infinite space...

The wisdom that is reflective discernment and stabilization regarding the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity, is knowledge of equanimity toward formations.

The wisdom that is reflective discernment and stabilization regarding the perception of the base of infinite space for the purpose of attaining the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, is knowledge of equanimity toward formations. [And so on] for the purpose of attaining the attainment of the base of nothingness...
The wisdom that is reflective consideration and stabilization regarding the perception of the base of infinite consciousness is knowledge of equanimity towards formations;

the wisdom that is reflective consideration and stabilization regarding the perception of the base of nothingness for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
These eight kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of serenity.
“What are the ten kinds of equanimity towards formations that arise by way of insight? It is the wisdom of reflective establishment in equanimity towards formations regarding arising,
occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, destiny, generation, manifestation,
birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair, for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry.”

Knowledge of arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, reflection, and composure regarding the equanimity towards formations is knowledge for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry; [knowledge] for the sake of attaining the path of once-returning...
pe... for the sake of attaining the fruit of once-returning... pe... for the sake of attaining the path of non-returning... pe... for the sake of attaining the fruit of non-returning... pe...

The wisdom that, through reflective contemplation, remains steadfast regarding arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, destiny, manifestation, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair, for the sake of attaining the path of arahantship—this is knowledge of equanimity toward formations.
[It is the wisdom] for the sake of attaining the fruition of arahantship... pe ...for the sake of attaining the dwelling in emptiness... pe ...

"Knowledge of equanimity towards formations is wisdom that reflects upon and becomes established in arising, occurrence, signs, accumulation, rebirth-linking, for the sake of attaining the attainment of the signless dwelling.

Thus, equanimity consisting in the mode of reflecting upon and becoming established in the hindrances and so forth, as it has been handed down, is what is called "equanimity towards formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*). It arises by way of insight (*vipassanā*) in these ten ways.
In this context, "reflecting upon the hindrances" means reflecting upon the five hindrances as things to be abandoned;

the sense is that one has discerned them. "Abiding" refers to the state of equanimity (*majjhattatā*) that arises through the absence of active effort even toward their abandonment, because one has already become oriented toward abandoning the hindrances.
"In the equanimity regarding formations" refers to the equanimity toward those things designated as hindrances, by virtue of not exerting further effort toward their abandonment.

The meaning is: "in the equanimity regarding formations. This same method applies to applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth, as well as to arising (*uppāda*) and the rest.
Therein, "arising" refers to the appearance here of the aggregates due to past kamma as a condition. "Occurrence" refers to the continued process of those [aggregates] having thus arisen.
"Sign" (*nimitta*) refers to everything belonging to the three planes of existence, because it appears as a sign.
"Accumulation" (āyūhana) refers to the karma that serves as the cause for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the future. "Rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) refers to arising in the future.

"Destination" (gati) refers to the specific realm of existence in which that rebirth-linking occurs. "Generation" (nibbatti) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates. "Arising" (upapatti) refers to the occurrence of the resultant state.
"Birth" (jāti) refers to birth conditioned by becoming, which serves as the condition for aging and so forth. Aging, death, and the rest are indeed well known.
And here, only the five beginning with arising (*uppāda*) are stated as the objects of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*);
the rest are synonyms for them. For this pair—“origination” (*nibbatti*) and “birth” (*jāti*)—is a synonym for both arising and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

This pair—“destiny” (*gati*) and “reappearance” (*upapatti*)—should be understood as referring to the process of existence (*pavatta*), while “aging” (*jarā*) and the others refer to the sign (*nimitta*). Is it not so?
And here, in the four sections on the paths, fifteen terms are stated: five root terms beginning with “arising” (uppāda) and ten synonymous terms beginning with “going” (gati);
however, in the six sections on the attainment of fruition, only the five root terms are stated.
If one asks why that is, it is because when equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) has become sharp, the path—which is capable of abandoning the defilements—[arises].
The root terms were stated together with their synonyms in order to demonstrate the sharpness of that [equanimity] by way of its actual existence;

however, it should be understood that the root terms alone were stated in order to show that even equanimity toward formations, though weak, becomes a condition for the fruit because the fruit is peaceful by nature due to its lack of exertion and because it depends upon the path.
In that context, among the four sections on the paths beginning with "for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry," one of the paths—emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—is mentioned.
However, among the four sections on the fruits beginning with "for the sake of entering the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry," the wishless attainment of the fruit is to be understood.
Why? Because [the other two] are mentioned as "for the sake of entering the dwelling of emptiness" and "for the sake of entering the dwelling of signlessness."
Because the two attainments of fruition are mentioned separately. For, by way of emerging from the contemplation of impermanence, there is the signless path;

likewise, at the time of the attainment of fruition, there is the signless attainment of fruition. By way of emerging from the contemplation of suffering, there are the wishless path and attainment of fruition.
By way of emerging from the contemplation of non-self, there are the void path and attainment of fruition.

This should be understood according to the method of the Suttas. And having done so, ten kinds of insight-wisdom consisting in equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-vipassanā-paññā*) have been mentioned:

four which serve as the cause for the arising of the path by way of the voidness (*suññatā*) and other liberations; likewise four by way of the wishless fruit-attainment (*appaṇihita-phalasamāpatti*);

and two by way of the abiding in voidness (*suññatavihāra*) and the signless abiding (*animittavihāra*). However, equanimity towards formations belonging to serenity (*samatha-saṅkhārupekkhā*) [occurs] in the process of absorption (*appanāvīthiyā*).
The knowledge consisting of development (bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa) that has reached its peak at the stage immediately preceding the path is [the equanimity of insight].

However, the equanimity termed "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" which occurs in such passages as, "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity," is called the equanimity of feeling (vedanupekkhā).

The equanimity characterized by neutrality in investigation which occurs in such passages as, "He abandons what exists, what has become; he attains equanimity," is called the equanimity of insight (vipassanupekkhā).
Therein, that which "exists" and "has come to be" is the pentad of aggregates; one abandons it by means of the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*).

"One attains equanimity" means that one attains equanimity toward the pentad of aggregates—which has the three characteristics already seen—by investigating the characteristic of formations (*saṅkhāra-lakkhaṇa*), just as one does when investigating the characteristics of a snake whose three coils have been seen.

However, that equanimity which is included among the "mere-enumeration" factors such as zeal (*chanda*) and so forth, and which serves as the cause for the simultaneous occurrence of co-nascent states, is called "equanimity as specific neutrality" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

That equanimity which is mentioned in the passage, "And he dwells in equanimity," and which produces non-partisanship even toward that supreme bliss, is called "meditative equanimity" (*jhānupekkhā*).

But that equanimity which is mentioned in the passage, "The fourth jhāna is purity of mindfulness due to equanimity," and which is purified of all opposing factors and remains inactive even while suppressing those opposing factors, is called "equanimity as purity" (*pārisuddhupekkhā*).

In this context, the sixfold equanimity, the equanimity of the divine abodes, the equanimity of the enlightenment factors, the equanimity of specific neutrality, the equanimity of jhāna, and the equanimity of purification are in meaning one and the same: the equanimity of specific neutrality.

However, this distinction arises from the difference in their respective states, just as there is a distinction for a single being according to whether he is a child, a youth, an elder, a general, a king, and so forth.

It is like a division. Therefore, it should be understood that where there is equanimity with regard to the six bases (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), there is no equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) and so forth;
or conversely, where there is equanimity as a factor of enlightenment, there is no equanimity with regard to the six bases and so forth.

And just as these [two types of equanimity] are identical in meaning, so too are equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity in insight (*vipassanupekkhā*). For they are simply wisdom (*paññā*) itself, distinguished by way of its function.

It is divided into two kinds. For example, when a man has entered his house in the evening and, searching with a staff of thorny wood, sees a snake lying in the rice-bin, he looks at it, wondering, "Is it a snake or not?
Upon seeing its three-pointed hood, he becomes free from doubt; then, while investigating whether it is a snake or not a snake, there is a state of equanimity.

In the same way, when one who has initiated insight sees the three characteristics through the knowledge of insight, the equanimity that arises during the discernment of the impermanent nature and so forth of formations is called "insight-equanimity" (*vipassanupekkhā*).
It is like that man who, having seized the snake firmly with his foot and stick, thinks: "How can I handle this snake without harming it, yet without letting it bite me?"

Just as for one who seeks only the mode of releasing with the thought "let him release," there is equanimity toward grasping, so too, the equanimity toward the grasping of formations for one who sees the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze because of having seen the three characteristics—this is equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Thus, when insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) is established, equanimity regarding formations is also necessarily established. By this, however, [it is shown that] in the processes of investigating and grasping...

They are divided into two types by way of their function, which is designated as "equanimity. Furthermore, energy-equanimity (*vīriyupekkhā*) and feeling-equanimity (*vedanupekkhā*) are distinct from one another and from the remaining [types] in terms of their actual meaning.
As for the classification of these ten kinds of equanimity according to plane, person, and so forth, it is to be understood in the same manner as explained in various other places.
Showing that it should be understood [in this way], he said: "Thus, even this tenfold [equanimity]," and so forth. Therein, "by way of plane, person, consciousness, and object" means:

by way of plane, such as "the six-factored equanimity belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)," and so on. By way of person, such as "the six-factored equanimity belongs only to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*);
the equanimity of the divine abodes belongs to all three—ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), those in training (*sekkha*), and those beyond training (*asekkha*)," and so on.

From the perspective of the person (*puggala*). From the perspective of consciousness (*citta*), as in: “The sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) is associated with a mind accompanied by joy and equanimity,” and so forth.

From the perspective of the object (*ārammaṇa*), as in: “The sixfold equanimity has six objects; the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) has mental phenomena as its object,” and so forth.

By way of the summary of the aggregates (*khandhasaṅgaha*), the single-moment wholesome triad (*ekakkhaṇakusalattika*), and the concise [classification], it is said: “Equanimity of feeling (*vedanupekkhā*) is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).”

"Those [factors] are included, while the other nine are included by the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)"—this is by way of inclusion within the aggregates. The sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*)—namely, equanimity as the divine abiding (*brahmavihāra*), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), equanimity as purity of jhāna, and equanimity as specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*)—are identical in meaning. Therefore, when one of these exists at a single moment, the others do not;

the same should be understood for equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity in insight (*vipassanupekkhā*). As for equanimity regarding feeling (*vedanupekkhā*) and equanimity regarding energy (*vīriyupekkhā*)...

"Arising in a single moment"—thus it is according to the mode of a single moment. "The six-factored equanimity is indeterminate; the equanimity of the divine abodes is both wholesome and indeterminate;
likewise the rest; but the equanimity of feeling may also be unwholesome"—thus it is according to the wholesome triad.
"In brief, these ten are only four states by way of energy, feeling, specific neutrality, and knowledge"—thus it is according to the mode of summary.
Now, having determined the characteristics and other qualities of the equanimity of jhāna intended here, he says, “But as to its characteristic, etc.
Therein, “having the flavor of non-exertion” means its function is to counteract the inclination toward even that sublime pleasure.
“Manifested as non-activity” means that although the perfection of pleasure has been attained, it stands manifesting itself by remaining unoccupied with that pleasure.
The meaning is that it presents itself there as being inactive toward the associated states.

Because its function is not manifest there—being overwhelmed by applied thought (vitakka) and other factors which bring about agitation and elation in the associated dhammas—it is said, "due to its unmanifest function," referring to the fact that the function of equanimity (tatramajjhattatā) is absent there, whereas here it is manifest. For this very reason, he says, "for it is unmanifest," and so forth.

Now, regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending," the word "is said" (*vuccati*) must be supplied. By the term "remembers" (*sarati*), it is shown that the word "mindful" (*sato*) functions as the agent.
"Clearly comprehends" (*sampajānāti*) means he understands correctly. "By way of the person" (*puggalena*) means by way of referring to the person.
It has the characteristic of remembering, thinking, and being present; thus it is "characterized by mindfulness. It is the opposite of forgetfulness.
Its function (*rasa*) is non-forgetfulness, as its duty is not to forget. It stands ready by way of guarding against defilements, or it establishes protection [against them];
thus, it has protection as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). Non-delusion is the correct understanding of things, or non-delusion is the opposite of delusion;
this is its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), thus it has non-delusion as its characteristic. Its function is investigation.

“Going to the further shore. Investigation (*pavicaya*) is inquiry (*vīmaṃsā*). Granted that, in comparison with access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) and so forth, even the first and second jhānas are subtle;

however, this [third jhāna] is described as such “because of the grossness of those lower jhānas,” and that grossness should be understood as consisting in the presence of the coarse factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*). Some say it is due to the “abundance of mental factors (*cetasika*).”
And they say: "Like a man on the ground" means that it is like a man's movement upon the ground; thus it is said.
"The movement is pleasant" means that within those jhānas, the movement is pleasant.

"The function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not manifest there" is said because there is no need to state, "This specific thing is being done with difficulty. By the abandoning of the gross factors...
As for the meaning "subtlety," this may indeed occur in the second jhāna as well;

nevertheless, because the mindfulness and wisdom here are particularly predominant in their subtlety—due to the abandoning of the gross factor known as rapture (*pīti*) while joy and bliss continue to exist mostly in a state of inseparability—it is said, "of a man," and so forth.
One who drinks from a cow is "a cow-drinker" (*dhenupaga*); [it refers to] the milk of the cow.
"Drinking" is what is meant. "He might again approach rapture" means that the jhāna could become partaking of decline;
the sense is that he might achieve the second jhāna itself. Therefore he said, "It would be associated with rapture.

And this [jhāna] is called "exceedingly sweet bliss" with reference to the bliss of the third jhāna; its exceeding sweetness is due precisely to the absence of rapture, whose nature is to be exultant and elated.
It should be understood. "This" refers to the two phrases, "mindful and clearly comprehending.

Regarding the statement, "and he experiences pleasure with the body," one might ask: how can there be an experience of pleasure without mental application (*ābhoga*)? To this he says, "Even though... and so forth.
Since that pleasure is associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*), he states this point as follows:
One should connect [the text] by saying: “He experienced pleasure with the body. This, however, is the summarized meaning here:

even though there is no such mental application (ābhoga) as “I am feeling pleasure,” one who possesses jhāna is said to experience mental pleasure through the mental aggregate (nāmakāya), and physical pleasure through the production of material form that is the cause of physical pleasure. “Of him” means of the one possessing jhāna. That which...
"Or else" means either that [pleasure] or whatever pleasure associated with the body of names (nāmakāya) has been described.

"By its origination" means: because the material body (rūpakāya) of this one possessing the jhāna is suffused by the exceedingly refined matter originating from that [pleasure], therefore it should be connected as showing this meaning.
"Of which" refers to the material body. "By being suffused" means by being pervaded. Just as...
For just as pleasure arises when a body touched by water encounters such a tangible object, so too does it arise for one whose body is touched by these forms produced by the jhāna-consciousness.
"Even when emerged from jhāna" means even when emerged from the meditative absorption.
"One would experience pleasure" refers to the contact with the remaining types of form produced by mindfulness, alongside the forms produced by consciousness.

"One might experience bodily pleasure with arisen body-consciousness. "This matter" refers to the matter consisting in the experience of mental and bodily pleasure, according to the method already stated.
"Yaṃ" is a particle used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "because. Therefore he said, "by reason of which jhāna.

With the intention that the words beginning with "they proclaim" (ācikkhanti) have the sense of praising, he said, "the intention is 'they praise'. "What? is a question regarding the manner of praising.
"Attained to the perfection of happiness" means having reached the ultimate limit of happiness. "Through attachment to happiness" means through clinging to happiness.
In such instances, full awareness (*sampajañña*) is already included by the mention of mindfulness (*sati*);

since only mindfulness is mentioned here in the text, it is stated simply as "mindful" (*satimā*) because of his established mindfulness, while "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) was mentioned previously.
Or because it has been so stated. "Unafflicted" means unafflicted because it is unmixed with defilements (*kilesa*).
At the moment of jhāna, only mental pleasure is obtained in the primary sense; thus it is said, "he experiences pleasure with the body of mind.
"The third" should be understood according to the sequence of counting as the third, following the method explained below.
The Discussion of the Third Jhāna is finished.
Regarding the Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna:
because it was stated [in the previous section] that "previously," a challenge is raised as to "when, then, does their abandoning take place? In response, he says: "Of the four..."

The connection is: "it should be understood thus. Regarding the phrase "not stated according to the order of abandoning," here "order of abandoning" refers to the sequence in which the abandoning factors arise.
If that were the order used, one would have to say, "pain, grief, pleasure, and joy"; why, then, is it stated differently? To this he says: "In the *Indriyavibhaṅga*," and so forth.
“By the order of the summary” means by the order of the summary as it occurs thus: “the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief.
Now, the connection [of the question] is: why is cessation stated only in relation to the jhānas? And where does the arisen faculty of pain occur?
The faculty of pain that has arisen through its own conditions and has not been suppressed.
When he asks, "And where does it cease without remainder?", he is asking for the place of cessation and the cause of cessation. Therefore, even though the answer to the question "Where?
is "Here," the locative case should be understood as expressing the reason (*hetu*). For the faculty of pain, which would otherwise arise, does not arise due to the sign of the power of jhāna.
It is said that "it ceases without remainder. "Exhaustive cessation" (*atisayanirodha*) is thorough abandoning;

"calming by way of the direct opposite" (*ujupaṭipakkhena vūpasama*) is mere cessation (*nirodha*), which is simply abandonment. Regarding the phrase "with different adverting": this refers to an adverting consciousness different from that adverting by which the absorption path arises, or to multiple instances of adverting.
For in the absorption path, the access concentration involves a single act of adverting, whereas the other [the mundane path] involves multiple instances of adverting, occurring many times.
Because it causes [the body] to pervade. Fatigue arising from an uneven posture is the affliction caused by an uneven seat.
"By the pervading of rapture" is said because rapture has the function of pervading, or because the sublime material qualities produced by rapture spread throughout the body. Therefore he said:
"The whole body is suffused with pleasure. Since the body touched by these sublime material qualities is one whose body is suffused with pleasure, how [could there be pain]?
Because of the affliction caused by sitting on uneven ground and so forth, which gives rise to suffering, he said, "because it is not struck down by its opposite.

As for the word *pi* (also/even) in the phrase "even with the conditions of applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārapaccaye pi*), that particle is used out of place; it should be brought forward and connected with the word "of that which has been abandoned" (*pahīnassāpi*).

And this phrase, "of the faculty of mental grief even though it has been abandoned," should be connected with the words "there might be an arising" (*siyā uppatti*). The word *etaṃ* refers to the faculty of mental grief.

This is connected with the phrase "it arises. From the statement, "As I was reflecting and examining for too long, my body grew weary and my mind became exhausted," it should be understood that weariness of body and mind has initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained examination (*vicāra*) as their conditions.
In the phrase "with the development of initial application and sustained examination," one must supply the words "the faculty of mental distress arises" and connect them here.
“*Tatthassa siyā uppatti*”: there, in the vicinity (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna, there might be the arising of that faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*), even though it has been abandoned.
And here, when some say, “By saying ‘there might be its arising,’ it is shown that even for those who have attained the jhāna, there is the arising of mental grief;
and by this, it is indicated that hatred (*dosa*), like greed (*lobha*), exists as a nature that is not itself an hindrance (*anīvaraṇa-sabhāva*).”
For mental grief does not arise without hatred; nor should any contradiction with the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi* be considered here.

This is because, in that text, the grief that arises taking a lost meditative absorption (*jhāna*) as its object is demonstrated, since it is impossible for grief to arise taking an unlost absorption as its object; thus, for those who have attained the absorptions, grief is entirely absent.
Furthermore, it is impossible to say that [depression] does not arise, because it has arisen even for one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*);
yet, it is certainly not the case that such a person has fallen away from jhāna. That [argument] is incorrect, because depression, by its very nature, is not an obstruction (*nīvaraṇa*).
If it were [an obstruction], it would arise even for beings in the fine-material and immaterial realms; however, it does not arise there. For this reason, in the immaterial realm (*ārūpa*),...
In such passages as "dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there are the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance," the hindrances of ill-will and worry are not mentioned;

yet this is not because they lack the status of being hindrances, for even sensual desire and the others are spoken of by the term "hindrance" only because they resemble hindrances despite not being actual hindrances. As for what was said...

“Because it arises even for one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṣṭasamāpatti*)”—this too is not a valid reason, because one falls away from *jhāna* due to the arising of mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
However, it should be understood that when one has fallen away due to a minor condition, those of similar character restore them to their original state with little difficulty.
The phrase “it might arise therein for him,” on the other hand, is a hypothetical statement.
This is for the purpose of showing that dissatisfaction (*domanassa*) has not yet been abandoned at the moment of access (*upacāra*). For it is said: "But certainly not within absorption (*appanā*).
If, however, dissatisfaction were to arise at that time, it should be understood that even the first jhāna would have been lost.

Although the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) has already been abandoned, it is described as being "near" because, like rapture (*pīti*), it is not far away. This refers to the stage of access characterized by different adverting (*nānāvajjana-upacāre*).
Showing that even what has been abandoned might arise again from time to time because it has not been struck down by its opposite—
a factor of abandonment— he said, "having reached absorption," and so forth. Because such repetition is desirable,
just as before the path-moment two or three rounds of impulsion proceed as similar contemplations, so too here, prior to the round of absorption—
They say that two or three rounds of impulsion occur accompanied by equanimity alone.

"He brought together" means he collected; the sense is that he spoke after having gathered [the points]. "Subtle" means subtle because they are not gross like pleasure and pain due to their lack of manifestation;
for that very reason, they are difficult to discern because their intrinsic nature must be inferred. "Of one who is corrupt" means of one whose application is corrupt.
The meaning is "of one who is difficult to tame. "It is possible to cause him to grasp" means that by way of removing other [wrong] views, it is possible to cause him to grasp;
this is the intended sense. "To the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind"—this should be understood as this very fourth jhāna.
"For the purpose of showing the condition" means for the purpose of showing the condition that serves as the means for attainment. Therefore he said: "the abandoning of suffering, etc."
“Indeed, these are its conditions. And by the phrases “the abandoning of suffering,” etc., it is the first jhāna and so forth that are intended here in a figurative sense.
They are said to be “abandoned” because it is stated: “through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana).

“These” refers to feelings such as pleasure and so forth. Pleasure is a condition for mental joy (somanassa) in the sense that it is produced by clothing, perfumes, ointments, flowers, ornaments, cosmetics, and so on.

Bodily pleasure is a condition for mental joy (*somanassa*). Because of the statement, “Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust lies latent in pleasant feeling,” he said, “Mental joy is a condition for lust.
Because of the statement, “Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in painful feeling,” it was said, “Mental grief (*domanassa*) is a condition for hatred (*dosa*).”
"By the destruction of pleasure and so forth" means by the abandoning of pleasure and so forth.

Regarding the term "neither-painful-nor-pleasant": here, "not painful" (*adukkha*) means that which is not pain; it is distant from pain. Because there is no pain therein, it is therefore said, "by the absence of pain.
The same method applies here to the term "not pleasant" (*asukha*). "By this" refers to the statement consisting of the negation of both pain and pleasure.
"Being the opposite" is stated here because the third feeling is to be attained by means of transcending suffering and so forth;
it is not because of being a direct antithesis like wholesome and unwholesome states.

"Characterized by the experience of what is contrary to the desirable and undesirable" means [the experience] of an object that is neutral, which is the opposite of the desirable and undesirable, or [the experience] of the desirable and undesirable in a neutral manner.
It has the characteristic of experiencing. For that very reason, its function is neutrality. Its manifestation is non-obvious;

unlike pleasure and pain, it does not have a manifest mode of appearance, but rather a non-obvious mode of appearance that must be inferred from them, like the path of a deer on a rocky ridge behind one's back.

Here, "cessation of pleasure" refers to the preliminary stage (upacāra) of the fourth jhāna; since this [equanimity] has that as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), it is called "having the cessation of pleasure as its proximate cause."

Regarding the phrase "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*), he says it is a compound word formed by eliding the latter member of the first term; thus, it means "the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity.

When equanimity—which is thoroughly purified of all adverse states and is not occupied with suppressing them—is present in the fourth jhāna, mindfulness is perfectly pure, just as wisdom is when it consists in the act of gladdening.
And it is said to be "very clear" because he says: "It is the purity of mindfulness; that is performed by equanimity (upekkhā) and not by anything else.

If it is the state of neutrality (tatramajjhattatā) that is intended here by the term "equanimity," how is it stated that mindfulness alone is the purity? To this he says: "Not exclusively," and so forth.
"By means of mindfulness as the head" means making mindfulness the foremost limb, or making it the primary factor.

Even so, with reference to the inquiry as to why it is said here specifically that there is "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*), the passage beginning with "In this regard, although...

was stated. Therein, although the state of neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*) exists in the three lower jhānas, there is no purity because of the overcoming of its opposites and the deficiency of its supporting conditions; likewise for those [factors] associated with it.
In order to demonstrate this meaning—that there is purity here due to the absence of those [defilements]—the passage beginning with “Just as, however” was spoken by way of a simile.
“Overpowered by the sun’s radiance” means because it is being overwhelmed by the sun’s light. Like a crescent moon that has waned, even though it is night, it possesses a gentle nature;
and since a crescent moon shines only on a night that is similar [in its gentleness], it is included within that category.
He said, "By way of his own serenity, or by way of being helpful to those who are like him, on a night [of similar character]. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The discussion of the fourth jhāna is finished.
The discussion of past lives.
12. Since even the fourfold immaterial jhāna that occurs by way of the cultivation of dispassion toward form is included within the fourth jhāna, he said, "the four jhānas.
It is indeed appropriate to speak of "the four jhānas" by way of those [factors], since one-pointedness of mind is common to all four jhānas, just as it is for the purpose of emerging from existence;
however, this is also the case for the capacity to induce insight (vipassanā) and the capacity to induce direct knowledge (abhiññā).

But since the quality of being the basis for cessation belongs exclusively to the fourth jhāna, how can it be said that this [quality] is common to all four jhānas? It is because they serve as successive bases.

For even the basis of a basis is called simply a "basis," and the cause of a cause is called simply a "cause," just as one says, "the meal was prepared by means of grass. And having established it thus:
In the exposition of the purpose, the inclusion of the eight attainments is justified. "Bases for one-pointedness of mind" means bases for the concentration of the mind;

the meaning is that they are bases for dwelling in happiness in this very life. For it is by way of one-pointedness of mind that dwelling in happiness in this very life is described, and this is stated with reference to those who have destroyed the taints through dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka). Therefore he said: "With one-pointed minds, [they dwell] happily during the day..."
“We shall dwell [here]. “Bases for the arising of existence” means bases for rebirth within the realms of existence (*bhava*).

He said, “having remained without consciousness for seven days,” because they enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for a period of seven days. But why do they enter cessation for exactly seven days?

Because they establish such a temporal limit; and that is generally because the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnaka-kappa*) of beings who subsist on nutriment cannot persist beyond that duration.

Because one who has eaten food on a single day can sustain himself for only seven days. Now, what is this so-called attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), who attains it, who does not attain it, where do they attain it, why do they attain it, and how does its attainment come about? It is said: regarding this— * **What is the attainment of cessation?** It is the temporary cessation of the mental aggregates (*nāma-khandhā*) and the cessation of the physical life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*). * **Who attains it?** Only non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants; no others. * **Where do they attain it?** Only in the fine-material sphere (*rūpa-loka*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpa-loka*), never in the sense-sphere (*kāma-loka*). * **Why do they attain it?** For the purpose of dwelling in peace for a time, and for the purpose of demonstrating that even when the mind is absent, the body can still be maintained by the force of past karma. * **How does its attainment come about?** It occurs through a specific sequence of meditative absorption. First, one enters the first jhāna and emerges; then, having emerged, one reviews the jhāna and the defilements abandoned through it. Next, one enters the second jhāna and emerges; then, having emerged, one reviews the jhāna and the defilements abandoned through it. This process continues through all four jhānas. Then, one enters the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and finally the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having emerged from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one reviews it and the defilements abandoned through it. Then, with the mind directed toward cessation, one enters the attainment of cessation. Upon emerging from the attainment, one reviews it and the defilements abandoned through it. Finally, one enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception again, and from there, one descends back through the stages of the formless attainments until reaching the first jhāna. Emerging from the first jhāna, one reviews it and the defilements abandoned through it. This is the method of attainment. Regarding the duration: it lasts for as long as the meditator intends, up to a maximum of seven days. If he intends to emerge after one day, he emerges after one day; if he intends to emerge after two days, he emerges after two days; and so on, up to seven days. Beyond that, the force of the life-faculty and the karma that maintains the body is exhausted, and he passes away. Why? Because the attainment of cessation is a state of total suspension of mental activity, and thus it cannot be sustained for longer than seven days. Once the force of the karma that maintains the body is spent, death occurs. Therefore, the maximum duration is seven days. Furthermore, it is said that the attainment of cessation is the most peaceful of all states, more peaceful than the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is itself the most peaceful of all meditative attainments.

Just as the ocean is deeper than any lake or pond, so too is the attainment of cessation more peaceful than any other attainment. It is the supreme state of tranquility, free from the turbulence of both mind and matter. It is the ultimate refuge for those seeking liberation from the suffering of conditioned existence. By attaining this state, the noble ones demonstrate that even in the absence of consciousness, the physical body can persist through the power of past volitions, thereby providing a profound demonstration of the nature of dependent origination and the continuity of karmic energy. Thus, the attainment of cessation is a unique and extraordinary phenomenon in the Buddhist path, accessible only to those who have reached the highest stages of spiritual development.
What is this so-called attainment of cessation? It is the non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors by way of successive cessation.

Who enters it and who does not? All ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*), as well as non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants who have not attained the eight attainments, do not enter it; however, non-returners who have attained the eight attainments do enter it.

And those whose taints are destroyed enter [these attainments]. Where do they enter them? In the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*). Why? Because of the presence of successive attainments (*anupubbasamāpatti*) there.
However, in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), the arising of the first jhāna and so forth does not even exist; therefore, it is impossible to enter them there. Why do they enter them?
Because, becoming weary of the diversity of the occurrence of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), they think: "In this very life..."
"Having become mindless and having attained cessation, which is Nibbāna, we shall dwell in happiness. How does its attainment come about?

For one who has exerted himself by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), performed the preliminary duties, and is bringing the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) to cessation—it is in this way that its attainment occurs for him.
For he who exerts himself solely by way of serenity attains the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"He stands having reached" means: even one who strives by means of insight alone stands having reached the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

However, one who, having striven by means of both [tranquility and insight], brings about cessation in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters that attainment. This is the summary here.
But this is the detailed explanation: here, a bhikkhu desiring to enter cessation, having entered the first jhāna...
Having emerged from that, one contemplates those formations there as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Furthermore, this insight is threefold: insight that grasps formations, insight of the attainment of fruition, and insight of the attainment of cessation.
Among these, insight that grasps formations—whether dull or sharp—is indeed the proximate cause for the Path.
Insight leading to the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti-vipassanā) is indeed suitable when it is sharp, being similar to the development of the path (maggabhāvanā).
However, insight leading to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti-vipassanā) is suitable when it is neither too dull nor too sharp;

therefore, with insight that is neither too dull nor too sharp, he contemplates those formations. Then, having entered the second jhāna... [and so on] ...then, having entered the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana).
Having emerged from that state, he likewise contemplates formations there.

Then, having entered the base of nothingness and emerged, he performs the fourfold preliminary duty: not disturbing what is bound by various ties, honoring the Saṅgha, summoning the Teacher, and delimiting the duration of the journey.
In this context, "not disturbing what is tied separately" means that whatever belongs to this bhikkhu—
whether it be his bowl and robes, a bed and chair, a dwelling place, or any other kind of requisite— that is not tied together with him but remains separate,
he should ensure that it is not disturbed and does not perish through the influence of rain, water, wind, thieves, rats, and so forth.
It should be resolved in this way. Herein, the method of resolution is as follows:
"May this and that not be consumed by fire, nor swept away by water, nor destroyed by wind, nor carried off by thieves, nor gnawed by rats and the like, within these seven days.
When it has been resolved thus, for those seven days no danger whatsoever shall befall it.
However, if it is not formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhahata*), it may be destroyed by fire and so forth; this is what is called "non-disturbance of what is bound separately.
But as for that which is bound together—whether it be the lower garment and upper robe, or a seat where one is sitting—there is no need for a separate act of resolution there;
the meditative attainment itself protects it.

"Waiting upon the Saṅgha" means waiting for or looking toward the community of bhikkhus; the meaning is that until that bhikkhu arrives, the formal act (saṅghakamma) of the Saṅgha is not to be performed. And here, "waiting" is not a preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*) for him;
rather, the preliminary duty is the mental advertence (*āvajjana*) to wait. Therefore, he should advert thus: "If, during these seven days..."
"If the Saṅgha wishes to perform any formal act, such as a *apalokana-kamma*, while I am sitting having entered cessation, I shall emerge at that very moment as soon as no monk comes to call me.
Having made this resolve and entered cessation, he indeed emerges at that time. However, for one who does not do so, if the Saṅgha...
Having assembled and not seeing him, they asked, "Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?
When it was said, "He has entered cessation," they sent a certain bhikkhu with the instruction, "Call him.
Then, as soon as that bhikkhu stood within hearing distance and said, "The Saṅgha awaits you, friend," he emerged from it. Thus it is grave.

For this is indeed called the Saṅgha’s command; therefore, having directed one's attention to it, one should attain the attainment in such a way that one emerges exactly as before. Regarding the "Teacher’s summons":

here too, the preliminary duty is precisely the directing of attention to the Teacher’s summons; therefore, that too should be directed to in this manner. The rest should be understood according to the previous method.
"Limitation of the duration" means the limitation of the life-span. By this monk, regarding the limitations of the duration...
The skillful one should reflect, "Will my life-formations continue for seven days or will they not?

and only after such reflection should he enter the attainment. For if he enters without reflecting on whether his life-formations will cease within seven days, his attainment of cessation is unable to ward off death; death occurs within that cessation.
Because there is no interval before emerging from the attainment, one must enter this [attainment] after having adverted to it.
For while it is permissible not to advert to the remaining [factors], this one must indeed be adverted to; thus it is said.
Having thus entered the base of nothingness and emerged, and having performed this preliminary duty, he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, after skipping one or two thought-moments, he becomes mindless and touches cessation (*nirodha*).
But why do thoughts no longer arise for him beyond those two moments? It is because this is the preliminary application (*payoga*) for cessation.
For this bhikkhu, having yoked together the two factors of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), this ascent through the eight attainments is the gradual cessation (*anupubbanirodha*).
The application is not for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; because it is the application for cessation, no further consciousnesses arise beyond those two.
This is because even prior to approaching the seat of enlightenment, the Bodhisatta had already produced the fourth jhāna in his final existence.
At that time, however, it had merely been produced; it was not yet a foundation for insight (vipassanā) and so forth.

Therefore, it is stated as being distinguished from that [previous state] by saying, "produced at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "A foundation for insight" means a foundation for insight at the commencement of insight.
The same principle applies here to "a foundation for direct knowledge" (abhiññā). For at the very first commencement of the Buddhas, by means of the foundational jhāna—

It served a specific purpose; it was not for the sake of attaining the higher paths, the fruition-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*), the superknowledges (*abhiññā*), or the mastery of powers (*vaḷañjana*) beyond that.
For from the moment of attaining full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), every function of knowledge and concentration is dependent upon mere wish.
"Accomplisher of all tasks" means the accomplisher of all tasks such as the successive dwellings (*anupubbavihāra*). "Bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities."

In this context, it should be understood that the fourth jhāna is the bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities upon the Blessed One precisely because it serves as the basis for insight and direct knowledge (*vipassanā-abhiññā*).
For path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) has omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and omniscience has that [path-knowledge] as its proximate cause;
this is the Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*). And at the very moment of attaining that, all the qualities of a Buddha came into the hands of the Blessed One.
And the attainment of the Path is dependent upon the fourth jhāna.
Having stated, "He entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna," because the word "he" was used, [the commentator] said, "I myself.
Regarding the phrase "thus concentrated," here the word "thus" (evaṃ) refers to the concentration of the fourth jhāna established by the sequence of the attainment of the three preceding jhānas.
"‘For the purpose of illustration’ means he said: ‘Thus: this is an illustration of the sequence of the fourth jhāna.

The meaning is that it is an illustration of both that fourth jhāna and the path by which it is attained—that is, the sequence of concentration through which the concentration of the fourth jhāna was obtained;
thus it is an illustration of both. Therefore he said: ‘By this... it is stated. In that context, by this..."
"By means of the sequence" refers to the sequence beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.

Although the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) indicates the concentration of the fourth jhāna together with the concentration of arrival, it is specifically the concentration of purity of mindfulness that is primary because it serves as the basis for psychic power;
therefore, he says, "concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna. [This refers to] that which is purified of all opposing states and defilements.
Even when equanimity toward the adverse is present and unoccupied, the fourth jhāna and the states associated with it become perfectly pure and clear;
however, because the teaching there is given under the heading of mindfulness, it says,
"purified by the state of purity of mindfulness and equanimity," meaning by the occurrence of the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity.

The meaning is as follows: The specific mode of occurrence due to a particular condition for purification itself is its state of being "brightly pure" (*pariyodāta*), just as the radiance of well-polished gold results from its being rubbed.
Therefore, it is said: "Because of its very purity, it is 'brightly pure' (*pariyodāte*); that is to say, it is 'radiant' (*pabhassare*).
By the destruction of the conditions for pleasure and so forth—namely, of pleasure and joy, and of pain and grief, respectively—...
By means of the suppression of those things conditioned by lust and hatred. It is said: "Pleasure is a condition for joy; joy is a condition for lust;
pain is a condition for grief; grief is a condition for hatred.

Just as lust and the rest are called "stains" (*aṅgaṇāni*) because they are impurities of the mind, so too they are called "defilements" (*upakkilesā*) in the sense that they defile by approaching [the mind].
He said: “And because it is without blemish (anaṅgaṇa), it is free from defilement (vigatupakkilesa). Therefore he said: “For by means of a blemish (aṅgaṇa), the mind becomes defiled”;
the meaning is that it is obstructed and afflicted. “Because it is well-developed” (subhāvitatta) means because it has been thoroughly developed by bringing it to a state of proficiency.
Therefore he said: “Having attained mastery,” through the fourteenfold or fivefold training consisting of adverting and so forth.
The meaning is: "it has come to be brought under control. For a mind that is being brought under control is called "pliant" (*mudu*);
thus, a mind being brought under control is said to be "pliant" like well-polished leather or well-prepared lac because it has attained a state of proficiency.

"Capable of work" (*kammakkhama*) means capable of performing works such as the supernormal powers of transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*). "Both of those" refers to the pair consisting of pliancy and adaptability (*kammaniya*).
In the passage beginning with *nāhaṃ*, the word *na* has the sense of negation. *Ahaṃ* is the Teacher’s designation of himself. *Bhikkhave* is his address to the monks.
*Aññaṃ* means other than the state of mind that is presently being described. *Ekadhammampi* means even a single dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

The connection is with the phrase *na samanupassāmi* (“I do not perceive”). This is the meaning here: “Monks, by means of my omniscient knowledge, I do not perceive... [the rest of the sentence follows].
Even upon examining, I do not perceive any other single thing which, through the attainment of mastery, being developed,
and through repeated practice and cultivation, becomes so exceptionally supple and wieldy due to its pliancy and fitness for action as this mind.
He says "this mind" because it is evident both to himself and to them.
Just as the aforementioned states such as purity do not disappear, so too the well-developed mind established therein is described here as "steadfast" and "having reached imperturbability.
Therefore, he said: "Because it is established in these qualities such as purity, it is steadfast;
and because it is steadfast, it has reached imperturbability. Just as softness and wieldiness are characterized by the attainment of mastery, [so too is this state].
Thus, even the attainment of mastery is characterized by softness and wieldiness;
therefore it is said: "or because they abide under one's own control due to their state of softness and wieldiness.

For just as a cause is determined by its effect, so too a cause is determined by its effect; thus, stability through immovability and the attainment of imperturbability [are indicated] among the associated states.

It is said, "Because it is embraced by faith and the other [faculties], it has reached imperturbability," because it occurs through the power of the faculties such as faith, which—by virtue of their stability and their unworkability by opposing states—are possible.
Now, in order to explain in detail this very meaning that was stated briefly, it is said, "Embraced by faith," and so forth. Therein:

"Embraced by faith" means that a mind thus well-developed and brought to mastery leads, through the power of faith as previously described, to the direct realization of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge;
it is embraced by such faith and supported by the aforementioned power of faith. "By lack of faith" means by its opposite, lack of faith (*assaddhiya*).
"By means of a cause": it does not waver, meaning it does not move or shake; rather, it stands solely by way of bringing about higher distinction.
The meaning in "sustained by energy" and so forth should be understood by this same method. However, this is the distinction:
"sustained by energy" means supported by energy that accomplishes mastery and taming. "Sustained by mindfulness" refers to what has been stated above... [text truncated]
It is supported by mindfulness which, through frequent cultivation, pursues the courses of wholesome states such as non-forgetfulness;
it is embraced by concentration, being supported by the state of composure that accomplishes non-distraction right there;
and it is embraced by wisdom, characterized by the discernment of those factors that are conducive or non-conducive to that very cultivation.
It is supported by wisdom (*paññā*). "Attained to illumination" means accompanied by the illumination of knowledge (*ñāṇobhāsa*).
For, seeing the side of defilement as it truly is through that knowledge—which has become an illumination and is augmented by the aforementioned concentration—one becomes terrified and ashamed of it;
thus one overcomes it and is not overcome by it. Therefore he said: "It is not shaken by the darkness of defilements. By this, [the mind] is encompassed by knowledge.

It demonstrates the power of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). "Endowed with eight factors" means endowed with these eight factors: being concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, pliant, wieldy, and established in imperturbability through the concentration of the fourth jhāna.
Alternatively, it means that these are the factors of a concentrated mind.

“‘Concentrated’ (samāhita): one should understand the meaning as being endowed with the eight factors already mentioned, taking ‘concentration’ not merely as a constituent factor, but rather as the attainment of stability and imperturbability separately.

‘Capable of directing’ (abhinīhārakkhama) means capable of directing [the mind] for the purpose of the various supernormal powers (iddhividhā) and so forth, and thus suitable for bringing them into manifestation.
Therefore he said: ‘of those states to be realized through direct knowledge (abhiññā)...’”
“for the realization of direct knowledge.

Granted that the attainment of the first jhāna occurs only after suppressing the hindrances, and the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth occurs only through the subsiding of applied thought and the rest;
nevertheless, those [hindrances] have not become distant from or departed from them to the same extent as they have in those [higher stages].

From the fourth jhāna onwards, its state of being utterly pure and bright is said to result from its thorough liberation from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth—which cause mental turbidity, agitation, and restlessness; thus he says, "from the hindrances... [down to] ...bright.
Regarding the phrase "of those things opposed to the attainment of jhāna," here the Elder Master Dhammapāla [interprets it as] "of those conditions for the attainment of jhāna."
Having adopted the reading, this reading—"of those things opposed to the attainment of jhāna"—is rejected.
For he [the commentator] stated: "Of those things conditioned by the attainment of jhāna" means having the attainment of jhāna as their cause, or arising in dependence upon the attainment of jhāna.
"Evil" means base. "Within the range of desire" means within the sphere of desire, or submerged by the power of desire.
“Alas, would that the Teacher might teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus by way of questioning me!”—such are the instances of conceit, deceit, hypocrisy, and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “covetousness and so forth,” those very same states are included.
Furthermore, covetousness here should be understood as that which cannot be suppressed by the first jhāna, and conceit and the rest are its concomitants, being conditions for the attainment of jhāna.
Because they are being practiced. However, those hindrances that are suppressible are included by the mention of the "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

But how is it that those which cannot be suppressed by the first *jhāna* disappear here? This is stated thus by way of the practice of effacement (*sallekha*)—according to the principle that "all wholesome states are the opposites of all unwholesome states"—in order to show the state of the *jhāna* as being non-adherent. As for those [factors] herein...

With the intention that by these words, “of covetousness and so forth belonging to the sense-sphere,” anger, resentment, sensual lust, ill will, and the like are included, they reject the reading “conditions for the attainment of jhāna” and claim the reading should be “opposites to the attainment of jhāna.
That is merely their own opinion, because such a reading does not exist at all; [the correct term is] “opposites to the attainment of jhāna.”
And because it is both the hindrances themselves and their concomitants, it would be inappropriate to speak again of their absence and disappearance after having already spoken of their removal.
But is it not the case that this meaning is found in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and the Vattha Sutta, since only gross evil states are intended there?
True, that is so; however, here [the reference is] to one who has attained the fourth jhāna.

Because they are stated by way of [their] subtlety, only those subtle ones are included here; however, the reference to the suttas is made on account of their commonality as "defilements of the limbs.
For it is said, "in accordance with the suttas," and not "by way of the suttas.
This must certainly be accepted in this way, because even for some who have attained jhāna, there is the occurrence of the sphere of desire (icchāvacara).
The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla himself, having adopted the reading "conditions for the attainment of jhāna," rejected the reading "counter-factors to the attainment of jhāna.
In both the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada* on the *Visuddhimagga*, the meaning of this very reading—"conditions for the attainment of jhāna"—is explained;
therefore, this reading alone should be accepted, and its meaning is also to be understood according to the method already stated.
It should be understood that for this reason, the reading "icchāvacarānan" (of those within the range of desire), meaning "of those who have descended into the range of desire—
that is, those occurring under the influence of desire— namely, the various kinds of causes for anger," must also be regarded as incorrect;
and for that very reason, this reading is not presented at all in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"By attaining the state of being a basis for success" means by attaining the state of being the foundation (*padaṭṭhāna*) for success.

"By the fulfillment of development" means because the development capable of bearing the directing of the will (*abhinīhāra*) is complete, owing to the absence of anything further to be done beyond this point.
"By attaining a refined state" means by having been led to a state of excellence precisely for that reason, in the sense of being supreme.
And by way of not being satisfied, through the attainment of a state of refinement. Both of these are statements of the cause for the stability of development;
that is, it is stable because of having reached a state of refinement through fully perfected development. “Reached the imperturbable” (*āneñjappatta*) is a qualification of its stability.
Therefore he said: “stable in such a way as to have reached the imperturbable. In this interpretation, [the phrase is read as] “stable, having reached the imperturbable.”
Both [of these] constitute one factor; furthermore, "being concentrated" (*samāhita*) is also one factor.
It is for this reason, with reference to its distinction from the first alternative, that it is said: "Thus, it is endowed with eight factors.
He recollects his past lives, or the recollection of those past lives is *pubbenivāsānussati*; it is that [recollection], together with its basis and other conditions...

Because it arises dependently. To elaborate upon the meaning stated in brief as "the knowledge for the purpose of recollecting past lives," he first shows the past lives and then, in order to show the mindfulness and knowledge regarding them, he says "past lives" and so forth.
In that context, the word "previously" (pubbe), based on such statements as "even one birth," is intended here to have the past existence as its object.
He said, "In past births. The word *nivāsa* (abiding) has the sense of an action-noun (*kamma-sādhana*);

and since there is no phenomenon that abides apart from the aggregates (*khandha*), he said, "the aggregates that have been inhabited" (*nivutthakkhandhā*). Here, "having been inhabited" means existing within the continuum (*santāna*);
and having become such, they have arisen and proceeded one after another, having appeared therein and then vanished—thus he said, "inhabited."
"Having been dwelt upon and experienced, they have arisen and ceased within one's own continuum.

Having thus explained the meaning of the word *nivāsa* (dwelling) by way of phenomena included within one's own continuum, he now speaks generally, saying "or phenomena that have been dwelt upon (*nivutthadhammā*) are 'dwelt upon' (*nivutthā*).

To explain this, he says "by dwelling in the range (*gocaranivāsena*)," and so forth. For even those things that constitute the range [of consciousness] are [considered "dwelt upon"] through the cultivation of that range.
When they have been cultivated, experienced by way of being made an object, and dwelt upon, they are said to be "inhabited.
These, moreover, are of two kinds because they are the domain of both one's own consciousness and the consciousness of others. To show both of these, the words beginning with "of oneself" are stated.

Therein, after saying "cognized by one's own consciousness," the statement "delimited" is used to indicate that those phenomena which are inhabited by dwelling upon their domain are not cognized by consciousness alone.
It is "merely cognized" (viññātamattā); rather, it is stated for the purpose of illustrating this meaning:

that this knowledge grasps by delimiting [the object] in exactly the same way as it was previously grasped by means of wisdom (paññā) which delimited it through specific distinctions such as name, clan, complexion, gender, food, and so forth.
Alternatively, the connection is: "even what has been cognized by another consciousness is experienced. It is not only one's own [consciousness].

The meaning is: "by consciousness," or rather, "known by the consciousness of others. Here too, the word "delimited" (*paricchinnā*) should be brought in and connected; or else, it means "delimited as being known by the consciousness of others.
And the purpose for including that [word] should be stated in the same manner as previously explained.
And because those [past lives] were indeed experienced and delimited by others in past births, and because those [beings] who experienced them have also attained final nibbāna,
one can understand their past activity by following the currently existing mental continuum of those [beings]; thus,
in order to show the past lives that have reached their culmination as the object of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), [the Buddha said:]...

It is said: “In the recollection of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth (*chinnavaṭumaka*), and so forth. Those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth are the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*);

their recollection is the “recollection of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth. Some say that by the word “and so forth,” the recollections of the Private Buddhas (*paccekabuddha*) and the disciples of the Buddha (*buddhasāvaka*) are included.
Furthermore, all those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth have attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
Because they have cut off the path of *saṃsāra*, "recollection of them" means recollection of their practice.
That practice, in brief, has the characteristic of grasping the six objects; thus, those [objects] are here included by way of grasping what was cognized by the consciousness of others.
Therefore, [this refers to] all those who have attained final Nibbāna, whose states were not cognized by one's own consciousness in previous births.
The recollection of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples should be understood as the "recollection of those whose cycle of rebirths has been severed" (*chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇa*). By the word "etc.

(*ādi*) here, however, is included the recollection—by means of one's own consciousness—of those who have not yet attained final Nibbāna in previous births, skipping over the sequence of their currently existing aggregates and proceeding by way of a "lion’s leap" (*sīhokkantika*).
These, moreover, are the aforementioned "recollection of those whose cycle of rebirths has been severed" and so forth.

These [qualities] are obtained only for Buddhas. For it is not the case that the Blessed Buddhas of the past perceived in this way, developed the path in this way, realized the fruits and Nibbāna in this way, and disciplined those to be disciplined in this way; there is no scope for the knowledge of others in this regard in any respect.
However, those things which were known by one's own consciousness in previous births [remain accessible] even when [the Buddha] has attained final Nibbāna.

Because they are bound to the aggregates, the disciples merely recollect. That mindfulness by which one recollects past lives should be brought forward and connected as "the recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*).
"I directed my mind" means that having withdrawn the mind from the object of jhāna, I sent it toward past lives;
the meaning is that I made it incline toward past lives, lean toward past lives, and tend toward past lives.

In the Pāli text, regarding the word *abhininnāmesi*, because it is an activity of a Supreme Person (*uttamapurisa*), the meaning becomes clear when the word "I" (*aham*) is supplied here for the pronoun "he" (*so*);
thus it is said, "He, I. "Of many kinds" (*anekavidham*) means manifold, by way of various realms of existence, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and so forth.
"By modes" (*pakārehi*) means together with the aspects of name, clan, and so on; and this is the instrumental case used in conjunction with the word *saha*.
"Pavattitaṃ" means set forth by way of teaching. Therefore he said "saṃvaṇṇitaṃ," which has the sense of being detailed.
"Nivāsaṃ" is a general term that includes its specific subdivisions;
showing these subdivisions by way of their desire for exposition, he said, "the continuum dwelling here and there. "Anugantvā anugantvā" means following along by way of the movement of knowledge.
"Having followed, having followed. In *anudeva*, the letter *d* has come about by way of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
Having said "he directed [his mind]," because it was stated "I recollect," the prefix *anu-* indicates a recollection that occurs immediately after the directing of the mind;
thus he said, "it shows that one recollects at the very moment the mind has been directed. The preliminary work (*parikamma*) must be stated.

"‘Siyā’ means: ‘A beginner monk who wishes to recollect his past lives, having returned from his alms round after the meal, gone into seclusion, and entered the four jhānas in succession, should emerge from the fourth jhāna—the basis for direct knowledge—and advert to his very last sitting position,’ and so forth;
thus it refers to the preliminary work for the knowledge of past lives."
The preliminary task (*pubbakaraṇa*) should be stated.
"In order to show the manner in which it was undertaken" means in order to show the classification of the past lives (*pubbenivāsa*) that have been recollected.
