"Even a single birth" (*ekampi jātiṃ*) means even a single existence (*bhava*). For that [existence] is produced by a single kamma, is delimited by its beginning and end, and contains within it a variety of constituent phenomena (*dhamma*).
The continuity of the aggregates (*khandhappabandho*) is intended here by the term “birth” (*jāti*), because it is born; thus it is called “birth. Therefore he said: “Even a single...

[the] continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*). “Declining” means wasting away or perishing. A “eon” (*kappa*) refers to an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*). In its actual sense, however, it is time;
its decline should be understood in terms of the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) occurring at that time. “Increasing”...

The term *vivaṭṭakappa* (aeon of expansion) follows the same principle here as well. However, although the "destruction" (*khaya*) of time is mentioned in such passages as, "Time consumes [all], time devours beings;

all things indeed pass away with time," that sense of destruction is not intended here, as it would lead to an undesirable consequence. *Saṃvaṭṭana* means dissolution or destruction; *saṃvaṭṭa* is the state of being dissolved.
That which remains in its state after dissolution is the *saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī* (the period of stability following dissolution). It is because these [periods] are rooted in that [process].
"Taṃpubbakattā": because it precedes that. "Vivaṭṭanaṃ" means manifestation or expansion; alternatively, "vivaṭṭo" means increase.
"Tejasā saṃvaṭṭo" means dissolution by fire; thus, "tejosaṃvaṭṭo. "Saṃvaṭṭasīmā" means the boundary of dissolution. "Saṃvaṭṭati" means it perishes. "Sadā" means at all times;
the meaning is "during all three periods of dissolution. "Ekaṃ buddhakkhettaṃ" refers here to that which is...
This was stated with a specific intention; in order to define and demonstrate that, it is said: “The Buddha-field is threefold,” and so forth.

To the extent that the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge—beginning with the knowledge of rebirth-linking—is fully manifested by its own inherent force, intensified by the fruit of merit, all of that is called the field for the production of the Buddha-sprout; thus he says, “the birth-field.”
"Extending as far as ten thousand world-systems. Regarding the phrase "its power prevails":

here, it is said because a possessor of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind, having stood anywhere within a world-system included in his sphere of authority and performed a protective chant (*paritta*) for his own sake, remains one for whom the protection has been performed even when he goes to another world-system. Alternatively, there...

When a protective chant (paritta) is recited for the benefit of all beings while standing within a single world-system (cakkavāḷa), the power of that chant must indeed be effective for all beings within the sphere of its command;

it is said that "its power prevails" because the deities there must accept the protection. Furthermore, regarding what was stated as "or as far as one might wish," this refers to the field of its objective range.
The Blessed One, intending to declare that he can both make himself known by his voice and manifest his own form at one and the same moment, said:
"Or as far as he might wish. "Wherever" means in whatever region or field of objects, infinite and immeasurable.
"Whatever he wishes, that he recollects" is because his state of being depends solely upon his mere wish.

Whatever the Buddha’s knowledge wishes to recollect, that it recollects. By the phrase "one field of authority perishes," the limit of the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*) from the horizontal direction is stated.
"Is reconstituted" (*saṇṭhahantaṃ*) means expanding (*vivaṭṭamāna*) or arising.
Its destruction and its reconstitution have been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*; therefore, we too [have explained them] previously under the term "Knower of the World."
Since this commentary on the meaning was already stated in the course of the relevant section, it is not repeated here.

Having thus explained the contraction and so forth as an incidental digression, he now says, "But these contractions and expansions that have been mentioned," etc., in order to show the manner of recollecting them as they were attained.
Therein, "among these" (*etesu*) is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*), [referring] from the whole collection of eons of contraction and expansion.

Because many eons of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*) and so forth are being extracted [from the sequence]. In the phrase "in this eon of dissolution" (*amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe*), the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as having been elided.
And by that [elision], which has the sense of non-restriction, the inclusion of the other incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) is established.
Alternatively, the phrase "in this eon of dissolution" is used because the eon of dissolution was taken from the beginning of the text.
This has been stated. For even therein, his wandering through existences (*bhava*) and so forth for some time is found.

Or, this should be understood as a demonstration of those existences (*bhava*) and so forth in which his rebirth occurred while an eon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*) was taking place. In the phrases "in an existence" (*bhave vā*) and so forth, it refers to an existence such as the sense-sphere (*kāma-bhava*) and so on;

or to a womb such as the egg-born (*aṇḍaja-yoni*) and so on; or to a destiny (*gati*) such as that of the gods (*deva*) and so on; or to a station of consciousness (*viññāṇa-ṭṭhiti*) such as "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions" and so forth.

Or in a dwelling of beings, or among the classes of beings such as the kṣatriyas. Since this knowledge of recollecting past lives has come down through the Blessed One, he spoke thus—“of such a name, whether Vessantara or Jotipāla,” and so forth—showing the meaning by way of his name and other details.
“Having rice, meat, and boiled rice as food” is said with reference to his time as a householder. “One who eats fallen fruit” [refers to his time as a forest-dweller].
"Vāti" refers to the time of ascetics and so forth. "One who eats fallen fruit" means one whose food consists of fruits that have fallen of their own accord.

Regarding the phrase "of those distinguished as with-material and without-material," here "with-material" refers to joy and so forth based on household life, while "without-material" refers to joy and so forth based on renunciation.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is an inclusion of happiness born of seclusion, happiness born of concentration, and others.
Desiring to show that same meaning already stated above by analyzing it, he says, "Or else," and so forth. Therein, "amutrāsi" is a general designation;
or it is an ellipsis for the desire for detail, meaning "amutra amutra āsi" (he was here and there).
Regarding the phrase "recollection as far as desired for one who ascends step by step," here "for one who ascends" refers to [the process] in reverse order.
"Of one ascending to past lives by means of knowledge. "Of one returning" means of one who, having gone as far as desired by way of recollecting past lives, returns again.
"Reviewing" is the reviewing of what has been recollected and what has not yet been recollected.
"Therefore" is a reference back to the reason for the meaning already stated; it refers to the state of reviewing on the part of one who is returning.
It has been said: "Arising here" means arising here in this final existence (*carimabhava*). "Immediately after" refers to the immediately preceding past.
"There" means in such-and-such an existence. "Arose" means I was born. "By those deities" means by the Tusita deities. "Of one clan" means of one clan with the Tusita clan.
This refers to the state at the conclusion of the continuum (*santāna*) of the Great Bodhisattvas.
With the intention that what is called "producing rebirth in the world of the gods" is indeed unafflicted by unwholesome karma, it was said: "But suffering is merely the suffering of formations.
However, even for sons of the gods who possess great merit, there is certainly contact with undesirable objects at times, such as when the signs of their impending death appear;
therefore, it is not the case that "there is never the occurrence of even the suffering of suffering."
It can be said that the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*) should be understood as the arising and ceasing of phenomena.

The passage beginning with "seventy-five... and ending with "...is limited" is stated according to the calculation of human years. However, there, by the calculation of celestial years, it is only four thousand.
The word "iti" is a demonstrative of the meaning already stated; and this is shown to be according to what is appropriate, not according to sequential order.
He said, “By way of name and clan,” and so forth. It is pointed out (*uddisīyati*) because, being otherwise unintelligible, when asked, “Who is this by name?
one points him out by means of his name and clan, saying, “Tissa the Gotama. “By complexion and so forth” means by way of the delimitations of complexion, nutriment, feeling, and life-span.

In the phrase “sāmoti,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning with” (*ādi-attha*) or the sense of “manner” (*pakāra-attha*). By that, it means “by such diversity as beginning with these and having such a manner.”
It has been shown. "Name and clan are the description" means that name and clan are the description because by means of them a being is described.
"The others are the modes" means that the others—the color and so forth—are the modes because by means of them a being is made known (ākārīyati) as soon as they are seen.
To explain in detail the very point that was stated briefly as "but not without distinction," he said, "For the sectarians... and so forth.
In this context, "sectarians" (*titthiya*) refers to those belonging to other sects. These are the ascetics and others who maintain the doctrine of karma and the doctrine of action.

Since, among the forty [discourses] such as the *Brahmajāla*, only the recollection of forty eons of world-contraction and expansion is mentioned for the sectarians, he says "not beyond that," and then states the reason for this by saying "because their wisdom is weak," and so forth.
This shows that application to insight (vipassanā) is the specific cause for the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).

For this very reason, it should be understood that because they possess powerful wisdom, the ordinary disciples (*pakatisāvaka*), excluding the Chief Disciples and the Great Disciples, can indeed recollect even a hundred eons or a thousand eons.
It is for this same reason that it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "The ordinary disciples [can recollect] even a hundred eons..."
"Because they possess powerful wisdom, they indeed remember even a thousand eons. For such is their aspiration (*abhinīhāra*):

the aspiration for merit and knowledge of those great disciples, the foremost disciples, and the paccekabuddhas—respectively corresponding to a hundred thousand eons, more than that, and two incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*)—is thus measured by way of time;
it is the perfection of the enlightenment of disciples and paccekabuddhas.

It is established. If the range of the supernormal knowledge (*abhiññāñāṇa*) of those various noble ones (*ariya*) were limited by the time it takes to complete the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), then in that case, even the Buddhas would fall into being limited. Therefore, he said: "But for the Buddhas, there is no limitation.
This is because of the statement, "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge," and thus [the knowledge] of the Buddhas is like the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Even for the knowledges of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), there is no such thing as a limitation regarding their own respective objects; thus, whatever they wish to know, they certainly know that very thing.

Alternatively, although there is a limitation by way of time, because the provisions for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-sambhāra*) are preeminent through the mastery of causes, skillful means, and so forth, there is indeed no limitation to the power of the manifestation of the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramitā*).
Since there is no such thing, how could there be the super-knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) that arises from it? Therefore, he said: "But for the Buddhas, there is no limitation.
In the past, there is no limitation of time such as "this many incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa)," just as there is none for the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) regarding the future.
Hence he said: "As far as they wish, so far do they recollect."
Having thus shown the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussaraṇa*) of the five types of persons by way of the division of time, he now says, "And the sectarians...
and so forth, in order to show the specific mode of its occurrence by way of grasping the object.

Regarding the phrase "they remember the succession of aggregates (*khandhapaṭipāṭi*)," here "succession of aggregates" means the sequence of the aggregates; and that indeed occurs by way of reverse order, starting from the moment of death (*cuti*).
However, some here say that "the sequence of the postures is the sequence of the aggregates.
To clarify this very point through its opposite, he said, "setting aside the sequence," and so forth.

In that context, "by way of death and rebirth-linking" means: having observed the death of oneself or another in this or that state of existence, one grasps the rebirth-linking itself without touching upon anything in between.
Just as blind people walk without letting go of their staff, so too do they recollect without letting go of the sequence of the aggregates;

thus he said, "For them, like the blind, there is no reaching their desired destination. The term "disciples" (sāvaka) is stated in its general sense, including both ordinary disciples, great disciples, and chief disciples.
For even ordinary disciples [recollect] by means of the sequence of the aggregates.
They recollect them; they also transmigrate by way of death and rebirth-linking due to their powerful manifestation, as do the eighty great disciples.
However, for the two chief disciples, there is no function of the sequential succession of aggregates.

Having seen the death of one individual existence, they see the rebirth-linking; then, having again seen the death of another, they see the rebirth-linking—in this way, even by way of death and rebirth-linking.

They go by passing through. This is a world-established fact: just as, for example, at the time of midday during the autumn season, the various forms within a four-walled house are perfectly manifest to a man with sight.
However, while there might be a lack of range for him regarding those forms that are more subtle or obstructed by walls and such, this is certainly not the case for the Buddhas in knowing them.

The knowable object that is desired does not fall outside their range; rather, illuminated by the light of their knowledge, it becomes perfectly clear and distinct, like an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand.
Thus, because the veil over the knowable has been thoroughly abandoned, he says, "But the Buddhas," and so forth.
In this context, "by way of the lion’s stride" means by way of the lion’s gait and movement. "Whatever place they desire" means in whatever location...
In whatever aeon, in whatever existence, and whatever place they wish to know, they remember all of it;
indeed, they remember everything they wish to know, and do not fail to remember.

For Buddhas, there is no function of following the sequence of the aggregates (*khandha*), nor is there any function of transferring by way of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*). For them, [the knowledge extends] back through many millions of aeons.
Or whether above or below, whatever place they desire becomes clearly manifest.
Therefore, just as those reciting a passage consisting of a formulaic repetition (peyyāla-pāḷi) abbreviate and rehearse by taking only the beginning and the conclusion—such as "the first jhāna...
[pe] ...the fifth jhāna"—and not word by word, so too, even many millions of eons are abbreviated like a formulaic repetition.
Whatever they desire, entering by means of knowledge right there and then, they proceed in the manner of a lion’s descent.
And for those proceeding in this way, their knowledge— just like an arrow shot by a master archer such as Sarabhaṅga who has practiced the art of piercing a hair—
is not obstructed by trees, creepers, or other obstacles along the way, but falls precisely upon the target.
It does not cling and it does not become dispassionate; thus, throughout successive births, it neither clings nor becomes dispassionate.
Not clinging and not becoming dispassionate, it takes up exactly whatever place it desires.
The aggregates in past existences, along with the names and clans associated with them—all these are included within "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*).
He said: "What does it know? It knows former abodes. Because delusion (moha) is like darkness (tama) in the sense of concealing, he said: "That very delusion," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of producing illumination" (*obhāsakaraṇaṭṭhena*): it is called "producing" (*karaṇa*) because it is to be produced;

"illumination-producing" (*obhāsakaraṇa*) means that illumination itself is the production, in the sense of being produced as the state of illumination by its own conditions. The remainder is words of praise.
This is stated because it makes known the specific modes of activity that dispel their opposites.
Regarding the phrase "ignorance is destroyed," it should be understood that by this, the meaning of "knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of "discerning" (*vijānana*) is also illuminated. Why?

Because by the statement "knowledge has arisen," it shows that ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, and demonstrates that its status as an opposite consists in its being something to be abandoned, while knowledge is that which abandons it.
This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. By this, darkness is dispelled and destroyed. Why? Because it refers by extension to the meaning: "because light has arisen.
In the sense of burning and tormenting the defilements (*kilesa*), energy (*vīriya*) is called "heat" (*ātāpa*); thus he says, "ardent through the heat of energy," which means "possessing energy.
"Of one whose mind is directed" means of one whose mind is applied toward the accomplishment of the intended goal.
The phrase "as one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute" implies that this applies to anyone else like himself.
"Devoted to striving" means being intent upon the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*). The rest here is easy to understand because it is both plain and follows the method already stated.
The Discourse on Past Lives is concluded.

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye (Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathā). 13. "In death" (*cutiyā*) means in the process of passing away (*cavane*). "In rebirth" (*upapāte*) means in the process of arising (*upapajjane*). This locative case is used here in the sense of proximity; what is meant is:
"in the vicinity of the moment of death" and "in the vicinity of the moment of rebirth. For thus he will say later: "But those who are near to death," and so forth.
"By which knowledge" means by which knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). For it is precisely by the knowledge of the divine eye that the passing away and rebirth of beings is known.

"The preliminary work should be stated" means: "A clansman who is a beginner and desires to produce the knowledge of the divine eye must, in every respect, make the jhāna based on a kasiṇa object—the foundation for direct knowledge—capable of being directed toward the higher knowledges."
"Among these three kasiṇas—the fire kasiṇa, the white kasiṇa, and the light kasiṇa—one should make one of them proximate;
having made it the object of access concentration, one should expand it and establish it. In such ways, the preliminary work for the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) should be stated.

"I am he" means "I am that person who has performed the mental resolve. "Because of its similarity to the divine" means: that which exists in the heavens (*divi*) is "divine" (*dibba*); [it belongs] to the gods...

“Eye of clarity” (*pasādacakkhu*); the meaning is that it is similar to that divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). The phrase “resembling the divine” is an illustration by way of a lower comparison, because this [eye] possesses even greater power than the divine eye of the deities.
Now, in order to clarify that resemblance to the divine, the passage beginning with “For the deities...
is stated. Therein, “produced by well-performed kamma” refers to the excellence of having abundant faith, purified vision, seeing the benefits [of virtue], and so forth.
It is produced by well-performed conduct (*sucarita*), that is, by meritorious action (*puñña-kamma*) which generates rebirth among the devas.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "bile, phlegm, blood, etc.," diseases such as those caused by wind (*vāta*) are included. "Unobstructed" (*apalibuddha*) means unafflicted.

Because it is unafflicted by bile and the like, and because of the loftiness of the karma, its freedom from defilements (*upakkilesa-vimutti*) should be understood; for karma is indeed free from the faults of defilements.
Just as a crop free from weeds and other defects becomes an abundant fruit that is unsullied, so too this [eye] is described by way of its cause as "pure" or "having a pure result" (*sukka-vipāka*).

By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even at a distance," it is included that the eye is capable of receiving even a subtle object. "The physical eye" (*pasāda-cakkhu*) refers to the four great elements...

The eye has the characteristic of clarity (*pasāda*). "Produced by the power of the development of energy" means that because all wholesome development succeeds precisely through the exertion of energy, all wholesome development is the development of energy; or, specifically, the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) endowed with the formations of striving is the development of energy.
That which is produced by the influence of this is "produced by the power of the development of energy. It consists of knowledge (*ñāṇamaya*).

The eye is the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*). "Just like that" means it is similar to that [divine eye] because of its freedom from defilements and its capacity to receive objects even when they are distant or subtle.
It is said to be "attained by way of the divine abode" (*dibbavihāra*) because it is attained through the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) known as the divine abodes.
Because it has been attained. By this reason, he states its divine nature (*dibba*). "Because it is dependent on a divine abode" means:
because it proceeds by depending on the divine abode known as the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), which has reached its highest excellence through the possession of the eight factors;
or, because it is dependent on the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna—which is included within the divine abodes, associated with itself, and serves as its condition.
The meaning here should be understood in this way: they are called *dibba* (divine) because they possess great radiance (*mahājutika*) through the grasping of light;
because they are to be attained through the assistance of the light of the *kasiṇa*; and because they themselves possess the quality of pervading the light of knowledge.

Indeed, even that which possesses great radiance is called *dibba*, as in such expressions as "this celestial (*dibba*) mansion. They are called *dibba* because they have a great course (*mahāgati*), that is, because their movement is worthy of honor (*mahanīya*).
The meaning is "one whose activity is wonderful. Indeed, his activity is wonderful because of his seeing forms situated beyond walls and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "all that," they say it is stated with reference to the fivefold meaning mentioned above.

However, some maintain that since grammarians accept the root *div* in the senses of "splendor" (*juti*) and "motion" (*gati*), [the terms] mean "one of great splendor" (*mahājutika*) and "one of great motion" (*mahāgatika*).
It is with reference to these two points that it was said. Therefore, they say that the statement "it should be understood according to the science of grammar" was spoken to show this meaning:
"It is called *dibba* because it shines (*dibbati*) and illuminates; it is called *dibba* because it moves (*gacchati*) and proceeds unhindered.
However, the Elder Master Dhammapāla says:
“The preparation made by a yogin for the attainment of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) is, in its true sense, called ‘the desire for victory over its opposites.

Furthermore, one who possesses the divine eye and supernormal power (iddhimā) may engage in worldly transactions characterized by giving and receiving—such as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and others did—by way of receiving the speech of deities and bestowing the Dhamma.
Thus, [these qualities] are comprised of what is known as the desire for victory in abiding, eloquence in transaction, and proficiency in movement.”
"Because this knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) is established as the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) by way of its meaning,

and since those who are experts in grammar also accept the word *divu* in those very senses, it was said: 'All that should be understood according to the science of grammar (saddasattha).'"— Thus he spoke.
“In the sense of seeing” means by way of the state of seeing visible forms. For it is with the eye that beings see visible forms.
Just as the physical eye, when presided over by consciousness, functions as if pointing out what is even or uneven, this [mental eye] does not function in that same way.
Rather, it performs the function of the eye even more excellently than that; thus he said, “It is like the eye because it performs the function of the eye.”
“‘The eye’: in order to explain the meaning stated in brief—that it is for the sake of purification of view—the passage beginning with ‘For he who’ was spoken.
He grasps the annihilationist view because, not seeing rebirth from another [existence], he grasps the annihilationist view, thinking:
‘Right here this being is annihilated; so it is with others as well. He grasps the view of the manifestation of a new being because of his attainment of jhāna.”
He grasps [the view] like one who holds to fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannika*).

For instance, having passed away from the realm of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) and been reborn here, he goes forth into homelessness and, having attained supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*), recollects his past lives;
yet, seeing only this present rebirth and being unable to recollect any birth beyond it in the non-percipient realm, he thinks: "I am of fortuitous origin; I did not exist before."
“Having not existed, I have now become a being; other beings too are just like me”—thus one adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings.
In the same way, this [person] too, seeing only the descent into a womb and failing to see the passing away, adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings.
Now, showing another reason for purification, he says: “Or because of being free from the eleven defilements,” and so forth.
“Yathāha” indicates the textual passage found in the *Upakkilesa Sutta*.

For there, having addressed these three sons of good family—Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimila—and wishing to show them the Dhamma, [the Blessed One said]: “Anuruddhas, why would you not be disturbed by these?
Even I was formerly disturbed by these eleven defilements (*upakkilesa*), including clinging (*upādāna*). Thus he showed it.
“Anuruddha, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, I perceived light and saw forms;
however, that light of mine soon disappeared, as did the vision of forms.
Then, Anuruddha, this thought occurred to me: ‘What now is the cause, what is the condition, for the disappearance of my light…’”
‘...and the vision of forms disappears. Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me: ‘Doubt has arisen in me;
because of that doubt, my concentration has lapsed; when concentration has lapsed, the radiance has disappeared and the vision of forms has vanished.
I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again.’”
“Thus, Anuruddha, while dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived both light and forms.
Yet before long, that light of mine vanished, as did the vision of forms.
Then, Anuruddha, this thought occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my light has vanished?’”
"And the vision of forms. Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me: "Non-attention has arisen in me, and because of that non-attention, my concentration has lapsed;
when concentration has lapsed, the radiance and the vision of forms have disappeared.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again."
Having begun the teaching with the words, "It is not non-attention," this was said: "Then I, Anuruddha, having understood that doubt is a defilement of the mind," and so forth.
In that context, "doubt" refers to the Great Being’s various kinds of forms [seen] after he had increased his light and [beheld them] with the divine eye.
Doubt arises in one passing by, thinking, "What indeed is this? However, forms appeared to me through the power of attention;
while seeing forms, doubt arose. Therefore, thinking, "Now I shall not attend to anything," he becomes silent.
It is with reference to this attainment of silence that it is said: "non-attention. As for "sloth and torpor" (*thina-middha*), something...

For one who does not attend [to the object], sloth and torpor arise; for in such a state, because of the absence of expansive attention, sloth and torpor arise. As for "trembling": having dispelled sloth and torpor, by means of the attention as it was undertaken, one extends light toward the Himalayas;
while looking at the generous ogres, cannibal demons, pythons, and so forth, trembling arises.

*Chambhitattaṃ*: trembling. *Uppilāvitattaṃ*: elation; this is the state of elation that arises for one who dispels fear by thinking, "The danger I saw was not perceived when looked at with the natural visual consciousness; what kind of danger is there in something imagined regarding what was not seen?
It is based on one's own skill in self-reflection. *Duṭṭhullaṃ*: bodily sloth.
“‘I exerted intense energy for the purpose of calming sloth and torpor and agitation;
because of that, a powerful rapture—characterized by elation, detrimental to mental concentration, and worldly in nature—arose in me,’ [he thought].
As he relaxed his energy, coarseness of body, bodily distress, and bodily lethargy arose.”
*Accāraddhavīriyaṃ* (excessive energy) arises when one, thinking "defilement arose because my energy was lax," again exerts energy.

*Atilīnavīriyaṃ* (excessively slack energy) arises when one, thinking "this occurred because I exerted energy," again relaxes the energy. *Abhijappā* (longing) is directed toward the world of the gods.

Craving arises as he beholds the assembly of gods after increasing his light. It is called *abhijappā* because it yearns (*jappati*) by way of adhering with the thought, “May it be so for me”; thus, it is craving.
Regarding “perceptions of diversity”: [he thinks], “While I was attending to a single type of form, craving arose;
now I shall attend to forms of various kinds,” and at times he turns his face toward the world of the gods.
When, at the appropriate time, he increases [his attention] toward the world of humans and attends to various kinds of forms, there arises "perception of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*).
It is called "perception of diversity" because it is a perception of what is diverse, that is, of various natures. Regarding the phrase "due to excessive contemplation":
"As I was attending to various kinds of forms, a perception of diversity arose; whether desirable or undesirable, it was of one and the same kind."
"Thinking, 'I shall attend to form,' for one who attends in that way, there arises an excessive contemplation of forms;
*atinijjhāyitattaṃ* is the act of looking upon them with excessive, further contemplation. 'They appear' means the light arisen from the preliminary work (*parikamma*).
'And I do not see forms' refers to being intent on attending to the light of the preliminary work by means of the divine eye."

"I do not see forms; indeed, I do see forms. Having pervaded the place where he stands with that light of preliminary work (*parikamma-obhāsa*), he sees the various forms that have become the objective range of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—
“Anuruddha, for the whole night, for the whole day, and for the whole day and night, this thought occurred to me:
‘What now is the cause, what is the condition, why it is that I perceive light but do not see forms,
while I see forms but do not perceive light— for the whole night, for the whole day, and for the whole day and night?’”
"By day and night. Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:

"At whatever time I do not attend to the sign of forms but attend to the sign of light, at that time I perceive light but do not see forms. But at whatever time I do not attend to the sign of light [but attend to the sign of forms]..."
"I attend to it thus: 'Indeed, at that time I see forms, yet I do not perceive light—whether for the whole night, or for the whole day, or for the whole day and night.
This includes such passages from the Canon as these.
“Human” (*mānusaka*) means belonging to humans; it refers to a visible object that has become the range of human experience.

It is called “beyond the human” (*atikkantamānusaka*) because it is seen as a form distinct from others—such as those of the divine, the invisible, or the subtle. Such a form is said to have “transcended the human sphere”; thus he says: “by seeing forms after having transcended the human sphere.”
In this context, "within the range of humans" (*manussūpacāra*) means a place frequented by humans; the intended meaning is an object that can be grasped by the eye-door in its natural state.
Having thus shown it by way of the object (*visaya*), he now says "or human" (*mānusakaṃ vā*) and so forth, in order to show it by way of the subject (*visayin*).
Even there, the surpassing of the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) should be understood as occurring precisely through the surpassing of its function. By means of the divine...
"By the eye": even by means of the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa), it is impossible to see certain forms because of the extreme brevity and extreme subtlety of the moment.
Furthermore, the object of the divine eye is a present form, and that [object] must exist as a pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya);
moreover, there is no occurrence of a sublime state (mahaggata) without the preliminary work of adverting (āvajjana), nor does a form arise while it is actually in the process of arising.

It is capable of being an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) whether it is existing or in the process of dissolving; therefore, it is well said that one cannot see matter at the moments of death and rebirth with the divine eye.
If the knowledge of the divine eye has only matter as its object, then why is it said, "I see beings"? Because for the most part...

This was said because of seeing the form belonging to the continuum of a sentient being (*sattasantānagatarūpa*). Alternatively, they say it was spoken by way of conventional designation (*vohāra*) because of its being the cause for the apprehension of a "sentient being.
The connection is: "those who are passing away" are what is intended. "Of such a kind" means those who do not possess the moments of death and rebirth.
He said, "because it is associated with the outflow of delusion (*mohanissanda*)," meaning that karma which has delusion as its decisive support (*upanissaya*) is inferior and yields inferior fruit.
And the state of being a decisive support through delusion (mohūpanissayatā) is to be understood from the abundance of the occurrence of delusion prior to a wholesome deed (*kusalakamma*).

Since a wholesome deed defiled by such an occurrence of delusion produces only inferior birth and so forth, inferior birth and the rest are said to be the outflow-results (*nissandaphala*) of delusion; thus he says, "of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so forth. "Hīḷita" means censured.
"Despised" (*ohīḷita*) means especially censured. "Contempted" (*uññāta*) means known for its lowliness. "Disregarded" (*avaññāta*) means specifically understood as being base.
"Because it is associated with the outflow of non-delusion" (*amoha-nissandayuttattā*): here, non-delusion is described as occurring both by way of association and by way of the preceding stage;
and by this, he indicates [the state] in one possessing a three-rooted rebirth-linking (*tihetuka-paṭisandhika*). "Its opposite" (*tabbiparīta*) refers to that state of being despised and so forth.

"In the opposite case" means when it is not despised, not reviled, approved, and not disregarded; that is, it is honored. "Beautiful" means having a lovely color. "Ugly" means having an unlovely color.
Now, this quality of being beautiful or ugly occurs respectively because of the presence or absence of non-hatred (*adosa*) as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for karma;
thus he said, "Because it is associated with the outflow (*nissanda*) of non-hatred," and so forth. [This refers to] the state of having non-hatred as its decisive support.
And this should be understood as occurring through the activity of a mental continuum permeated by loving-kindness (*mettā*) and other such qualities.

"The beautiful as ugly" is stated here by way of shape (*saṇṭhāna*). For the word *vaṇṇa* (color/appearance) can also mean shape, as in such passages as "having manifested a large elephant-appearance.
However, the meaning stated first was expressed specifically by way of color. "Beautiful" (*sundaraṃ*).
"Those who have gone to a good destination (gati) are 'well-gone' (sugata)," he said; the meaning is "reborn in a happy destination.
Sentient beings whose disposition is free from greed, who are generous and devoid of stinginess, become well-gone and prosperous through karma supported by non-greed;

thus he said, "or because they are endowed with the outflow of non-greed, they are wealthy and possess great riches. Those who have gone to a miserable destination are "ill-gone" (duggata); thus he said.
“*Duggatigate*”: Beings whose disposition is dominated by greed are greedy and stingy;

because of their karma based on greed, they become wretched and deformed. Thus it is said: “Or, because of being joined with the outflow of greed, [they are born] among the poor, where food and drink are scarce.

*Upacitaṃ* means performed in such a way that it brings about a fruit. For when an action is performed in a manner that makes it capable of yielding a fruit, it is thus performed as *upacitaṃ*. By the words “*cavamāne*,” etc.,...
The function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) has been described; this refers to the activity of the possessor of the eye by way of its object.
The phrase "by the former ones" is said with reference to the words beginning with "with the divine eye. Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādīhi*), the particle *ca* is elided;

therefore, the meaning is that the function of the divine eye is described by these [words] beginning with "with the divine eye... I see," as well as by those beginning with "passing away. By this, however—
"By the phrase" means by this sentence: "I understand beings according to their karma. For a "phrase" (*pada*) is a sentence (*vākya*), since meaning is traversed or understood by means of it.

Regarding the expression "experiencing great suffering," it should be understood that after seeing the form with the knowledge of the divine eye, one knows their experience of suffering by means of a sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*) alone. "He" refers to one who stands having seen the beings in hell directly before him.
One who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye attends to it in this way:

having entered the foundational jhāna out of a desire to know the karma that leads those hell-beings to hell, and having emerged from it, he attends to it by means of the preliminary work (*parikamma*).
The passage beginning with "What indeed... shows the method of attending. Having thus performed the preliminary work, [he enters] the foundational jhāna.
For one who has emerged from that attainment, adverting consciousness arises taking that [attainment] as its object. When that has ceased, four or five impulsion moments (javana) arise.
Of these, the first three or four—named preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū)—belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The fourth or fifth is the absorption consciousness (appanā-citta) belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and associated with the fourth jhāna. Therein:
The knowledge that arises together with that attainment-consciousness (appanā-citta) should be understood as the knowledge of the passing away according to karma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa).

As for the statement, "There is no separate preliminary work," this is said with the intention that there is no separate preliminary work for the knowledge of the passing away according to karma apart from the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa). And this must be accepted; otherwise, [the status] of the knowledge of the passing away according to karma...
There would simply be no state of loftiness (mahaggatabhāva). This same principle applies even to the seeing of devas.

Here, the mention of hell-beings and devas should be regarded as merely illustrative; for one who has attained the divine eye and so desires may proceed in this very manner toward those belonging to other destinies as well.
For he will say: "By the mention of the states of misery, he indicates the animal realm," and so forth, and "by the mention of the happy destiny..."
And it is said: “The human realm is also included. That karma which leads to hell is its object; thus, it is “having that karma as its object.
Regarding the phrase “in the Phārusaka forest, etc.,” the word “etc. includes the Cittalatāvana forest and others.
And just as for this [knowledge], there is no separate preliminary exercise (parikamma) for the knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), so too...

This also demonstrates that there is no separate preliminary stage for the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*). Regarding this, he states the reason: "For these two have the divine eye as their basis.

The intention here is as follows: just as one who has attained the divine eye increases light directed toward the hells and so forth, and having seen beings such as those in hell, perceives the karma conducive to rebirth in hell and so on that was previously accumulated by them.
When the mind has been refined by such an undertaking and by the corresponding attention, he knows it as it truly is; thus,
whenever he desires to know the future personal existence immediately following that of any particular being, he directs his light toward that specific being and,
by means of the knowledge of the destination according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), [he perceives] the karma accumulated in the past or in the present that brings about its rebirth.

Having seen this, one who desires to know the future personal existence that is to be produced in various ways understands it as it truly is when the mind has been refined by such a undertaking and by the corresponding attention. This same method applies to subsequent personal existences as well.
This is called the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa). Since these two [knowledges] are accomplished only when the divine eye-knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) exists, and not when it is absent.
Therefore it was said: "These succeed together with the divine eye.
Regarding "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*): it is misconduct committed by the body, or misconduct arising from the body;

thus, it is "badly conducted" (*duṭṭhu caritaṃ*) by means of the body, or it is "badly conducted" because it arises from the body due to its being rotten with defilements (*kilesapūtikattā*). It should be applied in this way according to the respective order.
And here, by "body" (*kāya*), the body of nutriment (*copana-kāya*) is intended. Unwholesome bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is that which proceeds by way of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*);

it is bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*). Since the continuity (*santāna*) in which an action has been performed and accumulated does not lose its nature of being subject to ripening (*vipāka*)—provided there is no interruption of nutriment—it must be said that this continuity is indeed accompanied by that [action].
Thus he says: "Possessed (*samannāgatā*) means having become endowed (*samaṅgībhūtā*)."

"Having become those who desire what is harmful" means that, unlike mothers and fathers toward their children, or teachers and preceptors toward their dependents, they do not become well-wishers, but rather become reproachers and slanderers.

"By the destruction of virtues" means by the demolition and ruin of existing virtues; this is the meaning. But is it not the case that even through the final ground (the charge of a pārājika offense), the slander is indeed the destruction of virtues?
This is true; however, in this context, "virtues" (guṇā) refers specifically to the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and so forth.
Therefore, the destruction of virtue (sīlaparidhaṃsana) is mentioned separately. For this reason, he said: "There is no ascetic practice (samaṇadhamma) for these," and so on.
By "ascetic practice," he means moral restraint (sīlasaṃyama). "Knowing" (jānaṃ vā) means knowing the noble state (ariyabhāva) of the one whom he reviles. Or "not knowing" (ajānaṃ vā).

Or perhaps not knowing. In this context, whether one knows or does not know is irrelevant; the state of being noble (ariyabhāva) alone is the criterion. Therefore he said: "In either case, it is indeed a slander against the noble ones. However, they say:

"But for one who does not know that [the person] is noble, and who proclaims the presence of noble qualities there with a mind free from ill will, there is no destruction of those qualities; thus, for him, there is no slander against the noble ones. This is grave.
"Kamma" refers to a grave deed because it resembles an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense; however, it is curable through confession, unlike an *ānantariya*, which is incurable.
"And for the purpose of making that manifest" means for the sake of explaining its nature as being grave and so forth. "He felt disgust for that" means he felt disgust for that elder.
Or he loathed that action. "Aticchāto" means one who is excessively overcome by hunger.

"Mahallako" should be understood as censuring him through the destruction of his virtues, on the grounds that he does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate for ascetics, or even the mere conventional conduct of the world.
"He did what is shameful for us" means, "Such a thing was done by one who calls himself an ascetic."
The intention was: "Having said this, we are unable to lift our heads.

Knowing [the truth] all along, the Elder asked, "Friend, do you have a firm footing in this Dispensation? The other replied, "I am a stream-enterer," meaning that the realization of the Truths constitutes a firm footing in the Dispensation.
Out of compassion for him, the Elder [said], "An arahant whose taints are destroyed has been slandered by you," and [revealed] himself...
"He made it manifest. "By that, his [kamma] became natural" means the intention is that by that [act], his kamma did not become an obstruction to the Path.

However, because he was already a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and had completely abandoned those states leading to the woeful planes (*apāya*), that kamma was simply incapable of acting as an obstruction to heaven for him.
Regarding the phrase "one who is older than oneself," here [it refers to one who has] "sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture..."
"He should ask for forgiveness," as stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. Stream-enterers and once-returners do not forgive even out of malice;
nor would other noble ones, though desiring his welfare, fail to ask for forgiveness for the sake of future restraint. Therefore, he says, "if he does not forgive.
If he is senior to oneself, one should remain standing; here too, it should be understood that "one should sit in the kneeling posture (*ukkuṭika*)."
It is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. For it is said there:
"If he has gone away to another region, he should ask for forgiveness either by going himself or by sending a co-resident (*saddhivihārika*).
If he is unable neither to go nor to send anyone, then [he should ask] those monks who are living in that monastery."
Having gone into his presence, if he is junior, one should sit in the *ukkhuṭika* posture;
if he is senior, one should proceed according to the method prescribed for elders, saying: "Venerable sir, I said such-and-such to the Venerable [Name];
may that Venerable one forgive me," and thus ask for forgiveness. Even if he does not forgive him in person, this very same procedure must be performed.
Furthermore, this is also said there:
"If he is a monk wandering alone, neither his place of residence nor his destination is known;
he should go into the presence of a wise monk and say: 'Venerable sir, I am such-and-such a person, and I have [seen] this venerable one do this and that...'"
“I said [this], and as I remember it again and again, remorse arises; what should I do? This is what should be said.
He will reply, “Do not worry; the Elder forgives you; let your mind be pacified.
Then, facing the direction where the Noble One has gone, one should raise one’s joined palms and say, “May he forgive me.”
"Parinibbutamañcaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to the place where an act of worship is performed. Regarding the phrase "it becomes as it was before," some say that the intention is this:
when one has done such a deed, one's own mind gains confidence, and thus that action does not become an obstruction to heaven (*saggāvaraṇa*) nor an obstruction to the Path (*maggāvaraṇa*).
This is stated in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, in the commentary on the *Mātaṅgacarita*.
“Against the Great Being— whose mental continuum was well-composed through the perfection of virtue and view,
which had been brought to success by the cultivation of the perfections and fulfilled by dwelling in various meditative attainments; who was suffused with great compassion—

the harsh speech consisting of the curse known as ‘insulting the Noble Ones’ was [only] seen to be experienced in this very life, because of the Great Being’s status as a distinguished field and because of the speaker’s own harsh disposition.”
"If he had not asked forgiveness from the Great Being after making the offering, it would have become ripe for fruition on the seventh day.

But because the Great Being was asked for forgiveness, the result was warded off by the excellence of that act; thus it reached a state of non-fruition due to its becoming a 'lapsed karma' (*ahosikamma*).
For this is the natural law regarding both the evil of reviling the Noble Ones and [karma] to be experienced in the present life."
Since it was spoken by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, when that deed was thus forgiven, its ripening was warded off by the perfection of the performance [of the act of forgiveness];

consequently, it attained the state of being a "deed that has become past" (*ahosikamma*) and reached the condition of being non-ripenable. Thus, it should be understood here that it becomes neither an obstruction to heaven nor an obstruction to liberation.
"Those whose view is perverted are 'those of perverted view' (*viparītadassanā*). In the sense of being undertaken, they are 'undertakings' (*samādāna*);

those for whom there are undertakings of action are 'those who have undertaken actions' (*kammasamādānā*). By way of wrong view, they are 'those who have undertaken actions of wrong view' (*micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā*).

Alternatively, taking the word 'by way of' (*vasena*) as having the sense of cause, they are 'those who, by way of wrong view, cause others to undertake actions,' thus they are 'those who have undertaken actions of wrong view.'"
Demonstrating this meaning, he said, "By way of wrong view," and so forth. The phrase "those who...

and incite others" should also be construed as "undertakers of the kamma of wrong view. The passage beginning with "one endowed with virtue" is stated with reference to one who possesses the Path and whose faculties are matured;
however, in the case of one standing in the highest path (the Arahant), there is simply nothing further to be said. Alternatively, it refers to those included within the highest path.
In this same way, virtue and the other factors are to be understood. For one who stands in the highest path, the attainment of the goal (*aññārādhanā*) is certain in this very life;
for others, it is not certain. "The goal" (*añña*) here refers to Arahatship. Regarding the phrase "in this very manner" (*evaṃsampadamidam*): here, *sampadā* means "accomplishment" or "fulfillment";
thus the meaning is "an accomplishment that does not fail in this way. Just as that [attainment] is inevitably destined to occur, so too is this.

This has been stated. For just as the fruit arises immediately after the path without any interval, so too it shows that for this person, rebirth-linking occurs in hell immediately after death without any interval.
Indeed, throughout the entire word of the Buddha, there is no simile stated with greater force than this one. Regarding the phrases beginning with "without abandoning that speech," etc.:
With reference to reviling the noble ones, one is said to abandon speech when saying, "I will not speak such words again";
one is said to abandon mind when thinking, "I will not give rise to such a state of mind again";
and one is said to abandon view when abandoning it with the thought, "I will not take up such a view again. One who does not act accordingly—

He neither abandons nor relinquishes it. "As he was brought, so he is placed in hell" means that just as he was brought by the wardens of hell and placed in hell, so indeed is he placed in hell; there is no obstacle whatsoever to his rebirth in hell.
Herein, this is the logical justification: one who reviles the Noble Ones and goes to hell does not abandon that [kamma] once it has been taken up, just like wrong view.
And here, by the statement beginning with "without abandoning that speech," it is shown that for one who has not abandoned it, reviling the Noble Ones is an obstacle and brings harm;

however, by abandoning it—namely, by confessing the transgression and asking for forgiveness—it is no longer an obstacle or harmful, just as an offense is no longer such once it has been cleared through confession. [This applies to] what should not be done by way of wrong view.
"There is no evil so great that even the state of being a 'morsel' (khāṇu) in saṃsāra would not result from it," thus he said:
"Bhikkhus, wrong view is the foremost of evils.
"Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata’s body stands with the conduit to existence cut off; this very body and [the body] external..."
In such passages as "and name-and-form," the word *kāya* here refers to the five aggregates; thus he says, "the breaking up of the body" means the relinquishing of the acquired aggregates.

Since for one not free from lust, after death there is only the grasping of the form of another existence, he says, "after death" means "in the seizing of the aggregates produced immediately thereafter. That by which one remains...
"The body breaks up by way of its very cessation," thus he said: "With the breaking up of the body" means with the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
It brings happiness from this, thus it is *aya*; merit is what he called "merit-regarded *ayas*.

Happiness comes from this, thus it is *āya*, the means for achieving happiness through meritorious deeds and so forth. Therefore he said: "Or because of the absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness. "Vivasa" [means...]

Because they must turn according to the power of karma, they are unable to turn according to their own will; thus, "vivasā" means those from whom will (*vasa*) has departed, which is to say, those who do not exercise mastery.
That which goes (*iyati*) and is tasted (*assādīyati*) is "ayo"; he says "ayo signifying enjoyment (*assāda*). By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "of the nāga kings, etc.," there is an inclusion of garuḷas and others. "Like asuras" means like the *peta*-asuras.
"So hi" means that asura host. "From all heights" (sabbasamussayehi) means from all heights of prosperity; what is meant is "one who is attached to all prosperity.

"By way of the opposite of what was stated" refers to the opposite of the meaning stated for the phrases beginning with "bodily misconduct," namely: "well-conducted" (sucarita), or "beautiful conduct" (sobhanaṃ caritaṃ), [is called] "good conduct" (sucarita) because it is blameless, and so forth.

Because of the statement, “Go from here, sir, to a happy destination,” the human realm is indeed a happy destination; thus he said, “By the inclusion of ‘happy destination,’ the human realm is also comprised.
The rest here is easy to understand, as it follows the method already explained and its meaning is clear.
The discussion on the knowledge of the divine eye is finished.

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhayañāṇakathā). 14. "Having insight as its proximate cause" means having insight as its foundation (*padaṭṭhāna*). And insight is threefold according to the distinction between the persons who possess it.

For in the case of Great Bodhisattvas and Pacceka-Bodhisattvas, it consists of self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), because it has been developed through knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*).

In others, it is born of instruction from another because it is developed through knowledge consisting of what has been heard. It is described in many ways in the *Visuddhimagga* by way of various approaches for discerning the elements— such as "having emerged from any one of the remaining fine-material or immaterial jhānas, except for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—
by way of various approaches for discerning those respective elements taught under the heading of the "definition of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*) via the immaterial door.

It is analyzed according to various methods. Furthermore, for the great Bodhisattvas, by way of twenty-four hundred thousand million methods, it brings about the attainment of the womb of preliminary knowledge—which serves as the foundation for the noble path-knowledge that is the support of omniscience—and leads it to maturity;
it is supremely profound, more subtle and delicate than anything else, and not shared with others.
This is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), which is called "the great diamond-knowledge" (*mahāvajiraññāṇa*) in the commentaries.
And by way of its functional manifestation, it is divided into twenty-four hundred thousand varieties;

with this as its basis, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that the Teacher enters daily are said to number twenty-four hundred thousand. This is the mode of practice of insight for the Buddhas.
In this *Paramatthamañjūsā*, the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*, [the path] has been shown by way of enumeration; it should be taken from there by those who seek it.

Because it exhausts and utterly cuts off the taints (*āsava*), the noble path is the "destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*); the mention of the path of Arahantship is by way of the highest description.
Showing that "knowledge regarding the destruction of the taints" is "knowledge of the destruction of the taints," he says: "And therein this..."

Having stated "knowledge," he said "because it is included therein" (*tappariyāpannattā*) to show that the locative case in "in destruction" (*khaye*) refers to the locus (*ādhāra*), not to the object (*visaya*).
"This is suffering" (*idaṃ dukkhaṃ*) is a demonstration of the Noble Truth of Suffering being grasped through direct perception at that time.

"So much is suffering" (*ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ*) is a demonstration of its being grasped as delimited. "There is nothing more than this" (*na ito bhiyyo*) indicates that it has been grasped without remainder.
It is the vision of the state already grasped. Therefore he said, "All suffering-truth," and so forth.
"By penetration through the characteristic of its own essence" means by penetrating without confusion the characteristic defined as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

And "penetration without confusion" means that when that knowledge is active, there is subsequently no confusion regarding the determination of the specific form and other qualities of suffering. Thus...
[This refers to] the process of occurrence. Therefore he said: "He directly knew it as it truly is. "Producing" means bringing about.
"Having reached that state" means having come to that *nibbāna* which serves as the cause by way of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for the Path.

For it is said that the attainment of both by a person who possesses both is the "attainment of both. Alternatively, "having reached" (*patvā*) means by reason of reaching. "Non-occurrence" (*appavatti*).

It is the sign of non-occurrence (*appavatti*). Alternatively, it is "non-occurrence" (*appavatti*) because they do not occur therein; that is, Nibbāna. "Of that" refers to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*).
"Leading rightly" means leading correctly by way of realization (*sacchikiriyā*).

"By way of defilements" means by way of the defilements known as the taints (*āsava*). Since the taints are a synonym for the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), [the cessation] is included within that category.
There is also a method of exposition regarding the origin and so forth of the remaining truths; therefore, it is said, "by way of method" (*pariyāyato*).
The construction is: "showing [them] as the truths. And here, only the taints (*āsava*) are mentioned because the passage begins with "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
For it is by means of liberation from the taints that liberation from all defilements is expressed. "This is suffering" is [to be understood] as it really is (*yathābhūtaṃ*).
Because the mixed path is taught here by means of the phrase "he directly knew" (*abbhaññāsi*) and so forth, it is said: "He speaks of the path that has reached its culmination together with insight.

And herein, although it is said "he directly knew [the truths] as they really are" because the penetration of the truths was then in the past tense, the words "knowing thus, seeing thus" are used by taking their presentness at the time of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

The description was made by way of the present tense. And while it is true that from the moment of the path onwards until the present, [the fruit] is indeed of the past time, its being of the past time must first of all be understood by way of the moment of fruition; thus he said:
“By ‘was liberated,’ he shows the moment of fruition. Alternatively, “of one who knows and sees” is a description of the cause; that is, by reason of knowing and by reason of seeing.

The construction is: "the mind was liberated even from the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*). Furthermore, by the inclusion of the "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*) here, it should be understood that the "taint of views" (*diṭṭhāsava*) is also included, since the view of existence is likewise subsumed under the "taint of existence," just as lust for existence is.
For, through the reviewing of abandoned defilements, even existing karma does not lead to rebirth in the future.
“He knows, ‘Birth is exhausted’; and because he understands through the reviewing of the path and so forth that the holy life has been lived, etc., it is therefore said:
‘By means of [the phrases] “birth is exhausted,” etc., this is its plane. In this context, “its” (*tassa*) refers to the knowledge of reviewing.
“Its plane” (*bhūmi*) means its sphere of activity. Having clarified the intention with which the challenge was posed by the words beginning with “But what is...,” [the author continues:]
Desiring to state the resolution, he said, "Not yet for him," and so forth. The intention is that his past birth has not been exhausted by the cultivation of the path;
he states the reason for this as "because it was already exhausted previously. The construction is: "His future birth has not been exhausted.
And the term "future" is spoken figuratively, having taken the commonality of being future. Therefore he said:
“Because there is no effort regarding the future. For application is possible only with respect to what exists, not with respect to what does not exist; this is the intended meaning.

However, it is the specific distinction of the future that is intended here, and even in the case of its destruction, effort is indeed applicable. Therefore he said, “But as for the path,” and so forth.
By the words “but as for” and so on, [he shows] that the cultivation of the path occurs precisely through the removal of the causes of future births.

The state of being exhausted (khīṇabhāva) is made manifest. Regarding the phrase "in one, four, or five-aggregate existences," the mention of the three types of existence is for the purpose of showing, according to the method already stated, that birth has been exhausted without remainder.
"That" refers to the aforementioned birth; "he" refers to the Blessed One.
As for the so-called "dwelling in the holy life" (brahmacariyavāsa), it is here simply the production of the path as the holy life; thus he said, "it is finished."

When right view proceeds by way of accomplishing the tasks such as full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding the four truths, the proceeding of right intention and the other factors in accordance with the direct realization of full understanding regarding the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), and their proceeding by way of the direct realization of abandonment (*pahāna*) and so forth regarding the remaining truths, is indeed evident.
Therefore it was said: "by way of the direct realization of full understanding, abandonment, verification, and cultivation through the four paths."
“*Nāparam itthattāya*”: these modes are *itthaṃ*; their state is *itthattaṃ*, meaning “for that purpose.

However, those modes intended here are thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) and so forth, which constitute the activity of the Noble Path; thus he says, “in this way, for the sake of the state of the sixteen functions.
For these [functions] become manifest and appear to one who reviews the Path through the power of the Path, among thorough knowledge and the rest.

And since abandonment itself is the exertion, and the others exist for its sake, he said, "or for the destruction of the defilements. Alternatively, this was stated by way of reviewing the defilements that have been abandoned.
Regarding the passage, "He directly knew: 'There is no further state of being here,'" there is this other method:

"itthattāya" is a dative (sampadāna) used in the sense of the ablative (nissakka). Thus, the meaning is: from this state of being, from this suchness (itthambhāvato), from this very kind [of existence].
Now, there is no further continuity of future aggregates for me beyond this present continuity of aggregates;
rather, these five aggregates, known as my final existence, stand without a foundation once they have been fully understood, like trees whose roots have been cut.
For a foundation exists only when its root is not fully understood. As it is said: "If, monks, in the case of physical nutriment..."
“There is lust, there is delight, there is craving; therein consciousness is established and has grown,” and so forth.
They understood that these five aggregates, through the cessation of the final consciousness, will go out like a fire without fuel.
“Encompassed by reviewing knowledge” means it is not merely [the attainment] as in the case of the first two knowledges.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Showing" means showing by way of conclusion; for it has already been shown previously in its essential form (*sarūpato*).
The rest here is easily understood because it follows the method already stated.
By the phrase "born three times," however, this is what he shows: "O Brahmin, I am indeed born through the first knowledge (*vijjā*)."

Because he is older and more venerable than all others due to the absence of anyone born before him or born simultaneously with him—how much more so since he has been "born" three times through the three types of higher knowledge (*vijjā*)—it should be connected thus:

"Having made known the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsāñāṇa*) by means of the knowledge of past states (*atītaṃsañāṇa*)," because of their commonality in having the past as their object and because the latter exists as a consequence of the former. In this regard:

"Knowledge of the past" means unimpeded knowledge regarding the past portion, which consists of the aggregates, bases, and elements of the past. Since the knowledge of the divine eye has a present object,
and since the knowledge of rebirths according to karma and the knowledge of the future are accomplished by means of the divine eye itself—
and because the knowledge of others' minds is established only for one who is already established in the divine eye— it is considered an ancillary knowledge to the divine eye.

It is said: "The knowledge of the past and future through the divine eye. In this context, "by the divine eye" means by the knowledge of the divine eye together with its peripheral range (*saparibhaṇḍa*).
"Past and future portions" (*paccuppannānāgatamsa*) refers to the present portion and the future portion; the knowledge therein is "knowledge of the past and future portions.
This occurs precisely through the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*), just as it does for the knowledge of omniscience.

Because the Buddha-qualities that are not shared with others—such as the unique knowledge of the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the other exclusive Buddha-dharmas—also come to fruition through the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), it is said:
"By the destruction of the taints, all mundane and supramundane qualities. Therefore he said: "Having manifested all the qualities of omniscience.
The discussion on the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is concluded.
The Discourse on the Expression of Gratitude for the Teaching 15. *Pītivipphāraparipuṇṇagattacitto*: one whose body and mind are filled with the pervasion of rapture.
*Aññāṇaṃ* means "of ignorance"; for, due to its connection with the word *dhī*, this accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. *Abhikkantā*: excellent.
In this context, the meaning is "transcended" or "departed," hence he said, "it is seen in the sense of destruction. For it is for this very reason that it is said, "the first watch has departed.
And "more excellent" (*abhikkantataro*) means exceedingly desirable and delightful;
since such a thing is called beautiful and auspicious (*bhaddako*), he said, "it is seen in the sense of beauty. Who? Among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—who?
"Who? means "mine. "Feet" means "the two feet. "By means of psychic power" means by means of such divine majesty (*deviddhi*).
"By fame" means by such a retinue and distinction. "Shining" means glowing brightly. "By his lovely appearance" means by an exceedingly beautiful, desirable, and handsome complexion;
"by his color" means by the hue of his skin and the radiance of his body. "Illuminating all"—that is, making everything radiant.
The meaning of the verse is: "Disā" means illuminating the ten directions like the moon and like the sun, making them one mass of radiance and one mass of light.
"Abhirūpe" means in one of sublime form, one endowed with perfect beauty.
Regarding the two statements, "Excellent, O Gotama! Excellent, O Gotama!", [the word] "sādhu" is used twice.
Having shown the meaning by means of the repetition "Gotama, Gotama," he spoke the words beginning with "In fear, in anger" in order to determine its specific scope.
Therein, repetition occurs in cases of fear, as in "A thief, a thief! or "A snake, a snake!"; in cases of anger, as in "Pierce, pierce! or "Strike, strike!";
in cases of praise, as in "Excellent, excellent!"; and in cases of haste, as in "Go, go! or "Reap, reap!"

In expressions such as “Come, come,” it signifies wonder (*kotūhala*). In expressions such as “Thinking ‘the Buddha, the Buddha’,” it signifies amazement (*accharā*). In expressions such as “Come forward, venerable sirs;

come forward, venerable sirs,” it signifies laughter (*hāsa*). In expressions such as “Where is my only son? Where is my only son? it signifies sorrow (*soka*). In expressions such as “Oh, what happiness!

Oh, what happiness! it signifies confidence (*pasāda*). The word *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated (*avutta-samuccaya*). By this, [it includes] censure (*garaha*), disrespect (*asammāna*), and so forth.

The inclusion [of these terms] should be understood. Therein, in expressions such as "wicked, wicked," it is used in the sense of censure. In expressions such as "handsome, handsome," it should be understood as being used in the sense of disrespect.
Showing that this is not stated twice by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), but rather by way of two distinct meanings, he says: "Then..."
He spoke the words beginning with "excellent" (*abhikkanta*). This was stated in the neuter gender in view of the word *vacana* (speech).
However, since that speech of the Blessed One is the teaching of the Dhamma, it is said: "That is to say, the Lord Gotama’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Alternatively, this is merely a demonstration of the meaning; therefore, the change in gender and case-ending should be understood according to the sense.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "From the destruction of faults" means from the eradication of defilements such as lust (*rāga*).

"From the attainment of qualities" means from the accomplishment of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). Since those qualities which the teaching brings about must be shown, and among them the primary qualities should be indicated, the text says "from the generation of faith (*saddhā*) and from the generation of wisdom (*paññā*)" in order to first show those primary qualities. Faith is the foremost...

For mundane qualities have wisdom as their foremost, while supramundane ones have it as their head. Regarding the phrases "meaningful" (*sāttha*) and so forth: it is "meaningful" because of its perfection in the purpose of virtue (*sīla*) and the other trainings;

it is "well-phrased" (*sabyañjana*) because of its perfection in natural expression. It is "clear in its words" (*uttānapada*) due to the employment of easily understood terminology, and "profound in meaning" (*gambhīrattha*) due to the difficulty of understanding its meaning because of its subtle and delicate nature.
It is "pleasant to the ear" (*kaṇṇasukha*) due to the employment of sounds that are smooth, soft, and sweet.

Because it reaches the heart through its vast, pure, and lovely meaning; because it does not exalt oneself by dispelling pride and conceit, nor disparage others by crushing stubbornness and hostility;
because it is cooled by compassion through its activity motivated by the desire for welfare and its pacification of others' feverish passion and the like;
because it is brightened by wisdom through its dispelling of the darkness of the defilements; and because it is delightful to the senses through its sweetness like the song of the cuckoo.

The meaning should be understood as follows: because it is capable of withstanding scrutiny due to its perfectly pure meaning that is not contradicted by what precedes or follows; because it is pleasant to hear due to its very beauty when it enters the range of hearing; and because it is beneficial when investigated, owing to its being set forth with a disposition toward welfare.
By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etc. includes the turning back of the wheel of saṃsāra, the setting in motion of the wheel of the True Dhamma, and the dispelling of false doctrines.

The inclusion [of right speech] should be understood through such points as: establishing right speech, uprooting the unwholesome roots, planting the wholesome roots, closing the doors to the states of misery, opening the door to the path to heaven, pacifying the outbursts of defilements, and eradicating the underlying tendencies.
"Placed face-down" means placed face-down by someone; "naturally facing downwards" means being face-down by its very nature.

It has arisen. "He should uncover" means he should open it. "Taking by the hand" means that without saying "Go facing east or facing north," etc., he should take him by the hand and show him, saying, "This is the path without doubt; go thus.
"The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight" means the fourteenth day in the dark fortnight. "He should turn what was face down over" means...
One should turn upside up a vessel that lacks a base for what is to be placed within it, by means of providing it with a state of being a base.

The two phrases—“turned away from the True Dhamma because it was produced face-downward” and “established in the non-True Dhamma because it was set down face-downward”—should be applied accordingly, not according to their numerical order.
Granted, sensual desire and the other hindrances are also concealers by virtue of their nature as hindrances; yet...
Wrong view, moreover, is especially concealing because it causes beings to adhere to what is false; thus he said, "concealed by the thicket of wrong view.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the supreme fault.

All paths leading to the states of misery are called "bad paths" (kummagga) because they are contemptible paths; and because they are the direct opposites of right view and the other factors of the Path, wrong view and so forth [are so designated].
The eight states of wrongness are the wrong path. For it is precisely with reference to their being the opposites of both [the right path and the right view] that it is said:
"by one who is explaining the path to heaven and liberation. The lamp supported by ghee and such is not as bright as that supported by oil; hence the mention of an "oil-lamp.
