"By these modes" means by these various types of similes to be illustrated, such as those of turning upside-down back upright, uncovering what is hidden, and so forth.
Or rather, by these aforementioned methods of demonstrating that he is not of the nature of one who lacks flavor (arasarūpa) and so forth;
by the methods of manifesting his own divine abidings; by the means of manifesting the threefold clear knowledge (vijjā); and by the methods of manifesting his own quality of omniscience.
Therefore, it was said: "The Dhamma has been proclaimed in many ways."
The discourse on the expression of appreciation for the teaching is finished.
Regarding the "manner of showing confidence":
"manner of showing confidence" refers to the honor that should be performed by those who have confidence. In the phrase "I go for refuge," the word *iti* is indicated as being elided.
He said, "I go for refuge. For here, this verb "to go" (gacchati) is not transitive—taking two objects—like verbs such as "to lead" (nī).
Therefore, just as one says "he leads the goat to the village," it is not possible to say "I go Gotama for refuge";
rather, one must say "I go [to him] for refuge. Consequently, in this context, the word "iti" is indicated as being elided.
It should be understood that *saraṇa* means a refuge; therefore he said "the ultimate resort" (*parāyaṇa*).

And the state of being an ultimate resort arises through the prevention of what is harmful and the accomplishment of what is beneficial; thus he said, "The protector from misfortune and the provider of welfare.

Regarding "from misfortune" (*aghassa*), they say it means from suffering (*dukkha*), but the meaning "from evil" (*pāpa*) is more appropriate; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. *Saraṇa* means...
In this context, showing that "going" means associating with that intention and likewise knowing it, he said: "Thus, by this intention," and so forth.
Therein, in the phrases such as "I go," each preceding term is explained by the succeeding one.

Alternatively, "associating" (bhajana) is approaching with the intention of seeking refuge; "service" (sevanā) is remaining in his presence; and "waiting upon" (payirupāsana) is performing the duties and counter-duties.
"Upaṭṭhāna" (approaching) thus indicates in every respect the state of having no other refuge. Regarding the word "gacchāmi" (I go), he says "yesaṃ hi...
and so forth to show how the meaning "how shall I understand? is obtained.

By the two phrases "adhigatamagge" (to those who have attained the path) and "sacchikatanirodhe" (to those who have realized cessation), only those established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*) are shown, not those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*).

Demonstrating this, he said: "And for those practicing according to the instruction. Now, is it not the case that even a "good worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is said to practice according to the instruction?

Although he is so called, in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), only those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*) should be described thus, and not others, because they lack entry into the fixed course of rightness (*niyāmokkama*). For it is only they who [are described as] "not falling into the states of misery..."

"...is maintained," it is said. For by entering the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), there arises the possibility of being freed from the states of misery (*apāya*). Regarding the word "it is declared" (*akkhāyati*):

here the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner. By this, it includes the Sutta passage: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them," as well as the phrase "in detail."

Or [it may be understood] by this [phrase]. And here, both the Noble Path and Nibbāna are called "Dhamma" in the primary sense: the Noble Path because it is the means of deliverance, and Nibbāna because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose.

For it is by obtaining Nibbāna as its object-condition that the Noble Path accomplishes its purpose; nevertheless, regarding the Noble Fruits, there is the statement beginning with, "Because that faith has not yet subsided," and so forth.
Because the defilements eradicated by the Path possess the function of pacification and abandonment, because they are conducive to deliverance, and because they culminate in deliverance;

and because the Dhamma of the scriptures is the cause for the attainment of the Dhamma that leads to deliverance—it is precisely in this manner, according to the method stated, that the status of being "Dhamma" is obtained. Furthermore, this meaning is indeed established by the text itself.
Showing this, he said, “Not merely,” and so forth.

“The fading away of lust” (*rāgavirāga*) is stated as the Path; for it is by means of this that all lust—including its divisions such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*)—fades away and is abandoned.
Thus, the Path is called the fading away of lust. “Unshakable and sorrowless” refers to the Fruit, because of [the absence of] that which is reckoned as agitation (*ejā*).

The fruit is described as "unperturbed and sorrowless" because, through the complete exhaustion of craving, both sorrow—which is characterized by inward brooding—and its arising have been entirely eliminated.
It is "not repulsive" in the sense of being non-opposed to anything, since it demonstrates an absence of conflict; or rather, the meaning is that it is desirable and sublime.
It is "proficient" because it occurs in a state of mastery, or because it manifests distinguished qualities. As it has been said:
“Perceiving no harm, O Brahmā, I spoke with skillful ease the sublime Dhamma among men. This is the construction: it means that all the aggregates of Dhamma have been explained.

By the phrase “comprising view and virtue,” this refers to what was said thus: “That noble view which is emancipating, leading the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering—one dwells having attained conformity in view with such a view.”

Regarding the view, it means "he dwells having attained conformity in virtue through such virtues as those described as 'virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration,'" by way of the state of being unified;
the meaning is: by way of conformity in both view and virtue. "Unified" (*saṃhata*) means joined together.
The meaning is "assembled. For noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), even when situated far apart anywhere, are indeed united by the harmony of their own qualities.
And "the eight persons who see the Dhamma" means that there are four pairs according to the dyads of persons, or eight individuals according to the persons themselves;
they are "seers of the Dhamma" because of their direct vision of the Noble Dhamma. [They are called] "those who have gone for refuge" by way of going to the three objects of refuge.
By going [to the Buddha] three times, he announced the three goings for refuge. "He announced" means he made known what was in his heart by means of speech.
The Discourse on the Manner of Faith is concluded.
The Discourse on Going for Refuge.

Since proficiency in the goings for refuge requires an analysis of their scope, classification, fruit, defilement, and the person who goes for refuge—just as there is an analysis of these very factors—it is said:
“For the sake of proficiency in the goings for refuge, the refuge... [and so forth]... should be understood,” because without that [analysis], the going for refuge itself is impossible.
Therein, regarding the term *saraṇa* (refuge): first, from the standpoint of the word-meaning (*padatthato*), it is called a refuge (*saraṇa*) because it destroys (*sarati*).
This term should be understood by way of the word *sara* having the sense of "destroying" (*hiṃsattha*).

Therefore, for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, it destroys—that is, it eliminates—all suffering, including the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭabhaya*), mental terror, physical pain, and whatever suffering is comprised within the miserable destinies.
This is a designation specifically for the Triple Gem. Alternatively, [it may be explained] by its causing one to proceed toward what is beneficial (*hita*).
By enjoining beings to their welfare through such instructions as, “Monks, dwell possessed of perfected virtue,” and by turning them away from what is harmful;
and by turning them away from what is disadvantageous through means such as the vision of danger, as in, “Now, the ripening of the taking of life is evil, and its future consequence is evil”;
[compassion] destroys the fear of beings—that fear which is caused by the non-engagement in what is beneficial and the engagement in what is harmful.

The Buddha destroys calamity by bringing about its cessation. The Dhamma, known as the Path, dispels the fear of beings by enabling them to cross the wilderness of existence; the other [the Saṅgha] does so by bestowing consolation.
The Saṅgha dispels the fear of beings by causing them to obtain abundant fruits through even small acts of giving and through the honors they offer.
Because it possesses the state of being the unsurpassed object of offerings, for this reason as well, one takes refuge in the Triple Gem according to the method explained through analysis:
"The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced rightly.

By means of the profound respect born from such praise of the Triple Gem, one shakes off wrong views, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so forth; thus, with defilements destroyed, one takes refuge in that very Triple Gem.

“Refuge,” “destination,” “protection,” and “shelter”—thus, when these terms are employed, the arising of consciousness that occurs in the mode of being intent upon them is “going for refuge” (*saraṇagamana*).
This is because it is defined as “that by which one goes for refuge. A sentient being endowed with that aforementioned arising of consciousness “goes for refuge”;
by means of the arising of consciousness in the manner described, [one thinks]: “These Three Jewels are my refuge.”
"These are the ultimate resorts"—thus one approaches, frequents, serves, and attends upon them; or alternatively, the meaning is that one knows and awakens to this.
In this way, first, the refuge, the act of going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—these three should be understood.
Regarding the classification of going for refuge, there are two kinds of refuge: supramundane and mundane. Of these, the supramundane...

For those who have seen the Truths, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), by means of the total eradication of the defilements associated with going for refuge, it becomes, in terms of its object, one that has Nibbāna as its object;
and in terms of its function, it succeeds in respect of the entire Triple Gem. For in actual meaning, the attainment of the Four Truths is itself the supramundane going for refuge.

Therein, the Dhamma of Nibbāna is [realized] through the clear realization of direct knowledge (sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya), and the Dhamma of the Path is [realized] through the clear realization of development (bhāvanā-abhisamaya).

While being penetrated, it accomplishes the purpose of going for refuge; however, the qualities of the Buddha that fall within the range of disciples are accomplished through the realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*), and likewise the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha.
Therefore it is said: "It succeeds with respect to all three Jewels by way of function.
And when it succeeds, it succeeds simultaneously, not sequentially as in the case of the mundane, but through the penetration of non-delusion (*asammohapaṭivedha*).
Because it has been penetrated. As for those who say, "The going for refuge does not proceed by having Nibbāna as its object;

rather, because the Path has been attained, it is simply 'attained'—just as certain worldly sciences such as the threefold knowledge (tevijjā) and so forth are attained [upon reaching their respective goals]," for them, the going for refuge would be merely mundane and not supramundane. And that is incorrect, for both kinds [of going for refuge]...
Because it is desirable. However, mundane going for refuge succeeds by way of its object through the suppression of the defilements of going for refuge characteristic of worldlings;

having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object, it consists in meaning of the acquisition of faith regarding the bases such as the Buddha—expressed as "The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened"—and right view preceded by that aforementioned faith, [occurring] in the ten...
Among the bases for the performance of merit, this is called the rectification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*).

Here, it should be understood that by the phrase "acquisition of faith" (*saddhāpaṭilābha*), taking refuge dissociated from knowledge is shown, such as in the case of children who are encouraged by their mothers and others.
By the phrase "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*), however, taking refuge associated with knowledge is shown, [namely] the Buddha’s state of being perfectly enlightened.
This is because one correctly perceives, by way of mundane awakening, the excellence of the Dhamma and the excellence of the Saṅgha’s practice through right method.
This mundane going for refuge occurs in four ways: by surrendering oneself, by making that one’s supreme resort, by entering into the state of a pupil, and by prostration.
Among these, "surrendering oneself" means: "Starting from today..."

“I surrender myself to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha”—thus is the relinquishing of one’s own personal existence for the sake of crossing over the suffering of *saṃsāra* to the Buddha and the others.
“Taking them as one’s supreme refuge” means the state of having them as one’s supreme refuge, thinking:

“From this day forward, may you consider me one who has the Buddha as his supreme refuge, the Dhamma as his supreme refuge, and the Saṅgha as his supreme refuge. This is the act of entering into discipleship.
"Taking today as the beginning, 'regard me as one who says: "I am a resident pupil of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, and of the Saṅgha"'—this is the undertaking of the status of a disciple.
Prostration means: 'Taking today as the beginning, regard me as one who says:

"From this day forth, I shall perform only the three acts of salutation, rising from my seat, joining my palms, and respectful service toward the Buddha and the other two [the Dhamma and the Saṅghha]."'"
Thus, there is the supreme act of self-surrender toward the Buddha and the others. For by performing even one of these four modes, the going for refuge is indeed accomplished.
Furthermore: "I surrender myself to the Blessed One; I surrender myself to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; [I surrender] my life..."
"I renounce; my very self is renounced, my very life is renounced.
For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection"—thus too should the surrendering of oneself be understood.
"Indeed, may I see the Teacher; indeed, may I see the Blessed One; indeed, may I see the Sugata..."

“I see him, I see the Blessed One; indeed, I see the Perfectly Enlightened One, I see the Blessed One alone”—thus should the acceptance of discipleship by the Elder Mahākassapa be understood, just like his going for refuge.
“Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town.”
"Revering the Fully Awakened One and the excellent nature of the Dhamma:

‘We shall wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain... [as before] ...the excellent nature of the Dhamma’”—in this way, one’s taking of refuge, such as that of Āḷavaka, Sātāgira, Hemavata, and others, should be understood as having that as their ultimate resort. Is it not so?
[Objection: These individuals, such as Āḷavaka and others, attained the refuges by way of the Path itself;

how then can it be said that their going for refuge consisted in having that [Dhamma] as their ultimate resort? [Response: Even though they attained the refuges by way of the Path, it was stated thus because they proclaimed the mode of having that as their ultimate resort through such words as, "I shall wander from village to village. Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat...

Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name, saying: “I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama;
I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama. In this way, too, prostration by falling flat is to be understood.
Furthermore, this [prostration] is fourfold, by way of kinship, fear, teacherhood, and worthiness as a recipient of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*).

Among these, the going for refuge occurs through prostration caused by worthiness as a recipient of offerings, and not through the other three types of prostrations proceeding from kinship, fear, and so forth.
For it is by way of excellence that one takes refuge, and it is by way of excellence that one breaks [the precepts]; therefore, whether one is a Śākyan or a Koliyan...
Or, if one pays homage thinking, "The Buddha is our relative," the taking of refuge has not been undertaken.

Or, if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power; if he were not saluted, he might even cause me harm," the taking of refuge has not been undertaken.
Also, if one—whether during the time of being a Bodhisatta or at the time of Buddhahood—recalls something learned in the presence of the Blessed One...
“One should enjoy wealth with one part, employ labor with two parts,
and set aside the fourth part as a reserve for times of misfortune.

Having received such instruction concerning matters pertaining to this visible world, if one pays homage [to the teacher], thinking, “He is my teacher,” while not having actually received [the teaching], [that is a transgression].
One who expects instruction that is for the sake of the future life and leads to liberation performs only the prostration toward those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
However, when one pays homage [to the Buddha] thinking, "This one is the foremost among those worthy of offerings in the world," by that very act the refuge has been taken.
And for a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a lay follower woman (*upāsikā*) who has thus taken refuge, even if a relative has gone forth among other sects—
“Even for one who pays homage thinking, ‘This person is my relative,’ the going for refuge is not broken, let alone for one who has not gone forth.
Likewise, it is not broken for one who pays homage to a king out of fear; for if he were not honored, being revered by the whole kingdom, he might even cause harm.
Similarly, it is not broken for one who pays homage even to a teacher of some craft, even if they be a member of another sect (tīrthika), thinking, ‘This person is my teacher.’”
Thus should the classification of going for refuge be understood.
The discussion on going for refuge is finished.
Now follows the discussion on the fruit of going for refuge.
And here, regarding the going for refuge that is supramundane, the four fruits of recluseship are the fruition-result (*vipākaphala*).

This is because it is the noble path itself that is intended as the "supramundane going for refuge. However, the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is the benefit-result (*ānisaṃsaphala*).
For this has been said:
“But whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering.”
And the Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
“This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
by coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.”
Furthermore, the fruit of its benefits should be understood by way of not falling into the view of permanence and so forth. For this has been said:

"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent, should regard anything as pleasant, or should regard any phenomenon as a self, or [should deprive] his mother of life..."

“...one might kill one’s mother, kill one’s father, kill an arahant, with a malicious mind draw blood from a Tathāgata, or cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or point to another teacher—this is impossible.
However, for the worldly going for refuge, the attainment of existence and the attainment of wealth are indeed the fruits. For this has been said:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to the plane of misery;
having cast off the human body,”
“They will fulfill the body of a god.
Furthermore, it is said:
“Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...”
He approached him... [as before] ...and as Sakka, lord of the devas, was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:
"It is good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha;
it is because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
“They are reborn there. They surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, divine beauty, happiness, fame, sovereignty, and divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
This same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha as well.
Furthermore, the specific excellence of the fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others as well.

For instance, in the Velāma Sutta, it is said that [the merit of one who goes for refuge] is equal to that of eighty-four thousand golden bowls, silver bowls, and bronze bowls—each measuring a quarter-part of a *karīsa*—filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion, and adorned with every kind of ornament; and likewise, it is equal to eighty-four thousand elephants...
By way of relinquishing eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand milch cows,
eighty-four thousand maidens, eighty-four thousand couches, eighty-four thousand millions of garments,
and immeasurable food consisting of various kinds of hard and soft edibles, for more than seven months...
Giving for seven consecutive years at the time of the Pavāraṇā festival is more fruitful than giving to a single stream-enterer;
giving to a hundred stream-enterers is more fruitful than giving to a single once-returner; giving to a single non-returner is more fruitful than that;
giving to a single arahant is more fruitful than that; giving to a single paccekabuddha is more fruitful than that; and giving to a perfectly enlightened Buddha is the most fruitful of all.

It was declared: "A gift given to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is more fruitful than that; building a monastery for the sake of the Saṅgha of the four quarters is more fruitful than that; and going for refuge is even more fruitful than that. For this has been said:
"Householder, compared to the great gift which the brahmin Velāma gave as an offering, if one were to feed a single person endowed with right view, this would be more fruitful than that."
Ādi. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.
The Discussion on the Fruit of Going for Refuge is finished.
Now begins the Discussion on the Defilements and the Analysis of Going for Refuge.
And therein, the mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth regarding the three objects;
it is not of great radiance, not brilliant, impure, and unpurified, and it does not have great extension or loftiness.
And herein, "ignorance" means the non-knowing of the qualities of the Triple Gem, that is, delusion regarding them. ["Is he a Buddha?"...]

"Doubt" (*vicikicchā*) refers to uncertainty, as expressed in such phrases as "Is it so, or is it not so? "Wrong knowledge" (*micchāñāṇa*) should be understood as a perverted grasp resulting from imagining that his [the Buddha's] qualities are actually non-qualities.
However, there is no defilement in the supramundane going for refuge. Furthermore, the mundane going for refuge is of two kinds:
blameworthy and blameless. Of these, the blameworthy consists in [taking refuge] in other teachers and so forth.
It arises through such acts as making oneself one's own master, and its fruit is undesirable; however, it is blameless at the time of death.
For mundane going for refuge, like the undertaking of the training rules, is not restricted by a specific time limit and lasts only as long as life itself;
therefore, it ceases with the breaking up of the aggregates, and because it lacks karmic ripening, it is fruitless. But for the supramundane [going for refuge], there is none at all.
The breach: for even in another existence, a noble disciple does not point to another teacher. Thus, both the defilement and the breach of going for refuge should be understood.
But why is purification not included here? Is it not the case that the demonstration of purification also serves for proficiency in this matter?
This is true; however, because it is already indicated by implication through the mention of "defilement" (saṃkilesa), it was not explicitly included.
For purification occurs through the absolute non-arising of those causes of defilement, such as ignorance and so forth, and through the abandoning of those that have already arisen.
In this way, the elaboration regarding "refuge" and "going for refuge," and so on, should be understood here.
Showing the reason for not including this aforementioned elaboration here, he says: "But if that were spoken here," and so forth.
In that context, "from the description of going for refuge" means from the description of going for refuge as stated in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
The discussion on the defilements and the analysis of going for refuge is finished.
The Discussion on the Declaration of Lay Status (*Upāsakattapaṭivedanākathā*).
"Let it be held thus" means "let it be known thus. Here, "Who is a lay follower? is a question regarding the specific nature [of the term];

therefore, what is meant is: "What is the characteristic of a lay follower? "Why? is a question regarding the cause. By that, [the question is: by what causal basis does the word "lay follower" [arise]?
This shows that the term is established with reference to that person. Therefore he asks: "Why is he called a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
For the cause for the application of a word to its referent is the reason for the existence of that state in the object denoted by it.

"What is his virtue? means: what kind of virtue does this lay follower have; by how much virtue does he become one who is "endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanna*)? "What is his livelihood? (*ko ājīvo*)...
What is right livelihood? Since that occurs through the avoidance of wrong livelihood, that too is analyzed.
What is failure? It refers to the failure of which virtue or of which livelihood; for there is either an injunction or a prohibition regarding what immediately precedes it.
The same principle applies here to success as well.
"This miscellaneous matter is to be understood"—how is it to be understood? It is said: Who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
Any householder among the kṣatriyas and others who has gone for refuge to the Three. For here, the going for refuge itself is the cause, not distinctions such as birth and so forth.
For this has been said: "From the time, Mahānāma, that one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha..."
“He has gone [for refuge]. It is to this extent, Mahānāma, that one is a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

Why is he called a *upāsaka*? Because of his attendance (*upāsana*) upon the Three Jewels. By that very act of going for refuge, it is meant that he attends upon them through the performance of duties with care, and by means of devotion, reverence, and great respect. For he attends upon the Buddha; thus he is a *upāsaka*.
An *upāsaka* (lay follower). He is called an *upāsaka* because he waits upon (*upāsatī*) the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

What is his virtue? It consists of the five abstentions (*veramaṇiyo*). Here, "abstentions" refers to the fact that "wrongdoing" (*vera*)—namely, immorality such as killing living beings—is called *vera*;
because one refrains from, destroys, and eliminates that [wrongdoing], they are the five abstentions (*viratiyo*), since abstention is their primary characteristic.
Regarding that virtue: for this has been said, "Insofar as, Mahānāma, a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life,
from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
to this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous."
What is livelihood? It is the making of one’s living by means that are righteous and equitable, having abandoned the five kinds of wrong trade. For this has been said:
“Monks, there are these five trades that a lay follower should not engage in. Which five?
Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons. These, monks, are the five trades that a lay follower should not engage in.”
And here, "trade in weapons" refers to the sale of weaponry after having made it oneself, had it made by another, or obtained it already made.

"Trade in living beings" refers to the sale of human beings. "Trade in meat" refers to the sale of meat after having raised deer, pigs, and so forth, like butchers and the like, and prepared the meat.
"Trade in liquor" refers to the preparation of any kind of intoxicant and its...

Trade. "Poison-dealing" means trading in poison after having prepared it or collected it. In this context, it should be understood that the trade in weapons is declared improper because it is a cause for harming others;
the trade in living beings because it renders them unfree; the trade in meat and poison because they are causes of killing;
and the trade in intoxicants because they are a basis for negligence.
What is failure? That which is the failure, breach, anger, and provocation of that very virtue and livelihood—this is its failure.
Furthermore, it should be understood that whatever makes him an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), as well as defiled and censured, is also his failure.
And in terms of their actual nature, these consist of five states, beginning with lack of faith. As it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower is a *caṇḍāla* among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and one who is despised among lay followers.
What are the five? He is faithless; he is immoral; he is a superstitious omens-seeker;
he believes in auspicious signs, not in kamma; and he seeks outside here for those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). Therein...”
And he performs meritorious deeds.

Herein, “disparaging the lay follower” means one who is inferior to a lay follower. Lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) is the opposite of faith (*saddhā*) regarding the Buddha and so forth, as well as regarding karma and its fruit; it is wrong resolve (*micchā-adhimokkha*).
One who is possessed of such lack of faith as described is “faithless. By way of the aforementioned failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*), [he is so called].

He is immoral. One who possesses the auspiciousness of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—which is reckoned as a "superstitious rite" (kotūhalamaṅgala) imagined by foolish people, thinking, "By this [rite] such-and-such auspiciousness comes about"—is one who relies on superstitious rites. He "believes in auspiciousness" means he believes only in auspiciousness divided into the categories of what is seen and so forth.
He "does not believe in karma" means he does not believe in the ownership of one's actions (kammassakata). "Outside of this" means...

"Outside of this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha" means in the systems of outsiders (*bāhiraka*). "He seeks one worthy of offerings" means that perceiving someone who has practiced wrongly as being worthy of offerings, he searches for such a person.
"He performs a prior service" means that he performs wholesome deeds, such as giving and honoring, beforehand.
And here, by treating the seeking of one worthy of offerings and the performing of a prior service as one, five qualities are to be understood.

What is his accomplishment? That very perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and perfection of livelihood (*ājīvasampadā*) is his accomplishment, as well as those five qualities beginning with faith (*saddhā*) which constitute his being a "jewel" and so forth. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a lay follower becomes a jewel among lay followers, a lotus among lay followers, and a white lotus among lay followers.
With which five? He is endowed with faith, he is virtuous, he does not rely on superstitious omens..."
“Kamma is what prevails; kamma is what one inherits, not auspicious charms; one does not seek those worthy of offerings outside of this [dispensation], but rather performs meritorious deeds here.
And herein, because he generates delight in all four assemblies, the lay follower himself is the jewel—the “lay-follower-jewel.”

Just as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is like a lotus by virtue of his virtues, beauty, fame, reputation, and fragrance, so too is he to be understood as a "lay follower-lotus" (*upāsaka-paduma*), and likewise as a "lay follower-white-lotus" (*upāsaka-puṇḍarīka*).
The rest here is to be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding failure. Thus, this miscellaneous discussion beginning with "Who is a lay follower?
should be understood in detail. However, this miscellaneous discussion is not elaborated upon here.
Showing the reason, he said: “Because it makes [the burden] too heavy,” and so forth.

“In the beginning” (*ādismiṃ*) means in the sense of “beginning. “At the limit” (*koṭiyaṃ*) means at the ultimate limit. “By way of the dwelling” (*vihāraggena*) means by way of the section of the room;
that is, by way of the specific section where they reside, such as: “For those living in this chamber, this jackfruit is reached,” and so on.
The meaning is as follows: *ajjataṃ* means simply "today. By the phrase "endowed with life" (*pāṇehi upetaṃ*), he demonstrates that his going for refuge extends to the very end of his life;
thus, having said "as long as my life continues," and so forth, he again honors the Triple Gem with his life and maintains his going for refuge.
In this way, he clarifies the intention that had arisen in that brahmin.
He said, “I indeed,” and so forth. “Approached with life” means: as long as my life-breaths endure, I have approached for refuge.
One who approaches does not do so merely by words, nor merely by a single arising of the thought;
rather, the meaning here should be understood as having approached for as long as life lasts by way of relinquishing one’s life.
“Let him consent” means let him accept; since that acceptance is a mental undertaking, he said, “let him agree.

“A member of the body” (kāyaṅga) means they call the body itself a member, or else a member of the body such as the head and so forth is a “member of the body”; what is meant is a limb or part of the physical frame.
“A member of speech” (vācaṅga) refers to a member or component of speech such as “very well, let it be so,” and so on. The touching of a member of speech—
It should be understood as the very proceeding by means of speech. "Within oneself alone" means within one's own mental continuum (*cittasantāna*).
"Having exercised patience" means having set patience in motion; what is meant is that one has generated a liking [for the teaching].
There is also a reading, "having maintained patience," which means that having maintained the liking that had arisen within oneself alone, one has made it manifest through a verbal expression.

But how did the Brahmin of Verañjā understand the Blessed One’s consent? For it was not possible for him to know the movement of the Blessed One’s mind through direct perception; therefore, if one asks why it is said, "having understood the Blessed One’s consent," [the answer is as follows]:
although he could not know the movement of the mind through direct perception, nevertheless, by his skill in observing outward signs (*ākāra*), [he understood].
Showing that he knew [the answer] through inference by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he said, "If the ascetic Gotama...
and so forth. "By skill in discerning the mode" means by proficiency in knowing the mode of mental activity;
it is said to mean proficiency in discerning the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). "Radiant with the joining of ten nails" refers to the ten [fingers] on two hands.
It was shining brightly through the joining together and unification of the fingernails. "Añjali" means the hollow of the hands.

"Paṭimukhova" means facing [the Blessed One] directly; the meaning is that he did not turn his back on the Blessed One. "Vanditvā" means having paid homage by prostrating with the five points of the body.
The discussion on the declaration of lay discipleship is concluded.
**The Discourse on Famine (Dubbhikkhakathā)** 16. *Susassakālepi*: even during times when the crops are abundant. *Atisamagghepi*: even when prices are extremely low; the meaning is:
even at such times when people receive a great deal of grain—both paddy and cooked food—in exchange for giving away only a small amount. *Sāliādidhaññaṃ*: rice and other kinds of grain.

“Grain” refers to rice and so forth; “vegetables” refers to mung beans, black gram, and the like. He says, “‘Dvīhitika’ is a compound with the middle term elided (majjhapadalopī) and the external sense retained (bahirattha), meaning ‘that in which there is effort (īhita) occurring in two ways’,” thus showing that it is a bahubbīhi compound.
He says, “‘Effort’ (īhita) means striving (īhana); this word ‘īhita’ is a noun derived from the action (bhāvasādhana),” and thus states, “‘Effort’ is called movement (iriyā).
In this context, “movement” (iriyā) means activity (kiriyā). To the question, “Whose activity is this? he replies, “Movement of consciousness (cittairiyā).”
The meaning is "mental activity" or "mental application. For this very reason, it is said: "the striving of the mind.
But how is it that the striving here occurs in two ways? To this he says: "Shall we obtain? and so forth. Therein, "Shall we obtain?
is stated with reference to those in a miserable state. However, "Shall we be able to live, or not? is stated with reference to those who are powerful.
It should be understood as follows. "Bhikkhamānā" means begging. There is also a reading "duhitikā"; there too, the meaning should be understood according to the same method already stated.
For this designation arises through the substitution of the word "du-" for the word "dvi-. Alternatively, it is "duhitikā" because effort (īhita) here is difficult;
that is, no application can be carried out with ease, thus it is "duhitikā," meaning an application of livelihood that is hard to perform.
Alternatively, having changed the letter *u* in the word *du* to *va*, this is the analysis (*niddesa*) as "dvīhitikā"; thus he says "or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth.
"Byādhi" and "roga" are synonyms for "āturatā" (affliction). By this, he shows that there is a certain class of disease called *setaṭṭikā*.
That disease, moreover, arises from the corruption of parasites (*pāṇaka*). It is said that a certain parasite [attacks] a knot located in the middle of the stalk.
It is pierced; because it has been pierced, even the tip of the rice stalk, though emerged, is unable to take up milk. Therefore he said, "with its milk cut off," and so forth.
"Sown grain" means grain that has been planted.
"Therein" means in Verañjā. It is called *salākāvutta* because a mere tally-stick (*salākā*) is used there for measurement.
This is an expression formed by the elision of the latter member of the compound *purimapada*. Therefore he said: "It turns out to be merely a tally-stick (*salākā*).
The meaning is that whatever was spoken or sown therein became nothing more than a mere tally-stick; no fruit was produced.

Furthermore, by the word *sampajjati*, he shows that in the phrase "spoken as a tally-stick" (*salākāvutta*), the word *vutta* has the sense of "resulting" or "coming into being. Regarding the term *salākāya*:
"By means of a tally made from bamboo, *vilīva* wood, palm leaves, and so forth. "In the presence of those who sell grain":
those who sell grain are "grain-sellers"; the meaning is "in their vicinity. "Among buyers": among those who take grain. "Having bought": having taken [the grain].
"At the place for preparing grain": in a location near the storehouse; it is said to mean "at the place for threshing grain."
"Appreciative of color" refers to one who examines *kahāpaṇa* coins. "Not easy to subsist by means of the *paggaha*"—*paggaha* means that which is held out;

thus it is the alms-bowl (*patta*). The meaning is: "by means of that *paggaha*, [that is] by means of the bowl. What is intended is that it is not possible to subsist by wandering for alms while holding the bowl.
For this very reason, he said: "The alms-gathering by means of the *paggaha*," and so forth. "Not easy" refers to the state of being easy.

"Here there is none" means they are not easy [to find]. "Having wandered for alms" means for the purpose of wandering for alms; for some maintain that the particle *tvā* can also express the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

They came from the Northern Region (*Uttarāpatha*), or those whose dwelling is the Northern Region are called *Uttarāpathaka*; however, according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*), what should have been called *Uttarāpathaka* is stated as *Uttarāhaka*.
Therefore he said, "those who dwell in the Northern Region," and so forth. Or else, it is simply *Uttarāpathaka*.
The reading of the Pāli text should be understood as it stands. However, some explain the meaning in another way, saying: “They bring superior (uttara) or excellent goods, thus they are ‘uttarāhakā’;
or, they take a higher or greater price, thus they are ‘uttarāhakā’,” and so forth.
“In the place where horses arise” means in the source or breeding-ground of horses. “Verañjā” means in Verañjā; for here the locative sense is intended.
This is a term of application (*upayogavacana*). "Mandira" means a stable for horses.

"They were known as *assamaṇḍalikā*" means that because they were constructed in a circular form, they became well-known as *assamaṇḍalikā*. And because there were many such horse stables thus constructed, the plural number was employed.
Some also say that each *assamaṇḍalikā* is a place for ten horses to reside. [Horses] capable of enduring long journeys.
“They are not” means they are not capable of persisting for a long time; what is meant is that they do not continue for a long duration.
With the intention that the southern direction from the Ganges is an unsuitable location while the northern direction is a suitable location, he said, “For those [are not],” and so forth.
Those born on the southern bank of the Ganges are the people of the Southern Land (Dakkhiṇāpatha). “He is our Buddha”—thus...

"Buddhamāmaka" means "those who come to me as Buddha. The same applies to the remaining terms. "Paṭiyādetuṃ" means to prepare. "By way of a regular meal" (*niccabhattasaṅkhepena*) means by way of a fixed meal.
Regarding "at the time of morning" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*), he says "the meaning is 'at the time of morning'" because this accusative case is used in the sense of a locative.
Alternatively, to show that this accusative case expresses the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*), [he gives an example] of how the meaning of continuous connection [is expressed].
Showing that this is possible, he says, "at the time of the morning," and so forth. "Thus" means when the meaning is being stated in the manner just described.

Now, one might ask: even those sitting in a monastery sit having already put on their inner robe (*antaravāsaka*); therefore, why was it said, "having put on [the inner robe]"? To this he replies: "by way of changing the monastery-robe," and so forth.

And regarding "the changing of the dwelling and the undergarment": even when one is seated in the monastery, at the time of entering the village again, one should lift up the undergarment that was already worn, adjust it here and there, and put it on properly;
thus it should be understood as "the undergarment itself. For this very reason it is said:
"For they were not unworn by him prior to that. "Taking bowl and robe" means having taken both the bowl and the robe.
And here, "taking" does not mean only by means of the hand; rather, it is intended to show that it is simply holding in whatever manner possible.
Thus he provides the application of the meaning according to what is appropriate with the words, "with hands [taking] the bowl," and so forth.
"In every place reached" means in each successive spot within the precincts of the hermitage. Having pounded [it] repeatedly in the mortar...
Regarding the phrase "they consume": why then do those bhikkhus act in this way and consume it themselves?
Is it because it is not permitted to have a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who makes things allowable) cook rice-gruel or a meal on their behalf, or to cook it oneself before consuming it?
To answer this, he says: "There was no *kappiyakāraka* for the elders," and so forth. [This refers to] the state of being allowable or unallowable.
Having stated that it is not appropriate for monks to act in this way without regard [for the rules], he further said, "And it is not permissible," showing that it is also an unallowable state.
He spoke of "living with few possessions" because of the absence of having many belongings due to the maintenance of vessels and such.
"Each their own portion" means their respective shares. "Free from anxiety" means...
They were devoid of effort in anything other than the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). "Tadupiyaṃ" means corresponding to that. "Pisati" means to grind into powder.
He said "by one possessing merit," and so forth, because the work to be performed through specific merits and knowledges is pleasing. "Naṃ" refers to that handful of rice.
From the statement "not from that time onwards," it should be understood that even the Blessed One’s wandering for alms prior to that is being shown.
*Laddhā* means having obtained. Alternatively, the reading is *laddho*, meaning that the position of attendant was not obtained.

But when did the Elder obtain the position of attendant? It is said: Once, it seems, while the Blessed One was traveling along a highway together with the Elder Nāgasamāla, he reached a fork in the road. The Elder stepped aside from the path and [said], "Blessed One, I..."
“I am going by this path,” he said. Then the Blessed One said to him, “Come, bhikkhu; let us go by this way.
He replied, “Very well, Blessed One, take your bowl and robe; I shall go by this path,” and he began to set his bowl and robe on the ground.
Then the Blessed One said, “Bring them, bhikkhu,” and having taken the bowl and robe, [he proceeded].
He set out. As that bhikkhu was traveling by the other path, bandits robbed him of his bowl and robes and split open his head.
Thinking, "The Blessed One is now my refuge, and no other," he approached the Blessed One while blood was still flowing.
When the Blessed One asked, "What is this, bhikkhu? he reported what had happened. Then—
The Blessed One comforted him, saying, "Do not worry, monk; it was precisely for this reason that we prevented you.
On another occasion, however, the Blessed One went from the Pācīnavaṃsa Migadāya to Jantugāma together with the elder Meghiya.
There too, after Meghiya had walked for alms in Jantugāma, he saw a beautiful mango grove on the riverbank and said, "Blessed One..."
"Take your bowl and robe; I shall perform the duties of a recluse in this mango grove," he said.
Although the Blessed One discouraged him three times, he went away. Being obsessed by unwholesome thoughts, he returned and reported what had happened.
To that as well, the Blessed One replied, "It was precisely because we perceived this very reason that we discouraged you."
Having spoken thus, he gradually arrived at Sāvatthī.
There, seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber and surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old;
some monks, when told 'let us go by this path,' go by another, while others [take] my bowl and robe..."
“They place it on the ground; know him as my constant attendant monk. A sense of spiritual urgency arose among the monks.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said:
“Venerable sir, desiring only you, I fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable eon plus a hundred thousand aeons. Is it not so that one of such great wisdom as I—”
“An attendant is appropriate; I shall serve you,” he said. The Blessed One refused, saying, “Enough, Sāriputta!
In whichever direction you dwell, that direction is indeed not empty. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas;
I have no need for an attendant from you. By this same method, [he refused] Mahāmoggallāna first...
Having made [this request], the eighty great disciples rose up. The Blessed One rejected them all.
But the Elder Ānanda remained silent. Then the monks said to him: "Friend, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus requests a place for an attendant;
you too should request one. He replied: "Friends, what kind of place is it that is called 'obtained by request'?"
[He thought: "What, does the Teacher not see me? If he approves, he will say, 'Let Ānanda attend upon me.
Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Ānanda need not be urged by another; knowing it himself, he will attend upon me.
Thereupon the monks said, "Arise, friend Ānanda! Arise, friend Ānanda! [Attend] upon the One of Ten Powers!"
“Ask for it,” they said. The Elder rose and requested eight boons: the four refusals and the four entreaties. The four refusals are as follows:
“Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robe he himself has received;
if he will not give me almsfood; if he will not allow me to dwell in the same Perfumed Chamber; if he will not accept an invitation [to a meal].”
"Having taken these, I will not go; in this way I shall attend upon the Blessed One.
When it was asked, "But what disadvantage do you see here, Ānanda?", he replied, "If I were to receive these things, venerable sir, there would be those who would say:
'Ānanda enjoys the exquisite robes obtained by the One of Ten Powers; he enjoys the almsfood [obtained by the One of Ten Powers].'"
“He dwells in a single fragrant chamber, he goes to a single invitation, and while receiving this gain, he attends upon the Tathāgata;
what burden could there be for one who attends in such a way? Thus he requested these four refusals.
These are called the four requests: “If, venerable sir, the Blessed One will go to the invitation accepted by me, and if I...”
May I have the opportunity to see the Blessed One at the very moment that the assembly comes from across kingdoms and across districts;
may I have the opportunity to approach the Blessed One at the very moment that doubt arises in me;
and likewise, may I receive from him, upon my arrival, whatever Dhamma the Blessed One has taught in my absence.
“I shall speak thus, and in this way I will attend upon the Blessed One. When it was asked, “But what benefit do you see in this, Ānanda?

he replied, “In this case, venerable sir, faithful sons of good family who find no opportunity with the Blessed One say to me, ‘Venerable Ānanda, please accept almsfood at our house together with the Blessed One tomorrow.’”
If the Blessed One does not go there, I will not find the opportunity to show myself to the assembly and dispel their doubts at the very moment they desire it.
People will say, "Why does Ānanda attend upon the One of Ten Powers, yet the Blessed One does not grant him even this much favor?
And in the absence of the Blessed One, they will ask me, "Friend, [why is this so?]"
“Ānanda, where was this verse, this sutta, and this Jātaka taught? If I were not able to determine that, there would be those who would say:

“Friend, you do not even know this much; why did you wander for so long a time, following the Blessed One like a shadow, never leaving him? Therefore, even regarding the Dhamma taught in his absence, I...
“I wish to speak further,” he said, and he made these four requests. The Blessed One granted them as well.
Having thus obtained these eight boons, he became a constant attendant.
It was for the sake of that very position that he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over a hundred thousand eons.
Having arrived, he became the foremost of the attendants and served the Blessed One.

Indeed, from the time he attained the position of attendant, the Elder served the Blessed One with various duties such as providing two kinds of water, three kinds of tooth-sticks, massaging the feet, rubbing the back, and sweeping the Gandhakuṭi and its surrounding courtyard. Thus did he serve.
Thinking, "At this particular time, it is fitting for me to obtain such-and-such from the Teacher; it is fitting for me to perform such-and-such," he would produce each of those things.
Taking a large staff-lamp, he would circumambulate the Gandhakuṭi courtyard nine times during a single night.
For he thought: "If sloth and torpor should overcome me when the Blessed One calls upon me..."
“I would not be able to give a reply. Therefore, throughout the entire night he does not let go of his staff-lamp from his hand;
thus, with reference to the fact that he has not obtained a fixed position as an attendant, it is said:
“but he has not obtained the status of an attendant. “A fixed attendant” (nibaddhupaṭṭhāka) means a regular attendant (niyatupaṭṭhāka).

There were none [fixed]. However, during the Blessed One’s first awakening, there were many who served him without a fixed status; showing these, he said, "Sometimes the Elder Nāgasamāla," and so forth.
Because he was both a kinsman (*ñāti*) and preeminent (*seṭṭha*) due to his possession of highly praised virtues, he is called "the most excellent kinsman" (*ñātiseṭṭha*).
In such circumstances, this alone is appropriate; thus, the giving of prepared food during times of distress is indeed [proper].
The intention is that it is more appropriate for a kinsman to do so.
"By means of Māra’s enticement" (mārāvaṭṭanāya) means by means of the mental turning about caused by Māra; what is meant is: by means of the delusion of mind produced through Māra’s power.
For this very reason he said, "having enticed and deluded," and so forth. "Let alone... even that Māra would entice."
Because of the manifestation of unwholesome kamma accumulated during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, which had found its opportunity at that moment.
For it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"In the dispensation of Phussa, I reviled the disciples..."
"Eat and consume barley, but do not eat with attachment.
"By the ripening of that karma, I ate barley for three months;
invited by a brahmin, I then dwelt in Verañjā."
“With a mind obsessed” means with a mind enveloped; the meaning is that the mind is overcome.
“They came at the conclusion of the turning back” means they came after having been turned back by Māra. “Because of inability” means because of incapacity.
“Of alms brought forth” means of alms being brought after having been cooked. “Of regular giving” means for such a period of time...
"Let us give it to the Blessed One," having thus determined and set aside the gift as a regular meal (*niccabhatta*). "Of the cloth offered":
of the cloth that was brought to the monastery and given with the thought, "This is for the Buddha’s use of the four requisites.
"It does not endure": it is not able [to remain]. "By way of the bringing of alms-food": by means of the effort involved in bringing the alms-food. "The fathom-wide radiance": (*byāmappabhāya*)...

[It was filled] with a radiance extending one fathom (vyāma) all around. Here, it should be understood that the obstruction consists in the eclipsing of the secondary marks (anubyañjana) and the fathom-wide radiance.
For this very reason, he said: "Even of the moon, the sun, the devas, and the brahmas," and so forth. Because the secondary marks and the fathom-wide radiance are joined together as one, it is said:
"Having reached the region of the secondary marks and the fathom-wide radiance. [This refers to] the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
An "obstacle" (*antarāya*) is an obstruction regarding the phenomena to be known (*ñeyyadhamma*).
When it was said, "The Blessed One heard the sound of a mortar," if one asks whether he heard the sound of a mortar that had arisen spontaneously, [the text] says:
"Of those pounding rice that had been soaked for a long time," and so forth. "Beneficial in meaning" (*atthasañhita*) means that which accomplishes a purpose (*payojana*).
"Connected with what is harmful" (*anatthasañhita*) means words based on what is harmful. The locative case is used in the sense of "seeking to destroy.
Since destruction is accomplished by that [path] against which it is directed, it is said that the destruction of such speech is brought about by that very path; thus it is stated:
"By the path itself, the destruction and eradication of such speech is meant. Alternatively, one might consider the locative case to be used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*).
"It says thus" is how it should be understood. And the eradication of the statement should be known as occurring through the eradication of the defilements rooted in it.
It is called an "ākāra" (mode) because it produces (*ākaroti*) a fruit that is commensurate with itself, having its own boundaries and limits;
thus he said, "by modes means by causes. "Connected with an occasion" means that which proceeds based on a present circumstance.

"By making the transgression evident through that question" means: having made manifest the transgression committed by that bhikkhu through such questions as "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you [did this]?
The purpose of making the transgression manifest is for the sake of authorizing the laying down of this training rule, [asking]:
"For what purpose is this training rule being prescribed?"
“There is nothing further to be said”: because of the method already stated previously, this shows that there is nothing new here to be said.
Therefore he says, “For it has already been said before,” and so forth. “Excellent, excellent!”—this is a reduplicated expression used for praise;
thus he says, “encouraging the Venerable Ānanda. “In two ways” refers to those [ways] consisting of the teaching of the Dhamma and the laying down of the training rules.
"In two circumstances. "Taking one" means taking the reason stated as "I shall teach the Dhamma.
"In such a time of famine" (*evaṃ-dubbhikkhe*) means in a time or place where alms-food (*bhikkhā*) is obtained with difficulty;
this is an explanation of the meaning of "where food is hard to obtain" (*dullabha-piṇḍe*). [This is] because of having many belongings due to the necessity of carrying vessels and other such items.

It is said, "by this lightness of livelihood," because of its absence [of hardship]. However, it is said, "and by this austerity (sallekha)," because there is no further aspiration [beyond] thinking that "this much alone is sufficient for maintenance.

Regarding the phrase "a famine has been won": here, *dubbhikkha* means the absence of alms (*bhikkhā*), as in expressions such as "free from flies" (*nimmakkhika*). For it is precisely the absence of alms that constitutes the distress of the mind caused by them.

Because it was non-existent, it was conquered by the bhikkhus and brought under control. "Greed was conquered" means that even greed in the form of covetousness—which, for the sake of material gain, gives rise to the offenses of interrupting the night or the rains retreat—did not exist among them;
thus, greed consisting of craving for material things was conquered. "Improper conduct was conquered" means:
"We shall make a living by trading in our virtues, proclaiming superhuman qualities to one another for the sake of material gain. This [conduct] was conquered.
Because such conduct of desire was absent, the aforementioned conduct of desire was conquered.
The phrase "or thought" is stated with reference to the fact that not even a mere arising of a mental state occurred.
Furthermore, the phrase "or distress" is stated to show that there was no affliction of the mind through repeated grieving.

"Or the breaking of the night" means that either the breaking of the night by staying outside until dawn after having gone on account of a seven-day business was not performed, or because he did not go anywhere even for the sake of a seven-day task.

For the term "breaking of the night" is a conventional expression in the Aṭṭhakathā with reference to being away from home on account of a seven-day task; and for this very reason, in the commentary to the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*:

Having stated, "This, however, is the decision regarding the breaking of the night (*ratticcheda*) outside of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*)," it is explained that "it is not permitted for one who has not been invited to go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma," and so forth, thus detailing only the seven-day business (*sattāhakaraṇīya*). It is also said in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Having gone on account of a seven-day task, not even a single bhikkhu broke the night. And having done so, the breaking of the night—
It should be understood that the definition of the interruption of the night is stated here [only] because it occurs by way of a seven-day business and not otherwise.
Furthermore, since the interruption of the night is also mentioned when the cause for interrupting the rains— namely, a deficiency of requisites— is present,
it is established that where such a cause for interrupting the rains exists, it is permissible to go even on account of a seven-day task.
This is stated in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, and it is well-stated in the section concerning the interruption of the rains residence in the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*:

"Now at that time, in a certain monastery, the village of the monks who had entered for the rains was plundered by bandits. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow you to go to where the village is.'"
This is because it accords with the following passage from the Commentary: "In this case, if the village is not far away, one should go there for alms and then return to the monastery to stay.
If it is far away, the dawn should be made to rise after a seven-day interval. If that is not possible, one should stay right there in a suitable place.
For indeed, when one has stayed in the village for alms...
Since the Blessed One, stating that there is no offense even when the rains retreat is interrupted due to a lack of food, said, "Bhikkhus,
I allow you to go to whatever village [you may need]," the absence of almsfood is a cause for interrupting the rains retreat.
In this regard, the statement from the Aṭṭhakathā, "If one has gone far away, dawn should be made to rise after every seven days," applies when such a cause for interrupting the rains retreat exists.
This establishes the point that it is permissible to go on a seven-day business mission.
As for what was stated by someone else—"The 'breaking of the night' is said with reference to a seven-day business; having gone on a seven-day mission, the breaking of the night..."
"Or else, even a single bhikkhu did not break the rains retreat," so it is said in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

Therefore, some say that when there is a reason for breaking the rains retreat, it is permissible to perform the seven-day business (*sattāhakicca*). However, the holders of the Vinaya do not accept this;
therefore, the intention of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) should be investigated."
That, however, is merely an attempt to cause confusion in others while being confused oneself.
For no reason is found for the Vinaya-dharas’ reluctance, since it contradicts the Aṭṭhakathā and lacks logical consistency.

Indeed, if the reason that establishes there is no offense even when interrupting the rains-residence were valid, then it would follow that it is not permissible to go on a seven-day mission without interrupting the rains-residence.

What is the reasoning? The statement, "Let us enter the rains residence there during the later period," illustrates the appropriate reflection of those monks, but it does not illustrate a specific purpose.
For indeed, since the interruption of the rains residence is permissible due to famine, there is no offense even if one interrupts the rains during the earlier period;
likewise, there is no offense even if one goes with the intention of not entering the rains during the later period.
There is no fault, because the day for the later invitation (*pacchimikā vassūpanāyikā*) has not yet arrived.
"They do not conceive anything" means they do not conceive [pride] toward any quality by way of esteem. "Having manifested" means having manifested by way of qualities such as jhāna already attained.
Regarding the conduct of desire that occurs in such a manner when there is care for the belly, as stated in the passage: "We shall resolve upon virtue afterwards."
"Because of the state of impurity and the absence of purity in livelihood, one must strive again and establish oneself in restraint"—thus he said, "Later we shall resolve upon virtue. What is this?
It is stated by way of censure. It is rice prepared with fine grains of rice and basted with meat broth.
*Sālimamsodanaṃ*. "He will despise" means he will think with a sense of contempt;
it is said that he will think of it as something base and inferior. Therefore he said, "he will treat it with contempt and disdain.
*Oññātaṃ* means known as being placed below or made inferior. *Avaññātaṃ* is a synonym for that very same thing. *Svāyaṃ* means "this one."
“Country”: by this practice—that is, by the practice fulfilled at Verañjā, which was extremely difficult to perform.
“Depending on you”: depending on this practice of fewness of desires belonging to you. “Those reckoned as fellow-celibates”:
the group of six and others are meant. “Sitting among you”: sitting in your midst, sitting together with you.

It has been said. "O māna" means overweening pride (*atimāna*). Here, it is overweening pride itself that is called "o māna" because of its inferiority, and not the conceit that comes from despising others.
Having thus construed the text here as, "Ānanda, future generations will look down upon the fine rice and meat that were won by you, the true men," they explain the meaning. This is what is meant:
"Because you were satisfied with whatever was obtained and cut off your aspiration for fine rice and meat,
and because future generations will be unable to sever their aspirations for that fine rice and meat which has been conquered and overcome by you, they will hold it in contempt.
The Discourse on Famine is finished.
The Discourse on the Lion’s Roar of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. 17.
Regarding the phrase "the Venerable": whether one says "the Venerable," or "Devānampiya" (Beloved of the Gods), or "Bhadda" (Fortunate One), this is a term of endearment;
thus he said, "‘The Venerable’ is a word of affection. For when those of a discerning nature address another with affection, they say "Sir" or "Devānampiya."
They address him as "Venerable" (āyasmā) or "Friend" (āvuso). Therefore, "Friend" is used for addressing him in his presence, while "Venerable" is used when he is out of sight;
this too is a form of conventional address. Since these terms are spoken out of affection, reverence, and deference, it is said:
"This is a designation based on reverence and deference. He is called Mahāmoggallāna because of the greatness of his qualities, not Cūḷamoggallāna.
Regarding "because of its existence," he said: "And it is great because of the greatness of its qualities.

*Pappaṭako* refers to an extremely sweet essence of the earth, resembling a layer of mud, which arises on the lower surface of the great earth where water stands in contact with the earth's foundation and which is submerged by a flood of water in that region of ground. That [essence] would not be for me.
"Suitable" means: "To act without having asked for permission would not be appropriate for me.

And by acting without asking for permission, he thought, "Just as the Blessed One does whatever he wishes without asking for permission, so shall I too," thereby making himself equal to the Blessed One;
thus it was as if he acted out of pride. Therefore he said: "It was like a seizing of the yoke with the Blessed One..."

“...would have been made together with another. For grasping by making oneself a pair or a couple equal to another is “grasping as a pair” (*yugaggāha*), which is the apprehension [thinking], “What distinction is there for me?
“Accomplished” (*sampanna*) means endowed with excellence.
Here, however, it is the excellence of flavor (*rasasampatti*) that is intended, because the general term is used in a specific sense.
“From the standpoint of being well-prepared. Therefore he said: “‘Well-prepared’ means sweet and of good flavor; this is the meaning. For there are three ways of being well-prepared:
by way of being complete, by way of being possessed [of all parts], and by way of being sweet. In that regard:
“The rice-fields are well-prepared, O Kosiya, and the crows eat the grain;”
“I inform you, O Brahmā; I am not able to stop them.

This is what is called “perfectly complete and accomplished” (*paripuṇṇasampanna*). For even that which is perfectly complete is called “accomplished” (*sampanna*) because it has spread out all around.
“By means of this Pātimokkha restraint, one is endowed, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, and accomplished.”

“Endowed with” (*samannāgato*) refers to being fully possessed (*samaṅgī-sampanna*). For one who has truly attained (*samma eva patto*) and reached (*gato*) [the state] is called “endowed” (*sampanno*).
“In that case, there is a tree endowed with fruit and possessed of fruit” (*tatrassa rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca*); this refers to being endowed with sweetness (*madhura-sampanna*).
It should be understood that it is this “endowment with sweetness” which is intended here. “Possessed of fruit” (*upapannaphalo*) means having abundant fruit.
"Assa" means of the lower surface of the earth. "For the purpose of illustrating by way of a simile" means for the sake of demonstrating through a comparison.
"Anīḷaka" means faultless. And here, its faultlessness consists in being free from flies and the like; thus he said "nimmakkhika" and so forth. "Nimmakkhika" means there are no flies there.
And here, by the word "makkhikā," the fly's sting is also included by way of general usage.
They say it means "taken. For that very reason, it is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"In order to clarify the meaning of this term 'free from flies' (*nimmakkhika*), it is said 'free from fly-eggs' (*nimmakkhikaṇḍaka*); the meaning is that it is devoid of flies and their eggs.
However, our own preference here is as follows: "Fly-eggs" (*makkhikaṇḍa*) are the eggs of flies; [the term] means "there are no fly-eggs here."
"Free from fly-eggs": by this, its being devoid of flies' eggs is stated;
however, by "free from flies," the total absence of flies themselves is stated. This, it is said, is "honey," namely the honey made by small bees.
"Of all honeys" refers to those made by large bees, bumblebees, and so forth. "Supreme" means the most excellent. "Best" means the most praised.
“Surasanti” means having a beautiful flavor. “Ojavantanti” means possessing extreme vitality (*ojas*).
With the words “this is a request,” he turns away from the purpose of acceptance, encouragement, and so forth. “Ekaṃ hatthanti” means one palm of the hand.
To clarify the meaning already stated—“I shall manifest”—he says, “I shall make it like the earth.”
It has been said. By the phrase "Is this indeed the earth, or is it not?
he demonstrates the anxiety that arises because the fashioned earth resembles the natural earth, thinking: "Is this our own earth, or is it another?
A *nigama* is a village with a constant and abundant income; it means a large village where great wealth is generated.
He indicates the prima facie position by stating, "This is not a perversion. But why is this not a perversion? He says:
"For the range of psychic power (iddhi) of one possessing psychic power is inconceivable. The intention is that, by the very power of psychic power, such a perversion will not occur for those beings.
Now, showing the acquisition of a perversion in another way, he says: "In this manner..."
"Panā" and so forth. "Reproaching" means reproaching in their presence. "Slandering" means reviling them behind their backs. [Objection:
But was it not the case that after prohibiting the going for alms to Uttarakuru, the reason was not stated as to why beings would even incur perversity?
Therefore, what is the reason here? To this he says: "In this regard, although... and so forth. Even if... [text continues]

Although this has been stated, it is understood that for the very same reason—the fact that beings might also acquire the perversions (*vipallāsa*)—the Blessed One prohibited going to Uttarakuru for alms; therefore, showing that this same reason must be applied here as well, he said:
"It should be understood in the manner previously explained. [The phrase] "even the perversions" (*vipallāsampi*).
The intention is that even though the phrase "they might acquire existence" (*sattā paṭilabheyyun*) was not explicitly stated here, it should be brought forward and connected [to the context].

Its meaning should also be understood as being exactly like what was stated previously. However, he speaks with reference to the alternative interpretation of the meaning stated later, beginning with "but they might thus acquire perversion" (*evaṃ pana vipallāsaṃ paṭilabheyyun*).
As for what was stated there—"having produced those qualities..."—[it refers to the following].
Regarding the statement, "In times of famine, having turned over the earth, they consumed the papphataka-plant food," one should apply the interpretation here as follows:
having removed that [previous state] and produced those qualities, they went to Uttarakuru during a time of famine, walked for alms, and consumed [the food].
As for the phrase "with a single stride of a footstep" (*padavītihārena*), here the "striding of a foot" (*padassa vītiharaṇa*) means its placing down.
"Padavītihāra" means the placing of a foot; therefore, it is said "by a single placing of a foot.
The distance to be traversed by a single step is the space between two feet when walking normally, which is the measure of a fist (muṭṭhiratana); therefore [it is so called].
"Having resolved upon the mere measure of a mat" means having resolved upon the measure of a mat, which is the size of a fist.
The discourse on the Lion’s Roar of Mahāmoggallāna is concluded.
18. The Discourse on Requesting the Formulation of the Discipline (*Vinayapaññatti*).

Regarding the phrase "formulation of the discipline," this is said with reference to training rules (*sikkhāpada*) not previously formulated. For the Elder [Mahākassapa] [was concerned with] those training rules already formulated...
Setting aside [the previous matter], he spoke with reference to the training rules now to be formulated and the recitation of the Pātimokkha, saying:
"Bhagavā, this is the time; Sugata, this is the time for the Bhagavā to formulate a training rule for his disciples and to recite the Pātimokkha. And the Bhagavā—
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why formerly there were fewer training rules and more bhikkhus established in final knowledge?
But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why now there are more training rules and fewer bhikkhus established in final knowledge? “It is so, Ananda.”
“Bhaddāli, when beings are declining and the true Dhamma is disappearing,
there are more training rules and fewer bhikkhus who remain established in higher knowledge. Bhaddāli,
the Teacher does not lay down a training rule for his disciples until certain things that are the basis for the taints appear within the Saṅgha.”
In this *Bhaddāli Sutta*, even though certain rules have already been laid down, it is said with reference to those yet to be laid down:
"Sāriputta, the Teacher has not yet laid down a training rule for his disciples.

And in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on this very passage, the statement, "Even cooking for oneself is not befitting a recluse and is not permitted," refers to the "breaking of the night" (*ratticchedo*).
The statement, "or whether the interruption of the rains-residence has been made," should be understood as the authority for the existence of the training rules (sikkhāpada) previously laid down.
Because the remaining training rules and the recitation of the Pātimokkha were established through the request of the Elder, he said, "in order to show the source from the very beginning.
"Of one who has gone into seclusion" means of one who has approached a place secluded from people.
By that absence of association with a group, he expresses the physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) of the Elder. "Of one who has retired into solitude" (*paṭisallīnassa*):
because of the withdrawal of the mind from wandering among various objects, it means of one who has properly settled within, whose mind is not scattered therein.

By that absence of mental association (*cittasaṅgaṇikā*), he expresses his prior-stage mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). "For a long time" (*ciram*): this is the accusative case used in connection with an absolute duration, referring to time.
“Endures for a long time” means that its persistence is stated without distinction over a long period.
“He is not able to do this” means he is not able to determine this.
Having shown the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he now says “But the Elder Mahāpaduma,” etc., in order to present the Theravāda position. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says “he is not able.”
Because one who knows this is nevertheless unable to discern it correctly, they say that [the teaching] was spoken [for such a person].
"Of one who has reached the pinnacle of the sixteenfold wisdom" refers to the instruction given in the *Anupada Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*:
"Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is of great wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta is of vast wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta is of radiant wisdom..."
“Sāriputta, monks, has swift wisdom; Sāriputta, monks, has sharp wisdom; Sāriputta, monks, has penetrative wisdom.
