Thus, there are six types of wisdom beginning with “great wisdom” as they appear in that very sutta, along with the wisdom of the nine successive attainments and the wisdom of the path to Arahantship. Of these sixteenfold divisions of wisdom, he [Sāriputta] reached the highest pinnacle within the domain of the disciples.
But why did the Blessed One here speak only of the long-lasting and short-lived nature of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the seven Buddhas beginning with Vipassī,
and not of twenty-five Buddhas as in the *Buddhavamsa* teaching, or even more than that?
[It is because] the teaching of realization (*paṭivedhasāsana*) of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones still persists even today by way of absolute certainty, and has not disappeared.
Reciting those very names, he spoke here of the long-lasting or short-lived nature of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Blessed Ones beginning with Vipassī.
For it is only their disciples who remain in the Suddhāvāsa realm both then and now, because the disciples of others have attained final Nibbāna.
It is said that the disciples of the Buddhas Siddhattha, Tissa, and Phussa [likewise] remained in the Suddhāvāsa realms.
They say that those who arose [in this dispensation] attained Arahantship immediately upon their arising—just like Upaka and others—and passed away into Parinibbāna before long;
they did not remain as disciples in various places for the full duration of their lifespan.
However, the rule regarding "neither first nor last" applies to a single world-system in terms of beings who transmigrate from one existence to another.
It should be understood that this does not contradict [the statement] "it is desired.
There is no purpose here in making such distinctions as "an uncommon cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*) and "a common condition" (*sādhāraṇa-paccaya*),
because the inquiry here concerns the reasons for the short duration and the long duration of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of Vipassī and the other Buddhas.
Regarding the word "impulsion" (*codanā*), he says: "Both 'cause' (*hetu*) and 'condition' (*paccaya*) are synonyms for 'reason' (*kāraṇa*).
He says "by that, its fruit" and so forth because the word *hetu* is here used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning "it causes (*hinoti*) the fruit [to arise].

However, the word *hetu* is not unfit to be used in the sense of an agent (*kattusādhana*) as well; for it can mean "it goes toward (*hinoti*) the state of being a cause for the fruit. Depending on that...
"It comes and occurs" means that, depending on that cause, its fruit comes, occurs, and is produced; this is the meaning.
"They became lazy" means they became inactive, they became lacking in effort; this is the meaning.
However, that lack of effort was not due to indolence, so he said, "not lazy through indolence," meaning they did not become lazy by way of indolence.

Regarding this, he states the reason with the words beginning “for not,” and so forth. By the phrase “or laziness,” he indicates the absence of unwholesome states that proceed from dullness and torpor (*thina-middha*).

By the phrase “or slackness of energy,” however, he refers to a lack of enthusiasm for teaching the Dhamma to anyone whatsoever—even to one who carries a load of food or is a hunter—based on the statement: “Even in the absence of laziness, he teaches the Dhamma with due care.”
He shows that [the teaching] does not exist [for others] because the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma occurs with an equal effort on the part of all.

Therefore he said, “For the Buddhas,” and so forth. “With slackened energy” means those whose energy has declined; the sense is that they are inactive. “With intensified energy” means those with superior energy;

the sense is that they possess great exertion. “With speed” means with swiftness. “Those who hold the Dhamma dear” (dhammagaruno) means those for whom the Dhamma is of high value. “Those who have reverence for the Dhamma” means...
They have reverence for the Dhamma. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, the lifespan was eighty thousand years;
during that of Sikhī, seventy thousand years; and during that of Vessabhū, sixty thousand years.
Thus it is said: "In their time, beings were long-lived. *Abhisamenti* means they penetrate [the truth].
“Because it is faultless” means because there is an absence of the fault of transgression.

It is said that the training precepts of instruction were established not by way of offenses—such as declaring, “In this transgression, such-and-such an offense occurs”—but rather by way of teaching the Dhamma, beginning with, “Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from the taking of life.
Therefore, they are called the “training precepts of command” by way of the seven classes of offenses.
"Unprescribed. The phrase "at the end of each six years" should be understood as an ellipsis.
Alternatively, since it is said "once each" with reference to the day of conclusion for each six-year period, this genitive case is used in relation to that.
Thus, the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus throughout the whole of Jambudīpa performed the Uposatha at one and the same place.
[The question] "What is that place? is answered with the words "In the royal capital of Bandhumatī," and so forth.
At that time, Isipatana was a park named Khema; however, because it had been granted as a sanctuary where deer lived without fear, it was called Migadāya (the Deer Park).
It is with reference to this that it is said, "in the Khema Migadāya."

"Ten or even twenty thousand bhikkhus dwell unmixed" means that ten or even twenty thousand bhikkhus dwell without being in contact with persons of a different class (*visabhāga*). However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:
"All those great monasteries capable of accommodating twelve thousand bhikkhus are like the Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, and Cittalapabbata monasteries."

And it is said, "they were. "Uposathārocikā" means those who announce the Uposatha. It is said that those deities, when one year had elapsed, would go here and there and announce: "Venerable sirs, one year has indeed passed;
five years now remain. At the end of five years, the royal capital Bandhumatī must be approached."
“...for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Likewise, when two years had passed, they announced: “Venerable sirs, two years have indeed passed;
four years remain. At the end of four years, the royal capital Bandhumatī must be approached for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
In this same manner, [they announced] when three, four, and five [years had passed].
They announced [the news] after the rains had passed. Therefore it was said: “Venerable sirs, one year has passed,” and so forth.
“Possessed of power” means possessed of power through supernormal psychic power (*iddhānubhāva*). “Those monks, it is said,” he says referring to those who travel by means of the power of deities.
“At the edge of the eastern ocean” means in a region near the eastern ocean. “The duty of those traveling” refers to that which must be performed by those who are traveling.
The duty of maintaining the lodgings and so forth. "The Uposatha hall" means the place for performing the Uposatha ceremony.
"They have indeed gone" means they have gone by the power of the deities. "All of them" refers to everyone who has gone by their own power and by the power of the deities.
In passages such as "Patience is supreme," one endures the censure of others, the harm done by others, and obstacles to one's virtues such as cold and heat.

It endures and patiently accepts, thus it is *khanti*. Furthermore, because it specifically heats, intensely heats, and dispels the states that are the opposites of virtue (*sīla*) and the other perfections, it is the supreme and highest *tapo* (asceticism). Enduring and being patient is *titikkhā*;
this is a synonym for *khanti* itself. For etymologists explain the word *titikkhā* as meaning "patience" (*khamā*); therefore, such is the meaning here.
It should be understood that "the supreme austerity is indeed patience, which is defined as endurance" (*titikkhā*). The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme.
It is called *bhava* because it destroys one existence with another, or because it binds through the state of craving for existence;
or alternatively, it is reckoned as *vāna* because, for one who still possesses craving, it destroys or binds karma along with its fruit so as to produce renewed existence in the future.
Nirvana has emerged from craving that has gone; it is so called because of the absolute absence of that craving therein.
Furthermore, the Buddhas declare that Nirvana is supreme in every respect, by way of such qualities as being peaceful, sublime, subtle, auspicious, and secure.
For one who harms others is not a renunciant—meaning one who, due to a lack of patience in endurance, injures or oppresses another.
He harms; he is not truly called one who has gone forth, because he does not cause that which ought to be gone forth to go forth.
Furthermore, the fourth line is a synonym for the third line, as there is no difference in meaning.
For "not a renunciant" is a synonym for "not a śramaṇa," and "one who harms others" is a synonym for "one who oppresses others."
Alternatively, "one who harms others" means one who harms virtue (*sīla*).
For virtue is called "the other" in the sense of being supreme, because the word *para* denotes what is best, as in such expressions as "one who knows the higher and lower persons.
The meaning is that a recluse who, by harassing any living being whatsoever, becomes a harmer of others and a destroyer of his own virtue, is not truly a renunciant.

Alternatively, one who harms others due to a lack of patience characterized by forbearance—even if he deprives another of life, down to a mere gadfly or mosquito—is not truly a renunciant. Why is that?
Because the stain of evil has not been removed from him; it has not been cast out. For this is the defining characteristic of a renunciant:
“Because he has cast out the stain from himself, therefore he is called a renunciant.”
Even one who does not injure or kill, but nevertheless harasses another with sticks and the like, is not a recluse (samaṇa) while thus harassing another.
Why? Because he has not stilled (samita) his harassment. For it is said that "one is called a recluse because of having stilled [evil]";
this indeed is the characteristic of a recluse. Indeed, it is stated: "Because of having stilled evil deeds, one is called a recluse."

Furthermore, while reciting the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus, the Blessed One—since the discourse on the Pātimokkha is centered on virtue (*sīla*), and since hatred (*dosa*) is specifically the adversary of virtue—spoke at the outset, "Patience is the supreme austerity," in order to show the method for its suppression.
By that, the means for warding off the undesirable was stated; however, by the inclusion of the term "forbearance" (*titikkhā*),...

By both of these, the meaning is shown as follows: "Having overcome both the discontent that has arisen regarding what is undesirable and the delight that has arisen regarding what is desirable, he dwells.
Because it pacifies craving and its concomitants, the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme.

In this context, by the mention of *khanti* (forbearance), the absence of failure in application is shown; by the mention of *titikkhā* (endurance), the absence of failure in disposition is shown. Likewise, by the mention of *khanti*...
By the inclusion of "forbearance" (titikkhā), the non-offending toward others even when they commit offenses is shown.

Having thus demonstrated the Pātimokkha through the method of positive concomitance (anvaya) by way of its causes, the words beginning with "na hi" are now spoken in order to demonstrate it through negative concomitance (byatireka).
By this, it is shown that the taking of life from beings and the harming of others with hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth, constitutes "injury to others" (parūpaghāta).
It is called "afflicting others. Thus, for anyone, the seizure of their property,
the grasping [of their belongings], the deceiving, the causing of mutual division, the striking at the vital points with harsh speech, the useless prattle, the coveting of what belongs to another,
the thinking of their destruction, and the wrong adherence— all these constitute injury and the afflicting of others.
This shows that by performing unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome deeds, one is neither a renunciant nor a *samaṇa*.

In the second verse, "of all evil" (*sabbapāpassa*) refers to all that is unwholesome—namely, all twelve types of unwholesome [deeds] and all blameworthy phenomena (*sāvajjadhamma*) comprised within every arising of consciousness.
"Non-doing" (*akaraṇa*) means non-arising; for "doing" indeed means the production of that [evil] within one's own continuum.
Non-doing and non-arousing are the negation of that [unwholesome state]. "Of the wholesome" means of the wholesome belonging to the four planes.

For this term "of the wholesome," because it will be stated later that "this is the teaching of the Buddhas," indicates both the noble path-dhammas and the wholesome dhammas of the three planes which serve as their requisites. "Attainment" (upasampadā) means the act of attaining. As for its meaning, however, it is...
The attainment and acquisition of the wholesome. "The purification of one’s own mind" means the brightening of one's own mind, the making of the mind luminous, its complete cleansing.

That, moreover, occurs through Arahantship. And here, because the mind of one who possesses the supreme path is said to be completely purified, whereas at the moment of the supreme fruit it is already purified.
It is because there is no further need for purification; therefore, with reference to the completion of purification, it is said:

"That, moreover, occurs through Arahantship. Thus, having abandoned all evil by means of the restraint of virtue, and having accomplished the wholesome by means of mundane and supramundane serenity and insight, the mind is to be purified by the fruit of Arahantship—this is what is meant.
The teaching, advice, and instruction of the Buddhas.
In the third verse, "non-reproach" means not reproaching anyone by way of speech. "Non-injury" means not causing injury to anyone by way of body or mind;
it refers to the non-infliction of injury even by way of the mind through such means as thinking of harm toward others.

Because it is to be avoided. Regarding the *pātimokkha*: that which is the *pātimokkha*—the preeminent, supreme virtue (*sīla*)—is called *pātimokkha* because it protects (*pāti*) one from the fears of unhappy destinies (*duggati*) and liberates (*mokkheti*) one from the fears of miserable states, or because it protects (*pāti*) that which is liberated (*mokkheti*).
And in that *pātimokkha*, "restraint" (*saṃvara*) is characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
Restraint (*saṃvara*). "Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññutā*) means knowing the measure in food by way of receiving and consuming it.
"A secluded lodging" (*pantañ ca sayanāsanaṃ*) refers to a dwelling place that is free from the bustle of crowds, devoid of people, and solitary.
Here, it should be understood that contentment with the four requisites is illustrated by means of only two requisites, due to their commonality as contentment with requisites.
Because the other two [factors] are also illuminated by way of the method of extraction (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*). Regarding "application to higher mind" (*adhicitte ca āyogo*):
the eight attainments of consciousness that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*) are "higher mind" (*adhicitta*); furthermore, only the path and fruit consciousnesses are "higher mind.
Application (*āyoga*) and devoted practice (*anuyoga*) toward that aforementioned higher mind is the meaning. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas" refers to this [teaching] for others.

Non-reproaching, non-harming, restraint according to the Pātimokkha, moderation in receiving and using [alms-food], resorting to secluded lodgings, and devotion to higher consciousness—this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these are the verses for reciting the Pātimokkha common to all Buddhas. Therefore, he said: "By this very method," and so forth.
"Until the end of the Dispensation" is said with reference to the limit of the instruction of the Buddhas currently existing;
it means that as long as the Buddhas endure, [the Uposatha] remains subject to recitation.
For it is the Buddhas alone who recite the *Ovāda-pātimokkha*, not the disciples. The connection is that it comes to be recited even during the first enlightenment.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* that the first enlightenment (*paṭhamabodhi*) is delimited by twenty years.

This was said by taking the phrase "the first enlightenment consists of twenty years" based on what was already stated below in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Indeed, during the first twenty years of the Blessed One’s enlightenment, there was no one who could be called a constant attendant. [This was stated] by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
However, it is stated that "of the forty-five years, the first fifteen years constitute the First Enlightenment.
This being the case, it would follow that the middle fifteen years constitute the Middle Enlightenment and the final fifteen years constitute the Last Enlightenment;
thus, the three Enlightenments would be equal in measure, which is also appropriate. For by means of the number fifteen, [the total] forty-five...

They fulfill the years. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), because the period of twenty years following the First Enlightenment is already included within the fifteen-year measure [of that era], it is stated:
"within the twenty-year interval of the First Enlightenment. This can also be understood in this way.
But is it not the case that even after some training rules (*sikkhāpada*) had been laid down, the *Āṇāpātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha as a formal command) was not yet permitted? Later...
Because it was authorized by the request of the Elder, how then can this be said:
"From the time of the promulgation of the training rules (sikkhāpada), however, only the *āṇā-pātimokkha* is recited"?

Even though the *āṇā-pātimokkha* was not authorized until after certain training rules had been promulgated, nevertheless, when a training rule has not yet been promulgated, there is no *āṇā-pātimokkha*.
However, in order to show this meaning—that [the offense] occurs only when it has been laid down—it is said: "from the time of the laying down of the training rule onwards.
"In the Eastern Monastery" refers to the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra), which received that designation because it was built in the eastern direction of Sāvatthī.
"In the Palace of Migāra’s Mother" refers to the great female lay disciple Visākhā, who had come to be known as "Migāra’s Mother" because she stood in the place of a mother to the merchant Migāra.
When the palace was built. "An impossibility" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause. "No occasion" (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition.
By both terms, he negates the very reason. "By which" (*yaṃ*) means by which reason. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the monks.
"Those who went forth in the presence of the face-to-face disciples" refers even to the very last ones, such as Subhadda.
He speaks with reference to those who have gone forth in the presence of the face-to-face disciples. The connection is that "various families" refers specifically to the Kṣatriya clan and so forth.

It should be construed either as "by way of high, low, eminent, noble, wealthy, and so forth families," or as "by way of high and low families, and by way of eminent, noble, wealthy, and so forth families.
In that regard, it may be by way of the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa [clans], or by way of the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and householders.

Or, noble birth is to be understood by way of the remaining [factors], while low birth is understood by way of the others. Or, it is by way of a family possessing excellent and most excellent wealth and so forth;

that is, by way of a family possessing enjoyment that is more or most excellent. The word "excellent" (*uḷāra*) is used again for the purpose of indicating an even higher degree of excellence, as in the expression "suffering of suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of both excellent and mediocre [wealth] is to be understood.
Having thus explained the meaning already stated—that they "guard the holy life" (brahmacariya)—he says, "they preserve the Dhamma of the scriptures for a long time.

Even if the training rules (sikkhāpada) had not been laid down, if there were those of the same birth and so forth, they would not have lost it, just as one does not lose the texts inherited from one's own family. But since even the training rules were not laid down, and these monks...
They do not belong to the same birth-class and so forth; therefore, in order to show the meaning of the phrase "they perish together," it was said: "Because they have the same names... [etc.
...therefore, harming one another," and so on. If this is so, why was it stated even in the section on long duration that "they have different names" and so forth?
Even though they possess different birth-classes and so on, the long-lasting presence of the Dispensation depends solely upon the promulgation of the training rules (sikkhāpada).
It was stated for the purpose of showing that the Dispensation endures for a long time precisely through the promulgation of the training rules (sikkhāpada).

It should be understood that this is because Buddhas promulgate a training rule when there exist beings to be trained even after their own final Nibbāna, but do not promulgate one when such beings do not exist.
Just as [one acts] by generating intimation (viññatti) consisting of the doors of body and speech...
Even though consciousness is occurring, it is said to "occur through the doors of body and speech" because it occurs by way of that very intimation;
this should be understood in the same manner. As for the word *tanti*, here *tanti* is a mere particle.

"By way of grouping into chapters (*vagga*), collections (*saṅgaha*), and fifties (*paṇṇāsa*)" means by way of the grouping into chapters such as the Sīlakkhandha-vagga and Mahāvagga, and by way of the grouping into fifties such as the Mūla-paṇṇāsa and Ajjhata-paṇṇāsa.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the *Saṃyutta* and other [nikāyas] is to be understood.

In the phrases "think thus" and "do not think thus," the term "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to the manner in which the instruction has been set forth, both by way of affirmation and by way of negation according to what was taught; and that [manner] pertains to right thoughts.
It proceeds by way of showing the mode of occurrence of wrong thoughts, for the purpose of clarifying both the benefits and the dangers.
Therefore he said: “One should think thoughts of renunciation and so forth—these three thoughts,” and so on.
Here, by the word “and so forth” (ādi), the inclusion of thoughts of non-ill-will and thoughts of non-cruelty is to be understood. In that context, renunciation (nekkhamma) is...
It is called "non-greed" (alobha) because it has emerged from greed; the "first jhāna" because it has emerged from the hindrances;
"all wholesome phenomena" because they have emerged from all unwholesome states; and "nibbāna" because it has emerged from all conditioned things.
A thought associated with renunciation (nekkhamma) by way of decisive support, association, and as its object is "a thought of renunciation" (nekkhammavitakka).

Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappo*). In the preliminary stage of the meditation on the foul (*asubhajjhāna*), it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); within the meditation on the foul itself, it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*);
and at the time when the path and fruit arise having made that meditation the basis, it is supramundane (*lokuttara*). Non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) is the opposite of ill-will (*byāpāda*);
or, alternatively, it is called non-ill-will because by means of it one does not cause anyone to be ill-willed—it is loving-kindness (*mettā*). It is associated with the aforementioned non-ill-will.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is non-ill-will applied thought. Prior to the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*), it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

when the first jhāna is attained by means of the cultivation of loving-kindness, it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); and at the time of the arising of the path and fruit, having made that jhāna the basis, it is supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) is compassion (*karuṇā*); it is so called because it is the opposite of cruelty, or because beings do not suffer through it.

The thought associated with that [compassion] is the thought of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā-vitakka*). In the preliminary stage of the meditation on compassion (*karuṇā-jhāna*), it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

when the first jhāna is attained by means of the cultivation of compassion, it belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); and at the time of the arising of the path and fruit, having made that jhāna its basis, it is supramundane (*lokuttara*).

But is it not the case that because non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*) are mutually inseparable, these thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and so forth—which arise by way of them—[would likewise be inseparable]?

Is there no definition of them as mutually unmixed? It is not that there is none. For when non-greed (alobha) is predominant—by way of its being determined, matured, manifested, and so forth—then the other two become concomitants of it.

Thus, when an arising of consciousness has non-greed as its predominance and renunciation (nekkhamma) as its weight, then the thought of renunciation (nekkhammavitakka), having gained its opportunity, [arises].

It is established. Furthermore, by way of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*), which has the characteristic of being free from fault and is associated with that [renunciation], there may arise for that very [state] the nature of non-ill-will thought (*abyāpādavitakka*);
and when the state of non-ill-will thought exists, because of its innate quality of not harming anyone, there may also arise the nature of non-cruelty thought (*avihiṃsāvitakka*).
These other two follow after that very same thought of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*).
Because they are not visible in their own form, one should infer that they exist when that [primary state] exists and do not exist when it does not;
thus it is that when a mental state has loving-kindness (*mettā*) as its predominant factor, the other two are concomitant with it,
and when a mental state has compassion (*karuṇā*) as its predominant factor, the other two are concomitant with it.
Regarding the phrase "thoughts of sensual desire, etc.," it should be understood that the word "etc. includes thoughts of ill will and thoughts of cruelty.
Among these, a thought associated with sensual desire is a "thought of sensual desire" (*kāmavitakka*). For here, there are two kinds of sensual desire:

sensual desire as an object (*vatthukāma*) and sensual desire as a defilement (*kilesakāma*). Within that, according to the category of sensual desire as an object, a thought associated with sensual desires by way of its objective referent is a "thought of sensual desire."
Regarding the side of the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*), however, it should be construed as "associated with sensual desire" by way of association (*sampayoga*).
Thought associated with ill will is "ill-will thought" (*byāpādavitakka*). Thought associated with cruelty is "cruelty thought" (*vihiṃsāvitakka*).
Among these, two arise in relation to both sentient beings and formations (*saṅkhāra*). For sensual-desire thought arises in one who thinks about beloved and agreeable sentient beings or formations.
Ill-will arises from the moment one looks upon an unpleasant or disagreeable being or formation with anger, continuing until its destruction;
however, cruelty does not arise toward formations. For there is no such thing as a formation that can be made to suffer;
[one thinks], "May these beings be slain, cut off, or destroyed."
However, it arises with respect to sentient beings at the time of thinking, "May they not come to be. Now, why is it said that "there is no formation (saṅkhāra) that is to be made to suffer"?
Is it not the case that even those things designated as "sentient beings" whom one wishes to make suffer are, in their actual essence (attha), nothing but formations?
True, this is so; yet, because they are bound by the sense-faculties and possess consciousness, they experience suffering.

Therefore, those things designated as "beings" which are the objects of harmful thought are intended [here]. However, with reference to those who do not experience suffering because they lack the application of the aforementioned characteristics, it is said: "Harmful thought does not arise regarding formations.
In the phrase "their minds were liberated from the taints without clinging," the term "from the taints" (*āsavehi*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative.
"Cittāni" (minds) is the plural form of the personal pronoun; "vimucciṃsu" (were liberated) is a passive construction. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:
"the minds were liberated by means of the outflows (*āsava*), which function as the agent, without grasping [them] as objects (*ārammaṇa*) through clinging (*anupādāya*).
Thus he said, "For their minds," and so forth. In the phrase "by whichever outflows," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent itself.

"Vimucciṃsu" (they were liberated) is a passive construction (*kamma-sādhana*). "They were not liberated by grasping those [objects]" means that those taints (*āsava*) were liberated—were set free—without grasping those minds by way of an object.

Here, "minds" (*cittāni*) is the accusative plural, while "vimucciṃsu" is an active construction (*kartṛ-sādhana*). "Ceasing through non-arising and cessation" means by way of what is termed non-occurrence in the future.
"The taints were ceased by means of cessation": they were liberated without grasping; that is, their minds were liberated without taking [them] as objects by way of making them objects.
"Their minds became blossomed" means their minds became fully opened through contact with the rays of preeminent knowledge.
"In reference to the preceding statement" means it is in reference to the statement previously spoken: "in a certain terrifying forest thicket."
Therefore he said: "Regarding what was stated, 'in that certain terrifying forest thicket,' therein. He said this word "katam" expresses the sense of an abstract noun (bhāvasādhana), meaning:
"it occurs in the state of being terrifying (bhiṃsanakata), that is, in the act of being terrifying (bhiṃsanakakiriyāyā).
The act of making something terrifying is "bhiṃsanakata"; it is in that state of being terrifying (*bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ*).
Now, showing another way of construing the meaning, he says "Or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth. In this alternative interpretation of the meaning, that which causes fear is *bhiṃsana*;

that which is *bhiṃsana* itself is *bhiṃsanaka*. When it should have been said, "the state of being *bhiṃsanaka* is *bhiṃsanakatta*," he says "in the state of being *bhiṃsanaka*" (*bhiṃsanakattaṃ*) after eliding the letter *t*, indicating that it is expressed thus. He explains: "In the state of being *bhiṃsanaka* means in the condition of being *bhiṃsanaka*."
“Meaning,” and so forth. The inclusion of the term “for the most part” (*yebhuyya*) should also be applied by way of having body hair (*lomavanta*), and not solely by way of body hair;

thus he says, “or for the majority,” and so forth. “By way of the human pair” (*purisayuga*) means by way of the human period, that is to say, by way of the lifespan measure of humans. “The very last one” (*sabbapacchimaka*).
"Like Subhadda"—this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. Taking the entire lifespan limit of the two types of persons existing at that time, it is said:

"One hundred thousand... [and so on]... eighty-eight. Regarding the phrase "only two human pairs," here a "human pair" (*purisayuga*) refers to the period during which two persons exist simultaneously;
this is merely a matter of terminology, for in actual meaning—
"Like one man for a pair of men": while the Blessed One was living, there was one pair of men, and after his final nibbāna, there was another;

thus it is said, "only two pairs of men. However, it should be understood that after the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, only one pair of men remained, and the holy life (brahmacariya) endured for exactly eighty thousand years.

20. "Pairs of disciples" (*sāvakayugāni*) means that the disciples themselves are the pairs of disciples. "By one who was unable" (*asambhuṇantena*) means by one who did not reach [the goal]. "Causing [her] to conceive a fetus" (*gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpentassa*) means causing her to conceive the "fetus of knowledge" (*ñāṇagabbha*) for the purpose of giving birth to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

21. "What is the connection? (*ko anusandhīti*) means what is the sequence of the preceding and following discourses; what is the relationship? It means this. "Regarding the request for the proclamation of the training rules" (*sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanāpekkhaṃ*):

it is called a "request" (*yācanā*) because it is requested; the "proclamation of the training rules" itself is the request, hence "the request for the proclamation of the training rules. "Regarding that" means depending upon that.

The locative expression refers to the request for the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*); what is meant is that the locative expression refers to the formulation of the training rule being requested.
For it is the very formulation of the training rule, as distinguished by the act of requesting, that is referred to by the word "therein" (*tattha*).
Therefore, he will later say: "therein, of that formulation of the training rule. As for the phrase "which was spoken":
“‘He shall lay down a training rule’—by this, the laying down of a training rule that was requested is meant; ‘requested’ is the meaning.
Therein, ‘of that laying down of a training rule’ means ‘of that laying down of a training rule which was being requested.
‘An improper time’ refers to an improper time for the laying down of a training rule.”
Regarding the term *āsavaṭṭhānīya*, it is said that the suffix *-anīya* here denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in the statement:

"The taints (*āsava*) reside in these. But what are those taints, and which phenomena serve as their locus? To this he says: "In which [there are] things pertaining to the present life and the future life," and so forth.

Those pertaining to the present life are such things as insults from others; those pertaining to the future life are the specific sufferings of the states of deprivation (*apāya*) in the woeful realms. These [phenomena] flow out (*āsavanti*).
They are called *āsava* (taints) because they flow forth according to various conditions. "Of these" refers to the taints such as the reproach of others and so forth.

"Those" refers to the states of transgression. To the question, "If there were no state that serves as a basis for a taint, what fault would there be in the formulation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), such that it was said thus?
he says: "For if he were to formulate [them]," and so forth. The intention is: "if he were to formulate them without seeing the fault of transgression. *Parammukhā*.

Abusive speech is speaking ill of others; accusing others by attributing faults to their words is "assailing others"; censuring them to their face is the "fault of reproach. The connection is "how indeed will he wrap himself up?
When used with the word *kathaṃ* (how), it should be understood as referring to the future tense.
*Anvāyiko* means a follower. *Bhogakkhandhaṃ* means a mass of wealth. They are called *ñātī* (relatives) because they are known as "these are ours."
In the sense of revolving by way of grandfather, father’s sons, and so forth, it is a "revolving"; relatives themselves are the revolving, thus it is "relatives’ revolving.
"Content with food and clothing as the maximum" means content with the maximum—that is, the highest degree—regarding food and clothing;
the meaning is that they are established in the state of excellence through the process of effacement (*sallekha*) regarding the search for food and clothing.
"Having food and clothing as their supreme limit" means that for them, food and clothing are indeed the highest and the ultimate limit;
they do not seek or expect anything beyond that which is free from worldly gain (*sāmiṣa*). Their state of being such is "having food and clothing as their supreme limit.
They are content with that state of having food and clothing as their supreme limit. Among those distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, who indeed could be...?

Among those monks, who indeed [is it]? "Becoming worldly bait" (*lokāmisabhūta*) means that, having become included within the world (*lokapariyāpanna*), it is to be grasped by defilements (*kilesa*); thus it is "become worldly bait.
"By way of the summary of renunciation" (*pabbajjāsaṅkhepena*) means precisely by way of the gateway of renunciation, such as "abstaining from taking life," and so forth.
"This" (*etaṃ*) refers to the non-performance of sexual intercourse and other such acts. "Firmness" (*thāma*) is the capacity for the act of enacting the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
The power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) is the capacity to penetrate all phenomena as they truly are.

"It might be disturbed" means it would become subject to agitation. To make this same point clear: "it would not remain in its proper place," meaning it would not remain in the position of its designation (*paññatti*).
"Unskilled" means he is unskilled and lacking in dexterity because he does not fully understand the proper time for treatment.
“Non-increase” means lack of progress; “misfortune” means suffering. “From the very beginning” means even before the abscess has formed.
“Having made the skin beautiful” means having made the skin attractive. “A foolish physician” means an unwise physician.
“And he brings me to the loss of blood”—this should be construed by changing the grammatical case (from accusative to dative).

"Having shown that it was the wrong time" means having shown that it was the improper time for the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Having allayed the illness" means having made him comfortable. "In his own teacherhood" (*ācariyake*):
the state of being a teacher or the activity of a teacher is "teacherhood" (*ācariyaka*); [the phrase refers to] in that state of his own teacherhood or in that activity of a teacher.
This locative case is used here in the sense of a cause or occasion (*nimitta*). "Of known power" means of manifest power.

"By way of abundance" means by way of the great number of those who have gone forth. "In the Dispensation, certain defilement-producing states do not arise" means that because lodgings are available in abundance, certain defilement-producing states rooted in avarice for dwellings (*āvāsamacchariya*) and so forth do not arise in the Dispensation.
By this method, the inclusion of the training rules concerning the purification of words (*padasodhamma-sikkhāpada*) and so on should be understood.
"Abundance of gain and greatness": "Gain" (*lābha*) refers to the requisites to be obtained, such as robes and so forth; its "greatness" (*mahatta*) means its excellence or its abundance.
"Learnedness" (*bāhusacca*) is the state of being one who has heard much. "Emerging improperly" (*ayoniso ummujjamānā*) means adhering by way of what is not the right method;
the meaning is that they understand erroneously. "Blending essence with essence" (*rasena rasaṃ saṃsanditvā*) means blending intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) with intrinsic nature.

Regarding the permitted spreaders and so forth, because they share the quality of pleasant contact, even though they possess the flavor of contact belonging to what is clung-to (*upādinnaphassarasa*), one perceives them as blameless;

thus, the meaning is that one blends the flavor of contact belonging to what is clung-to with the flavor of contact belonging to what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaphassarasa*) and brings them into a state of equality.
"Explaining the Teacher’s instruction as contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya" means [saying] such things as, "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way."
They teach by making the Teacher’s instruction contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.
Regarding the phrase "in this matter": it refers to the matter designated as the "Bhikkhu Saṅgha" as stated in the passage, "For the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Sāriputta, is free from vermin.
But how can there be a state of being thieves for those who are immoral? To this he says: "For they, having become non-recluses," and so forth. "Possessed of the nature of black things" means:
Because of his association with evil states characterized by immorality. "Radiant" means one whose character is radiant.
They are called "the essence" because the virtues such as morality are called "the essence" since they constitute the core of the holy life of the Dispensation.
"One possessing all inferior virtues" means one who has all lowly virtues, or one of little virtue. "He is a stream-enterer"—[this refers to] the Elder Ānanda.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Has entered the stream" means he has entered the stream of the Path (*magga-sota*).
Because it hears (*savana*) and pushes away (*pellana*) the opposing states without remainder, the Noble Path is called a "stream"; thus he says, "And 'stream' is a designation for this Path.
"Stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) refers to the person who is endowed with that [Path]. Having stated by this that one possessing the Path is a Stream-enterer, he explains that very same point:
Having established [the point] by way of an example, he now says "But here," and so forth, in order to identify and show the person intended in this context.
Here, the word *āpanna* (entered/attained) refers to the present time, as in such expressions as "one practicing for the realization of the fruit";
thus he says, "The name of the fruit has been given by means of the path. For by the path, a name is given to that which is similar to itself—whether it be the eightfold or the sevenfold [path].

Or, the name "stream of fruit" (phala-sota) was given because it flows toward the fruit; however, since it pertains to the past time, it may receive its name by virtue of its own inherent nature. For at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), it is said to "enter" the stream of the Path, whereas at the moment of the Fruit (phala-khaṇa), it has already entered.

It is called a "fall" (vinipāta) because it causes one to fall into that which is deformed, painful, and full of distress; it is that which casts one into the suffering of the states of misery (apāya). It is called "Dhamma" because...
This is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Therefore it was said: "It does not have the nature of casting oneself into the states of misery.
Alternatively, "dhamma" refers to unwholesome states such as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which hurl one into the states of misery.

Since that unwholesome state does not exist in him at all because it has been completely abandoned, he does not possess the nature of casting himself into the states of misery; therefore it was said: "He does not [cast] himself..."

"It is said that [the nature of those states] is to cause one to fall into the states of misery (apāya). Why?"—this asks for the reason why they possess the quality of not falling into the states of misery.
"Leading to the states of misery" means they cause one to go to the states of misery. "Having the nature of causing one to fall" means having the nature of arising [there].

"By means of the path obtained through the fixed course of rightness" means by means of the path attained through the fixed course of existence (bhava-niyāma) that leads correctly. Or, "fixed" means [fixed] at least from the seventh existence downwards.

It is "certain" (niyata) by virtue of the fact that [the remaining defilements] are destined not to arise again. "Enlightenment" (sambodhi) refers to enlightenment consisting of the three higher paths.

For it is that which awakens (sambujjhati) that is called "enlightenment," namely, the Noble Path. And since the first path has already been attained here, what remains is precisely that which must still be attained;
thus it is intended as something yet to be reached. Therefore he said: "one who will inevitably reach the three higher paths."
One who necessarily attains the three higher paths is a "reacher," namely, a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
The discussion on the request for the formulation of the discipline is concluded.
The discussion on the practice of the Buddhas.

22. *Anudhammatā* means a state of being in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*). *Anapaloketvā* is an explanation of the word [meaning] "without having asked for permission" (*anāpucchitvā*).
Regarding the phrase "setting out on a journey through the countryside" (*janapadacārikaṃ pakkamanti*), the particle *iti* is not explicitly stated here because it is understood;

this is likewise the case in other such instances. In that context, "journey through the countryside" (*janapadacārika*) refers to wandering (*caraṇa*) in the various districts (*janapada*). Wandering...

Or, "wandering" (*cāra*) is itself "wandering about" (*cārikā*); wandering about among the districts is "district-wandering" (*janapada-cārikā*). They set out for that; the meaning is that they go on a journey through the districts.
By the restrictive phrase "they indeed set out," he shows that it is not the case that they do not set out.
Having stopped at the words "they set out on a district-wandering," he spoke as follows in order to show the Blessed One’s procedure for setting out on a wandering: "On a district-wandering..."
"Moving about," and so forth. This wandering is of two kinds: hurried wandering and unhurried wandering.
Therein, "hurried wandering" refers to going quickly even from afar upon seeing a person capable of being enlightened, for the purpose of enlightening them;
this is to be seen in such instances as the Elder Mahākassapa’s going out to meet [the Buddha]. For the Blessed One, while going out to meet the Elder Mahākassapa...
In a single moment he traveled thirty *gāvutas* for the sake of Āḷavaka; likewise, thirty *yojanas* for the sake of Aṅgulimāla;
forty-five *yojanas* for Pukkusāti; one hundred and twenty *yojanas* for Mahākappina; seven hundred *yojanas* for the sake of Dhaniya;
and more than thirty *gāvutas* for the sake of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa, who was the co-resident disciple of the General of the Dhamma.

To travel two hundred yojanas is what is called a "hurried journey. However, traveling by way of successive villages, market towns, and cities, sustaining the world through daily alms rounds and so forth at a pace of one or half a yojana per day—this is called a "non-hurried journey.
While wandering on this [latter] journey, the Blessed One [traversed] the great circle, the middle circle, and the final circle.

He wanders within one of these three circles (*maṇḍala*). Since the term "wandering through the countryside" (*janapadacārika*) was used there, it is specifically this unhurried wandering that is intended here.
Explaining that very point in detail, he says: "The great circle, the middle circle," and so forth.
Therein, the "final circle" (*antimamaṇḍala*) refers to the small circle; or else, because it is included within the other circles, it is called the final circle.
The "inner circle" (abbhantarima-maṇḍala) is what is meant. As to the measurement of these circles, he said:
"Therein, the great circle is nine hundred yojanas," and so forth. Even a place measuring nine hundred yojanas is included within the Middle Country;
beyond that is not intended here, because [the Buddha] did not travel further due to his rapid journey. From the time of his departure...
For a hundred leagues all around the four sides of the place they have already visited, there is a single great clamor;
those who arrive first are permitted to offer invitations. In the other two circles, the honor descends toward the Great Circle (*mahāmaṇḍala*);
there, the Blessed Buddhas, staying for one or two days in various villages and market towns, [benefit] the great multitude by accepting material gifts.
They assist [others], and through the gift of the Dhamma, they increase the wholesome roots conducive to the turning away from saṃsāra; therefore it is said:
"Assisting the great masses in villages, market towns, and so forth, by means of the acceptance of material gifts," and so on. Regarding the phrase "serenity and insight are tender":
here, "tender insight" refers to the knowledge of discerning formations, the knowledge of overcoming doubt, and the knowledge of comprehension.

“Knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path” is a designation for the four kinds of knowledge. Furthermore, the nascent state of serenity (samatha) should be understood by way of access concentration (upacārasamādhi).
As for the statement, “If, however, during the rains retreat the serenity and insight of the bhikkhus are nascent,” this should be regarded as merely an illustration.
For it may also occur through other causes, such as the ripening of the knowledge of those to be trained (veneyya) within the Middle Region.
Desiring to wander on tour through the Middle Region, they depart only after having resided for four months.
"Having granted the inclusion of the invitation ceremony" means having granted it by way of giving permission.
"On the first day of Māgasira" means on the first day of the month of Māgasira; this is, according to current usage, the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Of them" means of those Buddhas. Because they are to be guided by them, it is said, "the beings to be guided by them.
And "beings to be guided" refers to those beings who are to be guided during the course of the wandering life.

That [he] stayed right there even until the month of Māgasira and [left] on the first day of the month of Phussa—this too should be understood as a mere illustration. Even regarding the four-month residence...
When the disciples to be trained by the Buddhas have faculties that are not yet matured, the Buddhas, awaiting the maturation of those faculties,
remain right there for another month, two, three, or four months, surrounded by a great community of monks. Then, departing in the same manner as before,
they continue to favor the world with their presence for seven, six, five, or four [months].

They complete their wandering tour within [three] months. By the restrictive phrase "only according to those who are ready to be trained" (*veneyyavaseneva*), he shows that they do not wander for the sake of robes and other such things.
For indeed, when wandering on a tour in any of these three regions, they do not wander for the sake of robes and so forth;
rather, it is for the sake of those who are poor, ignorant, aged, or sick, thinking: "When will the Tathāgata come and see us?"
"But while I am wandering on tour, the great multitude will have the opportunity to see the Tathāgata;

therein, some will clarify their minds, some will honor him with garlands and other offerings, some will give alms with ladles, and some, abandoning wrong view, will become possessed of right view. That will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time."
Thus they wander on tour out of compassion for the world.
Furthermore, the Blessed Buddhas wander on tour for four reasons: by means of walking about to ensure the comfort of their bodies;
with the desire to obtain the occasion for the arising of a teaching; for the purpose of laying down training rules for the monks; and in various places...
"For the sake of awakening those beings capable of being awakened whose faculties have reached maturity. Furthermore, for four other reasons the Blessed Buddhas go on tour:

thinking, "They will go for refuge to the Buddha," or "They will go for refuge to the Dhamma," or "They will go for refuge to the Saṅgha," or "I shall satisfy the four assemblies with a great rain of Dhamma. For yet other reasons...
For five reasons the Blessed Buddhas go on tour:

thinking, "They will abstain from the destruction of life," or "They will abstain from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
Furthermore, for eight reasons the Blessed Buddhas go on tour: [to teach] the first *jhāna*...
Or they will attain it; or a second [time]... pe ...or they will attain the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For eight other reasons as well, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, go on tour:
thinking that beings will attain the path of stream-entry, or the fruit of stream-entry... pe ...or will realize the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding the phrase "they move about as if gathering flowers": just as a garland-maker, upon seeing a large flowering grove, might stand there for a long time gathering flowers, but then—seeing the grove stripped bare of blossoms—abandons it without delay and goes elsewhere to wander gathering flowers;
even so, the Buddhas likewise [proceed] in whatever villages, market towns, and so forth.

There are many beings to be trained; having lived there for a long time and having trained them, they leave behind the proliferation (*papañca*) found in villages and other places that are empty of those to be trained, and instead live and wander elsewhere in villages and so forth where there are many to be trained.
For this very reason, even in a very small final circle (*antimamaṇḍala*), because there are many [beings] possessing the necessary support (*upanissaya*), it is "so much" [a great number].
They wander on tour for a period of seven months.
Because it is peaceful by nature, or because it is the cause for the subduing of defilements, it is "peaceful" (santa); and because it is the cause of happiness, it is "bliss" (sukha).
Thus it is said: "having made the peaceful and blissful Nibbāna the object. In the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*) refers to the field of birth.
"Of the ten-thousandfold world-system. This is stated with reference to gods and brahmās; however, humans who are to be enlightened are to be found within this very world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

Regarding "the surveying of beings capable of being enlightened": having first pervaded [the world] with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he subsequently spread out the net of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and [surveyed] those beings capable of being enlightened who had entered within it.
The surveying of the world. It is said that after the Buddhas have entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and emerged from it, they resolve their minds, thinking:
"May those beings who are capable and whose knowledge is matured, and who are to be disciplined by me this very day, appear before my knowledge.
Simultaneously with that mental application, one, two, or many such beings become accessible to discipline.
Those who are to be converted come within the range of the Buddha’s omniscient knowledge; this is the power of the Buddhas in this regard.
Once they have thus come within his range, he examines their decisive support (*upanissaya*), their past conduct, their prior causes, and the practice currently prevailing in them.
For when he applies his attention for the purpose of grasping those beings who are to be converted, first of all, by virtue of their very state as those to be converted—

There is attendance. Then, wondering "What indeed will happen?", and investigating some accomplishment by means of going for refuge and so forth, they look back upon their past supporting conditions (*pūrvopaniśraya*).
When it is announced that [the candidate] has entered [the assembly], or when he has entered the midst of the assembly. "Twice" means twice in one year.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, the monks would assemble twice each year:
at the time when the rains-retreat was approaching and at the time of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).

When the rains-retreat was near, even ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty monks would come in groups for the sake of their meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). The Blessed One [dwelt] together with them.
Having exchanged greetings, he asked, "Monks, why do you wander about when the time for entering the rains retreat is near?
Then they requested, "Blessed One, we have come for the sake of a meditation subject; please grant us a meditation subject.

According to their individual temperaments, the Teacher gave a meditation subject on foulness to those of a lustful temperament and a meditation subject on loving-kindness to those of a hateful temperament.
To one of deluded temperament, he explains: "Recitation, questioning, listening to the Dhamma at the proper time, and discussion of the Dhamma at the proper time—this is suitable for you.

For although the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is suitable for one of deluded temperament, in order to make him a fit vessel for the development of that meditation subject, one must first, through the removal of his confusion, engage him in recitation, questioning, listening to the Dhamma, and discussion of the Dhamma.
He engages them [in practice]. To one whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (vitakkacarita), he gives the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhāna).
For one whose temperament is characterized by faith (saddhācarita), the first six recollections (anussati) are especially suitable;

however, to show that this is the preliminary practice for engaging in those [recollections], he proclaims the excellence of the Buddha, the excellence of the Dhamma, and the excellence of the Saṅgha’s practice by means of inspiring discourses (pasādanīyasuttanta).

For one whose temperament is characterized by knowledge (*ñāṇacarita*), mindfulness of death, recollection of peace, the analysis of the four elements, and the perception of the repulsiveness of food are especially suitable.
To show the qualities that assist these, he preaches profound discourses connected with impermanence and so forth.
Having taken up the meditation subject, if it is suitable, they [should remain] right in the presence of the Teacher.
They dwell there. If it does not exist, they go while asking for a suitable dwelling place.
While dwelling there, by undertaking the three-month practice and striving with diligence, they become stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and even arhats.
Then, having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, they go into the presence of the Teacher and say, "Bhagavā, I [belong] to you..."
Having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in his presence, he attained the fruit of stream-entry...

[and so on] ...while others announce the qualities they have acquired, saying, "I have attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship," and request a meditation subject for the sake of attaining what they have not yet reached above that.

Therefore it is said: "Before the commencement of the rains retreat, for the purpose of receiving a meditation subject... and for the purpose of receiving a meditation subject for what lies further ahead."
Regarding the word *āyāma*: here the prefix *ā-* has the same meaning as in the word *āgaccha* (“come”), thus he says, “*Āyāma* means ‘come, let us go’”;

the sense is “come, let us go. The Blessed One addresses the Elder Ānanda with the word *Ānanda* because of his status as an attendant, not because there were no bhikkhus living near the Teacher at that time; for at that time, the Blessed One’s retinue consisted of five hundred [bhikkhus].
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus was nearby. However, the Elder announced to the bhikkhus, "Friends, take up your bowls and robes; the Blessed One wishes to go to such-and-such a place.
Because it is stated, "Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda," the genitive case *bhagavato* here [in the phrase *bhagavato paccassosi*] is indeed a word of address.
With the intention that [the listener] depends upon another related person, it is said: "He listened back to the word of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the term "of the Blessed One" (bhagavato) is a dative case used in connection with the act of listening back, just as in the expression, "he listens back to Devadatta.
Regarding the word *paccassosi*, the prefix *pati-* signifies "facing toward"; thus he says, "having become face-to-face, he heard. [This refers to] the Blessed One’s...
The intended meaning is that he, having turned toward the face [of the Buddha] and having consented, listened, rather than remaining indifferent.
Because that miracle was performed for the sake of a visitor, it is said, "starting from the city gate.
Regarding the phrase "with rays tawny with the essence of gold," here the word *rasa* is a synonym for water, and the word *piñjara* is a synonym for the color of gold; therefore—
The meaning is: "with rays golden in color, like a stream of molten gold. *Samujjotayamāno* means illuminating.
*Assa* refers to the brahmin Verañja. *Upnisīditukāmo* means desiring to sit near the Blessed One;
that is to say, desiring to approach the Blessed One and sit in his presence.
The connection in the text should be understood as: "O Brahmin, we have been invited by you; we have completed the rains-retreat.
It means "it should be given" (*dātabbo*), that is, it ought to be given. By saying "not non-existent" (*no asanto*), he indicates that it is not merely absent, but rather actually present.
Or, one may understand the meaning here without a change in grammatical gender; thus he says "or else," and so forth. By this, from the general statement—

Here, he shows that this is an indication in the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅganiddeso*). "No natthi" means "it does not exist for us" (*no amhākaṃ natthi*). Or, "no" is an explanation for "natthi. To the question "Of whom is there a desire not to give? he says "yathā" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "pahūtavittūpakaraṇānaṃ," here "vitti" means satisfaction; "vittūpakaraṇaṃ" is the instrument of satisfaction, meaning the cause of satisfaction. "Pahūtaṃ" [means abundant].
"Those who possess abundant wealth and requisites" refers to those who have various kinds of riches and equipment, such as money, grain, gold, silver, diverse ornaments, golden vessels, and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "Just as there is a lack of desire to give in those who are miserly and possess abundant wealth and requisites, we likewise have no such lack of desire to give. Regarding the phrase "How could this be obtained here?": here, the word *taṃ* (that) refers to that reason.
Or, it is that duty. "In this" means in the life of a householder. In the second alternative interpretation, however, *tanti* is the reference to the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*).
"In this" means within these three months; such is the meaning. *Yaṃ* either refers to the reason, or it is a reference to the action.
In the second alternative interpretation, however, *yaṃ* means "that which is the object to be given."
"Having persuaded him by saying, 'Enough with worrying about the hindrance of household life,'" means:
"O Brahmin, this was not done by the hindrance of household life, but rather by the influence of Māra"—thus he persuaded the Brahmin.

"Appropriate to that moment" means: whatever the state of his inclination was at that time, [the speech] was appropriate to that; such is the meaning. Of him who was then thus oriented toward the turning away from the world (*vivaṭṭa*).
Because there is an absence of the ripening of knowledge (*ñāṇaparipāka*), only the meaning based on the internal [state] is shown;

thus he said, "having demonstrated the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life" (*diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ sandassetvā*), which means having made it manifest through direct experience. "Wholesome states" (*kusale dhamme*) refers to wholesome states belonging to the three planes.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the wholesome states as they have been encouraged. "Him" (*naṃ*) refers to the brahmin. "Having inspired him" (*samuttejetvā*).
Having properly established [the mind] higher and higher, one brings about a state of sharpness and intensity through the performance of meritorious deeds.
Since that, in its actual meaning, serves to generate enthusiasm for those deeds, he said, "having made it enthusiastic.

Thus, through such enthusiasm for the performance of meritorious deeds, there arises both the possession of such qualities as these and the certain accomplishment of benefits pertaining to the present life and so forth; such is the nature of enthusiasm.
And having encouraged him by pointing out other qualities existing within him, he brought him to a state of perfect joy and satisfaction.
If the Blessed One rained down the rain of the Dhamma treasure, why then did he not attain distinction? Because of the absence of the requisite spiritual potential (*upanissaya*).
If this is so, why did the Blessed One rain down the rain of the Dhamma treasure for him in such a manner? It is said in reply:

—Even though he had no specific attainment, it should be understood that all his previous and subsequent discourses on the Dhamma were conducive to spiritual cultivation for the sake of attaining Nibbāna in the future.
For there is no teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One that is purposeless.
"A gift to be given for three months" means a gift to be given for the duration of three months. "On whichever day" means on whatever day.

23. *Buddhapariṇāyaka*: "The Buddha is the leader of this," thus it is *buddhapariṇāyaka*, namely the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "That which has the Buddha as its leader" means that the Buddha is the foremost.
"Having made [it] as much as needed" (*yāvadatthaṃ katvā*): the intention is that it was prepared with food for as long as there was need.
The refusal of alms-food brought forward to be given is by means of a hand-gesture (*hatthasaññā*).
It occurs either by means of a facial expression or by means of a verbal utterance; thus he said, "by a hand-signal," and so forth. Regarding the term *onītapattapāṇi*:

here, the word *onītapattapāṇī*—meaning "one whose hand has been removed from the bowl"—is a compound with a non-identical case relation (*bhinnādhikaraṇa-visaya*), specifically a *bāhirattha-samāsa*.
Therefore he said, "one whose hand has been removed from the bowl," and so forth. There is also a reading *onittapattapāṇi*; its meaning is that it has become separated (*onittaṃ nānābhūtaṃ*).
"Having removed the bowl from his hand"—that is, having cleared the bowl by removing the food (āmiṣa), he is one whose hand is free of the bowl;
thus, "one with the bowl removed from his hand. The meaning is that, having washed both his hands and the bowl, he sits down after setting the bowl aside in a secluded spot.
"On cloth made of cotton or silk" means on cloth made of cotton (*pattuṇṇa*) and on cloth made of silk (*paṭṭa*). Therein, in the case of the cotton portion...
"Bhavā" refers to pattuṇṇa; some also say they are specific types of *kosiya* (silk). "Paṭṭāni," however, are Chinese cloths (*cīnapaṭa*). Regarding "āyoga" and so forth:
"āyoga" means a shoulder-strap for carrying bags for bowls and the like. "Bhesajjatelānaṃ" means oils prepared by means of medicinal decoctions.
"Tumbāni" are oil vessels made of leather. The connection is that she gave each individual monk oil worth a thousand [pieces of money].

"Having performed a great sacrifice" means having given a great gift. "Seated after having paid homage together with his sons and wife" means seated after having paid homage along with his children and spouse.
"For three months" is used in the accusative case to express continuous duration.

It is said that [the teaching was given] "to one whose intention was fulfilled," because it was taught to fulfill the aspiration of one who sat thinking, "Today itself I shall hear the Dhamma to be heard for three months."
"Practicing. "Having followed" means having gone after.
Since Buddhas have no such things as dissatisfaction or agitation, he said, "having dwelt according to their own inclination or according to their own preference.
For "delighting" (*abhiranta*) and "delight" (*abhirati*) are one in meaning. Furthermore, this word *abhiranta* is a synonym for "liking" (*abhiruci*).

It is not a discourse on gratification. Furthermore, for one dwelling in some place due to the influence of gratification, there might arise a lack of delight there once the basis for that gratification has vanished;
however, this does not occur for those whose taints are destroyed, let alone for the Buddhas.

Therefore, because they possess no such lack of delight, there is no such thing as Buddhas departing elsewhere after having dwelt in a certain place out of a desire for delight; rather, they do so solely for the purpose of training those to be trained.
However, having stayed in some places, once that [purpose] was accomplished, they go elsewhere from there solely for the sake of training those to be trained;

this is what is meant here by "according to one's pleasure. "Without approaching Soreyya and the others" means without approaching cities such as Soreyya, which served as the routes for the Great Circuit (mahāmaṇḍala-cārikā).
"The landing-place of the Payāga" is a designation for both a village and a ford. "The river Gaṅgā."
The river named Gaṅgā. Regarding the term *tadavasarī*: here, the accusative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus he says, "he went by means of that, hence *tadavasarī*.
The discourse on the practices of the Buddhas is concluded.
Regarding the phrase *Samantapāsādikāya*: it is called *Samantapāsādikā* because it generates complete and universal confidence (*pasāda*); [it belongs] to that *Samantapāsādikā*.

Herein, in the expression "the state of being *Samantapāsādikā* of this *Samantapāsādikā*," the word *tatra* refers back to the preceding statement, while *idam* refers to the statement concerning the reason that is about to be explained. This is the construction: as for what was stated, "of the *Samantapāsādikā*..."

Regarding the phrase "of the Vinaya commentary," that commentary which was stated as the *Samantapāsādikā*—in its being *samantapāsādikā*, in its state of being *samantapāsādikā*, and in its quality of producing complete confidence, this [following] occurs.
To the question "What occurs?", he says: "From the lineage of teachers," and so forth.
"From the lineage of teachers" means from the succession of teachers stated [in the text] as "Upāli, Dāsaka," and so forth.

"By way of illustrating the distinctions of the origins and the subject matters" means by way of illustrating the distinctions of the origins (nidāna) and by way of illustrating the distinctions of the subject matters (vatthu). In this regard, the illustration of the distinctions of the origins should be understood by way of showing the external origins, the internal origins, and the origins of the training rules (sikkhāpada);
however, the elucidation of the Theravāda is the illustration of the distinctions of the subject matters.

“By avoiding other systems” means: by refuting the views of others who have practiced wrongly, as in such passages as, “In accordance with your own admission, you must expel the nun Mettiyā,” and so forth;
and precisely because of that, by establishing one’s own system, it is [purified] through the purification of one’s own system.
“By purifying the phrasing” means: the purification of the phrasing should be understood as the purification of the text according to the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*).
Or, having shown the etymology, the demonstration of the derivation of the words is the purification of the phrasing (*byañjana*).

"By showing the distinctions in the method of the analysis (*vibhaṅga*)" means by showing the distinctions in the method according to the appropriate manner of the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) beginning with "three kinds of women.
"To those who see clearly" means to those seeing correctly with the eye of knowledge; the meaning is "to those who investigate. "Uninspiring" means that which does not bring about confidence.

"Ettha" means "in the *Samantapāsādikā*. The connection is with the phrase "of the wise who clearly perceive. Therefore, it should be construed thus: "This commentary proceeds as the *Samantapāsādikā* itself.
To the question, "Of what [is this] a commentary, and by whom was it taught? he says: "Of the Vinaya," and so forth.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* known as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The commentary on the Verañjā Chapter is completed.
The first part is finished.
